Omissions, for instance, loaded on both the semantic and phonological working memory factors, which is not surprising given that a failure to respond can be the endpoint of several different breakdowns, including degraded conceptual knowledge, an inability to hold or activate a phonological code long enough to support production, or a reluctance to guess after repeated failures. This complexity is consistent with interactive and computational models, which suggest that damage to different parts of a distributed system can produce overlapping error profiles (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000; Ueno et al., 2011). It also fits with dual-stream and connectionist accounts, which propose that semantic and phonological processes interact during naming (Hickok & Poeppel, 2007; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).

The pattern of semantically-related errors was particularly complex, loading across phonological ability, speech quanta, executive-cognitive skill, and circumlocution. This challenges the intuitive equation of semantic paraphasias with a semantic deficit, as semantic errors can arise from impaired semantic representations, but also from deficient selection among competing lexical candidates, weak phonological support for the target word, or reduced inhibitory control (Schnur et al., 2006; Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006; Schwartz et al., 2006). Our data-driven solution is compatible with this heterogeneity, suggesting that semantic errors are better viewed as a multi-determined outcome than as a pure marker of semantic impairment. This, in turn, implies that interpreting semantic errors clinically requires attention to the surrounding profile of phonological, executive, and fluency abilities.

The involvement of executive-cognitive skill in the pattern of semantically-related errors also fits with evidence that domain-general control contributes to aphasic performance and recovery (Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Brownsett et al., 2014). Furthermore, the neural correlates of the three factors with distinct lesion profiles are consistent with previous research. Phonological working memory was associated with primary auditory cortex and adjacent regions, consistent with work implicating the left temporoparietal and auditory cortices in verbal short-term memory and phonological buffering (Buchsbaum & D'Esposito, 2008; Baldo & Dronkers, 2006; Leff et al., 2009). Semantic impairment was associated with the anterior temporal lobe, in line with evidence from semantic dementia, functional imaging, and stroke aphasia that this region is a transmodal semantic hub (Patterson et al., 2007; Binney et al., 2010; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Schumacher et al., 2019). Fluency was associated with the precentral gyrus, matching accounts of its role in articulatory planning and speech motor control (Hillis et al., 2004; Guenther, 2016; Basilakos et al., 2015).

The fact that a data-driven, error-informed model converged on these well-established brain-behaviour relationships provides some validation of our approach, suggesting that the factors capture real functional components rather than statistical artefacts. However, several factors had no unique lesion correlate, including output phonology, executive-cognitive skill, phonological discrimination, and circumlocution. There are several possible explanations for this. These abilities may depend on widely distributed networks, such that no single region is critical, or they may be supported by redundancy and reorganisation in the chronic stage (Fedorenko & Thompson-Schill, 2014; Hartwigsen & Saur, 2019). Lesion overlap in the sample may also have limited power to detect effects in areas lesioned in few patients, and shared variance among correlated deficits may have been removed when each factor was modelled in the same framework. The absence of a unique correlate should therefore not be taken as evidence that no neural basis exists.

Our study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. Firstly, the sample size was relatively small, which may have limited the power to detect effects in certain areas. Secondly, the lesion profiles were based on a single time point, which may not reflect the dynamic nature of language recovery. Thirdly, the error analysis was based on a limited set of error types, which may not capture the full range of errors produced by individuals with aphasia. Despite these limitations, our study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex relationship between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and lesion correlates in post-stroke aphasia. By combining multiple sources of information and using a data-driven approach, we were able to identify distinct neural correlates for phonological working memory, semantics, and speech fluency, and to shed light on the complex patterns of error-impairment relationships in aphasia. Future studies can build on this framework to further elucidate the neural basis of language and cognition in aphasia, and to develop more effective treatments for individuals with aphasia.

The alarming prevalence of insufficient physical activity worldwide has significant implications for public health, as it is a leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, various cancers, and premature mortality. According to estimates, physical inactivity is responsible for 6% to 10% of the global burden of major noncommunicable diseases and approximately 9% of premature deaths (Lee et al., 2012). Despite the well-established benefits of regular physical activity, a mere 25% of U.S. adults meet the national guidelines for both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities (Blackwell & Clarke, 2018; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018). This disparity is not evenly distributed, with adults in rural areas engaging in less leisure-time physical activity and exhibiting higher obesity rates compared to their urban counterparts. National estimates suggest that approximately 40% of rural residents are obese, compared to 33% in urban settings (Befort et al., 2012). The challenges faced by rural residents are further compounded by structural barriers, including limited access to recreational infrastructure, fewer programs, and constrained public health resources (Frost et al., 2010; Bauman et al., 2012).

Fortunately, a substantial evidence base has been established on strategies to promote physical activity at the population level. The Community Guide for Preventive Services, developed by the Community Preventive Services Task Force, recommends a multifaceted approach that encompasses informational, behavioral, and environmental strategies (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2016). Socioecological models also emphasize the importance of sustained behavior change, which is most likely to occur when individual-level support is combined with changes in the social, physical, and policy contexts in which people live (Sallis et al., 2006; Sallis et al., 2012). Community-wide multicomponent interventions, grounded in these principles, offer a promising means of shifting population activity levels. However, the evidence for such interventions is largely derived from urban and suburban settings, with a notable dearth of studies conducted in rural communities, particularly those with diverse and rapidly changing demographics.

The term "rural" is often used as a monolithic category, but it encompasses a wide range of communities with distinct characteristics. Micropolitan communities, defined as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 residents, occupy an intermediate position between rural towns and metropolitan areas. These communities often lack the resources and infrastructure of larger urban areas, making it challenging to adapt evidence-based recommendations to their unique contexts. The situation is further complicated in micropolitan communities that have become new immigrant destinations, such as those in the rural Midwest and South. The influx of immigrants from Latin America and other regions has led to rapid demographic change, with linguistically and culturally diverse newcomers settling alongside long-term residents (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Immigrant and Latino adults in the United States often report lower rates of leisure-time physical activity, and their activity patterns tend to decline with acculturation and time in the United States (Crespo et al., 1996; Marquez & Bryan, 2011).

Newcomers in these communities face numerous challenges, including language barriers, physically demanding work schedules, limited transportation, and unfamiliarity with local resources (Lichter, 2012). Interventions developed in other contexts cannot be assumed to translate directly to these settings, and the literature offers few examples of community-wide physical activity interventions designed for communities that are simultaneously rural and rapidly diversifying. One potential approach to bridging this gap is the use of lay health advisor models, which have been shown to improve health behaviors and outcomes in underserved and minority populations (Balcázar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). Evidence from Latino and rural communities suggests that peer-led walking groups and other group-based activities can increase physical activity while building social capital and local capacity for sustaining programs (Ayala et al., 2011; Cleland et al., 2012).

However, few studies have integrated a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations in a single community-wide effort, and fewer still have done so in a micropolitan new destination. To address this gap, it is essential to consider how evidence-based interventions are adapted and evaluated. Adaptation frameworks emphasize the systematic modification of intervention content, delivery, and context to improve fit while preserving core functions (Escoffery et al., 2018). Community-based participatory research principles stress shared decision-making between researchers and community partners throughout this process (Israel et al., 1998). Evaluation frameworks, such as RE-AIM, encourage assessment not only of effectiveness but also of reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, which are dimensions of particular relevance to resource-constrained settings (Glasgow et al., 1999).

In this context, community-wide interventions are often challenging to evaluate using a single design. A more comprehensive approach involves combining population-level surveillance with longitudinal cohort data, observational measures of the environment, and qualitative and process data. This can provide a more complete understanding of what changes, for whom, and why. The Active Ottumwa project, a community-wide intervention aimed at increasing physical activity in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents, offers a unique opportunity to address these gaps. Ottumwa has experienced significant demographic change linked to employment in meatpacking and related industries, with a growing Latino population. As part of a community-academic partnership, local organizations and researchers are working together to design and implement an intervention that integrates a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations. The early implementation of Active Ottumwa is described in this paper, with a focus on the challenges and opportunities associated with adapting evidence-based interventions to a micropolitan new destination. The development of the Active Ottumwa intervention was a collaborative effort, with residents and community partners playing a crucial role in shaping the initiative. By adapting strategies recommended by the Community Guide, our goal was to increase physical activity among residents of a micropolitan new destination community. The Community Guide's recommendations were tailored to fit the specific needs of Ottumwa, a mid-size rural community undergoing significant demographic changes due to immigration. The initiative's core component was the use of trained lay health advisors, or physical activity leaders, who were responsible for delivering group-based activities such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga.

The overarching research question guiding this study was whether a multicomponent, lay health advisor-based intervention could effectively increase physical activity among residents of Ottumwa. To address this question, we also explored several secondary research questions, including the reach of the intervention across different population subgroups, the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted strategies, and the contextual factors that facilitated or constrained implementation. This report aims to contribute to the existing literature in three key ways. Firstly, it extends the evidence base on physical activity promotion to a setting that is underrepresented in the literature: a mid-size rural community undergoing immigration-driven demographic change. Secondly, it provides a transparent account of the process of adapting and integrating evidence-based, multilevel strategies through a community-academic partnership. This includes the training and deployment of 45 physical activity leaders and the execution of a five-channel communication campaign. Thirdly, it presents a multi-method evaluation design that combines a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, observational data, key informant interviews, and project records, which may serve as a model for evaluating community-wide interventions in similar settings.

The Active Ottumwa intervention was developed within a community-academic partnership in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents located in the southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa is a new immigrant destination, with a growing Latino and Pacific Islander population drawn to the area by the meatpacking and related industries. As a result, the city is more ethnically and linguistically diverse than most rural Iowa communities. The partnership brought together university researchers, local public health and healthcare organizations, city and parks officials, schools, faith-based organizations, and residents. Throughout the project, partners played an active role in prioritizing physical activity as a health concern, reviewing intervention materials for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, and interpreting early findings. This collaborative approach was guided by the principles of community-based participatory research, as outlined by Israel et al. (1998).

We employed a single-community, pre-post design with multiple data sources to evaluate the intervention. A convergent mixed-methods framework guided the evaluation, with quantitative and qualitative data collected in parallel and integrated at the interpretation stage (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). The study protocol was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent in English or Spanish. To develop the intervention, we selected strategies from the Community Guide for Preventive Services recommendations for physical activity (Task Force on Community Preventive Services, 2002; Kahn et al., 2002) and adapted them through a review of local assets, barriers, and resources with our community partners.

The intervention comprised three categories of approaches: behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy. The central strategy used a lay health advisor model, where physical activity leaders were recruited through partner organizations, workplaces, churches, and neighborhood networks, with a focus on reaching residents who were bilingual or trusted in immigrant communities. Eligible leaders were aged 18 years or older, lived or worked in Ottumwa, and were willing to lead or support at least one activity for 12 months. Leaders completed a structured training program of approximately 8 hours, covering physical activity guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018), group facilitation, safety and injury prevention, motivational communication, and program logistics. The training content was informed by social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), emphasizing self-efficacy, modeling, and social support. Leaders then established community-based walking groups, tai chi classes, and yoga classes in locations and at times chosen by participants.

In addition to the behavioral and social approaches, we developed a community-wide communication campaign delivered over five channels: local print media, radio, social media, community events with printed materials, and signage or flyers placed at partner sites. Messages were tested with community members, and key materials were produced in English and Spanish. The campaign promoted the benefits of physical activity, publicized local opportunities including leader-led groups, and encouraged use of existing parks and trails. We also worked with city and parks partners to identify and promote low-cost changes that support activity, such as wayfinding and trail signage, publicized walking routes, and improved access to existing facilities. Furthermore, we documented policy discussions and actions relevant to active living, including shared-use arrangements and municipal planning efforts.

The evaluation of the Active Ottumwa intervention followed the RE-AIM framework (Glasgow et al., 1999), assessing reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. Our evaluation methods comprised a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, systematic observation, key informant interviews, and project records. To assess population-level change, we conducted repeated cross-sectional surveys of adult Ottumwa residents at baseline and at the end of the intervention period. Households were sampled from an address-based frame, and one adult per household was selected using the next-birthday method. Residents could complete the survey online, by mail, or by interviewer-assisted telephone or in-person administration, in English or Spanish. The survey instrument assessed leisure-time and transportation-related physical activity using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form (Craig et al., 2003), along with perceived neighborhood environment, social support for activity, self-efficacy, awareness of Active Ottumwa messages and programs, and sociodemographic characteristics.

In addition to the cross-sectional survey, we recruited a cohort of adult residents through community events, partner organizations, leader networks, and direct outreach, including both people who participated in leader-led programs and those who did not. Participants completed baseline and 12-month assessments, with additional follow-up planned. Data collection included self-reported physical activity (Craig et al., 2003), sociodemographic and health characteristics, and psychosocial measures. A subsample of participants wore hip-mounted accelerometers for 7 days, with valid wear defined as at least 10 hours per day on at least 4 days (Troiano et al., 2008). By providing a detailed account of the intervention's development, implementation, and evaluation, we aim to inform practitioners and researchers seeking to translate evidence-based recommendations into the diverse rural communities where they are most needed. The collection of height, weight, and blood pressure data was conducted by trained staff adhering to standard protocols, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of these measurements. To maximize retention, we employed a range of strategies, including flexible scheduling, the use of bilingual staff, reminder contacts through multiple modes, and modest incentives for participation. The effectiveness of these strategies was evaluated by calculating the proportion of baseline participants who completed the 12-month assessment. We also compared the baseline characteristics of completers and non-completers to assess potential differential attrition, which is crucial for understanding the representativeness of our sample.

Our observational data were collected using the System for Observing Play and Recreation in Communities (SOPARC), a well-established method for estimating the number, activity level, and demographic characteristics of individuals using public spaces such as parks, trails, and other areas (McKenzie et al., 2006). Trained observers conducted scans at fixed target areas multiple times daily across different days and seasons. To ensure the reliability of our observations, a subset of scans was double-coded, allowing us to assess interrater reliability using Cohen’s kappa. Observations were scheduled both before and after the implementation of campaign and environmental components to evaluate changes in the use of these spaces over time.

To gain a deeper understanding of the perceptions and experiences of stakeholders, we conducted semi-structured interviews with a purposively sampled group of key informants. This included physical activity leaders, city officials, representatives from healthcare and educational institutions, and leaders from immigrant communities. The interview guide was informed by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), focusing on perceived barriers and facilitators, community readiness, the acceptability of the intervention, and prospects for sustainability. Interviews lasted between 30 to 60 minutes, were conducted in either English or Spanish, and were audio-recorded and professionally transcribed. To ensure the accuracy of Spanish-language transcripts, they were translated and checked by a bilingual team member. We continued recruiting participants until thematic saturation was reached, as recommended by Guest et al. (2006).

Project records played a critical role in documenting the implementation processes and reach of our intervention. These records included detailed information on the number of leaders recruited, trained, and retained, along with their demographic characteristics. We also tracked the number, type, location, and frequency of activity sessions, attendance counts, leader activity logs, campaign outputs, dissemination dates, and notes from partner meetings. To assess fidelity, we compared the activities as implemented with the planned protocol and classified any documented adaptations by type and rationale.

Our analytical approach will be guided by the RE-AIM framework, which evaluates the reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance of interventions. We will use descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, medians, and proportions, to summarize leader characteristics, session attendance, campaign exposure, and participant characteristics. Reach will be estimated as the proportion of survey respondents and cohort members reporting participation in Active Ottumwa activities. We will examine the representativeness of participants by comparing them with the Ottumwa population using chi-square tests and standardized differences.

For cross-sectional survey data, we will evaluate changes between baseline and follow-up in meeting aerobic physical activity guidelines using weighted logistic regression, adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, education, and income. Continuous outcomes, such as weekly minutes of activity, will be modeled using linear or generalized linear models, applying appropriate transformations for skewness. For the cohort, we will employ linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to estimate change from baseline to 12 months (Fitzmaurice et al., 2011), and generalized estimating equations (Liang & Zeger, 1986) for binary outcomes. Our models will include time, exposure to the intervention (participation in leader-led activities and campaign awareness, modeled as dose), and their interaction, with adjustments for covariates. We will address missing data through multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption and conduct sensitivity analyses to examine complete-case results and inverse-probability weighting for attrition.

Accelerometer data will be summarized as daily minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity using established cut points. Observational SOPARC data will be analyzed as counts of users per scan, using Poisson or negative binomial regression to compare pre- and post-implementation periods, adjusting for season, day type, and area. Statistical significance will be indicated by two-sided P values below.05, and we will emphasize effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals. All analyses will be conducted using Stata or R.

The analysis of interview transcripts will utilize directed content analysis (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005), with an initial codebook based on CFIR constructs and the iterative addition of inductive codes. Two coders will independently code a subset of transcripts, resolve discrepancies by consensus, and calculate intercoder agreement before coding the remainder using qualitative analysis software. To ensure the validity of our findings, community partners will review summarized findings as a member-checking step. We will integrate quantitative and qualitative results through joint displays to explain variation in reach, implementation, and effectiveness.

The implementation of Active Ottumwa followed the three categories of strategies recommended by the Community Guide for Preventive Services: behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy approaches (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2017). Results are reported using RE-AIM dimensions where applicable (Glasgow et al., 1999). At the time of writing, the project was in its second year of intervention delivery.

A key component of our intervention was the recruitment and training of physical activity leaders, termed physical activity leaders (PALs). We recruited 45 PALs across two training cohorts (n = 26 and n = 19), leveraging churches, worksite wellness programs, the community college, ethnic community organizations, and the local school district for recruitment. The mean age of PALs was 44.3 years (SD 12.1; range 21–71), with 38 (84.4%) being women. The demographic composition of our PALs broadly reflected that of the target community, with 21 (46.7%) identifying as Hispanic or Latino, 3 (6.7%) as Pacific Islander, and 21 (46.7%) as non-Hispanic White. Notably, 28 PALs (62.2%) reported a language other than English as their primary language at home, and 17 (37.8%) delivered sessions in Spanish or bilingually. All 45 PALs completed the 8-hour core training, and 41 (91.1%) remained active at 12 months after training, indicating a high level of engagement and retention among our PALs.

The PALs established 34 recurring physical activity groups, including 22 walking groups, 7 tai chi classes, and 5 yoga classes. Over the first 18 months of implementation, 1,846 sessions were documented in PAL logs, with a median of 48 sessions per group (interquartile range [IQR] 26–71). Mean attendance was 9.4 participants per session (SD 4.2), and 612 unique individuals attended at least one session, equivalent to approximately 2.4% of the city’s adult population. The demographic profile of participants showed that 71.6% were women, 38.4% identified as Hispanic or Latino, and 52.1% were aged 50 years or older. Among participants attending at least four sessions (n = 347), the median number of sessions attended was 14 (IQR 7–29), with walking groups accounting for 64.9% of all sessions, tai chi for 20.8%, and yoga for 14.3%. These findings suggest a strong uptake and engagement with the physical activity groups among the target population. The demographic breakdown of participants in our chi and yoga sessions revealed some interesting trends. Notably, chi sessions drew the highest proportion of adults aged 60 years or older, with a remarkable 58.2% of participants falling into this age group. In contrast, yoga sessions were more popular among younger adults, with 44.0% of participants under the age of 40. These findings suggest that different types of physical activity may appeal to different age groups, and that tailored approaches may be necessary to effectively promote physical activity across the lifespan.

A key component of the Active Ottumwa initiative was a comprehensive communication and informational campaign, which utilized five distinct channels to reach the community. These channels included local radio broadcasts in both English and Spanish, a local newspaper, social media platforms, printed materials distributed through community venues, and signage and banners along walking routes. Over the course of the campaign, we broadcast 1,240 radio spots, including 608 in Spanish, and published 36 newspaper features or columns. Our social media efforts generated 214 posts, which in turn yielded 48,310 impressions and 3,972 engagements. Additionally, we distributed 18,500 printed materials through 52 community sites and installed 31 route signs. The campaign's reach and impact were substantial, with 41.7% of respondents in our cross-sectional community survey reporting awareness of the Active Ottumwa name or logo.

The survey also provided valuable insights into the relative effectiveness of different communication channels. Awareness of the campaign was highest among respondents who reported seeing printed materials (27.3%) or hearing radio broadcasts (22.6%), while social media (12.9%) and newspaper (11.4%) were less effective in reaching the community. Furthermore, we observed significant disparities in awareness based on educational attainment, with respondents having less than a high school education reporting lower levels of awareness (28.5%) compared to those with at least some college education (47.2%). This difference was statistically significant (χ² = 19.4, p < 0.001), highlighting the need for targeted outreach efforts to reach vulnerable populations. In contrast, we did not observe significant differences in awareness between Hispanic (39.1%) and non-Hispanic (42.6%) respondents (p = 0.41).

In addition to the communication campaign, the Active Ottumwa initiative also incorporated environmental and policy approaches to promote physical activity. Working in collaboration with the city parks department, public works office, and school district, our project team and community partners conducted audits of 14 walking routes and 6 parks using the Community Pedestrian Audit Tool. These audits identified a mean of 5.2 environmental barriers per route, with missing or damaged sidewalks (38%) and inadequate lighting (24%) being the most common obstacles. Based on these findings, our partners installed lighting and wayfinding markers on 4 routes, and the city council adopted a resolution to prioritize sidewalk repairs near 3 elementary schools. Moreover, two worksites and one school district adopted written policies allowing walking breaks or community use of facilities outside school hours, demonstrating the potential for policy changes to support physical activity.

Recruitment and retention of participants were critical components of the longitudinal cohort study. We enrolled 402 adults through door-to-door outreach, community events, and PAL networks, with a mean age of 47.6 years (SD 15.3) and a predominance of women (64.7%). The cohort was diverse, with 33.1% of participants self-identifying as Hispanic or Latino, 7.5% as Pacific Islander, 51.2% as non-Hispanic White, and 8.2% as other race or ethnicity. Nearly one-third (31.8%) of participants reported less than a high school education, and 44.3% reported annual household income below $35,000. At baseline, the mean body mass index was 30.1 kg/m² (SD 6.7), and 38.6% of participants met the criteria for obesity. We achieved a high retention rate, with 331 participants (82.3%) completing follow-up assessments at 12 months. While attrition was slightly higher among men (23.1%) than women (14.6%; p = 0.02) and among participants younger than 35 years (24.8%) than among those aged 35 years or older (15.9%; p = 0.03), we did not observe significant differences in attrition by ethnicity or education.

At baseline, 46.5% of cohort participants reported meeting the federal aerobic guideline of at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per week, based on self-report using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form. The median self-reported weekly moderate-to-vigorous activity was 120 minutes (IQR 20–300). Among the 214 participants who wore accelerometers for at least four valid days, the mean daily wear time was 13.1 hours (SD 1.4), and the mean moderate-to-vigorous activity was 19.8 minutes per day (SD 15.6). Notably, only 18.2% of participants met the guideline based on accelerometer-measured activity, which was substantially lower than the self-reported proportion. This discrepancy is consistent with known overreporting in questionnaire-based measures. We also observed differences in physical activity patterns by ethnicity, with Hispanic participants reporting more occupational activity but fewer minutes of leisure-time activity (median 30 vs. 60 minutes per week; p = 0.008) than non-Hispanic participants.

Preliminary findings from the 12-month follow-up assessments indicate a positive trend in physical activity levels. The proportion of participants meeting the federal aerobic guideline increased from 46.5% to 54.4% (absolute change +7.9 percentage points; McNemar p = 0.01), and the median weekly minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity increased from 120 to 150 (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.004). In a mixed-effects model adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, education, and season, the estimated mean change was +24.6 minutes per week (95% CI 8.3 to 40.9). Among accelerometer-wearing participants with valid data at both time points (n = 158), the mean moderate-to-vigorous activity increased by 2.7 minutes per day (95% CI 0.4 to 5.0; p = 0.02). Participants who reported attending at least one PAL-led session (n = 119) showed larger gains in self-reported weekly activity (+46.2 minutes; 95% CI 21.5 to 70.9) than those who did not (+14.8 minutes; 95% CI −3.9 to 33.5), although this comparison was not randomized and should be interpreted cautiously.

To gain a deeper understanding of the initiative's impact, we collected qualitative and observational data. Key informant interviews (n = 22) conducted at 12 months revealed that PALs were viewed as trusted and culturally credible messengers, with 81.8% of informants identifying PAL-led groups as the most visible component of the initiative. Commonly cited barriers to physical activity included winter weather, limited childcare, and variable work schedules, particularly for shift workers in meatpacking and manufacturing. Direct observation of walking routes (n = 1,120 observation periods across 10 routes) recorded a mean of 11.8 people per hour per route, representing a 26% increase relative to the pre-intervention mean of 9.4 (p = 0.03). While differences varied by route and season, these findings suggest that the initiative is having a positive impact on community physical activity levels.

This paper provides an overview of the design and early implementation of the Active Ottumwa initiative, a community-wide, multicomponent intervention aimed at promoting physical activity in a micropolitan new destination community. While effectiveness findings are not yet available, our preliminary results suggest that evidence-based recommendations from the Community Guide for Preventive Services can be adapted to a mid-size rural setting with a rapidly diversifying population. In the second year of implementation, we have trained 45 lay health advisors (physical activity leaders) to deliver behavioral and social strategies such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga. The communication campaign has been completed across five channels, and the longitudinal cohort has been recruited and has completed baseline and 12-month follow-up assessments. As we continue to evaluate the initiative's impact, we are hopeful that our findings will inform the development of effective strategies to promote physical activity in similar communities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a complex and multifaceted condition, characterized by a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture that ultimately lead to significant activity limitations. The etiology of CP is attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain, and it is often accompanied by a range of comorbidities, including disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, perception, behavior, and epilepsy. As the most common cause of physical disability in childhood, CP poses a substantial and sustained burden on affected individuals, their caregivers, and the healthcare system as a whole. This burden is multifaceted, encompassing not only the physical manifestations of the condition, such as pain, contractures, hip displacement, and scoliosis, but also the significant psychosocial and economic implications, including reduced participation and substantial lifetime costs.

Spasticity is a dominant feature of CP, affecting the majority of children with the condition. It is characterized by a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes, resulting from the hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex. Over time, spasticity combines with weakness, impaired selective motor control, and altered muscle growth, leading to a range of secondary musculoskeletal problems, including shortened muscle-tendon units, fibrotic change in muscle, and fixed contractures. The management of CP is inherently multidisciplinary, incorporating a range of interventions, including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses, oral antispastic drugs, intramuscular botulinum toxin A, intrathecal baclofen, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and orthopedic surgery. While evidence supports the efficacy of several of these interventions, particularly botulinum toxin, casting, and goal-directed training, their effects are often modest or transient, and they are not without limitations.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of complementary and alternative therapies, including traditional medicine approaches, which are widely used alongside conventional rehabilitation in East Asia. One such approach is acupotomy, also known as needle-knife therapy, which was developed in China in the 1970s. This technique integrates the principles of traditional acupuncture with those of modern minimally invasive surgery, utilizing a stainless-steel needle with a flat blade at its tip to puncture the skin, cut, release, or dissect fibrotic or adherent soft tissue. The proposed mechanisms of action are multifaceted, including the release of local tension and adhesions, improved local microcirculation, modulation of inflammatory mediators, and reduced abnormal mechanical stress on connective tissue.

In the context of CP, the rationale for using acupotomy is that releasing shortened or fibrotic muscle-tendon units and myofascial restrictions may reduce passive resistance to stretch, improve joint range of motion, and facilitate motor training. Clinicians in China and Korea have also proposed that acupotomy at selected sites could alter afferent input and reduce excitability of the spinal stretch reflex arc, although direct evidence is limited. Acupotomy is typically applied to the muscles and tendons most affected, such as the adductors, hamstrings, gastrocnemius-soleus, and cervical or paraspinal structures, and is usually delivered as a short course in combination with rehabilitation training.

While clinical research on acupotomy has grown in recent years, primarily in China, the evidence base is not without its limitations. Randomized and non-randomized studies have reported improvements in muscle tone, joint mobility, gross motor function, and activities of daily living when acupotomy is added to rehabilitation in children with spastic CP. However, systematic reviews have noted important methodological limitations, including small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and a high or unclear risk of bias. Furthermore, acupotomy involves cutting soft tissue, which distinguishes it from filiform needling in terms of technique, tissue effect, and risk profile, and therefore, evidence on acupuncture cannot be assumed to apply to acupotomy.

The reported adverse events associated with acupotomy, including bleeding, infection, nerve injury, and procedural pain, are particularly relevant in children, and safety must therefore be assessed together with efficacy. Despite the growing use of acupotomy for CP, several gaps remain in our understanding of its efficacy and safety. To date, no comprehensive systematic review has quantitatively evaluated randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP across outcomes, and the primary studies vary widely in terms of participant age, CP subtype and severity, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, acupotomy technique, treatment frequency, comparators, and co-interventions. This heterogeneity makes it challenging for clinicians to interpret the findings, and the methodological quality of these trials, including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting, has not been systematically appraised.

The present study aimed to address these gaps by systematically evaluating the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. Specifically, we sought to determine whether, in children and adults with CP, acupotomy alone or combined with conventional rehabilitation is more effective than rehabilitation alone, sham treatment, or other active comparators in improving spasticity, gross motor function, joint range of motion, and activities of daily living, and whether it is acceptably safe. We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance to ensure the rigor and transparency of our review. This study makes three key contributions to the existing literature. Firstly, it provides the first structured synthesis of randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of its efficacy and safety. Secondly, it assesses the methodological quality of the included trials, providing a critical appraisal of the evidence base. Finally, it evaluates the certainty of the evidence using a structured approach, such as GRADE, enabling guideline developers and clinicians to make informed decisions about the use of acupotomy in multidisciplinary CP care. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for cerebral palsy (CP), while also evaluating the risk of bias and certainty of evidence for each outcome. To achieve this, we conducted a thorough search of multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, among others, using a combination of controlled vocabulary and free text terms related to the condition and intervention. Our search strategy was designed to capture all relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of acupotomy in children and adolescents with CP, with no language restrictions.

The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO prior to the commencement of the search, and the study was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. We adhered to the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, which provided a framework for the design, conduct, and reporting of our review. As our analysis relied solely on published data, ethical approval was not required. Our eligibility criteria were defined using the PICOS framework, which enabled us to clearly specify the participants, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and study design that were relevant to our review.

In terms of participants, we included children and adolescents aged 0-18 years with a diagnosis of CP, regardless of subtype or Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level. We excluded studies that focused on motor impairment from other causes, as our primary interest lay in the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. The experimental intervention was acupotomy, also known as needle-knife or miniscalpel-acupuncture, which combines acupuncture with soft-tissue release. We excluded studies that combined acupotomy with other traditional Chinese medicine modalities, unless these modalities were also applied to the control group.

Our primary outcome of interest was gross motor function, as measured by the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-88 or GMFM-66). Secondary outcomes included muscle tone or spasticity, activities of daily living, range of motion, quality of life, and total effective rate, as defined by the original trials. We also evaluated safety outcomes, such as adverse events, including infection, bleeding, nerve injury, needle breakage, and treatment discontinuation. Only parallel-group RCTs were eligible for inclusion, while quasi-randomized trials, non-randomized studies, case reports, animal experiments, and reviews were excluded.

To identify relevant studies, we employed a comprehensive search strategy that combined controlled vocabulary and free text terms related to the condition and intervention. We applied a filter for randomized trials to ensure that only relevant studies were captured. The full search strings for each database are provided in the Supplemental Digital Content. After removing duplicates, two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by a full-text assessment against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by a third reviewer. The selection process is illustrated in a PRISMA flow diagram.

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized, piloted form. The form captured information on study characteristics, including first author, year, country, sample size, age, CP subtype, GMFCS level, acupotomy technique, co-interventions, comparator, treatment length, follow-up, outcomes, and adverse events. For each outcome, we extracted the post-treatment mean and standard deviation (SD), or the change from baseline when only that was reported. When data were missing or unclear, we contacted the corresponding authors to request additional information. If means and SDs were not reported, we estimated them from medians and ranges or interquartile ranges using established methods.

To evaluate the risk of bias, we used the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, which assesses the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Each domain was rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. Given the procedural nature of acupotomy, blinding of participants and therapists is challenging; therefore, we paid particular attention to the blinding of outcome assessors and the potential influence of knowledge of allocation on parent-reported outcomes.

The certainty of evidence for each primary and key secondary outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, which considers risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. We rated the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Statistical analysis was performed using R (version 4.3) with the meta and metafor packages, and Review Manager 5.4 was used to generate risk-of-bias figures. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided P <.05. For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, we calculated the mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence interval (CI). When trials used different scales for the same construct, we employed the standardized mean difference (SMD) as Hedges' g.

Dichotomous outcomes, including total effective rate and adverse events, were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. For rare adverse events, we used the Mantel–Haenszel method without continuity correction or the Peto odds ratio when events were very sparse. Due to the expected clinical heterogeneity in acupotomy protocols, co-interventions, and CP phenotypes, we pooled effect sizes under a random-effects model with inverse-variance weights. Our analysis aimed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP, while also identifying methodological shortcomings in the existing literature and offering recommendations for the design, conduct, and reporting of future trials. Our analysis employed a random-effects model to synthesize the results of 18 randomized controlled trials, using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator to compute the between-study variance, denoted as τ². The weight of each trial, wᵢ, was inversely proportional to the sum of the within-study variance, vᵢ, and τ². To ensure the accuracy of our confidence intervals (CIs), we utilized the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment, which is particularly suited for small numbers of trials. This adjustment has been shown to provide better coverage in such cases (IntHout et al., 2014). Additionally, we calculated 95% prediction intervals to provide insight into the expected range of effects in future settings, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of the treatment's potential impact.

To assess the heterogeneity among the trials, we employed Cochran's Q test, with a significance level set at P < 0.10, and quantified it using the I² statistic. The I² statistic, expressed as a percentage, helps in understanding the proportion of variance that can be attributed to heterogeneity rather than chance. Following established guidelines (Higgins et al., 2003), we interpreted I² values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% as indicative of low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. For outcomes with ten or more trials, we conducted prespecified subgroup analyses and random-effects meta-regression to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. These analyses considered several factors, including the subtype of cerebral palsy (CP), the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level, age (<6 vs ≥6 years), the type of comparator (conventional rehabilitation, acupuncture, or sham), whether acupotomy was used as monotherapy or add-on therapy, and the duration of treatment (≤4 vs >4 weeks). To evaluate differences between subgroups, we used a chi-square test for interaction.

Sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of our findings. These included (i) leave-one-out omission of each trial to assess the influence of individual studies on the overall estimate, (ii) excluding trials at high risk of bias to evaluate the impact of study quality, (iii) excluding trials with imputed means and standard deviations (SDs) to consider the effect of data imputation, and (iv) comparing fixed-effect with random-effects estimates to explore the difference in results based on the model used. For outcomes reported in at least ten trials, we assessed small-study effects and publication bias using contour-enhanced funnel plots, Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997), and the trim-and-fill method (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). Furthermore, to determine whether the cumulative evidence was sufficient to draw firm conclusions, we conducted a trial sequential analysis for the primary outcome, with a type I error of 5%, a power of 80%, and the minimal clinically important difference of the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM) as the anticipated effect (Wetterslev et al., 2008).

When quantitative synthesis was not deemed appropriate due to significant clinical or methodological heterogeneity, we opted for a narrative summary of the results. Our literature search, which spanned multiple databases including PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed, yielded 1,426 records. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 96 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Following the application of our inclusion criteria, 18 randomized controlled trials were included in the qualitative synthesis, all of which contributed to at least one meta-analysis, as detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram (Page et al., 2021).

The characteristics of the included trials were diverse. The 18 trials, published between 2010 and 2023, enrolled a total of 1,284 children, with 646 in acupotomy groups and 638 in control groups. The sample sizes of the trials ranged from 40 to 120 participants, with a median of 66. The majority of the trials (16) were conducted in mainland China, with one trial each in South Korea and Taiwan. The mean age of the participants varied from 2.1 to 12.4 years, and males constituted 58.7% of the total. The spastic subtype of cerebral palsy was the most common, with 13 trials exclusively enrolling children with spastic cerebral palsy and 5 trials including mixed subtypes. The GMFCS levels, where reported, were primarily I-III in 11 trials and I-V in 4 trials (Palisano et al., 1997). Acupotomy was consistently applied to spastic muscle insertions, tendons, or paravertebral and cervical soft-tissue tension points. The treatment frequency varied, with once weekly applications in 9 trials, once every 2 weeks in 6 trials, and twice weekly in 3 trials. The total duration of treatment ranged from 4 to 24 weeks, with a median of 12 weeks. In 12 trials, acupotomy was used as an adjunct to conventional rehabilitation (including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, or both) and was compared with rehabilitation alone. Four trials compared acupotomy with manual acupuncture, and two compared it with botulinum toxin type A injection, each combined with rehabilitation. The primary outcomes assessed included the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-88 or GMFM-66) in 12 trials (Russell et al., 1989), the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) in 9 trials (Bohannon & Smith, 1987), activities of daily living (ADL) scales in 7 trials, and clinician-rated total effective rate in 14 trials.

An assessment of the risk of bias in the included trials, using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (Higgins et al., 2011), revealed that 11 trials (61.1%) reported adequate sequence generation, typically using random number tables. However, only 4 trials (22.2%) described adequate allocation concealment. Due to the invasive nature of acupotomy, blinding of participants and personnel was judged to be at high risk in 15 trials, although 6 trials (33.3%) reported blinding of outcome assessors. The risk of attrition bias was deemed low in 16 trials, with dropout rates ranging from 0 to 9.2%. Selective reporting bias was unclear in most trials, as protocols were seldom registered; only 2 trials had prospective registration. Notably, no trial was judged to be at low risk in all domains, as detailed in Supplemental Digital Content 2.

The analysis of gross motor function, based on 12 trials involving 868 participants, showed that acupotomy-based treatment resulted in a significantly greater improvement in GMFM total score compared to control interventions. The mean difference was 6.84 points (95% CI 4.92 to 8.76; P < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 61%, τ² = 5.37, P = 0.003 for Cochran Q). The benefits of acupotomy were most pronounced in Dimension D (standing) and Dimension E (walking, running, jumping) of the GMFM. Subgroup analyses provided insight into the sources of heterogeneity, as presented in Supplemental Digital Content 3. Notably, treatment duration emerged as a significant factor, with treatments lasting at least 12 weeks yielding a larger effect (MD 8.21, 95% CI 6.03 to 10.39; I² = 42%) compared to those lasting less than 12 weeks (MD 4.97, 95% CI 2.65 to 7.29; I² = 38%; P for interaction = 0.04). However, the effects did not differ significantly between children aged 6 years or younger and those older than 6 years. 

Our comprehensive analysis, including sensitivity analyses and assessments for publication bias, provides a nuanced understanding of the efficacy of acupotomy in improving gross motor function in children with cerebral palsy. The findings suggest that acupotomy, particularly when used in conjunction with conventional rehabilitation and for durations of at least 12 weeks, may offer significant benefits in terms of gross motor function improvement. However, the substantial heterogeneity among the trials and the variability in treatment protocols underscore the need for further research to standardize treatment approaches and to explore the long-term effects of acupotomy in this patient population. The efficacy of acupotomy, a technique that combines acupuncture with a miniature surgical blade, in children with cerebral palsy (CP) has been evaluated in this systematic review and meta-analysis. Our analysis of the included randomized trials suggests that acupotomy, often used in conjunction with conventional rehabilitation, is associated with greater improvements in gross motor function, as measured by the GMFM-88, compared to rehabilitation alone. Specifically, the mean difference (MD) in GMFM-88 scores was 7.13 (95% CI 4.76 to 9.50) for younger children and 6.22 (95% CI 2.97 to 9.47) for older children, with no significant interaction between age groups (P for interaction = 0.62). Furthermore, when compared to manual acupuncture or botulinum toxin controls, the pooled MD was 3.88 (95% CI 0.41 to 7.35), based on three trials.

In addition to its effects on gross motor function, acupotomy was found to significantly reduce muscle spasticity, as measured by the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS). Nine trials, involving 640 participants, reported a mean difference in MAS scores of -0.52 (95% CI -0.71 to -0.33; P < 0.001), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 48%). Notably, among the five trials that reported the proportion of children with a reduction of at least one MAS grade, acupotomy was superior, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.46 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.75; I² = 12%). However, when compared to botulinum toxin A in two trials involving 118 participants, no significant difference in MAS change was observed (MD -0.09, 95% CI -0.34 to 0.16; I² = 0%).

The impact of acupotomy on activities of daily living (ADL) and overall efficacy was also assessed. Seven trials, involving 512 participants, used ADL scales, including the Barthel Index and the Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory. The results showed that acupotomy improved ADL performance, with a standardized mean difference of 0.74 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.03; I² = 55%), which is considered a moderate effect according to conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). Moreover, fourteen trials, involving 1,020 participants, reported a higher total effective rate with acupotomy (88.4%, 450/509) compared to control treatment (72.8%, 372/511), resulting in a pooled RR of 1.21 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.29; P < 0.001) with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). The number needed to treat was approximately 6.

Adverse events were reported in ten trials, involving 782 participants. The results showed that adverse events occurred in 9 of 392 children (2.3%) in the acupotomy groups and 6 of 390 (1.5%) in the control groups, with a risk ratio of 1.38 (95% CI 0.55 to 3.45; P = 0.49; I² = 0%). The adverse events in the acupotomy groups were primarily transient and mild, including local pain or bruising, minor local infection, and temporary post-procedural fatigue. No serious adverse events, nerve injuries, or treatment-related withdrawals were reported. However, it is worth noting that eight trials did not report adverse events systematically, which may limit the accuracy of these findings.

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted sensitivity analyses and evaluated publication bias. Leave-one-out analysis showed that no single study materially changed the pooled GMFM estimate (MD range 6.21–7.35, all P < 0.001). Excluding the four trials at highest risk of bias resulted in a similar but slightly smaller effect (MD 5.97, 95% CI 3.85 to 8.09; I² = 53%). Switching to a fixed-effect model yielded an MD of 6.12 (95% CI 5.30 to 6.94). Funnel plot asymmetry was apparent for the GMFM outcome, and Egger's test was significant (P = 0.03; Egger et al., 1997). The trim-and-fill method imputed three missing studies and gave an adjusted MD of 5.64 (95% CI 3.58 to 7.70). Egger's tests were not significant for MAS (P = 0.21) or total effective rate (P = 0.18).

The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework (Guyatt et al., 2008). The results showed that the certainty of evidence was low for GMFM and ADL scores, downgraded for risk of bias and inconsistency (and for suspected publication bias in GMFM). The certainty of evidence was moderate for MAS, downgraded for risk of bias, and low for total effective rate due to unblinded subjective assessment and imprecision in some trials. The certainty for adverse events was very low owing to inconsistent reporting and few events.

The biological plausibility of the observed effects is supported by the underlying mechanisms of CP. Spasticity and contracture in CP arise from upper motor neuron lesions and secondary changes in muscle and connective tissue, including sarcomere elongation, extracellular matrix stiffening, and reduced muscle fiber length (Mathewson & Lieber, 2015; Graham et al., 2016). Acupotomy is intended to release adhesions and tension in fascia, tendons, and muscle insertions through minimally invasive cutting and stretching at selected sites. Several mechanisms may explain the benefits of acupotomy, including mechanical release, modulation of local fibroblast behavior, and spinal and supraspinal modulation of stretch-reflex excitability (Langevin et al., 2011).

Our findings are consistent with the broader CP literature, which favors goal-directed, task-specific training, botulinum toxin for focal spasticity, and selected surgical or neurosurgical interventions (Novak et al., 2020). Botulinum toxin type A reduces tone and improves function in the short term, but effects wane after about three months, and repeated injections are costly (Multani et al., 2019). Acupotomy offers a potentially lower-cost alternative or adjunct, particularly in settings with limited access to toxin or orthopedic services. Previous reviews of acupuncture and related Chinese medicine modalities for CP have reported favorable but low-certainty effects, with much of the evidence published in Chinese-language journals and conducted in a single national health care context (Wang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020). Our results are consistent with this pattern and add evidence specific to blade-based needling.

In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that acupotomy is a promising technique for improving gross motor function, reducing muscle spasticity, and enhancing activities of daily living in children with cerebral palsy. While the certainty of evidence is generally low due to methodological limitations and publication bias, the direction of effect is biologically plausible, and the findings are consistent with the broader CP literature. Further research is needed to fully establish the efficacy and safety of acupotomy in this population, particularly in diverse healthcare settings and with longer follow-up periods.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental component of natural language processing pipelines, providing crucial input for downstream tasks such as entity linking, relation and event extraction, question answering, and knowledge base population. The progress made in NER to date has been largely driven by a handful of shared benchmarks, including the CoNLL-2003 shared task data and OntoNotes. These benchmarks have enabled the development of highly effective neural sequence labelling architectures, from BiLSTM-CRFs to contextualised pretrained representations, which have achieved impressive performance gains. However, this success is closely tied to the way these benchmarks represent the task, with each token belonging to at most one entity mention and a small label inventory, typically ranging from four to eighteen types. This coarse-grained view of NER, while effective for certain applications, discards much of the semantic content of natural language, where entity mentions often contain other entity mentions.

Consider, for example, the mention "University of California, Berkeley", where the organisation contains a state and a city, or "the Bank of China", where a financial institution contains a country. Such nested structure is pervasive in various domains, including news and biomedical text, and the inner mentions often play a crucial role in downstream tasks. A relation extractor that only sees the outer organisation, for instance, cannot recover the fact that the organisation is located in, or named for, a particular country. Moreover, nested mentions provide valuable insights into how names are compositionally constructed, which can aid in disambiguation and linking. Unfortunately, the flat annotation guidelines used in most benchmarks force annotators to choose a single span, usually the outermost or the one that best fits a narrow set of types, resulting in models that are blind to the more nuanced structure of natural language.

The research community has long recognised this limitation, and early work on nested NER explored various approaches, including cascaded or layered tagging, discontinuous or parse-based methods, and mention hypergraphs. More recent methods have built on these foundations, incorporating techniques such as layered and stacked neural taggers, transition-based systems, and span-enumeration models. However, the evaluation of these methods has been limited to a narrow set of resources, primarily the ACE 2004 and 2005 corpora and GENIA. While these corpora provide some insights into nested NER, they are limited in their coverage, with ACE containing a small number of coarse entity types and shallow nesting, and GENIA restricted to the biomedical domain with a specialised ontology. As a result, models for nested NER are often tested on data that does not fully exercise their capabilities, and conclusions about their effectiveness may be specific to the idiosyncrasies of these corpora.

In parallel, fine-grained entity typing has developed as a separate line of research, with work on larger type inventories demonstrating the benefits of richer types for downstream inference. However, fine-grained resources are often built using distant supervision, which introduces noise, or are focused on typing already-identified mentions rather than detecting them. Moreover, these resources typically do not annotate nested structure, with some notable exceptions, such as BBN's pronoun coreference and entity type corpus, which provides a hierarchical inventory of 64 types over the Wall Street Journal. Despite these efforts, no existing dataset combines broad coverage of entity types, genuinely nested annotation, and a widely studied and linguistically well-understood text source.

This paper addresses this gap by presenting NNE, a manually annotated dataset of fine-grained, nested named entity mentions over the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB). Our annotation comprises 279,795 mentions of 114 entity types, with up to six layers of nesting, and builds on the BBN type hierarchy, extending it to capture additional distinctions. By choosing the PTB as the base text, we leverage the existing syntactic and semantic annotations, including PropBank and the CoNLL-2003 NER annotation, enabling comparison and joint modelling with these resources. The alignment of nested entity boundaries with constituent boundaries also allows for the study of how syntax can inform nested NER and how entity structure can inform parsing.

The creation of NNE is motivated by the need for a dataset that satisfies three key requirements. First, it must be large enough to train and reliably evaluate high-capacity neural models. Second, it must have a sufficiently rich type inventory to make nesting semantically meaningful, rather than an artefact of a few coarse classes. Third, it must be annotated consistently, with guidelines and quality control that give confidence in the gold standard. To achieve this, we describe not only the resulting data but also the annotation scheme, the process by which annotators were trained and guided, and measures of inter-annotator agreement. We also provide a quantitative analysis of the data, characterising the distribution of types, the depth and structure of nesting, and the relationship between entity structure and the PTB's syntax.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we release NNE, the largest manually annotated nested NER dataset for English, covering the entire WSJ portion of the PTB with 279,795 mentions across 114 fine-grained types and up to six layers of nesting. Second, we provide a detailed description of the annotation scheme and process, including type definitions, handling of ambiguous cases, and agreement statistics, to facilitate understanding, extension, and replication of the resource. Third, we offer a quantitative analysis of the data, providing insights into the characteristics of nested NER in newswire text and the potential applications of NNE in future research. The study of nested and fine-grained entity recognition has been hindered by the lack of a comprehensive dataset that captures the complex relationships between entities and their underlying syntactic structure. To address this gap, we have developed the Nested Named Entity (NNE) corpus, which provides a detailed annotation of entity structure and type distributions, as well as an examination of how annotation relates to the underlying syntactic structure. Our goal is to provide a benchmark for evaluating the performance of existing nested NER approaches and to encourage the development of new techniques that can effectively handle the challenges of nested and fine-grained entity recognition.

To create the NNE corpus, we annotated the complete Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB), which spans sections 00-24. The PTB is a widely used resource that provides a rich annotation of part-of-speech tags, constituency structure, and semantic role and coreference layers. By annotating the WSJ portion of the PTB, we can study nested entity structure in conjunction with existing syntactic and semantic information. We retained the original tokenization of the PTB to ensure that mention boundaries align with the treebank, and annotators were able to see neighboring sentences to resolve ambiguous types.

Our annotation scheme began with the BBN Pronoun Coreference and Entity Type Corpus, which was already annotated over the same WSJ text. We extended this scheme by incorporating ideas from the Extended Named Entity Hierarchy, the ACE guidelines, and the GENIA ontology. Through several rounds of pilot annotation on held-out documents, we refined our type inventory, adding, merging, or splitting types as necessary to ensure that frequent phenomena had suitable labels. The final scheme consists of 114 types organized in a three-level hierarchy, with top-level categories including person, organization, geopolitical entity, location, facility, event, product, work of art, law, language, and several numeric and temporal families.

Annotators were instructed to choose the most specific applicable type for each mention, allowing the hierarchy to be collapsed to coarser labels when needed. Guidelines defined a mention as a contiguous token span that refers to an entity of one of the scheme's types, and names, numeric expressions, and temporal expressions were annotated, while pronouns and generic common-noun phrases were not. Nesting was permitted to arbitrary depth, subject to the constraint that any two mentions must be either disjoint or strictly nested, with no partially overlapping spans allowed. Identical spans with different types were permitted only in documented cases of genuine type ambiguity, such as metonymic uses.

To ensure consistency and accuracy, the annotation procedure involved a team of trained annotators with linguistics backgrounds, who received a guideline document and supervised practice before working on the main corpus. We developed a browser-based interface for efficient span selection and hierarchical type assignment, which supported keyboard shortcuts, type search over the hierarchy, and visual display of nested mentions. The tool pre-populated candidate annotations from the existing BBN labels where compatible, and annotators then corrected, extended, and re-typed them. Every sentence received full manual review, and annotators were encouraged to flag uncertain cases rather than guess.

To evaluate the quality of the annotations, we measured inter-annotator agreement on a subset of documents that were annotated independently by multiple annotators from scratch. Since chance-corrected coefficients such as Cohen's kappa are poorly defined for this task, we followed Hripcsak and Rothschild (2005) in treating one annotator's labels as the reference and computing precision, recall, and F1 for the other. We report agreement at three granularities: unlabeled span match, match at the top level of the hierarchy, and match at the full fine-grained type. This allows us to separate disagreements about where mentions are from disagreements about what they are.

We also compared agreement at different nesting depths to determine whether inner mentions are harder to annotate than outermost ones and examined confusion between types to identify systematically ambiguous distinctions. Finally, we computed descriptive statistics over the final corpus, including the number of mentions, the frequency of each type, the distribution of mention lengths in tokens, and the distribution of nesting depths. These statistics provide a detailed understanding of the characteristics of the NNE corpus and can inform the development of new models and techniques for nested and fine-grained entity recognition.

In addition to the NNE corpus, we provide standard training, development, and test splits, as well as an evaluation of existing nested NER approaches as baselines. This will enable researchers to assess the performance of their models on the NNE corpus and to compare their results to those of other approaches. We hope that the public release of the NNE corpus will encourage the development of new techniques for nested and fine-grained entity recognition and will support research on how entity structure interacts with syntax, linking, and other downstream applications. By providing a comprehensive and carefully annotated dataset, we aim to advance the state of the art in entity recognition and to facilitate further research in this important area. 

Furthermore, the NNE corpus offers a unique opportunity to study the relationships between entity structure and syntactic structure, which can inform the development of more effective models for entity recognition. The corpus can also be used to investigate the impact of nesting depth and type granularity on the performance of entity recognition models, and to explore the use of syntactic and semantic features to improve entity recognition. By making the NNE corpus available to the research community, we hope to stimulate further research in these areas and to contribute to the development of more accurate and effective entity recognition systems.

Overall, the NNE corpus is a significant contribution to the field of natural language The distribution of nesting depth in our annotated corpus reveals a complex landscape of embedded mentions. To quantify this phenomenon, we defined depth as the length of the longest chain of mentions containing a given token, and also examined the frequency of mentions that contain or are contained within other mentions. Furthermore, we analyzed the parent-child type pairs that characterize the semantic relationships captured by nesting, which provides a richer understanding of the annotation. 

In order to compare our annotation to traditional flat NER resources, we computed the proportion of mentions and sentences that would be discarded by a flat annotation scheme, which only retains outermost mentions. This analysis highlights the significant amount of information that would be lost by ignoring nested mentions. For our experiments, we adhered to the conventional PTB division, utilizing sections 02-21 for training, section 22 for development, and section 23 for testing. The remaining sections, which are distributed with the corpus, can be allocated as additional data for future research.

To demonstrate the utility of our dataset, we trained and evaluated several published nested NER approaches that represent distinct modeling strategies. These included a transition-based model, a hypergraph model, and a layered sequence-labeling model, as well as a flat BiLSTM-CRF tagger trained solely on outermost mentions. All systems were tuned on the development set and evaluated once on the test set, using exact-match span-level precision, recall, and F1 as the evaluation metric, which requires identical boundaries and fine-grained type matching. We report micro-averaged scores overall and broken down by nesting depth, as well as performance on frequent versus rare types, to provide a more nuanced understanding of the results.

The NNE annotation spans the entirety of the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank, encompassing 49,208 sentences and approximately 1.17 million tokens. The annotation contains 279,795 entity mentions, with an average of 5.7 mentions per sentence. Notably, every one of the 114 entity types in the hierarchy is attested in the corpus, although the type distribution is heavily skewed, with the ten most frequent types accounting for 51.6% of mentions. The prevalence of nesting in the annotation is striking, with 57.6% of mentions embedded in at least one other mention, and annotations reaching six layers of nesting, albeit with a rapid decline in frequency at deeper levels.

The density of nesting in NNE is significantly higher than in other resources, such as ACE-style datasets or GENIA, where nesting is limited to a small set of coarse types or biomedical categories. In contrast, NNE contains roughly six times as many mentions as the English CoNLL-2003 data and more than twice as many as ACE2005. Furthermore, 31.4% of mentions in NNE share their exact token span with another mention of a different type, underscoring the structural and lexical complexity of the annotation.

The patterns of nesting in NNE are strongly typed, with numeric and temporal types accounting for 44% of mentions at depth 2 or deeper, often serving as modifiers within larger expressions. Organization and person names comprise the majority of the remaining nested material, with common structures including locations within organization names and person names within title phrases. The five most common parent-child type pairs account for 27.8% of all nested mentions, indicating that a small number of structures carry a significant portion of the nesting signal.

To assess the quality of the annotation, we conducted a detailed analysis of inter-annotator agreement. Trained annotators worked over the PTB's existing sentence and tokenization boundaries, with a subset annotated twice for agreement.
