The results showed a mention-level F1 of 94.1 when both span and type were required to match exactly, and 96.7 when type was compared only at the parent level of the hierarchy. Disagreements were concentrated in a small number of confusable type groups, with distinguishing organization: other from organization: corporation and facility versus geopolitical usages of place names being the most common sources of error.

In terms of experimental splits, we followed the standard PTB convention, using sections 02-21 for training, section 22 for development, and section 23 for testing. This yields a test set of 2,416 sentences and approximately 14,000 test mentions. We also evaluated several representative nested-NER approaches, scoring exact match of both span and fine-grained type over all layers. A flat BiLSTM-CRF tagger trained only on outermost mentions achieved 91.0 F1 on that layer, demonstrating that flat recognition of the top-level structure is relatively straightforward, but also highlighting the significant amount of information that is discarded by ignoring nested mentions.

When the same architecture was applied as a cascade, with one tagger per nesting layer, it reached 75.9 precision, 70.4 recall, and 73.0 F1 over the full set of mentions. These results underscore the challenges and opportunities presented by nested NER, and demonstrate the value of our annotated corpus in supporting the development of more sophisticated models that can capture the complex, hierarchical structure of real-world text. By providing a rich, high-quality annotation of nested mentions, we aim to facilitate advances in NER and related areas of natural language processing, and to support the creation of more accurate, informative, and effective models of language understanding. The quest for more accurate and informative named entity recognition (NER) has led to the development of various models and datasets. One such model, which builds mention structures incrementally (Wang et al., 2018), achieves a precision of 77.4, recall of 71.8, and F1 score of 74.5. Another approach, utilizing a hypergraph representation (Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), adapted to the 114-type inventory, yields an F1 score of 76.1 on the development set. Notably, all systems perform significantly lower than those reported on the CoNLL-2003 dataset, which is consistent with the inherent difficulty of predicting fine-grained, nested entities.

The disparity between the best nested system and the outermost-only tagger, approximately 16 F1 points, can be attributed to both the complexity of the label space and the accumulation of errors through layers. Moreover, performance varies substantially by depth and frequency. For instance, the cascaded model achieves an F1 score of 85.2 at the outermost layer, but this score drops to 70.3 at depth 2, 58.9 at depth 3, and below 40 at depths four and above, where training examples are scarce. Recall is the primary weakness at greater depths, as errors at outer layers often propagate or leave inner mentions unrecovered. Furthermore, performance correlates with type frequency, with types having more than 1,000 training mentions averaging an F1 score of 80.7, whereas types with fewer than 100 average a mere 38.4.

Certain types, such as numeric and temporal ones, are recognized more reliably, with F1 scores of 93.5 for MONEY, 95.1 for PERCENT, and 88.7 for DATE. In contrast, fine-grained organization and location subtypes, as well as less frequent categories like event and product subtypes, prove to be the most challenging. An error analysis of the transition-based model's outputs on the development set reveals that 41% of errors are type confusions with correct spans, 33% are boundary errors, and 26% are missed or spurious mentions. Notably, over half of the type confusions occur within a single parent category, suggesting that the hierarchical structure of the inventory could be leveraged by future models.

The introduction of the NNE corpus, a fine-grained nested named entity corpus covering the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank, provides a valuable resource for the community. With 279,795 mentions drawn from 114 entity types and up to six layers of nesting, NNE is considerably larger and more densely annotated than commonly used nested NER benchmarks like ACE2005 (Walker et al., 2006) and GENIA (Kim et al., 2003). The annotation of the PTB also situates NNE alongside rich existing layers, including constituency structure (Marcus et al., 1993), PropBank predicate-argument structure (Palmer et al., 2005), and coreference and entity annotation from OntoNotes (Hovy et al., 2006).

A key observation underlying this work is that flat NER schemes discard a substantial amount of semantic information. In NNE, a large proportion of mentions are nested inside other mentions, and nesting is not confined to a small set of exotic constructions. Typical examples include organizations containing geopolitical entities, person names embedded in organization names, and numeric or monetary expressions inside longer quantity phrases. Standard flat datasets like CoNLL-2003 (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) and the OntoNotes NER layer retain only the outermost or a single selected span, rendering downstream systems trained on them incapable of recovering inner entities.

The combination of fine granularity and nesting in NNE offers a unique opportunity to study the relationship between named entity structure and syntactic structure. Many nested mentions align with noun phrase constituents, but not all do, and the mismatches are informative, indicating where the PTB's flat NP bracketing conceals internal structure and where entity boundaries diverge from syntactic ones. This suggests potential applications in joint modeling of syntax and entities, as well as in evaluating the utility of syntactic features for nested recognition. The alignment with PropBank and coreference annotation also enables investigation of whether entity types and nested structure improve semantic role labeling, relation extraction, or entity linking.

More broadly, nested and fine-grained entities may support applications such as question answering and information extraction in the financial domain, where compound mentions carry the information users seek. For instance, a company name containing a place name or a monetary amount embedded in a description of a transaction may be crucial for answering specific questions or extracting relevant information. However, several limitations of NNE should be acknowledged. First, the corpus covers a single genre and period of text, namely financial newswire from the late 1980s, which may limit the transferability of models trained on it to contemporary news, social media, or other domains. Second, although annotation followed a detailed scheme and was conducted by trained annotators, fine-grained nested annotation is inherently challenging, and decisions about mentions, nesting, and type assignment are subject to genuine ambiguity, resulting in some noise in the labels.

Despite these limitations, NNE offers a valuable testbed for evaluating and improving nested NER models, particularly in the context of fine-grained and structurally deep mentions. The long tail of the 114-type inventory is likely to expose weaknesses in current models that are invisible on coarse-grained benchmarks, and handling deep nesting will require models that go beyond a fixed number of labeling layers. As the field continues to evolve, we anticipate that NNE will play a crucial role in driving innovation and improvement in nested NER, ultimately enabling more accurate and informative entity recognition in a wide range of applications.

The prevalence of code clones, which are fragments of source code that are identical or similar to one another, is a well-documented phenomenon in modern software systems. Studies have shown that between 5% and 20% of the code in typical large systems is cloned, with developers creating clones for a variety of reasons, including copy-and-paste reuse, language limitations, and deliberate performance or stability trade-offs. The debate over whether clones are harmful has been ongoing for over a decade, with some research associating them with inconsistent updates, propagated defects, and increased maintenance effort, while others have found that clones can be short-lived, stable, or even beneficial in specific contexts.

One of the practical consequences of clone detection is that it can leave developers with a triage problem. Clone detectors can report thousands of clone groups for a mature project, and not all clones are equally important. Developers with limited time must therefore decide which clones are worth refactoring, a process that can be time-consuming and requires a deep understanding of the context of each clone instance. Refactoring is not without its costs, however, as it can introduce regressions or entangle components that were intentionally kept separate. As a result, refactoring every detected clone is neither feasible nor desirable, which motivates the need for clone recommendation, the task of identifying the clones that developers are likely to find worth removing.

Prior research has approached clone recommendation from two complementary angles. The first approach focuses on the present state of the code, assessing whether a clone group is a good refactoring candidate based on its structural and syntactic properties, such as cohesion, coupling, size, and location within the class hierarchy or package structure. The second approach uses the past history of the project, mining version histories to determine how clone peers evolved, for example, whether they changed together, how often they were modified, and whether they were modified inconsistently. Clones that repeatedly co-change are plausible candidates for refactoring because the duplication imposes a recurring maintenance burden.

While there has been progress in clone recommendation, existing approaches face several limitations. Each tool considers only a restricted set of factors, chosen mostly on the basis of the authors' intuitions about what makes a clone worth refactoring. It remains unclear whether the factors used so far are sufficient, whether they overlap, or whether other properties of clones carry additional predictive signal. For example, features describing the evolution of an individual clone, such as how long it has existed, how often it has been edited, and who edited it, have received much less attention than co-change relations between clone peers. Furthermore, syntactic differences between peers are seldom combined with spatial relations such as same-file or same-package placement.

Another limitation of existing approaches is that much of the earlier evaluation relied on small data sets, manually labeled ground truth, or a single project, which makes generalization hard to assess. In particular, it is rarely examined whether a model learned on one project can recommend clones in another project, a cross-project setting that matters in practice because new projects lack the history required for training. Additionally, the literature offers little systematic comparison of which categories of factors contribute most to recommendation accuracy, or of which learning algorithms are best suited to the task. Without such comparisons, tool builders cannot make informed decisions about which information is worth the cost of collecting.

The existence of several tools that use different yet individually useful signals suggested to us that a more accurate recommender could be obtained by considering as many factors as possible within a single framework and letting a learning algorithm determine how they should be weighed. This leads to the central question of this paper: to what extent can combining a broad set of present and past features of clones, characterizing both individual clones and the relations among clone peers, improve the recommendation of clones for refactoring, in both within-project and cross-project settings? We further ask which categories of features are most informative and how sensitive the results are to the choice of learning algorithm.

To answer these questions, we present CREC, a learning-based approach to clone recommendation. CREC takes a set of software repositories as input and automatically mines their histories to identify clone groups that developers actually refactored (R-clones) and clone groups that persisted without being refactored (NR-clones). This automatic labeling removes the need for manual annotation and yields a training set that reflects real developer decisions at a scale unattainable by hand. For each clone group, CREC extracts 34 features in five categories: the content of individual clones, the evolution behaviors of individual clones, and the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. A classifier trained on these features then predicts whether a new clone group should be recommended for refactoring.

We evaluated CREC on six large open-source projects. In the within-project setting, where the classifier is trained and tested on data from the same project, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%. In the cross-project setting, where the classifier is trained on other projects and applied to an unseen one, it achieved an F-score of 76%. We compared CREC against the state-of-the-art approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014) on the same data set. Our results show that CREC outperforms the existing approach, demonstrating the benefits of combining a broad set of present and past features of clones. We also examined the importance of different categories of features and the sensitivity of the results to the choice of learning algorithm, providing insights into the factors that contribute most to recommendation accuracy.

Overall, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring and highlights the importance of considering a broad set of features in clone recommendation. Our findings have implications for the development of clone detection and recommendation tools, suggesting that a more comprehensive approach to clone analysis can lead to more accurate and effective recommendations. By providing a framework for evaluating the importance of different features and learning algorithms, our study contributes to the ongoing effort to improve the accuracy and usefulness of clone recommendation tools. The development of effective clone management tools is crucial for maintaining the quality and integrity of software systems. To address this challenge, we have designed and evaluated a novel approach, CREC, which leverages machine learning to recommend clones for refactoring. Our approach has achieved significant improvements over a state-of-the-art baseline, with F-scores of 83% and 76% in within-project and cross-project settings, respectively. This substantial enhancement is particularly noteworthy when historical data from the target project is unavailable.

To gain a deeper understanding of the factors that contribute to these results, we conducted a thorough analysis of the contribution of each feature category and compared the performance of several widely used learning algorithms. This paper presents the following key contributions: (1) an automated approach to building ground truth, which enables the construction of large training and evaluation sets without manual labeling; (2) the largest feature set to date for clone recommendation, comprising 34 features that integrate present and past information; (3) a learning-based recommender, CREC, which accurately recommends clones for refactoring; and (4) an empirical analysis of factors and algorithms, providing insights to guide the design of future clone-management tools.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by providing background and motivating examples in Section 2. Section 3 describes the design of CREC, including the extraction of refactored and non-refactored clone groups, the feature set, and the classifier training. The experimental setup and results are presented in Section 4, while Section 5 discusses threats to validity. A review of related work is provided in Section 6, and we conclude with a summary of our findings and implications in Section 7.

Our study was guided by three research questions. First, we sought to determine the accuracy with which CREC recommends clone groups for refactoring in within-project and cross-project settings, compared to a state-of-the-art baseline. Second, we aimed to quantify the contribution of each feature category to the overall performance of CREC. Third, we investigated the impact of the choice of learning algorithm on the effectiveness of CREC. To address these questions, we designed CREC as a three-stage approach: (1) automatic construction of a labeled data set of refactored clone groups and non-refactored clone groups from version histories; (2) extraction of 34 features capturing the present and past of each clone group; and (3) training and applying a classifier that predicts whether a clone group deserves refactoring.

We selected six open-source Java projects with long, well-maintained Git histories as the subject projects for our study. These projects, namely Ant, Cassandra, jEdit, JGit, Lucene, and Tomcat, were chosen based on three criteria: more than 5,000 commits, at least eight years of development, and varied application domains and sizes. To keep the analysis tractable, we sampled snapshots at release tags and at every 100th commit between releases, yielding a total of 1,412 snapshots. This sampling approach is common in clone-genealogy research, where the unit of analysis is the evolution of clones across versions rather than individual commits.

For each snapshot, we detected Type-2 and Type-3 clones using NiCad, with a minimum size of 10 lines, a maximum dissimilarity threshold of 30% after pretty-printing and identifier normalization, and blind renaming. Clone fragments were grouped into clone groups, where each member is similar to the others in the group. We then mapped clone groups across consecutive snapshots using a location- and similarity-based mapping, resulting in a set of clone genealogies that describe how each group was created, changed, and removed.

To automatically label refactored and non-refactored clone groups, we detected refactorings between successive snapshots using RefactoringMiner, which reports Extract Method, Pull Up Method, Move Method, Extract Superclass, and related operations with high precision. A clone group was labeled as refactored if its genealogy ended due to the disappearance or dissimilarity of at least two fragments, and a clone-removal refactoring was detected involving at least two fragments of the group in the same commit interval. Clone groups that survived at least five consecutive snapshots or at least one year without any clone-removal refactoring were labeled as non-refactored. Groups with ambiguous histories were discarded, and two authors manually validated a random sample of 300 labeled groups, achieving a high level of agreement with the automatic labels.

The final data set consisted of 1,028 refactored clone groups and 4,876 non-refactored clone groups. CREC computes 34 features at the snapshot immediately preceding the labeling event, which are organized into five categories: code features, evolution-history features, spatial features, syntactic-relation features, and co-change features. These features capture various aspects of the present and past of each clone group, including its content, evolution, spatial relations, and syntactic differences.

Code features, which describe the present content of a clone group, include metrics such as average lines of code, number of tokens, number of peers, cyclomatic complexity, and cohesion. Evolution-history features, which describe the past of each clone, include metrics such as age, number of commits touching it, number of distinct authors, time since last change, and change frequency. Spatial features characterize the location of clone peers, including same method, same file, same package, or different modules, as well as file-path distance and inheritance relation between enclosing classes. Syntactic-relation features capture the differences between clone peers, including token-level and AST-level similarity, number of differing statements, and gap lines in Type-3 clones.

In the next section, we present the results of our experimental evaluation, which demonstrate the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring. We also discuss the implications of our findings and provide insights into the design of future clone-management tools. The task of recommending clones for refactoring is a complex one, and our approach, CREC, relies on a comprehensive set of 34 features to identify refactored clone groups (R-clones) and distinguish them from non-refactored ones (NR-clones). These features can be broadly categorized into several groups, including code metrics, history features, and co-change features. Code metrics, such as size, complexity, and cohesion, provide insights into the structure and organization of the code, while history features, including the number of commits and authors involved, offer a glimpse into the evolution of the codebase over time. Co-change features, which capture the history shared by peers, are also essential in understanding how different parts of the codebase are related and how they have changed together.

To compute these features, we utilized a JavaParser-based analyzer for code metrics and mined history features from git log and git blame. We also employed a set of co-change features, including the number of commits in which peers changed together, the ratio of co-changes to total changes, and the consistency of change. These features were then normalized using min-max normalization on the training data to prevent feature dominance and ensure that all features are on the same scale. We also examined pairs of features with high correlation (Spearman |ρ| > 0.95) for redundancy, but none were removed, as tree-based learners are robust to collinearity.

Our default learning algorithm was Random Forest, with 200 trees and the square root of the feature count considered at each split. We also trained C4.5 decision trees, Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, and support vector machines with an RBF kernel using Weka, with parameters tuned via grid search in inner three-fold cross-validation. To address the class imbalance issue, where R-clones constitute only about 17% of the data, we applied SMOTE to the training folds, oversampling the minority class to a 1:1 ratio, while retaining the natural distribution in the test folds.

In evaluating CREC, we employed two settings: within-project and cross-project. In the within-project setting, we performed stratified ten-fold cross-validation on each project, repeated ten times with different random seeds. To reduce temporal leakage, we constructed folds such that clone groups from the same genealogy never appeared in both training and test sets. In the cross-project setting, we used leave-one-project-out validation, where the classifier was trained on five projects and tested on the sixth. We report precision, recall, and F-score for the R-clone class, as well as the area under the ROC curve (AUC), to account for threshold effects.

We compared CREC with the approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014), which recommends clones using design, context, and history features with a decision-tree learner. We reimplemented their approach from the published feature descriptions and ran it on the same data and folds, with the same SMOTE preprocessing, to ensure a fair comparison. To analyze the contribution of each feature category, we conducted two analyses: training with each feature category alone and training with all categories except one (ablation). We also ranked individual features by information gain and by the mean decrease in Gini impurity of the Random Forest.

The results of our evaluation are promising, with CREC achieving a mean precision of 85%, a mean recall of 81%, and a mean F-score of 83% in the within-project setting. The per-project F-scores ranged from 79% to 87%, with the best result on the project with the most training instances and the lowest on the project with the fewest R-clones. In the cross-project setting, the mean precision was 79%, the mean recall was 73%, and the mean F-score was 76%, with per-project F-scores between 68% and 82%. The 7-point F-score drop relative to the within-project setting suggests that refactoring practices differ across projects, but a substantial part of the signal transfers. The area under the ROC curve was 0.91 within projects and 0.84 across projects, indicating that the classifier ranks R-clones above NR-clones even when its decision threshold is not tuned.

In comparison with the state-of-the-art approach, CREC improved the F-score by 13 percentage points within projects and by 26 points across projects, corresponding to relative improvements of 18.6% and 52.0%. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the 60 paired cross-validation runs showed that the differences are significant in both settings (p < 0.01), and Cliff's delta indicated a large effect size (δ = 0.71 within projects, δ = 0.83 across projects). These results suggest that CREC is a robust and effective approach for recommending clones for refactoring.

To mitigate potential threats to validity, we took several precautions. To reduce construct risk from automatic labeling, we manually validated a sample of automatically extracted instances and used conservative inclusion criteria. To limit internal risk from tool error, we ran NiCad with default, previously validated settings. For generalizability, we included projects from different domains, although all subjects are Java open-source systems, which is a limitation we discuss later. Our dataset consists of six subject projects, with CREC's automatic extraction procedure identifying 1,437 R-clones and 4,912 NR-clones. The per-project number of R-clones ranged from 118 to 346, and because the classes are imbalanced, we balanced the training folds by random undersampling of NR-clones and evaluated on untouched test folds.

Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring, both within and across projects. The approach is robust, with a large effect size compared to the state-of-the-art approach, and it provides a reliable means of identifying R-clones and distinguishing them from NR-clones. While there are limitations to our study, including the focus on Java open-source systems, the results suggest that CREC has the potential to be a valuable tool for software developers and maintainers seeking to improve the quality and maintainability of their codebases. The performance of our clone recommendation model, CREC, was evaluated on a dataset of 34 features across five categories, including content features of individual clones, evolution-history features, spatial relations among clone peers, syntactic relations, and co-change relations. Notably, the baseline model's performance degraded more sharply across projects, with an F-score of 0.83, suggesting that its feature set is more dependent on project-specific characteristics such as local naming and structural conventions. In contrast, CREC's inclusion of evolutionary and co-change relations appears to generalize better across projects.

To better understand the contribution of individual feature categories, we examined the performance of each category in isolation. The results showed that, within projects, the F-scores for the individual categories ranged from 62% for spatial features to 74% for co-change features, with content, history, and syntactic features falling in between. Across projects, the corresponding F-scores were lower, ranging from 55% for spatial features to 67% for co-change features. These results suggest that co-change features are the most informative single category in both settings, which is consistent with the idea that clones that change together are more costly to maintain and therefore more worth merging.

We also explored the combination of features that describe the present state of the code and those that describe its history. Combining all present-oriented features (content, spatial, syntactic) yielded F-scores of 76% within projects and 67% across projects, whereas combining all past-oriented features (history, co-change) yielded 79% and 71%. The union of these two sets of features reached 83% and 76%, indicating that the two perspectives are complementary rather than redundant.

To further evaluate the importance of each feature category, we performed a leave-one-category-out ablation study. Removing co-change features caused the largest drop in performance, with the within-project F-score decreasing from 83% to 76% and the cross-project F-score decreasing from 76% to 67%. Removing history features also had a significant impact, lowering the F-scores to 78% and 70%, while removing content features lowered them to 80% and 72%. The removal of spatial or syntactic features had smaller but consistent effects, reducing the F-scores by 2 to 3 points in both settings. These results support the decision to retain all five categories, as every ablation reduced performance.

In addition to evaluating the importance of each feature category, we also examined the feature importance using the mean decrease in Gini impurity. The top 10 most important features were drawn from all five categories and included metrics such as the number of co-changes between clone peers, the proportion of commits in which all peers changed consistently, and the age of the clone group. The top three features alone accounted for 27% of the total importance, highlighting the value of considering a diverse set of features when recommending clones for refactoring.

We also compared the performance of random forest with five other classifiers using the same features and splits. The results showed that random forest and gradient boosting, both ensembles of trees, outperformed the other classifiers by at least 4 points within projects and 8 points across projects. The difference between the two ensembles was small and not statistically significant, whereas random forest was significantly better than every non-ensemble classifier. This result suggests that the relation between the features and refactoring decisions is nonlinear and involves interactions among features, which tree ensembles model well.

Furthermore, we performed sensitivity analyses to examine the impact of the amount of training data on the performance of our model. The results showed that, in the within-project setting, using 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% of the training data produced F-scores of 70%, 76%, 80%, 82%, and 83%, indicating that performance largely saturated at about 80% of the data. Under the original class distribution, without undersampling, recall decreased by 9 points and the F-score by 5 points, confirming that balancing the training data is beneficial.

Our evaluation demonstrates that CREC is accurate and generalizes across projects better than prior work. The results show that combining information about the present state of the code with its history is beneficial for clone recommendation. In the within-project setting, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%, compared with 70% for the state-of-the-art baseline, an improvement of 13 percentage points. The gap widened in the cross-project setting, where CREC reached 76% and the baseline fell to 50%, a difference of 26 points. This pattern suggests that the baseline's smaller feature set captures project-specific regularities that do not transfer well.

Several explanations for CREC's robustness are plausible. First, prior work has shown that clones differ in their maintenance consequences, and that harmfulness depends on how clones evolve rather than on their mere existence. Features that describe change history, such as how often a clone has been modified or how often its peers have changed together, express this dependence more directly than static similarity does. Second, developers refactor clones only when removal is both beneficial and feasible. Benefit is reflected by co-change and inconsistent-change behavior, while feasibility is reflected by spatial and syntactic relations, such as whether peers share a file, class, or inheritance hierarchy. A model that observes only one of these dimensions will misclassify clones that score highly on one but poorly on the other. This is consistent with our results, which show that combining present and past information about both individual clones and clone peers is essential for accurate clone recommendation.

Malaria remains a paramount parasitic disease globally, with the World Health Organization estimating approximately 219 million cases and 435,000 deaths in 2017, predominantly in the African Region, which accounted for about 93% of cases and 94% of deaths (World Health Organization, 2018). The significant progress achieved in the early 2000s, through scaled-up vector control, the introduction of artemisinin-based combination therapy, and improved diagnostics, which collectively reduced the global burden by around 40% (Bhatt et al., 2015), has stalled in several high-burden countries. A critical challenge in malaria control is its heterogeneity; transmission intensity varies not only over small geographical distances but also across different seasons and years, influenced by a complex interplay of factors including climate, land use, vector ecology, human movement, socioeconomic conditions, and the coverage of interventions (Gething et al., 2011; Kabaria et al., 2017). This heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of national averages, as they mask the specific foci and periods of risk that are crucial for effective control and elimination strategies. The issue is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where resources are limited, making targeted interventions essential. 

To address this challenge, spatio-temporal modelling has emerged as a central tool for characterizing the heterogeneity of malaria transmission. By elucidating how disease risk varies jointly over space and time, these models support a range of critical applications, including the mapping of disease burden, early warning systems for epidemics, the identification of hotspots and high-risk periods, and the evaluation of interventions (Hay et al., 2009; Pigott et al., 2015). The rapid expansion of this field can be attributed to several factors. The increasing availability of georeferenced data, such as national household surveys with GPS coordinates (e.g., Demographic and Health Surveys and Malaria Indicator Surveys), health facility records from routine information systems like DHIS2, and parasite rate databases compiled by the Malaria Atlas Project (Guerra et al., 2007; Gething et al., 2011), has been pivotal. Additionally, advancements in satellite remote sensing now provide high-resolution environmental data, including rainfall, temperature, vegetation indices, and other relevant measures (Hay et al., 2006). Computational advances, particularly in hierarchical Bayesian geostatistical inference, have made it feasible to apply complex models to large datasets, with techniques such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) with the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach allowing for flexible modelling (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011).

The methodologies employed in spatio-temporal modelling of malaria are diverse and depend on the nature of the data and the objectives of the analysis. For area-level data, models often involve Poisson or negative binomial likelihoods to account for the count of cases in each area over time, incorporating expected counts or population at risk, covariates, spatially structured and unstructured random effects, temporal terms, and space-time interactions (Besag et al., 1991; Knorr-Held, 2000). For point-referenced survey data, geostatistical binomial models are common, which include Gaussian processes with Matérn covariance to capture spatial and temporal dependencies (Diggle et al., 1998; Gething et al., 2012). Other approaches include spatial scan statistics for cluster detection (Kulldorff, 1997), generalized additive models, spatio-temporal autoregressive and distributed-lag models for climate-driven forecasting, machine learning techniques such as random forests and boosted regression trees, and mechanistic or hybrid models that combine transmission dynamics with spatial structure (Smith et al., 2012; Reiner et al., 2015). Each of these approaches is based on distinct assumptions regarding stationarity, dependence structure, interaction between space and time, and the relationship between covariates and risk, and the choice of approach is further influenced by the scale of analysis and the quality and completeness of the underlying data.

The covariates included in these models are equally diverse, reflecting the multifactorial nature of malaria transmission. Environmental and climatic variables, such as temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation indices, elevation, and hydrology, are frequently used due to their biological relevance to vector and parasite development (Craig et al., 1999; Mordecai et al., 2013). Socioeconomic indicators, housing quality, urbanization, population density, access to healthcare, intervention coverage (including insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, and treatment), and human mobility are also considered, although their inclusion is less standardized and they are often less consistently available and measured. Decisions regarding lagged effects, spatial resolution matching, collinearity, variable selection, and handling covariates that are themselves modelled or interpolated are made inconsistently and often without clear justification. Similarly, the practices used to validate models vary, ranging from simple in-sample fit statistics (such as deviance information criterion, R²) to out-of-sample cross-validation, spatial block validation, and prospective forecast evaluation using proper scoring rules (Roberts et al., 2017; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007), with the neglect of residual spatial and temporal autocorrelation potentially leading to overestimation of predictive performance.

While existing reviews have addressed various aspects of this landscape, a comprehensive overview that synthesizes the full range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates, and validation strategies across different settings is lacking. Earlier syntheses have focused on specific topics, such as the use of geographic information systems and remote sensing in malaria epidemiology (Hay et al., 2006; Eisele et al., 2012), early warning systems and climate-based forecasting (Thomson et al., 2006; Zinszer et al., 2012), mapping of parasite prevalence (Hay et al., 2009), or particular techniques. The absence of a systematic comparison of the diverse methodologies, covariates, and validation strategies employed in spatio-temporal modelling of malaria hinders researchers and national malaria control programs aiming to develop models for burden estimation, forecasting, or intervention targeting, as they lack consolidated guidance on the applicability and effectiveness of different methods under various data conditions.

This knowledge gap is particularly significant in LMICs, where data are often sparse, noisy, and reported at aggregated administrative scales, and methodological choices can directly influence resource allocation. Given the heterogeneity in aims, designs, and outcomes across the literature, a scoping review is more appropriate than a conventional systematic review with meta-analysis. A scoping approach enables the mapping of the extent, range, and nature of the evidence, the identification of key concepts and gaps, and the establishment of a foundation for best-practice recommendations (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010; Tricco et al., 2018). The overarching goal of such a review is to provide a comprehensive framework that can guide the development and application of spatio-temporal models for malaria control, ultimately contributing to more effective and targeted interventions against this persistent and heterogeneous disease. The question at the heart of this review is a pressing one: what approaches have been employed to model the spatio-temporal dynamics of malaria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and what covariates and validation techniques have been used to inform these models? To address this question, we have identified five key objectives. Firstly, we aim to provide a detailed description of the aims and settings of existing spatio-temporal malaria modelling studies, including the spatial and temporal scales employed and the data sources utilized. Secondly, we seek to catalogue and classify the various statistical and mathematical modelling frameworks that have been applied to this problem. Thirdly, we will summarize the covariates that have been included in these models and how they have been processed. Fourthly, we will document the procedures used to validate and assess the performance of these models. Finally, we hope to identify methodological gaps and derive recommendations to guide future modelling decisions.

This review makes three significant contributions to the field. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive and structured synthesis of spatio-temporal malaria modelling efforts over the past five decades, incorporating not only peer-reviewed literature but also grey literature that may have been overlooked by conventional searches. Secondly, it explicitly links modelling choices to data characteristics, spatial scale, and purpose, thereby enabling a more transparent and informed approach to method selection. Thirdly, it highlights underutilized methods, weaknesses in validation and reporting, and priority areas for research, ultimately supporting the development of more rigorous and reproducible modelling approaches in the settings where they are most needed.

Our review follows the PRISMA-P reporting guidance (Moher et al., 2015) and is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017076427). The methodological framework for this scoping review is based on the work of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the Joanna Briggs Institute (Peters et al., 2015). The protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement (Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015) and was registered with PROSPERO before the screening process began. The final review will be reported using PRISMA guidance, including a flow diagram of study selection. We opted for a scoping design because our primary aim is to map the range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates, and validation practices employed in malaria modelling, rather than to pool effect estimates.

The review process proceeds through five stages: (1) identifying the research question, (2) identifying relevant studies, (3) selecting studies, (4) charting the data, and (5) collating, summarizing, and reporting the results. Our research question is focused on the spatio-temporal modelling approaches, covariates, and validation techniques used to assess the burden of malaria in LMICs within the limits of malaria transmission. Eligibility criteria were structured using the Population–Concept–Context framework. The population of interest comprises human malaria cases, infection prevalence, incidence, or mortality, at any spatial scale from household to continental. The concept of interest is the application of statistical, mathematical, or geostatistical models that explicitly incorporate both spatial and temporal dimensions, such as Bayesian hierarchical models, spatio-temporal geostatistical models, space–time scan statistics, generalized additive or autoregressive models with spatial structure, and mechanistic models with spatial components. The context is any LMIC, as defined by the World Bank income classification, lying within the spatial limits of malaria transmission (Gething et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2008).

Studies were included if they were published between January 1968 and April 2018, in any language for which translation was feasible, and as primary research, methodological papers, theses, or technical reports. We excluded studies that were purely spatial or purely temporal with no joint modelling, those conducted in high-income or non-endemic settings, those that considered only vector distribution or entomological outcomes without human burden, and commentaries, editorials, or narrative reviews without original modelling. Reference lists of excluded reviews were hand-searched for eligible primary studies.

To identify relevant studies, we will conduct a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete, MasterFILE Premier, CINAHL, and MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, as well as Google Scholar. The search strategy was developed in collaboration with an information specialist and combines controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH) with free-text terms in three concept blocks joined by the Boolean operator AND: (i) malaria ("malaria" OR "Plasmodium" OR "falciparum" OR "vivax"); (ii) spatio-temporal methods ("spatio-temporal" OR "spatiotemporal" OR "space-time" OR "geostatistic" OR "Bayesian hierarchical" OR "disease mapping" OR "geographic information system" OR "remote sensing" OR "kriging" OR "CAR model" OR "INLA"); and (iii) burden or outcome terms ("prevalence" OR "incidence" OR "burden" OR "transmission" OR "mortality" OR "risk"). Terms within each block are joined by OR. A country-level filter listing LMICs, adapted from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care group filter (Cochrane EPOC, 2017), will be used to improve specificity. The search will be piloted in PubMed, peer-reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al., 2016), and adapted to the syntax of each database. Due to the large number of records returned by Google Scholar, the first 200 hits for each search string will be screened (Haddaway et al., 2015).

In addition to searching databases, we will also seek out grey literature through various channels, including OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the World Health Organization Global Malaria Programme repository, the Malaria Atlas Project, the MEASURE DHS and Malaria Indicator Survey publications, conference proceedings of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Multilateral Initiative on Malaria, and institutional repositories of African universities. Furthermore, we will contact experts in malaria spatial epidemiology to identify unpublished work.

All records will be exported to EndNote, where duplicates will be removed, and then imported into Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016) for screening. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, then abstracts, then full texts against the eligibility criteria. Before formal screening, a calibration exercise on a random sample of 50 records will be undertaken to refine the criteria and ensure consistent interpretation. Inter-rater agreement at each stage will be quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. A kappa of at least 0.61 will be considered substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977). Disagreements will be resolved by discussion, and where consensus cannot be reached, by a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be recorded and reported in the PRISMA flow diagram.

To facilitate data extraction, a standardized data charting form will be piloted on ten studies and iteratively refined. This form will capture key information about each study, including the study design, data sources, spatial and temporal scales, modelling approach, covariates, validation techniques, and outcomes. By systematically charting this information, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of spatio-temporal malaria modelling and identify areas for future research and improvement. Our systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the methodologies employed in spatial epidemiology studies of malaria. To achieve this, we will conduct a thorough data extraction process, where two reviewers will independently chart data from included studies, with a third reviewer verifying a 10% random sample to ensure accuracy. The extracted variables will encompass a wide range of study characteristics, including bibliographic details, country and region, spatial scale and unit of analysis, study period and temporal resolution, data source, malaria outcome, study aim, modelling framework, and model validation and performance assessment techniques.

To illustrate the types of models we anticipate encountering, consider a typical Bayesian space-time formulation for count data, such as Yit ~ Poisson(Eit θit), where log θit = α + xitᵀβ + ui + vi + γt + δit, with ui representing a spatially structured effect, vi an unstructured effect, γt a temporal effect, and δit a space-time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000). Geostatistical alternatives to this model replace ui with a latent Gaussian field S(s,t) with Matérn covariance (Diggle and Giorgi, 2019). In cases where key information is missing, we will contact the authors to request additional details.

In accordance with scoping review guidance, we will not conduct a formal risk-of-bias assessment, as this is not required for our study (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005). Instead, we will descriptively appraise the reporting transparency of each study, including whether data sources, model specification, priors, convergence diagnostics, and validation procedures were stated, and whether uncertainty was quantified and mapped. This will enable us to inform best-practice recommendations for future studies.

Our synthesis and analysis will involve summarizing the charted data descriptively, using frequencies and proportions to show the distribution of studies by year, geographic region, spatial scale, outcome, and model class. We will also conduct a qualitative thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) to group and evaluate studies around four themes: aims, spatio-temporal methodology, covariates employed, and model validation techniques. This analysis will be conducted inductively in NVivo by two reviewers, with themes developed through iterative discussion. Furthermore, we will cross-tabulate studies by method and aim, and by covariate class and spatial scale, to identify methodological trends, gaps, and areas of consensus. Our findings will be synthesized into recommendations for model choice, covariate selection, and validation, which will be explicitly linked to the characteristics of the data and the intended use of the model.

It is worth noting that patients and the public were not involved in the design of this review, as it uses only published and publicly available data. Consequently, ethical approval is not required. However, we plan to disseminate our results through a peer-reviewed publication and presentations at malaria and spatial epidemiology conferences, to ensure that our findings are accessible to relevant stakeholders.

Our search, which covered the period from January 1968 to April 2018, identified 6,214 records, including 5,873 from electronic databases and 341 from grey literature sources. After removing duplicates, 4,232 records were screened by title and abstract, resulting in the exclusion of 3,801 studies. A further 244 studies were excluded at the full-text review stage, leaving 187 studies that met the inclusion criteria and entered the thematic synthesis. Inter-reviewer agreement was substantial to almost perfect at both stages, with Cohen's κ = 0.82 for title and abstract screening and κ = 0.87 for full-text review. Disagreements were resolved by consensus without the need for a third reviewer.

The included studies span a range of years, with the earliest eligible study published in 1999, during a period when geostatistical methods were first being applied to malaria survey data (Kleinschmidt et al., 2000; Diggle et al., 2002). The number of publications increased steeply thereafter, with 12 studies (6.4%) appearing before 2005, 41 (21.9%) between 2005 and 2010, and 134 (71.7%) between 2011 and April 2018. The majority of studies were from sub-Saharan Africa (128; 68.4%), followed by Asia (38; 20.3%) and the Americas (15; 8.0%). Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Mali, and Mozambique were the most frequently studied African countries, while Thailand, India, and Indonesia predominated in Asia, and Brazil, Colombia, and Peru in the Americas.

In terms of spatial scale, 71 studies (38.0%) worked at the subnational or district level, 62 (33.2%) at the national level, 31 (16.6%) at the village or household level, and 23 (12.3%) were continental or multi-country analyses, such as the Malaria Atlas Project (Hay et al., 2009; Gething et al., 2011; Bhatt et al., 2015). The outcomes modeled were mainly clinical incidence or case counts (82; 43.9%) and parasite prevalence (74; 39.6%), with fewer studies examining entomological indices, malaria mortality, or other outcomes such as anaemia or treatment-seeking.

Data sources varied, with 78 studies (41.7%) using routine health management information systems or passive surveillance, 69 (36.9%) using national household surveys, and 24 (12.8%) using active surveillance, cohort, or purpose-designed cross-sectional surveys. The principal aim of 98 studies (52.4%) was disease mapping or risk estimation, including prediction at unsampled locations, while 46 (24.6%) examined environmental, climatic, or socioeconomic determinants of malaria, 24 (12.8%) developed forecasting or early-warning systems, and 19 (10.2%) evaluated interventions such as insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, or mass drug administration.

Our table-level synthesis revealed considerable methodological heterogeneity, with Bayesian hierarchical models being the most common (63 studies; 33.7%). Most of these were geostatistical models, highlighting the importance of accounting for spatial autocorrelation in malaria epidemiology. However, the diversity of approaches and models used in the included studies underscores the need for a comprehensive synthesis of the literature to inform best practices in spatial epidemiology. The analysis of malaria burden has become increasingly reliant on spatio-temporal modeling, particularly in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). This trend is driven by the growing availability of georeferenced survey and surveillance data, global malaria mapping initiatives, and advances in computational power that enable hierarchical Bayesian inference for large datasets. A key aspect of these models is the incorporation of a Gaussian random field, which can be represented as y(s,t) | p(s,t) ~ Binomial(n(s,t), p(s,t)), with logit p(s,t) = x(s,t)ᵀβ + S(s) + u(t) + ε(s,t), where S(s) is a spatially structured Gaussian process, typically with a Matérn covariance, u(t) is a temporal effect, and ε is an unstructured error term, as described by Diggle et al. (2002) and Gosoniu et al. (2006).

Our review of 187 studies reveals a diverse range of methodological approaches, with 41 studies employing Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation and 22 using integrated nested Laplace approximation with the stochastic partial differential equation approach, as introduced by Rue et al. (2009) and Lindgren et al. (2011). The latter approach has gained popularity since 2012, reflecting the growing recognition of its utility in modeling complex spatial and temporal patterns. The proportion of studies using Bayesian approaches has increased significantly, from 18.2% of studies published before 2011 to 41.0% of those published from 2011 onwards, underscoring the value of these methods in accounting for uncertainty and complexity in malaria modeling.

Frequentist regression approaches, including generalized linear and additive models with spatial autocorrelation terms, simultaneous or conditional autoregressive structures, or generalized estimating equations, were used in 39 studies (20.9%). Spatial scan statistics and other cluster detection methods were employed in 25 studies (13.4%), often to identify hotspots, as described by Kulldorff (1997) and Bejon et al. (2010). Time-series methods, such as seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average models and wavelet analyses, were used in 21 studies (11.2%), primarily for forecasting purposes. Machine-learning or ensemble approaches, including boosted regression trees and random forests, were applied in 14 studies (7.5%), while mechanistic or mathematical transmission models coupled to spatial data were used in 11 studies (5.9%). The remaining 14 studies (7.5%) employed other or hybrid techniques.

The treatment of temporal structure varied across studies, with 58 studies (31.0%) analyzing discrete time slices or aggregated periods separately, 47 (25.1%) including first-order autoregressive or random-walk temporal effects, and 31 (16.6%) using harmonic or other seasonal terms. A full space–time interaction term was fitted in 29 studies (15.5%), while only 12 studies (6.4%) allowed non-stationary spatial covariance. Notably, 32 studies (17.1%) were purely spatial in their estimation, despite using multi-year data, highlighting the need for more nuanced consideration of temporal dynamics in malaria modeling.

The choice of covariates also varied widely, with environmental and climatic covariates used far more frequently than socioeconomic or health-system covariates. Rainfall, temperature, and vegetation indices (NDVI or EVI) were the most commonly used covariates, appearing in 141 (75.4%), 128 (68.4%), and 112 (59.9%) studies, respectively. Elevation, humidity, distance to water bodies, and land cover were also commonly used, as were climate-driver indices such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation. Most remotely sensed data came from MODIS, TRMM, or WorldClim products. Socioeconomic and demographic variables, including intervention coverage, household wealth indices, population density, urban–rural classification, and distance to health facilities, were used less frequently, appearing in 74 (39.6%), 69 (36.9%), 58 (31.0%), 41 (21.9%), and 27 (14.4%) studies, respectively.

Covariate selection was typically based on stepwise or univariable screening, with 96 studies (51.3%) using these methods. Fewer studies employed Bayesian variable selection or penalized regression, with only 17 (9.1%) using these approaches. Model validation was reported in only 97 studies (51.9%), with 90 (48.1%) reporting no validation beyond model fit. Information criteria (AIC, BIC, or DIC) were used for model comparison in 108 studies (57.8%). Predictive accuracy was summarized using various metrics, including mean absolute or root mean squared error, correlation between observed and predicted values, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and coverage of prediction or credible intervals.

The interpretation of these findings will be structured around three key themes: model class, covariates, and predictive performance. Malaria models in LMICs span a continuum from regression with residual spatial correlation to geostatistical models with Gaussian random fields, areal conditional autoregressive formulations, and mechanistic or hybrid models. A generic formulation can be represented as g(μit) = β₀ + xᵀit β + S(si) + T(t) + ψ(si, t) + εit, where μit is expected prevalence or incidence at location i and time t, xit is a vector of covariates, S is a spatially structured effect, T is a temporal trend or seasonal term, ψ is a space–time interaction, and ε is unstructured error. The review will examine how studies parameterize each component, with particular attention to the specification of the interaction term, which is critical for capturing the complex spatial and temporal dynamics of malaria transmission.

The choice of covariates is also a critical aspect of malaria modeling, with climatic and environmental predictors expected to dominate due to their biological basis in vector and parasite development. However, the review will also examine whether this dominance reflects scientific rationale or data convenience, and whether socioeconomic factors, housing, urbanization, human movement, and intervention coverage are adequately accounted for in these models. Ultimately, the goal of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of malaria modeling, highlighting areas of consistency, idiosyncrasy, and deficiency, and identifying opportunities for future research and improvement.

The persistence of homogeneous leadership in organizations, despite decades of diversity initiatives and a growing commitment to equal opportunity, is a striking phenomenon. In many professions, women, racial and ethnic minorities, and other nondominant group members enter in substantial numbers, only to see their representation dwindle at each successive step of the career ladder. This pattern is particularly evident in what can be termed upward mobility career systems, where careers unfold as a series of evaluations and promotions that progressively narrow the pool of candidates. For instance, in academia, women earn roughly half of doctoral degrees in many fields, yet they remain underrepresented among full professors and in senior leadership positions. The "leaky pipeline" metaphor, often used to describe this phenomenon, is somewhat misleading, as it implies a passive loss of talent rather than the outcome of repeated decisions made by identifiable individuals at specific points in the system.

The fact that this pattern persists in organizations that explicitly espouse meritocratic values is particularly puzzling. As Castilla and Benard (2010) have noted, a paradox of meritocracy can arise, where organizations that emphasize meritocratic values can actually exhibit greater bias in favor of dominant group members. This is because the belief in one's own objectivity can lead decision makers to relax their vigilance, making them more susceptible to moral licensing and less likely to monitor their own behavior. Furthermore, the criteria used to evaluate merit are often constructed or reweighted to favor certain candidates, as merit is rarely defined in a way that is independent of who displays it. Decades of research have shown that stereotypes can shape the evaluation of competence, the attribution of success, and the interpretation of ambiguous performance information, particularly when evaluation criteria are ambiguous, accountability is low, and time is short.

Gatekeepers, who control access to valued resources and positions, occupy a pivotal position in this process. They are often members of the dominant group, having been successful under existing rules, and are therefore prone to reproduce homophilous patterns of selection. However, the majority of diversity interventions are directed elsewhere, focusing on fixing the nondominant group member through mentoring, networking, or leadership training, or changing attitudes broadly through diversity training for all employees. While these approaches may have some benefits, the evidence suggests that they have modest and often short-lived effects, and that mandatory training can even provoke resistance.

In contrast, programs that target the people and procedures at decision points, such as accountability, transparency, and task forces responsible for diversity outcomes, have been shown to be more effective. However, these types of interventions have been relatively understudied, and the available evidence is limited. Two further limitations characterize the literature on diversity interventions. First, much of the evidence on bias comes from laboratory or vignette experiments, which, while valuable for demonstrating mechanisms, say little about how bias operates in the collective, repeated, and politically embedded decision processes of real organizations. Second, systemic approaches, which view inequality as an emergent property of interacting parts of an organization, have been advocated for some time, yet they are rarely translated into concrete guidance for practitioners.

As a result, change agents, including diversity officers and consultants, are left with broad principles but few specifics on what an intervention should contain and why it should work. The empirical base for "what works" in systemic interventions is thin, and rigorous evaluations in naturally occurring organizational settings remain scarce. This article seeks to address these gaps by asking: What design specifications should systemic diversity interventions meet if they are to engage gatekeepers, improve the quality of decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems? I use the term design specifications in the sense of design science, referring to general, evidence-informed prescriptions that state the properties an intervention should have to produce a desired outcome in a class of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation.

To derive these specifications, I draw on research on the paradox of meritocracy, bias in evaluation, and group decision processes to identify the mechanisms through which gatekeepers reproduce inequality and the leverage points at which they might be disrupted. I also ground the specifications in the limited empirical evidence on systemic interventions, examining three illustrative examples from academic settings: a bias literacy program, participatory modeling of organizational dynamics, and participant observation of decision making in committees. Universities offer a particularly informative context because their career systems are archetypal examples of upward mobility, their gatekeeping processes are formalized and visible, and their commitment to meritocratic ideals is especially strong.

The contribution of this article is threefold. First, I extend the diversity literature by shifting the unit of intervention from the disadvantaged individual or the undifferentiated workforce to the gatekeepers and the decision-making processes they control. Second, I provide a set of design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that can be applied in a variety of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation. Finally, I demonstrate the value of a design science approach to developing and evaluating diversity interventions, which can help to build a more robust and evidence-based field of practice. By focusing on the mechanisms and leverage points that shape the behavior of gatekeepers, we can develop more effective interventions that address the root causes of inequality in upward mobility career systems. This research endeavors to bridge the gap between the study of bias and organizational change by examining the decision-making processes that underlie systemic diversity interventions. To achieve this, I have developed a set of design specifications that synthesize the existing evidence on effective interventions, with a focus on features such as engagement, self-generated insight, and attention to the decision process. Each specification is accompanied by a concrete example of a successful intervention, providing a foundation for future evaluation research and inspiration for diversity officers and consultants. By combining these contributions, I aim to make systemic change in the composition of the upper echelons of career pyramids a more tractable and evidence-based pursuit.

The research approach employed in this study follows a design science methodology, which seeks to generate prescriptive knowledge in the form of design specifications. These specifications take the form of general statements that outline the conditions under which a particular outcome can be achieved, and are judged on their utility and the plausibility of their underlying mechanisms. Given the scarcity of rigorous evaluations of systemic diversity interventions, I drew on three sources of input in an iterative, abductive process. Firstly, I conducted a theoretical analysis of the paradox of meritocracy in upward mobility career systems. Secondly, I undertook a purposive review of the existing evidence on interventions. Thirdly, I developed a formal sketch of how bias in gatekeeping decisions accumulates across a career pyramid. By moving back and forth between these sources, I refined the design specifications until each was tied to an identified mechanism, at least one empirical example, and a plausible implementation route.

The scope of this research is focused on upward mobility career systems, which are organizations in which individuals progress through hierarchical stages, with advancement decided by gatekeepers who evaluate candidates against criteria of merit. Examples of such systems include academia, professional service firms, and large public bureaucracies. A systemic diversity intervention is defined as one that targets the decision-making processes, structures, or routines through which advancement occurs, rather than solely focusing on the attitudes or skills of individuals from nondominant groups. Nondominant group members are those whose social category is underrepresented at higher organizational levels and who are subject to negative stereotyping or reduced status in the evaluative context.

To identify and select intervention evidence, I conducted a comprehensive search of major databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar, for English-language publications from 2000 to 2022. The search strings combined terms related to the intervention level, target, topic, and setting. I supplemented the database search with backward and forward citation tracking from key works, as well as reports from funded programs such as the U.S. National Science Foundation ADVANCE initiative and the European structural change projects. Studies were included if they described an intervention aimed at influencing gatekeepers' evaluations, selections, or promotions, or altering the structures or routines within which they operate, and reported some form of outcome evidence. Interventions aimed solely at individual development of nondominant group members, or one-off awareness sessions without follow-up, were excluded.

Given the limited evidence base, I employed a purposive, criterion-based selection approach to identify exemplary cases that maximized variation in the mechanism of change. Three interventions in academic settings were chosen, each engaging gatekeepers through a different route. The first was a bias literacy program, which equips gatekeepers with the knowledge and strategies to recognize and counter biases in their evaluations. The second was participatory modeling, which involves gatekeepers and other stakeholders in the construction of a formal or semiformal model of the career system, allowing them to see how local decisions aggregate into pyramid-level representation. The third was participant observation, in which a researcher-practitioner observes actual decision meetings and provides feedback to gatekeepers on the discursive and procedural patterns that shape their evaluations.

For each intervention, I extracted the target group of gatekeepers, core activities, theory of change, implementation conditions, outcome measures, and reported effects and limitations. I then coded the material using a mechanism-oriented template adapted from realist evaluation, seeking to understand what it was about the intervention that produced change, for whom, and under what conditions. The coding process involved three passes: firstly, open descriptive categories were coded; secondly, these categories were clustered into higher-order mechanisms drawing on the literatures on stereotyping, accountability, and structured decision making; and thirdly, each cluster was translated into a design specification and checked against disconfirming cases to identify boundary conditions. Specifications were retained when they were supported by at least two independent sources, or by one empirical source and a well-established theoretical mechanism, and were flagged as provisional otherwise.

To clarify why modest gatekeeper bias yields large representation gaps at the top, and to provide a transparent basis for the participatory modeling example, I developed a formal model of bias accumulation. This model illustrates how biases in gatekeeping decisions can accumulate across a career pyramid, resulting in significant representation gaps at the top. By providing a clear understanding of the mechanisms underlying bias accumulation, this model can inform the development of more effective interventions aimed at promoting diversity and inclusion in upward mobility career systems. The career advancement process can be conceptualized as a multistage pipeline, where individuals progress through a series of promotion stages (Martell et al., 1996; Nielsen & Börjesson, 2022). To better understand the dynamics of this process, consider a system with K promotion stages, where pk represents the promotion probability for dominant group members at stage k. The nondominant group's promotion probability, on the other hand, is pk(1 − δk), with δk ∈ [0,1) denoting the proportional reduction in promotion probability due to biased evaluation. 

At each stage, the share of nondominant group members can be calculated using the formula fK = f0 ∏{k=1}^{K}(1 − δk) / [ f0 ∏{k=1}^{K}(1 − δk) + (1 − f0) ]. This formula highlights the cumulative effect of biased evaluation across multiple stages. For instance, if the nondominant group's share at entry is f0 = 0.50, and the proportional reduction in promotion probability is constant at δ = 0.10, then after K = 5 stages, the nondominant group's share at the top would be approximately 0.37. This disparity arises despite the fact that no single stage exhibits a dramatic gap, underscoring the insidious nature of cumulative disadvantage.

The meritocratic belief that selection is unbiased can lead to the attribution of these gaps to individual differences, which, in turn, can increase bias (Castilla & Benard, 2010). To illustrate the potential impact of interventions, the model can be used heuristically to demonstrate how reducing δk at selected stages or increasing the number of transparent, structured stages can shift fK. Although the parameters used in this model are illustrative, the model itself is not intended for estimation or inference, and no statistical hypothesis testing was performed.

To ensure the credibility of the synthesis, several steps were taken. Multiple evidence types were used to triangulate each specification (Denzin, 2012), and coding decisions were thoroughly documented in an audit trail. The distinction between mechanisms supported by empirical evidence and those inferred theoretically was made explicit. Furthermore, disconfirming evidence, including reports of backlash, tokenism, and symbolic compliance (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016; Kaiser et al., 2013), was sought to inform the specifications on voluntariness, accountability, and follow-up. 

However, the approach is not without limitations. The purposive sampling strategy, the dominance of Western academic settings in the evidence, and the reliance on published accounts that may overrepresent successful interventions all contribute to the limitations of this synthesis. As such, the specifications presented here are empirically informed, testable propositions rather than established causal laws.

The synthesis focused on three intervention families implemented in academic settings: bias literacy programs, participatory modeling, and participant observation of gatekeeping meetings. Each intervention was evaluated against the paradox of meritocracy (Castilla & Benard, 2010). Due to differences in design and outcome measures across interventions, effects are reported in their original metrics, followed by a comparison in terms of the design specifications they support. Three types of outcomes were relevant across cases: gatekeeper cognition (awareness, self-efficacy, and bias), decision processes (criteria, deliberation, and evidence use), and representation at successive career transitions.

In the academic systems examined, the share of nondominant group members declined at each transition, a phenomenon known as representation loss across the pyramid. To quantify this loss, let pk denote the proportion of nondominant group members at career stage k, and let rk represent the relative advancement ratio, or the odds of promotion from stage k−1 to stage k for nondominant relative to dominant group members. The expected representation at stage k can then be calculated as pk = (p{k−1} · rk) / (p{k−1} · rk + (1 − p{k−1})). 

In one case, participatory modeling, women constituted 47% of doctoral graduates but only 38% of assistant professors, 31% of associate professors, and 19% of full professors. The implied ratios were r ≈ 0.70 at the hiring transition, 0.73 at the tenure transition, and 0.52 at promotion to full professor. These ratios were not explained by differences in pipeline size at each stage. Simulations that held rk = 1 at every stage produced a full-professor share of about 41% within a 25-year horizon, while a simulation that raised only the final-stage ratio to 0.85 produced a share of about 27%. These findings suggest that gatekeeping at several transitions compounds, and a single-point intervention cannot close the gap on its own, consistent with cumulative-disadvantage accounts (Valian, 1998; Martell et al., 1996).

Controlled evidence on bias education is mixed but informative. In a cluster-randomized trial of a habit-breaking workshop, Carnes et al. (2015) found that intervention departments showed significantly greater increases in gender-bias awareness, self-efficacy to promote equity, and reported action than controls, although no immediate difference in climate measures was observed. The effect sizes on self-efficacy were small to moderate (Cohen's d ≈ 0.2–0.4). Similarly, Devine et al. (2012) found that a 12-week bias-habit-breaking intervention reduced implicit race bias scores relative to controls, but these effects were concentrated among participants who reported high concern about discrimination and faded in later follow-up.

Evidence from faculty settings is consistent with this pattern. Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) demonstrated that an identical laboratory manager application was rated less competent and offered a lower starting salary when the applicant was labeled female, with bias being equally strong among female and male raters. This suggests that the problem lies in shared cultural schemas rather than in the identity of the rater. In the bias literacy program examined, the strongest outcomes appeared when training was embedded in actual decision tasks. Search committee chairs who completed a 90-minute session and then worked with a trained facilitator during the search were more likely to define evaluation criteria before reviewing files and to use a standardized rating rubric.
