The IEDB's story is one of continuous growth and development, and its impact on the field of immunology will continue to be felt for years to come. As the research community continues to explore the complex interactions between the immune system and pathogens, allergens, and tumors, the IEDB will remain a vital tool, supporting the discovery of new epitopes, the characterization of immune responses, and the development of novel immunotherapies. The IED The Immunome Epitope Database (IEDB) has undergone significant enhancements to bolster its capabilities as a comprehensive, reliable, and user-oriented resource for the immunological and broader biomedical research communities. These developments encompass four primary areas: (i) expansion of the data curation scope to incorporate a wider range of epitope types, (ii) improvements to the data model and ontologies to facilitate enhanced integration with external resources, (iii) updates to the associated prediction and analysis tools, and (iv) plans for future development. 

To identify relevant literature, we employed scheduled PubMed queries that combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for epitopes, antibodies, T cell responses, and MHC ligands, as previously described (Vita et al., 2015). The retrieved abstracts were then ranked using a supervised text-classification approach trained on previously curated and rejected references (Vita et al., 2010). This approach enabled us to prioritize the most relevant articles for manual review by our curators, who possess training in immunology. The curators meticulously reviewed each article to determine whether it contained epitope-specific experimental data, and eligible articles were subsequently curated in full, including figures, tables, and supplementary files.

The standing scope of the IEDB encompasses a broad range of topics, including B cell, T cell, and MHC ligand elution and binding assays in any host species and in various contexts, such as infectious, allergic, autoimmune, and transplant settings (Peters et al., 2005; Salimi et al., 2010). In line with earlier NIAID-directed priorities, we also conducted targeted curation sweeps for specified pathogens and disease categories, including the NIAID Category A–C priority pathogens, allergens, and a defined set of autoantigens. For each article, our curators recorded a comprehensive set of data, including the epitope structure and source antigen and organism, the host and its immunization or exposure history, the assay type and readout, the effector cell or antibody characteristics, and the restricting MHC molecule where relevant.

Each epitope was linked to its source molecule through UniProt (UniProt Consortium, 2017) or NCBI Protein records, ensuring seamless integration with external resources. In cases where a defined epitope structure was not reported, we recorded the data as a non-peptidic or discontinuous epitope using ChEBI identifiers or, for conformational B cell epitopes, residue positions on a Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure (Berman et al., 2000). Peptide-MHC binding measurements were captured as IC50 or KD values (nM) or as qualitative categories (positive-high, positive-intermediate, positive-low, negative), while T cell and B cell assay outcomes were recorded as positive or negative, with the corresponding quantitative measure when available.

To ensure the accuracy and reliability of our curated data, we implemented a quality control process that involved double-checking a random subset of each curator's records, with discrepancies resolved by consensus with senior curators. Data completeness was also assessed against a standard set of required fields, guaranteeing that our data met the highest standards of quality and consistency.

The IEDB's data model is aligned with community ontologies, enabling seamless integration with external resources and facilitating hierarchical queries. Assay types, experimental conditions, and cell types were annotated with the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (Bandrowski et al., 2016) and the Cell Ontology, while diseases were annotated with the Disease Ontology, organisms with NCBI Taxonomy, molecules with ChEBI and the Protein Ontology, and MHC molecules with the MRO ontology and IMGT/HLA nomenclature (Robinson et al., 2015). Ontology terms were imported using the OBO Foundry conventions (Smith et al., 2007) and refreshed on each release cycle, ensuring that our data remained up-to-date and consistent with the latest developments in the field.

The search interface of the IEDB was designed and implemented through an iterative process driven by user feedback, helpdesk requests, usage logs, and periodic usability sessions with external immunologists and bioinformaticians. The web interface was built on a server-side framework with a relational back end and a JavaScript front end, allowing for efficient and flexible querying of our curated data. New functionality was prioritized based on the frequency of related support requests and the need for manual post-processing of exported files. Each feature was thoroughly tested against curated reference queries with known results before release, ensuring that our tools met the highest standards of performance and reliability.

In addition to its comprehensive data curation and search capabilities, the IEDB also provides a range of tools for data export, integration, and reporting. Search results can be exported as comma-separated files containing the complete curated fields for each epitope, assay, and reference, while summary reports are generated dynamically from the query results. These reports include distributions of epitopes by source organism, assay type, MHC restriction, and host, as well as direct links to the underlying records. Cross-references to external resources, such as PubMed, UniProt, GenBank, PDB, and IMGT/HLA, are also provided, facilitating seamless integration with other resources and tools.

The IEDB Analysis Resource provides a suite of predictive and analytical tools that operate on curated data and user-supplied sequences (Kim et al., 2012). For MHC class I binding, we offer a range of methods, including artificial neural network, stabilized matrix method (Peters and Sette, 2005), and NetMHCpan-based methods (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017), as well as a consensus approach. For MHC class II, we provide consensus methods that combine the SMM-align, NN-align, combinatorial library, and structure-based predictors (Wang et al., 2008), along with NetMHCIIpan (Andreatta and Nielsen, 2016). Linear and discontinuous B cell epitope prediction relies on BepiPred and DiscoTope (Larsen et al., 2006; Kringelum et al., 2012), providing a comprehensive set of tools for epitope analysis and prediction.

The performance of our tools was evaluated through automated benchmarking against newly curated data that were not available during method training, using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and Spearman rank correlation for quantitative measurements (Trolle et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014). Binding was classified as positive at an IC50 threshold of 500 nM unless otherwise specified, and epitope conservancy across sequence sets was calculated as the fraction of sequences containing an epitope at a user-defined identity threshold. Epitope clustering was performed using a greedy algorithm that assigns peptides to the cluster of the longest or most representative sequence, with a minimum sequence identity threshold between 70% and 100%. Population coverage was estimated by combining HLA allele frequencies from published studies, providing a comprehensive framework for epitope analysis and prediction.

In conclusion, the IEDB has undergone significant enhancements to its data curation, search interface, and analysis tools, cementing its position as a leading resource for the immunological and broader biomedical research communities. Our ongoing efforts to expand the data curation scope, improve the data model and ontologies, and develop new tools and features will ensure that the IEDB remains a comprehensive, reliable, and user-oriented resource for years to come. The analysis of population data in conjunction with each epitope's set of restricting alleles is predicated on the assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and independent loci, as previously described by Bui et al. in 2006. To better understand the composition and growth of the database, we computed summary statistics and conducted statistical analyses directly from the production database at a fixed release date. This involved counting distinct epitope structures, curated references, and assay records, which were then stratified by various categories, including assay category (e.g., B cell, T cell, MHC binding, MHC ligand elution), source taxonomic group, and disease category. Notably, epitopes were only counted once per distinct structure, regardless of the number of assays or references that reported them, whereas assays were counted as individual records, and each reference was counted only once. 

To estimate growth over time, we compared counts between consecutive releases, revealing a significant increase in the number of curated references and epitope-associated assays. The proportions of positive assays were calculated per category, accompanied by exact binomial 95% confidence intervals, which allowed for a more nuanced understanding of the data. Furthermore, differences between proportions were assessed using chi-square tests, while continuous quantities, such as binding affinities, were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests due to their non-normal distributions. Prior to correlation analysis, binding affinity values were log-transformed to ensure more accurate results. All tests were two-sided, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05, and were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure when multiple comparisons were performed. The analyses were carried out using a combination of Python (SciPy and pandas) and R, which provided a robust framework for data analysis. 

The Immunome Epitope Database (IEDB) is freely accessible at www.iedb.org, and all data and tools described here can be used without registration. The full dataset is available for bulk download under open-access terms, and user support is available through the website help desk. As of the 2018 release, the IEDB contained curated data from approximately 20,000 references, representing more than 1.5 million experiments that characterized roughly 600,000 unique peptidic and non-peptidic epitopes, as previously reported by Vita et al. in 2015. A comparison with the 2014 release revealed a notable increase in the number of curated references (about 28%) and the number of epitope-associated assays (nearly 40%), with the majority of this growth stemming from T cell and MHC ligand data. 

The distribution of assay records was notable, with MHC binding and elution assays together accounting for about 1.2 million records, T cell assays for about 400,000, and B cell and antibody assays for about 350,000. Antibody data remained the most heterogeneous in format, reflecting the variety of epitope definitions, which ranged from linear peptides to discontinuous conformational residues. The source organism category revealed that infectious disease epitopes remained the largest category, with epitopes from viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotic parasites making up about 70% of unique epitopes. Specifically, HIV-1, hepatitis C virus, influenza A virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Plasmodium falciparum each contributed more than 10,000 curated epitopes. 

In contrast, epitopes from allergens, autoantigens, and transplant-related antigens made up about 9%, 11%, and 2% of the database, respectively. Human was the most common host, accounting for about 60% of records, followed by mouse (about 25%), and non-human primates, chimpanzees, and other species making up the remainder. The most frequently characterized HLA class I alleles were HLA-A02:01, HLA-B07:02, and HLA-A01:01, with the 100 most-studied alleles accounting for more than 85% of class I binding assays. This highlights the limited coverage of less common alleles, which remains a challenge in the field. 

A major focus of the recent curation effort was tumor-associated antigens and neoepitopes, in collaboration with cancer immunotherapy groups. Since the 2015 update, we have curated more than 1,000 additional references on cancer immunology, adding approximately 9,000 unique cancer-related epitopes and bringing the cancer subset to more than 15% of all T cell epitope entries. Within this subset, melanoma antigens such as MART-1, gp100, and NY-ESO-1 had the most extensive characterization. We also curated a growing body of patient-specific neoepitopes identified by exome sequencing and mass spectrometry, including both mutated epitopes and their wild-type counterparts. 

Newly introduced curation fields now record whether an epitope arises from a somatic mutation and capture the assay context, such as tetramer staining, ELISPOT, or cytotoxicity, in a form that can be searched. In response to user feedback and web usage analysis, which showed that the original search interface was difficult to use for researchers who needed summaries rather than record lists, we redesigned the main search page to give access to more than 40 searchable fields. A new result view groups records by epitope, assay, or reference, significantly cutting the time needed to navigate large result sets. 

In a usability evaluation with internal and external volunteers, the median time to retrieve the T cell epitopes for a defined pathogen and HLA restriction fell from about 4 minutes with the earlier interface to under 90 seconds with the redesigned one. Result tables can now be exported to Excel or CSV with user-selected columns, and a search can be saved as a URL for sharing and reproducibility. We also introduced a "Reports" function that generates graphical summaries of the results of any query, which has been well-received by the community. 

For example, a query for human T cell epitopes from influenza A virus returns about 3,000 epitopes in under a minute, with the report showing that these are concentrated in a small number of proteins, namely nucleoprotein, matrix protein 1, and hemagglutinin, which together account for more than half of the epitopes. The ImmunomeBrowser tool, which maps epitope positivity onto antigen sequences, was expanded to cover antibody and MHC ligand data in addition to T cell data. For a given antigen, it computes the response frequency score (RFscore) across the tested subjects, with corrections for sample size, and can also be restricted to specific HLA alleles. 

When applied to a data set of about 1,200 curated dengue virus T cell assays, it identified NS3 and NS5 as the most immunodominant proteins in human subjects, in agreement with the original studies. The Epitope Cluster Analysis tool was upgraded to support clustering by sequence identity thresholds from 50% to 100% through a web interface, which has been used to reduce redundancy in data sets. For instance, it was used to condense a set of about 5,000 HIV-1 epitopes to roughly 2,300 clusters, demonstrating its utility in streamlining epitope analysis. These improvements to the IEDB have significantly enhanced its functionality and usability, providing researchers with a more efficient and effective means of exploring and analyzing immunological data. The Immunome Epitope Database (IEDB) has undergone significant updates to enhance its predictive capabilities and usability. Notably, the IEDB Analysis Resource now boasts 20 tools for predicting and analyzing epitopes, with a particular focus on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II binding predictions. The incorporation of NetMHCpan 4.0, trained on both binding affinity and eluted ligand mass spectrometry data, has improved the accuracy of MHC class I binding predictions. In a benchmarking study utilizing newly curated T cell and ligand data, the ligand-trained version of NetMHCpan 4.0 achieved an impressive average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94 for eluted ligands, outperforming the previous affinity-only version, which had an AUC of 0.91.

In addition to these updates, the consensus method for MHC class II binding predictions has been refreshed with new training sets, resulting in a substantial increase in the number of alleles with available predictions. Specifically, the number of alleles with predictions has risen to over 5,000 for class I and approximately 1,000 for class II, largely due to the implementation of pan-specific methods. Furthermore, an MHC class II binding prediction benchmark has been introduced, which is updated automatically with weekly data releases, enabling methods developers to compare tools on previously unpublished data.

The IEDB Analysis Resource has proven to be a highly utilized tool, with over 150,000 prediction jobs served in the most recent annual period, originating from more than 15,000 unique users across over 90 countries. Notably, approximately 25% of these jobs were submitted through the REST API or downloadable command-line versions, highlighting the resource's versatility and accessibility.

To enhance the utility of antibody epitope data, we have established links between IEDB B cell epitope records and three-dimensional structures in the Protein Data Bank. This integration has resulted in the cross-referencing of approximately 1,900 antibody-antigen complexes, with contact residues derived from the structure and displayed on the epitope page. Moreover, we have strengthened links to UniProt, NCBI Taxonomy, and the Ontology of Biomedical Investigations, leading to the annotation of over 95% of epitopes with a standardized source antigen identifier. The full database is also available as monthly downloadable XML and CSV files, which have seen a significant increase in downloads of around 60% over the past two years, suggesting growing use in large-scale computational studies.

As the IEDB has been publicly accessible for over a decade, our focus has shifted from accumulating data to making this complex body of data usable. The curation of the epitope literature has reached a scale where the primary bottleneck is no longer the availability of records but rather the ability of users to formulate precise queries, interpret heterogeneous results, and compare them across experimental contexts. To address this challenge, we have introduced improvements to query and reporting functionality, aimed at enabling investigators to move from broad questions to defensible, reproducible subsets of records without requiring specialist knowledge of the underlying data model.

A crucial aspect of the IEDB is its design as a repository of experimental observations, rather than consensus conclusions. Each record is tied to a specific assay, host, disease state, and, increasingly, a specific MHC restriction, preserving the provenance of every claim and allowing users to apply their own stringency. This approach also acknowledges that apparent contradictions, such as the same peptide being reported as both immunogenic and non-immunogenic, often reflect real differences in assay sensitivity, donor selection, or MHC background rather than curation errors. Consequently, our reporting tools prioritize transparent summaries, exposing the number of assays, subjects, and references underlying each statement, over single-valued annotations.

The scope of the IEDB is both a strength and a limitation. The database's coverage across pathogens, allergens, autoantigens, and transplant antigens, as well as across antibody, T cell, and MHC binding contexts, enables cross-disease comparisons that are otherwise difficult, including systematic analyses of the features distinguishing immunodominant from subdominant determinants. However, the distribution of data is far from uniform, with records concentrated on a limited number of well-studied organisms and a small set of common HLA alleles, mostly prevalent in populations of European descent. As a result, analyses that aggregate across the database can inherit these biases, and estimates of population coverage, as well as the performance of predictive tools trained on these data, may be less reliable for underrepresented alleles and emerging or neglected pathogens.

The relationship between the IEDB and prediction methods is also noteworthy. The database underpins the training and evaluation of widely used tools for MHC binding and, more recently, for T cell immunogenicity and B cell epitope prediction. The continuing growth of quantitative binding data has improved the accuracy of these predictors, particularly for alleles with initially sparse data. Nevertheless, the field's most pressing problem is no longer whether a peptide can bind an MHC molecule but whether it will be presented, recognized by a T cell repertoire, and elicit a functional response. For these questions, the available data are scarcer, noisier, and less standardized, with negative results, essential for learning discriminating features, being comparatively underreported in the literature and therefore in the database.

Several limitations of the present approach should be acknowledged. Manual curation, although yielding a high level of accuracy and contextual detail, is resource-intensive and cannot keep pace with the growth of the literature without prioritization. Our curation therefore focuses on defined categories of interest, and records outside those categories, or in publications where the data are not readily extractable, may not be included. Furthermore, the IEDB's design and implementation are not without challenges, and we recognize the need for ongoing improvements to ensure the database remains a valuable resource for the scientific community.

The social and economic factors that shape population health and health inequalities are well-established, with income, housing, employment, education, social connectedness, and the physical environment all playing a significant role (Dahlgren & Whitehead 1991; Marmot 2010). In primary care, where most people first seek help for health concerns, many patients present with problems that are rooted in social, emotional, or practical difficulties rather than clinical disease. General practitioners in the UK, for instance, report that a substantial proportion of their consultations are driven by non-clinical needs, such as loneliness, debt, housing difficulties, or unemployment (Torjesen 2016; Polley et al. 2017). These consultations can be time-consuming and often result in prescribing or onward referral that fails to address the underlying issue.

As health systems grapple with the challenges posed by ageing populations and rising numbers of people with long-term conditions, there is a growing interest in approaches that connect patients with sources of support outside the healthcare system (Naylor et al. 2016). One such approach is social prescribing (SP), which enables health professionals in primary care to refer patients with non-clinical needs to local, non-clinical services and activities, typically provided by community, voluntary, and social enterprise organisations (Friedli & Watson 2004; Brandling & House 2009; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Examples of these services include befriending schemes, arts and exercise programmes, volunteering opportunities, gardening groups, and welfare, debt, and employment advice. In many models, patients are not referred directly to the activity, but rather to a "navigator," "link worker," or "community connector," who assesses their needs, helps them identify goals, and supports them in accessing appropriate community resources (Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015; Polley et al. 2017).

SP is not just a referral pathway, but an attempt to build partnerships between the health and social sectors to address the wider determinants of health in a more coordinated way. As a result, policy interest in SP has grown, with national strategy documents in England, Scotland, and Wales promoting its use, and a rapid expansion of link worker roles planned within primary care networks (NHS England 2016). Despite this momentum, the evidence base for SP remains limited, with several systematic and scoping reviews highlighting methodological weaknesses in primary studies, including the absence of control groups, small samples, high attrition, short follow-up, and inconsistent outcome measurement (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Mossabir et al. 2015; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Some evaluations have reported improvements in psychological well-being, self-reported health, social connectedness, and reductions in healthcare utilisation (Dayson & Bashir 2014; Cawston 2011), but the reliability of these findings is uncertain, and reviews have generally concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether SP is effective or cost-effective (Bickerdike et al. 2017).

A further challenge is the heterogeneity of SP services, which differ in their aims, target populations, referral routes, the presence and role of a navigator, and the range and quality of community activities available (Husk et al. 2016; Bickerdike et al. 2017). This heterogeneity complicates the interpretation of outcomes and the transfer of lessons across settings. Moreover, whether an SP service achieves its intended effects depends not only on what the intervention is, but also on how it is implemented and delivered. Complex interventions that cut across organisational boundaries are shaped by contextual factors, such as leadership, funding arrangements, workforce stability, inter-organisational relationships, and the readiness of the settings in which they are introduced (Greenhalgh et al. 2004; Damschroder et al. 2009). Partnerships between general practices and small third-sector organisations may be particularly vulnerable to these influences, given the differences in culture, governance, resources, and professional language, as well as the often-precarious funding arrangements of voluntary organisations.

Weak implementation can undermine an otherwise promising intervention, and null findings in effectiveness studies may reflect implementation failure rather than inherent ineffectiveness. Conversely, understanding the conditions under which SP services are successfully established and sustained could help explain variation in reported outcomes and inform the design of future services and evaluations. Existing syntheses have paid limited attention to these questions, with most reviews focusing on outcomes and implementation issues treated as secondary findings or described only in relation to individual evaluations (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). A realist review protocol has set out to explore what works, for whom, and in what circumstances (Husk et al. 2016), but to our knowledge, no systematic review has specifically collated and synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services.

This review aims to address this gap by identifying and synthesising the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services based in general practice and involving a navigator. We restricted the scope to this model for two reasons: first, the presence of a navigator is a defining feature of many contemporary SP services and represents the model most prominent in current policy; second, restricting the scope to a more clearly specified service model allowed a more coherent synthesis than would have been possible across the full range of loosely related referral schemes. By focusing on implementation and delivery, we aimed to identify the modifiable factors that decision-makers can influence, rather than outcomes that may not be directly actionable without an understanding of the mechanisms and contexts that produce them.

This review makes three key contributions. First, it provides the first systematic synthesis of barriers and facilitators to implementing and delivering navigator-based SP services in general practice, drawing on a broad search of published and grey literature. Second, it offers a nuanced understanding of the complex factors that shape the implementation and delivery of SP services, highlighting the importance of contextual factors, such as leadership, funding arrangements, and inter-organisational relationships. Third, it provides guidance for commissioners, service managers, and providers who are currently making decisions about how to establish and scale up SP services, with little consolidated guidance on likely challenges and enabling conditions. By shedding light on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, this review aims to inform the development of more effective and sustainable SP services that can improve the health and well-being of patients and communities. This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services, with a focus on identifying the key factors that influence their success. To achieve this, we employed a three-pronged approach. Firstly, we conducted a thorough search of the literature to identify all relevant studies, regardless of their design or methodology. This involved searching multiple electronic databases, as well as scouring the grey literature and consulting with experts in the field. Secondly, we appraised the methodological quality of the included studies using a tool specifically designed for assessing the quality of mixed-methods research. This enabled us to transparently evaluate the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn from the available evidence and highlight any shortcomings in the reporting of SP evaluations. Thirdly, we translated the findings into practical considerations that can inform the planning and delivery of future SP services, while also identifying priorities for further research on the implementation of SP.

In terms of design and reporting, our review followed the principles outlined by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) for undertaking systematic reviews in healthcare, and we reported our findings in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. Our review protocol was developed a priori and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), ensuring that our approach was systematic and transparent. Given the complexity of SP services and the diversity of study designs and outcomes, we opted for a narrative synthesis using thematic analysis rather than statistical pooling. This approach allowed us to integrate the findings from a wide range of studies and identify key themes and patterns that can inform the implementation and delivery of SP services.

For the purposes of this review, we defined Social Prescribing (SP) as a service based in or linked to general practice, through which patients with predominantly non-clinical needs are referred to a navigator or link worker. The navigator assesses the patient's needs and connects them to local non-clinical services and activities, typically provided by the third sector. We excluded studies that did not involve a navigator or link worker, such as direct referral by a clinician to a single activity without a navigation or assessment step.

Our eligibility criteria were structured around the population, intervention, context, and outcomes of interest. We included studies of any design (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods) that reported factors, experiences, or perceptions relating to the implementation or delivery of SP services. Relevant participants included commissioners, managers, general practitioners, and other practice staff, navigators, third-sector providers, and patients. We were interested in identifying barriers and facilitators to implementation, as well as the organisational and contextual determinants of SP services. As such, studies were not required to report clinical effectiveness outcomes, and we included peer-reviewed articles and grey literature, provided they contained primary data and a sufficiently described methodology.

Our search strategy involved searching eleven electronic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, using a combination of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary related to social prescribing and primary care. We deliberately did not apply filters for study design to maximise sensitivity and ensure that we captured all relevant studies, regardless of their methodology. In addition to searching electronic databases, we also searched the grey literature using OpenGrey and consulted the websites of relevant organisations, such as the King's Fund and the Health Foundation. We contacted experts in the field and examined the reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic reviews to identify any additional studies that may have been missed.

Once we had identified all relevant studies, we imported the records into reference management software and removed duplicates. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, and full texts of potentially relevant records were obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. We recorded the reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage and assessed inter-rater agreement at the title and abstract screening stage using Cohen's kappa.

To extract data from the included studies, we developed a standardised data extraction form, which was piloted on two studies and refined before use. One reviewer extracted data from each included study, and a second reviewer checked the extracted data for accuracy and completeness. We collected information on the author, year, and country of the study, as well as the study aims, design, setting, and funding. We also extracted information on the description of the SP service, participant characteristics, sample size, data collection and analysis methods, and reported barriers and facilitators to implementation and delivery.

To appraise the methodological quality of the included studies, we used the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), Version 2011. This tool permits the appraisal of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods designs within a single framework, making it well-suited to our review. Two reviewers independently rated the relevant criteria for each study, and scores were expressed as the percentage of criteria met. For mixed-methods studies, the overall score was taken as the lowest score across the qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods components. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and we used the quality assessment to describe the strengths and limitations of the available evidence, rather than as a criterion for exclusion.

Overall, our review provides a comprehensive overview of the implementation and delivery of SP services, highlighting the key factors that influence their success and identifying priorities for further research. By synthesising the findings from a wide range of studies, we aim to inform the planning and delivery of future SP services, ultimately improving the health and wellbeing of patients with non-clinical needs. Our approach to data analysis was iterative and reflexive, with the process of exclusion informing our interpretation of the findings and our confidence in each emerging theme. Given the heterogeneity of study designs, settings, and outcomes, we opted for a narrative synthesis, guided by the principles outlined by Popay and colleagues (2013) and the thematic analysis approach described by Thomas and Harden (2008) for systematic reviews of qualitative and mixed evidence. This involved a three-stage process. Initially, we immersed ourselves in the text labelled as results or findings in each study, including participant quotations, and coded the data line by line, applying codes inductively to segments that described factors facilitating or impeding the implementation or delivery of social prescribing (SP) services. 

As we compared codes across studies, we grouped them according to conceptual similarity and organised them into descriptive themes, which we then classified as facilitators, barriers, or both. Through iterative discussions among the review team, we refined these descriptive themes into higher-order analytical themes, considering the relationships between themes and their possible interpretation in the context of implementation processes. To ensure the consistency of our coding framework, one reviewer used NVivo software to code the data, while a second reviewer independently coded a subset of the studies (approximately one third) and we discussed and resolved any differences in interpretation. The final themes were agreed upon by all authors. 

To assess the robustness of our synthesis, we examined whether the themes were supported by studies of higher and lower methodological quality and noted instances where a theme relied on a single study or on studies scoring 25% or lower on the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). We also summarised quantitative data on implementation, such as referral numbers or staff turnover, descriptively, using these data to contextualise the thematic findings without formal statistical testing. As our review relied on published and publicly available sources, ethical approval was not required. 

The electronic searches of eleven databases yielded 4,873 records, and grey literature searching and reference list checking identified a further 126 records. After removing duplicates, we screened 3,785 unique records by title and abstract, excluding 3,689 as clearly irrelevant. We then assessed the full texts of 96 records for eligibility, excluding 88 studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria: 31 did not describe a service involving a navigator, 24 were not based in or linked to general practice, 19 did not report factors related to implementation or delivery, 9 were commentaries or editorials without empirical data, and 5 were duplicate reports of included studies. 

Eight studies, reported in eight documents, met all inclusion criteria and were included in the synthesis (Grant et al., 2000; Grayer et al., 2008; Friedli et al., 2012; Dayson & Bashir, 2014; Bertotti et al., 2015; Kimberlee, 2015; Moffatt et al., 2017; Rempel et al., 2017). The agreement between the two reviewers at the full-text stage was substantial (κ = 0.78). The characteristics of the included studies were diverse: all eight studies were conducted in the United Kingdom, with five in England, two in Scotland, and one across multiple sites in England and Wales. Publication dates ranged from 2000 to 2017, with six of the eight studies (75%) published after 2012. 

Four studies were published in peer-reviewed journals, and four were evaluation reports identified through the grey literature. The study designs were also varied, with three using a mixed-methods design, three being qualitative, and two being quantitative descriptive studies. The sample sizes for the qualitative components ranged from 8 to 46 participants (median 21), comprising navigators, general practitioners (GPs), practice managers, commissioners, and representatives of voluntary sector organisations. The quantitative components included between 87 and 1,003 referred patients (median 304). The services were described under different labels, including "social prescribing," "community referral," "Well-being Service," and "Link Worker programme." The number of participating general practices per service ranged from 1 to 23. 

Navigators were employed by voluntary sector organisations in five services, by the National Health Service in two, and by a joint arrangement in one. Seven of the eight studies explicitly aimed to evaluate outcomes as well as process, but only three provided a dedicated process or implementation evaluation. The methodological quality of the included studies, as assessed using the MMAT (version 2011), was variable, with a median quality score of 25% (range 0–75%). Two studies scored 0%, three scored 25%, two scored 50%, and one scored 75%. No study met all four criteria applicable to its design. 

Among the six studies with a qualitative component, four (67%) clearly described how findings were derived from the data, and only two (33%) considered the relationship between researchers and participants. Of the five studies with a quantitative component, none reported a sampling strategy that was clearly representative of the target population, and only one reported a response rate above 60%. Among the three mixed-methods studies, none adequately justified the use of a mixed-methods design or described the integration of qualitative and quantitative findings. In line with the review protocol, no study was excluded on the basis of quality. 

Our thematic analysis of the extracted data produced nine themes relating to factors that facilitate and hinder implementation and delivery. These themes were: implementation approach; legal agreements; leadership, management, and organisation; staff turnover; staff engagement; relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders; characteristics of general practices; local infrastructure; and funding. The most frequently reported theme was relationships and communication, which featured in seven of the eight studies (88%), followed by leadership, management, and organisation (n = 6; 75%), characteristics of general practices (n = 5; 63%), and local infrastructure (n = 5; 63%). Staff turnover and legal agreements were each reported in only two studies (25%). 

Four studies (50%) described the approach taken to implementation, with services introduced incrementally, beginning with a small number of pilot practices before expanding, reported as easier to adapt to local circumstances (Dayson & Bashir, 2014; Bertotti et al., 2015). Conversely, three studies reported that short lead-in times and rapid roll-out resulted in unclear referral pathways, inconsistent use of referral forms, and low referral rates in the first six months (Friedli et al., 2012; Kimberlee, 2015; Rempel et al., 2017). In one service, the proportion of practices actively referring rose from 41% to 71% over a period of 12 months, highlighting the potential for services to develop and improve over time. 

The findings of our review highlight the complexity and variability of social prescribing services, with multiple factors influencing their implementation and delivery. Our study provides insights into the key themes that facilitate and hinder the implementation of social prescribing services, including the importance of relationships and communication, leadership, management, and organisation, and the characteristics of general practices. These findings have implications for the development and delivery of social prescribing services, highlighting the need for a tailored and flexible approach that takes into account the local context and the needs of the target population. By examining the factors that facilitate and hinder implementation, our review aims to inform the development of effective social prescribing services that can improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities. 

Furthermore, our study underscores the importance of considering the methodological quality of the included studies and the potential limitations of the review. The variable quality of the included studies, particularly in terms of the sampling strategy and response rate, may have impacted the robustness of the findings. However, by using a systematic and transparent approach to data extraction and synthesis, we aimed to minimise the risk of bias and ensure the reliability of the results. Our review provides a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on social prescribing services, highlighting the need for further research on the implementation and delivery of these services.

The findings of our study have implications for the development and delivery of social prescribing services, highlighting the need for a tailored and flexible approach that takes into account the local context and the needs of the target population. By examining the factors that facilitate and hinder implementation, our review aims to inform the development of effective social prescribing services that can improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities. Future research should focus on evaluating the effectiveness of social prescribing services, exploring the experiences of patients and navigators, and examining the impact of different implementation approaches on service outcomes. The implementation of Social Prescribing (SP) services in general practice settings has garnered significant attention in recent years, with a growing body of research highlighting the complexities and challenges involved. A notable example of this is the phased relaunch of SP services, which has been shown to yield retention rates of up to 78% when accompanied by dedicated engagement events (Bertotti et al., 2015). Furthermore, the presence of legal agreements, such as data-sharing agreements and information governance protocols, has been identified as a crucial factor in facilitating feedback to GPs on patient progress, with their absence or protracted negotiation often resulting in delayed service start-up (Dayson and Bashir, 2014; Moffatt et al., 2017).

In addition to these structural factors, the importance of strong leadership and clear management structures cannot be overstated. Services that have a named project lead, regular steering group meetings, and defined lines of accountability have been found to be more resilient to change (Grayer et al., 2008; Bertotti et al., 2015). The role of navigators, in particular, has emerged as pivotal in mitigating isolation and role ambiguity, with clinical and managerial supervision, as well as peer support meetings, serving as essential components of their support system (Friedli et al., 2012; Rempel et al., 2017). However, staff turnover has been identified as a significant barrier, with the loss of navigators often interrupting relationships with practices and causing patient waiting lists to lengthen (Friedli et al., 2012; Rempel et al., 2017).

The engagement of practice staff is also a critical factor, with those who understand the purpose of the service and receive regular feedback being more likely to refer patients (Dayson and Bashir, 2014). Conversely, GP scepticism about the evidence base, concerns about duplication of existing services, and perceived lack of time to refer have been cited as barriers (Dayson and Bashir, 2014). Referral rates have been found to vary markedly between practices within the same service, ranging from 0.4 to 11.2 referrals per 1,000 registered patients over 12 months (Dayson and Bashir, 2014).

The theme of relationships and communication has emerged as a dominant factor in the implementation of SP services. Trusting, well-established relationships between navigators, general practice staff, and voluntary sector providers have been found to facilitate delivery, with co-location of navigators within practices being particularly beneficial (Grayer et al., 2008; Bertotti et al., 2015). Face-to-face feedback loops, shared case review meetings, and a single point of contact at each provider have also been identified as facilitators. However, barriers such as poor communication on referral outcomes, mismatched expectations about the navigator role, and differences in organisational culture between the medical and voluntary sectors have been reported (Dayson and Bashir, 2014; Moffatt et al., 2017).

Communication with patients has been found to be less frequently addressed, although clear explanation of the service by the referring clinician has been associated with higher uptake (Kimberlee, 2015). The characteristics of general practices have also been identified as influencing implementation, with larger practices with multidisciplinary teams, established links to community organisations, and prior experience of quality improvement projects being more receptive (Brandling and House, 2009). Small practices, on the other hand, have reported insufficient space for navigators and limited administrative capacity (Friedli et al., 2012).

The local infrastructure has also emerged as a critical factor, with the availability of a diverse, accessible third-sector offer facilitating appropriate referral (Husk et al., 2016). However, limited capacity, waiting lists for activities, transport difficulties in rural areas, and short-term funding of voluntary organisations have been identified as barriers (Polley et al., 2017). Funding insecurity, typically 12-month contracts, has been linked to difficulties in retaining staff and sustaining partnerships (Husk et al., 2016).

This systematic review has synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services based in general practice and involving a navigator. Despite the limited evidence base, with most studies being of low methodological quality, a coherent set of influences has emerged. These relate to the implementation approach, legal agreements, leadership, management and organisation, staff turnover, staff engagement, relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders, characteristics of general practices, and the local infrastructure.

Two features of the findings stand out. Firstly, most of these determinants operate at the level of organisational and inter-organisational processes rather than at the level of the individual patient or intervention. Secondly, the review found few published studies that examined implementation as a primary objective. The prominence of relationships, communication, and leadership is consistent with the wider literature on integrated and cross-sector working (Damschroder et al., 2009; Greenhalgh et al., 2004). SP is a clear example of such an intervention, as it depends on collaboration between sectors that differ in funding, culture, accountability, and professional language.

The reliance on time-limited contracts and the lack of robust infrastructure, workforce planning, and evaluation have been identified as significant concerns (Husk et al., 2016; Polley et al., 2017). The dependence of SP on a viable local third sector is a further structural vulnerability, with the scarcity, under-resourcing, or inability of community organisations to absorb additional referrals constraining the value of the navigator's work (Kimberlee, 2015). In a period of austerity and reductions in voluntary sector funding, this raises the question of whether SP can deliver its intended benefits without parallel investment in the underlying infrastructure and workforce.

The notion that the loss of one sense can be offset by the enhancement of others has a long history, dating back to philosophical and early psychological thought. This idea is deeply ingrained in popular culture, where blind individuals are often perceived as having a more acute sense of smell, touch, or hearing, which enables them to navigate a world primarily designed for the sighted. In the context of olfaction, this notion is reinforced by anecdotal reports from blind individuals themselves, who frequently rely on their sense of smell to recognize people, locate places, and evaluate food and objects (Wakefield, Homewood, & Taylor, 2004). Olfaction is a particularly intriguing case, as it is a chemical sense that has a relatively weak link to the visual system in everyday behavior, yet is closely tied to cognition, emotion, and memory (Herz & Engen, 1996). The theoretical foundation for expecting compensatory adaptations in olfaction lies in the neuroplasticity literature, which has shown that in congenitally and early blind individuals, the occipital cortex is not simply silent, but is instead recruited for a range of non-visual functions, including Braille reading, auditory localization, speech comprehension, and verbal memory (Sadato et al., 1996; Röder et al., 2002; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny, 2017).

Behavioral studies have often reported superior performance in blind individuals on tasks such as pitch discrimination, sound localization, and tactile acuity, although these findings are not uniform and depend on task demands and the age at which vision was lost (Collignon, Voss, Lassonde, & Lepore, 2009; Wan, Wood, Reutens, & Wilson, 2010). Moreover, neuroimaging studies have suggested that olfactory stimulation may engage regions beyond the classical olfactory network in blind individuals, such as the occipital areas, which are typically associated with visual processing (Kupers et al., 2011; Araneda et al., 2016). These results indicate that cross-modal reorganization could, in principle, have consequences for olfactory perception. However, the behavioral evidence for enhanced olfactory abilities in blind individuals is far less consistent.

Olfactory function is a complex and multifaceted construct, comprising several partly separable components, including lower-level, sensory-driven abilities such as detection threshold and odor discrimination, as well as higher-order abilities that involve cognitive and linguistic processes, such as cued and free odor identification (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997). Performance on these tasks depends on a range of factors, including semantic memory, verbal ability, and attention, in addition to sensory sensitivity (Cain, 1979; Larsson, 1997). It is possible that blindness could selectively affect some of these components, for example, by improving higher-order processing through increased attention to olfactory cues, without altering peripheral sensitivity.

Empirical findings, however, do not clearly support either a general or a selective enhancement of olfactory abilities in blind individuals. Several studies have reported lower olfactory thresholds in blind compared to sighted participants (Cuevas, Plaza, Rombaux, De Volder, & Renier, 2009; Beaulieu-Lefebvre, Schneider, Kupers, & Ptito, 2011), while others have found no difference (Smith, Doty, Burlingame, & McKeown, 1993; Rosenbluth, Grossman, & Kaitz, 2000) or even poorer performance in blind individuals (Wakefield et al., 2004). Similarly, studies of odor discrimination have yielded mixed results, with some reporting an advantage for blind participants (Cuevas et al., 2009) and others reporting equivalent performance (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska, Sorokowski, & Karwowski, 2013). The picture for odor identification is also mixed, with some investigations showing superior free or cued identification in blind participants (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Cuevas et al., 2009), while others have found no group differences (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska et al., 2013).

The heterogeneity in methods used across studies may partly explain these discrepancies. Studies differ in the psychophysical procedure used, the odorants tested, the criteria for sample selection, and the way blindness is characterized. Moreover, many studies have small samples, which limits statistical power and increases the probability that observed effects, whether positive or null, are unreliable (Button et al., 2013). Participant characteristics, such as age and sex, are also a source of uncertainty, as olfactory function declines with age and differs between women and men, with women often outperforming men on several olfactory measures (Doty & Cameron, 2009; Sorokowska et al., 2017). If the age or sex composition of blind and sighted samples differs, or if these factors moderate the effects of sensory deprivation, estimates of group differences could be distorted.

Most importantly, the timing of vision loss may be critical, as plasticity is thought to be greatest during sensitive periods of development, so early or congenitally blind individuals might show larger compensatory effects than those who lose their sight later in life (Voss, Lepore, Gougoux, & Zatorre, 2010; Collignon et al., 2009). Yet, studies of olfaction have often combined early and late blind participants, or have not reported onset in sufficient detail, making it difficult to determine whether the timing of blindness matters. Narrative reviews have summarized parts of this literature (Sorokowska, 2016; Kupers & Ptito, 2014), and they generally conclude that evidence of superior olfaction in blindness is equivocal. However, narrative approaches are vulnerable to selective citation and cannot quantify the magnitude or consistency of effects, nor assess whether the published record is distorted by selective reporting.

Publication bias is a particular concern in this field, as an intriguing and intuitively appealing finding of superior performance in blind people may be more likely to be published than a null result, which would inflate the apparent evidence for compensation (Rothstein, Sutton, & Borenstein, 2005). Meta-analytic methods, on the other hand, allow the combination of effect sizes across studies, the examination of heterogeneity, the testing of moderators, and the application of procedures that detect and adjust for small-study effects (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Duval & Tweedie, 2000). To our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively synthesized the evidence on olfactory abilities in blind individuals across the full range of olfactory functions. The present work therefore provides a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing blind and sighted individuals on four outcomes: odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. By using meta-analytic methods, we aim to provide a more comprehensive and quantitative understanding of the relationship between blindness and olfactory abilities, and to shed light on the mechanisms underlying any potential compensatory effects. Our investigation into the relationship between blindness and olfactory performance was motivated by a fundamental question: does blindness confer an advantage in olfactory abilities, and if so, does this advantage vary between sensory-driven tasks, such as threshold and discrimination, and higher-order tasks, such as identification? To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive meta-analysis, taking care to assess and correct for publication bias, which can significantly influence estimates of effect sizes. Additionally, we performed exploratory moderator analyses to examine whether factors such as participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness (early vs. late) contribute to variability in effect sizes across studies.

This research contributes to the field in three key ways. Firstly, it provides the first comprehensive quantitative estimate of olfactory performance in individuals with blindness, replacing anecdotal summaries with precise effect sizes and confidence intervals. Secondly, it examines whether the published literature supports the notion of compensatory plasticity in olfaction, once publication bias is taken into account. Thirdly, it identifies methodological gaps, such as small sample sizes and inconsistent reporting, that can inform the design of future research on sensory compensation.

Our review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009) and followed recommendations for meta-analysis in the behavioral sciences (Borenstein et al., 2009; Cooper et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria, outcomes, and analytic strategy for the primary analyses were predefined prior to data extraction. The analyses of moderators were exploratory in nature.

To identify relevant articles, we conducted a comprehensive computerized search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO, supplemented by Google Scholar. The search terms combined keywords related to blindness (e.g., blind, visual impairment, visual deprivation) with terms related to olfaction (e.g., olfact, smell, odor, odour, chemosens). We imposed no restrictions on publication year and covered records from database inception until the date of the final search. We also screened the reference lists of all eligible articles and relevant narrative reviews, and searched for conference abstracts and unpublished dissertations to minimize the risk of missing unpublished data. When essential statistics were missing, we contacted corresponding authors via email.

Studies were included in our analysis if they met the following criteria: (a) compared a group of blind participants with a group of sighted controls, (b) assessed at least one of four olfactory outcomes (odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, or free odor identification), (c) used human participants, and (d) reported data sufficient to calculate an effect size. Blindness was defined as congenital or acquired total blindness or severe visual impairment, as described by the original authors. Studies were excluded if they lacked a sighted control group, if participants had additional conditions known to affect olfaction (e.g., neurodegenerative disease, Kallmann syndrome, head trauma, or chronic rhinosinusitis), or if the data were reported only for subjective ratings of odor properties or for olfactory-related tasks that did not map onto the four outcomes.

We defined the four olfactory outcomes as follows: odor threshold tasks estimated the lowest concentration at which an odorant could be detected, typically using a staircase or forced-choice procedure (e.g., Sniffin' Sticks). Discrimination tasks required participants to identify the odd item among three odorants presented in a triangle test. Cued identification required selection of the correct label from a list of alternatives, whereas free identification required participants to name the odor without any response options. Because threshold is generally considered a sensory-driven function and identification a higher-order function dependent on semantic and mnemonic processes (Hummel et al., 1997), we analyzed the four outcomes separately.

When studies reported more than one measure within an outcome (e.g., several odorants or subtests), we averaged them to obtain one effect size per study and comparison. When separate early-blind and late-blind groups were compared with the same sighted group, we handled the shared control group as described below.

Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, who screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third author. Data were extracted using a standardized form, which recorded authors and year, country, sample size per group, mean age, proportion of women, onset of blindness (early/congenital vs. late), olfactory test used, and the statistics necessary to compute effect sizes. Inter-coder agreement was high (Cohen's κ >.90 for categorical variables), and discrepancies were resolved through consensus.

We classified studies as early blind when blindness was congenital or began in early childhood (typically before the age of 5 years, or as defined by the authors), and as late blind otherwise. The effect size was computed as the standardized mean difference, Hedges' g, with positive values indicating better performance in blind than in sighted participants. For threshold tasks, in which lower scores reflect higher sensitivity (in studies reporting concentration), the sign was reversed accordingly. The effect size was calculated using the formula d = (Mblind − Msighted) / SDpooled, with SDpooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + (n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)], and the small-sample correction g = d × [1 − 3 / (4(n₁ + n₂) − 9)]. The sampling variance was calculated as vg = (n₁ + n₂)/(n₁n₂) + g² / (2(n₁ + n₂)) multiplied by the squared correction factor. When only t or F values were reported, they were converted to d using standard formulas (Borenstein et al., 2009). For nonparametric tests, we converted exact p values or z statistics to equivalent effect sizes. When a study contained two blind subgroups compared with one control group, we combined the subgroups into one group (computing pooled means and standard deviations) for the main analyses and treated them separately only in the onset moderator analysis, where the shared control group's sample size was divided between the comparisons to avoid inflating the sample size. When conducting meta-analyses, it is essential to account for the potential issue of double-counting, as highlighted by Higgins and Green (2011). To address this, we employed a random-effects model, which is particularly suitable when the true effects are expected to vary across studies due to differences in samples and procedures. The weighted mean effect was calculated using the formula ĝ = Σ wᵢgᵢ / Σ wᵢ, where wᵢ = 1 / (vᵢ + τ²), and τ² represents the between-study variance. To improve the accuracy of our confidence intervals, we utilized the Knapp-Hartung adjustment, which is particularly useful when dealing with a modest number of studies (Knapp & Hartung, 2003).

To assess heterogeneity, we relied on Cochran's Q, τ², and I² = max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100, and also calculated 95% prediction intervals, following the guidelines outlined by Higgins, Thompson, and Deeks (2003) and IntHout, Ioannidis, Rovers, and Goeman (2016). Furthermore, we examined outlying and influential studies using studentized residuals, Cook's distance, and leave-one-out analyses, as recommended by Viechtbauer and Cheung (2010).

Given the potential for publication bias, we employed several complementary methods to evaluate small-study effects and publication bias, as no single method is universally effective. We visually inspected contour-enhanced funnel plots and tested for funnel asymmetry using Egger's regression test (Egger, Davey Smith, Schneider, & Minder, 1997) and Begg's rank correlation test. Additionally, we applied the trim-and-fill procedure (Duval & Tweedie, 2000) to estimate the number of potentially missing studies and the adjusted effect. We also utilized PET-PEESE meta-regression (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014), which involves regressing the effect size on its standard error or variance, and p-curve analysis (Simonsohn, Nelson, & Simmons, 2014) to evaluate the evidential value of significant results. Notably, we avoided using the Fail-safe N as the primary indicator due to its known limitations (Becker, 2005).

In our moderator analyses, we exploratorily examined three moderators: mean participant age (continuous), proportion of women in the total sample (continuous), and onset of blindness (early vs. late, categorical). For continuous moderators, we used mixed-effects meta-regression, whereas categorical moderators were analyzed through subgroup analyses with a pooled estimate of τ² across subgroups. Moderator tests were conducted using Wald-type tests with the Knapp-Hartung adjustment. It is essential to note that we only analyzed moderators when data were available for at least ten studies (continuous) or at least three studies per subgroup (categorical), and we did not apply corrections for multiple testing, given the exploratory nature of our analysis.

To assess the risk of bias, we used an adapted checklist that covered the clarity of blindness definition, matching of groups on age and sex, control for smoking and nasal health, use of validated olfactory tests, and blinding of the experimenter. Quality scores were used descriptively and in sensitivity analyses. All analyses were performed using R (R Core Team) with the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010), supplemented by the dmetar and weightr packages for ancillary analyses. We set the threshold for statistical significance at α =.05, two-tailed.

Our literature search identified studies comparing olfactory performance in blind and sighted adults, yielding a final sample that covered four olfactory domains. Eighteen studies assessed odor threshold (N = 1227; 590 blind, 637 sighted), 14 studies evaluated odor discrimination (N = 940; 455 blind, 485 sighted), 14 studies examined cued odor identification (N = 968; 468 blind, 500 sighted), and 7 studies investigated free odor identification (N = 443; 224 blind, 219 sighted). It is worth noting that many publications reported more than one olfactory measure, resulting in the same participants contributing to more than one domain-specific analysis. Consequently, each domain was analyzed separately, and no study was included in the same analysis twice. Effects were expressed as Hedges' g (Hedges & Olkin, 1985), with positive values indicating better performance in the blind group. Threshold scores were reversed where lower values indicated greater sensitivity.

For each study, the standardized mean difference was calculated as g = J · (Mblind − Msighted) / SDpooled, with J = 1 − 3/(4(n₁ + n₂ − 2) − 1). Effects were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, as implemented in the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010). Heterogeneity was quantified using Cochran's Q and I² = max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100% (Higgins et al., 2003).

Our analysis of odor threshold revealed a small advantage for blind participants, with an uncorrected random-effects model yielding g = 0.28 (95% CI [0.05, 0.51], z = 2.39, p =.017). However, heterogeneity was substantial (Q(17) = 52.4, p <.001; I² = 68%; τ² = 0.14), with individual effect sizes ranging from g = −0.41 (Smith et al., 1993) to g = 1.02 (Cuevas et al., 2009). Notably, fewer than half of the 18 comparisons were individually significant. Visual inspection of the funnel plot suggested asymmetry, with small studies exhibiting larger positive effects, a finding confirmed by Egger's regression test (intercept = 2.14, p =.018). The trim-and-fill procedure imputed five missing studies on the left side of the funnel, resulting in an adjusted estimate of g = 0.09 (95% CI [−0.15, 0.33]), which does not differ from zero. Leave-one-out analyses demonstrated that the uncorrected estimate was unstable, with g ranging from 0.21 to 0.33, and the lower confidence bound crossing zero in seven of 18 iterations.

In contrast, our analysis of odor discrimination across 14 studies yielded a pooled effect of g = 0.21 (95% CI [−0.04, 0.46], z = 1.64, p =.101), with moderate to high heterogeneity (Q(13) = 33.1, p =.002; I² = 61%; τ² = 0.10). Egger's test indicated funnel plot asymmetry (intercept = 1.87, p =.041), and the trim-and-fill procedure imputed three studies, reducing the estimate to g = 0.07 (95% CI [−0.19, 0.33]). Both the uncorrected and corrected results suggested no reliable difference between blind and sighted participants. Leave-one-out analysis produced estimates between 0.15 and 0.27, none of which were significant.

For cued odor identification, the uncorrected pooled effect across 14 studies was small and significant (g = 0.30, 95% CI [0.07, 0.53], z = 2.56, p =.010), with considerable heterogeneity (Q(13) = 35.8, p <.001; I² = 64%; τ² = 0.12). The largest positive effects emerged from small samples (n < 30 per group). Egger's test again suggested small-study effects (intercept = 2.31, p =.016), and the trim-and-fill procedure imputed four studies, resulting in a corrected estimate of g = 0.17 (95% CI [−0.04, 0.38]). While the uncorrected result indicated a significant advantage for blind participants, the corrected estimate was no longer significant, highlighting the importance of considering potential biases in the analysis.

Our findings underscore the complexity of olfactory perception in blind and sighted individuals, with results varying across different domains of olfaction. The presence of substantial heterogeneity and potential publication bias highlights the need for cautious interpretation of the results. By employing a range of statistical methods to address these issues, we aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between blindness and olfactory performance, acknowledging the limitations and uncertainties inherent in meta-analytic research. The relationship between blindness and olfactory abilities has garnered significant attention, with many studies investigating whether the absence of visual input enhances one's sense of smell. Our meta-analysis aimed to synthesize the existing literature on this topic, examining four distinct domains: odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued identification, and free identification. The uncorrected pooled effects across these domains were uniformly small and positive, ranging from g = 0.21 to g = 0.38, with three of the four domains reaching nominal significance. However, it is essential to note that these effects were also characterized by substantial heterogeneity, which may be indicative of underlying publication biases.

To address this concern, we employed the trim-and-fill method to adjust for potential small-study effects. This correction resulted in a notable reduction in the estimated effects, with the corrected values ranging from g = 0.07 to g = 0.15. Furthermore, the confidence intervals for these corrected estimates included zero, suggesting that the initial findings may have been inflated by publication bias. The funnel plots, which are often used to visually inspect the distribution of study effects, revealed the characteristic asymmetry expected when small studies with positive findings are overrepresented. This pattern is consistent with the presence of publication bias, which can lead to an overestimation of the true effect size.

In an effort to identify potential moderators that could account for the observed heterogeneity, we conducted exploratory analyses examining the impact of mean participant age, proportion of women in the combined sample, and onset of blindness (early vs. late). These analyses were necessarily exploratory, given the limited number of studies in each domain, and the results should be interpreted with caution. The meta-regression analyses revealed that age was unrelated to effect size in all domains, with negligible explanatory power (R² < 4%). Similarly, the proportion of women in the samples did not predict effect sizes in any of the domains. The subgroup comparisons based on the onset of blindness also failed to yield significant differences between early-blind and late-blind participants.

The absence of significant moderator effects suggests that the observed heterogeneity may be attributable to other factors, such as differences in experimental design, stimulus selection, or participant characteristics. However, it is also possible that the true effect size is simply too small to be reliably detected, given the current state of the literature. Our findings are consistent with the notion that compensatory plasticity in blindness may be more pronounced in other sensory modalities, such as audition and touch. The existing literature has consistently demonstrated enhanced pitch discrimination, sound localization, and Braille-related tactile acuity in blind individuals, which are often accompanied by cross-modal recruitment of occipital cortex.

In contrast, the olfactory system appears to be less dependent on visual input for spatial calibration, and the loss of vision may not generate the same functional pressure for compensatory reorganization. While neuroimaging studies have reported structural and functional differences in olfactory-related regions in blind people, our results suggest that these neural differences do not necessarily translate into reliably measurable behavioral advantages. This conclusion is consistent with the idea that the relationship between blindness and olfactory abilities is more complex than previously thought, and that any potential behavioral effects may be too small or too nuanced to be detected using current methodologies.
