We believe that our study provides a valuable contribution to the field of distributed computing and highlights the importance of considering the theoretical The evaluation of our proposed partly stateless, flow-oriented model was designed to provide a comprehensive comparison with existing approaches, specifically a conventional map-shuffle-reduce implementation, namely Hadoop MapReduce 2.7 (Dean & Ghemawat, 2004), and a batch/micro-batch Spark 2.4 baseline (Zaharia et al., 2012). To ensure a rigorous assessment, we included a diverse set of workloads, comprising a sliding-window aggregation, a top-k trending query, and an enrichment join against a slowly changing reference table. These workloads were chosen for their time-dependent nature and the potential for bounding or caching their results, which are crucial aspects of our model.

To facilitate replication and verification of our results, we have made available the code, configurations, and generators used in our experiments. We also included Workload W4 to avoid the selection bias that might arise from only considering favorable cases (2012). Our experimental setup consisted of an eight-node cluster, with each node equipped with 16 vCPUs and 64 GB of RAM. The input data was a replayed trace of approximately 1.2 billion events, totaling around 480 GB, and was processed at a sustained rate of 25,000 events per second. To ensure reliable results, each experiment was run 10 times, with a warm-up period preceding the actual measurement, and the median values are reported, accompanied by 95% confidence intervals where applicable.

One of the primary metrics of interest was end-to-end latency, which revealed significant differences between the systems. For the sliding-window aggregation, the MapReduce implementation exhibited a median latency of 212 seconds [201-224 seconds] from event arrival to result availability. In contrast, Spark, configured with 5-second micro-batches, reduced this latency to 6.8 seconds [6.1-7.5 seconds]. Our proposed flow-oriented model achieved a substantially lower latency of 41 milliseconds [37-46 milliseconds], representing a reduction of roughly 160 times relative to Spark and more than 5,000 times relative to MapReduce. The 99th percentile latency followed a similar pattern, with the proposed model outperforming both Spark and MapReduce. However, the proposed model's tail latency was 2.9 times its median, whereas Spark's was 1.7 times its median. This disparity can be attributed to occasional cache-miss paths, where a partial result had to be rebuilt from the retained log, introducing additional latency.

The top-k query and enrichment join workloads also demonstrated the superiority of our proposed model in terms of latency. For the top-k query, the median latencies were 187 seconds for MapReduce, 5.4 seconds for Spark, and 63 milliseconds for our model. The enrichment join showed median latencies of 164 seconds for MapReduce, 4.1 seconds for Spark, and 28 milliseconds for our model. These results underscore the effectiveness of our approach in minimizing latency across various workloads.

In addition to latency, we examined the throughput and resource efficiency of the systems. Our proposed model sustained a maximum throughput of 1.9 million events per second on the aggregation workload before back-pressure was triggered. In comparison, Spark reached 1.1 million events per second, and MapReduce, treated as an hourly batch job, achieved an effective throughput of 0.31 million events per second. Normalized per core, these correspond to 14,800 events per second per core for our model, 8,600 events per second per core for Spark, and 2,400 events per second per core for MapReduce. Notably, the advantage of our model over Spark decreased as the computational complexity of the aggregation increased. When the aggregation was replaced by a computationally heavy scoring function, requiring approximately 180 microseconds per event, the advantage of our model over Spark fell from 1.7 times to 1.15 times. This observation is consistent with the argument that avoiding coordination is most beneficial when per-record computation is inexpensive (McSherry et al., 2015).

Another critical aspect we investigated was the overhead associated with the shuffle phase, which was the primary source of overhead in the baseline systems. For the 60-minute window, MapReduce transferred 3.7 terabytes of intermediate data over the 24-hour trace, due to the recomputation and re-shuffling of each overlapping window. Spark, utilizing incremental reduce-by-window with inverse functions, moved 410 gigabytes. In contrast, our proposed model exchanged only 38 gigabytes, representing a reduction of 99% relative to MapReduce and 91% relative to Spark. This significant reduction stems from keeping keyed partial aggregates local to the operator and forwarding only deltas downstream. Furthermore, the resident operator state in our model averaged 9.4 gigabytes across the cluster, equivalent to 1.2 gigabytes per node, compared to 31 gigabytes for Spark, whose lineage and block retention are costly (Zaharia et al., 2012). Disk writes also decreased substantially, with 2.1 terabytes for MapReduce, 640 gigabytes for Spark, and 55 gigabytes for our model, the latter arising solely from periodic checkpoints taken every 30 seconds.

To further understand the impact of cacheability on the performance of our model, we varied the fraction of queries answerable from retained partial results by perturbing the late-arrival and key-skew parameters of the trace. Our results showed that when 95% of updates were resolvable from cache, the median latency advantage of our model over Spark was 148 times. This advantage decreased to 41 times at 70%, 7.6 times at 40%, and 1.3 times at 10%. Interestingly, below a cache-resolvable fraction of approximately 8%, extrapolated from a logistic fit with an R² value of 0.97, Spark's micro-batch approach matched or outperformed our model in terms of both latency and throughput. This finding indicates that our approach is not universally superior and that problems requiring global, unbounded re-aggregation, such as a full-history join with no temporal locality, remain better suited to batch execution, aligning with the long-standing caution regarding the generality of stream processing (Stonebraker et al., 2005).

We also evaluated the fault tolerance and recovery capabilities of our model by injecting single-node failures at random points during the run, with 20 trials per system. The mean recovery time, defined as the time until output latency returned to within 10% of its pre-failure median, was 74 seconds [66-83 seconds] for MapReduce task re-execution, 19 seconds [16-23 seconds] for Spark, and 3.2 seconds [2.6-3.9 seconds] for our proposed model. Recovery in our model relied on replaying the retained log from the last checkpoint and on idempotent, stateless stages that could be restarted without coordination. Although this approach introduced a short window of duplicate emissions, with an average of 0.004% of output records being delivered twice before deduplication by sequence number, no records were lost in any of the 20 trials. However, exactly-once output semantics were only guaranteed after the deduplication step, which is a weaker intermediate guarantee compared to transactional systems like Flink (Carbone et al., 2015). Notably, checkpointing reduced peak throughput by 6.3% relative to a checkpoint-free run.

To assess the scalability of our model, we scaled the cluster from 2 to 16 nodes and observed the throughput on the aggregation workload. The throughput grew from 0.49 million events per second to 3.4 million events per second, achieving a parallel efficiency of 87% at 16 nodes. In comparison, the corresponding efficiencies for Spark and MapReduce were 74% and 69%. The efficiency losses in our model were mainly attributed to key skew. When the key distribution was made Zipfian (s = 1.2), the hottest partition handled 23% of all traffic, and the 16-node efficiency fell to 61%. This degradation was mitigated to 78% by splitting hot keys with a two-stage partial aggregation, albeit at the cost of 11 milliseconds additional median latency.

Finally, we considered the cost implications of our model. Using on-demand cloud pricing at the time of the experiments, the cluster hours needed to serve the aggregation workload for 24 hours with a 1-second freshness target were 192 node-hours for our proposed model. In contrast, Spark required 384 node-hours, with micro-batch intervals tuned to 1 second, and MapReduce could not meet the target at any tested cluster size up to 32 nodes. This significant reduction in cost underscores the potential of our approach to provide efficient and scalable processing of streaming data, making it an attractive solution for a wide range of applications. The cost of Spark drops to 96 node-hours, surpassing the proposed model's 128 node-hours, when a relaxed 5-minute freshness target is applied, primarily due to the latter's retention of always-on operators and in-memory state. This stark difference underscores the economic argument's strong dependence on the freshness requirement. A closer examination of the results reveals order-of-magnitude improvements in latency, shuffle volume, and recovery time for cacheable, time-dependent problems. However, these gains gradually diminish as the conditions approach those for which map-shuffle-reduce was originally designed, namely, high cache applicability, computational intensity, or freshness tolerance.

At the heart of this paper lies the central claim that a significant class of problems currently addressed with map-shuffle-reduce pipelines is, in fact, poorly suited to this model. Specifically, time-dependent problems whose solutions can be bounded, windowed, or cached are more efficiently handled through a partly stateless, flow-oriented formulation. This approach avoids the unnecessary cost of repeatedly materializing, shuffling, and recomputing data that changes slowly or is only relevant for a short horizon. It is essential to interpret these results as supporting a design principle rather than a general refutation of batch-oriented processing. Map-reduce and its descendants remain well-suited to large, unbounded-latency, embarrassingly parallel scans, which was the original design target (Dean & Ghemawat, 2004).

The advantages of the proposed model stem primarily from a shift in what is considered the unit of work. In traditional map-shuffle-reduce, the dataset serves as the unit, triggering a pass over or re-aggregation of a large collection with each new piece of information. In contrast, the flow-oriented model treats the event or a small, bounded window of events as the unit, with the applied function retaining only the necessary state to answer time-bounded questions. This perspective aligns with earlier arguments advocating for stream processing to prioritize data in motion as the primary abstraction and avoid storing data before processing (Stonebraker, Çetintemel, & Zdonik, 2005). It also resonates with the view that batch and streaming processing represent two ends of a continuum rather than separate systems (Akidau et al., 2015).

When a solution can be cached, the reduction step evolves from a global recomputation into an incremental update. This transformation explains why the most significant gains are observed when the working set implied by the time bound is small relative to the historical corpus. The result also has implications for the sociology of the field, as highlighted in the abstract. The adoption of cluster-based Big Data tooling has often been driven by perceived inevitability, marketing value, and technical need. However, several studies have shown that many real analytic workloads are sufficiently small to fit within a single machine's memory or storage (Appuswamy et al., 2013), and that carefully crafted single-threaded programs can outperform sizable clusters running general-purpose frameworks (McSherry, Isard, & Murray, 2015). Furthermore, profiling work on Spark-style engines suggests that disk and network bottlenecks are less common than assumed, with CPU and serialization overheads playing a more significant role (Ousterhout et al., 2015). These observations lend credence to the present argument, suggesting that a model eliminating unnecessary shuffles and materialization by design should yield savings without requiring exotic engineering.

In relation to existing architectures, the proposed model shares similarities with, but is distinct from, the Lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers and merges their outputs (Marz & Warren, 2015). Critics have noted the cost and error-prone nature of maintaining two code paths for the same logic (Kreps, 2014). Our formulation addresses this critique by utilizing a single functional description of the computation and varying only the amount of retained state. It also aligns with systems like Flink, Naiad, and Storm, which provide stateful dataflow with differing consistency and recovery guarantees (Carbone et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2013; Toshniwal et al., 2014). The key distinction lies in the emphasis on statelessness as the norm, introducing state only when justified by the problem's temporal structure. This approach simplifies functions, making them easier to reason about, replicate, and restart after failure. It also connects to the observation that monotonic, coordination-free computations can be distributed with fewer consistency mechanisms (Hellerstein & Alvaro, 2020).

Several limitations constrain the conclusions drawn from this work. Firstly, the benefits are contingent upon the problem's temporal structure. If the answer depends on arbitrary historical data, such as iterative graph algorithms, large-scale model training, or ad hoc joins across the full corpus, the bound or cache assumption fails, and a batch or iterative engine is likely a better choice (Zaharia et al., 2012). Secondly, caching and partial statelessness shift complexity from the framework to the application designer, requiring domain knowledge to choose appropriate window sizes, eviction policies, and tolerance for stale results. An incorrect choice may silently degrade correctness. Thirdly, the treatment of fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics is less mature compared to established systems, whose lineage-based recovery and checkpointing have been refined over years of production use. In a flow-oriented design, replay of in-flight events and reconstruction of cached state after failure remain open engineering concerns. Fourthly, the evaluation is restricted to the workloads and scales considered, and performance at much larger scales, under skewed key distributions, or with heterogeneous hardware may differ. The comparison with tuned production deployments of mature frameworks may not generalize. Finally, the trade-off between latency and consistency is inherent in distributed systems (Abadi, 2012), and our model makes this trade-off explicit without removing it.

The implications of this work are multifaceted. For practitioners, the primary implication is that the choice of processing model should commence with an analysis of the problem's temporal and state requirements, rather than the availability of a popular platform. A useful initial question is whether the answer can be computed from a bounded window or an incrementally maintainable summary. If so, a flow-oriented design is likely to reduce infrastructure, latency, and operational burden. If not, a batch framework is justified. For system designers, the results encourage the development of frameworks that make bounded state and caching first-class, declarative concepts, allowing developers to leverage these features without manual implementation. This would narrow the gap between batch and streaming programming models that current systems are still addressing. For researchers, the work suggests the need for benchmarking that reports cost and performance in a way that reflects the temporal structure and state requirements of real-world problems, facilitating a more informed choice of processing models.

The burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, and cancer, is a pressing global health concern, accounting for approximately 70% of deaths worldwide, with a disproportionate impact on low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2018). The importance of primary care in addressing this burden cannot be overstated, as it is widely regarded as the optimal setting for delivering the continuous, coordinated, and person-centred care that chronic conditions require (Starfield et al., 2005; Kruk et al., 2018). As a result, a plethora of interventions have been developed to improve the detection, management, and long-term support of individuals with NCDs in primary care, encompassing strategies such as structured self-management education, decision support for clinicians, task-shifting to nurses and community health workers, audit and feedback, and multicomponent models of integrated care (Wagner et al., 2001; Coleman et al., 2009).

While many of these interventions have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews of such trials have revealed that their effects are often modest and heterogeneous, with similar interventions yielding markedly different results in different settings (Smith et al., 2016; Tricco et al., 2012). This heterogeneity is not surprising, given the complex nature of interventions in primary care, which typically involve multiple interacting components, target multiple levels (patients, providers, practices, and organisations), require tailoring to local circumstances, and depend on the behaviour of numerous actors (Craig et al., 2008; Hawe et al., 2004). The effects of these interventions are shaped by the context in which they are delivered, including the structure and financing of the health system, workforce availability, and local social and cultural norms (Pfadenhauer et al., 2017).

Conventional trials, which report only whether an intervention "worked" on average, are limited in their ability to explain why an effect was or was not observed, whether the intervention was delivered as intended, which components were responsible for any change, or how the findings might transfer to other settings. Null results are particularly challenging to interpret without this information, as they may reflect a flawed intervention theory, poor implementation, or an unsuitable context (Oakley et al., 2006). To address these limitations, process evaluations (PEs) have been advocated, with the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions defining their purpose as examining implementation (what is delivered, and how), mechanisms of impact (how delivered activities produce change), and contextual factors that shape both (Moore et al., 2015).

By answering questions of for whom, how, and why interventions have an impact, PEs help distinguish implementation failure from theory failure, identify unintended consequences, and provide the information needed to refine interventions and support scale-up. Earlier frameworks for describing implementation, including those of Steckler and Linnan (2002), Baranowski and Stables (2000), and Grant et al. (2013), and widely used theory-based approaches such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), normalisation process theory (May and Finch, 2009), and RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 1999), have similarly emphasised the need to examine reach, fidelity, dose, and adaptation alongside outcomes. The MRC guidance further stresses that PEs should be underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory or logic model, so that data collection and analysis are directed at the hypothesised causal pathway rather than being purely descriptive (Moore et al., 2015; De Silva et al., 2014).

Despite this guidance, there is concern that PEs are inconsistently conducted and reported. Reviews in other fields, such as school-based health promotion and public health, have found that PEs often lack explicit theoretical grounding, apply inconsistent definitions of constructs such as fidelity and context, and rely on convenience samples or purely descriptive data (Oakley et al., 2006; Bonell et al., 2012; Grant et al., 2013). Where theory is absent, it is difficult to judge whether the right processes were examined, and findings from one PE are hard to compare with, or build upon, those of another. Improvements in reporting have been proposed, including the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) and the TIDieR checklist for describing interventions (Pinnock et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2014), but it is unclear how far these have influenced practice in primary care.

Several existing syntheses bear on this topic, but leave important gaps. Systematic reviews of barriers and facilitators to implementing chronic disease interventions have mostly drawn on qualitative studies or focused on single conditions, such as diabetes self-management or hypertension control, and have not examined how the underlying evaluations were designed (Gagliardi et al., 2011; Jeet et al., 2017). Reviews of PEs, in contrast, have concentrated on public health, school, or community settings, where the organisational features of primary care, such as gatekeeping, multidisciplinary teams, continuity of care, and payment systems, are less salient. To our knowledge, no review has systematically described the methods used in PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions for NCDs, assessed the extent to which they follow recognised guidance, and synthesised their findings on implementation barriers and facilitators across conditions and health systems.

This omission is significant, as primary care interventions are increasingly being adapted for and tested in diverse settings, including low-resource health systems, where many of the assumptions underpinning interventions developed in high-income countries may not hold (Kruk et al., 2018; Legido-Quigley et al., 2013). We therefore conducted a systematic review of PEs alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for individuals with NCDs, using the MRC guidance for process evaluation as an organising framework. Our review had two primary aims: first, to describe and appraise the methods used in these PEs, including the use of intervention theory and theoretical frameworks, the choice of data collection and analytic approaches, sampling, and the integration of qualitative and quantitative data; and second, to synthesise the principal findings of these evaluations regarding barriers and facilitators to implementation, with attention to the context in which interventions were delivered.

This review makes three key contributions. Firstly, it provides the first comprehensive overview of how PEs in primary care chronic disease research are being designed and reported, identifying strengths and weaknesses that can inform methodological practice and the application of the MRC guidance. Secondly, it offers a cross-condition synthesis of recurring implementation challenges, which may be more useful to intervention developers and health system decision-makers. Finally, by examining the extent to which PEs follow recognised guidance and the factors that influence their quality, this review aims to contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable primary care interventions for NCDs, which can be adapted and implemented in diverse settings. The development of effective interventions for non-communicable diseases in primary care settings is a complex and multifaceted challenge. Despite the growing body of research in this area, there remains a need for a more nuanced understanding of the factors that influence the implementation and sustainability of these interventions. Our systematic review of process evaluations conducted alongside randomized controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive overview of the current state of the field.

To achieve this, we conducted a systematic review of process evaluations that were conducted in conjunction with randomized controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. Our protocol was registered in PROSPERO prior to the commencement of screening, and our review is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. We utilized the UK Medical Research Council's guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions as a framework for both data extraction and appraisal, which emphasizes the importance of describing the intervention and its causal assumptions, examining implementation, exploring mechanisms of impact, and considering contextual influences on delivery and outcomes.

Our eligibility criteria were defined using the Population, Intervention, Context, and Study design elements. We included studies that reported a process evaluation, which we defined as a study that assessed implementation, mechanisms of impact, or context, alongside a randomized controlled trial. The trial intervention had to be delivered in primary care or community-based primary health care settings and aim to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, mental health conditions, and musculoskeletal disorders. Interventions could be targeted at patients, providers, practices, or the wider health system. We excluded studies of infectious diseases, those conducted solely in hospital or specialist settings, trials with no process evaluation component, and process evaluations reported only as protocols without results.

Our search strategy combined three concept blocks: process evaluation terms, primary care terms, and non-communicable disease terms, together with a trial filter to identify randomized designs. We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, CINAHL, EMBASE, and Global Health, from 1998 to June 2018. Our search terms were developed in collaboration with an information specialist and piloted against a set of known process evaluations. We also supplemented our electronic searches by hand-searching the reference lists of included studies and relevant methodological reviews, and by checking trial registries and linked publications to identify companion papers reporting process evaluation findings.

Study selection was conducted independently by two reviewers, who screened titles and abstracts against our eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating where consensus could not be reached. We calculated agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage using Cohen's kappa. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded.

Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, structured around the UK Medical Research Council's framework, which was piloted on five studies. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and a third reviewer checked a random sample of extractions for accuracy and consistency as quality assurance. We extracted a range of information, including bibliographic details, country and income setting, clinical condition, description of the intervention using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) items, level of intervention, trial design, and the timing of the process evaluation relative to the trial.

We also extracted information on the process evaluation methods, including whether the authors stated an explicit intervention theory or logic model, whether an existing theoretical or implementation framework was used, the process evaluation research questions, the components assessed, data collection methods, sampling strategy and sample size, the respondents included, analytic approach, and whether qualitative and quantitative data were triangulated or integrated. Furthermore, we recorded whether the process evaluation findings were used to interpret trial outcomes. For findings, we extracted all reported barriers and facilitators to implementation, together with the authors' interpretations and illustrative data, where available.

Rather than excluding studies on quality grounds, we appraised the methodological characteristics of process evaluations against the UK Medical Research Council's guidance to describe the field and to identify strengths and weaknesses. Our appraisal criteria included clarity of intervention theory, a priori specification of process evaluation questions, appropriateness of sampling, use of multiple data sources, transparent analysis, and consideration of context. Qualitative components were additionally assessed with reference to the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist, with the aim of contextualizing the weight placed on individual findings rather than determining inclusion.

Our data synthesis was conducted in two parts. First, we summarized the methodological data descriptively using frequencies and proportions, stratified by country income group, intervention level, and whether a theoretical framework had been used. We cross-tabulated the presence of an explicit intervention theory against these characteristics and used Fisher's exact test to explore associations. Our findings provide valuable insights into the current state of process evaluations in primary care settings, highlighting areas of strength and weakness, and informing the development of future interventions that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of different settings. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more effective and sustainable interventions that can be implemented and maintained at scale, thereby improving outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases in primary care settings. 

In addition to the methodological data, we also conducted a thematic analysis of the process evaluation findings, which revealed a range of barriers and facilitators to implementation. These findings have important implications for the development of future interventions, highlighting the need for careful consideration of the complex interplay between intervention design, implementation context, and patient and provider factors.

Our review also highlights the importance of using theoretical frameworks to inform the design and evaluation of complex interventions. The use of such frameworks can help to identify potential barriers and facilitators to implementation, and can inform the development of strategies to address these challenges. Furthermore, our review emphasizes the need for greater attention to the role of context in shaping the implementation and effectiveness of complex interventions.

Our review highlights the need for ongoing research and evaluation in this Our analysis of the included process evaluations (PEs) was conducted in three stages. Initially, where cell counts were small, we treated these analyses as exploratory and did not adjust for multiple comparisons, recognizing the limitations of our findings in these instances. Next, we employed thematic synthesis, as outlined by Thomas and Harden (2008), to synthesize findings on barriers and facilitators. This involved two reviewers independently coding extracted text line by line, using an inductive approach to generate descriptive codes. These codes were then grouped into descriptive themes, which were compared across studies, conditions, and settings to identify patterns and inconsistencies.

In the third stage of our analysis, we developed analytical themes that went beyond the original studies to interpret why implementation succeeded or failed. To ensure that our synthesis addressed the context-mechanism-outcome relationships emphasized in the MRC guidance, we mapped our themes onto the health system building blocks proposed by the World Health Organization (2007). These building blocks include service delivery, workforce, information, medicines and technologies, financing, and leadership and governance. Our coding frameworks were discussed in team meetings to ensure consistency and validity, and a third reviewer reviewed a sample of coded data to check for consistency and the plausibility of the themes. We managed our data using NVivo and Microsoft Excel.

It is worth noting that our review focused on the implementation barriers and facilitators reported by the original authors, and we did not seek to link them to effect sizes. As a result, we did not formally assess the certainty of evidence. However, we did note where PE findings were used to explain null or heterogeneous trial results, as this indicated the interpretive value of the PE. The searches for our review identified a total of 14,532 records, which were then screened and filtered to identify relevant studies. After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, we assessed 412 full texts, of which 69 PEs met our inclusion criteria and were included in the synthesis.

The most common reasons for excluding full texts were that the paper described a trial protocol or outcome evaluation with no process component, that the study was not nested in a randomised trial, and that the intervention was not delivered in primary care. Agreement between the two reviewers at full-text screening was good, with a kappa statistic of 0.81. The majority of the included PEs were published recently, with 55% published between 2014 and June 2018. The PEs were conducted in a range of settings, with 59% conducted in high-income countries, including the UK, the USA, the Netherlands, Australia, and others. The remaining 41% were conducted in low- and middle-income countries, with the most common settings being South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America.

The target conditions for the interventions varied, with diabetes being the most common (28%), followed by cardiovascular disease and hypertension (25%), chronic respiratory disease (14%), depression and other common mental disorders (13%), multimorbidity (9%), cancer (6%), and other conditions (6%). The interventions themselves were complex, with a median of three components, ranging from two to seven components. The most frequent components were training or education of health professionals (70%), patient self-management support (57%), care pathway or protocol redesign (45%), decision support or information technology (32%), and task-shifting to nurses or community health workers (29%).

In terms of study design, 64% of the PEs used a mixed-methods design, while 25% were qualitative only and 12% were quantitative only. Data collection varied, with 55% of PEs collecting data concurrently with the trial, and 45% collecting data only after the trial had ended. The most common data sources were semi-structured interviews (75%), followed by questionnaires or surveys (42%), routine or audit data (35%), focus groups (30%), non-participant observation (22%), documentary analysis (20%), and audio-recorded consultations (12%). The median number of data sources per PE was three, with an interquartile range of two to four.

Participants in the PEs were most often health professionals (86%), followed by patients (68%), managers or policy-makers (26%), and carers (7%). Sampling was described in 88% of the PEs, with purposive sampling being the most common approach. Maximum-variation strategies were used in 18 of the PEs that employed purposive sampling, for example, sampling across high- and low-performing practices or across urban and rural sites. Data saturation or an equivalent stopping criterion was reported in 36% of the PEs.

The analytic approaches used in the PEs varied, with thematic analysis being the most common (63%), followed by framework analysis (29%), content analysis (12%), and grounded theory (8%). Some studies used more than one approach. Among the mixed-methods PEs, 82% explicitly integrated qualitative and quantitative findings to explain how the intervention worked. Reporting of the PEs was inconsistent, with only 70% of papers using the term "process evaluation" in the title or abstract.

Using the components of the MRC guidance (Moore et al., 2015), we found that 67% of the PEs assessed implementation fidelity, 55% assessed dose, 48% assessed reach, and 59% examined context. Mechanisms of impact were investigated in 42% of the PEs, and unintended consequences were looked for in 25%. However, only 16% of the PEs assessed all of fidelity, dose, reach, context, and mechanisms. Fewer than half of the PEs (45%) specified the research questions before data collection, and only 20% reported that the PE protocol had been published or registered before the trial analysis.

The use of an intervention theory was also varied, with 43% of the PEs being underpinned by a clearly articulated theory. This meant that an explicit description of how the intervention was expected to produce change was provided. In the other 57% of PEs, the assumed mechanisms were implicit or not described. Of the 30 PEs with a clear theory, 22 used an existing theoretical or implementation framework, such as Normalization Process Theory, the MRC complex interventions framework, or the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. The remaining eight presented a bespoke logic model or causal pathway.

We found that studies with a clear intervention theory were more likely to assess mechanisms of impact (70%) than those without (21%), and more often reported on context (87% vs 38%). The use of an intervention theory did not differ markedly between high-income and low- and middle-income settings. A further 19% of the PEs applied a framework only at the analysis stage, usually to code interview data, and not to design the PE. Overall, our analysis highlights the importance of using a clear intervention theory and assessing implementation fidelity, dose, reach, context, and mechanisms in PEs. By doing so, researchers can gain a better understanding of why interventions succeed or fail, and how they can be improved to achieve better outcomes. The analysis of 69 process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomized controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases revealed three cross-cutting themes that explained why many interventions were implemented poorly or had limited impact. A significant mismatch between intervention design and local needs was a major concern, with 38 PEs (55%) highlighting this issue. This mismatch was often due to a lack of consideration for the priorities, resources, and expectations of patients and providers who were meant to use the interventions. For instance, 31 PEs (45% of the total) described content or delivery that was poorly matched to patient circumstances, such as educational materials that were culturally inappropriate or of low literacy relevance. Furthermore, 22 PEs (32%) reported that practitioners saw the intervention as adding to their workload without addressing the problems they considered important, particularly in cases of multimorbidity where single-disease protocols were difficult to apply.

The lack of formative research during intervention development was also a notable issue, with only 12 PEs (17%) reporting the use of needs assessment or user-centered piloting. In contrast, 24 PEs reported facilitators related to fit, with 17 attributing it to local adaptation or stakeholder involvement in design. This highlights the importance of involving local stakeholders in the design process to ensure that interventions are tailored to the specific needs and context of the target population.

The second theme that emerged was the unclear roles and responsibilities of key actors, which was reported in 44 PEs (64%). This lack of clarity often led to confusion about who was accountable for delivering intervention components, with 33 PEs (48%) identifying role ambiguity between doctors, nurses, and community health workers. Insufficient training or supervision was also a common issue, with 19 PEs (28%) reporting this problem. Moreover, 16 PEs (23%) reported that patients did not understand their own part in the intervention, such as in shared decision-making or home monitoring. Facilitators, reported in 27 PEs (39%), included clearly defined role descriptions, local clinical champions, and regular feedback or supervision.

The third theme that emerged was the health system context, which was reported in 47 PEs (68%). Governance, financing, and workforce factors that had not been anticipated often adversely affected implementation, with 32 PEs (46%) citing workforce shortages, high turnover, or competing demands. Funding structures, including lack of reimbursement for new activities or unreliable supplies of medicines and equipment, were also a common issue, with 26 PEs (38%) reporting this problem. Furthermore, 18 PEs (26%) cited fragmented governance or poor integration with existing information systems and referral pathways. These barriers were reported in both high-income and low- and middle-income settings, although medicine stock-outs and community health worker remuneration were mentioned almost exclusively in the latter. Facilitators included alignment with existing policy priorities (n=15, 22%) and managerial support (n=21, 30%).

The principal findings of this review highlight two key messages. First, the conduct and reporting of PEs were highly variable, with fewer than half of the studies (30/69) underpinned by an explicit intervention theory. This lack of theoretical grounding is concerning, as it makes it difficult to decide what to measure, to distinguish theory failure from implementation failure, or to interpret null trial results. Second, the barriers to implementation clustered around three recurring problems: a mismatch between what the intervention was designed to achieve and local needs, unclear roles and responsibilities for key actors, and unanticipated features of the health system context. These issues are largely failures of design and anticipation rather than of delivery, suggesting that many interventions reached the trial stage without sufficient formative work.

The findings of this review are consistent with the existing literature on implementation science. The MRC guidance on process evaluation positions PEs as a means of examining implementation, mechanisms of impact, and context. Earlier reviews of PEs in other fields, including public health and school-based interventions, have reported similar shortcomings in theoretical grounding and in the explicit analysis of mechanisms. The relatively strong use of purposive sampling and the triangulation of qualitative and quantitative data are encouraging, reflecting the methodological pluralism recommended for complex interventions. However, triangulation was seldom used to test hypotheses derived from a prior theory, so it more often described than explained.

The three themes that emerged from this review align with the wider implementation literature. The mismatch between intervention and local need echoes the argument that interventions developed centrally and imposed on practices struggle to achieve fit with existing workflows and priorities. Role ambiguity has been reported for task-shifting and team-based chronic care, where responsibilities for screening, follow-up, and self-management support are redistributed among nurses, community health workers, pharmacists, and physicians without clear negotiation of accountability. The influence of health system context is consistent with systems-oriented frameworks, which emphasize that financing arrangements, supply chains, referral pathways, and workforce capacity determine whether an evidence-based intervention can be sustained.

The implications of this review are significant for both research and practice. First, PE reporting needs greater consistency, with a common structure for describing the intervention, fidelity, dose, reach, and context. A reporting standard specific to PEs, comparable to CONSORT for trials or TIDieR for interventions, would improve comparability and allow future syntheses to move beyond description. Journals and funders could require that PE protocols be registered or published, and that trial and PE findings be cross-referenced. Second, interventions should be underpinned by explicit, testable theory, ideally developed with stakeholders and informed by existing frameworks. Logic models or theories of change that specify assumed mechanisms and contextual preconditions would allow PEs to test whether those assumptions held.

In conclusion, this review highlights the importance of careful consideration of the local context, clear roles and responsibilities, and adequate health system support in the design and implementation of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. By addressing these issues, researchers and practitioners can increase the likelihood of successful implementation and improve health outcomes for patients with chronic diseases. Furthermore, the development of a reporting standard for PEs and the use of explicit, testable theory in intervention design can help to improve the quality and consistency of PEs, ultimately leading to more effective and sustainable interventions.

Lactococcus lactis is a crucial component of mesophilic starter cultures used globally in the production of cheese and other fermented dairy products. The role of starter bacteria in these processes is multifaceted, as they rapidly convert lactose into lactic acid, thereby controlling spoilage and pathogenic microbiota, driving curd formation and syneresis, and contributing to the development of texture and flavor (Smid and Kleerebezem, 2014). Beyond acidification, L. lactis also plays a significant role in flavor development through its proteolytic and peptidolytic activities, amino acid catabolism, and the production of volatile compounds such as diacetyl, acetoin, and others derived from citrate and pyruvate metabolism (Smit et al., 2005; Cocaign-Bousquet et al., 2002).

The success of dairy fermentation processes hinges on the viability and metabolic activity of the starter culture, which must withstand a series of stresses. These stresses occur in two phases: first, during starter production, concentration, and storage, where freezing, freeze-drying, and cold storage can be detrimental; and later, during cheese manufacture, where heat, osmotic, acid, and oxidative stress can impact the starter's performance (van de Guchte et al., 2002; Papadimitriou et al., 2016). Among these challenges, oxidative stress is often underappreciated but pervasive. Although L. lactis is aerotolerant, it lacks a complete respiratory chain unless exogenous heme is provided, and its defenses against reactive oxygen species (ROS) are limited (Duwat et al., 2001).

In the presence of oxygen, enzymes such as NADH oxidase and pyruvate oxidase generate hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, which can damage DNA, proteins, and membrane lipids, leading to growth arrest and loss of viability (Rochat et al., 2006). The introduction of oxygen during various stages of dairy processing, including handling, pumping, stirring, and vat filling, as well as the large-scale propagation of starters under non-anaerobic conditions, further exacerbates oxidative stress. Moreover, oxygen influences the metabolic fate of pyruvate, diverting flux from lactate towards acetate, acetoin, and diacetyl, which has implications for flavor development (Lan et al., 2006). Consequently, strains with improved oxygen tolerance are of practical interest, as they could exhibit more consistent performance in industrial environments and provide an additional route to modulate aroma formation.

Cultivating L. lactis under respiratory conditions, i.e., in the presence of heme and oxygen, can improve biomass yield and robustness (Duwat et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2012). However, this approach requires specific process modifications and is not universally applicable to all dairy applications. Furthermore, strain improvement in food microorganisms is constrained by regulatory and consumer perceptions, and genetically modified organisms are not widely accepted in the dairy sector. As a result, non-recombinant approaches such as spontaneous mutant selection and adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) have become attractive alternatives (Bachmann et al., 2012).

ALE leverages the capacity of bacteria to acquire beneficial mutations under sustained selective pressure and has been used to enhance various industrially relevant traits in lactic acid bacteria, including acid and thermal tolerance, osmotolerance, growth in specific substrates, and bacteriophage resistance (Derkx et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2020). A notable feature of this approach is that selection under one stress often results in cross-protection against other stresses, due to the overlap in cellular responses and global regulatory changes (Mols and Abee, 2011). Selecting for a trait that depends on a global physiological response, such as the integrity and remodeling of the cell envelope, could therefore yield strains with generally more robust phenotypes.

The cell envelope is the primary barrier against environmental insults, and its stress response is well characterized in L. lactis. Envelope-targeting agents trigger the CesSR and other two-component systems, which induce a regulon that includes genes involved in cell wall biosynthesis, modification of the envelope, and protein quality control (Martínez et al., 2007; Roces et al., 2012). Lcn972, a non-lantibiotic bacteriocin produced by L. lactis IPLA972, inhibits cell wall biosynthesis in sensitive lactococci by binding to lipid II, the cell wall precursor, at the septum, thereby impairing septum formation and cell division (Martínez et al., 1996; Martínez et al., 2008; Roces et al., 2009). Its narrow spectrum, restricted to L. lactis, and its mode of action make it a suitable agent to impose controlled cell envelope stress on lactococcal starters.

Previous studies have demonstrated that the response to Lcn972 involves the CesSR system, the overexpression of the stress-inducible protein encoded by the lcn972 resistance-associated locus, and the activation of genes of unknown function (Roces et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2008; Tymoszewska et al., 2017). Notably, resistance to Lcn972 in mutants of the laboratory strain L. lactis IPLA947 or its derivatives has been linked to altered growth, cell wall properties, and metabolic regulation, which may influence how cells handle other stresses (Roces et al., 2012). However, whether resistance to cell wall-active bacteriocins can be harnessed to improve the technological robustness of an industrial starter remains unexplored.

L. lactis IPLA947 is a well-characterized, phage-resistant dairy starter used in the manufacture of artisanal and industrial cheeses, with good acidifying properties and a sequenced and annotated genome (Rodríguez-Alonso et al., 2009; Flórez et al., 2016). Given its industrial relevance, it is an appropriate model to test whether cell envelope stress-driven adaptive evolution can generate variants with enhanced technological traits. Any improvement in stress tolerance must not compromise the core functions of the starter, namely rapid acidification, stable lactose-to-lactate conversion, and an adequate contribution to flavor. Trade-offs between stress resistance and growth, which are well described for mutants affected in global regulators or carbon catabolite control (Ferenci, 2016), can render stress-tolerant variants useless for dairy applications.

In this study, we applied adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress by consecutively exposing L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing doses of Lcn972 and screened the resulting derivatives for cross-protection against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that resistance to this envelope-active bacteriocin would select for variants with modified envelope physiology and/or metabolic regulation, conferring a more robust phenotype in the presence of oxygen. We characterized the selected mutant, L. lactis R5, regarding its technological traits and stress tolerance, with a focus on understanding the underlying mechanisms driving its improved performance. Our findings provide insights into the potential of adaptive evolution as a tool for strain improvement in the dairy industry, highlighting the importance of considering the complex interplay between cell envelope stress, metabolic regulation, and stress tolerance in the development of more robust starter cultures. The quest for robust and efficient dairy starters has driven research into the development of strains that can thrive in a variety of environments and withstand the stresses inherent to starter production and storage. Our investigation focused on the adaptation of Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, a well-characterized dairy starter strain, to the bacteriocin Lcn972, with the goal of obtaining a stable, oxygen-tolerant derivative that retains the desirable technological properties of the parental strain. To achieve this, we employed a strategy of adaptive evolution, where the strain was consecutively exposed to increasing concentrations of Lcn972, allowing it to develop resistance while maintaining its growth and metabolic capabilities.

The parental strain, Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, was grown in M17 broth supplemented with 0.5% glucose (GM17) or in reconstituted skim milk (RSM) at 30 °C, with stocks stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol. Lcn972 was produced and partially purified from L. lactis IPLA972 supernatants using cation-exchange chromatography, as previously described (Martínez et al. 1996), and its activity was quantified by agar well diffusion assay against L. lactis subsp. cremoris MG1363. To promote respiratory metabolism, hemin (5 µg/ml) was added to GM17 where indicated (Duwat et al. 2001).

The adaptive evolution process involved diluting an overnight culture of IPLA947 1:100 in GM17 containing a sub-inhibitory concentration of Lcn972, initially set at 0.5× the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), and incubating for 24 h. The culture was then transferred daily into fresh medium with the Lcn972 concentration raised stepwise whenever growth was visible (OD600 > 0.5). After approximately 30 transfers, equivalent to around 200 generations, the final population was plated on GM17 agar, and isolated colonies were tested for Lcn972 MIC. Clones with the highest MIC were selected and passaged ten times (about 70 generations) in GM17 without bacteriocin to assess phenotypic stability. One stable clone, designated R5, was chosen for further characterization. The identity of R5 relative to the parent strain was confirmed through RAPD-PCR fingerprinting with primer OPA-3 (Ward and Roberts 1994) and by verifying the absence of bacteriophage-induced changes via plaque assays.

To evaluate the stress tolerance of R5, we conducted a series of experiments. First, we assessed its survival after a hydrogen peroxide challenge. Exponential-phase cultures of both IPLA947 and R5 were harvested, washed, and resuspended to approximately 10^8 CFU/ml. Hydrogen peroxide was added to final concentrations of 5–20 mM, and cells were incubated at 30 °C for 30 min. After neutralizing the residual H2O2 with catalase, viable counts were determined by plating serial dilutions on GM17 agar. Survival was calculated as a percentage, and log reductions were also determined.

Next, we examined the growth of R5 under aerobic and anaerobic conditions. Cultures were grown in GM17 at 30 °C with orbital shaking at 200 rpm (aerobic) or statically in sealed tubes filled to the top (limited oxygen). Specific growth rates were calculated from the slope of ln(OD600) versus time during the exponential phase. To assess respiratory metabolism, growth experiments were performed in GM17 with and without hemin, and growth, final OD600, and biomass were compared. Dissolved oxygen levels were measured using a fiber-optic oxygen sensor in selected experiments.

The performance of R5 as a dairy starter was evaluated in milk acidification experiments. Reconstituted skim milk was inoculated with 1% (v/v) of overnight cultures of IPLA947 or R5, washed in sterile saline, and incubated at 30 °C. Aerated cultures were shaken at 200 rpm, while static incubation in filled bottles served as the low-oxygen control. pH was recorded continuously using a data logger or measured at defined intervals. The maximum acidification rate, time to reach pH 5.3, and final pH after 24 h were calculated from the pH curves.

We also investigated the survival of R5 during cold storage and freeze-drying. For cold storage, cells from stationary-phase cultures were harvested, resuspended in RSM or in 0.9% NaCl, and stored at 4 °C for 28 days, with viable counts determined weekly. Freeze-drying was performed on cells harvested in late exponential phase, washed, and resuspended in 10% (w/v) skim milk supplemented with 5% sucrose. Aliquots were frozen at −80 °C for 2 h and lyophilized for 24 h. Survival was calculated as the ratio of CFU/ml after versus before freeze-drying, and viability was monitored after 1 and 3 months of storage at 4 °C.

Finally, we manufactured experimental miniature cheeses using pasteurized whole cow’s milk inoculated with IPLA947 or R5 as the starter culture. The cheese-making process involved warming the milk to 32 °C, adding starter, CaCl2, and commercial chymosin, followed by coagulation, cutting, stirring, scalding, draining, molding, and pressing. Cheeses were ripened at 12 °C for 30 days, during which counts of lactococci, pH, and the profile of sugars and organic acids were determined. Lactose, galactose, lactic acid, acetic acid, citric acid, and other organic acids were quantified by HPLC from milk fermentations and cheeses.

Our results indicate that the R5 derivative, obtained through adaptive evolution under Lcn972 stress, exhibits enhanced resistance to hydrogen peroxide and improved growth under aerobic conditions, while retaining the desirable technological properties of the parental strain. Notably, R5 displays an increased capacity to produce acetoin, a compound of interest in dairy fermentations. These findings support the use of cell envelope stress as a driver of intra-strain diversification in industrial lactococci, offering a promising approach for the development of robust and efficient dairy starters. The analysis of volatile compounds in 30-day curds was performed using headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled to gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS), a technique that allows for the detection of volatile compounds in a non-destructive manner. Specifically, 3 g of grated cheese was equilibrated at 40 °C for 10 minutes, and then volatiles were extracted for 30 minutes using a DVB/CAR/PDMS fibre (Supelco). The compounds were subsequently desorbed at 250 °C and separated on a DB-WAX capillary column with a temperature gradient from 40 to 220 °C. Mass spectra were acquired in electron impact mode (70 eV), and compounds were identified by comparison with NIST library spectra, retention indices, and authentic standards when available. The relative abundance of each compound was expressed as peak area ratios to the internal standard, 2-methyl-3-heptanone.

Statistical analysis was performed on all experiments, which were conducted with at least three independent biological replicates, unless otherwise stated. Data are presented as means ± standard deviation, and differences between the R5 and IPLA947 strains were analyzed using two-tailed Student's t tests or one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test for multiple comparisons. Normality and homogeneity of variance were verified using Shapiro-Wilk and Levene's tests, respectively, and non-parametric Mann-Whitney tests were used when necessary. For the analysis of volatile compounds, peak area ratios were log-transformed before analysis, and a principal component analysis was performed to visualize differences between cheese groups. To account for multiple comparisons, a false discovery rate correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) was applied. Differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. All analyses were performed using R (version 4.1) and GraphPad Prism 8.

The isolation of a stable Lcn972-resistant mutant, designated R5, was achieved through consecutive exposure of L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing concentrations of Lcn972 in M17 broth supplemented with glucose (GM17). After five rounds of exposure, the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) for the population increased from 40 to more than 640 arbitrary units (AU) ml⁻¹. The R5 clone was selected based on its ability to retain the resistant phenotype (MIC ≥ 640 AU ml⁻¹) after approximately 100 generations of growth without bacteriocin, indicating a stable genetic change rather than a transient physiological adaptation. The level of resistance exhibited by R5 was comparable to that reported for spontaneous Lcn972-resistant mutants of L. lactis IPLA947 and other strains (Roces et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2008).

Under standard anaerobic conditions in GM17, the R5 and parental strains displayed similar maximum specific growth rates (0.62 ± 0.03 and 0.60 ± 0.02 h⁻¹, respectively; P > 0.05), suggesting that the acquisition of resistance did not incur an obvious fitness penalty. However, when challenged with hydrogen peroxide, the R5 strain exhibited significantly improved survival compared to the wild type. Cells in exponential phase were exposed to 5 mM H₂O₂ for 30 minutes, and survival was calculated as N/N₀. The wild type showed a reduction of approximately 3.1 log units, whereas R5 decreased by only 1.4 log units, resulting in a difference in survival of roughly 1.7 log units (P < 0.01). This corresponds to a 50-fold greater survival under oxidative challenge for the R5 strain. In contrast, survival after exposure to other stresses, including heat (52 °C), acid (pH 4.0), and 0.3 M NaCl, did not differ significantly between the strains (differences < 0.4 log units), suggesting that the improvement was relatively specific to oxidative stress.

To evaluate the impact of the R5 phenotype on growth, aerated cultures (shaking at 200 rpm) were established in GM17. Under these conditions, the wild type slowed markedly, with a specific growth rate of 0.35 ± 0.02 h⁻¹, whereas R5 grew at 0.48 ± 0.03 h⁻¹, representing a 37% increase (P < 0.01). Additionally, R5 reached a higher final optical density at 600 nm (1.9 ± 0.1 versus 1.5 ± 0.1). In static cultures, however, the differences were negligible. The relative growth advantage of R5 in the presence of oxygen was consistent with its greater tolerance to peroxide, a major product of NADH and pyruvate oxidase-type reactions in lactic acid bacteria (Condon, 1987; Marty-Teysset et al., 2000).

In reconstituted skim milk (10% w/v) cultures incubated at 30 °C with agitation to aerate the medium, the wild type reduced the pH to 5.2 ± 0.1 after 24 hours, whereas R5 reached 4.7 ± 0.1 (P < 0.05). Final viable counts were approximately 0.5 log CFU ml⁻¹ higher for R5 (9.2 versus 8.7 log CFU ml⁻¹). In non-aerated milk, however, the acidification curves were superimposable, with both strains reaching pH 4.6 within 8 hours and showing equal maximum acidification rates (approximately 0.012 pH units min⁻¹ at the steepest part of the curve). Thus, the benefit of the mutation was confined to oxygenated conditions.

L. lactis can switch to respiratory metabolism when supplemented with heme and oxygen, resulting in higher biomass and improved survival (Duwat et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2012). To determine whether the improved oxygen behavior of R5 extended to respiration-permissive conditions, cultures were supplemented with 1 µg ml⁻¹ hemin and aerated. Both strains displayed the expected increase in biomass relative to cultures without heme (final OD₆₀₀ of 3.0–3.3 for both), and the specific growth rates did not differ statistically (0.55 ± 0.03 h⁻¹ for the wild type and 0.57 ± 0.02 h⁻¹ for R5). Similarly, survival after 7 days of storage in the stationary phase at 4 °C was equivalent in respiratory and fermentative cultures, with a loss of 0.3–0.6 log units in each. The benefit of R5 was thus masked by heme, which presumably confers oxygen detoxification through the respiratory chain and catalase activity.

Storage under cold conditions was also examined for cells suspended in milk. After 21 days at 4 °C, viable counts decreased by 0.5 ± 0.2 log units for the wild type and 0.4 ± 0.2 for R5 (P > 0.05). Survival after freeze-drying in 10% skim milk with 5% sucrose was 38 ± 6% for the wild type and 41 ± 7% for R5, and after 3 months at 4 °C, the remaining viability was again indistinguishable (approximately 0.8 log reduction in both). These results suggest that the R5 strain does not exhibit a significant advantage in terms of survival under cold storage or freeze-drying conditions. The introduction of the R5 mutation in L. lactis IPLA947 resulted in a strain with enhanced tolerance to oxidative stress, as evidenced by its improved survival in the presence of H₂O₂ and its faster growth in aerobic conditions. However, this increased robustness did not translate to improved performance during cold storage or lyophilization, suggesting that the benefits of the mutation are relatively specific. To further characterize the effects of the R5 mutation, we examined the fermentation profile and acidification of the strain in cheese-like conditions. We found that the mutation did not alter the metabolic performance of the starter, with lactose consumption and organic acid production remaining similar to those of the wild-type strain. After 24 hours of fermentation at 30 °C, the lactose concentration decreased from 47.5 ± 0.8 g l⁻¹ to 2.1 ± 0.4 g l⁻¹ in the wild-type strain and to 2.3 ± 0.5 g l⁻¹ in the R5 strain. The lactic acid concentrations were also similar, with values of 41.2 ± 1.5 g l⁻¹ and 40.6 ± 1.2 g l⁻¹, respectively. Additionally, the levels of acetic and formic acid, as well as citrate, were not significantly affected by the mutation.

We also investigated the impact of the R5 mutation on cheese manufacture and the production of volatile compounds. Experimental miniature cheeses were produced using either the wild-type or R5 strain as the sole starter, and the resulting cheeses were analyzed for their volatile compound profiles. The curd pH and moisture content were equivalent for both strains, with values of 5.3 ± 0.1 and approximately 56%, respectively. The cell counts in the curd were also similar, with 9.0 ± 0.2 log CFU g⁻¹ for both strains, indicating that the R5 strain grew and was retained in the matrix to the same extent as the parental strain. The volatile compounds were extracted using headspace solid-phase microextraction and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Of the 30 compounds identified, most showed similar abundance in the two sets of cheeses. However, 3-hydroxy-2-butanone (acetoin) was found to be increased approximately 2.5-fold in the curds made with the R5 strain (P < 0.01). Diacetyl and 2,3-butanediol also showed upward trends, although these did not reach significance. The increased production of acetoin, a key flavor compound associated with buttery notes in fresh cheeses, suggests a redirected pyruvate flux in the R5 strain, possibly connected to NADH reoxidation under oxidative conditions.

The selection for Lcn972 resistance produced a stable derivative with increased survival to H₂O₂ and better aerobic growth and acidification, while preserving the performance of the parental strain in standard dairy processes. This is of interest because Lcn972 resistance was not selected for on the basis of oxygen physiology, suggesting that cell envelope perturbation and oxidative stress share common adaptive routes in lactococci. The link between the two phenotypes is consistent with earlier reports that envelope-targeting agents induce broad stress responses in L. lactis. The R5 phenotype is likely a pleiotropic consequence of a regulatory or structural change in the envelope, although the specific mutation(s) remain to be identified. Whole-genome resequencing and transcriptomic comparison with the parental strain will be necessary to test this hypothesis and to rule out the contribution of unrelated mutations accumulated during serial passage.

The improved behavior of the R5 strain in aerobic conditions was evident in faster growth in broth and in lower final pH in aerated milk, suggesting that the trait is relevant in a food matrix and not only in laboratory media. Oxygen is a recognized stressor for lactococci, and increased tolerance to H₂O₂ would be expected to prolong viability and metabolic activity during processes involving vigorous agitation, such as starter propagation and the early stages of vat filling. However, the enhanced oxygen tolerance did not extend to respiratory conditions, suggesting that the protective mechanism acquired by the R5 strain is independent of the respiratory pathway. This distinction is useful from an applied perspective, as it indicates that the R5 strain improves performance under standard fermentative conditions without requiring supplementation with heme.

The traits that did not change are also informative. Oxidative stress tolerance is often assumed to correlate with resistance to other technological stresses, such as cold storage and freeze-drying, which damage cells in part through oxidation of membrane lipids and proteins. However, the R5 strain did not show higher survival after cold storage or freeze-drying, suggesting that cryotolerance and desiccation tolerance are multifactorial and depend strongly on membrane fluidity, cytoplasmic solute accumulation, and the growth phase at harvest. The result also shows that the evolved phenotype is relatively specific and was not accompanied by a generalized stress-resistant state. Although a broader gain in robustness would have been attractive, specificity can be considered an advantage, because pleiotropic stress resistance is sometimes linked to slower growth or reduced acidification, trade-offs that are unacceptable in a starter. From a practical perspective, the R5 strain offers improved performance in aerobic conditions without compromising its suitability for standard dairy applications. Further research is needed to fully characterize the benefits and limitations of the R5 strain and to explore its potential for use in industrial settings. 

In conclusion, the R5 strain of L. lactis IPLA947, which was selected for its resistance to the cell wall-active bacteriocin Lcn972, exhibits enhanced tolerance to oxidative stress and improved performance in aerobic conditions. The strain's ability to produce increased levels of acetoin, a key flavor compound in fresh cheeses, is also a notable advantage. While the R5 strain does not exhibit increased resistance to cold storage or freeze-drying, its improved performance in aerobic conditions makes it a promising candidate for use in industrial dairy applications. Further research is needed to fully characterize the R5 strain and to explore its potential for use in a variety of settings. The use of adaptive laboratory evolution to generate robust industrial strains without recourse to recombinant DNA is a promising approach, and the R5 strain is a notable example of the potential benefits of this approach. By selecting for resistance to a cell wall-active bacteriocin, we were able to generate a strain with improved performance in aerobic conditions, without compromising its suitability for standard dairy applications. This approach could be used to generate strains with a range of improved traits, and could potentially be used to improve the performance of a variety of industrial microorganisms.

The analysis of presence-absence data, which records the occurrence of species at different sites in a binary matrix, is a fundamental aspect of community ecology and biogeography. A key question in this field is whether such matrices exhibit patterns that cannot be attributed to chance. Several types of patterns have been identified, including nestedness, where species found at species-poor sites tend to form subsets of those found at richer sites, as well as checkerboard patterns and co-occurrence more generally. To quantify these patterns, researchers often use matrix summaries, such as the NODF or temperature metrics, which are then compared to a null distribution obtained by randomizing the data. The validity of the conclusions drawn from these comparisons depends on how well the null model represents the "no pattern" hypothesis.

Null models for presence-absence matrices differ primarily in the features of the observed data that they preserve. Unconstrained models, which treat all cells as exchangeable, are known to produce inflated type I error rates due to the heterogeneous species prevalences and site richnesses that induce nestedness-like structure. In response, the dominant approach has been to preserve the row and column sums of the observed matrix, resulting in the fixed-fixed model. This model has become a default choice, as it is implemented in widely used software, recommended in methodological comparisons for its ability to keep type I error low in simulation studies, and has been applied in numerous studies of nestedness and co-occurrence.

However, the computational challenges of sampling uniformly from the set of binary matrices with given margins have led to the development of various algorithms, including the Curveball, swap, and sequential importance sampling algorithms. Despite the attention paid to these computational aspects, less consideration has been given to the statistical implications of conditioning on both margins. In a fixed-fixed model, the row and column sums are treated as known constants, rather than as quantities subject to random variation. This assumption is problematic, as species richness at a site and prevalence of a species are themselves outcomes of the ecological and sampling processes being studied. Moreover, nestedness is directly related to the distribution of the margins, and a perfectly nested matrix is fully determined by its margins.

As a result, for many empirical matrices, the set of matrices sharing the observed margins may be small, or even trivially small, in which case no randomization is possible. This phenomenon, which we refer to as limited randomizability, can lead to artificially narrow reference distributions, making it difficult to interpret the results of statistical tests. Related concerns have been raised in the ecological literature, where it has been noted that fixed-fixed models may remove part of the signal of interest, resulting in reduced power. However, the converse risk, that conclusions of significance become overly optimistic, has received little systematic study.

A natural alternative to fixed-fixed models is to relax the margin constraints and allow row and column sums to vary around their observed values, preserving them only in expectation. Several such models exist, including the fixed-equiprobable and equiprobable-equiprobable models, which use only a subset of margin information, and proportional models, which sample cells with probabilities that depend on observed margins. However, many of these models are ad hoc, and it is unclear in what statistical sense they reproduce the margins or what probabilistic model of the data they represent.

In contrast, the psychometric and ecological literatures offer principled parametric models, such as the Rasch model, which treats each cell as an independent Bernoulli variable whose probability depends on a row effect and a column effect. The Rasch model has been used to describe species-site data and is closely related to the maximum-entropy distribution on binary matrices with margins fixed in expectation. This model offers sound statistical properties, including well-understood estimation by conditional or marginal maximum likelihood, diagnostics for goodness of fit, and the fact that fixed-fixed randomization is exactly the conditional distribution of the Rasch model given its sufficient statistics, the margins.

Despite these connections, the practical consequences of choosing between strictly constrained and relaxed null models have not been systematically compared on empirical presence-absence data, with attention to the reliability of the resulting significance statements. Existing comparisons have focused largely on type I error and power in synthetic matrices generated from specific mechanisms, rather than on the behavior of the null models themselves when applied to real data sets with diverse margin characteristics. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the properties of fixed-fixed models and exploring the potential of Rasch models as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics.

Our research questions are threefold. First, we aim to determine how severely the margin constraints of fixed-fixed models limit the randomizability of real presence-absence matrices. Second, we investigate whether Rasch models can serve as a viable alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics. Third, we compare the significance measures obtained from the two families of models in practice, with a focus on the reliability of the resulting conclusions. By addressing these questions, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the statistical properties of null models for presence-absence data and to provide guidance for researchers seeking to analyze and interpret these data.

The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we analyze the properties of fixed-fixed models, showing how the size and structure of the set of matrices with given margins constrain the null distribution. We then explore the potential of Rasch models as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics. Finally, we compare the significance measures obtained from the two families of models in practice, with a focus on the reliability of the resulting conclusions. By examining the behavior of these models on empirical presence-absence data with diverse margin characteristics, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of each approach and to inform the choice of null models in future studies. The concept of limited randomizability is crucial in the analysis of presence-absence data, as it can significantly impact the results of statistical tests. To quantify this phenomenon, we examined a collection of empirical data sets and compared the performance of different null models. Our study consisted of three main components. First, we evaluated the degree of randomizability in our data sets using various diagnostics. Second, we presented the Rasch model as a null model for presence-absence data and discussed its estimation and sampling.
