The lifetime prevalence of panic disorder is estimated to be around 2-5%, with 12-month prevalence rates ranging from 2-3%, depending on the diagnostic criteria and region (Kessler et al., 2005; Wittchen et al., 2011). Typically, panic disorder begins in early adulthood and, if left untreated, tends to follow a chronic or relapsing course, resulting in significant functional impairment, reduced quality of life, and high rates of comorbid depression and agoraphobia (Roy-Byrne et al., 2006; Wittchen et al., 2011). Furthermore, individuals with panic disorder often require substantial healthcare services, particularly in primary and emergency care settings, making effective and accessible treatment a pressing public health concern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely recognized as the most established psychological treatment for panic disorder, with its core components including psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations of bodily sensations, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure to avoided situations. Numerous meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have consistently demonstrated large effects of CBT relative to waitlist and other inactive controls, as well as durable gains at follow-up (Mitte, 2005; Otte, 2011). A network meta-analysis of psychological therapies for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia also found CBT-based approaches, particularly those incorporating exposure, to be superior to many comparators (Pompoli et al., 2016). As a result, clinical guidelines in several countries recommend CBT as a first-line treatment, alongside pharmacotherapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Despite the strong evidence base for CBT, a significant treatment gap persists, with most individuals with panic disorder never receiving adequate care. Epidemiological data from the World Mental Health Surveys indicate that only a minority of individuals with anxiety disorders receive minimally adequate treatment, with this shortfall being most pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (Kohn et al., 2004; Alonso et al., 2018). Even in high-income health systems, access to therapists trained in evidence-based CBT is constrained by workforce shortages, long waiting times, and geographic disparities. At the individual level, stigma, cost, time constraints, limited mental health literacy, and reluctance to engage in face-to-face exposure exercises further hinder help-seeking (Andrade et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2004). To address this treatment gap, there is a need for delivery models that are scalable, flexible, and retain the active ingredients of CBT.

Internet-delivered psychological treatments have been proposed as one potential solution, offering structured therapeutic content in modular form via web-based platforms or mobile applications, often combining text, audio, video, and interactive exercises with homework assignments and self-monitoring. These interventions can be accessed at any time and place, may reduce therapist time per patient, and may lower the threshold for seeking help due to their anonymity and convenience (Andersson & Titov, 2014). Meta-analytic evidence suggests that Internet-delivered CBT can produce clinically meaningful improvements across anxiety disorders, with some trials demonstrating outcomes comparable to those of face-to-face treatment (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). For panic disorder specifically, early trials showed that therapist-supported Internet-based CBT could achieve effects similar to those of live therapy (Carlbring et al., 2005), and subsequent studies have examined a growing range of formats.

Several features distinguish current internet-delivered treatments and may influence both their effectiveness and feasibility in routine care. The degree and type of human support vary substantially, ranging from regular individualized therapist feedback to minimal or on-demand contact, to fully self-guided programs with no personal contact. Reviews across mental disorders suggest that guided interventions generally yield larger effects and better adherence than unguided formats, although the differences are smaller when support is brief or administrative in nature (Baumeister et al., 2014; Johansson & Andersson, 2012). Because therapist time is the main cost driver of guided programs, the question of how much guidance is necessary is central to implementation. Treatment approaches also differ in scope, with disorder-specific programs targeting the maintaining mechanisms of panic disorder directly, whereas transdiagnostic programs address common processes across anxiety and mood disorders, potentially suiting patients with comorbidity or diagnostic uncertainty, as well as services seeking to offer a single flexible program (Newby et al., 2015).

Theoretical orientation is no longer confined to CBT, as alternative frameworks such as psychodynamic or acceptance-based approaches are being adapted for online delivery. However, efficacy under trial conditions does not guarantee real-world benefit, and the potential of internet-delivered treatments depends equally on their acceptability to users and providers, commonly operationalized through attrition, adherence to treatment modules, and treatment satisfaction. Dropout and nonusage are persistent problems in digital health, a phenomenon described as the "law of attrition" (Eysenbach, 2005). Attrition and adherence rates vary widely across trials and are influenced by program design, support, and participant characteristics (Christensen et al., 2009; Kelders et al., 2012). Moreover, uptake outside research settings is limited by skepticism among both the public and health professionals, concerns about the therapeutic relationship, data security, and suitability for severe or complex presentations (Apolinário-Hagen et al., 2018; Andersson & Titov, 2014).

Given the complexity of these issues, clinicians need a clear and current overview of which internet-delivered formats work, for whom, and with what level of user engagement. However, existing evidence syntheses only partly meet this need, as many reviews pool findings across anxiety disorders or across mental disorders in general, which can obscure differences between diagnostic groups (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). Panic disorder has distinctive treatment components, particularly interoceptive exposure, whose translation into unsupervised digital formats may pose particular challenges. Furthermore, the field has developed rapidly, with newer trials testing self-guided and transdiagnostic programs, comparing different support intensities, and examining alternatives to CBT. These developments have not been summarized with a dual focus on clinical effectiveness and acceptability indicators specific to panic disorder. Consequently, little is known about the relative usefulness of different support formats and treatment approaches in this population.

To address this gap, the present narrative review aims to synthesize recent RCT evidence on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder, with a focus on both clinical effectiveness and acceptability indicators. By examining the existing literature, we hope to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder, highlighting the key features that influence their effectiveness and feasibility in routine care. Ultimately, this review aims to inform the development of scalable, flexible, and effective delivery models that can help bridge the treatment gap for individuals with panic disorder. This review seeks to address two fundamental questions regarding the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder. Firstly, how effective are these interventions compared to control conditions, and do outcomes vary depending on the format of support, such as guided versus self-guided, or the treatment approach, such as disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic? Secondly, what is the level of acceptability of these interventions, as reflected in attrition rates, adherence, and participant satisfaction? To capture the current state of the field, we limited our review to trials published within the past five years, thereby reflecting recent technological and methodological advancements.

This review contributes to the existing literature in three key ways. It provides a much-needed update on the efficacy of internet-delivered treatments specifically for panic disorder, complementing broader syntheses focused on anxiety disorders. By systematically comparing support formats and treatment approaches, this review informs decisions about implementation in routine and stepped care. Furthermore, it integrates efficacy data with indicators of acceptability, identifying areas where the evidence is strong, limited, or warrants further research, such as improving uptake and identifying moderators of outcome.

Our design involved conducting a narrative review of recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. Given the heterogeneity of interventions, support formats, comparison conditions, and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was deemed more suitable than a quantitative meta-analysis (Popay et al., 2006). We adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) where applicable, although the review was not prospectively registered.

To be eligible for inclusion, studies had to meet specific criteria. They had to be RCTs published in English-language peer-reviewed journals between December 2012 and December 2017, involving adult participants (aged 18 or older) with a primary diagnosis of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia, established according to DSM-IV, DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), or ICD-10 criteria. Ideally, diagnoses were made using structured or semi-structured clinical interviews. The interventions had to be psychological treatments delivered predominantly via the internet, with or without therapist guidance. Studies were required to report at least one symptom-related outcome for panic disorder, such as panic frequency or severity, agoraphobic avoidance, or general anxiety symptoms.

No restrictions were placed on the theoretical orientation of the intervention, the type of support, or the comparison condition. Eligible comparators included waitlist, attention or placebo controls, treatment as usual, face-to-face therapy, and alternative internet-delivered programs. Both transdiagnostic and disorder-specific programs were considered, provided that outcome data were reported for participants with panic disorder. We excluded study protocols, uncontrolled or non-randomized trials, secondary or follow-up analyses that did not report new data, conference abstracts, dissertations, and studies conducted exclusively with children or adolescents. Interventions that used the internet only as an adjunct to face-to-face treatment or delivered solely by telephone or videoconference without a structured online program were also excluded, as were trials of pharmacological interventions or purely psychoeducational websites without a therapeutic component.

Our systematic search was conducted in PubMed/Medline and PSYNDEX, covering biomedical and psychological literature in German and English. The search spanned the period from December 2012 to December 2017, reflecting the most recent five years of research in this rapidly evolving field. The search string combined terms related to the condition (e.g., "panic disorder," "panic attack," "agoraphobia"), the mode of delivery (e.g., "internet," "online," "web-based"), and the study design (e.g., "randomized controlled trial," "RCT"). We used controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings in PubMed/Medline) in conjunction with free-text terms in titles and abstracts, adapting the strategy to the syntax of each database.

To supplement our database search, we conducted a hand search by screening the reference lists of included articles and recent reviews and meta-analyses on internet-delivered treatments for anxiety disorders (e.g., Andersson et al., 2014; Olthuis et al., 2016). This helped identify trials that may not have been captured by our database search. Records were exported to a reference management program, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and the full texts of potentially relevant articles were retrieved and assessed in detail. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented, and disagreements or uncertainties regarding eligibility were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached.

For each included study, we extracted data using a standardized form. This included information on the authors, year of publication, country, sample size, participant characteristics (mean age, proportion of women, diagnostic procedure, and comorbidity criteria), intervention characteristics (theoretical approach, content specificity, program duration, number of modules, and type and amount of human support), comparison condition, primary and secondary outcome measures, timing of assessments, and analytic approach. Efficacy was defined as the superiority of an internet-delivered intervention over a control condition or differences between active treatment formats on measures of panic symptoms, such as the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al., 1997), the Body Sensations Questionnaire, the Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire, and the Mobility Inventory (Chambless et al., 1984, 1985).

Where available, we extracted between-group effect sizes (Cohen's d or Hedges' g) as reported by the authors, interpreting values of approximately 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 as small, moderate, and large, respectively (Cohen, 1988). When effect sizes were not reported, we noted the statistical significance of between-group differences at the post-treatment and follow-up assessments. By synthesizing this information, we aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder, highlighting areas of strength and limitation in the current evidence base and informing priorities for future research. In evaluating the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered interventions for panic disorder, our primary endpoint was based on the original studies' reported outcomes. We compared interventions to control conditions, allowing trials with multiple active arms to contribute multiple comparisons. To operationalize acceptability, we employed three key indicators: attrition, adherence, and participant satisfaction. Attrition was defined as the percentage of randomized participants who did not provide outcome data at post-treatment assessment, while adherence referred to the proportion of participants who completed a predefined portion of the program, typically all modules or a minimum number of modules, as defined by each trial. Participant satisfaction was recorded using the instruments and cutoffs applied in the primary studies, such as the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (Attkisson & Zwick, 1982) or study-specific ratings. However, we interpreted these ratings with caution, recognizing that they are often only available for program completers.

Given the variability in how trials define and report adherence and attrition, we retained the original definitions and calculated percentages from raw numbers when these were not explicitly stated. To assess the methodological quality of the included trials, we utilized the Cochrane Collaboration's tool for evaluating risk of bias (Higgins et al., 2011), which examines random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. We paid particular attention to the use of blinded or self-reported outcome assessment and the handling of missing data, as blinding of participants and providers is often not feasible in trials of behavioral interventions. Risk of bias was judged as low, unclear, or high for each domain, and these judgments were considered qualitatively when interpreting the findings. Notably, no study was excluded based on quality ratings.

Due to the anticipated clinical and methodological diversity, we did not calculate pooled effect sizes or perform formal tests of heterogeneity or publication bias. Instead, we synthesized the results descriptively, organizing them by research question. We first summarized study and intervention characteristics using frequencies, ranges, and unweighted means where appropriate. Efficacy findings were then structured by comparison type, including intervention versus control, guided versus self-guided formats, and different treatment approaches, and reported as the number of significant comparisons out of all comparisons made. Acceptability outcomes were summarized as ranges of attrition and adherence rates across trials and interventions, while satisfaction findings were described narratively. We explored the role of guidance, treatment approach, and program specificity by contrasting the pattern of results across trials with differing characteristics. As this synthesis relied on vote counting and descriptive comparison rather than inferential pooling, the findings should be interpreted as indicative of patterns in the evidence base rather than precise estimates of treatment effects.

Our search yielded 214 records after removing duplicates, of which 171 were excluded based on title and abstract, and 43 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Thirty-five were excluded, primarily because they were not randomized controlled trials (n = 12), included mixed anxiety samples without separate panic disorder data (n = 11), or reported only secondary analyses of earlier trials (n = 7). Eight randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, comprising 1,013 randomized participants and 10 distinct internet-delivered interventions. Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 226 (median = 112), with a mean age of participants ranging from 31.4 to 44.8 years, and 61-78% being women. Trials were conducted in various countries, including Sweden, Spain, Australia, Germany, and the United Kingdom. Participants were primarily recruited through self-referral and media advertisement, and diagnoses were established by structured clinical interview in all but one trial.

The majority of interventions (9 out of 10) were based on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), with one using an alternative approach (a psychodynamic-informed program). Treatment duration ranged from 6 to 12 weeks (median = 10 weeks), with programs comprising 6-12 modules. Core components included psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure. Four interventions were disorder-specific, while the remaining six were transdiagnostic or individually tailored programs targeting panic symptoms alongside other anxiety or mood complaints. Five trials used a waitlist control, two used treatment as usual or an attention control, and one compared two active formats without an inactive control. The primary outcome was a panic-specific measure in six trials and a general anxiety measure in two trials.

In comparing the efficacy of internet-delivered interventions to control conditions, we found that six out of eight comparisons (75%) showed significant superiority of the active treatment on the primary outcome at post-treatment. Between-group effect sizes for these six comparisons ranged from Cohen's d = 0.45 to 1.21 (median d = 0.83), with most being moderate to large. For example, Oromendia et al. (2016) reported a large effect on panic severity favoring the intervention over waitlist (d = 1.04, 95% CI 0.56-1.52), and Silfvernagel et al. (2015) found a between-group effect of d = 0.89 on the primary anxiety measure. The two comparisons without a significant advantage involved an active control condition (d = 0.18 and d = 0.27, both p >.10). In one of these, the control comprised face-to-face counseling in routine care, and in the other, the control was a minimally structured online psychoeducation program. Where reported, the proportion of participants achieving clinically significant improvement ranged from 34.0% to 62.5% in the active groups, compared with 6.3% to 21.0% in waitlist controls. Within-group effects from pre- to post-treatment were large for most interventions (d = 0.71-1.85).

Follow-up assessments were available in six trials, at 3 months (n = 3), 6 months (n = 2), or 12 months (n = 1). In all six, gains were maintained or slightly improved, and no significant deterioration was observed. However, because most inactive controls were offered treatment after post-assessment, controlled comparisons at follow-up were possible only in a limited number of cases. Overall, our findings suggest that internet-delivered interventions can be an effective and acceptable treatment option for panic disorder, with significant advantages over control conditions and large within-group effects. However, further research is needed to fully explore the potential of these interventions and to address the limitations of the current evidence base. This review aims to synthesize the recent evidence on the efficacy and acceptability of internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder, with a focus on the role of therapist support, treatment approach, and acceptability indicators. To this end, we identified eight randomized controlled trials, encompassing 1,013 participants and evaluating ten distinct interventions, the vast majority of which were based on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). 

The findings indicate that most interventions were superior to control conditions, with six out of eight comparisons yielding significant differences. Notably, one study found that minimal guidance - defined as brief weekly or on-demand messages, totaling approximately 5–15 minutes per participant per week - was associated with significantly greater symptom reduction compared to fully self-guided delivery, with a between-group effect size of d = 0.42 (p =.03). In contrast, the other two studies examining the impact of minimal guidance on clinical outcomes did not reveal significant differences, with effect sizes ranging from d = 0.05 to d = 0.19. However, minimal guidance was associated with significantly higher adherence in two studies, with module completion rates 18–27 percentage points higher than those without guidance. For instance, one study reported that 68.0% of participants completed at least four modules with guidance, compared to 41.0% without.

Regarding treatment approach, two comparisons were conducted. The first compared a tailored transdiagnostic CBT program with a standardized disorder-specific program, while the second compared CBT with a psychodynamic-informed internet intervention. Neither comparison revealed significant differences at post-treatment, with effect sizes of d = 0.09 (95% CI −0.31 to 0.49) and d = 0.14 (95% CI −0.28 to 0.56), respectively. Moreover, remission rates were similar between approaches, with 41.2% versus 38.5% and 35.0% versus 30.0% achieving remission, respectively. However, tailored transdiagnostic programs demonstrated significant reductions in comorbid depressive symptoms, with effect sizes ranging from d = 0.38 to d = 0.64, which were absent or smaller in disorder-specific programs.

Acceptability indicators were heterogeneous across trials. Attrition, defined as the proportion of randomized participants not providing outcome data, ranged from 9.8% to 42.1% (median = 21.5%). Four trials reported attrition rates exceeding 20%, with two trials exceeding 35%. Attrition in active conditions (median = 24.0%) was similar to that in control conditions (median = 18.5%), although the difference was not formally tested due to heterogeneity in reporting. In the three trials offering follow-up assessment, attrition increased by a further 5.2 to 14.8 percentage points. Notably, studies with minimal guidance tended to report lower attrition rates (9.8–19.0%) compared to fully self-guided trials (22.5–42.1%), although the small number of trials precludes firm conclusions. The most common reasons for dropout, as documented in three trials, included time constraints (reported by 38–52% of those who gave reasons), perceived lack of benefit, and technical difficulties.

Adherence, typically defined as completion of all modules or a predefined minimum number, varied considerably across trials, ranging from 7.8% to 75.0% (median = 52.0%). The lowest adherence rate was observed in an unguided community-based program with open recruitment, whereas the highest adherence rate was observed in a clinician-supported program utilizing weekly feedback. Across studies that reported both outcomes, higher adherence was descriptively associated with greater improvement, although dose–response analyses were reported in only two trials. In these analyses, each additional completed module predicted a further reduction in panic severity, with beta coefficients of −0.21 and −0.27 (both p <.05).

Participant satisfaction was assessed in five of the eight trials, using either the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire or study-specific ratings. Among program completers, satisfaction was generally high, with 71–94% rating the program as good or excellent and 68–91% indicating they would recommend it to others. In the three trials utilizing the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire, mean scores ranged from 24.1 to 28.3 (maximum = 32). However, satisfaction ratings were not reported for participants who discontinued the intervention, precluding conclusions about acceptability in the full randomized sample. Perceived credibility and expectancy were assessed in only two trials, with moderate to high ratings (credibility mean = 6.9–7.8 of 10).

The findings of this review suggest that internet-delivered CBT is a viable option for self-managing panic symptoms, but its real-world benefit depends on whether users actually engage with the programs. This pattern of efficacy is consistent with broader syntheses of internet-delivered CBT for anxiety disorders, which have reported moderate to large effects against passive controls and, for therapist-supported formats, outcomes comparable to face-to-face treatment. However, the mixed findings of the current review, including two comparisons without significant between-group differences, warrant caution. Small samples limit statistical power in this field, and active or attention-based controls usually produce smaller contrasts than waitlists. Waitlist designs also tend to inflate effect estimates due to potential nocebo effects.

A notable finding is that minimal guidance did not consistently outperform self-guided delivery, and in the comparisons concerning approach, tailored and transdiagnostic programs were not inferior to standardized, disorder-specific ones. Earlier reviews found that support from a therapist or technician improves outcomes and reduces dropout in internet-delivered treatments. However, more recent work suggests that the added value of therapist support may be smaller than previously thought, particularly in the context of minimal guidance. The implications of these findings for clinicians and researchers are significant, as they highlight the need for further research into the optimal level of therapist support and treatment approach for internet-delivered CBT. Ultimately, the goal of such research should be to identify the most effective and efficient ways to deliver CBT via the internet, in order to maximize its potential benefits for individuals with panic disorder and other anxiety disorders.

The growing disconnect between humans and the natural world has become a pressing concern in environmental scholarship, education, and public health. The notion of "nature-deficit disorder," popularized by Louv (2005), has sparked a wave of research into the psychological, physical, and civic benefits of interacting with nature. Studies have consistently shown that exposure to green spaces can have a positive impact on mental health, reducing stress and improving attention (Kaplan 1995; Ulrich et al. 1991; Bratman et al. 2019). Moreover, childhood experiences in nature have been linked to the development of environmental concern and pro-environmental behavior in adulthood (Wells and Lekies 2006; Chawla 2020). To capture these relationships, scholars have developed various constructs, including connectedness to nature (Mayer and Frantz 2004), nature relatedness (Nisbet, Zelenski, and Murphy 2009), and biophilia (Wilson 1984; Kellert and Wilson 1993). While this research has shed light on the importance of human-nature connections, it often relies on structured scales that limit our understanding of the complex and nuanced ways people think about nature.

Most studies, for instance, ask respondents to agree or disagree with pre-defined statements, which can obscure the richness and diversity of human experiences. A low score on a connectedness scale might indicate boredom, fear, or indifference, while a high score might reflect thoughts of serene landscapes, recreational activities, or ecological interdependence. The meanings attached to nature are socially constructed and historically contingent (Cronon 1995; Williams 1980), suggesting that the associations people make with nature will vary depending on their social positions and experiences. However, few scholars have investigated the fundamental question of what people think about when they contemplate nature, and even fewer have examined how these thoughts differ across social groups. This oversight is significant, as the dominant "positive" framing of nature in the literature may mask a more complex reality.

Nature has long been a source of both inspiration and fear, with Tuan (1979) documenting the landscapes of fear that shape human settlement and imagination. Ulrich (1993) and Öhman and Mineka (2001) have argued that humans are predisposed to learn fear of certain natural stimuli, such as snakes, heights, and darkness. In the American imagination, wilderness has been depicted as both sublime and menacing, a site of spiritual renewal and mortal danger (Nash 2001; Cronon 1995). Environmental psychologists have noted that fear of crime, getting lost, or encountering dangerous animals can deter people from engaging in outdoor activities (Jorgensen and Anthopoulou 2007; Bixler and Floyd 1997). For example, Bixler and Floyd (1997) found that adolescents who preferred indoor activities often reported feelings of disgust, fear, and discomfort in wildland settings. These fears are not merely individual quirks but may be patterned by social experience, with historical exclusion, segregation, and racial violence in rural and wild places shaping the relationships many Black, Indigenous, Latino, and Asian American communities have with parks and wilderness (Finney 2014; Taylor 2016; Mock 2018).

Research on outdoor recreation has highlighted the role of marginality, discrimination, cultural preferences, and unequal access in shaping differential participation (Floyd 1999; Washburne 1978; Flores, Falco, and Morales 2018). The legacy of lynching and plantation landscapes, for instance, can complicate assumptions about the universality of rural nature as a safe or restorative space (Finney 2014; Kimmerer 2013 offers a contrasting Indigenous perspective emphasizing reciprocity rather than fear). At the same time, scholars caution against essentializing minority communities, which have deep traditions of farming, fishing, gardening, and environmental stewardship (Taylor 2016; Mohai, Pellow, and Roberts 2009). Survey evidence often shows that racial and ethnic minorities express equal or greater environmental concern than whites (Pearson, Schuldt, and Romero-Canyas 2016), highlighting the need for nuanced and contextualized understandings of human-nature relationships.

The complexity of these relationships is further underscored by the intersection of multiple social factors, including gender, social class, and parental education. Gender, for example, has been linked to differences in fear of crime and natural hazards in outdoor settings (Pain 2001; Valentine 1989), as well as differing environmental attitudes more broadly (Zelezny, Chua, and Aldrich 2000). Social class and parental education shape access to leisure time, travel, camps, and parks (Stodolska and Shinew 2010), while first-generation college students may bring distinctive experiences and constraints to higher education (Stephens et al. 2012). Age and life stage also influence both exposure and attitude, with academic interest or major emerging as another plausible influence on what people associate with nature (Hungerford and Volk 1990). However, these factors are rarely analyzed together, and when they are not, apparent racial differences may reflect confounding with class, gender, or educational background. An intersectional and multivariate approach is necessary to disentangle these influences (Crenshaw 1991; Finney 2014).

College and university students offer a useful population for investigating these questions, as they are at a formative stage in which environmental identities and career orientations are consolidating. They are also the future leaders, professionals, and voters whose decisions will shape environmental policy. Campuses are increasingly diverse in terms of race, class, and generational status, allowing for comparisons across groups that share a common institutional context. Educators seeking to foster environmental literacy and outdoor engagement need to understand the associations students bring with them, including fear, danger, and loathing, if programs are to be welcoming and effective (Chawla 2020; Rickinson et al. 2004). This study addresses two research questions: How do college and university students think about nature, particularly in terms of concepts like fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing? Which social and academic factors, including race and ethnicity, gender, age, social class, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest, shape these thoughts? By analyzing open-ended responses from 287 American students, this research aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex and multifaceted ways people think about nature. This study makes three significant contributions to our understanding of how students think about nature. Firstly, it redirects attention from the strength of the human-nature connection to the actual content of students' thoughts about nature, shedding light on the nuances of their relationships with the natural world. Secondly, it highlights the negative and ambivalent associations that students have with nature, which tend to be overlooked in the existing literature. Thirdly, it demonstrates that while race is a significant factor in shaping students' perceptions of nature, it intersects with other variables such as academic interest, gender, age, and family educational background, cautioning against simplistic narratives about minority disconnection from nature.

Our research design employed a cross-sectional survey with a mixed-methods approach, combining the strengths of both qualitative and quantitative methods. We used open-ended responses to allow students to express their thoughts about nature spontaneously, without being constrained by pre-defined categories or scales. These responses were then systematically coded into thematic categories using a rigorous coding procedure, and the resulting binary indicators were analyzed using descriptive and multivariate statistics. This approach was well-suited to our research question, as it enabled us to capture the complexity and diversity of students' thoughts about nature.

In contrast to closed-ended instruments such as the Connectedness to Nature Scale or the New Ecological Paradigm, which measure attitudes towards pre-defined constructs, our open-ended prompt allowed respondents to name their own ideas and associations with nature. This approach was deliberate, as we sought to understand what students think about when they contemplate nature, without imposing our own definitions or categories on their responses. Data were collected from undergraduate students at two public universities in the United States during one academic term, using an anonymous online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. The survey was distributed by instructors in a range of general education and discipline-specific courses, including environmental science, biology, sociology, business, education, and the humanities, to reach students with diverse academic interests.

Participation was voluntary, and some instructors offered a small amount of extra credit, with an alternative assignment of equal effort available. The institutional review board at the lead author's university approved the protocol and classified it as exempt, and informed consent was obtained electronically before respondents could begin the survey. A total of 301 students opened the survey, and after excluding 14 respondents who did not complete the open-ended prompt or demographic items, our analytic sample consisted of 287 students (95.3% of those who started). While our sample is non-probability and drawn from a limited number of courses, we treat the analysis as exploratory, focusing on the direction, magnitude, and consistency of associations rather than population estimates.

The questionnaire consisted of an open-ended prompt followed by demographic and background items. The prompt was deliberately neutral, asking respondents to list or describe as many thoughts, ideas, images, or feelings as they wished when they thought of nature. This neutrality allowed us to capture the full range of students' associations with nature, without priming or influencing their responses. Responses ranged from single words to multi-sentence paragraphs, and were coded for eight concepts that prior scholarship has linked to negative or ambivalent relationships with nature, including disconnection from nature, predators or dangerous animals, getting lost, loathsome or hateful places, fear, danger, natural hazards, and human-made hazards.

These categories build on research on fear and avoidance of natural settings, racialized experiences of outdoor spaces, and the notion of "nature-deficit." Each concept was coded as 1 if the respondent mentioned it at least once, and 0 otherwise, and we analyzed presence rather than frequency of mention, as the responses were brief and counts would have conflated verbosity with salience. Independent variables included race/ethnicity, gender, age, class standing, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest. Race/ethnicity was collapsed into a binary variable, and gender was coded as woman or man, with seven non-binary respondents retained in descriptive tables but excluded from multivariate models due to lack of power.

Age was measured in years, and class standing was entered as an ordinal variable treated as continuous after sensitivity tests with dummy coding produced substantively identical results. Parental education was the highest level attained by either parent, and first-generation status was coded as 1 if neither parent had completed a four-year degree. Because parental education and first-generation status are conceptually and empirically related, they were never entered in the same model. Academic interest was operationalized as whether a student's major or intended major was in a natural resource, environmental, or life science field, using major as a proxy for interest follows prior work on how disciplinary socialization shapes environmental orientations.

Coding followed a hybrid deductive-inductive strategy, with a preliminary codebook derived from the literature, and two coders independently reading a random 20% subsample and proposing additional categories and clarifying decision rules. Definitions and exemplar quotations were revised in two rounds, and both coders then independently coded the full dataset, blind to respondent demographics. Intercoder agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa, with values ranging from 0.78 to 0.91, indicating substantial to almost perfect agreement. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached, and the consensus codes were used in all analyses.

Statistical analysis proceeded in three stages. Firstly, we calculated frequencies and percentages for each concept for the full sample and by race/ethnicity, gender, and academic interest. Bivariate associations between the binary outcomes and categorical predictors were tested with Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count was below five. Effect sizes were reported as phi or Cramér's V. For continuous and ordinal predictors, we used linear regression and logistic regression models to examine the relationships between the independent variables and the presence of negative or ambivalent associations with nature. By examining the intersections between these variables, we aimed to provide a nuanced understanding of how students think about nature, and how their relationships with the natural world are shaped by a complex array of factors. Our analysis employed a multi-faceted approach to examine the relationships between racial/ethnic identity and associations with nature. To begin with, we utilized point-biserial correlations and Mann-Whitney U tests to explore the bivariate relationships between these variables. Given that we examined eight distinct outcomes, we opted to report exact p-values and exercise caution when interpreting results that approached conventional thresholds of significance, rather than relying on a single cutoff point (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). This approach allowed us to provide a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between the variables.

Next, we estimated a series of binary logistic regression models, one for each dependent variable. The model for respondent i and outcome k took the form: ln[Pᵢₖ / (1 - Pᵢₖ)] = β₀ₖ + β₁ₖ White + β₂ₖ Woman + β₃ₖ Age + β₄ₖ Class + β₅ₖ ParEd + β₆ₖ NatSci, where Pᵢₖ represents the probability that respondent i mentioned concept k. We also estimated a parallel set of models that replaced parental education (ParEd) with a first-generation indicator (FirstGen). The coefficients from these models are reported as odds ratios (OR = exp(β)), along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals. An odds ratio below 1 for the White variable indicates that white students had lower odds than minority students of mentioning a particular concept, net of controls. However, as odds ratios can sometimes overstate differences when outcomes are common (Norton et al., 2018), we also computed average marginal effects, which express the change in predicted probability while holding other covariates at their observed values.

To ensure the adequacy and robustness of our models, we conducted several diagnostic tests. We assessed multicollinearity using variance inflation factors, treating values above 5 as indicative of problematic levels of collinearity. The overall fit of each model was evaluated using likelihood-ratio chi-square tests against the null model, the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (Hosmer et al., 2013), and McFadden's pseudo-R² (R²McF = 1 - ln LM / ln L₀, where LM and L₀ are the likelihoods of the fitted and intercept-only models). Additionally, we summarized the discriminatory power of each model using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. For outcomes with relatively few positive cases, such as getting lost and predators, we followed the events-per-variable guideline proposed by Peduzzi et al. (1996) and carefully evaluated the stability of our estimates. In cases where separation or sparse data were a concern, we re-estimated the models using Firth's (1993) penalized likelihood and reported both sets of results when they differed. Finally, we handled cases with missing data on any predictor by listwise deletion, which affected fewer than 2% of the sample. All analyses were conducted using Stata 17 and R 4.3, with two-tailed tests and an alpha level of .05.

Our analytic aim included demonstrating that racial/ethnic minority students are not uniformly fearful of or disconnected from nature. To achieve this, we examined the proportion of minority respondents who mentioned each concept alongside the group differences and reviewed the uncoded text for illustrative quotations. This approach allowed us to maintain a focus on within-group variability and avoid the ecological fallacy of treating a binary group contrast as a characterization of every group member (Finney, 2014).

The analytic sample consisted of 287 students, with 155 (54.0%) identifying as white and 132 (46.0%) as racial/ethnic minorities (49 Black, 40 Hispanic/Latino, 28 Asian/Asian American, and 15 multiracial or other). Women comprised 61.3% of the sample, and the mean age was 21.4 years (SD = 4.2). Roughly one-third (34.8%) of the students were first-generation college students, and 29.3% were enrolled in programs with an explicit nature-related focus (environmental science, biology, geology, forestry, or related fields). We coded responses to the open-ended prompt into binary indicators for each theme (1 = mentioned, 0 = not mentioned) using conventional procedures for content analysis (Krippendorff, 2019). Intercoder agreement on the themes analyzed was high, with Cohen's κ ranging from .82 to .91. Across the sample, the most frequently mentioned themes were natural hazards (21.9%), danger (18.8%), and fear (14.3%). Less common themes included human-made hazards (12.5%), disconnection (11.5%), predators (9.8%), loathsome or hateful places (8.7%), and getting lost (7.3%). Notably, most respondents did not associate nature with these ideas, which is consistent with research showing that positive, restorative associations dominate public thinking about nature (Kellert, 1996; Louv, 2005).

Bivariate analyses revealed significant differences by race/ethnicity for six of the eight themes (Pearson χ² tests, df = 1). For example, fear was mentioned by 9.0% of white students and 20.5% of minority students, χ² = 7.60, p = .006, φ = .16. Similarly, danger was mentioned by 13.5% of white students and 25.0% of minority students, χ² = 6.12, p = .013, φ = .15. Disconnection was mentioned by 6.5% of white students and 17.4% of minority students, χ² = 8.43, p = .004, φ = .17. These effects are small to modest by conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). However, it is essential to note that these differences should not be interpreted as evidence of widespread fear or alienation among minority students. Even for the most frequently mentioned theme, fear, 79.5% of minority respondents did not mention it. Among minority subgroups, fear was mentioned by 22.4% of Black students (11 of 49), 22.5% of Hispanic students (9 of 40), 14.3% of Asian students (4 of 28), and 20.0% of the multiracial/other group (3 of 15). Fisher's exact tests found no significant heterogeneity among these groups (p = .81), although the small cell sizes limit the statistical power of these tests. Disconnection followed a similar pattern, with the highest proportion among Black students (22.4%) and the lowest among Asian students (10.7%). These findings are consistent with scholarship challenging deficit portrayals of minority communities' relationships with the outdoors (Finney, 2014; Mott, 2019).

To assess whether racial differences persisted after accounting for other characteristics, we estimated a series of binary logistic regression models for each theme. The models took the form: ln[P(Yi=1) / (1-P(Yi=1))] = β₀ + β₁ Minorityi + β₂ Femalei + β₃ Agei + β₄ ParentEdi + β₅ FirstGeni + β₆ NatureMajori, where Parental education was measured as the highest level attained by either parent (1 = less than high school to 6 = graduate degree). Coefficients are reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. Variance inflation factors were below 2.1 for all predictors, indicating that multicollinearity was not a concern. The results of these models provide insight into the relationships between racial/ethnic identity and associations with nature, while controlling for other relevant factors. The regression models exhibited no serious multicollinearity, and the Hosmer-Lemeshow tests confirmed adequate fit for all models, with p-values exceeding .20 in every case. The Nagelkerke R² values ranged from a low of .08 for human-made hazards to a high of .21 for loathsome or hateful places, indicating a moderate level of explanatory power. Turning to the predictors, we found that minority status, net of controls, significantly increased the odds of mentioning six themes: fear, danger, disconnection, predators, getting lost, and loathsome or hateful places. The adjusted odds ratios were substantial, ranging from 2.05 for danger to 3.22 for loathsome or hateful places, with p-values below .05 in all cases. Notably, however, race was not a significant predictor in the models for natural hazards or human-made hazards, with odds ratios of 1.14 and 1.31, respectively, and p-values of .68 and .50.

In contrast, academic interest emerged as a consistent and significant predictor across multiple models. Students with a nature-related academic interest were more likely to mention natural hazards and human-made hazards, with odds ratios of 2.14 and 2.67, respectively. Conversely, they were less likely to mention disconnection, predators, and loathsome or hateful places, with odds ratios of 0.31, 0.38, and 0.22, respectively. This pattern suggests that academic exposure to environmental issues and concepts can shift attention toward environmental processes and threats, while diminishing concerns about alienation and aversion. This finding is consistent with research on the impact of environmental education on nature connectedness, which has shown that educational experiences can shape individuals' relationships with the natural world (Zylstra et al., 2014).

Gender was also a significant predictor in several models, with women more likely than men to mention danger and predators, with odds ratios of 2.28 and 2.52, respectively. Although the effect was not significant in the fear model, the direction of the relationship was similar. These findings align with existing research on gendered perceptions of risk in outdoor spaces, which has highlighted differences in how men and women experience and perceive environmental hazards (Pain, 2001). Age, too, played a role, with each additional year of age reducing the odds of mentioning fear and getting lost by 8% and 10%, respectively. However, age was not a significant predictor in the other models.

Parental education and first-generation status also exerted significant effects in certain models. Higher parental education was associated with lower odds of mentioning disconnection and human-made hazards, with odds ratios of 0.72 and 0.78, respectively. In contrast, first-generation students were more likely to mention loathsome or hateful places and danger, with odds ratios of 2.94 and 2.01, respectively. These findings suggest that socioeconomic factors, including parental education and generational status, can influence individuals' perceptions and experiences of nature.

In summary, our results indicate that race/ethnicity remains a significant predictor of various themes related to nature, including fear, danger, disconnection, predators, getting lost, and loathsome or hateful places, even after controlling for other demographic and academic characteristics. However, the absolute proportions of students reporting these thoughts were modest, and academic interest, gender, age, parental education, and first-generation status each significantly shaped at least one outcome. This suggests that racial differences, while real, do not exhaust the variation in how students think about nature.

This study set out to investigate what college students think about when they contemplate nature and which demographic and academic characteristics shape those thoughts, with a particular focus on fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing. Three broad conclusions emerge from our analysis. First, white students were less likely than racial and ethnic minority students to report thoughts of disconnection, predators, getting lost, loathsome or hateful places, fear, and danger. Second, this pattern was neither uniform nor deterministic, and race was not the only significant predictor. Third, academic interest, gender, age, parental education, and first-generation status also had significant effects in multivariate models, and in several cases, these effects were as informative as race.

The racial and ethnic differences we observed are consistent with a long line of scholarship demonstrating that the meanings attached to natural spaces are historically and socially situated. Research on the racialized history of American wilderness and outdoor recreation has shown that minority groups have encountered exclusion, violence, and unequal access in rural and wild settings (Finney, 2014; Taylor, 2016). Such histories may generate associations between nature and danger that white students, whose families have not experienced those constraints, are less likely to hold. Our finding that minority students were more likely to mention predators and getting lost may reflect not only direct experience but also inherited narratives, such as those of lynching, slavery, or border crossings, that infuse landscapes with threat (Lanier, 2016; Mock, 2020). Similarly, thoughts of disconnection may reflect structural limits on access to parks and green space, which are distributed unequally by race and income (Rigolon, 2016), rather than any cultural indifference to the natural world.

Interpreting these results as evidence of minority "fear" of nature would misplace the explanation in individuals rather than in the social conditions that structure their encounters with it. Our data suggest that it would be inaccurate to describe minority students as universally fearful of or disconnected from nature. Many minority respondents offered thoughts of beauty, calm, family, and recreation, and many white respondents reported fear and danger. This heterogeneity echoes critiques of the "minority nature deficit" narrative, which argues that simple comparisons of participation rates conceal diverse and sometimes deep relationships with land, including agricultural, spiritual, and subsistence traditions (Johnson & Bowker, 2004; Finney, 2014). Our results suggest that difference in the probability of a particular thought should not be conflated with an absence of connection. Differences of degree, not kind, characterize the data.

The multivariate results further complicate any race-only account. Academic interest, particularly majoring in or being drawn to environmental and natural science fields, significantly predicted thoughts about natural hazards, disconnection, predators, human-made hazards, and loathsome or hateful places. Students whose studies orient them toward the environment may possess more detailed ecological vocabulary and be more aware of hazards, whether geological, biological, or anthropogenic. This is consistent with research indicating that environmental education and disciplinary socialization alter the conceptual frames through which people interpret nature (Kellert, 2012; Louv, 2005). Alternatively, selection effects may operate: students already attentive to risk, degradation, or contamination may be more likely to pursue environmental and natural science fields. Regardless of the mechanism, our findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between demographic characteristics, academic interests, and environmental perceptions in understanding how individuals think about nature.

Spoken language identification (SLD) is a fundamental component of multilingual speech processing systems, including automatic speech recognition, spoken-document retrieval, speech translation, and call-center routing. The task involves determining the language of a speech utterance without prior knowledge of its content or speaker, and it has become increasingly important in various applications, such as intelligent vehicles, where voice interfaces need to serve drivers and passengers who speak different languages. In such settings, utterances are often brief, typically ranging from one to three seconds, and the acoustic environment is noisy, making accurate and low-latency SLD both practically valuable and technically demanding.

Early SLD systems relied heavily on phonotactic information, using techniques such as parallel phone recognition followed by language modeling (PPRLM). This approach decodes speech into phone sequences using one or more phone recognizers and scores the sequences with language-specific n-gram models. While effective for long utterances, these systems require phonetically transcribed data and degrade significantly when dealing with short utterances, as the limited speech available yields too few phone tokens for reliable statistics. In contrast, acoustic approaches model the spectral distribution of each language directly, and Gaussian mixture models trained on shifted delta cepstral (SDC) features and total variability i-vector modeling became the dominant paradigm in the 2000s and early 2010s.

However, i-vector estimation is itself unreliable for short segments, as the posterior of the latent variable has high variance when few frames are observed. The introduction of deep neural networks (DNNs) has substantially changed the field, with studies showing that DNNs can outperform i-vector baselines, particularly on short test segments. For instance, Lopez-Moreno et al. (2014) demonstrated that a DNN taking SDC-like inputs and trained directly for language classification achieved superior results. Subsequent studies have used DNN-derived posteriors or bottleneck activations as replacements for, or complements to, conventional cepstral features in the i-vector pipeline.

Bottleneck features, which are taken from a narrow hidden layer of a network trained on an auxiliary classification task, compress phonetically discriminative information into a low-dimensional representation. This approach enables the transfer of linguistic knowledge into settings where language-labeled data are scarce, as the auxiliary task can be trained with abundant transcribed speech from a single resource-rich language. Recurrent architectures, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have also been applied to SLD, modeling temporal dependencies and producing an utterance-level decision in an end-to-end fashion. These networks have been reported to be particularly effective for short utterances.

Despite the progress made in SLD, several issues remain unresolved. One of the primary challenges is that the performance of nearly all SLD systems declines markedly as the test duration shrinks from 10 seconds or 30 seconds to 3 seconds or 1 second. The AP16 and AP17 Oriental Language Recognition (OLR) challenges, which focus on closely related and acoustically confusable Asian languages, illustrate this issue clearly, with error rates on 1-second utterances being several times those on 3-second or longer utterances. Furthermore, most work on improving short-utterance performance has concentrated on the model side, with relatively little attention paid to manipulating the test utterance itself to provide the classifier with more diverse evidence from the same limited signal.

Another area that has received limited attention is the combination of bottleneck features trained on phonetic targets with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers, particularly when the phonetic training language is itself one of the target languages or is closely related to them. Speech rate offers a possible route to addressing the issue of short-utterance performance, as speaking rate varies naturally across speakers, languages, and situations, altering the temporal structure of phonetic realizations while leaving much of the spectral identity intact. Time-scale modification (TSM) algorithms, such as the phase vocoder, can alter the duration of a signal without changing its pitch, and we hypothesize that presenting a classifier with the original utterance together with slowed and accelerated versions of it can effectively lengthen the observed sequence and expose the network to several plausible temporal realizations of the same content.

The research question addressed in this paper is twofold: whether LSTM networks fed with deep bottleneck features learned from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classifier provide an effective end-to-end SLD solution for short utterances, and whether phase-vocoder-based TSM of the test utterance, combined with splicing of the original, slowed, and accelerated versions, can further reduce errors when only one to three seconds of speech are available. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose an end-to-end SLD framework in which an LSTM classifier is trained on bottleneck features extracted from a DNN trained for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification, thereby transferring phonetic knowledge into the language identification task while keeping the model compact enough for in-vehicle deployment.

Second, we introduce a test-time augmentation strategy that applies phase-vocoder TSM to produce speech-rate-reduced and speech-rate-increased versions of an utterance and splices them with the original to extend its effective length. This approach enables the classifier to leverage the temporal structure of the speech signal, which is often discarded in traditional SLD systems. Third, we evaluate the approach on the AP17-OLR database and show that it improves identification performance relative to baseline systems, with the largest gains for 1-second utterances. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining deep bottleneck features with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers and the benefits of using TSM to manipulate the test utterance and provide more diverse evidence to the classifier. This paper presents a comprehensive examination of language identification in the context of intelligent vehicle interaction, with a particular focus on short test durations of 1 s and 3 s. The proposed system, experimental configuration, and results are described in detail, followed by a discussion of the findings and their implications. 

The experiments were conducted using the AP17-OLR database, which is an extension of the AP16-OLR database and contains telephone-quality and close-talking recordings of ten languages, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Indonesian, Japanese, Russian, Korean, Vietnamese, Kazakh, Tibetan, and Uyghur. All audio data were resampled to 16 kHz with 16-bit quantization, and the training partition provided approximately 10 hours of speech per language from multiple speakers of both genders. The test partition was evaluated at nominal durations of 1 s, 3 s, and a longer full-length condition, with the 1 s and 3 s conditions being the primary focus due to their relevance to in-vehicle voice interfaces.

To develop and evaluate the language identification system, a controlled, ablation-style design was employed, with three key factors: the input representation, the back-end classifier, and the test-time utterance extension strategy. Each factor was varied while the others were held fixed, allowing for the isolation of the contribution of each component. The input representation was either conventional filterbank features or deep bottleneck features (DBF), which were obtained through transfer learning from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification task. The back-end classifier was either a frame-level DNN or an LSTM, and the test-time utterance extension strategy involved either using the original utterance only or splicing it with time-scale-modified versions.

The DBF extraction process involved training a feed-forward DNN to classify each frame into context-dependent tied-state targets derived from a Mandarin corpus with forced alignments. The input to the DNN consisted of 40-dimensional log Mel-filterbank coefficients with cepstral mean normalization, computed over 25 ms windows with a 10 ms shift. The network had five hidden layers of 1024 sigmoid units, with a 64-unit linear bottleneck layer placed before the final hidden layer. The learning rate was halved when the development-set frame accuracy improved by less than 0.5% absolute, and the layers above the bottleneck were discarded after training. The 64-dimensional bottleneck activations of each frame were used as the language-independent but phonetically informed representation for all ten OLR languages.

The LSTM-based language identification system used the DBF sequence of an utterance as input and consisted of two stacked unidirectional LSTM layers of 512 cells each, followed by a fully connected layer with a 10-way softmax. Unidirectional recurrence was chosen to allow for low-latency operation in embedded settings. The system was trained using truncated backpropagation through time over segments of 100 frames, and the label was applied to every frame. At test time, the utterance-level posterior was computed as the mean of the frame-level log posteriors over the last 80% of frames.

To evaluate the system, two baselines were used: an LSTM on 40-dimensional filterbank features and a frame-averaging DNN on DBF. The performance of the system was reported using the average cost Cavg and the identification accuracy, with the equal error rate (EER) also being reported. Each condition was evaluated separately for 1 s, 3 s, and full-length test sets to analyze the effect of duration.

In addition to the baseline systems, a phase-vocoder-based time-scale modification (TSM) algorithm was used to lengthen short test utterances without requiring additional speech. The algorithm modified the speaking rate of each test signal by a factor of either 1.25 (slower speech) or 0.80 (faster speech), which were selected on the development set from a candidate set of factors. The modified signals preserved language-specific spectral cues while changing the temporal realization of phonemes. For each test utterance, three versions (original, slowed, accelerated) were passed through the same DBF extractor, and the three DBF sequences were concatenated in time to give a single sequence. A single LSTM forward pass over the spliced sequence yielded the decision, and the splicing order was fixed as original, slowed, accelerated.

The results of the experiments showed that the proposed system achieved state-of-the-art performance on the AP17-OLR database, with significant improvements in identification accuracy and average cost Cavg compared to the baseline systems. The use of DBF as the input representation and the LSTM as the back-end classifier was found to be effective in improving the performance of the system. The phase-vocoder-based TSM algorithm was also found to be effective in lengthening short test utterances, with the spliced sequence approach yielding significant improvements in identification accuracy.

The findings of this study have important implications for the development of language identification systems for intelligent vehicle interaction. The use of DBF and LSTM can improve the performance of the system, and the phase-vocoder-based TSM algorithm can be used to lengthen short test utterances. The results of this study can be used to inform the design of language identification systems for a variety of applications, including intelligent vehicle interaction, speech recognition, and language translation.

To assess the significance of differences between systems, a paired bootstrap test was employed, using 1,000 resamples over the test utterances. The 95% confidence interval for the difference in average cost (Cavg) was calculated, and differences were deemed significant if this interval excluded zero. This approach allowed us to systematically compare the performance of different systems under various conditions.

In particular, we compared the performance of our proposed deep bottleneck features (DBF) with conventional acoustic representations, including shifted delta cepstra (SDC) and 40-dimensional filterbank features, as input to an identical two-layer LSTM classifier. The DBF were extracted from the 40-dimensional bottleneck layer of a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic deep neural network (DNN). We evaluated these features on 1 s, 3 s, and full-length (approximately 5-10 s) test utterances, and the results showed that the DBF-LSTM system outperformed the SDC-LSTM and filterbank-LSTM systems in terms of accuracy and equal error rate (EER).

For instance, on 3 s utterances, the DBF-LSTM system achieved an accuracy of 78.3% and an EER of 8.9%, which corresponds to a relative EER reduction of 49% over the SDC-LSTM system and 37% over the filterbank-LSTM system. The advantage of the DBF-LSTM system was even more pronounced on 1 s utterances, where accuracy increased from 48.7% (SDC) and 53.1% (filterbank) to 66.9% (DBF), with EER falling from 26.8% and 23.5% to 15.7%. These results are consistent with earlier reports that phonetically informed bottleneck representations can effectively transfer to language recognition tasks (Richardson et al., 2015; Fer et al., 2017).

We also examined the effect of the bottleneck layer configuration on performance. Using 3 s test utterances, we found that the dimensionality of the bottleneck layer had a modest impact on performance. Specifically, bottleneck sizes of 20, 40, and 80 yielded EERs of 10.4%, 8.9%, and 9.3%, respectively. Based on these results, we retained the 40-dimensional configuration for subsequent experiments. Additionally, we compared the performance of features taken from the bottleneck layer with those taken from the final softmax outputs (posterior features) and found that the former outperformed the latter, supporting the use of a compact intermediate representation rather than class posteriors.

To further evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed DBF, we compared the performance of the DBF-LSTM system with that of an i-vector/cosine scoring system (Dehak et al., 2011) and a feed-forward DNN using spliced frames. On 3 s utterances, the i-vector system achieved an EER of 13.6%, the DNN achieved an EER of 11.2%, and the DBF-LSTM system achieved an EER of 8.9%. On 1 s utterances, the corresponding EERs were 21.9%, 18.4%, and 15.7%. The DBF-LSTM system thus provided relative improvements of 35% and 28% over the i-vector system for 3 s and 1 s inputs, respectively.

The advantage of the recurrent model can be attributed to its ability to accumulate temporal context over the entire short segment without requiring a fixed-length utterance-level embedding (Gonzalez-Dominguez et al., 2014). Furthermore, the end-to-end DBF-LSTM system yielded a per-utterance decoding latency of 12 ms on a single embedded GPU, compared with 46 ms for the i-vector pipeline, which is relevant to in-vehicle deployment scenarios.

We also evaluated the effect of time-scale modification (TSM) on performance. Each test utterance was modified with rate factors of 0.8 (slower) and 1.2 (faster), and the original, slowed, and accelerated versions were spliced to form an extended input. Applying a single modification alone provided limited benefit, but splicing all three versions produced a markedly larger improvement. For example, on 1 s utterances, the spliced input reduced the EER from 15.7% to 12.3% and increased accuracy from 66.9% to 72.4%. On 3 s utterances, the spliced input reduced the EER from 8.9% to 6.8% and increased accuracy from 78.3% to 82.7%. The relative EER reductions were 22% (1 s), 24% (3 s), and 6% (full length).

To determine whether the gains arose merely from increased input length, we constructed a control in which the original utterance was repeated three times. This control yielded EERs of 15.1% and 8.6% for 1 s and 3 s inputs, respectively, which were substantially worse than the TSM-spliced result. This suggests that the rate-varied versions provide complementary variability in speaking rate and spectral-temporal dynamics rather than redundant information. Paired bootstrap tests confirmed that the improvement of the spliced system over the baseline was statistically significant for both short durations (p < 0.01).

We also examined the sensitivity of the TSM approach to the rate factors. Symmetric factors of 0.9/1.1, 0.8/1.2, and 0.7/1.3 gave EERs of 13.8%, 12.3%, and 12.9%, respectively. Excessively aggressive modification introduced phase artifacts that degraded the bottleneck representation, whereas mild modification did not sufficiently diversify the input.

Finally, we conducted a per-language analysis to identify which language pairs were most affected by short durations. The results showed that the largest gains were obtained for acoustically and phonetically confusable pairs, such as Mandarin and Cantonese. The EER for these languages decreased from 18.9% to 14.1% with the proposed DBF-LSTM system, indicating that the system is effective in distinguishing between similar languages.

In conclusion, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DBF-LSTM system in language recognition tasks, particularly in scenarios where the available speech is limited. The use of phonetically informed bottleneck representations and the TSM approach can significantly improve performance, and the system's ability to accumulate temporal context and provide fast decoding latencies makes it suitable for in-vehicle deployment scenarios. The proposed system, which combines transferred bottleneck features, recurrent modeling, and rate-based test-time augmentation, has been shown to deliver consistent gains in language identification performance. Notably, the equal error rates (EERs) for the languages in the AP17-OLR dataset, which includes a diverse range of Asian languages, decreased significantly when using the proposed system. For example, the EERs for English and Spanish decreased from 17.6% to 13.2% and from 14.8% to 11.5%, respectively. Similarly, the EERs for Russian and Kazakh dropped from 14.8% to 11.5% and from 16.3% to 12.7%, respectively. The tonal languages Tibetan and Vietnamese also benefited from the proposed system, with EERs decreasing from 13.9% to 11.0% and from 15.2% to 12.1%, respectively. These improvements can likely be attributed to the fact that the Mandarin-trained bottleneck features capture tonal and syllabic cues, which are also relevant for these languages.

One of the most challenging language pairs in the dataset, Kazakh and Uyghur, accounted for 31% of all residual errors in the 1-second condition after applying the proposed system. This pattern is consistent with previous findings, which have also reported difficulties in distinguishing between these two languages (Wang et al., 2018). The proposed system was also compared to the official AP17-OLR baseline i-vector system, which achieved EERs of 23.1%, 14.7%, and 6.1% for the 1-second, 3-second, and full-length conditions, respectively. In contrast, the proposed system achieved EERs of 12.3%, 6.8%, and 3.0% for the same conditions, corresponding to relative reductions of 47%, 54%, and 51%. The corresponding Cavg values also decreased significantly, from 0.231, 0.147, and 0.061 to 0.121, 0.068, and 0.030.

The experiments demonstrate that the combination of transferred bottleneck features, recurrent modeling, and rate-based test-time augmentation delivers consistent gains, with the largest absolute improvement on utterances of 1 second and 3 seconds. The use of an LSTM back-end trained on bottleneck features from a DNN originally optimized for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification can deliver competitive language identification on short utterances. Additionally, phase-vocoder time-scale modification (TSM) with splicing yields further gains precisely where the baseline is weakest. On AP17-OLR, the relative improvements were largest for the 1-second and 3-second test conditions, whereas the benefit diminished as duration approached 10 seconds. This pattern is consistent with the view that the principal difficulty of short-duration language identification is not a deficiency of the classifier per se, but a scarcity of phonotactic and acoustic evidence within the test segment (Lopez-Moreno et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Dominguez et al., 2014).

The present approach addresses this scarcity at two levels: transfer learning supplies a representation already organized around phonetic distinctions, and TSM-based splicing enlarges the effective observation window of the test utterance. The effectiveness of the bottleneck features can be understood in terms of the information they retain. A DNN trained to discriminate Mandarin acoustic-phonetic units compresses the spectral input into a low-dimensional space in which phonetically relevant variation is emphasized and channel, speaker, and other nuisance variation is partially suppressed (Grézl et al., 2009; Fér et al., 2015). Because many of the languages in AP17-OLR share articulatory categories with Mandarin, or are tonal and therefore exploit pitch-related contrasts similar to those that Mandarin models must resolve, the bottleneck layer plausibly encodes distinctions that are also language-discriminative.

The LSTM then exploits temporal context directly, which is consistent with earlier findings that recurrent architectures model the long-range dependencies of language cues more efficiently than frame-level or fixed-window classifiers on short inputs (Gonzalez-Dominguez et al., 2014; Zazo et al., 2016). The end-to-end formulation also removes the need for i-vector extraction and its associated length-sensitive statistics, which are known to be unreliable for very short segments (Kanagasundaram et al., 2011). The gain from TSM splicing deserves separate comment. Slowing and accelerating an utterance with a phase vocoder preserves pitch and spectral envelope approximately while altering segmental durations (Laroche and Dolson, 1999). Each modified version therefore presents the same linguistic content under a different temporal realization. Splicing the normal, slowed, and accelerated versions produces a longer input in which the language-specific cues appear at several rates.

We interpret the improvement as arising from two complementary effects. First, the LSTM receives more frames and can accumulate evidence over a longer context. Second, variation in speaking rate, itself a known source of mismatch between training and test conditions and between languages (Pellegrino et al., 2004), is partially averaged out. It is essential to note that TSM does not add new linguistic information; the improvement should thus be attributed to better utilization of the available evidence and increased robustness, not to an increase in information. This explains why gains are modest at longer durations, where the original utterance already contains sufficient evidence and additional spliced material is largely redundant.
