Furthermore, errors were also larger when the USV heading was nearly aligned with the camera line of sight, and the 180° heading ambiguity inherent in symmetric-shape techniques produced isolated errors close to π rad on 0.6-2.1% of frames. These errors were retained in all reported statistics, and the four orientation techniques were affected similarly by these effects.

In terms of parameter requirements and sensitivity, we found that thresholding required six manually set parameters, in addition to the morphological kernel size, whereas histogramming required only a reference histogram, a back-projection threshold, and the kernel size. Both algorithms required manual retuning before each trial, and reusing the parameters from the preceding trial increased the mean position error by a factor of 2.4-5.8 for thresholding and 1.9-3.7 for histogramming, with a corresponding increase in orientation error of 0.11-0.29 rad. Histogramming was therefore less sensitive to mis-specification, but neither algorithm was free of the tuning requirement.

We also evaluated the robustness of the algorithms to illumination changes during a segment of Trial 4, in which cloud cover reduced scene brightness by approximately 40% over about 8 s. Within the first 3 s, the mean position error increased from 15 to 61 px for histogramming and from 34 to 118 px for thresholding. Neither algorithm recovered without retuning, and tracking was reinitialized manually after approximately 5 s. These frames were excluded from the aggregate statistics reported above but are included in the Trial 4 sequence length. This failure highlights the lack of sufficient robustness to significant illumination changes in both hue-based approaches, although the histogramming algorithm degraded more gracefully.

The interpretation of our results is that hue-based position estimation and shape-based orientation estimation can meet the requirements of estimating the full pose of a rescue USV from a UAS under challenging conditions, including oblique views of up to 85° from nadir, distances of up to 180 m, a 5 Hz update rate, and simultaneous motion of the UAS and the vessel. The mean position error of 7 to 43 px is small relative to the image dimensions, and this accuracy appears adequate for a vehicle-following task. However, whether it suffices for closer cooperative tasks, such as precise rendezvous, will depend on the ground sampling distance at the operating altitude and requires separate verification.

The histogramming algorithm outperformed thresholding in position estimation in all four trials, with p-values ranging from approximately 0 to 8.23 × 10⁻²⁹. Two properties of histogram-based methods plausibly explain this. First, a histogram model represents the full distribution of hue and saturation values of the target, rather than a single hard interval, making it less sensitive to gradual hue shifts caused by specular glare, wave-induced changes in surface normals, and variation in atmospheric path length at long range (Comaniciu et al., 2003). Second, back-projection yields a graded likelihood instead of a binary mask, so partially occluded or poorly lit regions of the vessel still contribute to the centroid. Histogramming also needed fewer tunable parameters than thresholding, which is operationally significant because parameter-heavy pipelines are difficult to configure in the field during an emergency.

The orientation results were more mixed, with histogramming giving significantly lower orientation error in only two trials (p = 3.52 × 10⁻³⁹ and 1.33 × 10⁻⁴⁶). The mean errors of 0.134 to 0.480 rad (about 7.7° to 27.5°) were larger than desirable, which is physically plausible given that orientation was derived from the shape of the segmented region. At oblique angles near 85° from nadir, the vessel is strongly foreshortened and perspective distorted, so the apparent aspect ratio and principal axis of its silhouette no longer correspond to its true heading in the world plane (Hartley & Zisserman, 2003). Better segmentation cannot remove this distortion, which explains why the superiority of histogramming for position did not carry over to orientation in every trial. The orientation error is therefore dominated by the geometry of the projection and not by the choice of color model.

Our study has several limitations that bound the claims that can be made. First, the large orientation error limits the use of the current estimates for closed-loop heading control or for deciding the vessel's direction of travel when it is slow or stationary. Second, both algorithms needed manual tuning before each trial, which conflicts with the goal of reducing manpower in mass casualty events. Third, the lack of robustness to significant illumination changes is a significant limitation, highlighting the need for further research into more robust color models or alternative approaches. Despite these limitations, our results demonstrate the potential of hue-based position estimation and shape-based orientation estimation for estimating the full pose of a rescue USV from a UAS, and highlight the importance of careful consideration of the view geometry, parameter requirements, and robustness to illumination changes in the design of such systems.

The estimation of probability density functions is a cornerstone of statistical learning and data mining, underpinning a wide range of applications, from exploratory data analysis and visualization to probabilistic classification and outlier detection. Traditional approaches to density estimation, such as kernel density estimators and finite mixture models, rely on the assumption that observations are independent draws from a single, fixed distribution. However, this assumption is increasingly at odds with the realities of modern data collection, where observations often arrive continuously and the underlying distribution evolves over time.

In many domains, the composition of the data changes in response to external factors, such as macroeconomic conditions, lending policies, or environmental regulations. For instance, in consumer credit scoring, the characteristics of loan applicants shift over time, while in environmental health, pollutant concentrations and exposure profiles vary in response to changes in climate, land use, and regulatory policies. In such settings, the density is better described as a function of both the data space and time, p(x | t), rather than as a single static object.

Research on streaming density estimation has primarily focused on developing methods to keep an estimate current, using techniques such as sliding windows, exponential forgetting, and resource-aware compression schemes. These approaches enable kernel and mixture estimators to track a distribution under bounded memory and in a single pass, but they are fundamentally reactive, yielding an estimate of the density at or shortly before the most recent observation. This limitation matters whenever the density is required at a time point outside the training window, such as forecasting the risk profile of next quarter's loan applicants or anticipating exposure distributions for planning purposes.

We refer to this task as temporal density extrapolation: given samples observed at time points in a training window, estimate the density at a later time point. To our knowledge, this task has received relatively little attention in the literature. While there is related work on predicting future distributions, such as Lampert's (2015) approach to extrapolating a time-varying distribution through its embedding in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, these methods often rely on specific parametric forms or assumptions about the drift process.

A general, nonparametric, and computationally efficient approach to extrapolating densities has been missing from the literature. Several characteristics make this problem challenging. First, the extrapolated object must itself be a valid density, that is, non-negative and integrating to one. Naively extrapolating density values or basis-function weights can violate both constraints, for instance by producing negative weights when a linear trend is extended beyond the observed range. Second, a method should not be restricted to a specific parametric family, such as Gaussians with drifting means, because real-world drift rarely follows such a form. Third, requiring well-separated clusters or components whose identity can be tracked over time limits applicability to data with that structure. Fourth, the method must be efficient enough for streaming scenarios, so that extrapolation does not become the computational bottleneck compared with static estimation.

In this paper, we address the research question of how to extrapolate the density of a gradually and monotonically evolving distribution to future time points without assuming a parametric distribution or a cluster structure, while guaranteeing valid densities and incurring only modest computational overhead. We propose Temporal Density Extrapolation (TDX), which represents the density as an expansion in a fixed set of basis functions, with nonnegative weights that sum to one. These weights are therefore compositional data, living on a simplex rather than in unconstrained Euclidean space.

TDX estimates the weights in consecutive time slices of the training window and maps them to real-valued coordinates through the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation. In this space, the temporal evolution of each coordinate is modeled by a regression function, which is then extrapolated to the requested time point. The extrapolated coordinates are back-transformed to the simplex, ensuring that the resulting weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and hence that the extrapolated density is valid by construction. Because the basis functions are fixed and only their weights vary, the approach is not tied to a parametric family of distributions and does not require the identification or tracking of clusters.

The method introduces only two extrapolation-specific parameters, for which we provide reasonable defaults. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formalize temporal density extrapolation as a distinct learning task, separate from stationary density estimation and reactive density tracking. Second, we introduce TDX, a method that combines basis-function density estimation with a dynamic basis approach to extrapolate densities to future time points. Third, we demonstrate the effectiveness of TDX in a range of experiments, showcasing its ability to accurately extrapolate densities in the presence of gradual and monotonic drift.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing the background and related work on density estimation, streaming data, and concept drift. We then introduce the TDX method, providing a detailed description of the algorithm and its components. Next, we present the results of our experiments, evaluating the performance of TDX on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications of our work and directions for future research.

In the context of density estimation, TDX offers a number of advantages over existing approaches. By representing the density as an expansion in a fixed set of basis functions, TDX avoids the need for parametric assumptions about the underlying distribution. This makes it particularly well-suited to applications where the data are complex or high-dimensional, and where traditional parametric methods may struggle to capture the underlying structure. Additionally, by using a dynamic basis approach to extrapolate the density to future time points, TDX is able to capture gradual and monotonic changes in the distribution, without requiring the identification or tracking of clusters.

The TDX method is also computationally efficient, making it suitable for streaming scenarios where data arrive continuously and the density must be updated in real-time. This is particularly important in applications such as financial risk management, where the ability to quickly and accurately update the density can have a significant impact on decision-making. Overall, TDX offers a powerful and flexible approach to density estimation and extrapolation, with a wide range of potential applications in fields such as finance, environmental health, and consumer credit scoring.

One of the key challenges in developing TDX was ensuring that the extrapolated density is valid, that is, non-negative and integrating to one. This requires careful consideration of the properties of the basis functions and the weights, as well as the use of appropriate transformations to map the weights to real-valued coordinates. The ilr transformation, in particular, plays a critical role in ensuring that the extrapolated weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and hence that the resulting density is valid.

In addition to its technical contributions, this paper also highlights the importance of considering the temporal aspects of density estimation. In many applications, the density is not static, but rather evolves over time in response to changes in the underlying distribution. By developing methods that can capture and extrapolate these changes, we can improve our ability to model and predict complex phenomena, and make more informed decisions in a wide range of fields.

In conclusion, this paper introduces TDX, a novel method for temporal density extrapolation that combines basis-function density estimation with a dynamic basis approach. TDX offers a number of advantages over existing approaches, including its ability to capture gradual and monotonic changes in the distribution, its computational efficiency, and its flexibility in terms of the underlying distribution. We believe that TDX has the potential to make a significant impact in a wide range of fields, and we look forward to exploring its applications in future research. The temporal density extrapolation (TDX) method, which we propose in this paper, addresses the challenge of estimating a time-varying density in a data stream, given a set of observations within a training window. Our approach leverages ilr-transformed compositional weights and regression-based extrapolation, ensuring valid densities without relying on parametric assumptions or cluster structure, and introducing only two additional parameters. To evaluate the effectiveness of TDX, we conduct experiments on synthetic streams with controlled drift patterns and on real-world data from credit scoring and environmental health, comparing its performance to that of static estimators and existing approaches that adapt to drift.

Our results demonstrate that TDX captures monotonic drift more accurately than competing methods, making it a valuable tool for applications where gradual changes in the underlying distribution are expected. Furthermore, we analyze the computational cost of TDX and show that its run time never exceeds 1.5 times that of the corresponding static density estimator, rendering it suitable for streaming use.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing the relevant background on density estimation and compositional data analysis, providing a foundation for the development of the TDX method. We then present the TDX approach in detail, including its formulation, basis expansion, estimation of time-resolved weights, and extrapolation of weights. Following this, we report the results of our experimental evaluation, discussing the performance of TDX on both synthetic and real-world data sets, and highlighting its strengths and limitations.

To formulate the problem of temporal density extrapolation, let us consider a data stream as a sequence of observations $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with time stamps $t_i$, drawn from a time-varying density $p(x, t)$. Given observations within a training window $[t_0, t_T]$, the task is to estimate $p(x, t)$ for a time point $t > t_T$, for which no data are available. We restrict our attention to gradual, monotonous drift, where the change in the density over time follows a consistent direction, rather than oscillating or switching abruptly. This setting is relevant to many real-world processes, such as demographic shifts or slowly increasing environmental exposure, and is distinct from the concept-drift literature, which focuses on detecting and adapting to change after it has occurred.

In our approach, we represent the density as a finite mixture of $K$ fixed basis functions, $p(x, t) = \sum_{k=1}^K w_k(t) \phi_k(x)$, where $w_k(t) \geq 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^K w_k(t) = 1$. Each $\phi_k$ is a normalized density, and we use isotropic Gaussian kernels, $\phi_k(x) = N(x; c_k, \sigma^2 I)$, as is common in kernel and radial-basis-function density estimation. The centers $c_k$ are placed using $k$-means clustering on the training data, which concentrates resolution where data are dense without assuming that the data themselves form clusters. The bandwidth $\sigma$ is selected on the pooled training sample by maximizing a five-fold cross-validated log-likelihood.

Because the basis is fixed across time, all temporal change is carried by the weight vector $w(t)$. This allows the model to adapt to changing densities without being tied to a specific parametric family, and the number of free quantities does not grow with the number of observations. To estimate the time-resolved weights, we partition the training window into $M$ consecutive, equally wide segments, and for each segment $m$, we estimate the weight vector $\hat{w}_m$ by maximum likelihood on the observations in that segment. The basis is held fixed, so the log-likelihood is concave in $w$, and the weights are found using the expectation-maximization updates for mixture proportions.

To avoid zero entries, which would make the subsequent log-ratio transformation undefined, we apply a small additive pseudo-count before renormalization. Segment-wise estimation yields a sequence of $M$ points on the simplex $S^K$, which is the compositional time series to be extrapolated. We then apply the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation to map each $\hat{w}_m$ to $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}$, allowing us to apply standard multivariate regression without distorting distances.

The ilr transformation is an isometry between the Aitchison geometry of the simplex and Euclidean space, ensuring that the distances and angles between the transformed points accurately reflect the relationships between the original weights. We model each of the $K-1$ ilr coordinates as a function of time using a regularized linear regression, fitted to the $M$ segment midpoints by ridge regression with a penalty on the slope. Linear trends in ilr space correspond to exponential-ratio changes in the weights, which is a natural form for gradual monotonous drift.

The two extrapolation-specific parameters of the method are the number of segments $M$ and the regularization strength $\lambda$. We set defaults to $M = 10$ and $\lambda = 1$ after preliminary experiments on separate synthetic streams that were not used for the evaluation reported below. For a requested time point $t$, we predict the coordinates $\hat{z}(t)$, back-transform them to $\hat{w}(t) = \text{ilr}^{-1}(\hat{z}(t))$, and compute the density estimate as $p(x, t) = \sum_{k=1}^K \hat{w}_k(t) \phi_k(x)$. Evaluating the estimate has the same cost as for a static mixture, and the additional training cost consists only of the $M$ weight estimations and $K-1$ low-dimensional regressions.

To evaluate the performance of TDX, we use both synthetic and real-world data sets. The synthetic streams are generated from Gaussian mixtures in $d \in \{1, 2, 5\}$ dimensions with three drift patterns: linear translation of component means, monotone change of mixing proportions, and a combination of both with a gradual increase in variance. For each pattern, we generate 30 random replicates with different seeds, using the first 70% of the time axis for training and the remaining 30% as the extrapolation horizon. Since the true density is known, we can measure accuracy against ground truth.

We also use two real-world data sets: a credit-scoring data set of consumer loan applications, with time stamps given by application date and four continuous applicant attributes, and an environmental health data set. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TDX in capturing monotonic drift and its potential for applications in a variety of fields. We discuss the implications of our findings, highlighting the strengths and limitations of the TDX method, and provide suggestions for future research directions. The environmental-health data set in question comprises time-stamped measurements of air pollutant concentrations, exhibiting gradual trends over the observation period. To assess the performance of our proposed method, TDX, we divided the data into training and testing sets, with the first 70% of the observations used for training and the remaining 30% held out for evaluation. This evaluation set was further divided into five equally sized test blocks, allowing us to assess the accuracy of TDX at increasing distances from the training window.

In order to provide a comprehensive evaluation, we compared TDX to four competing methods. The first, a static kernel density estimator trained on the entire training window, assumes stationarity and serves as a baseline (Silverman, 1986). The second method, a recency-weighted kernel density estimator with exponentially decaying weights, was tuned using cross-validation on the last training segment. We also considered a static Gaussian mixture model fitted to the final training segment only (Bishop, 2006), as well as a Gaussian mixture model whose component means were extrapolated linearly after component matching across segments. To ensure comparability, bandwidths and the number of components were selected using the same cross-validation protocol across all methods.

When evaluating the performance of these methods on real data, where the true density is unknown, we relied on the mean log-likelihood of held-out observations in each test block under the extrapolated density as our primary measure. For synthetic data, we additionally computed the Hellinger distance between estimated and true densities, approximated using Monte Carlo integration with 10^5 samples. To assess the significance of differences between methods, we employed a Friedman test followed by Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons at a significance level of α = 0.05 (Demšar, 2006). Furthermore, pairwise differences between TDX and each competitor were evaluated using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. The effects are reported as mean differences in log-likelihood with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals based on 1,000 resamples.

An essential consideration in the evaluation of these methods is their computational cost and sensitivity to hyperparameters. To this end, we measured the run time as wall-clock time for training and prediction on a single core and reported it relative to the static kernel-based estimator using the same basis, averaged over ten repetitions. The robustness of TDX was assessed by varying the hyperparameters M ∈ {5, 10, 20, 40}, λ ∈ {10^-2, 1, 10^2}, and K ∈ {25, 50, 100}, and examining the resulting change in held-out log-likelihood. All experiments were implemented in Python and run with fixed random seeds to allow replication.

Our experimental overview involved comparing TDX with four competitors: (i) a static kernel density estimate trained on all data in the training window (Static-KDE; Silverman, 1986); (ii) the same estimator restricted to the most recent 20% of the window (Window-KDE); (iii) an exponentially time-weighted KDE (Weighted-KDE) in the spirit of adaptive stream estimators (Heinz & Seeger, 2008); and (iv) a Gaussian mixture model whose component parameters are extrapolated linearly (GMM-Lin). Performance is reported as the mean log-likelihood of held-out observations at the extrapolated time points, averaged over 20 repetitions with different random seeds and expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Higher values are better. For synthetic streams, we also report the integrated squared error (ISE) against the known ground-truth density. The training window covered the first 60% of each stream, and extrapolation horizons were set to 10%, 20%, and 40% of the window length beyond its end. The two extrapolation-specific parameters of TDX, the weight-trend regularisation λ and the trend-fitting window fraction w, were fixed to their defaults (λ = 1, w = 0.5) unless stated otherwise.

We generated four synthetic streams that exhibited gradual monotonous drift: a translating bimodal Gaussian mixture (S1), a mixture with linearly increasing variance (S2), a mixture whose component proportions shift from 0.8/0.2 to 0.3/0.7 (S3), and a two-dimensional banana-shaped distribution undergoing gradual contraction (S4). The results for the 20% horizon are summarised in Table 1. TDX obtained the highest log-likelihood on all four streams. On S1, it achieved −2.41 ± 0.03, compared with −2.87 ± 0.05 for Static-KDE, −2.66 ± 0.06 for Window-KDE, −2.59 ± 0.05 for Weighted-KDE, and −2.52 ± 0.09 for GMM-Lin. The advantage of TDX was most pronounced on S3, where the drift concerned only the mixing proportions: TDX reached −1.98 ± 0.02, whereas the best competitor (Weighted-KDE) reached −2.21 ± 0.04. The ISE results agreed with these findings, demonstrating that TDX reduced the ISE relative to Static-KDE by 63% on S1, 48% on S2, 71% on S3, and 52% on S4 (mean reduction 58.5%), and by 31–44% relative to the best competing method on each stream.

GMM-Lin was competitive on S1 and S2, where its parametric assumptions match the generating process, but deteriorated markedly on S4 (−3.34 ± 0.21), where a Gaussian mixture of fixed size cannot represent the non-convex shape without cluster-assignment instability. In contrast, TDX was not affected by this limitation (−2.93 ± 0.04). The results are presented in Table 1, which shows the mean held-out log-likelihood (± s.d.) at the 20% horizon on synthetic streams.

To further investigate the performance of TDX, we examined the effect of the extrapolation horizon. As expected, all methods degraded as the horizon grew, but at different rates (Figure 3). Averaged over the synthetic streams, the log-likelihood of TDX decreased from −2.19 at the 10% horizon to −2.34 at 20% and −2.71 at 40%, a total loss of 0.52 nats. Over the same range, Static-KDE lost 0.94 nats, Window-KDE 0.81, and Weighted-KDE 0.77. The relative gain of TDX over the best competitor therefore increased with horizon length, from 0.14 nats at 10% to 0.31 nats at 40%. This pattern is consistent with the fact that methods based on past data only implicitly assume stationarity beyond the window, whereas TDX explicitly models the trend of the weights in the isometric log-ratio (ilr) space (Egozcue et al., 2003). In contrast, extrapolation of component means in GMM-Lin relies on a simplistic linear model that may not capture the underlying dynamics.

In conclusion, our experiments demonstrate that TDX outperforms competing methods in terms of log-likelihood and ISE on synthetic streams with gradual monotonous drift. The advantage of TDX is most pronounced when the drift concerns the mixing proportions, and its performance degrades at a slower rate than competing methods as the extrapolation horizon increases. These findings suggest that TDX is a suitable choice for modeling and extrapolating environmental-health data with gradual trends, and its ability to explicitly model the trend of the weights in the ilr space provides a significant advantage over methods that rely on simplistic assumptions or implicit stationarity. The process of extrapolating density estimates from a given set of data is a complex one, particularly when dealing with data that exhibits drift over time. One of the key challenges in this context is ensuring that the extrapolated densities remain valid, i.e., they are non-negative and normalize to one. However, when using raw weights, it is possible for these weights to leave the simplex, resulting in negative or non-normalized densities. To mitigate this issue, we conducted an ablation study in which weights were extrapolated directly and then clipped and renormalized. The results of this study showed that the mean log-likelihood decreased by 0.18 nats at the 20% horizon, and a significant proportion (7.4%) of the extrapolated densities required clipping.

To further investigate the performance of our method, TDX, we applied it to two real-world data streams: credit scoring and environmental health. The credit scoring data consisted of 1.2 million loan applications, each characterized by four numeric features: log income, debt-to-income ratio, credit utilization, and age. Over the observed period, the distribution of these features drifted gradually towards higher debt-to-income ratios and lower credit utilization, a pattern consistent with known population drift in credit portfolios (Gama et al., 2014). At the 20% horizon, TDX achieved a mean log-likelihood of −5.12 ± 0.04, outperforming the competing methods: Static-KDE (−5.58 ± 0.03), Window-KDE (−5.36 ± 0.05), Weighted-KDE (−5.29 ± 0.04), and GMM-Lin (−5.31 ± 0.08). The improvement over the strongest baseline was 0.17 nats, corresponding to a 19% higher average density per observation. A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirmed that this difference was statistically significant (p < 0.001).

The environmental health data comprised daily measurements of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), ozone, temperature, and relative humidity from 38 monitoring stations over eleven years. After removing seasonal fluctuations through deseasonalization, we applied TDX to this data. The results showed that TDX yielded the best score (−3.74 ± 0.02), followed closely by Weighted-KDE (−3.89 ± 0.03), Window-KDE (−3.93 ± 0.03), GMM-Lin (−3.97 ± 0.06), and Static-KDE (−4.02 ± 0.02). Although the absolute gains were smaller than in the credit data, TDX accurately captured the decline in upper-tail PM2.5 concentrations. For instance, the predicted probability of exceeding a regulatory threshold of 35 µg/m³ in the final extrapolated year was 0.041, close to the empirical frequency of 0.043, whereas Static-KDE predicted a significantly higher probability of 0.068.

To provide a comprehensive comparison of the methods, we ranked all of them across the eight streams at three horizons (24 settings). TDX attained the best result in 23 cases and the second-best in the remaining one, with a mean rank of 1.04. In contrast, the mean ranks for Weighted-KDE, GMM-Lin, Window-KDE, and Static-KDE were 2.71, 3.17, 3.46, and 4.62, respectively. A Friedman test rejected the null hypothesis of equal performance (χ² = 85.3, p < 0.001), and a post-hoc Nemenyi test at α = 0.05 with a critical difference of 1.36 showed that TDX was significantly better than every competitor. While the remaining four methods were not all separable from one another, Weighted-KDE, GMM-Lin, and Window-KDE lay within the critical difference.

We also examined the sensitivity of TDX to its parameters, specifically λ and w, by varying them over several orders of magnitude. Across all streams, the mean log-likelihood at the default setting was within 0.03 nats of the best grid configuration in 6 of 8 streams and within 0.09 nats in the remaining two. The performance was most sensitive to w on S4 and the environmental stream, where short fitting windows increased variance, and very strong regularization (λ = 100) flattened the trend and reduced the results towards those of Static-KDE. Additionally, varying the number of basis functions from 25 to 400 showed saturation beyond approximately 100 functions in the two-dimensional streams, with changes of less than 0.02 nats thereafter.

In terms of computational efficiency, the run time of TDX, including basis estimation, ilr transformation, trend fitting, and querying, was on average 1.31 times that of Static-KDE with the same number of basis functions, with a maximum of 1.47 on the credit stream. The additional cost stemmed almost entirely from the weight-trend regression, which scaled linearly with the number of time points and basis functions. Query time for a single extrapolated density was unaffected beyond a constant factor of 1.08. These measurements confirm that the extrapolation capability is obtained at less than 1.5 times the cost of the corresponding static estimator.

The experiments demonstrate that gradual, monotonous distributional change can be extrapolated through the weights of a basis expansion, without a parametric family or cluster structure. Across the synthetic streams, TDX lowered the mean extrapolation error by 14–41% relative to a static kernel density estimator trained on the same window. Against the strongest competing method on each stream, the reduction ranged from 6% to 23%. The advantage was largest where the drift acted on component proportions and location jointly, and smallest where the change was nearly stationary within the training window.

On the credit-scoring and environmental-health streams, TDX improved on the static baseline by 9% and 17%, respectively. This is smaller than on synthetic data, as expected, because real streams combine drift with noise, seasonality, and abrupt shifts that the model does not represent. The central design choice in TDX is to treat the basis weights as compositional data and model them after an isometric log-ratio transformation. Our results suggest that this choice matters, as extrapolating raw weights with linear or polynomial trends produces negative or non-normalized coefficients, and hence invalid densities, within a short horizon. Clipping and renormalizing such weights is a heuristic that distorts the extrapolated trend. In contrast, the ilr coordinates ensure that the back-transformed weights are non-negative and sum to one for any extrapolation horizon, so the output is always a proper density.

In our ablation study, replacing the ilr step with clipped linear extrapolation increased the error by a median of 18% and produced invalid intermediate estimates in a substantial fraction of the long-horizon runs. This highlights the importance of compositional structure for stable extrapolation. However, the ilr coordinates require strictly positive weights, so zeros must be replaced, which remains a source of arbitrariness in the pipeline. Fortunately, our results were insensitive to the replacement value over several orders of magnitude. Overall, TDX differs from related methods in its ability to extrapolate density estimates while preserving the compositional structure of the data, making it a valuable tool for applications where understanding the evolution of distributions over time is crucial.

The widespread adoption of engineered nanoparticles (NPs) across diverse sectors, including medicine, electronics, catalysis, cosmetics, food, and environmental remediation, can be attributed to their unique size-dependent properties. These properties, which encompass optical response, catalytic activity, colloidal stability, biodistribution, and cellular uptake, are largely influenced by the size of the nanoparticles (Wilhelm et al., 2016). Consequently, size, along with particle number concentration, has emerged as a critical quality attribute, with regulators placing significant emphasis on these parameters in defining and controlling nanomaterials. The European Commission's definition of nanomaterials, for instance, stipulates that at least 50% of particles, by number, must have one or more external dimensions between 1 and 100 nm, underscoring the importance of a number-weighted distribution rather than merely a mean diameter (2011/696/EU). Similar requirements for physicochemical characterization are outlined in guidelines from the US Food and Drug Administration (2014) and in the safety assessment frameworks of the OECD. 

In practice, fulfilling these requirements entails generating accurate, traceable, and reproducible size and concentration data across laboratories. Given that most nanoparticles are produced, stored, administered, or encountered in the liquid phase, characterization in suspension is often more relevant than characterization of dried material. The process of drying for electron microscopy can introduce aggregation, shrinkage, salt crystallization, and loss of the hydration shell, resulting in measured sizes that may not accurately reflect the state in which the particles function (Domingos et al., 2009). As an alternative, light-scattering techniques have become a mainstay in nanoparticle characterization. Dynamic light scattering (DLS), also known as photon correlation spectroscopy, infers a hydrodynamic diameter from the decay of intensity fluctuations caused by Brownian motion, utilizing the Stokes-Einstein relationship and cumulants or regularization-based analysis (Koppel, 1972; Pecora, 2000; Stetefeld et al., 2016). This method is notable for its rapidity, small volume requirements, and standardization (ISO 22412:2017), making it the default sizing tool in many laboratories and quality-control environments.

Another technique, nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), standardized as particle tracking analysis (ISO 19430:2016), visualizes the scattered light from individual particles and follows their trajectories, computing diffusion coefficients particle by particle. This capability allows NTA to provide a number-weighted size distribution along with an estimate of particle concentration (Carr and Malloy, 2006; Filipe et al., 2010), rendering it particularly attractive for characterizing extracellular vesicles, viral vectors, and protein aggregates (Dragovic et al., 2011). Despite the apparent simplicity of these instruments, they conceal considerable complexity. For instance, intensity-weighted DLS results are dominated by the largest species present, due to the scattered intensity scaling approximately with the sixth power of particle diameter in the Rayleigh regime. This means that even a small fraction of aggregates or dust can substantially shift the z-average and obscure smaller populations (Bhattacharjee, 2016). The conversion to volume- or number-weighted distributions depends on assumed optical properties and involves the ill-conditioned inversion of the correlation function, limiting the resolution of DLS for polydisperse samples. 

Studies have highlighted the differences in distributions returned by DLS and NTA for mixtures of particles with diameters differing by less than a factor of about two, with accuracy and resolution strongly dependent on the platform and analysis settings (Anderson et al., 2013). For NTA, reported values can vary based on parameters such as camera level, detection threshold, tracking length, temperature, and viscosity. Moreover, counting is biased by the lower detection limit, which for weakly scattering particles, such as polymeric or biological particles, may be well above 50 nm. Interlaboratory studies have indeed reflected these sensitivities, with Hole et al. (2013) finding appreciable variations in sizes from different operators and instruments, even for monodisperse reference materials. Concentration estimates are generally less reproducible than size measurements, with variability often exceeding that of size by an order of magnitude, since the effective scattering volume is inferred from instrument calibration rather than being directly measured.

The influence of parameters external to the instrument, including sample preparation, dilution medium, ionic strength, pH, sample temperature, adsorption to tubing and cuvettes, and the presence of contaminants, further contributes to the final uncertainty. However, few studies have considered these influences within a single, coherent framework. To address this, orthogonal methods that do not rely on light scattering can offer complementary information and a route to validation. Electron microscopy, for example, yields direct, number-based dimensions with nanometer resolution, albeit on dried specimens and with limited statistics. Atomic force microscopy provides accurate height measurements on substrates, while tunable resistive pulse sensing measures particles individually through changes in ionic current, providing both size and concentration (Vogel et al., 2011). Single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (spICP-MS) quantifies the mass of the target element per particle, hence determining particle size and number concentration for metallic NPs at ng L⁻¹ levels (Laborda et al., 2014).

Separation-based approaches, such as field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering and analytical ultracentrifugation, resolve populations before or during detection, offering additional capabilities. Small-angle X-ray scattering and differential centrifugal sedimentation further expand the toolkit. Each technique responds to a different physical property—hydrodynamic, projected, mass-equivalent, Stokes, or sedimentation diameter—meaning that results should not be expected to agree numerically. Apparent discrepancies may reflect real differences in the measurand (Domingos et al., 2009), a distinction that the literature has seldom made explicit for end-users, who are often presented with a single "size" value without a statement of its definition or uncertainty.

Existing reviews tend to delve deeply into individual techniques or compare them empirically for selected reference materials, but there is a notable absence of a consolidated account that connects the physical principles of light-scattering methods to the practical variables determining measurement uncertainty. Moreover, there is a need to set these methods beside non-optical approaches in terms of applicability and limitations. This gap is significant because the growing regulatory emphasis on validated, fit-for-purpose methods requires users to understand the origins of uncertainty and how it can be controlled. The central question addressed in this perspective is: which factors most strongly govern the accuracy and reproducibility of NP size and concentration measurements obtained by DLS and NTA, and how do these methods compare with alternative technologies in suspension?

This work aims to make three key contributions. First, it summarizes the principles, capabilities, and limitations of the main techniques for characterizing NPs in liquid, encompassing both light-scattering and non-scattering approaches. Second, it presents a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa-type) analysis of the principal contributors to uncertainty in size and concentration determination by NTA and DLS, categorizing them into sample, instrument, operator, and data-analysis factors. By elucidating these factors and their interplay, this perspective seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding and mitigating the uncertainties associated with nanoparticle characterization, ultimately contributing to the development of more reliable and reproducible measurement protocols. Our aim in this Perspective is to provide a comprehensive examination of the techniques used to characterise nanoparticles in liquid suspension, with a particular focus on identifying areas where uncertainty can be reduced. To achieve this, we first conducted a thorough literature and standards survey, which involved searching peer-reviewed articles, international standards, and regulatory guidance published between 1990 and 2022. Our search terms included a range of relevant keywords, such as "nanoparticle", "particle size distribution", and "dynamic light scattering", which were combined using Boolean operators to capture studies related to measurement uncertainty, reproducibility, and reference materials.

We prioritised three types of sources: inter-laboratory comparisons, studies using certified or well-characterised reference materials, and documentary standards and guidance, including ISO 22412 for DLS and ISO 19430 for particle tracking analysis. Regulatory definitions and data requirements were taken from the European Commission Recommendation on the definition of nanomaterial and guidance issued by the European Food Safety Authority and the US Food and Drug Administration. We included reports in our analysis only when the measurand, sample preparation, and instrument settings were described in sufficient detail to allow for comparability.

Our framework for comparing technologies involved assessing each technique against a fixed set of attributes extracted from the selected literature. These attributes included the physical principle and quantity measured, nominal working size range, and lower and upper practical concentration limits. We also considered the weighting of the reported distribution, capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples, and the requirement for dilution, labelling, separation, or other sample manipulation. Additionally, we evaluated the traceability of the result to the SI, reported repeatability, and between-laboratory reproducibility, expressed as relative standard deviation (RSD) where available.

To compare the performance of different techniques, we extracted values manually from published studies, with discrepancies resolved by consensus between two reviewers. For example, we recorded the percentage difference between the DLS z-average diameter and the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) modal diameter for monodisperse polystyrene latex and gold NPs. We also examined the theoretical basis for light-scattering measurements, including the standard relationship between the decay rate of the intensity autocorrelation function and the translational diffusion coefficient for DLS.

Our analysis of DLS involved using the Stokes-Einstein relation to obtain the hydrodynamic diameter, as well as cumulants analysis and regularised inversion to provide size distributions. We noted the dependence of scattered intensity on d⁶ in the Rayleigh regime as a key source of bias in polydisperse samples. For NTA, we considered the video-based tracking of individual scatterers undergoing Brownian motion, using the mean squared displacement to compute the diffusion coefficient and obtain the hydrodynamic diameter.

We also examined the limitations of these assumptions using published comparisons between NTA and DLS for protein aggregates, liposomes, and metallic NPs. To further understand the sources of uncertainty, we conducted a cause-and-effect analysis for four combinations of technique and measurand: NTA size, NTA concentration, DLS size, and DLS concentration or derived count rate. This analysis followed the principles of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, involving the decomposition of the measurement model into input quantities and the collection of candidate influence factors from the literature survey and instrument operating principles.

These factors were assigned to six branches: Sample, Dispersant, Sample preparation, Instrument, Method settings, and Operator and data handling. Each factor was classified according to whether it primarily affects the accuracy (bias) or the precision (random error) of the measurement. By examining the complex interplay between these factors, we aim to provide guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, required measurand, and regulatory context.

Ultimately, our goal is to help scientists generate size and concentration data that satisfy regulatory expectations and can be meaningfully compared between laboratories. By providing a detailed methodological treatment and identifying areas where uncertainty can be reduced, we hope to contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable characterisation techniques for nanoparticles in liquid suspension. This, in turn, will facilitate the safe and effective use of nanoparticles in a range of applications, from medicine to environmental remediation.

Our study had three stages: a structured literature and standards survey, a comparative evaluation of technologies, and a cause-and-effect analysis of the measurands "hydrodynamic size" and "particle number concentration". The literature and standards survey involved searching Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed, and screening titles and abstracts for relevance to colloidal suspensions in the nominal range 1 nm–1 µm. We prioritised inter-laboratory comparisons, studies using certified or well-characterised reference materials, and documentary standards and guidance.

The comparative evaluation of technologies involved assessing each technique against a fixed set of attributes, including the physical principle and quantity measured, nominal working size range, and lower and upper practical concentration limits. We also considered the weighting of the reported distribution, capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples, and the requirement for dilution, labelling, separation, or other sample manipulation.

The cause-and-effect analysis involved constructing an Ishikawa diagram separately for four combinations of technique and measurand: NTA size, NTA concentration, DLS size, and DLS concentration or derived count rate. We followed the principles of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, involving the decomposition of the measurement model into input quantities and the collection of candidate influence factors from the literature survey and instrument operating principles.

By examining the complex interplay between these factors, we aim to provide guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, required measurand, and regulatory context. Our analysis highlights the importance of considering the physical principle and quantity measured, as well as the nominal working size range and practical concentration limits, when selecting a technique for characterising nanoparticles.

We also emphasize the need for careful sample preparation, including dilution, labelling, separation, or other sample manipulation, to ensure accurate and reliable measurements. Additionally, our analysis underscores the importance of considering the weighting of the reported distribution, capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples, and the requirement for traceability to the SI.

By providing a detailed methodological treatment and identifying areas where uncertainty can be reduced, we hope to contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable characterisation techniques for nanoparticles in liquid suspension. This, in turn, will facilitate the safe and effective use of nanoparticles in a range of applications, from medicine to environmental remediation.

In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive examination of the techniques used to characterise nanoparticles in liquid suspension, with a particular focus on identifying areas where uncertainty can be reduced. By examining the complex interplay between influence factors and providing guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, required measurand, and regulatory context, we aim to facilitate the development of more accurate and reliable characterisation techniques for nanoparticles. Ultimately, our goal is to help scientists generate size and concentration data that satisfy regulatory expectations and can be meaningfully compared between laboratories, facilitating the safe and effective use of nanoparticles in a range of applications. The evaluation of precision, or random variability, of the measurand is a crucial aspect of any measurement technique. In this review, we assigned a qualitative rank of "major", "moderate", or "minor" to each factor influencing the measurement, based on the magnitude of effects reported in the studies reviewed. For instance, a factor was considered "major" if it altered the reported mean size or concentration by more than 20% in controlled experiments. We also examined how factors interact with one another, such as the interplay between particle concentration and multiple scattering in dynamic light scattering (DLS), or the relationship between camera level and detection threshold in nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA).

Our assessment of non-scattering techniques, including analytical ultracentrifugation, field-flow fractionation, size-exclusion and hydrodynamic chromatography, tunable resistive-pulse sensing, single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, small-angle X-ray scattering, and microscopy methods like transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy, and atomic force microscopy, was guided by two key considerations. Firstly, we sought to determine whether each technique measures particles in their native liquid state, and secondly, we examined the type of diameter reported, be it hydrodynamic, geometric, equivalent-sphere, or mass-derived. The potential for combining techniques orthogonally was evaluated by comparing the measurands and weightings of each pair of techniques, as outlined by Hackley and Clogston (2007) and Bhattacharjee (2016).

Given the diversity of materials and protocols employed in the source studies, a formal meta-analysis was not undertaken. Instead, quantitative values were summarized descriptively as ranges, medians, and relative standard deviations (RSDs). Repeatability and reproducibility were reported in accordance with the definitions outlined in ISO 5725. Where a study provided replicate measurements, the coefficient of variation was either taken directly or computed from the reported means and standard deviations. Differences between techniques were deemed meaningful when they exceeded the combined expanded uncertainty (coverage factor k = 2) reported by the original authors. In cases where uncertainties were not reported, a conservative threshold of 10% was used for size and 30% for number concentration, reflecting the typical between-laboratory variability described for NTA and DLS.

Our conclusions regarding technique suitability were grounded in the weight of evidence across independent studies, rather than relying on single reports. Conflicting results were retained and discussed in context, providing a nuanced understanding of the strengths and limitations of each technique. However, it is essential to acknowledge the limitations of our approach, including the restriction to English-language publications and the absence of a formal risk-of-bias assessment, which may have introduced selection bias. Furthermore, the cause-and-effect rankings are qualitative and dependent on the instrument platforms and software versions described in the source literature, and should therefore be regarded as a structured guide for method validation and uncertainty budgeting, rather than a substitute for laboratory-specific uncertainty evaluation.

In comparing the performance of light-scattering techniques for size determination, we found that DLS and NTA yielded hydrodynamic diameters that agreed with certified or microscopy-derived values to within 2-10% for monodisperse reference materials. However, this agreement broke down for mixtures and polydisperse samples. For example, cumulants-based DLS typically returned z-average diameters of 62-66, 101-106, and 203-208 nm for polystyrene latex standards with nominal diameters of 60, 100, and 200 nm, respectively, with polydispersity indices below 0.08 (Bell et al., 2012; Hole et al., 2013). In contrast, NTA returned number-weighted modal diameters of 58-65, 96-104, and 195-210 nm for the same materials, with relative standard deviations of 3-8% between replicate captures of at least 1,000 valid tracks (Filipe et al., 2010). The agreement between the two methods held for narrow unimodal populations, but diverged for heterogeneous suspensions. In a 1:1 number mixture of 100 nm and 200 nm latex, NTA resolved two populations centered at approximately 102 nm and 199 nm, whereas batch DLS returned a single peak at 168-181 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.19-0.24.

The quantitative range of NTA was bounded at both ends, with linear responses observed between approximately 2 × 10⁷ and 1 × 10⁹ particles mL⁻¹ for 100 nm latex, and recoveries of 85-110% against gravimetrically prepared dilutions. Below this range, counting statistics dominated the error, with coefficients of variation above 25%. Above it, overlapping trajectories led to undercounting of up to 40% at 5 × 10⁹ particles mL⁻¹ (Hole et al., 2013). Inter-laboratory comparisons revealed greater variability in concentration than in size, with coefficients of variation for size between operators ranging from 4-7%, whereas for concentration, they ranged from 20-35%. The largest contributions to this variability arose from camera level, detection threshold, and syringe-pump flow settings (Bell et al., 2012). Changing the detection threshold from 3 to 7 (instrument units) reduced the reported concentration of 60 nm latex by about 55% and shifted the modal diameter upwards by 8-12 nm, because the dimmest particles were progressively excluded.

DLS is not an intrinsic counting method, but concentration can be estimated from count rate under defined optical conditions. Count rate scaled linearly with number concentration for 100 nm latex from 10⁹ to 10¹² particles mL⁻¹ (R² > 0.99). Absolute number concentrations estimated this way had uncertainties of 30-60% unless refractive index, particle shape, and scattering angle were independently known (Stetefeld et al., 2016). Multiple scattering became appreciable above roughly 10¹² particles mL⁻¹ for 200 nm particles and reduced the apparent diameter by 10-25% at higher concentrations unless backscatter geometry (173°) or cross-correlation was used.

A cause-and-effect analysis of uncertainty, using the Ishikawa framework, grouped influences on measurement into five categories: sample, instrument, dispersant, operator/method, and data analysis. For DLS size, the dominant contributions were sample polydispersity and the presence of aggregates or dust. A single 1 µm aggregate present at a concentration of 10⁶ particles mL⁻¹ can significantly alter the measured size distribution, highlighting the need for careful sample preparation and characterization. The operator/method category also played a significant role, with factors such as camera level, detection threshold, and syringe-pump flow settings influencing the measured concentration and size. By understanding the interplay between these factors, researchers can optimize their measurement protocols and minimize uncertainty, ultimately leading to more accurate and reliable characterization of nanoparticles. The characterization of nanoparticles in suspension is a complex task, fraught with challenges that can significantly impact the accuracy of measured size and concentration. Even a small fraction of impurities, on the order of 10⁻⁵, can increase the z-average of a 60 nm suspension by 15-30%. Moreover, temperature plays a subtle yet systematic role, with a 1 °C error in sample temperature resulting in a 2.4% change in the viscosity of water, which in turn affects the calculated hydrodynamic diameter by a similar amount. The use of a nominal viscosity for a dispersant containing 150 mM NaCl or 1% protein can introduce a further bias of 1-5% (Bell et al., 2012). 

Ionic strength, on the other hand, has a profound effect on the electrical double-layer thickness, which can significantly influence the apparent hydrodynamic diameter of nanoparticles. For instance, 30 nm gold nanoparticles exhibit a decrease in apparent hydrodynamic diameter from approximately 52 nm in 1 mM NaCl to 38 nm in 100 mM NaCl, a reduction of nearly 27%. This decrease can be attributed to the compression of the Debye length from about 9.6 nm to 0.96 nm (Varenne et al., 2016). 

In the case of nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), several factors contribute to the uncertainty of the measured diameter, including optical settings such as camera gain, shutter, and detection threshold, as well as viscosity, temperature, tracking length, and the sampled volume. Notably, the number of completed tracks plays a crucial role in determining the standard error of the mean diameter, with fewer than 200 tracks resulting in a standard error above 5%, while 1,000-2,000 tracks reduce it to 1-3%. 

The refractive index of the particles also has a significant impact on detection, with particles having a higher refractive index being more easily detectable. For example, silica particles (n ≈ 1.46) in water have a lower detection limit of about 70-80 nm, compared to 20-30 nm for gold and 40-50 nm for polystyrene (n ≈ 1.59) under comparable laser power and camera settings (Filipe et al., 2010; Hole et al., 2013). This has important implications for the detection of polydisperse biological particles such as extracellular vesicles (n ≈ 1.37-1.40), which are often under-detected below approximately 70-90 nm, resulting in reported concentrations that represent only a fraction of the total population. 

In contrast to light scattering-based methods, non-scattering technologies such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) offer complementary approaches with different compromises. TEM, for instance, provides a number-weighted mean diameter of 59.8 ± 2.1 nm (n > 500particles) for 60 nm latex, but sample drying and contrast agents can introduce shrinkage or flattening artefacts of 5-15% for soft or hydrated particles (Domingos et al., 2009). AFM, on the other hand, offers sub-nanometre height resolution, with a typical expanded uncertainty of ±1-2 nm in z, although lateral broadening by tip convolution can inflate measured widths by 10-20 nm for particles under 50 nm. SAXS, meanwhile, provides a volume-weighted mean diameter of 28.9 nm with a relative standard uncertainty below 2% for 30 nm gold, as well as ensemble information on polydispersity (Stetefeld et al., 2016). 

Fractionation methods, such as asymmetric-flow field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering (AF4-MALS) and differential centrifugal sedimentation, can improve the resolution of mixtures. AF4-MALS, for example, can separate 60, 100, and 200 nm latex in a single run with baseline resolution greater than 1.5, recovering 80-95% of injected mass, while differential centrifugal sedimentation can resolve populations differing by as little as 5-10% in diameter, with a repeatability of 0.5-1% (Varenne et al., 2016). However, the latter method requires accurate particle density, and an assumed density error of 0.05 g cm⁻³ for latex can produce a 2-3% bias in diameter. 

Tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS) and single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (SP-ICP-MS) offer additional approaches for characterizing nanoparticles. TRPS can count particles from approximately 50 nm to 10 µm on a particle-by-particle basis, yielding concentrations within 10-15% of nominal values from 10⁷ to 10¹⁰ particles mL⁻¹, subject to pore blockage and calibration with a matched standard. SP-ICP-MS, meanwhile, determines the number concentration and mass-equivalent diameter of 30nm gold at 10⁵-10⁸ particles mL⁻¹, with transport-efficiency uncertainty of 5-10% and size detection limits of about 15-20 nm for gold and 40-80 nm for silver or titanium oxide, depending on the isotope and background (Domingos et al., 2009). 

The data collectively demonstrate that no single technique can provide both size and concentration with expanded uncertainties below 10% for all material classes. Instead, orthogonal pairing of techniques, such as combining NTA or DLS with TEM or AF4-MALS, can reduce the combined uncertainty for polydisperse or low-contrast samples to approximately 5-10%. This highlights the importance of using multiple techniques to obtain a comprehensive understanding of nanoparticle suspensions. 

A key conclusion of this perspective is that each method reports a different, operationally defined measurand, whether intensity-weighted hydrodynamic diameter, number-weighted trajectory-derived diameter, volume-equivalent diameter, or radius of gyration. These quantities converge only for monodisperse, spherical, non-interacting particles. Our analysis of dynamic light scattering (DLS) and NTA reveals that most uncertainty arises not from instrument hardware but from the interaction of sample properties (polydispersity, refractive index, concentration, and medium) with the assumptions built into data analysis. 

For DLS, the dominant source of bias is the strong dependence of scattered intensity on particle size. In the Rayleigh regime, intensity scales approximately with the sixth power of diameter, so a 100 nm particle scatters roughly 10⁶ times more light than a 10 nm particle of the same material (Bohren and Huffman 1983). This means that a small population of aggregates or dust can dominate the correlation function and shift the cumulant Z-average upwards, even if it is negligible by number. This explains the frequent discrepancy between DLS and number-based methods in polydisperse samples and highlights the importance of reporting and interpreting the polydispersity index (PDI). Values below about 0.1 are generally taken to indicate near-monodispersity, whereas values above 0.3 make the Z-average a poor descriptor of the sample (ISO 22412:2017; Hackley and Clogston 2011). 

Inversion algorithms such as CONTIN and non-negative least squares can, in principle, resolve multimodal distributions, but the problem is ill-posed. Populations that differ by less than a factor of about three in diameter are rarely resolved reliably (Stetefeld et al., 2016). NTA overcomes some of these limitations by tracking individual particles and calculating diameters from the Stokes-Einstein relation applied to each trajectory, giving a number-weighted distribution and a direct estimate of concentration. However, our analysis identifies a distinct set of influential parameters, including camera level, detection threshold, and shutter settings; the number of tracks acquired; temperature and viscosity; and the sample's refractive index and scattering cross-section. Because small or weakly scattering particles fall below the detection threshold, NTA concentration is size-dependent. For low-refractive-index particles such as liposomes and extracellular vesicles, the effective lower limit lies well above the nominal 30 nm, often at 70-100 nm, and the apparent concentration is consequently underestimated. 

In conclusion, the characterization of nanoparticles in suspension is a complex task that requires a comprehensive understanding of the limitations and biases of different techniques. By combining multiple approaches and considering the operational definitions of each measurand, researchers can obtain a more accurate and complete description of nanoparticle suspensions. Ultimately, the development of new methods and the refinement of existing ones will be crucial for advancing our understanding of nanoparticles and their applications in various fields.

Electrotherapy has become a staple in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, offering a non-invasive and cost-effective means of alleviating pain, preventing muscle atrophy, and promoting tissue repair. One of the most common applications of electrotherapy is transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), which has been widely used to manage postoperative pain following orthopedic surgery. Additionally, neuromuscular and high-voltage stimulation have been employed to maintain quadriceps strength after knee arthroplasty and ligament reconstruction. Low-intensity direct current, also known as galvanic current, is another modality used in clinical settings for iontophoresis, wound management, and tissue repair.

The appeal of these electrotherapeutic modalities lies in their ease of integration into physiotherapy programs, particularly during the postoperative period when pain and limited mobility often hinder active exercise. However, a significant and growing proportion of patients undergoing rehabilitation have metallic orthopedic implants, such as plates, screws, and joint prostheses, which raises concerns about the safety of applying electrotherapy in close proximity to these implants. The proximity of electrodes to the implant site is a common occurrence, and therapists are often faced with the dilemma of whether to use electrotherapy in such cases.

Current clinical guidelines are conservative and often contradictory, with many textbooks and manufacturer instructions listing metal implants as a contraindication or precaution for electrotherapy. This cautious approach is largely based on theoretical concerns and extrapolation from other modalities, rather than direct experimental evidence. The primary concern is that the implant, being more conductive than the surrounding tissue, may concentrate current density at its edges or surfaces, leading to Joule heating and thermal injury to bone, muscle, or skin.

The physical mechanisms underlying electrotherapy are distinct from those of other modalities, such as shortwave diathermy and microwave therapy, where the risk of tissue heating around metal is well-documented. The power dissipated per unit volume is described by the equation p = J²/σ = σ|E|², where J is the current density, E is the electric field, and σ is the tissue conductivity. A highly conductive implant, however, short-circuits the electric field in its interior, resulting in minimal field and dissipated power inside the metal, while enhancement of the field is expected mainly at sharp edges and at the metal-tissue interface.

Whether this enhancement is sufficient to produce clinically relevant temperature rises at the amplitudes used in therapy is an empirical question that remains to be answered. High-frequency electromagnetic exposures, such as those encountered in magnetic resonance imaging and diathermy, have been extensively studied, and implant heating has been evaluated through phantom experiments, numerical dosimetry, and standardized test methods. In contrast, transcutaneous electrotherapy delivers low-frequency currents or short pulses via surface electrodes, and the relevant quantities are current density under the electrodes, charge per phase, and the total energy delivered.

Results from high-frequency studies cannot be directly applied to this regime, and the empirical literature on low-frequency electrical stimulation in the presence of implants is surprisingly limited. Most evidence comes from case series, retrospective reports, and the experience of patients with cardiac pacemakers, where the primary concern is device interference rather than heating. A few studies have examined neuromuscular stimulation in patients with metal fixation or arthroplasty without reporting adverse events, and in vitro and animal work on electrical stimulation to promote bone healing has often used metal electrodes or implants as part of the stimulating circuit.

However, these studies were designed to evaluate efficacy rather than thermal safety, and they rarely measured temperature at the implant site. Consequently, the prohibition of electrotherapy over metal implants is based largely on theoretical reasoning and extrapolation from other modalities, rather than on direct experimental data. This evidence gap leads to uncertainty and inconsistent practice, with some practitioners withholding an effective therapy and others using it without a scientific safety basis.

Direct current is a critical case in this regard, as it flows continuously in a single direction, potentially carrying or redirecting a substantial fraction of the current and heating locally. Prolonged use of direct current may also cause galvanic effects at the implant surface. If heating is not observed with direct current under realistic therapeutic conditions, it is reasonable to expect that pulsed, lower-average-current modalities, such as TENS and high-voltage stimulation, would also be safe from a thermal perspective. Nonetheless, these different waveforms have never been compared experimentally in a single controlled setup containing a metallic implant.

A practical safety threshold is needed to determine the thermal safety of electrotherapy near implants. Tissue damage depends on both temperature and exposure time, and a sustained rise of a few degrees above normal body temperature is generally considered the limit beyond which cellular injury becomes a concern. Standards for implants in the electromagnetic field context commonly use a temperature rise of about 2 to 3 °C as an acceptance criterion. Adopting a conservative increase of 3 °C as the threshold of concern provides an objective, clinically meaningful endpoint for judging whether electrotherapy near implants might induce thermal harm.

The aim of the present study was to determine experimentally whether therapeutic electrical currents can heat a metal orthopedic implant. Using a tissue-equivalent model system, we investigated the thermal effects of different electrotherapeutic modalities on a metallic implant, with a focus on direct current, TENS, and high-voltage stimulation. Our results will provide valuable insights into the safety of electrotherapy in patients with metallic implants, helping to inform clinical practice and ensure the effective and safe use of these modalities in musculoskeletal rehabilitation. Our investigation focused on the thermal effects of three commonly used electrotherapy modalities - high-voltage stimulation (HVS), transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), and galvanic current (GAL) - on a titanium orthopedic implant. To this end, we designed an in vitro experimental study that would assess the temperature changes at the implant and in the surrounding medium during prolonged exposure to these modalities at therapeutic intensities. A key aspect of our study was the comparison of these temperature changes against a predefined threshold of 3 °C, which is considered a critical limit beyond which tissue damage may occur. The rationale behind this threshold is rooted in the thermal dose literature, which suggests that sustained tissue temperature elevations of 1-3 °C are generally tolerated, whereas larger elevations may cause harm. This threshold is also consistent with the standards outlined in ASTM F2182 and ISO/TS 10974, which recommend a 2-3 °C limit for implant heating.

To our knowledge, this is the first experimental evaluation of the thermal effects of direct current, in combination with pulsed low-frequency currents, on a metallic orthopedic implant. Our findings are intended to provide a much-needed evidence base for clinical decision-making and to inform the revision of guidelines concerning electrotherapy in patients with orthopedic implants. The study's design and rationale were centered on addressing a critical knowledge gap in the field, and our results have significant implications for the safe and effective use of electrotherapy in patients with metallic implants.

The model system used in our study consisted of a titanium osteosynthesis plate embedded in a tissue-equivalent medium, which was designed to mimic the electrical and thermal properties of human tissue. The primary outcome of interest was the maximum temperature change at the implant surface relative to baseline during and after stimulation. A rise of more than 3 °C was predefined as the threshold of concern, beyond which tissue damage may occur. This threshold is consistent with the thermal dose literature and the standards outlined in ASTM F2182 and ISO/TS 10974.

The test phantom used in our study was a rectangular acrylic container filled with a gelled saline medium, which was prepared according to the standards outlined in ASTM F2182-11a. The medium had a conductivity of approximately 0.47 S/m at 22 °C, which is close to that of human muscle at low frequencies. The use of a gelled medium prevented convective heat transport, ensuring that the recorded temperature changes reflected local power deposition rather than fluid mixing. The conductivity of the medium was verified before each session using a calibrated conductivity meter, and the medium was allowed to equilibrate to room temperature (22 ± 1 °C) for at least 12 hours before each experiment.

A commercially available, medical-grade titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) straight plate was fixed in the center of the phantom at a depth of 2 cm below the surface, with its long axis parallel to the line connecting the electrode pair. Two of the plate's screw holes contained titanium screws to reproduce a typical fixation configuration. In a second configuration, the plate was positioned directly beneath one electrode to represent a worst-case geometry with maximal current density. A control run without a plate was performed for each stimulation condition to separate implant-related heating from heating of the medium or electrodes.

We tested three stimulation modalities using clinical devices commonly found in physiotherapy practice. High-volt stimulation (HVS) used twin-peak monophasic pulses at a frequency of 100 Hz, while transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used a symmetrical biphasic rectangular waveform at a frequency of 80 Hz. Galvanic current (GAL) used continuous direct current at an intensity of 0.1 mA/cm² electrode area, which is the upper limit generally recommended to limit electrochemical skin effects. Each modality was delivered at two intensities: a "therapeutic" level and a "maximum" level. The therapeutic level was defined as the intensity producing a strong but comfortable sensation in a pilot of five healthy volunteers, while the maximum level was the highest output the device could deliver into the phantom load without alarm or compliance cutoff.

Delivered current and voltage were monitored using a digital oscilloscope across a 10 Ω series shunt resistor, and root-mean-square (RMS) current was calculated. Since Joule heating in a conductive medium scales with the square of current density, we also estimated the specific absorption rate to enable comparison with the temperature data. Under the assumption of negligible heat loss over a short interval, the initial temperature rise rate follows the equation ΔT/Δt ≈ SAR/c, where c is the specific heat capacity of the medium.

Electrodes were self-adhesive carbon-rubber pads coupled with conductive gel and positioned on the phantom surface 8 cm apart, flanking the implant. For GAL, polarity was assigned so that, in separate runs, the anode and then the cathode lay directly over the plate. Electrodes were replaced between sessions to avoid electrode degradation. Temperature was recorded with fiber-optic probes, which are immune to electromagnetic interference and do not distort the electrical field. Four probes were used: two placed in direct contact with the plate, one in contact with the screw head, and one reference probe in the medium 10 cm from the plate and electrodes to account for ambient drift. A fifth probe was placed under an electrode to document electrode-site heating.

The experimental procedure involved allowing the phantom to stabilize until the baseline drift was below 0.1 °C over 5 minutes, followed by a 5-minute baseline temperature recording.
