Stimulation was then applied continuously for 30 minutes, which equals or exceeds typical clinical treatment durations, followed by a 10-minute recovery recording. For GAL, an additional 10-minute recording was made after reversing the polarity. The temperature data were analyzed to determine the maximum temperature change at the implant surface relative to baseline during and after stimulation, and the results were compared against the predefined threshold of 3 °C.

Our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the thermal effects of electrotherapy on a metallic orthopedic implant, and our findings have significant implications for the safe and effective use of electrotherapy in patients with metallic implants. The results of our study will inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for the use of electrotherapy in patients with orthopedic implants, and will help to minimize the risk of adverse effects associated with electrotherapy in this patient population. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of considering the thermal effects of electrotherapy on metallic implants, and underscores the need for further research in this area to ensure the safe and effective use of electrotherapy in patients with orthopedic implants. To investigate the cumulative effects of prolonged exposure, we conducted a series of experiments with a 60-minute duration. Each combination of modality, intensity, and plate position - with the plate, without the plate, and with the plate under the electrode - was repeated five times, in a randomized order generated by a computer. The randomized order and the minimum 60-minute interval between runs helped minimize any potential carryover effects. Additionally, the phantom was either replaced or re-equilibrated whenever the baseline temperature deviated by more than 0.5°C from the target temperature of 22°C. This rigorous protocol ensured that our results were not confounded by thermal drift or other extraneous factors.

Given the potential for electrochemical reactions at the metal surface to be influenced by the polarity of the galvanic electrode, we visually inspected the plate after each galvanic current (GAL) run for any signs of gas formation or discoloration. Moreover, we measured the pH of the gel adjacent to the plate at the start and end of the longest exposure using a flat-surface pH electrode. These precautions were necessary to ensure that our findings were not compromised by unforeseen chemical reactions.

The primary outcome of interest was the maximum temperature increase (ΔTmax) recorded by the probe during stimulation, corrected for any simultaneous changes in the reference probe temperature. This correction was essential to account for any ambient temperature fluctuations that might have occurred during the experiment. We defined ΔTcorr(t) as [Tprobe(t) − T̄baseline,probe] − [Tref(t) − T̄baseline,ref], where Tprobe(t) and Tref(t) represent the temperatures of the probe and reference at time t, respectively, and T̄baseline,probe and T̄baseline,ref are the mean baseline temperatures of the probe and reference. Secondary outcomes included the time to reach ΔTmax, the heating rate during the initial 5 minutes (estimated using linear regression), the temperature difference between the plate and control (no-plate) conditions, as well as the root mean square (RMS) current and estimated specific absorption rate (SAR) for each setting.

Data analysis was performed using SPSS version 25 (IBM) and R version 4.0. We present our data as mean ± standard deviation, accompanied by 95% confidence intervals. Prior to conducting any statistical tests, we verified the normality of our data using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Our main hypothesis was that ΔTmax would not exceed 3°C, a threshold commonly used in standardized test methods for heating of implants (ASTM International, 2013). We tested this hypothesis using one-sided one-sample t tests against 3°C for each condition, and also compared the upper 95% confidence bound with the threshold. To evaluate differences between implant and no-implant conditions, as well as between modalities, we employed a two-way analysis of variance (modality × plate condition), followed by Tukey post hoc comparisons. In cases where the assumptions of these tests were violated, we used Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests instead. Furthermore, we calculated the Pearson correlation between RMS current and ΔTmax to investigate any potential relationships between these variables. We set the significance level at α = 0.05 and applied Bonferroni correction to account for multiple comparisons. With five replicates per condition and an expected standard deviation of 0.3°C, our experimental design had a power of over 80% to detect a difference of 0.8°C between conditions.

Before initiating each trial, we allowed the phantom to equilibrate to a mean baseline temperature of 22.1 ± 0.3 °C (range 21.6–22.7 °C) at all probe sites. In the 30-minute sham runs, where the electrodes were in place but no current was applied, the maximum drift at any probe was found to be 0.2 °C. This drift was monotonic and identical in phantoms with and without the plate, leading us to establish 0.2 °C as the practical noise floor of our setup. Notably, this value is well below the 3 °C criterion, providing a comfortable margin for our measurements. The fiber-optic probes used in this study were not affected by the stimulation, and signal traces recorded in the first seconds after current onset exhibited no step artifacts or discontinuities, which can sometimes be observed with metallic thermocouples in electromagnetic fields (Shellock, 2002). The delivered current and voltage were verified on an oscilloscope and found to agree with the device settings to within ±5% in every run, ensuring the accuracy of our stimulation protocol.

We conducted experiments using high-volt stimulation (HVS) with the plate in the current path, at the clinical maximum (twin-peak pulses, 100 Hz, peak voltage 150 V, mean current 1.8 ± 0.2 mA). The results showed a slow, small temperature increase over the 30-minute exposure, with a mean maximal rise (ΔTmax) of 0.4 ± 0.1 °C at the plate surface beneath the electrode and 0.3 ± 0.1 °C at the plate end. Probes located at the screw holes recorded a ΔTmax of 0.3 ± 0.1 °C, while the distant reference probe, which was not near the plate, rose by 0.2 ± 0.1 °C. At the intermediate setting (75 V), ΔTmax at the plate surface was 0.3 ± 0.1 °C. In all cases, the temperature increase occurred mainly during the first 10 minutes and then plateaued, suggesting that heat generation and dissipation reached a quasi-steady state rather than accumulating. The highest single reading across all HVS trials was 0.6 °C (n = 5 per intensity), recorded at the plate edge facing the cathode in one run, which was 2.4 °C below the threshold.

We also investigated the effects of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) using conventional biphasic TENS (80 Hz, 200 µs pulse width, 50 mA peak into the phantom load). The results showed a small temperature rise comparable to that observed with HVS, with a mean ΔTmax of 0.3 ± 0.1 °C at the plate surface, 0.2 ± 0.1 °C at the plate ends and screw holes, and 0.2 ± 0.1 °C at the reference probe. When we repeated the test in burst mode (2 Hz burst frequency, 100 µs pulses, 60 mA), ΔTmax at the plate surface was 0.3 ± 0.1 °C, with no meaningful difference from the conventional mode. The maximum single reading across all TENS runs was 0.5 °C. Given the short pulse width and low duty cycle, the time-averaged power was small, which is consistent with the observed small temperature changes. For a resistive load R, the mean Joule power is Pmean = Irms² · R, and with the measured rms currents (<3 mA for all pulsed settings), the dissipated power was in the low-milliwatt range, as expected (Robinson, 2008).

Galvanic current (GAL) was the only modality with a net unidirectional current, and thus, it was of particular concern. At 2 mA (current density 0.08 mA/cm² under the electrode), the mean ΔTmax after 30 minutes was 0.5 ± 0.2 °C at the plate surface and 0.4 ± 0.1 °C at the plate end. At 5 mA (0.2 mA/cm²), which is near the upper limit of typical clinical application, the corresponding values were 0.9 ± 0.2 °C and 0.7 ± 0.2 °C. When the exposure was prolonged to 60 minutes at 5 mA, to simulate the worst-case scenario, ΔTmax at the plate surface reached 1.1 ± 0.3 °C, the highest mean value in the study. The single highest reading was 1.5 °C, observed at the plate surface directly under the cathode, which is half the 3 °C threshold. The temperature at the electrode–phantom interface also rose slightly, up to 1.3 °C. The temperature rise at the implant site was found to be 0.3 ± 0.1 °C, indicating that a portion of the heating occurred at the electrode-gel interface, rather than at the implant itself, due to the higher contact resistance in the direct-current condition. Notably, we did not observe any evidence of abrupt thermal runaway or a temperature curve that continued to rise without plateauing. To further investigate this, we performed a linear regression analysis of temperature against time over the final 10 minutes of the 60-minute galvanic current (GAL) runs, which yielded a slope of 0.004 ± 0.003 °C·min⁻¹. This value does not differ significantly from zero, suggesting that the temperature increase was minimal and stable over time.

During the 5 mA, 60-minute GAL runs, gas bubbles were visible at the cathode surface, and we observed slight local discoloration of the gel near the anode, consistent with the electrochemical processes expected with prolonged direct current, as reported by Merrill et al. (2005). However, no visible changes were observed on the titanium surface in any of the runs. To determine whether the presence of the metal implant contributed to heating, we compared the temperature changes in phantoms with and without the implant under the same settings. The differences in maximum temperature change (ΔTmax) between the two conditions were negligible, with a maximum difference of 0.2 °C, which is within the noise floor.

For each modality, the mean difference in ΔTmax between the plate and no-plate conditions was small, with 95% confidence intervals that included zero. Specifically, the mean differences were 0.1 °C (95% CI -0.1 to 0.3) for high-voltage stimulation (HVS), 0.1 °C (95% CI -0.1 to 0.2) for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), and 0.2 °C (95% CI -0.1 to 0.5) for GAL at 5 mA for 30 minutes. The upper bounds of these intervals were far below the 3 °C threshold, indicating that the presence of the implant did not significantly contribute to heating.

A repeated-measures analysis of variance revealed a significant main effect of modality on ΔTmax at the plate surface (F(2, 12) = 14.6, p < 0.001), driven primarily by the GAL modality at 5 mA. Post hoc Bonferroni-corrected comparisons showed that GAL at this intensity produced a greater temperature increase than HVS (p = 0.002) and TENS (p = 0.001), whereas HVS and TENS did not differ significantly (p = 0.74). However, the effect of plate presence was not significant (p = 0.31), and there was no significant interaction between modality and plate presence (p = 0.48). Although the differences in ΔTmax between modalities were statistically reliable, they were small in absolute terms and did not have practical thermal importance, given the predefined criterion (Cohen, 1988).

Across all 90 trials, which included three modalities, multiple intensities, and five repetitions each, as well as sham and no-plate controls, no temperature increase exceeded 3 °C at any probe. The overall maximum temperature increase was 1.5 °C (GAL, 5 mA, 60 minutes), and the highest mean value was 1.1 °C. The pulsed modalities, HVS and TENS, never exceeded 0.6 °C at any site. Repeat runs yielded tight, reproducible results, with coefficients of variation for ΔTmax between repetitions ranging from 8-15% for pulsed currents and 18-27% for GAL. The larger values for GAL reflect the smaller absolute numbers and interface variability. The intraclass correlation between independent repeat measurements at the plate surface was 0.91 (95% CI 0.80-0.97), indicating good reproducibility.

These findings collectively demonstrate that all therapeutic electrical currents tested produced temperature changes in the model system that fell well within the predefined 3 °C limit, and that the presence of a titanium plate did not measurably increase heating, even under prolonged direct current. This study was designed to address a practical question that clinicians frequently encounter: whether electrotherapy delivered over or near an orthopedic implant can produce clinically relevant heating of the metal. Our results show that, across the three modalities tested (HVS, TENS, and galvanic current), temperature changes in the model system remained below the predefined 3°C threshold.

To our knowledge, this is the first experimental observation that prolonged exposure to a therapeutic direct current does not heat titanium plates. This finding is physically plausible and consistent with the limited literature, but its interpretation requires consideration of the mechanisms of heating, the differences between electrotherapy and other energy modalities, and the limitations of the model. Heating of a conductive implant by an applied current can arise from three principal mechanisms: resistive (Joule) heating in the implant or surrounding tissue, induced eddy currents in the metal from time-varying magnetic fields, and concentration of current density at the metal-tissue interface.

For a conductor of resistance R carrying current I, the dissipated power is P = I²R. A titanium plate of several centimeters in length and a few millimeters in cross-section has a resistance on the order of micro- to milliohms, whereas the surrounding electrolyte or tissue has a resistance of tens to hundreds of ohms. Because the plate is a much better conductor than its surroundings, any current diverted through it dissipates very little power in the metal itself. Even if the entire therapeutic current (typically below 100 mA for galvanic stimulation and far lower on average for TENS) passed through the plate, the resulting power would be negligible.

Tissue heating, in contrast, depends on the local current density J and tissue conductivity σ, with volumetric power density approximated by J²/σ. The dominant determinant of heating in clinical electrotherapy is thus the current density under the electrodes, which is limited by electrode size and patient tolerance, rather than the presence of a highly conductive implant. This reasoning explains why the three tested modalities behaved similarly, and why our observation for direct current is not surprising despite the persistent clinical assumption to the contrary.

The contraindication of electrotherapy over metal is largely inherited from shortwave and microwave diathermy, in which radiofrequency electromagnetic fields induce currents in metal and produce well-documented, sometimes severe, heating at implant sites (Shields et al., 2002; Nutt et al., 2001). Such fields operate at megahertz or gigahertz frequencies, at which eddy currents and dielectric absorption are substantial. HVS, TENS, and galvanic currents, on the other hand, operate at frequencies from zero to a few kilohertz, with negligible induction, and are delivered through surface electrodes by conduction rather than radiation. Extending the diathermy contraindication to these modalities therefore lacks a clear physical rationale, a point noted in earlier reviews of electrotherapy precautions (Houghton et al., 2010).

Although we found no thermal hazard, heating is not the only conceivable risk associated with electrotherapy over metal implants. Electrochemical considerations, such as the potential for electrode corrosion or the release of metal ions, must also be taken into account. However, these risks are generally considered to be low, and the benefits of electrotherapy in promoting tissue repair and reducing pain often outweigh the potential risks. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the safety and efficacy of electrotherapy in patients with metal implants, but our findings provide a foundation for the development of evidence-based guidelines for the use of electrotherapy in this population.

The practice of continuous deployment (CD) has become increasingly prevalent in software engineering, as it enables organizations to automatically build, test, and release code changes to end users through an automated deployment pipeline (Humble and Farley, 2010). By adopting CD, organizations can shorten release cycles, obtain faster customer feedback, and reduce the manual effort associated with releasing software. Industry surveys have consistently shown that frequent, automated deployment is associated with better organizational performance and faster recovery from failures (Forsgren et al., 2018). A crucial enabler of CD is infrastructure as code (IaC), which involves provisioning and configuring computing infrastructure through machine-readable scripts rather than manual procedures (Humble and Farley, 2010; Rahman et al., 2019a).

Tools like Puppet, Chef, and Ansible allow practitioners to specify the desired state of servers, services, and dependencies in source code, which can then be version-controlled, reviewed, tested, and executed repeatedly and consistently across environments. However, treating infrastructure as software also exposes it to the defects that affect any other software artifact. A defect in an IaC script can propagate to every machine on which the script is executed, compromising the reliability of the entire deployment pipeline. The consequences of such defects can be severe, as illustrated by the 2017 outage of Amazon's Simple Storage Service, which was caused by an erroneous operational command and affected a large number of dependent websites and services (Amazon Web Services, 2017).

Prior empirical work has shown that defects in IaC scripts are not rare. For example, Jiang and Adams (2015) observed that infrastructure code in open source projects co-evolves with, and is often as change-prone as, production code. Similarly, Rahman and Williams (2018) found that defect-related commits constitute a substantial share of the commits to IaC scripts in several open source repositories. Defective IaC scripts can cause frequent deployment failures and consume considerable developer effort, undermining the benefits that motivate CD in the first place.

Despite the importance of IaC, research on its quality remains sparse relative to its adoption in industry. A systematic mapping study found that few studies have examined the relationship between source code characteristics and script quality (Rahman et al., 2019a). While some studies have catalogued configuration smells in Puppet code (Sharma et al., 2016) and Chef (Schwarz et al., 2018), and proposed approaches for testing the idempotence and convergence of configuration scripts (Hanappi et al., 2016; Hummer et al., 2013), these studies rely heavily on smells and rules defined a priori by researchers or tool builders. They do not establish which properties of IaC source code are actually associated with defects observed in practice.

In the broader software engineering literature, source code properties have long been used to characterize and predict defects. Size, complexity, and change metrics are known to correlate with defect proneness in general-purpose languages (Nagappan et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2007). However, IaC languages differ markedly from general-purpose languages, as they are declarative or hybrid in nature, describe resources and their relationships rather than algorithms, and are dominated by configuration values, file paths, and invocations of external modules. Properties that matter in conventional code, such as inheritance depth or loop structure, may therefore carry little signal in IaC scripts, whereas properties specific to configuration, such as how values are specified or how dependencies are included, may carry considerable signal.

Given the lack of empirical evidence on the relationship between IaC source code properties and defects, practitioners lack data-driven guidance on where to focus code review and testing, and researchers lack a principled basis for building automated defect prediction models for IaC. To address this gap, we hypothesize that certain properties of IaC source code, such as the number of lines of code and the use of hard-coded strings as configuration values, are correlated with defective scripts. The objective of this paper is to help practitioners increase the quality of IaC scripts through an empirical study that identifies source code properties of defective IaC scripts.

To achieve this objective, we pursue three research questions: RQ1: What source code properties characterize defective infrastructure as code scripts? RQ2: Do practitioners agree with the identified source code properties? RQ3: How accurately can we predict defective infrastructure as code scripts using the identified source code properties? To answer RQ1, we apply qualitative analysis to defect-related commits mined from open source repositories, deriving candidate properties from the code changes that fixed defects and quantifying the relationship between each property and script defectiveness using statistical tests and effect sizes.

To answer RQ2, we survey practitioners to assess their level of agreement with each identified property, providing a check on whether the empirical findings match practitioner experience. To answer RQ3, we construct defect prediction models from the identified properties and evaluate them on 2,439 Puppet scripts drawn from four datasets collected from open source organizations, namely Mirantis, Mozilla, Openstack, and Wikimedia. We follow established practice in defect prediction by comparing several learners and reporting precision and recall, the measures that matter most to practitioners who must decide how much inspection effort to allocate (Hall et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2007).

Our analysis identifies 10 source code properties that correlate with defective IaC scripts, with lines of code and hard-coded string showing the strongest correlation with defective scripts. In the practitioner survey, the majority of respondents agreed with two properties: include, the property of executing external modules or scripts, and hard-coded string. Prediction models built on the identified properties achieve a precision of 0.70 to 0.78 and a recall of 0.54 to 0.67, suggesting that these properties carry practical predictive signal for IaC defects.

This paper makes several contributions to the field of software engineering, including a list of 10 source code properties of IaC scripts that correlate with defects, derived from defect-related commits in open source repositories, and a quantitative assessment of the strength of these correlations. Our findings provide a foundation for future research on defect prediction in IaC and offer guidance for practitioners seeking to improve the quality of their IaC scripts. By identifying the source code properties that are most strongly associated with defects, practitioners can focus their code review and testing efforts on the most critical aspects of their IaC scripts, ultimately improving the reliability and maintainability of their software systems. The relationship between script properties and defectiveness is a crucial aspect of infrastructure as code (IaC) development. Our analysis reveals that lines of code and hard-coded strings are the most strongly associated with defective scripts. To better understand this relationship, we conducted a comprehensive study that combines empirical evidence with practitioner perception. We developed defect prediction models using the identified properties and evaluated their precision and recall on a large dataset of 2,439 scripts from four organizations. This paper is organized as follows: we first provide background information on IaC and review related work, then describe our methodology, present our results, and discuss the implications for practitioners and researchers. Finally, we address potential threats to validity and draw conclusions.

Our research was motivated by three key questions: (RQ1) What source code properties characterize defective IaC scripts? (RQ2) Do practitioners agree that these properties are associated with defective scripts? (RQ3) How well can these properties predict defective scripts? To answer these questions, we conducted a three-phase empirical study. First, we applied qualitative analysis to defect-related commits to derive source code properties of defective IaC scripts. Second, we quantified the association between each property and defective scripts and surveyed practitioners on their agreement with these properties. Third, we built defect prediction models from the properties to evaluate their practical utility.

We focused on Puppet, a widely used declarative configuration management language in continuous deployment. Our datasets consisted of repositories from four organizations that use Puppet in production: Mirantis, Mozilla, OpenStack, and Wikimedia. We selected these repositories based on three criteria: (1) at least 11% of the files in the repository had to be Puppet scripts, (2) the repository had to be under active development with at least two commits per month, and (3) the repository had to contain enough history to support defect mining. We cloned each repository and extracted the full commit history using the PyDriller library, resulting in a total of 2,439 scripts.

To identify defect-related commits, we followed the approach of Rahman and Williams (2018) and classified a commit as defect-related if its message described the correction of a defect in a Puppet script. We applied a keyword filter on commit messages and retained only commits that modified at least one Puppet script. However, keyword matching alone can yield false positives (Herzig et al., 2013), so two raters manually inspected every retained message, together with the associated diff, to resolve any ambiguities. Commits that described feature additions, refactoring, or documentation changes were excluded. We measured inter-rater agreement using Cohen's κ (Cohen, 1960) and resolved any disagreements through discussion. A script was labeled defective if it was modified by at least one defect-related commit and neutral otherwise.

Our qualitative analysis (RQ1) involved applying open coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1998) to the code changes in the defect-related commits. The first author examined the lines removed or modified by each defect-fixing commit and recorded the code elements implicated in the defect. We grouped related codes into candidate properties through iterative comparison and gave each property a name and an operational definition. To evaluate the reliability of the resulting scheme, a second rater independently applied the definitions to a random sample of 200 defect-related commits, and we computed Cohen's κ. Disagreements prompted refinement of the definitions until the raters reached consensus, yielding a set of properties that could be computed automatically from script source code.

For each script, we computed the count of each property using a parser built on the Puppet language grammar, normalizing nothing except where noted, so that counts reflected raw code characteristics. We included lines of code (LOC) as a baseline property, as size is a well-established correlate of defects (Zhang, 2009). To quantify the relationship between each property and defective scripts, we compared the property's distribution in defective and neutral scripts within each dataset. Since property counts were non-normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk tests, p < 0.05), we used the non-parametric Mann–Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947) at α = 0.05, applying the Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple comparisons across properties. We quantified effect sizes using Cliff's δ (Cliff, 1993) and interpreted magnitudes using conventional thresholds (Romano et al., 2006). We also computed the median property value for defective and neutral scripts and ranked properties by their effect size.

To assess whether the properties reflect practitioner experience, we conducted a web-based survey (RQ2). For each property, the questionnaire provided its name, definition, and a short code example from a real Puppet script, then asked respondents to rate their agreement with the statement that scripts containing the property are more likely to be defective. Responses used a five-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932) from strongly disagree to strongly agree. We collected respondents' years of IaC experience and primary role and included an optional free-text field for comments. We distributed the survey to practitioners who had contributed commits to the studied repositories and to other open-source Puppet projects, as well as through public developer forums and mailing lists. Before deployment, we piloted the instrument with three practitioners, whose feedback led to clearer wording and the removal of ambiguous examples. Participation was voluntary and anonymous. We report agreement as the percentage of respondents choosing agree or strongly agree for each property and considered a property to have majority agreement when this percentage exceeded 50%. We analyzed the free-text comments using thematic coding.

Our results show that lines of code and hard-coded strings are the most strongly associated with defective scripts. We also found that practitioners generally agree with these findings, with majority agreement for most properties. Our defect prediction models, built using these properties, demonstrated good precision and recall on the large dataset of scripts. These findings have important implications for practitioners and researchers, highlighting the need for careful consideration of script properties in IaC development. We discuss these implications in more detail below, along with potential threats to validity and conclusions. To contextualize the quantitative responses, we undertook a comprehensive analysis of defect prediction, which is the focus of our third research question (RQ3). Specifically, we developed prediction models to investigate whether the identified properties can distinguish between defective and neutral scripts. Each script was represented by a feature vector comprising its property counts, allowing us to compare the performance of five commonly used learners in defect prediction: Classification and Regression Trees (Breiman et al., 1984), Random Forest (Breiman, 2001), Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, and a support vector machine (Lessmann et al., 2008). We trained these learners using default parameters in the scikit-learn library, ensuring a standardized approach across all models.

Given that defective scripts constituted a minority class in all four datasets, we applied the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (Chawla et al., 2002) to the training folds only. This approach prevented synthetic instances from leaking into the test data, thereby mitigating potential overfitting issues. To evaluate the performance of each model, we employed 10×10-fold cross-validation, repeating stratified 10-fold cross-validation ten times with different random seeds. This rigorous evaluation methodology allowed us to reduce variance stemming from a single partition (Tantithamthavorn et al., 2017). The performance of each model was measured using precision, recall, and the F-measure, which represents the harmonic mean of precision and recall. We summarized each metric as the mean across all 100 test folds, providing a comprehensive overview of the models' performance.

To determine whether the prediction models outperformed a naive baseline, we compared their performance with a classifier that labels scripts as defective with a probability equal to the training-set defect rate. We used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945) on the fold-level scores to assess the statistical significance of the differences between the models and the baseline.

Our study's design incorporates several features that mitigate potential threats to validity. Notably, the dual rating of commits and properties, with reported κ values, reduces subjectivity in the qualitative phases of the analysis. Furthermore, our separate analysis of four organizations helps to establish whether the findings can be generalized beyond a single codebase. The restriction of oversampling to training data, combined with repeated cross-validation, guards against optimistic bias in the prediction results. We have also made the property definitions and extraction procedures explicit, ensuring that the analysis can be replicated by other researchers.

Our investigation addresses four research questions, which we will discuss in turn. First, we examine which source code properties characterize defective scripts (RQ1). Second, we investigate how strongly each property correlates with defects (RQ2). Third, we explore how practitioners perceive these properties (RQ3). Finally, we assess how well the properties predict defective scripts (RQ4). Our datasets comprise 2,439 Puppet scripts from four organizations: Mozilla (322 scripts), OpenStack (1,383 scripts), Wikimedia (237 scripts), and GitHub (497 scripts). Of these scripts, 36.6% (893) were defective, with the proportion of defective scripts ranging from 28.4% (Wikimedia) to 41.2% (OpenStack).

Through open coding of 1,448 defect-related commits, we identified ten properties that are associated with defective scripts. Two independent raters coded the commits, achieving substantial agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.74; Landis and Koch, 1977). The properties include attribute (the count of attribute-value pairs), command (use of the exec resource to run shell commands), comment (lines of comment), ensure (specifying the state of a resource), file (use of the file resource), hard-coded string (configuration values specified as literal strings), include (execution of external modules or scripts), lines of code (LOC), require (declaring resource dependencies), and service (use of the service resource). The frequency of these properties varied in defect-related commits, with lines of code and hard-coded string being the most frequently associated with defect fixes, appearing in 41.3% and 37.8% of the coded commits, respectively.

To compare the normalized count of each property between defective and non-defective scripts, we used the two-sided Mann–Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947). We also assessed the effect size using Cliff's δ (Cliff, 1993), interpreting the results according to the thresholds established by Romano et al. (2006). To account for multiple comparisons, we applied a Bonferroni correction across the ten tests (α = 0.005). The results, which are summarized in Table 1, show that lines of code exhibited the strongest correlation with defective scripts (δ = 0.49), followed by hard-coded string (δ = 0.43). Defective scripts had a median of 87 lines, compared to 31 lines for non-defective scripts, and a median of 14 hard-coded strings, compared to 4 for non-defective scripts.

Our findings are consistent with prior research indicating that larger modules are more defect-prone in conventional software (Nagappan and Ball, 2005; Hall et al., 2012). Eight properties showed statistically significant differences after correction, with comment being the only property that was not significant (p = 0.071). Service was significant but negligible in magnitude. The ranking of the top two properties was stable across datasets, with lines of code having the largest effect size in three of the four datasets (δ between 0.44 and 0.53). In every dataset, lines of code and hard-coded string both exhibited at least medium effect sizes.

To gain a deeper understanding of how practitioners perceive the properties, we conducted a survey of 350 practitioners who had contributed to the repositories in our datasets. We received 56 responses (16.0%), with respondents having a median of 6 years of experience with configuration management. For each property, respondents rated their agreement that scripts with the property were more likely to be defective, using a five-point Likert scale. We counted ratings of "agree" and "strongly agree" as agreement. Only two properties received agreement from a majority of respondents: include (73.2%, 41 of 56) and hard-coded string (66.1%, 37 of 56). These findings suggest that practitioners are aware of the potential risks associated with these properties and take them into account when developing and maintaining Puppet scripts. The agreement among practitioners on the relevance of certain properties to defective scripts was notable, particularly with regards to the inclusion of external modules and the use of hard-coded strings. When asked to justify their agreement on the inclusion of external modules, respondents cited the potential for hidden dependencies on external modules to propagate failures to the including script. Similarly, the use of hard-coded strings was justified by noting that literal values, such as paths, ports, and package versions, are brittle and prone to variation across environments. In contrast, agreement on the remaining properties was relatively low, with lines of code receiving only 44.6% agreement, despite showing the strongest statistical correlation with defects. Attribute, require, and command also garnered limited agreement, at 39.3%, 35.7%, and 32.1%, respectively. The lowest levels of agreement were observed for comment and service, at 12.5% and 14.3%, which is consistent with their weak correlations in our previous analysis.

Interestingly, respondents with more than five years of experience tended to agree with the inclusion of external modules and hard-coded strings at slightly higher rates than their less experienced counterparts, although this difference was not statistically significant. This suggests that practitioner perception and measured correlation converge on the importance of hard-coded strings, but diverge on the role of lines of code. To further investigate the relationship between these properties and defective scripts, we constructed defect prediction models using the ten identified properties and five different machine learning algorithms: classification and regression trees, logistic regression, naïve Bayes, support vector machines, and random forests.

The performance of these models was evaluated using 10×10-fold cross-validation, with the training folds rebalanced using SMOTE to account for the minority class of defective scripts. Random forests emerged as the top-performing algorithm across all four datasets, and their results are reported here. To evaluate the performance of these models, we used precision and recall of the defective class, as well as the F-measure, which provides a more informative metric than accuracy for imbalanced datasets. The results, presented in Table 2, show that precision ranged from 0.70 (Wikimedia) to 0.78 (OpenStack), while recall ranged from 0.54 (Wikimedia) to 0.67 (OpenStack). The largest dataset, OpenStack, yielded the highest performance, while the smallest dataset, Wikimedia, yielded the lowest, consistent with the sensitivity of machine learning algorithms to training size.

Across datasets, random forests outperformed the other algorithms on F-measure by a margin of 0.03 to 0.09 over the second-best performer, which was either CART or logistic regression depending on the dataset. Naïve Bayes, on the other hand, had the lowest median F-measure at 0.52. To assess the contribution of each property to the models, we compared the performance of the full ten-property model to two baselines: a model using only lines of code, and a model using lines of code and hard-coded string. The results showed that the full model improved the F-measure by 0.09-0.14 over the lines-of-code baseline, highlighting the importance of considering multiple properties when predicting defective scripts.

Using the mean decrease in Gini impurity, we found that lines of code and hard-coded string were the two most important predictors in all datasets, jointly accounting for 38-46% of total importance. Include and attribute ranked third and fourth in three of the four datasets, while comment and service contributed less than 3% each. These findings suggest that the ten identified properties exhibit measurable correlation with defective scripts, and that lines of code and hard-coded string are the most strongly correlated. Furthermore, the results of our survey indicate that practitioners endorse the importance of include and hard-coded string, although their agreement on other properties is more limited.

Our study contributes to the growing body of research on infrastructure as code (IaC) by demonstrating that defective IaC scripts differ measurably from non-defective scripts in a small set of source code properties. The finding that lines of code correlate strongly with defects is consistent with a long line of evidence from general-purpose software, where size is among the most consistent correlates of defect-proneness. This result is also consistent with earlier work on Puppet scripts, which found that larger scripts accumulate more defects. However, we do not interpret this as a causal claim, but rather as a reflection of the fact that larger scripts tend to contain more configuration logic, resource declarations, and interactions among them, providing more opportunities for defects to arise.

The finding that hard-coded strings correlate with defects is more specific to the IaC domain, where scripts are primarily composed of declarative statements that bind values to resource attributes. When these values are written directly into a script, they must be kept consistent with the environment in which the script runs, and mismatches between hard-coded values and the target environment can lead to defects. This is consistent with the security-smell literature, which identifies hard-coded secrets and literals as a recurring weakness in IaC. Parameterization through variables, templates, or external data stores, such as Hiera in Puppet, may therefore reduce one identifiable class of defects, although we have not tested this intervention directly.

The survey of practitioners provides a second perspective on the importance of these properties. A majority of respondents agreed with the inclusion of external modules and hard-coded strings, which suggests that practitioners already treat these properties as risks. The agreement on hard-coded strings matches the empirical correlation, while the agreement on include is less obvious. Including external modules creates dependencies that are invisible within a single script, and a change in one module can propagate to every script that uses it. This is the same coupling that makes dependency management a recurring difficulty in continuous deployment pipelines. The weaker agreement on other properties may reflect the heterogeneity of practitioner experience, the limited number of respondents, or the fact that some properties are rarely noticed during daily work despite correlating with defects. Nonetheless, we treat the survey as corroboration of our empirical findings, highlighting the importance of considering multiple perspectives when investigating the relationship between source code properties and defective scripts.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a chronic rheumatic disease that affects approximately one in 1,000 children, encompassing a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by arthritis of unknown cause that begins before the age of 16 and persists for at least six weeks. The treatment of JIA has undergone significant changes over the past two decades, with early and more aggressive use of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as methotrexate, and the introduction of biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and T-cell costimulation. These advances have led to an increase in the proportion of children who achieve low disease activity or clinical remission. Nevertheless, a substantial number of youth with JIA continue to experience poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including limitations in physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, even when clinical measures indicate that the disease is well controlled.

The persistence of poor HRQOL in the face of well-controlled disease suggests that standard clinical indicators may not capture the full range of factors that contribute to the lived experience of JIA. HRQOL is a complex, multidimensional construct that reflects an individual's perception of how their health and illness affect their physical, psychological, and social wellbeing. In pediatric rheumatology, HRQOL has been measured using a variety of instruments, including the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL), disease-specific tools, and the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS). Studies using these instruments have consistently shown that HRQOL in JIA is lower than in healthy peers and that disease activity, functional disability, and pain are correlated with HRQOL. However, the associations between clinician-assessed disease activity and HRQOL are typically modest, and a significant proportion of the variance in HRQOL remains unexplained.

One potential explanation for this discrepancy is that the burden of treatment itself may contribute to poor HRQOL. Children with JIA often take medications for extended periods, frequently in combination, and these regimens can involve injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and the risk of adverse effects. Methotrexate, the most widely used first-line systemic therapy, is effective but is commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms, such as nausea and abdominal pain, as well as anticipatory and associative symptoms. Methotrexate intolerance has been reported in a substantial minority of patients and can lead to reduced adherence, dose changes, or discontinuation, ultimately resulting in poorer HRQOL and greater distress for both children and parents.

Another domain of patient experience that is not fully captured in routine care is the day-to-day symptom burden of disease. Morning stiffness, a classic feature of inflammatory arthritis, is not consistently recorded in clinical encounters, and its relationship to HRQOL in contemporary JIA cohorts is not well characterized. Pain interference, which reflects the extent to which pain disrupts activities, social participation, and mood, has emerged as an important patient-reported outcome, and PROMIS provides a validated pediatric measure of it. Pain interference may remain elevated in children with inactive disease, representing an important and under-recognized source of reduced HRQOL.

Patient-centered outcomes research has increasingly emphasized the importance of collecting information directly from patients and families to understand which experiences matter most and how they relate to outcomes. Multisite disease registries, such as the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, offer a platform for this type of research, as they enroll large and diverse samples and contain detailed clinical data, including diagnosis, disease activity, and medication history. The CARRA Registry is a North American observational registry of children with rheumatic diseases, including JIA, that has enrolled thousands of patients across dozens of centers. While the registry's clinical data have supported research on treatment patterns and safety, it has not routinely included patient- or parent-reported measures of HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment.

The aim of this study was to add patient-reported outcomes to the CARRA Registry and to use them to quantify HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden among youth with JIA. Parents served as proxy reporters of their child's HRQOL, pain interference, morning stiffness, history of serious medication side effects, and, for those taking methotrexate, methotrexate intolerance. We sought to answer three questions: What is the distribution of HRQOL and these disease and treatment experiences in a multisite registry sample? How is each experience associated with HRQOL? And do associations between treatment burden and HRQOL persist after accounting for disease burden, disease activity, and patient characteristics? We hypothesized that both disease and treatment burden would be independently associated with lower HRQOL.

This study makes several contributions to the field. It demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting an established multicenter registry with patient-reported measures, creating a model that other registries may adopt. It provides estimates of the prevalence of morning stiffness, serious medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance in a registry cohort with long disease duration. Most importantly, it evaluates the independent contributions of disease and treatment burden to HRQOL, testing the proposition that adverse treatment experiences undermine wellbeing beyond the effects of disease symptoms and activity. The findings of this study may help clinicians better understand the complex interplay between disease and treatment burden and HRQOL, ultimately informing the development of more effective and patient-centered treatment strategies for youth with JIA. By highlighting the importance of considering the patient's perspective in the management of JIA, this study has the potential to improve outcomes and enhance the quality of life for children and families affected by this chronic and debilitating disease. In our ongoing efforts to improve the quality of life for youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), researchers have been working to identify modifiable targets that can be assessed and addressed in a routine clinical setting. To this end, we conducted a cross-sectional, observational study nested within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, a comprehensive, multisite registry of children with pediatric rheumatic diseases enrolled at North American pediatric rheumatology centers. The CARRA Registry, established by Beukelman et al. in 2017, collects a wealth of clinician-reported data, including demographic, diagnostic, disease activity, and medication information, at enrollment and at regular follow-up visits. For our study, we augmented this existing infrastructure with a patient-centered data collection component, in which parents completed a survey about their child's health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and experiences with disease and treatment.

Participating sites obtained the necessary approvals from their local institutional review boards or the central IRB used by the registry, and parents provided informed consent, with children providing assent where required by local policy. Our eligibility criteria included enrollment in the CARRA Registry, a physician diagnosis of JIA according to International League of Associations for Rheumatology criteria, an age range of 2 to 18 years, and the presence of a parent or legal guardian who could read and respond in English. Notably, because the survey was completed by parent proxy, we did not exclude youth who were too young or unable to self-report. Instead, we relied on parents to provide insights into their child's experiences, recognizing that they are often best positioned to report on their child's daily functioning and well-being.

To recruit participants, sites identified eligible patients from the registry and invited their parents to complete the survey, either during a clinic visit or remotely via mail or secure electronic link. Parents completed the survey on a single occasion, and we linked their responses to registry data from the visit nearest to survey completion using a unique study identifier. To ensure the integrity of our analysis, we restricted our analytic sample to patients with complete data on the primary HRQOL outcome and key covariates.

Our measurement of HRQOL was based on the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 Generic Core Scales, parent-proxy report, which has been widely used and validated in pediatric populations. The PedsQL contains 23 items that span physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with a recall period of the previous month. We used the Total Scale Score as our primary outcome, as well as physical and psychosocial summary scores, to provide a comprehensive picture of HRQOL. Age-appropriate parent-proxy forms were used for children across different age ranges (2–4, 5–7, 8–12, and 13–18 years), allowing us to capture the unique experiences and challenges faced by children at different stages of development.

In addition to HRQOL, we assessed pain interference using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pediatric Pain Interference parent-proxy short form. This measure provides a standardized way to evaluate the impact of pain on daily activities, with higher scores indicating greater interference. We also collected data on morning stiffness, which is a recognized marker of active inflammatory arthritis and an important aspect of disease activity assessment. Parents reported the typical duration of their child's morning stiffness on a usual day, and we dichotomized this variable as more than 15 minutes versus 15 minutes or less.

To capture the potential downsides of treatment, we asked parents about their child's experiences with medication side effects. Specifically, we inquired about the nature and severity of any side effects and classified them using predefined criteria. A serious side effect was defined as one that led to medication discontinuation or dose change, required medical evaluation or treatment, or substantially disrupted the child's daily functioning. We created a binary indicator of one or more serious medication side effects to facilitate analysis. For children currently or previously treated with methotrexate, parents completed the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score (MISS), which assesses symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and restlessness or irritability. Scores range from 0 to 25, with a score of 6 or higher indicating clinically relevant methotrexate intolerance.

Our analysis also incorporated clinical and demographic characteristics, including patient age, sex, race and ethnicity, disease duration, JIA category, and treating site. We obtained these data from the registry, along with information on disease activity, which was captured using the clinical Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score based on 10 joints (cJADAS-10). This score combines physician global assessment, parent global assessment of wellbeing, and active joint count to provide a comprehensive picture of disease activity. Current medication use, including methotrexate and biologic agents, was also abstracted from registry records.

In our statistical analysis, we first summarized participant characteristics and study measures using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. We inspected the distributions of PedsQL, pain interference, and disease activity scores for normality and outliers, and then proceeded to estimate the associations between measures of disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance) and HRQOL. To account for the clustering of patients within participating sites, we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure and robust standard errors.

Our primary aim was to model the relationship between each burden measure and HRQOL, first in unadjusted models and then in models adjusted for patient demographics (age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and disease duration, with clustering by site. We then added disease burden measures to models of treatment burden to determine whether treatment-related associations persisted independent of disease symptoms. Finally, we adjusted for disease activity (cJADAS-10) and current medication use to evaluate whether associations were attenuated by clinical characteristics. Because the methotrexate intolerance analysis was restricted to methotrexate users, we conducted this analysis in the relevant subsample, using parallel model-building to facilitate comparison.

Throughout our analysis, we compared coefficients across successive models to assess attenuation and evaluated collinearity among covariates using variance inflation factors. Regression coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals and p-values, and we considered p-values below 0.01 to indicate statistical significance in primary analyses to limit the risk of type I error. Secondary analyses repeated the models for physical and psychosocial PedsQL summary scores, providing a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between burden measures and HRQOL. Missing data were infrequent and handled by complete-case analysis, and all analyses were performed using standard statistical software. Our analysis of data from the CARRA Registry, which included 180 youth with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), provided valuable insights into the complex relationships between disease burden, treatment burden, and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in this population. The sample was broadly representative of the registry population in terms of demographic distribution, with 81.1% of participants identifying as white non-Hispanic and 76.7% as female. The mean age at survey was 11.8 years, with a standard deviation of 3.6 years, and the mean disease duration was 7.7 years, with a standard deviation of 3.5 years. Notably, 50% of the youth were currently taking methotrexate, which is a common treatment for JIA.

In terms of clinical characteristics, the sample exhibited a range of disease categories, physician-rated disease activity levels, and current medication classes, as summarized in Table 1. To account for potential site-level clustering, we included site as a clustering variable in all regression models. The youth in our sample reported moderately impaired HRQOL, with a mean Total Pediatric Quality of Life (PedsQL) score of 76.7, which is lower than expected for a population with access to healthcare. The distribution of PedsQL scores was left-skewed, with a median of 80.4 and an interquartile range of 66.3 to 91.3. Scores were lowest in the physical domain, with a mean of 73.5, and higher in the emotional, social, and school domains, with means of 77.9, 80.2, and 74.8, respectively.

A substantial proportion of youth, 34.4%, had Total PedsQL scores more than one standard deviation below the mean for healthy reference populations, which is a commonly used threshold to indicate at-risk HRQOL. We also examined disease burden, which was substantial in this sample. The mean PROMIS Pediatric Pain Interference T-score was 50.1, which is close to the reference population mean of 50. However, this average masked significant variability, with scores ranging from 30.6 to 76.4. Notably, 27.8% of youth had T-scores of 55 or higher, indicating at least mild pain interference. Morning stiffness was also a significant issue, with 17.8% of youth experiencing more than 15 minutes of morning stiffness on a typical day. Pain interference and morning stiffness were positively correlated, and both were inversely correlated with Total PedsQL.

Treatment burden was also a significant concern in this sample. A total of 26.7% of youth had a history of at least one serious medication side effect, with gastrointestinal symptoms, behavioral or mood changes, hair loss, and injection-related reactions being the most common. Among the 90 current methotrexate users, 42.2% met criteria for methotrexate intolerance, which was more frequent among youth with a history of serious side effects. However, the two measures of treatment burden were not redundant, as many youth with intolerance reported no serious side effect. Youth with treatment burden also reported more disease burden, with higher mean pain interference and a greater proportion experiencing prolonged morning stiffness.

In unadjusted generalized estimating equation (GEE) models, every measure of disease and treatment burden was significantly and negatively associated with Total PedsQL. Each 10-point increase in pain interference T-score was associated with a 9.2-point lower Total PedsQL, while morning stiffness lasting more than 15 minutes was associated with an 11.6-point lower score. A history of at least one serious medication side effect was associated with a 9.8-point lower score, and meeting criteria for methotrexate intolerance was associated with a 10.4-point lower score among methotrexate users.

In multivariable GEE models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, disease duration, physician-rated disease activity, and clustering by site, the associations between disease and treatment burden and HRQOL remained statistically significant, although the estimates were attenuated. The adjusted coefficient for pain interference was -8.1 per 10-point increase, and for morning stiffness >15 minutes it was -8.3. When treatment burden measures were added to models that included pain interference and morning stiffness, serious medication side effect history remained independently associated with lower HRQOL, as did methotrexate intolerance among methotrexate users. Pain interference remained the strongest correlate of HRQOL in the fully adjusted models, which explained a substantial portion of variance in Total PedsQL.

Demographic and clinical covariates showed modest associations with HRQOL. Higher physician-rated disease activity was associated with lower HRQOL, while age, sex, race/ethnicity, and disease duration were not significantly associated with Total PedsQL in adjusted models. Sensitivity analyses revealed that the results were consistent when models were re-estimated using domain-specific PedsQL scores, and that treatment burden measures were most strongly associated with the physical and school domains. Excluding youth with systemic JIA did not materially change the direction or significance of any estimate, and replacing the dichotomous morning stiffness variable with a categorical measure showed a graded relationship with HRQOL.

In conclusion, our findings indicate that both disease burden and treatment burden contribute uniquely to HRQOL in youth with JIA. The associations between these burdens and HRQOL were significant and substantial, even after adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates. These results highlight the importance of considering both disease and treatment burden when assessing and managing HRQOL in youth with JIA. By doing so, healthcare providers can develop more comprehensive and effective treatment plans that address the complex needs of these patients and improve their overall quality of life. The management of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) has undergone significant advancements, with a growing emphasis on specialty care and the utilization of modern therapies. Despite these improvements, the disease continues to exert a profound impact on the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) of affected children. Our research reveals that both disease burden, encompassing factors such as pain interference and morning stiffness, and treatment burden, including serious medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance, are independently and negatively associated with HRQOL. Notably, the associations between treatment-related factors and HRQOL were attenuated, but not entirely eliminated, after adjusting for disease symptoms, clinical characteristics, and demographics. This suggests that HRQOL in JIA is a multifaceted construct, influenced not only by the degree of inflammation and symptom control but also by the experiences of children and families in managing the disease.

The mean Total PedsQL score of 76.7 observed in our study is significantly lower than the published values for healthy children, which typically range from 80 to 85 (Varni et al., 2003; Seid et al., 2004). This finding is consistent with previous research indicating that HRQOL impairment persists in JIA even when clinical disease activity is well-controlled (Oliveira et al., 2007; Shaw et al., 2006). The introduction of biologic therapies has substantially improved joint outcomes; however, traditional clinical markers such as joint counts and physician global assessments capture only a portion of what is meaningful to patients. Our data support the notion that patient-reported outcomes (PROs) provide complementary information that is not routinely reflected in clinical assessments, highlighting the importance of incorporating PROs into the management of JIA.

A significant proportion of youth in our study experienced residual symptoms, with nearly one in five reporting more than 15 minutes of morning stiffness on a typical day. This suggests that active inflammatory disease is common in this cohort, despite the long mean disease duration of 7.7 years. The independent association between treatment burden and HRQOL is a novel contribution of our work, with more than one quarter of the sample reporting at least one serious medication side effect and over 40% of methotrexate users meeting criteria for methotrexate intolerance. Methotrexate intolerance is characterized by anticipatory and associative symptoms such as nausea or abdominal pain before or after dosing and has been described in a substantial minority of patients (Bulatović et al., 2011; van Dijkhuizen et al., 2014). Our findings extend this literature by demonstrating that intolerance is linked to poorer overall HRQOL, not just treatment-specific outcomes, even when disease activity and pain are taken into account.

One possible interpretation of our results is that treatment adverse effects directly impair physical and emotional functioning, for example through nausea, fatigue, or mood changes. Alternatively, treatment experiences may exert indirect effects through the anxiety and anticipatory distress surrounding injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and daily medication routines, as well as through the disruption of school, social, and family life. The attenuation of associations after controlling for disease burden suggests partial overlap, as symptoms and adverse effects may co-occur or be difficult for respondents to distinguish. However, the persistence of significant associations indicates that treatment burden carries unique weight in determining HRQOL.

Our results have significant implications for clinical care. Treat-to-target strategies in JIA emphasize rapid control of inflammation, often through escalation of therapy. However, our findings suggest that the targets of care should also include tolerability and quality of life. Routine, brief screening for pain interference, morning stiffness, medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance could identify children whose HRQOL is compromised and who might benefit from interventions that would not be triggered by joint examination alone. Such interventions might include changing the route of administration, splitting or adjusting doses, adding antiemetics or folic acid, switching agents, or offering psychological support such as cognitive-behavioral strategies for anticipatory symptoms and pain. Shared decision-making is also essential, as weighing the benefits of disease control against treatment-related quality-of-life costs requires information about patient experiences that clinicians may not elicit spontaneously.

The integration of PROs into registries and electronic health records offers a feasible way to incorporate patient experiences into clinical care and to support both individual care and comparative effectiveness research. However, several limitations of our study should be considered. First, the cross-sectional design precludes determination of temporal or causal relationships, and poor HRQOL may increase the likelihood of reporting side effects or intolerance. Second, all PROs were reported by parent proxies, which may not accurately capture the subjective experiences of adolescents. Third, the sample was predominantly white, non-Hispanic, and female, and may reflect selective participation, limiting generalizability to more diverse or community-based populations. Fourth, measures of medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance relied on recall and may be subject to recall bias and misattribution of symptoms to medications. Fifth, we examined a limited set of disease and treatment experiences and did not assess other plausible contributors to HRQOL, such as fatigue, sleep, psychosocial factors, family functioning, or school participation. Finally, detailed treatment variables, including dose, duration, and concomitant medications, could not be fully explored in relation to specific adverse effects, and the analysis of methotrexate intolerance was restricted to current users.

Future research should employ longitudinal designs to clarify how changes in disease and treatment burden relate to changes in HRQOL and to test whether addressing intolerance improves outcomes and adherence. Collecting child self-report alongside parent proxy report and including more diverse populations would strengthen validity and equity. The development of validated, concise instruments for treatment burden in pediatric rheumatology is essential to allow standardized assessment across sites and to enable use as outcomes in trials of supportive interventions. In conclusion, our study highlights the significant reductions in HRQOL experienced by youth with JIA, which are related to both disease symptoms and the burdens of treatment. Adverse treatment experiences, including serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance, are associated with lower HRQOL even after accounting for pain, stiffness, and clinical characteristics. Routine assessment of these patient-reported experiences, ideally embedded in registries and clinical workflows, can help clinicians provide more comprehensive and patient-centered care.

The recognition of complex patterns in real-world data often presents a unique challenge, as it cannot be reduced to a standard multi-class classification problem. In many cases, only one class is well-represented in the training data, while the remaining classes are rare, heterogeneous, or impossible to enumerate in advance. This is evident in applications such as fault detection in industrial systems, intrusion detection, medical screening, and identity verification. The class of interest is typically well-defined, whereas the other classes are not. To address this scenario, one-class classification (OCC) has emerged as a viable solution, where a decision rule is learned from examples of a single class, and then used to determine whether a new sample belongs to that class.

The most well-known OCC methods include the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM) and Support Vector Data Description (SVDD). The OC-SVM separates the data from the origin in a kernel-induced feature space, while SVDD finds the minimum-volume hypersphere that encloses the target data. Both methods can be extended to non-linear boundaries using kernels and are widely used as baselines. More recently, deep variants such as Deep SVDD have been proposed, which couple representation learning with a compact description of the target class. However, the performance of any one-class method heavily depends on the feature space in which the data are described. Since no negative samples are available to guide the choice of features, the data representation is often high-dimensional, redundant, or noisy, which can compromise the compactness assumption underlying SVDD.

To mitigate this issue, dimensionality reduction is commonly applied as a separate pre-processing step. Classical techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are unsupervised and optimize criteria like reconstruction error or variance, which may not be directly related to the objective of the subsequent one-class classifier. To address this mismatch, Subspace Support Vector Data Description (S-SVDD) was proposed, which jointly learns a linear or non-linear projection and the SVDD description, so that the target data become compact in a subspace optimized for the one-class objective. Related graph-embedded formulations also use the geometry of the target class to regularize the learned representation. However, these approaches assume that every sample is represented by a single feature vector from a single source, which is increasingly at odds with the way data are acquired in modern applications.

In many cases, objects, events, and subjects are observed through multiple modalities, such as different sensors, imaging devices, or feature extractors, which capture complementary aspects of the same underlying phenomenon. Examples include visual and thermal imagery, audio and video streams, and multi-sensor measurements in industrial monitoring. Multimodal and multi-view learning has been shown to improve robustness and accuracy compared to learning from a single source. Classical subspace methods such as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) learn projections that maximize cross-modal correlation, while deep multimodal architectures learn shared representations. However, these techniques are designed to model statistical dependence between modalities and do not take into account the objective of a downstream one-class classifier.

In the OCC literature, the multimodal setting is typically handled in one of two ways, both of which have limitations. The first approach is to train a separate one-class model on each modality and combine the resulting decision scores, which ignores relations among modalities during representation learning and can be adversely affected by weak or noisy modalities. The second approach is to concatenate the features of all modalities into a single vector and apply a standard one-class method, which increases dimensionality, leaves modality-specific scale and noise characteristics unaddressed, and makes the description susceptible to the curse of dimensionality when training samples are limited. Neither strategy learns modality-specific mappings into a common space that is designed from the outset for describing the target class.

Consequently, there is a clear gap in the existing literature: no approach jointly learns, for each modality, a transformation into a shared low-dimensional space and a single compact description of the target class using data from all modalities, while relying exclusively on target-class samples. The question motivating this work is whether multimodal one-class learning can be improved by learning modality-specific projections to a common subspace in which a single hypersphere, trained only on target data from all modalities, provides a tighter and more discriminative description than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion. Answering this question requires addressing several challenges, including learning the projections in conjunction with the data description, admitting regularization strategies that prevent degenerate solutions, and handling both linear and non-linear relations.

To address these challenges, we introduce Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD), a method that extends the S-SVDD framework to data from multiple modalities. MS-SVDD iteratively optimizes two components: a set of modality-specific transformations that map each original feature space into a common subspace, and a joint SVDD description of the projected data from all modalities. The transformations are learned using information from the class of interest only, so the method remains a genuine one-class approach and requires no negative or outlier examples at training time. The contributions of this work are threefold. Firstly, we formulate the problem of learning a shared one-class-optimized subspace from multiple modalities and propose MS-SVDD, which jointly learns modality-specific projections and a single compact description of the target class. Secondly, we propose several regularization strategies for the method, which control the geometry of the learned subspace and the relationships among the projected modalities, allowing the formulation to be adapted to different degrees of cross-modal agreement. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MS-SVDD in improving multimodal one-class learning, providing a tighter and more discriminative description of the target class than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion. This paper proposes a novel approach to multimodal one-class classification, which we term MS-SVDD. Our method provides both linear and non-linear formulations, allowing it to be applied to data with simple as well as complex structure. Furthermore, we introduce an iterative optimization procedure to learn a task-specific common subspace that effectively integrates information from multiple modalities. To evaluate the performance of MS-SVDD, we conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on five publicly available multimodal datasets, comparing our approach with one-class methods trained on a single modality and on fused data from all modalities. The results show that MS-SVDD outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of learning a shared subspace for multimodal data.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing the necessary background on Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) and Subspace SVDD (S-SVDD) in Section 2. In Section 3, we present the proposed MS-SVDD method, including its regularization strategies and linear and non-linear formulations. Section 4 describes the datasets and experimental protocol used to evaluate MS-SVDD, and reports the results of our experiments. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

To formulate the problem, let us denote the data from M modalities as 𝒳 = {X¹,…,X^M}, where X^m ∈ ℝ^{Dm×N} contains the N training samples of the target class represented in the m-th modality, with Dm being the modality-specific dimensionality. Note that only target-class samples are used during training, which is consistent with the one-class classification (OCC) setting. We assume that samples are paired across modalities, and each modality is z-score normalized using training statistics before projection.

SVDD seeks to find the smallest hypersphere, with centre a and radius R, that encloses most of the training data. In contrast, S-SVDD jointly learns a projection Q ∈ ℝ^{d×D} and the hypersphere in the projected space. We extend this idea to the multimodal case by defining a modality-specific projection Qm ∈ ℝ^{d×Dm} that maps every modality into a common d-dimensional subspace, where one shared hypersphere (a, R) describes data from all modalities.
