Category D saw research as a socially situated process of constructing and testing understanding, which students explicitly equated with learning.

At the start of the course, nine of the 14 students (64%) described research in Category A, four (29%) in Category B, and one (7%) in Category C. No student articulated Category D. By the end of the course, the distribution had shifted, with one student (7%) in Category A, three (21%) in Category B, four (29%) in Category C, and six (43%) in Category D. Eleven of the 14 students (79%) moved to a more inclusive category, three (21%) remained in the same category, and none regressed. Of the nine students initially in Category A, seven moved to Category C or D, one moved to Category B, and one stayed in Category A. Three of the four students who moved beyond Category B did so by recognizing that the research question and design were open to their own judgment.

A typical initial statement was, "Research is when scientists find out something new and publish it" (Student 3, pre-course). The same student later said, "I used to think research was the results. Now I see that most of the work is deciding what to ask and how you could possibly know" (Student 3, post-course). This shift in understanding was evident in the increased attention to research processes, with 11 students (79%) mentioning researcher autonomy, 12 (86%) mentioning collaboration, and 10 (71%) mentioning how knowledge is constructed in the end-of-course interviews. In contrast, only three students (21%) mentioned researcher autonomy, one (7%) mentioned collaboration, and two (14%) mentioned how knowledge is constructed in the pre-course interviews. Students described autonomy as owning the question, "nobody gave us the answer, so we had to decide what counted as good evidence" (Student 9), and collaboration as negotiating interpretations of data with peers.

The explicit recognition that research and learning are the same kind of activity appeared only in the post-course interviews, in nine students (64%). These students described a change in their own approach to study, consistent with a shift from a surface to a deep approach as described by Marton and Säljö (1976) and Biggs (1999). Their accounts moved away from memorizing isolated facts for examinations and towards seeking meaning, relating ideas, and questioning sources. At baseline, 10 students (71%) characterized their learning in medical school mainly as memorization and reproduction. At follow-up, only four (29%) still did so, and the remaining 10 reported predominantly meaning-oriented strategies in at least some of their coursework. One student stated, "When I read a paper now I ask what they were trying to find out and whether I agree, and I've started doing that with lecture slides too" (Student 12). The five students who did not articulate the research–learning connection still demonstrated an increased focus on the processes of research, such as the importance of methodology and the role of collaboration.

Overall, our study provides insights into the ways in which undergraduate medical students' conceptions of research evolve over the course of an undergraduate research experience. By examining the changes in students' understanding of research and their approaches to learning, we can better understand how to support students in developing a deeper understanding of research and its relationship to learning. Our findings have implications for the design of undergraduate research experiences and highlight the importance of providing students with opportunities to engage in authentic research practices and to develop a sense of autonomy and collaboration in their learning. The relationship between students' conceptions of research and their approaches to learning is a complex and multifaceted one. Our study suggests that students who remained in Categories A or B, which represent a more nuanced and process-oriented understanding of research, were more likely to have experienced an epistemological shift, wherein their conception of research expanded to encompass a broader range of activities and values. This shift is consistent with the findings of Entwistle and Peterson (2004), who described a similar relationship between conceptions of knowledge and approaches to learning.

A thematic analysis of post-course interviews revealed five key themes that characterized students' engagement with the research process. These themes - an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, collaborative learning, and reflective learning - were identified in accordance with the methodology outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006), wherein themes are retained only when they appear across multiple groups. The distribution of students across these themes is notable: an inquiring mind, which encompassed curiosity and a willingness to question existing evidence, was reported by 12 students; synthesis of knowledge, which involved integrating clinical knowledge, literature, and personal data into a coherent argument, was reported by 11 students; active participation, which covered taking initiative in searching for literature, designing instruments, and seeking help from supervisors, was the most widely reported theme, with 13 students contributing to it; collaborative learning, which captured the process of explaining, challenging, and refining ideas with peers, was reported by 10 students; and reflective learning, which involved the reassessment of assumptions and strategies, was also reported by 10 students. Notably, nine students (64%) contributed to both collaborative and reflective learning themes, and these students were more likely to explicitly describe the link between research and learning.

However, despite these gains, the majority of students (13 out of 14, or 93%) reported experiencing difficulties in working within their groups. These difficulties can be categorized into four main areas: understanding the research process itself, prior learning experiences, differences in interpersonal communication styles, and problems rooted in existing social relationships. The first category, which included struggles with formulating a researchable question, choosing a design, and interpreting qualitative or mixed data, was reported by nine students (64%). The second category, which involved difficulties arising from prior learning experiences, such as feeling uncomfortable with ambiguity and the absence of a "correct" product, was reported by eight students (57%). The third category, which captured differences in how much group members valued interpersonal communication, was reported by seven students (50%). The fourth category, which involved problems rooted in existing social relationships, such as reluctance to challenge friends or perceived status differences within groups, was reported by six students (43%).

It is noteworthy that these difficulties were not evenly distributed across groups. All three groups containing students who ended in Category D, which represents a more fragmented and product-oriented conception of research, also contained students who remained in A or B. Furthermore, tensions were most often described in these groups, suggesting that the coexistence of students with differing conceptions of research can create challenges. However, some students reported that conflict and difficulties prompted reflection and growth, as exemplified by one student's comment: "the disagreement made us go back and justify why we chose that method" (Student 6). Others, however, reported that difficulties led to withdrawal of effort or unequal workload.

In summary, our study suggests that participation in a group-based undergraduate research course can lead to a qualitative shift in students' conceptions of research, wherein they move from a focus on outcomes to a more nuanced understanding of the research process. This shift is often accompanied by a recognition of the link between research and learning, and is associated with a deeper approach to learning. However, barriers to group work are common and can arise from both cognitive and social sources. The study's findings have implications for the design of undergraduate research courses and the role of research-based activity in medical education.

Our study's main finding - a qualitative shift in students' conceptions of research - is consistent with phenomenographic work on variation in how researchers and students experience research (Brew, 2001; Brew, 2003). Brew described conceptions ranging from research as a domino or layer-like accumulation of facts to research as a trading or journey-like process of making meaning. Our students' initial views resemble the more fragmented, product-oriented end of this range, while their later reflections moved toward relational and transformational understandings. This movement likely reflects the experiential nature of the course, wherein students encountered research as something people do, rather than something that is reported. This supports the view that students' conceptions change when they are placed in situations that expose the constructed nature of knowledge (Healey & Jenkins, 2009; Marton & Booth, 1997).

The link students drew between research and learning can be read as an epistemological change, wherein students moved from treating knowledge as something to be received and reproduced to seeing it as something to be questioned, synthesized, and justified. This corresponds to the distinction between surface and deep approaches (Marton & Säljö, 1976; Biggs & Tang, 2011) and to developmental accounts of epistemological belief, in which learners move from dualistic to more contextual understandings (Perry, 1970; Baxter Magolda, 2004). The themes we identified - an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, and collaborative and reflective learning - are characteristic of deep approaches, which involve an intention to understand, relating ideas, and active engagement.

In medical education, where curricula are often dense and examination-driven, strategic or surface approaches are common (Newble & Entwistle, 1986). Our findings suggest that undergraduate research can offer a context in which students recognize the value of understanding over memorization. Such recognition matters for lifelong learning and evidence-based practice, as graduates must continually appraise and integrate new knowledge (Frank et al., 2010). It also supports the argument that research-based activity should be treated as a pedagogy for learning, not only as a means of acquiring technical research skills. By providing students with opportunities to engage in authentic research experiences, we can help them develop a deeper understanding of the research process and its relationship to learning, and foster a more nuanced and contextual understanding of knowledge.

The increasing prevalence of infinite-dimensional data in modern statistical analysis has prompted a growing need for effective methods to ensure the privacy and security of sensitive information. Functional data analysis, which treats curves and surfaces as the fundamental units of observation, has become a crucial tool in this endeavor (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005; Hsing and Eubank, 2015). Similarly, shape analysis, which operates on objects defined on manifolds, and nonparametric statistics, which often produce functional estimators such as densities, regression surfaces, and covariance operators, also involve complex data structures that require careful consideration of privacy concerns.

Many of these data types are inherently sensitive, encompassing physiological trajectories from wearable devices, genomic profiles, mobility traces, and neuroimaging scans, among others. Even the release of summaries or aggregated forms of these data can potentially reveal identifying information about the individuals who contributed to them. To address this risk, Differential Privacy (DP) has emerged as a rigorous framework for quantifying and limiting the disclosure of sensitive information (Dwork et al., 2006). DP has become the standard for privacy-preserving data release in both academic and industrial settings (Dwork and Roth, 2014).

However, the application of DP to infinite-dimensional summaries remains less developed compared to its application to finite-dimensional vectors. The most common approach to achieving DP involves adding noise to a statistic, calibrated to its sensitivity. In finite dimensions, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms have been shown to accomplish this with well-understood trade-offs between privacy and accuracy (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork et al., 2014). Extending these mechanisms to function spaces requires careful consideration, as the properties of infinite-dimensional data can significantly impact the effectiveness of these approaches.

Recent research has made progress in addressing these challenges. Hall et al. (2013) demonstrated that for functional data, privacy can be achieved by adding a scaled Gaussian process to the target function, with calibration dependent on the sensitivity measured in the Cameron-Martin space of the process. Mirshani et al. (2019) generalized this result to arbitrary separable Hilbert spaces, while Awan and Slavković (2021) explored related mechanisms. These findings rely on a fundamental dichotomy: two Gaussian measures with different means are either equivalent or mutually singular (Feldman, 1958; Hájek, 1958), implying that privacy is only possible when the sensitivity lies in the Cameron-Martin space. This restriction limits the types of statistics that can be privatized using additive noise.

Moreover, additive mechanisms are not well-suited for outputs subject to geometric constraints, such as unit-norm eigenfunctions, positive semidefinite operators, or points on a manifold. In such cases, noise added to these objects typically leaves the constraint set, requiring ad hoc projection. The exponential mechanism, introduced by McSherry and Talwar (2007), offers a natural alternative. Instead of perturbing a statistic, this mechanism samples an output from a distribution whose density, relative to a base measure, is proportional to the exponential of a utility function scaled by the privacy budget and the utility's sensitivity. The exponential mechanism guarantees ε-DP under minimal assumptions and automatically respects the output space, as the base measure can be supported on the constraint set.

The exponential mechanism has connections to posterior sampling and Gibbs distributions (Wang et al., 2015; Minami et al., 2016; Dimitrakakis et al., 2017) and has been applied to various problems, including private PCA (Chaudhuri et al., 2013; Kapralov and Talwar, 2013), convex empirical risk minimization (Kifer et al., 2012), and private median and quantile estimation (Smith, 2011). Nevertheless, most existing theory concerns finite-dimensional or discrete output spaces, leaving several open questions for infinite-dimensional outputs. These include defining the mechanism when no uniform or Lebesgue measure exists, characterizing the sampling distribution of the privatized output, and determining the accuracy loss due to privacy relative to the intrinsic statistical error, asymptotically.

The conventional wisdom holds that privacy comes at no additional cost in large samples, as the noise required for privacy shrinks at a rate faster than the sampling error. However, the behavior of the exponential mechanism in this regard is less transparent, particularly when the utility is a general M-estimation criterion and the output space is infinite-dimensional. This paper addresses these gaps by formulating the exponential mechanism over a separable Hilbert space with respect to an explicitly chosen base measure, such as a Gaussian process. We demonstrate that the base measure is a genuine design choice, influencing the support of the output, its regularity, and the geometry in which accuracy is measured.

Our contributions include establishing conditions under which the resulting mechanism is well-defined, verifying that it satisfies ε-DP, and discussing the interaction between Gaussian-process base measures and the Cameron-Martin structure governing additive mechanisms. We also establish a Central Limit Theorem for the exponential mechanism under broad conditions, showing that the privatized output, after centering and scaling, converges weakly to a well-characterized Gaussian limit. This result provides a tractable description of the distribution of privatized outputs and is a first step toward valid inference from them.

In contrast to the prevailing view, we find that the privacy-induced Gaussian term is of the same order as the statistical error, causing the exponential mechanism to inflate the asymptotic variance by a constant factor dependent on ε. Although the mechanism remains consistent and converges at the √n rate, its asymptotic efficiency relative to the non-private estimator is strictly below one for any fixed ε. We characterize this inflation explicitly, describing it as an "apparent" negative result due to the mechanism's generality and strong pure-DP guarantee. This clarifies where gains from alternative mechanisms or relaxed privacy notions can be expected.

Finally, we apply our framework to functional principal component analysis (FPCA), a central tool for dimension reduction and exploratory analysis of functional data. We develop an ε-DP mechanism for estimating leading eigenfunctions of a covariance operator in a separable Hilbert space, which samples from a distribution on the unit sphere with a density relative to a chosen base measure. Our results provide a foundation for privacy-preserving functional data analysis and highlight the need for further research into the interplay between statistical inference, privacy, and the geometric properties of infinite-dimensional data. The development of a Gaussian-process-derived base measure, proportional to the exponential of the scaled Rayleigh quotient, marks a significant extension of the finite-dimensional Bingham-type mechanism proposed by Chaudhuri et al. (2013) to the functional setting. Notably, this approach obviates the need for discretizing curves and yields elements that satisfy the unit-norm constraint exactly, thus providing a more robust and efficient framework for analyzing functional data. 

To validate the efficacy of this method, we derive a sampling procedure and conduct a thorough examination of the privacy and asymptotic results for this case. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of the method through simulations and its application to two real datasets, varying sample size, privacy budget, and eigengap, and comparing accuracy with additive Gaussian-process mechanisms as proposed by Hall et al. (2013) and Mirshani et al. (2019). These simulations corroborate the asymptotic variance inflation predicted by our theoretical framework, underscoring the practical utility of private functional principal component analysis (FPCA) on sensitive functional data.

The organization of this paper is as follows: Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of differential privacy (DP) and the exponential mechanism, establishing notation for Hilbert-space-valued outputs. Section 3 delves into the development of the mechanism with general base measures, laying the groundwork for subsequent analyses. Section 4 presents the Central Limit Theorem and an efficiency analysis, crucial for understanding the theoretical underpinnings of our approach. Section 5 focuses on the development of private FPCA, a methodological innovation with significant implications for data analysis. Section 6 reports on simulations and data analyses, offering empirical insights into the method's performance. Finally, Section 7 concludes with a discussion of limitations and potential extensions, situating our contributions within the broader context of privacy-preserving data analysis.

To establish a common framework for our analysis, let H denote a separable Hilbert space equipped with an inner product ⟨·,·⟩ and norm ‖·‖. Consider a set of independent observations X₁, …, Xₙ in H, where each observation is bounded by a constant τ (i.e., ‖Xᵢ‖ ≤ τ), and let D represent the dataset comprising these observations. Two datasets are considered neighboring if they differ by exactly one observation. A randomized mechanism M is said to satisfy ε-differential privacy if, for any measurable set A and all neighboring datasets D and D′, the probability of M(D) being in A is less than or equal to e^ε times the probability of M(D′) being in A (Dwork et al., 2006). 

The finite-dimensional exponential mechanism, as introduced by McSherry and Talwar (2007), selects an output θ with a probability proportional to exp{εu(θ; D)/(2Δ)}, where u(θ; D) is a utility function, and Δ represents its sensitivity. However, in the infinite-dimensional setting, the absence of a Lebesgue measure necessitates defining the mechanism through a density with respect to a base measure μ on the output space Θ. This leads to the formulation of the mechanism's density as dPD/dμ(θ) = exp{ε u(θ; D)/(2Δ)} / ∫ exp{ε u(θ′; D)/(2Δ)} dμ(θ′), where Δ = supθ sup{D∼D′} |u(θ; D) − u(θ; D′)|. For bounded and measurable utility functions u, the normalizing constant is finite and positive, ensuring the mechanism's ε-differential privacy.

We proceed by taking μ to be a centered Gaussian process (GP) measure N(0, K) on H, with K being a trace-class covariance operator. This choice provides a well-defined reference distribution and facilitates sampling. Our asymptotic analysis is conducted under the scaling u(θ; D) = n·mn(θ), where mn(θ) = n⁻¹Σᵢ m(θ; Xᵢ) represents an M-estimation criterion. The sensitivity Δ is then of order O(1), and the density (1) concentrates around the maximizer θ̂ₙ of mn. 

For the central limit theorem, we assume the following conditions: (i) m(·; x) is bounded and twice Fréchet differentiable at the population maximizer θ₀; (ii) the Hessian −V = ∇²M(θ₀) is negative definite on the relevant tangent space; and (iii) μ has a density that is positive and continuous at θ₀ in finite-dimensional projections. We then examine the limiting law of √n(θ̃ₙ − θ̂ₙ), where θ̃ₙ denotes the privatized output, and compare its covariance, of order (ε/2Δ)⁻¹V⁻¹, with that of √n(θ̂ₙ − θ₀). The ratio of these covariances, denoted as ρ(ε) = tr{Cov(√n(θ̃ₙ − θ̂ₙ))}/tr{Cov(√n(θ̂ₙ − θ₀))}, quantifies the relative magnitude of privacy noise to statistical error and is empirically estimated in our simulations.

Our functional PCA mechanism is developed as follows: let Σₙ = n⁻¹ΣᵢXᵢ⊗Xᵢ denote the empirical covariance operator of the centered data. The leading functional principal component is the maximizer over the unit sphere S(H) of ⟨v, Σₙv⟩ (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005; Hsing and Eubank, 2015). Since the unit sphere has zero Gaussian measure in infinite dimensions, we define the utility on the whole space through its scale-invariant extension, u(w; D) = n⟨w, Σₙw⟩/‖w‖², for w ≠ 0. This utility is bounded, with Δ = τ², because replacing one observation changes ⟨w, Σₙw⟩/‖w‖² by at most τ²/n. We draw w from (1) with μ = N(0, K) and output v = w/‖w‖. This post-processing of an ε-DP output ensures that v is ε-DP (Dwork and Roth, 2014). 

Because the utility u is invariant to scale, the direction of w is the only quantity affected by the data. To obtain k components, we apply the mechanism sequentially to the deflated operator Σₙ^{(j)} = (I − Pⱼ)Σₙ(I − Pⱼ), where Pⱼ projects onto the previously released components. Each step receives a budget of ε/k, and basic composition yields a total privacy budget of ε. Data are centered using a fixed public mean or the mean is privatized separately using the GP mechanism of Hall et al. (2013) with a budget ε₀ that is subtracted from the total. Observations are clipped to ‖Xᵢ‖ ≤ τ before analysis, which is part of the mechanism and changes the target to the clipped population operator.

For the base measure, we select K to have eigenpairs (κⱼ, ψⱼ) with κⱼ = j⁻² and ψⱼ being the Fourier basis, corresponding to a Brownian-bridge-type prior. Sensitivity analyses also employ Matérn-type spectra (κⱼ = j⁻ᵃ, a ∈ {1.5, 2, 4}). Since exact sampling from (1) is not available in closed form, we utilize the preconditioned Crank–Nicolson (pCN) Metropolis–Hastings sampler (Cotter et al., 2013), which offers dimension-independent acceptance rates and is well-defined on H. The proposal is w′ = √(1 − β²)·w + βξ, with ξ ∼ N(0, K), and the acceptance probability is min{1, exp(ε[u(w′) − u(w)]/(2Δ))}. 

The step size β is tuned to achieve an acceptance rate of 0.25 ± 0.05 during burn-in. Each run consists of four chains of 25,000 iterations, with the first 5,000 iterations discarded and thinning by 20. Convergence is assessed using the Gelman–Rubin statistic (R̂ < 1.05) and effective sample size (> 200 per released draw). Functions are represented with the first J = 50 basis coefficients, and increasing J to 100 results in a change of less than 2% in the mean squared error in pilot runs. Since MCMC yields only approximate draws, the guarantee holds exactly only for the idealized setting, highlighting the importance of careful implementation and validation in practice. The development of the exponential mechanism has been a crucial step in enabling the release of differentially private statistical estimates. However, as noted by Wang et al. (2015), one of the limitations of this mechanism is the need for a bounded sampling space, which can be restrictive in certain applications. This limitation is also inherent in our implementation, and we will discuss its implications in the context of our results.

To investigate the properties of the exponential mechanism, we conducted a series of simulations. In the first scenario, we generated curves on the interval [0,1] using a Fourier basis with 10 terms, where the coefficients were drawn from a standard normal distribution truncated to the interval [-3, 3]. The eigenvalues of the covariance operator were chosen such that the leading eigengap was 2, and the almost-sure norm bound τ was set accordingly. In a second scenario, we considered a smaller eigengap, with the leading eigenvalue λ₁ = 1.2 and the second eigenvalue λ₂ = 1. We crossed sample sizes n ∈ {100, 500, 1000, 5000} with privacy budgets ε ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1, 5}, and repeated each experiment 500 times. We compared the performance of three procedures: (a) the non-private functional PCA estimator, (b) the proposed GP exponential mechanism, and (c) the Gaussian-noise covariance mechanism, which adds a Hilbert-Schmidt-valued GP perturbation to the sample covariance operator before eigendecomposition, as described in Dwork et al. (2014) and Mirshani et al. (2019). The noise was calibrated to achieve (ε, δ = n⁻²)-differential privacy, which provides a weaker guarantee than the exponential mechanism.

In addition to the simulated data, we also analyzed two benchmark datasets: the Canadian weather data, consisting of daily temperature curves at 35 stations (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005), and the Tecator near-infrared absorbance spectra, with 215 curves and 100 wavelengths (Ferraty and Vieu, 2006). We smoothed the curves using penalized B-splines, centered them, and rescaled them so that the norm bound τ was equal to the 95th percentile of the curve norms, clipping any curves that exceeded this bound. The bounds τ were treated as public information. We released the first three components of the functional PCA decomposition using the exponential mechanism, with privacy budgets ε ∈ {1, 5, 10}, and compared them to the non-private components.

To evaluate the accuracy of the estimates, we used the squared sine of the angle between the estimated and true leading eigenfunctions, L(v, φ₁) = 1 - ⟨v, φ₁⟩², and for the real data, we also considered the relative error with respect to the non-private estimate. We summarized the results using medians and interquartile ranges, as well as Monte Carlo standard errors. To assess the asymptotic claims, we regressed the log risk on log n within each ε to obtain empirical convergence rates. We estimated the ratio of the Monte Carlo variance of the scaled privacy noise to the variance of the non-private estimate, and checked the normality of the scaled privacy noise using Q-Q plots and Anderson-Darling tests.

All computations were carried out in R 4.3, and the code is available from the authors upon request. Our goal is to establish the large-sample behavior of the exponential mechanism, quantify the cost of privacy relative to statistical error, and evaluate the functional PCA mechanism in simulations and on real datasets.

First, we establish the asymptotic normality of the exponential mechanism. Let the mechanism release θ̃ from a density proportional to exp{-(ε/2Δn)·Mn(θ)} with respect to a base measure μ, where Mn is an empirical risk with global sensitivity Δn = Δ/n, and μ is either Lebesgue measure on a finite-dimensional space or a Gaussian process in a separable Hilbert space. Suppose Mn converges to a population risk M with a unique minimizer θ₀ and positive-definite Hessian H, and suppose the minimizer θ̂n is asymptotically normal with covariance Σ (van der Vaart, 1998). Then √n(θ̃ - θ₀) converges in distribution to N(0, Σ + (2Δ/ε)H⁻¹), which holds for any fixed ε > 0, and in the Hilbert space setting, it holds in the weak topology provided H⁻¹ is trace class relative to the covariance of μ. The mechanism is therefore √n-consistent and asymptotically Gaussian, in line with the behavior of other M-estimators (Wasserman and Zhou, 2010).

In a Monte Carlo check with n = 1,000 and d = 5, the empirical coverage of the nominal 95% region built from this limiting law was 94.3% (SE 0.7%) over 2,000 replications. The coverage of a region built from Σ alone, which ignores the privacy noise, was only 61.8% at ε = 1, demonstrating that the privacy noise is not asymptotically negligible. The second term in the limiting covariance does not vanish relative to Σ as n grows. For mean estimation of a bounded random element with ‖X‖ ≤ B, we have H = I and Δ = 2B. The ratio of privacy variance to statistical variance is then tr(2Δ/ε · I)/tr(Σ) = 4B/(ε σ²eff), where σ²eff = tr(Σ)/d. This ratio is constant in n. For a standardized setting with B = 3σeff, the variance inflation factor 1 + 12/ε is 25.0, 13.0, 7.0, and 3.4 at ε = 0.5, 1, 2, and 5, respectively.

We verified this numerically for the Hilbert-space mean with n ∈ {100, 500, 1,000, 5,000, 10,000}. The ratio of mean squared error to the non-private mean squared error was 12.4, 13.6, 12.9, 13.2, and 13.1 at ε = 1, which agrees with the theoretical value of 13.0 and shows no trend in n. By contrast, a calibrated Laplace-type mechanism with noise scale Δ/(nε) has noise variance of order n⁻², so its inflation factor tends to 1 (Dwork et al., 2006). The exponential mechanism is thus not asymptotically efficient in the usual sense. Its excess risk is of the same order as the statistical risk, and the constant is controlled by ε and the sensitivity of the score. This is the apparent negative result. However, the comparison is not entirely like-for-like, as the exponential mechanism needs no output-space boundedness assumption beyond that implied by the base measure, and it applies where additive noise is not well defined (McSherry and Talwar, 2007). The inflation factor can also be reduced by choosing a score with smaller sensitivity. Replacing the squared-error score with a trimmed version reduced Δ by 38% in our simulations and the inflation factor from 13.0 to 8.6 at ε = 1.

The functional PCA mechanism is designed for centered functional data X₁,…,Xₙ in a separable Hilbert space ℍ with ‖Xᵢ‖ ≤ τ. The leading eigenfunction φ₁ maximizes ⟨φ, Ĉn φ⟩ over the unit sphere, where Ĉn is the sample covariance operator. The score has sensitivity at most 2τ²/n. We release φ̃ from a density proportional to exp{(nε/4τ²)⟨φ, Ĉn φ⟩} with respect to a Gaussian-process base measure restricted to the unit sphere. The mechanism is designed to provide a differentially private estimate of the leading eigenfunction, while also controlling the error due to the privacy noise. By using the exponential mechanism, we can provide a rigorous guarantee of differential privacy, while also achieving a high level of accuracy in the estimation of the leading eigenfunction. The concept of differential privacy has been extensively studied in the context of finite-dimensional data, but its application to infinite-dimensional spaces, such as those encountered in functional data analysis, poses significant challenges. To address this, we developed a novel mechanism, denoted as ε-DP, which is a functional analogue of the Bingham-type mechanism for finite-dimensional principal component analysis (Chaudhuri et al., 2013). This mechanism operates by truncating the basis functions to a finite number, which we set to 50 in our experiments, and employing a Gibbs sampler on the sphere after a burn-in period of 1,000 iterations. Notably, increasing the number of basis functions from 50 to 100 resulted in a negligible change in the mean squared error, with a difference of less than 1.5%. Furthermore, subsequent eigenfunctions can be obtained by sequentially deflating the covariance operator, with the privacy budget allocated equally across components.

To evaluate the performance of our mechanism, we conducted a series of simulations. We generated curves using a Fourier basis with eigenvalues λ = (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125) and standard normal coefficients truncated to |ξ| ≤ 3. The loss was measured as 1 − ⟨φ̃₁, φ₁⟩², and we averaged the results over 500 replications. At ε = 1, the mean loss for the exponential mechanism was 0.214 (SE 0.009), 0.081 (0.004), 0.047 (0.002), and 0.020 (0.001) for sample sizes n = 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000, respectively. In contrast, the non-private estimator yielded losses of 0.037, 0.0071, 0.0036, and 0.0007, respectively. The loss of the exponential mechanism declines at a rate of √n, rather than at a faster rate, which is consistent with the non-negligible privacy term. Moreover, the ratio of private to non-private loss remained relatively stable across sample sizes, ranging from 5.8 to 13.2.

We also compared the performance of our mechanism to a Gaussian-process mechanism that perturbs the covariance operator (Mirshani et al., 2019). At n = 1,000 and ε = 1, the Gaussian-process mechanism had a loss of 0.131 (SE 0.006), which is nearly three times that of the exponential mechanism. However, the gap between the two mechanisms narrowed to 1.4-fold at ε = 5. The advantage of the exponential mechanism arises from the fact that it perturbs only the direction of the eigenfunction, rather than the full operator, and the added noise respects the unit-norm constraint. For the second to fourth components at n = 5,000 and ε = 4 (1 per component), the losses were 0.031, 0.058, and 0.112, which reflects the smaller eigengaps (Hall and Hosseini-Nasab, 2006).

In addition to simulations, we applied our mechanism to two real-world datasets. The first dataset consisted of the heights of 93 children measured at 31 ages (Tuddenham and Snyder, 1954; Ramsay and Silverman, 2005). We centered the curves and clamped them to a norm bound τ chosen at the 95th percentile. The non-private first component explained 82.4% of the variance and corresponded mainly to overall growth amplitude, while the second component (11.3%) captured the timing of the pubertal spurt. With ε = 1, the released first eigenfunction had an average inner product of 0.93 with the non-private one over 200 draws (interquartile range 0.89–0.97). At ε = 5, the average inner product rose to 0.99. However, the second component was recovered less well, with an average inner product of 0.71 at ε = 1 and 0.90 at ε = 5, which is consistent with the simulation results for small sample sizes and small eigengaps.

The second dataset consisted of 24-hour activity profiles for 2,848 participants from the NHANES 2003–2006 wave, averaged within participant to 96 fifteen-minute bins (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005). The first four non-private components explained 41.7%, 17.9%, 9.6%, and 6.2% of the variance. At ε = 1 per component, the first two privately estimated eigenfunctions had mean inner products of 0.98 and 0.94 with their non-private counterparts. The reconstruction error, measured as the relative squared L² error of rank-4 reconstruction, was 0.521 for the private estimates and 0.487 for the non-private ones, representing a 7% relative increase. At ε = 0.5, the increase was 15%. These results demonstrate that with a few thousand observations, the privacy cost is modest in practical terms for the leading components, even though it does not vanish asymptotically relative to the statistical error.

Our work has several key findings. First, we show that the exponential mechanism can be defined rigorously in a separable Hilbert space once a base measure, such as a Gaussian process, is chosen to replace the missing Lebesgue measure. Second, under mild regularity conditions, the resulting mechanism satisfies a Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which implies that the privatized estimator is asymptotically Gaussian around the target. Third, the scale of the privacy noise is asymptotically of the same order as the statistical error. We used these results to build an ε-DP mechanism for functional principal component analysis (FPCA) and evaluated it on simulated and real data.

The asymptotic results have important implications for the interpretation of our findings. The CLT is a positive result, as it shows that the exponential mechanism is well-behaved beyond finite-dimensional examples and that its output distribution can be characterized explicitly in the large-sample regime. This supports uncertainty quantification for privatized estimates, which is usually difficult for mechanisms without a tractable limiting law (Wasserman and Zhou, 2010; Karwa and Slavković, 2016). However, the negative result is that, for fixed ε, the privacy noise does not vanish relative to the sampling error. In our notation, both the estimator and the mechanism's perturbation are of order n^{-1/2}, so the limiting covariance is the sum of a statistical component and a privacy component, rather than being dominated by the former.

In the FPCA simulations, the mean squared error of the privatized leading eigenfunction was roughly 1.5 to 4 times that of the non-private estimator at ε = 1, and this ratio did not approach one as the sample size increased, as the theory predicts. By contrast, mechanisms with additive noise calibrated to global sensitivity typically add noise of order 1/(nε), which is asymptotically negligible (Dwork et al., 2006; Smith, 2011). We describe this result as "apparent" because it depends on how the mechanism is calibrated. The exponential mechanism is usually implemented with a utility whose sensitivity is bounded by a constant, and the temperature is set to match. This is a conservative approach, as the guarantee holds for worst-case neighboring datasets, whereas the asymptotic behavior reflects typical ones.

The increasing reliance on deep neural networks in high-stakes applications, such as autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and drug development, has highlighted the need for uncertainty quantification (UQ) in these systems. In these domains, a point prediction is rarely sufficient; rather, practitioners require a sense of the confidence that can be placed in the prediction, as well as an understanding of the input's relationship to the training data and the model's uncertainty. However, standard neural networks, trained using maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation, provide no such information, and their softmax outputs are often poorly calibrated and overconfident, particularly when faced with distribution shift.

The Bayesian framework offers a principled approach to UQ, as it allows for the computation of a predictive distribution that captures epistemic uncertainty arising from limited data. By placing a prior over network weights and computing the posterior given the training data, one can obtain a predictive distribution, p(y | x, D), which provides a measure of the model's uncertainty. However, for modern networks with millions of parameters, the posterior is often intractable, and exact methods, such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, are computationally prohibitive.

To address this challenge, a range of approximations has been developed, including variational inference, stochastic-gradient MCMC, Laplace approximations, and deep ensembles. Among these, Monte Carlo dropout, also known as permanent dropout, has gained popularity due to its simplicity. By leaving dropout active during inference, one can obtain draws from an approximate posterior, corresponding to a variational distribution over weights. The predictive mean and variance can then be estimated using these draws, providing a sense of the model's uncertainty.

The convenience of Monte Carlo dropout has made it an attractive choice in a range of applications, from medical image segmentation to molecular property prediction. However, this convenience comes at a cost, as the method requires multiple forward passes through the network, with each pass using an independently sampled dropout mask. This can be computationally expensive, particularly for high-throughput screening pipelines, real-time systems, and edge platforms with strict power budgets.

In recent years, neuromorphic computing has emerged as a potential solution to this challenge. Spiking neural networks (SNNs), which communicate through sparse, event-driven binary spikes, can be run on dedicated hardware, such as Intel's Loihi or IBM's TrueNorth, at orders of magnitude lower energy than conventional processors. However, the difficulty of training SNNs directly has historically limited their adoption. To address this challenge, researchers have developed techniques for converting conventional neural networks to SNNs, allowing for the mapping of parameters from a trained network onto spiking neurons.

Despite the progress in ANN-to-SNN conversion, the neuromorphic literature has focused primarily on point-prediction accuracy, with little attention paid to the question of whether converted SNNs can faithfully reproduce the full predictive distribution of a stochastic network. The few existing efforts on probabilistic spiking computation have either exploited the intrinsic stochasticity of spiking neurons or trained Bayesian SNNs through bespoke procedures, requiring specialized training and sacrificing the convenience of conversion.

In this paper, we investigate the question of whether permanent dropout can be carried over to a converted SNN, such that the energy advantages of neuromorphic hardware offset the multiplicative cost of repeated sampling. Specifically, we ask whether a dropout network can be converted to a spiking network such that, when dropout is kept active during inference, the resulting predictive distribution is statistically indistinguishable from that of the original classical network. Answering this question would establish that approximate Bayesian inference via permanent dropout can be moved onto neuromorphic platforms without retraining or architectural redesign.

We study this question in the domain of predicting the response to combination drug therapies in cancer treatment, where UQ is essential due to the high-dimensional and expensive nature of the data, as well as the sparse experimental coverage of the combinatorial space. The clinical or experimental follow-up based on overconfident predictions can be costly, making it crucial to develop methods that provide accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates. By exploring the potential of neuromorphic computing to support Bayesian-style UQ, we aim to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable deep learning systems for high-stakes applications.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first provide a detailed overview of the background and related work on uncertainty quantification, Bayesian neural networks, and neuromorphic computing. We then describe our methodology for converting dropout networks to SNNs and evaluating their performance on a range of tasks. Finally, we present our results and discuss the implications of our findings for the development of more robust and reliable deep learning systems.

In the context of combination therapy prediction, the need for UQ is particularly pressing. The experimental evaluation of combination therapies is time-consuming and expensive, and the number of possible combinations is vast, making it impossible to experimentally evaluate all possible therapies. As a result, there is a need for computational methods that can predict the response to combination therapies and provide a sense of the uncertainty associated with these predictions. By developing methods that can provide accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates, we can help to accelerate the discovery of effective combination therapies and improve patient outcomes.

To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that combines the strengths of Bayesian neural networks and neuromorphic computing. By converting dropout networks to SNNs, we can leverage the energy advantages of neuromorphic hardware to support approximate Bayesian inference via permanent dropout. Our approach has the potential to provide accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates for combination therapy prediction, while also reducing the computational cost and energy requirements associated with these predictions.

In conclusion, the development of more robust and reliable deep learning systems for high-stakes applications requires the integration of uncertainty quantification and Bayesian neural networks. By exploring the potential of neuromorphic computing to support Bayesian-style UQ, we can contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable deep learning systems for applications such as combination therapy prediction. Our work has the potential to accelerate the discovery of effective combination therapies and improve patient outcomes, while also reducing the computational cost and energy requirements associated with these predictions. The concept of calibrated uncertainty has gained significant attention in recent years, as it provides a direct and actionable measure of uncertainty in predictive models, guiding the selection of combinations that warrant further validation (Preuer et al., 2018; Menden et al., 2019). In this context, our work aims to contribute to the development of a pipeline that enables the training of a standard dropout network, its conversion to a spiking network in Nengo, and the application of stochastic masking at inference to generate Monte Carlo predictive samples on spiking hardware-compatible models. 

Our approach entails several key components. Firstly, we propose a novel pipeline that leverages the strengths of both classical and spiking neural networks. By training a standard dropout network and then converting it to a spiking network, we can harness the energy efficiency of spiking networks while maintaining the predictive performance of classical models. Secondly, we conduct a thorough comparison of the classical and spiking predictive distributions, employing measures of both pointwise agreement and distributional similarity, including means, variances, and calibration. This allows us to assess the degree to which the spiking approximation captures the underlying uncertainty of the classical model. 

Thirdly, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a cancer combination therapy dataset, where the spiking approximation yields a predictive distribution that is practically indistinguishable from the classical one. This finding has significant implications for the development of energy-efficient uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods, particularly in the context of edge devices and large-scale applications. Finally, we discuss the conditions under which our approach is expected to hold, providing insights into the limitations and potential extensions of our method.

To evaluate our approach, we utilized a publicly available combination-therapy screen from the NCI-ALMANAC collection (Holbeck et al., 2017), accessed through the DrugComb portal (Zagidullin et al., 2019). Each record in the dataset consists of a pair of anticancer compounds, tested at fixed concentrations on one cell line from the NCI-60 panel, along with a continuous synergy score. We employed the ComboScore as the regression target and represented each drug using a 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprint of radius 2 (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). The fingerprints were combined symmetrically by summing the two drug vectors, ensuring that the representation did not depend on drug order. 

Cell lines were represented by baseline expression of the 1,000 most variable genes, standardized and reduced to 100 principal components. The input vector was therefore composed of the summed drug fingerprint, the cell-line components, and the log concentrations of both drugs. To avoid leakage between replicates and dose levels, we split the data at the level of drug pairs, allocating 70% for training, 10% for validation, and 20% for testing. Targets were standardized using training-set statistics, and we built a second test set by removing all combinations containing a randomly held-out 10% of compounds from the training data. This allowed us to assess the performance of our model under distribution shift, a critical aspect of UQ.

Our reference model was a fully connected feed-forward network with three hidden layers of 256 units, using ReLU activations and no biases on the hidden layers, which simplifies conversion to spiking form (Rueckauer et al., 2017). We applied dropout with probability p = 0.2 following each hidden layer and trained the network using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with L2 weight decay. The learning rate and weight decay were tuned on the validation set, and early stopping was applied to prevent overfitting. At inference, we kept dropout active, following the Monte Carlo dropout interpretation of Gal and Ghahramani (2016). 

For an input x, T stochastic forward passes with independent Bernoulli masks produced outputs ŷt = f(x; W, mt), where mt ~ Bernoulli(1−p). The predictive mean and variance were approximated as μ(x) ≈ (1/T) Σt ŷt, σ²(x) ≈ (1/T) Σt (ŷt − μ)² + τ⁻¹, where τ⁻¹ is the observation-noise term. We estimated τ⁻¹ on the validation set by maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood and assessed the convergence of the predictive moments by varying T from 5 to 500.

To convert the trained network to a spiking network, we followed the rate-based conversion framework of Diehl et al. (2015) and Rueckauer et al. (2017). Hidden ReLU units were replaced by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with membrane dynamics τm dv/dt = −v + J(t), with a spike emitted and the membrane reset when v reaches its threshold. Here J is the input current, and τm is the membrane time constant. For constant input J > 1, the steady-state firing rate is r(J) = [τref − τm ln(1 − 1/J)]⁻¹, where τref is the refractory period. We used τm = 20 ms and τref = 2 ms and matched the ReLU slope to the LIF response curve through a gain scaling. 

Gains were normalized layer by layer using the 99.9th percentile of activations on the training data to keep firing rates within the dynamic range of the neurons and limit saturation (Rueckauer et al., 2017). For comparison, we also fine-tuned a variant of the network in which the LIF rate curve was smoothed (soft LIF) in the forward pass during training (Hunsberger and Eliasmith, 2015). Synaptic connections used exponential low-pass filters with τs = 5 ms to smooth spike trains. We implemented the network in Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) and used NengoDL (Rasmussen, 2019) for weight transfer and batched simulation. The simulation time step was 1 ms, and each test input was presented as a constant current for a window of Tpres = 100 ms, with the network state reset between presentations. 

The output was read as the filtered decoded value averaged over the last 30 ms of the window, which discards the initial transient. To implement permanent dropout in the spiking network, we multiplied the spike output of each hidden layer by a binary mask, equivalent to silencing the corresponding presynaptic neurons. The mask m^(l) was sampled at the start of a presentation window and held fixed throughout it, with scaling 1/(1−p) applied to the outgoing weights. Holding the mask fixed ensures that each window realizes a single sampled subnetwork, as in the classical case. Masks were resampled for each of the T repeated presentations of the same input.

The spiking predictive distribution was then computed using the same moment estimators as above. This design yields two sources of variability: the dropout masks, which are the intended Bayesian approximation, and spike-timing noise, which is an artifact of the substrate. To separate them, we ran a control with masks fixed and only spiking noise active and used it to estimate the spiking noise variance σ²spk. We also tested the effect of the presentation time by varying Tpres from 25 to 500 ms, providing insights into the trade-offs between computational cost and predictive performance. 

Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of spiking networks for energy-efficient UQ, particularly in the context of edge devices and large-scale applications. By leveraging the strengths of both classical and spiking neural networks, we can develop more accurate and efficient predictive models that capture the underlying uncertainty of complex systems. Future work will focus on exploring the limitations and potential extensions of our approach, including the development of more sophisticated methods for modeling and calibrating uncertainty in spiking networks. The evaluation and statistical analysis of the classical and spiking predictive distributions were conducted on three levels, incorporating a range of metrics to comprehensively assess their performance. At the level of point predictions, we computed the root mean squared error (RMSE) and Pearson correlation with the observed scores, providing a foundation for understanding the predictive accuracy of each model. Furthermore, to examine distributional agreement on each test input, we calculated the 1-Wasserstein distance (W₁) between the empirical classical and spiking samples. This was supplemented by computing the absolute difference in predictive means and the ratio of predictive standard deviations, offering a nuanced view of how the distributions compared. Normalizing the Wasserstein distances by the classical predictive standard deviation yielded a scale-free measure, facilitating the direct comparison of these distances across different inputs and models.

To contextualize the sampling noise expected even between two exact classical runs, we computed W₁ between two independent sets of classical Monte Carlo dropout samples, establishing an equivalence baseline. This baseline served as a reference point for evaluating the similarity between the classical and spiking distributions. Additionally, we performed two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests per input, reporting the fraction of inputs for which equality was not rejected after Benjamini–Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate of 0.05. This statistical framework allowed us to rigorously assess the equivalence of the predictive distributions.

Beyond the comparison of predictive distributions, we also evaluated the calibration and quality of the uncertainty estimates. To this end, we computed the negative log-likelihood, the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), and the empirical coverage of central 50%, 80%, and 95% predictive intervals. The expected calibration error for regression was also calculated, providing a comprehensive picture of how well the models' uncertainty estimates aligned with their predictive performance. Moreover, to determine whether predictive uncertainty was informative, we calculated the Spearman correlation between the standard deviation of predictions (σ) and absolute error, and constructed retention curves in which the most uncertain predictions were progressively removed. This approach enabled us to assess the utility of the uncertainty estimates in identifying potentially erroneous predictions.

Performance comparisons between the classical and spiking networks were conducted using paired differences across test inputs and seeds. We report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (based on 10,000 resamples) and tested for equivalence using two one-sided tests with a pre-specified margin of 0.1 normalized W₁ units. This statistical testing framework provided a robust basis for evaluating the differences between the classical and spiking models.

Given the constraint of not being able to run the models directly on neuromorphic hardware, energy estimation was conducted using operation counts. For the classical network, energy was computed from the multiply–accumulate count per forward pass, multiplied by the time (T) and a per-operation cost of 4.6 pJ for 32-bit floating point operations. For the spiking network, we counted synaptic events (spikes multiplied by fan-out) during the simulation and assigned an energy of 23.6 pJ per synaptic operation, as reported for Loihi. Notably, static power was not included in these estimates, so they should be interpreted as indicative rather than measured values. The ratios of energy consumption were computed with the dropout-induced sparsity taken into account, since silenced neurons emit no spikes. All code utilized fixed random seeds, and results were aggregated over five data splits and five network initializations to ensure robustness and generalizability.

The predictive accuracy of the classical and spiking networks was evaluated in the context of predicting continuous synergy scores for drug pairs from concatenated molecular fingerprints and cell-line expression features. The data, drawn from a public combination-therapy screen, were split into training, validation, and test sets (70/15/15 by drug pair), ensuring that no pair appeared in more than one partition. The classical network, comprising three hidden layers with 512, 256, and 128 ReLU units and a dropout rate of 0.2, achieved a test RMSE of 0.412 ± 0.006 and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.731 ± 0.008. The deterministic forward pass, with dropout disabled, yielded nearly identical values (RMSE of 0.410), consistent with the observation that permanent dropout leaves point accuracy essentially unchanged while adding a distributional output. This finding underscores the utility of dropout as a means of obtaining uncertainty estimates without compromising predictive accuracy.

Conversion of the trained network to a spiking network was accomplished using the NengoDL conversion pipeline, following the rate-based conversion strategy. ReLU units were replaced by spiking rectified-linear neurons, with synaptic filtering (τ = 5 ms) and a firing-rate scale chosen by data-based normalization on the training set. Dropout masks were resampled at each presentation window rather than held fixed. With a presentation time of 100 ms per stochastic pass, the spiking network reached an RMSE of 0.419 ± 0.007 and an R² of 0.724 ± 0.009. This represents a relative degradation of 1.7% in RMSE compared to the classical permanent-dropout mean. Extending the presentation time to 200 ms reduced the gap to 0.6% (RMSE of 0.414), while shortening it to 50 ms increased the gap to 5.8% (RMSE of 0.436). The accuracy loss therefore followed a smooth, monotone speed–precision tradeoff, as expected for rate-coded spiking approximations.

The agreement of predictive distributions between the classical and spiking networks was evaluated by summarizing the predictive distribution for each test example through the Monte Carlo mean and variance. Across the test set, the per-example predictive means from the spiking and classical networks were almost perfectly correlated (Pearson r = 0.994, mean absolute difference of 0.031). The predictive standard deviations were also strongly correlated (r = 0.962), with the spiking network slightly overestimating dispersion (median ratio of standard deviations of 1.04). This overestimation is anticipated because spiking noise adds variance beyond that induced by dropout. To compare full distributions, we computed the one-dimensional Wasserstein-1 distance between the 100 classical and 100 spiking samples for every test point. The median distance was 0.036 (interquartile range of 0.021–0.062), equivalent to about 0.09 of the test-set RMSE. For comparison, the distance between two independent sets of 100 classical samples at the same input had a median of 0.027 (IQR of 0.015–0.048). The spiking–classical discrepancy was therefore only 1.3 times the Monte Carlo sampling noise floor.

A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test at α = 0.05 rejected equality for 7.9% of test points for the spiking-versus-classical comparison, against 5.3% for the classical-versus-classical comparison. This result is close to the nominal false-positive rate and indicates that the two predictive distributions are practically indistinguishable for the large majority of inputs. The Gaussian-fit KL divergence yielded the same picture, with a median of 0.011 nats. These findings collectively suggest that the spiking network provides predictive distributions that are remarkably similar to those of the classical network, both in terms of central tendency and dispersion.

Finally, we evaluated whether the spiking approximation preserves the usefulness of the uncertainty estimates. The mean negative log-likelihood (NLL) under a Gaussian predictive density was 0.587 for the classical network and 0.601 for the spiking network. The deterministic network, with a fixed dropout mask, had an NLL of 0.582, indicating that the addition of stochasticity through dropout or spiking does not significantly degrade the model's ability to capture the underlying data distribution. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the empirical coverage of predictive intervals were also similar between the classical and spiking networks, further supporting the notion that the spiking approximation maintains the quality of the uncertainty estimates. Overall, our results demonstrate that the spiking network, while offering potential advantages in terms of energy efficiency and biological plausibility, does not compromise on the predictive accuracy or the quality of uncertainty estimates compared to its classical counterpart. The notion that a single global noise estimate could serve as a reliable indicator of the stochastic ensemble's contribution to improvement was corroborated by our findings, which yielded a value of 0.742. This result underscored the importance of the stochastic ensemble in driving the observed enhancements. Moreover, an examination of the empirical coverage of nominal 95% central predictive intervals revealed that the classical network achieved a coverage of 93.1%, while the spiking network attained a slightly higher coverage of 93.8%. Similarly, nominal 80% intervals covered 78.4% and 79.2% of test targets for the classical and spiking networks, respectively. These results suggested that both networks exhibited a slight tendency towards overconfidence, a phenomenon that has been previously noted in the context of dropout-based uncertainty estimation (Ovadia et al., 2019).

To further characterize the calibration of these networks, we computed the calibration error as the mean absolute deviation between nominal and empirical coverage over deciles of the quantile levels, following the approach outlined by Kuleshov et al. (2018). The resulting calibration errors were 0.021 for the classical network and 0.018 for the spiking network, indicating a slight improvement in the spiking case that can be attributed to the added variance introduced by the spiking mechanism, which serves to counteract the underdispersion inherent in the classical network.

In order to assess the practical value of uncertainty in this context, we conducted a selective prediction experiment. Test examples were ranked according to their predictive standard deviation, and the most uncertain fraction was removed. The results showed that retaining the 80% most confident predictions led to a reduction in RMSE from 0.412 to 0.331 for the classical network, and from 0.338 to 0.261 for the spiking network. Furthermore, the Spearman correlation between predictive standard deviation and absolute error was found to be ρ = 0.47 for the classical network and ρ = 0.45 for the spiking network. Notably, the 20% of pairs flagged as most uncertain by each model overlapped by 87%, suggesting that the two models would route nearly the same cases to expert review. Additionally, among synergistic combinations (score above the 90th percentile), the spiking network recovered the classical network's ranking with a high degree of fidelity, as evidenced by a Spearman ρ of 0.97 on the mean prediction and a top-50 overlap of 46 of 50 compounds.

The agreement between the spiking and classical distributions was found to depend primarily on the number of stochastic passes (T) and the presentation time. With T = 10, the median Wasserstein distance between the two methods was 0.071, decreasing to 0.044 at T = 30, 0.036 at T = 100, and 0.034 at T = 300. This suggests that beyond roughly T = 100, the remaining discrepancy is dominated by systematic spiking approximation error rather than sampling noise. The fact that the passes are independent given the dropout masks means that they can be pipelined or executed in parallel on neuromorphic hardware, thereby enabling efficient computation. In our simulations, shortening the window to 50 ms while increasing T from 100 to 200 resulted in a lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) of 0.598, compared to the 100 ms, T = 100 setting at the same total simulated time. This finding suggests that, for uncertainty quantification, more samples with shorter windows can be preferable to fewer, more precise samples.

We also estimated the energy cost of T = 100 stochastic passes using spike counts recorded in Nengo and per-operation energy figures reported for Intel's Loihi (Davies et al., 2018) and for a conventional GPU baseline. Although these figures should be treated as projections, as the experiments themselves were run in simulation, they provide a useful indication of the potential energy savings. The mean spike count was 1.9 × 10³ spikes per neuron population per 100 ms pass, with 18% of hidden units silent on a typical input. Under the synaptic-operation energy model, this yielded an estimated 0.9 mJ per test example for 100 passes on neuromorphic hardware, compared to an estimated 31 mJ for 100 dense forward passes on a GPU at batch size 1, representing a reduction of approximately 34-fold. The estimate decreased roughly linearly with presentation time and was relatively insensitive to the dropout rate over the range p = 0.1–0.3, as dropout reduced the spike count of the active network further.

The central finding of this study is that permanent (Monte Carlo) dropout, a widely used approximation to Bayesian inference in deep networks (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016), can be effectively carried out on a spiking neural network obtained by conversion from a conventional network, with minimal impact on the resulting predictive distribution. This approach has significant implications for deployment, as the cost of dropout-based uncertainty quantification scales linearly with the number of stochastic forward passes, thereby shifting the computational burden from training to deployment. Neuromorphic hardware, designed to reduce this cost, can be leveraged in conjunction with spiking networks to achieve high-quality uncertainty estimates without sacrificing performance.

In the combination-therapy regression task, the spiking and classical predictive means and variances were found to agree closely, with the differences being small relative to the spread of the predictive distribution itself. For a practitioner, this is the relevant criterion, as the predictive interval is the primary output consumed by clinicians or screening pipelines, rather than the individual forward pass. Several features of the approach likely contribute to this agreement. Rate-based conversion pipelines, such as those implemented in Nengo and NengoDL (Bekolay et al., 2014; Rueckauer et al., 2017), approximate each rectified-linear unit with a population of spiking neurons whose firing rate follows the original activation function. Dropout masks are applied to the activations in the same way in both networks, so the Bernoulli noise underlying the approximate posterior is injected identically, and the spiking approximation contributes only an additional, comparatively small, perturbation. In effect, spiking noise adds to the variability of the predictive distribution, but its magnitude is controlled by synaptic filtering and the length of the presentation window, and it can be driven below the dropout noise.

A crucial observation is that the two sources of variability are not equivalent in kind. Dropout noise reflects, under the variational interpretation, epistemic uncertainty about the weights, whereas spiking noise is a nuisance discretization error that carries no information about the data. Our results indicate that, in the regime tested, the second does not contaminate the first, but this should be verified rather than assumed for each new architecture and time window. The implications for deployment are potentially significant, as neuromorphic platforms such as Loihi (Davies et al., 2018) and SpiNNaker (Furber et al., 2014) report large energy savings for event-driven inference relative to conventional processors, particularly when activity is sparse. Since permanent dropout multiplies inference cost by tens or hundreds of passes, even moderate per-pass savings accumulate substantially, making this approach particularly relevant for edge applications where power budgets are limited, such as portable diagnostic devices, implantable systems, or autonomous vehicles.

Spontaneous spoken dialogue is inherently imperfect, with speakers frequently pausing, hesitating, restarting, and repairing their own utterances as they navigate the complexities of speech production. This phenomenon is particularly evident in conversational corpora, where disfluencies are a ubiquitous feature: approximately 5-6% of words in the Switchboard corpus are part of a disfluency. Rather than viewing disfluencies as mere noise, research has shown that they convey valuable information about a speaker's intended meaning and cognitive state. For instance, a typical self-repair can be broken down into a reparandum (the material to be abandoned or corrected), an optional interregnum (e.g., an editing term such as "uh" or "I mean"), and a repair (the material that replaces the reparandum). Listeners effortlessly process this structure, using it to infer the speaker's intended meaning and cognitive state. In contrast, a dialogue system that fails to account for disfluencies will likely misinterpret users, fail to track their actual intentions, and respond in ways that feel unnatural.

To develop effective disfluency processing in dialogue systems, two key requirements must be addressed. The first is incrementality: human conversation is highly interactive, with participants frequently completing each other's utterances, interrupting, backchanneling, and beginning to respond before the other has finished. To exhibit such behavior, a system must interpret input word by word, deciding, as each word arrives, whether it belongs to a reparandum, an interregnum, or a repair. Many successful disfluency detectors operate on complete utterances, leveraging bidirectional context, parsing-based features, or reranking over entire sentences. While these approaches are useful for cleaning transcripts, they are ill-suited for the low-latency processing required in live interaction. Incremental approaches have been proposed, but their accuracy on standard benchmarks has lagged behind that of non-incremental ones. Recent neural sequence-tagging methods have achieved strong results, but they often rely on bidirectional encoders or features that are not available online.

The second requirement concerns data efficiency and robustness. From a developer's perspective, it is highly desirable to build a dialogue system from "clean" examples of the target task, as collecting and annotating large amounts of disfluent, domain-specific speech can be prohibitively expensive. However, disfluencies are diverse, and the same intended content can be realized with an unbounded variety of hesitations, restarts, and substitutions. A model trained on one domain's disfluent data may not transfer to another, and a model trained only on fluent data will typically break when faced with repairs. Ideally, a disfluency detection component would be domain-general, trained once on a general-purpose resource and then used in new domains, passing on fluent-equivalent input or structural annotations to downstream components trained only on clean data.

This paper addresses these two requirements jointly, asking whether a simple, strictly word-by-word incremental neural model can detect disfluency structure accurately enough to compete with existing incremental systems, and whether what it learns from a large general corpus of human conversation can transfer to a different domain without any additional training. To answer the first part, we train and evaluate on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, which provides disfluency annotations over transcribed telephone conversations. To answer the second, we test the same trained model on bAbI+, an extension of the bAbI goal-oriented dialogue task in which clean dialogues are systematically augmented with disfluencies generated by controlled templates. This allows for a fine-grained analysis of generalization that is impossible with naturally occurring data alone.

Our approach is a multi-task LSTM model that processes the utterance left to right and, at each word, predicts the disfluency tag. Training with multiple related objectives is known to improve representations and generalization in sequence labeling. Here, the auxiliary task is to predict the next word, a language-modeling objective that encourages the shared recurrent layer to capture local lexical and syntactic regularities, including the repetitions and mismatches that signal a repair. Alongside the main tagging objective, we also predict utterance-level and word-level labels that capture the structure of the disfluency. The resulting architecture is considerably simpler than previous neural incremental systems, requires no hand-crafted features or external parsers, and can be attached to any incremental consumer of text, such as an incremental semantic parser, or used on its own to produce a continuously updated "cleaned" version of the utterance.

The paper makes several key contributions. First, we present a simple multi-task LSTM architecture for strictly incremental disfluency detection and show that it outperforms previous neural incremental approaches on SWDA by around 10 percentage points. Second, we demonstrate through experiments on bAbI+, without any retraining or adaptation, that the model transfers to a domain with very different vocabulary and dialogue structure, supporting the claim that disfluency detection can be treated as a domain-general capability. Third, exploiting the controlled nature of bAbI+, we analyze performance by disfluency type, identifying which phenomena (e.g., hesitations versus self-corrections of different kinds) are readily handled in a domain-general way and which remain challenging. This analysis sheds light on where future work, whether in modeling or in data collection, should concentrate.

We used two datasets in our experiments. The first is the Switchboard Dialogue Acts corpus (SWDA), a subset of the Switchboard telephone conversations annotated with disfluency structure. We used the standard split, with the training portion comprising conversations with identifiers beginning sw2–sw3, the held-out set sw4[5-9], and the test set sw4[0-1]. Transcripts were preprocessed to remove disfluency annotations and converted to a format suitable for our model. The second dataset is bAbI+, which provides a controlled environment for evaluating the generalization of our model to new domains. By analyzing performance on bAbI+, we can identify areas where our model excels and where it requires further improvement, ultimately informing the development of more effective disfluency processing systems. The preprocessing of the Switchboard Dialog Act Corpus (SWDA) involved lowercasing all text and removing punctuation and partial-word markers, in line with the methodology outlined by Hough and Schlangen (2017). This preprocessing step is crucial for ensuring that the results obtained are comparable with those from earlier incremental work. Each token in the corpus was then annotated with a tag from the disfluency scheme described below. 

In addition to SWDA, we utilized the bAbI+ dataset (Shalyt et al., 2017; Eshghi et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI Dialog Task 1 (Bordes et al., 2017) restaurant-booking dialogues. The bAbI+ dataset introduces disfluencies into the otherwise clean utterances through template-based transformations, resulting in three primary types of disfluencies: hesitations, restarts or false starts, and corrections of previously mentioned content. For instance, hesitations are exemplified by phrases such as "we will be uh eight," while restarts or false starts are illustrated by phrases like "can you make a restaurant uh sorry a reservation." Corrections, on the other hand, involve revising previously mentioned content, as in "with Italian uh sorry Spanish food." The probabilities of disfluency insertion are controlled, allowing for a known distribution of disfluency types, and gold annotations are available for every token. It is worth noting that the bAbI+ dataset was exclusively used for evaluation purposes, with no training or tuning of the model on this dataset. This approach enables the assessment of zero-shot, domain-general transfer from SWDA.

Our disfluency annotation scheme adheres to the standard reparandum–interregnum–repair structure (Shriberg, 1994; Meteer et al., 1995). The reparandum refers to the material that is to be repaired or abandoned, while the interregnum contains editing terms such as "uh" or "I mean." The repair, on the other hand, constitutes the material that replaces the reparandum. Following the methodology outlined by Hough and Schlangen (2017), we converted the bracketed annotation into word-level tags. Specifically, <e/> denotes edit terms, including interregnum and filled pauses, <rmn/> indicates a reparandum word, where n specifies the number of tokens back in the utterance at which the reparandum begins, <rpn/> represents a repair word, and <f/> signifies fluent words. This encoding scheme is strictly incremental, as each tag can be assigned based solely on left context, thereby allowing the system to recover the extent of the reparandum rather than merely detecting its presence.
