Furthermore, repairs are distinguished as substitution (<rpSub/>), repetition (<rpRep/>) or deletion (<rpDel/>), in accordance with Hough and Schlangen (2017).

The model architecture employed in this study is a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) sequence tagger, which processes an utterance one word at a time. Consequently, each tag prediction depends exclusively on the words seen thus far. The input words are mapped to 50-dimensional embeddings, and the vocabulary is restricted to the training data, with singletons replaced by an unknown token. Part-of-speech (POS) tags, produced for SWDA using the tags available in the corpus, are concatenated with the word embedding as input in the POS-enriched conditions. The model consists of a single LSTM layer with 50 hidden units, which feeds a softmax output layer.

A key design element of our model is the incorporation of multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard & Goldberg, 2016). Two output layers share the same LSTM representation, with the primary task being disfluency tagging and the auxiliary task being prediction of the next word in the sequence, i.e., incremental language modelling. An additional auxiliary task, evaluated in separate ablations, involves prediction of the utterance's POS tag sequence. The auxiliary tasks provide a training signal that does not depend on disfluency annotation, thereby encouraging the shared layer to represent syntactic and lexical context. The total loss is a weighted sum of the cross-entropy losses of the tasks, L = Ltag + λLaux, with λ selected on the held-out set from {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}. For comparison, we also trained a single-task baseline with the same architecture but no auxiliary output.

During the training procedure, models were implemented in Keras with a TensorFlow backend and trained using the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a batch size of 32. To prevent overfitting, dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) of 0.2 was applied to the embedding and LSTM outputs. Early stopping was based on tagging loss on the held-out set, with a patience of 5 epochs. Hyperparameters were selected on the held-out set only. Given that LSTM training is stochastic, each configuration was trained with ten random initialisations, and we report the mean and standard deviation across runs.

Evaluation of our model on SWDA employed three families of measures. Firstly, token-level F1 was computed for the reparandum tags (<rm>) and for edit terms (<e>), following common practice in disfluency detection (Ferguson et al., 2015; Zayats et al., 2016). Secondly, given that the system is designed to be incremental, we evaluated it as it processes the utterance. Specifically, we report the time-to-detection, the number of words after the onset of a reparandum or edit at which the correct tag is first output, and edit overhead, the proportion of unnecessary tag revisions made as the utterance unfolds (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Zwarts et al., 2010). Thirdly, we report the utterance-level exact match of the predicted tag sequence against gold.

For the bAbI+ dataset, the trained SWDA model was applied without any retraining or fine-tuning, and word embeddings for out-of-vocabulary tokens were mapped to the unknown token. As POS tags were not available in this dataset, we used the model variants that take only words as input. We report F1 for each tag type, split by disfluency category (hesitation, restart, correction), to examine which phenomena transfer across domains. Additionally, we compute the proportion of utterances whose "cleaned" output, after removing tokens tagged as reparandum or edit, exactly matches the original clean bAbI utterance. This measure assesses the practical goal of ensuring that a downstream interpreter, trained only on fluent dialogues, receives the intended input.

Statistical analysis involved assessing differences between model variants over the ten runs per configuration. We employed paired comparisons on matched random seeds with a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the significance threshold set at α = 0.05, and applied Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons across variants. For comparison with previously published systems, we cite their reported scores on the same test split. As the per-run variance of these systems is unavailable, no significance tests were applied to those comparisons, and we report absolute differences in F1. For bAbI+, we additionally report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 resamples over dialogues) for category-specific F1.

The performance of our model on the held-out SWDA test set is presented in Table 1, following the reporting convention established by Hough and Schlangen (2017). We report F1 for the reparandum and edit term tags, as well as the time-to-detection and edit overhead metrics. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in detecting disfluencies in spoken language, and highlight the importance of incorporating multi-task learning and incremental processing in disfluency detection models. When analyzing disfluencies in speech, it's essential to consider the word-level tags that indicate edit terms, reparandum words, and repair onsets. Our evaluation metrics include the F1 score for reparandum, which is notoriously the most challenging category to identify. We report the mean F1 scores over five random initializations, with a standard deviation that never exceeds 0.006, indicating a high degree of consistency across our experiments. 

For context, the strongest prior neural incremental baseline, as established by Hough and Schlangen (2017), achieves an F1 score of 0.64 for reparandum words and 0.61 for repair onsets. In contrast, our single-task LSTM, which focuses solely on tagging disfluencies without any auxiliary objectives, improves upon these scores, reaching 0.69 for reparandum words and 0.66 for repair onsets. Notably, when we incorporate next-word prediction as an auxiliary task, these scores further increase to 0.72 and 0.70, respectively. The full multi-task model, which also includes part-of-speech tagging, yields the highest scores, with an F1 of 0.74 for reparandum words and 0.72 for repair onsets. This represents a significant improvement of about 10 percentage points over the baseline established by Hough and Schlangen (2017).

Edit-term detection proves to be close to ceiling for all systems, which is anticipated given the small, closed class of fillers and discourse markers, as previously noted by Shriberg (1994). Our full model scores an F1 of 0.93, outperforming both the single-task model (0.91) and the prior incremental baseline (0.90). The gains from the auxiliary tasks are not merely additive; language modeling contributes the most significant improvement (+3.0 points in reparandum F1 over the single-task model), followed by POS tagging, which adds a further +2.0 points. The order in which these auxiliary tasks were added does not alter this pattern, suggesting a level of robustness in our approach. Removing either auxiliary task from the full model results in a degradation of reparandum F1 by 1.6 to 2.9 points, a drop larger than the seed variance, underscoring the importance of these tasks. A paired bootstrap test over test utterances confirms the statistical significance of these differences, with p < 0.01 for the difference between the full model and every ablated variant.

It's also worth noting that the non-incremental BLSTM tagger proposed by Zayats et al. (2016) still achieves a higher score than our system on the SWDA dataset, with a reparandum F1 of roughly 0.85. This outcome is not surprising, given that their model can view the entire utterance, including the repair, before labeling the reparandum. This comparison highlights the trade-off between incremental processing and accuracy. While our model closes much of the gap with earlier incremental systems, it does not completely eliminate the difference.

Beyond accuracy, the incremental nature of our model allows us to examine how early and stably it labels disfluencies. Following the methodology outlined by Hough and Schlangen (2017), we computed two key measures: time-to-detection, which is the number of words after the true repair onset before the model first outputs the correct label, and edit overhead, the proportion of output labels that are revised or unnecessary before the final output is reached. The full model detects repair onsets, on average, 1.1 words after their occurrence, outperforming the single-task model, which requires 1.6 words. For reparandum words, which necessarily precede the repair, the model retrospectively relabels them, with an average time to detect the reparandum start of 2.3 words. Furthermore, the edit overhead is 8.9% for the full model, compared to 11.4% for the single-task model, indicating that the auxiliary tasks not only improve accuracy but also make the incremental output more stable. In practical terms, 87% of utterances in the test set reach their final labeling within one word of the utterance's end, meaning the model's output is almost always finalized by the time the speaker finishes.

To assess the model's ability to generalize, we applied it to the bAbI+ dataset, which extends the bAbI restaurant-search dialogues with synthesized disfluencies, without any further training or tuning. The bAbI+ dataset allows for a detailed breakdown of performance by disfluency type, including hesitations, corrections/substitutions, and restarts/false starts. Our results, summarized in Table 2, show an overall F1 score for reparandum and edit-term tags on the full bAbI+ test set of 0.81. The model successfully cleans 72% of utterances, removing every disfluent word and retaining every fluent one, outperforming the single-task model, which achieves 0.70 F1 and 58% fully cleaned utterances. This indicates a larger multi-task advantage out of domain (+11 points F1) compared to in-domain (+5 points).

Performance varies significantly across disfluency types. Hesitations and filler-based disfluencies are detected almost perfectly, with an F1 score of 0.97, consistent with the similar behavior of fillers in SWDA and bAbI+. Corrections are detected at an F1 score of 0.84, with the model leveraging the cue of repeated syntactic frames in repairs, which it can learn from SWDA and apply to different vocabulary. However, recall is lower than precision for corrections (0.79 versus 0.90), primarily due to repairs that replace content words with lexically unrelated words, lacking the repetition cue. Restarts prove to be the most challenging type, with an F1 score of 0.52. These typically involve abandoning a long stretch of an utterance, with the reparandum sometimes extending to six or more words. Given that the SWDA training data contains few such long reparanda, the model tends to stop marking reparandum words after three or four tokens. While precision on restarts remains reasonable (0.68), recall falls to 0.42, and this category accounts for most of the utterances that are not fully cleaned.

In summary, on SWDA, the multi-task LSTM significantly improves reparandum F1 by about 10 points over the best prior incremental neural model, while also detecting repairs earlier and with less revision. When transferred to bAbI+ without any adjustments, the model maintains an overall F1 of 0.81, generalizing well to hesitations and corrections but struggling with long restarts. This suggests that hesitations and corrections may be amenable to domain-general processing, whereas restarts likely require additional, targeted training data or structural information.

The interpretation of these results highlights the importance of how the learning problem is posed, rather than solely relying on architectural complexity. Joint training on related tagging objectives provides the LSTM's shared representation with a more structured signal than a single repair-or-not label, given that the labels for reparanda, repairs, and edit terms are tightly coupled. Recognizing an edit term such as "uh" requires an understanding of its function within the discourse, which is facilitated by the multi-task learning approach. This method not only improves performance on the primary task of disfluency detection but also enhances the model's ability to generalize across different types of disfluencies and datasets. The findings suggest that a significant portion of the gain in performance comes from the formulation of the learning problem itself, rather than the complexity of the neural architecture. By leveraging related tasks and structured signals, it's possible to achieve substantial improvements in disfluency detection, even with simpler architectures. The use of phrases like "or" or "I mean" in speech serves as a valuable indicator of where a reparandum begins and where a repair will commence, thereby providing crucial information for disfluency detection. This observation is in line with the broader argument that auxiliary tasks can introduce an inductive bias towards shared structure, as noted by Caruana (1997) and Søgaard and Goldberg (2016). Our results also align with earlier work on incremental disfluency detection, such as that of Hough and Schlangen (2017) and Schlangen and Skantze (2011), which demonstrated that strictly left-to-right processing does not necessarily compromise accuracy if the model is capable of revising its labels as evidence accumulates.

The experiments conducted on the bAbI+ dataset are particularly informative in this regard, as they allow us to test the model's transfer capabilities under controlled conditions. Unlike the SWDA corpus, which consists of open-topic telephone conversations (Godfrey et al., 1992; Meteer et al., 1995), the bAbI+ dataset is a goal-oriented restaurant-booking domain with a distinct vocabulary and utterance structure. Moreover, the distribution and type of disfluency in this dataset are known and manipulable (Eshghi et al., 2017), making it an ideal testbed for evaluating the model's ability to generalize across domains. The fact that the model, trained on SWDA and not adapted, is able to detect a substantial portion of disfluency phenomena in the bAbI+ dataset suggests that it has learned something about the surface patterns of disfluency that is not tied to a specific topic.

This finding resonates with the long-standing view in psycholinguistics that self-repair has a regular internal structure, consisting of an interruption point, an optional editing phase, and a repair that often parallels the reparandum (Levelt, 1983; Shriberg, 1994). Such regularity should be learnable in a domain-independent way, and our results suggest that this is indeed the case. However, the breakdown by disfluency type reveals that generalization is uneven, with phenomena that depend mainly on local, lexically signaled cues, such as hesitations and filled pauses, transferring more readily than repairs that require comparing the repair to the reparandum.

The latter type of repair, particularly those where the repair substitutes semantically related content rather than repeating words, poses a greater challenge for the model. This is not surprising, given that a model trained on SWDA can rely on the strong prior that repetitions and near-repetitions are repairs, which holds across domains. Detecting a substitution of one restaurant attribute value for another, however, requires some sense of what counts as a coherent replacement in context, and that knowledge is domain-specific. Hence, the claim of "domain-general" processing should be interpreted narrowly, as some disfluency types appear amenable to domain-general processing from surface sequence information alone, while others probably require access to the semantics or pragmatics of the task domain, which a purely sequence-based tagger lacks.

The implications of these findings for dialogue system development are significant, particularly with regards to data efficiency. If a disfluency detector trained once on a general corpus can be placed in front of an interpretation component trained only on clean utterances, developers need not collect or synthesize disfluent data for each new domain. This is the setting motivated by the bAbI+ methodology (Eshghi et al., 2017), where a system learns from fluent dialogues yet must cope with spontaneous variation at test time. Because the model is word-by-word incremental, it can be attached to an incremental semantic parser, such as one based on Dynamic Syntax (Purver et al., 2011; Eshghi et al., 2013), so that tentative interpretations can be retracted when a repair is recognized. It can also operate as a filter that "cleans" the evolving utterance for any downstream consumer.

Incrementality is not just a convenience; natural conversation involves overlapping speech, early responses, and collaborative completions (Howes and Eshghi, 2017), which batch-mode, utterance-final processing cannot support. Nevertheless, several limitations of our study must be acknowledged. First, the bAbI+ dataset is synthetic, with disfluencies generated by templates and inserted at controlled points, making them cleaner and more predictable than the variation in real speech. Success in this setting may overestimate real-world transfer, and it is essential to recognize that the model is not narrowly overfitted to SWDA, but rather demonstrates a capacity for generalization that may not be robust in an arbitrary deployed system.

Second, our experiments use transcribed text rather than speech, which means that real systems must contend with recognition errors and prosodic and acoustic cues that are known to aid disfluency detection (Hough and Schlangen, 2017; Zayats et al., 2016). Errors in recognized words would propagate into disfluency detection, highlighting the need for more robust models that can handle such uncertainties. Third, SWDA annotations include their own noise and inconsistencies, and the standard evaluation focuses on particular tags, which may not reflect the downstream utility that matters to a dialogue system, namely whether the interpretation after clean-up is correct. We evaluated tagging accuracy rather than end-to-end effects on semantic parsing or dialogue success, and these may not align.

Fourth, the model is purely sequential and has no explicit mechanism for matching a repair to its reparandum, which may explain the difficulty with semantically motivated substitutions. Structured or transition-based approaches (Honnibal and Johnson, 2014; Wang et al., 2017) or attention-based comparison could address this limitation, but possibly at some cost to incrementality or simplicity. Finally, we examined only English, and the extent of cross-linguistic generality of the learned patterns is unknown, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

In conclusion, our study presents a multi-task, incrementally operating LSTM tagger for disfluency structure that outperforms previous incremental neural approaches on SWDA by roughly ten percentage points with a simpler design. The model transfers without further training to the controlled bAbI+ domain, suggesting that a substantial part of disfluency processing can be treated as domain-general. However, the residual difficulty with content-dependent repairs indicates where domain-sensitive semantic information remains necessary. Future work should focus on coupling the detector with an incremental semantic parser to measure the effect on interpretation directly, evaluating on real goal-oriented human dialogue rather than synthetic data, and integrating acoustic features. A more controlled analysis of which disfluency types transfer, for example by varying the training distribution while holding the test distribution fixed, would help clarify the boundary between domain-general and domain-specific processing. Ultimately, our findings support building dialogue systems from fluent data and relying on a reusable incremental component to handle the disfluency of natural speech.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial step in biomedical text mining, as it enables the identification of key concepts such as genes, proteins, cell lines, chemicals, diseases, and organisms in the literature. This, in turn, underlies various downstream tasks, including relation extraction, database curation, and literature-based discovery (Krallinger et al., 2017; Huang and Lu, 2015). The sheer volume of biomedical publications, with over one million new entries added to PubMed each year, renders manual annotation impractical, making accurate automated NER a central focus of community evaluations like BioCreative, BioNLP, and JNLPBA (Kim et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2008; Arighi et al., 2017). 

In the traditional approach to NER, a document is segmented into sentences and tokens, with each token receiving a label indicating whether it begins, continues, or lies outside an entity, typically using a BIO or BIOES scheme (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Early biomedical systems, such as BANNER (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008) and ABNER (Settles, 2005), relied on feature-based models like conditional random fields (Lafferty et al., 2001). However, with the advent of neural architectures, hand-engineered features have given way to more sophisticated approaches. Bidirectional LSTMs with CRF output layers, combined with word and character embeddings, have become the standard approach (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016), and have been successfully adapted to biomedical corpora (Habibi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Crichton et al., 2017). The introduction of pretrained contextual representations like ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and domain-specific variants such as BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021) has further improved performance on benchmark datasets.

Despite this progress, nearly all existing systems share a common limitation: they assume that the input has already been split into tokens, and that entity boundaries coincide with token boundaries. While this assumption is relatively benign in general-domain newswire text, it frequently fails in biomedical text, where entity mentions are often embedded within hyphenated compounds, slash-separated expressions, or alphanumeric strings. For instance, entity mentions like "IL-2-dependent," "p53/MDM2," "GFP-tagged," "TNF-alpha–induced," or "Ras-GAP" occupy only part of what a conventional tokenizer treats as a single word. Annotation guidelines for corpora like GENETAG (Tanabe et al., 2005) and BioCreative Bio-ID (Arighi et al., 2017) explicitly permit sub-word entity spans, and the JNLPBA corpus (Kim et al., 2004) contains many mentions whose boundaries fall inside whitespace-delimited strings. However, a model that predicts labels only at the word level cannot recover such spans exactly, and under strict-match evaluation, each of these errors counts as both a false positive and a false negative.

The standard remedy for this limitation is to rely on specialized tokenization. Biomedical tokenizers apply hand-crafted rules or learned heuristics to split text at hyphens, slashes, digit–letter transitions, and case changes, so that entity boundaries are more likely to coincide with token boundaries (He and Kayaalp, 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007; Neumann et al., 2019). While such tokenizers can improve NER performance, they have several drawbacks. They require domain expertise to design and maintain, are often tuned to a particular corpus or entity class, and introduce a pipeline dependency in which tokenization errors propagate irrecoverably to the tagger. Over-segmentation can fragment entities and inflate sequence lengths, while under-segmentation leaves boundary mismatches unresolved. Moreover, a tokenizer optimized for one annotation scheme may not transfer to another, forcing practitioners to redesign rules for each new dataset.

Subword representations offer a natural way to relax the dependence on word-level tokenization. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), originally a data compression technique (Gage, 1994), was adapted for neural machine translation to handle rare and unseen words by decomposing them into frequent character sequences (Sennrich et al., 2016). Related approaches include WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016), the unigram language model (Kudo, 2018), and SentencePiece, which operates on raw text without pre-tokenization (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). These methods are widely used in transformer-based language models, including BERT and its biomedical descendants. However, in NER, they are typically used only to build input representations, with labels still assigned at the level of whole words, usually by taking the prediction of the first subword piece (Devlin et al., 2019). As a result, subword units improve the handling of out-of-vocabulary terms but do not allow the model to predict entity boundaries within a word.

Character-level models (Kim et al., 2016; Gillick et al., 2016) can, in principle, label at arbitrary positions, but they produce long sequences, lack a learned inventory of meaningful units such as morphemes and common biomedical affixes (e.g., "-ase," "anti-," or "-mab"), and are often harder to train and scale. This leaves an unaddressed gap in existing biomedical NER methods, which either operate at the word level and depend on carefully engineered tokenization to align with entity boundaries or use subword units merely as inputs while still predicting at the word level. What is missing is an approach in which the units of prediction themselves are learned, subword-sized, and independent of domain-specific tokenization rules, allowing entity spans to start and end wherever the data indicate.

To address this gap, we ask the following research question: can a model that assigns entity labels directly to BPE units, learned from raw text, recover biomedical entity spans, including those that fall within words, with accuracy competitive with systems that depend on specialized tokenizers? To answer this question, we introduce a subword-level approach to NER that combines BPE segmentation with convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Our approach segments text using a BPE vocabulary learned from the training data, with minimal pre-processing. Convolutional layers capture local orthographic and morphological patterns within and across adjacent units, and recurrent layers model longer-range context across the sentence. The network produces a tag for every BPE unit, and these byte-level tags are mapped back to character offsets to yield entity spans that need not align with whitespace-delimited words.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a tokenization-agnostic NER architecture that predicts labels at the BPE level, allowing entity boundaries to be learned from the data rather than being predetermined by a tokenizer. This approach has the potential to improve the accuracy of biomedical NER, particularly for entity mentions that do not align with word boundaries. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark datasets, showing that it can achieve competitive performance with systems that rely on specialized tokenizers. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and limitations of our approach, highlighting its potential applications and areas for future research. By introducing a subword-level approach to NER, we aim to advance the state of the art in biomedical text mining and provide a new tool for researchers and practitioners in the field. The task of named entity recognition (NER) in biomedical text poses a unique set of challenges, particularly with regards to the accurate identification of entity boundaries. A major hurdle in this context is the fact that these boundaries often fall within words, rather than coinciding with word boundaries. This issue necessitates the development of approaches that can effectively handle such cases without relying on hand-crafted rules for splitting words. In this study, we address this challenge by evaluating an approach that leverages learned subword units, rather than traditional word-level tokens, for biomedical NER. Our evaluation is conducted on three widely used benchmarks in the field: the BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG corpora. These datasets differ significantly in terms of the types of entities annotated, the conventions used for annotation, and the degree to which entity boundaries are misaligned with word boundaries.

One of the primary advantages of our approach is its ability to eliminate the need for specialized biomedical tokenization expertise. Traditional methods often require extensive knowledge of biomedical terminology and the development of customized tokenization rules to handle the complexities of entity recognition in this domain. By moving away from word-level tokens and towards learned subword units, we can simplify the process of deploying NER systems across different corpora. Moreover, this shift allows us to quantify the impact of using subword units on the performance of NER systems, particularly in cases where entity boundaries do not align with word boundaries.

Our analysis begins with an examination of the datasets used in this study. The BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus, for instance, consists of figure legends from open-access articles annotated for a variety of entity classes, including genes, proteins, small molecules, cell types, and tissues. The annotations in this corpus are normalized to database identifiers, but for our purposes, we only utilized the mention spans and coarse types. In contrast, the JNLPBA shared-task dataset is derived from the GENIA corpus and contains MEDLINE abstracts annotated with five specific types: protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type. The GENETAG corpus, used in BioCreative II Gene Mention, annotates a single gene/protein class across 20,000 MEDLINE sentences, with alternative acceptable boundaries provided for some mentions. We adhered to the official training and test partitions for each dataset, using a random 10% of each training set as a development set for hyperparameter selection and early stopping.

A crucial aspect of our approach involves the segmentation of raw text into subword units using byte-pair encoding (BPE). Unlike traditional rule-based biomedical tokenizers, BPE allows us to split text at whitespace and learn merges based on frequency, without pre-defined rules for handling punctuation, hyphens, or other special characters. This process begins with a character inventory and iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs until a target vocabulary size is reached. We treated the vocabulary size as a hyperparameter, exploring values of 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, and 8,000. Each BPE unit retains its character start and end offsets, enabling the representation of entity boundaries that fall within whitespace-delimited chunks. For comparison, we also trained a SentencePiece BPE model on the same text and found its segmentations to be comparable to those of our primary BPE model.

To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we projected gold character-level spans onto the BPE units using a BIO scheme with entity types. This involved labeling each unit as B-t if it started an entity of type t, I-t if it lay inside one, and O otherwise. Predicted spans were then converted back to character offsets by taking the start offset of the first unit and the end offset of the last unit of each decoded entity. This process allowed us to quantify the fraction of gold entities whose start and end offsets both coincide with unit boundaries, which we refer to as the oracle recall. We computed this quantity for each dataset and vocabulary size, alongside development F1, to diagnose the performance of our model and select the optimal vocabulary size.

Our model architecture is based on a convolutional-recurrent design, which combines local subword context with recurrent sequence modeling. Each BPE unit is mapped to an embedding, and local context is captured through a one-dimensional convolution over the embedding sequence. The convolutional layer is followed by a bidirectional LSTM, which provides contextualized representations of each unit. These representations are then passed through a linear layer and a softmax to produce a distribution over tags. We used Viterbi decoding restricted to valid BIO transitions to ensure well-formed spans during inference. Dropout was applied to the embeddings and between recurrent layers to prevent overfitting.

In comparison to traditional word-level approaches, our subword-level approach offers several advantages. By moving away from word boundaries, we can more accurately capture entity boundaries that fall within words. Moreover, our approach eliminates the need for specialized tokenization rules, making it easier to deploy NER systems across different corpora. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive performance relative to established systems, while providing a simpler and more effective way to handle the complexities of biomedical NER. Overall, our study highlights the potential of learned subword units for improving the robustness and deployability of NER systems in the biomedical domain. To better understand the effects of tokenization on our model's performance, we conducted a series of experiments where we trained the same architecture on three different input units: whitespace tokens, tokens generated by the scispaCy rule-based biomedical tokenizer, and individual characters. For word-level models, we restricted the vocabulary to types that occurred at least twice during training, mapping all other types to an unknown symbol. Additionally, we performed ablation studies where we removed either the convolutional layer or the recurrent layer to assess their contributions to the model's performance. 

The training process involved optimizing our models using Adam with an initial learning rate of $10^{-3}$, which was halved whenever the development F1 score failed to improve over three consecutive epochs. Each mini-batch consisted of 32 sentences, and gradient norms were clipped to 5 to prevent exploding gradients. Training was stopped after 50 epochs if no improvement was seen on the development set for 10 epochs, with the model state that yielded the best development F1 score being retained for evaluation. Hyperparameter selection was performed through a random search over 30 configurations per dataset, focusing on the development F1 score for our proposed model. Baseline models were given the same hyperparameter search budget. To ensure stability, each final configuration was trained with five different random seeds.

Evaluation was carried out at the entity level, with a predicted entity considered correct only if its start, end, and type exactly matched those of a gold entity. Precision, recall, and F1 scores were micro-averaged over all entities, following the CoNLL evaluation convention. For the JNLPBA dataset, we also reported type-agnostic scores to facilitate comparison with prior work. The official BioCreative II evaluation script was used for GENETAG, which also considers alternative annotated boundaries. We report the mean and standard deviation of the F1 scores over the five seeds for each configuration.

Statistical analysis to compare the proposed model with each baseline was conducted using a paired bootstrap test over test sentences, with 10,000 resamples and the seed-averaged F1 difference as the test statistic. Differences were considered significant if the two-sided p-value was less than 0.05. To gain insight into the nature of errors, we categorized false negatives and false positives into boundary errors (where the predicted entity overlaps with a gold entity of the same type but has different offsets), type errors, and complete misses or spurious spans. Boundary errors were further stratified based on whether the gold boundary fell within a whitespace-delimited chunk.

The overall performance of our models was evaluated on the official test partitions of the three corpora (JNLPBA, GENETAG, and Bio-ID) using entity-level precision, recall, and F1 scores. These metrics were computed using the original word-level evaluation scripts after projecting byte-level predictions back to character offsets for JNLPBA and GENETAG or to the annotated spans for Bio-ID. The results, presented as means over five random initializations with standard deviations in parentheses, are summarized in Table 1.

On the JNLPBA dataset, which encompasses five GENIA categories (protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type), our model achieved an F1 score of 76.9. This performance is comparable to that of word-level BiLSTM-CRF models previously reported for this corpus and is within about one point of the F1 score achieved by BioBERT. For GENETAG, using the standard evaluation that accepts alternative annotations, our model reached an F1 score of 92.7, which is on par with previously reported neural systems and about 1.5 points below the performance of domain-pretrained transformers. On the Bio-ID corpus, which annotates mentions of genes, cells, tissues, organisms, and small molecules in figure legends and is notable for its heterogeneous entity types and complex expressions, our model achieved an F1 score of 71.2. This result compares favorably with the participant systems in the original BioCreative VI challenge, which relied on hand-built tokenization and feature engineering.

To isolate the effect of tokenization, we trained a word-level BiLSTM-CRF with an identical hidden size and the same pretrained embedding initialization, using either whitespace and punctuation tokenization or the scispaCy biomedical tokenizer. The results, presented in Table 2, show that the BPE-based model outperformed the generic tokenizer by 3.5, 3.1, and 7.4 F1 points on JNLPBA, GENETAG, and Bio-ID, respectively. It also outperformed the domain-specific scispaCy tokenizer by 1.0, 0.9, and 2.7 points on the respective datasets. The improvements were most significant on Bio-ID, which contains a large number of tokens that cross entity boundaries, such as fusion constructs and prefixed forms.

A paired bootstrap test indicated that the improvement over the scispaCy baseline was significant on Bio-ID (p < 0.001) and GENETAG (p = 0.02), with a borderline significance on JNLPBA (p = 0.07). We then quantified the impact of tokenization on entities whose boundaries did not align with those produced by the scispaCy tokenizer. These cases, which represented 3.1% of gold mentions in JNLPBA, 2.4% in GENETAG, and 8.9% in Bio-ID, are particularly challenging for word-level taggers, as they can never recover such mentions exactly. Our BPE model correctly recovered 41.7%, 46.3%, and 52.8% of these mentions on the three corpora, respectively, accounting for roughly one third to one half of its recall advantage over the word-level baseline. This analysis underscores the importance of tokenization in capturing complex entity boundaries in biomedical text and demonstrates the superiority of the BPE approach in handling such cases. The comparative analysis of boundary-aligned entities revealed that the two approaches differed by less than 0.6 F1 on every corpus, suggesting that the byte-level formulation does not compromise accuracy in cases where word-level segmentation is adequate. To further investigate the contributions of individual model components, we conducted ablation experiments on the JNLPBA and Bio-ID development sets, as reported in Table 3.

The results of these experiments indicate that removing the convolutional layers resulted in a reduction of 1.7 and 2.2 F1 points, while the removal of the recurrent layer led to a decrease of 2.9 and 3.7 points. These findings suggest that both components play a crucial role in the model's performance, with the BiLSTM providing the necessary long-range context to assign consistent entity types across a sentence. Furthermore, replacing BPE units with raw characters, equivalent to zero merge operations, led to a decrease of 2.6 and 3.3 F1 points, highlighting the importance of merged subword units in providing useful lexical information and facilitating optimization.

The CRF layer, on the other hand, yielded a smaller gain of roughly 0.8-0.9 points, indicating that while it contributes to the model's performance, its impact is relatively modest compared to the other components. To examine the effect of BPE vocabulary size on the model's performance, we varied the number of merge operations from 1,000 to 64,000, using a BPE vocabulary learned on approximately 2 million PubMed abstracts. The results showed that development F1 on JNLPBA increased from 75.4 at 1,000 merges to 77.8 at 16,000 merges, before declining slightly to 77.3 at 32,000 and 76.6 at 64,000. A similar pattern was observed on Bio-ID, which peaked at 72.4 with 16,000 merges.

These findings suggest that larger vocabularies result in rarer units with poorly trained embeddings, while smaller vocabularies produce long sequences that dilute context. Based on these results, we used 16,000 merges in all reported experiments. Notably, the average number of BPE units per word was 2.3 at this setting, and 96.8% of gold entity boundaries fell on a BPE unit boundary. The remaining 3.2% were resolved by tagging at the byte level rather than the unit level, as described in the Methods.

A closer examination of per-type performance on JNLPBA revealed that F1 ranged from 80.3 for proteins to 66.4 for RNA, with DNA (71.5), cell type (73.9), and cell line (68.8) falling in between. These patterns mirror those of prior systems, suggesting that our model is able to capture the nuances of biomedical entity recognition. On Bio-ID, the best-performing types were organisms (F1 84.6) and genes/proteins (75.9), while the lowest was tissue/organ (58.2).

To gain a deeper understanding of the model's strengths and weaknesses, we manually inspected 200 randomly sampled false positives and 200 false negatives from the Bio-ID test set. The results showed that boundary errors accounted for 38% of the total errors, type confusions for 27% (primarily between gene and protein annotations), and spurious or missed mentions for the remaining 35%. Among boundary errors, 61% involved nested or coordinated expressions, and only 9% were attributable to hyphenated or prefixed tokens, a category that dominated word-level errors in the baseline.

In terms of efficiency, our model's inference cost lies between that of character-level and word-level models, processing approximately 1,850 sentences per second on a single GPU. This is comparable to the word-level BiLSTM-CRF and character-level variant, and significantly faster than a BERT-base model fine-tuned on the same data. The model's relatively small size, with 9.8 million trainable parameters, makes it an attractive option for applications where computational resources or domain-specific preprocessing expertise are limited.

The central question of this work was whether a named entity recognition system could dispense with hand-crafted, domain-specific tokenization and still perform competitively on biomedical text. Our results suggest that this is indeed possible. By combining byte-pair encoding with convolutional and recurrent layers to assign tags at the subword level, we achieved performance comparable to word-level neural taggers of the BiLSTM-CRF family on BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG. Notably, our model did not require the rule-based tokenizers that biomedical pipelines usually depend on, which is significant because biomedical entity mentions often violate the assumption that entity boundaries coincide with whitespace or punctuation-delimited tokens.

The ability of our model to operate below the word level, making boundary decisions a learned property of the model rather than a fixed preprocessing step, is a key factor in its success. We attribute this to two properties of the architecture: first, BPE segmentation provides frequent biomedical morphemes and affixes with their own units, while rare strings decompose into smaller pieces, providing the morphological cues that character-aware models have long exploited; and second, the convolutional layers capture local orthographic patterns within and across adjacent subwords, while the recurrent layer propagates longer-range context needed to decide where a span begins and ends.

Our approach is related to byte- and character-level sequence labeling in multilingual settings, where explicit segmentation is likewise unreliable. The biomedical domain, with its dense and irregular nomenclature, appears to benefit similarly from subword tagging. The variation in results across datasets is consistent with this interpretation, with corpora whose annotation guidelines frequently place boundaries inside orthographic words benefiting most from subword tagging, whereas corpora in which entities largely align with conventional tokens leave less room for improvement over a good tokenizer.

The rapid proliferation of GPS-enabled mobile devices has led to an explosion in the growth of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs), such as Foursquare, Gowalla, and Yelp, where users share their physical presence at Points-of-Interest (POIs) through check-ins, tips, and reviews. This phenomenon has been extensively studied in recent years, with researchers like Bao et al. (2015) highlighting the potential of LBSNs to support a wide range of services, including urban planning, location-targeted advertising, and personalized travel assistance. Among these services, POI recommendation has emerged as a central task, as it enables users to explore their surroundings and helps businesses reach potential customers (Ye et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017). However, as the numbers of users and venues grow into the millions, effective POI recommender systems are needed to counter information overload and provide users with relevant and personalized recommendations.

Early POI recommenders were largely adapted from general-purpose collaborative filtering techniques, which learn latent user and POI representations through matrix factorization (MF) approaches. These approaches, such as those proposed by Koren et al. (2009) and Hu et al. (2008), approximate observed preferences by taking the inner product of the latent representations. However, since check-in data only record positive, implicit feedback, these methods typically treat unobserved entries as weighted negatives or optimize pairwise ranking objectives (Rendle et al., 2009). Nevertheless, researchers soon recognized that POIs differ from items such as movies or books because they are anchored in geographic space, and therefore, geographical context plays a crucial role in POI recommendation.

To address this issue, existing work has augmented collaborative filtering with spatial information, for example, by fitting power-law or kernel density models of check-in distances (Ye et al., 2011; Zhang & Chow, 2013), by embedding activity areas into latent factors (Lian et al., 2014), or by combining social, temporal, and categorical signals with geographical influence (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015). These studies consistently show that geographical context is a decisive signal, consistent with Tobler's (1970) first law of geography, which states that near things are more related than distant ones. Despite this progress, two challenges remain in POI recommendation. The first challenge is modeling non-linear user-POI interactions from implicit feedback. MF and its geographical extensions assume that preference is a linear function of latent factors, which limits their capacity to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior.

Deep learning offers a remedy to this challenge. Neural collaborative filtering replaces the inner product with a learned non-linear interaction function (He et al., 2017). Autoencoder-based models, such as AutoRec (Sedhain et al., 2015), the collaborative denoising autoencoder (Wu et al., 2016), and variational autoencoders for collaborative filtering (Liang et al., 2018), reconstruct a user's interaction vector through non-linear mappings and achieve strong top-N performance. However, these autoencoders compress a user's history into a single representation by uniformly aggregating the embeddings of all interacted items. In the POI setting, this is problematic because a user's check-ins are highly diverse, and a single user may frequent a workplace cafeteria, a gym, and a handful of tourist sites, each reflecting a different intention and with different significance for predicting future behavior.

The second challenge is incorporating context information, particularly geographical coordinates, into neural architectures. Most neural recommenders operate on identifiers alone, and the few that exploit location typically feed coordinates or discretized grid cells as additional input features (Yang et al., 2017). This design discards the continuous nature of geographic distance and does not express the underlying behavioral principle that a user who visits a POI is likely to visit its nearby and similar neighbors. Moreover, the data are extremely sparse, with typical LBSN check-in matrices having densities well below 1%. Propagating a user's preference to spatially adjacent venues is a natural way to mitigate sparsity and improve generalization. However, the question remains as to how to inject such neighborhood effects into a non-linear model in a principled, end-to-end trainable manner, rather than as a post-hoc re-ranking step.

These observations motivate the central research question of this paper: can a non-linear autoencoder framework adaptively weigh the multiple facets of a user's check-in history and explicitly encode geographical neighborhood influence, so as to produce more accurate POI recommendations from sparse implicit feedback? Attention mechanisms provide a promising route to the first goal. They were introduced to align and weigh elements of a sequence in neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and have since been generalized to self-attention, which relates elements of a single input to one another (Vaswani et al., 2017). In particular, multi-dimensional structured self-attention produces several attention distributions over the same input, each capable of focusing on a different aspect (Lin et al., 2017). This property suits POI recommendation, where a user's preferences are naturally multi-faceted.

For the second goal, kernel functions of spatial distance offer a smooth, differentiable measure of geographic proximity. The radial basis function (RBF) kernel, for instance, assigns high affinity to nearby locations and decays rapidly with distance. Building on these ideas, we propose SAE-NAD, an autoencoder with a Self-Attentive Encoder (SAE) and a Neighbor-Aware Decoder (NAD). The encoder applies multi-dimensional self-attention over the embeddings of a user's checked-in POIs and learns several attention weightings that distinguish the preference degrees of individual POIs along different aspects. These weightings are aggregated into a compact user representation. The decoder reconstructs the user's check-in preferences over all POIs and, crucially, makes a user's reachability to unvisited POIs higher when they are similar to and near the POIs the user has visited. This is realized through the inner product of POI embeddings, which captures similarity, combined with an RBF kernel over pairwise geographical distance, which captures proximity.

The model is trained end-to-end on implicit feedback, so the geographical influence is learned jointly with the user-POI relations rather than imposed through separate, hand-tuned components. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose SAE-NAD, a novel autoencoder-based framework for POI recommendation that models non-linear user-POI relations from implicit feedback while jointly leveraging attention-based preference modeling and geographical context. We design a self-attentive encoder that employs multi-dimensional attention to adaptively differentiate the importance of a user's checked-in POIs across multiple aspects, in contrast to prior autoencoders that weigh all interactions equally. We devise a neighbor-aware decoder that integrates POI embedding and geographical distance to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior. Overall, our approach provides a principled, end-to-end trainable framework for POI recommendation that effectively incorporates geographical context and attention mechanisms to produce more accurate recommendations from sparse implicit feedback. In this study, we propose a novel approach to Point of Interest (POI) recommendation, leveraging the strengths of both autoencoder-based collaborative filtering and geographical modeling. Our model, Self-Attentive Encoder-Neighbor Aware Decoder (SAE-NAD), incorporates a self-attentive encoder to capture complex user preferences and a neighbor-aware decoder to account for geographical context. By using a radial basis function (RBF) kernel to model the similarity between POIs based on their geographical distance, we can effectively raise the reachability of nearby and similar POIs, thereby enhancing the overall recommendation performance.

To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on three real-world Location-Based Social Network (LBSN) datasets, namely Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp. Our results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Furthermore, ablation analyses confirm that both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder contribute to the gains in recommendation performance.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by reviewing related work on POI recommendation and autoencoder-based collaborative filtering. We then formulate the problem and present the SAE-NAD model in detail, highlighting its key components and the intuition behind its design. Next, we describe the experimental setup and report the results of our evaluation, including the datasets used, the preprocessing steps taken, and the performance metrics employed. Finally, we conclude the paper by summarizing our findings and outlining directions for future research.

Our evaluation datasets consist of three public LBSN check-in datasets: Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp. Each check-in record contains a user identifier, a POI identifier, a timestamp, and the POI's geographical coordinates. Following common practice in POI recommendation, we removed users with fewer than 15 check-ins and POIs visited by fewer than 10 users to mitigate extreme sparsity and yield stable estimates. After filtering, the datasets contained 18,737 users, 32,510 POIs, and 1,278,274 check-ins for Gowalla; 24,941 users, 28,593 POIs, and 1,196,248 check-ins for Foursquare; and 30,887 users, 18,995 POIs, and 860,888 check-ins for Yelp.

Since the task is based on implicit feedback, each user is represented as a binary vector, where a value of 1 indicates at least one check-in at a particular POI. Repeated visits are collapsed into a single positive observation. For each user, we randomly assigned 70% of check-ins to training, 10% to validation for hyperparameter selection and early stopping, and 20% to testing. The split was repeated with five different random seeds to ensure robustness.

The problem formulation involves estimating, for each user, a reachability score for every unvisited POI and returning the top-k ranked POIs. Candidate sets for ranking comprise all POIs absent from a user's training and validation records. Our model architecture consists of an autoencoder that maps the user's binary vector to a latent representation and reconstructs a dense score vector over all POIs.

The encoder is a self-attentive encoder, which captures several aspects of user preference using multi-dimensional structured self-attention. Each POI has an input embedding, and the embeddings of the POIs visited by a user are stacked to form a matrix. The self-attention mechanism computes a weighted sum of these embeddings, where the weights are learned based on the user's preferences. The attended representation is then passed through a fully connected layer with a nonlinear activation to produce the user latent vector.

The decoder is a neighbor-aware decoder, which incorporates geographical context by adding a neighbor term to the scoring function. For each POI pair, we define the neighbor influence as the product of the inner product of the decoder-side POI embeddings and a radial basis function (RBF) kernel with bandwidth ρ. The final score is computed as the sigmoid of the sum of the user latent vector, the POI embedding, and the neighbor term. The RBF kernel decays smoothly with distance, allowing the model to capture both local and global geographical patterns.

We trained our model using a weighted binary cross-entropy loss function, where unobserved entries are treated as weak negatives and downweighted using a hyperparameter α. To avoid computing the loss over all POIs, we sampled five unobserved POIs per positive per epoch. Dropout with rate 0.5 was applied to the latent layer to reduce overfitting. Parameters were initialized using the Xavier scheme and optimized using Adam with a learning rate of 0.001 and mini-batches of 256 users. Training stopped if validation Recall@10 failed to improve for 10 consecutive epochs.

We searched the hyperparameter space by varying the embedding dimension, number of attention aspects, attention size, RBF bandwidth, negative weight, and regularization strength. Selection used the validation set, one factor at a time around a default configuration. Unless otherwise stated, the reported results use an embedding dimension of 50, three attention aspects, an attention size of 50, and an RBF bandwidth of 1 km.

Our baselines include representative methods from three families: classical implicit-feedback and geographical models, neural network-based models, and graph-based models. We compared SAE-NAD against these baselines using multiple ranking metrics, including Recall@k, Precision@k, and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@k). Our results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms the competing methods, with significant improvements in recommendation performance.

In conclusion, our study proposes a novel approach to POI recommendation, leveraging the strengths of both autoencoder-based collaborative filtering and geographical modeling. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we outline directions for future research, including exploring other architectures and incorporating additional contextual information. By developing more accurate and personalized POI recommendation systems, we can enhance the user experience and provide more effective recommendations for users in location-based social networks. The efficacy of various point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models has been extensively explored in recent years, with a plethora of approaches being proposed to tackle this complex problem. Our investigation focused on three primary categories of models: (i) matrix factorization-based methods, including weighted regularized matrix factorization (WRMF; Hu et al., 2008), Bayesian personalized ranking matrix factorization (BPRMF; Rendle et al., 2009), RankGeoFM (Li et al., 2015), and IRenMF (Liu et al., 2014); (ii) neural collaborative filtering models, such as neural collaborative filtering (NeuMF; He et al., 2017), CDAE (Wu et al., 2016), and Mult-VAE (Liang et al., 2018); and (iii) neural POI recommenders, including PACE (Yang et al., 2017) and ASMF (Ma et al., 2018). To ensure a fair comparison, we tuned the hyperparameters of these baseline models using the recommended ranges from their original publications, with the validation sets being identical to those used for our proposed model.

In addition to evaluating the performance of these baseline models, we also trained ablated variants of our proposed model, SAE-NAD, to isolate the contributions of its individual components. Specifically, we considered three variants: SAE-NAD without attention (referred to as "AE-NAD"), SAE-NAD without the neighbor term (denoted as "SAE-only"), and SAE-NAD with the neighbor term but without the RBF kernel (labeled as "SAE-NAD w/o RBF"). By examining the performance of these variants, we aimed to gain a deeper understanding of the relative importance of each component in our proposed model.

Our evaluation metrics consisted of Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Average Precision (MAP@k) at k = {2, 5, 10}, which are standard top-k metrics for POI recommendation (Liu et al., 2017). For a given user u, Precision@k was calculated as the ratio of the number of relevant POIs in the ranked top-k list (Ru^k) to the total number of recommended POIs (k), whereas Recall@k was defined as the ratio of the number of relevant POIs in Ru^k to the total number of test POIs (Tu). MAP@k, on the other hand, averages the precision values computed at the rank positions of correctly retrieved POIs within the top k. Users with no test POIs were excluded from the evaluation, and all metrics were averaged across users.

To ensure the reliability of our results, we performed statistical analysis using a two-sided paired t-test across five random splits and initializations, with significance determined at a p-value of 0.05. Since multiple metrics were tested, we applied the Holm-Bonferroni correction to control the family-wise error rate (Holm, 1979). The relative improvement of our proposed model over the strongest baseline was computed as (Mours - Mbest baseline) / Mbest baseline. Furthermore, we assessed the sensitivity of our model to the hyperparameters d, r, and ρ by varying one parameter at a time while holding the others at their default values. We also stratified users by their training check-in count (quartiles) to examine the robustness of our model to data sparsity. All experiments were implemented in TensorFlow and run on a single NVIDIA GPU.

Our results are summarized in Table 2, which reports the Precision@k (P@k), Recall@k (R@k), and MAP@k values for k = {5, 10, 20} on the Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp datasets. The values are averaged over five random splits, with 80% of the data used for training, 5% for validation, and 15% for testing. We compared the performance of our proposed model, SAE-NAD, with seven baseline models: WRMF, GeoMF, IRenMF, RankGeoFM, PACE, CDAE, and Mult-VAE. Our results demonstrate that SAE-NAD achieves the best performance on every dataset and metric. For instance, on the Gowalla dataset, SAE-NAD obtained P@10 = 0.1562, R@10 = 0.1317, and MAP@10 = 0.0845, outperforming the strongest baseline, Mult-VAE, which achieved 0.1388, 0.1156, and 0.0702, respectively. The relative gains of SAE-NAD over Mult-VAE were 12.5%, 13.9%, and 20.4% for P@10, R@10, and MAP@10, respectively.

Similarly, on the Foursquare dataset, SAE-NAD achieved P@10 = 0.1263, R@10 = 0.1581, and MAP@10 = 0.0953, surpassing the best baseline, PACE, which obtained 0.1117, 0.1392, and 0.0794, respectively. The improvements of SAE-NAD over PACE were 13.1%, 13.6%, and 20.0% for P@10, R@10, and MAP@10, respectively. On the Yelp dataset, which is the sparsest among the three, SAE-NAD obtained P@10 = 0.0618, R@10 = 0.0702, and MAP@10 = 0.0341, outperforming the strongest baseline, Mult-VAE, which achieved 0.0547, 0.0613, and 0.0278, respectively. The relative gains of SAE-NAD over Mult-VAE were 13.0%, 14.5%, and 22.7% for P@10, R@10, and MAP@10, respectively. The differences between SAE-NAD and the strongest baseline on each dataset and metric were statistically significant, with p-values less than 0.01 across the five splits.

Notably, the improvements of SAE-NAD over the best baseline were largest at k = 5 and decreased slightly as k grew. For example, on the Gowalla dataset, the P@5 gain of SAE-NAD over the best baseline was 14.8%, whereas the P@20 gain was 11.2%. This pattern suggests that our model is particularly effective at ranking the most relevant POIs at the top of the list, which is crucial in practical recommendation scenarios.

In addition to the primary results, several secondary trends emerged from our experiments. Firstly, the nonlinear models (PACE, CDAE, and Mult-VAE) consistently outperformed the linear factorization methods (WRMF and GeoMF). Averaged over the three datasets, Mult-VAE improved MAP@10 by 24.6% over WRMF, which supports the premise that user-POI interactions are poorly captured by inner products in a latent space. Secondly, geographically aware factorization models (IRenMF and RankGeoFM) outperformed their geography-agnostic counterpart (WRMF). For instance, on the Gowalla dataset, IRenMF and RankGeoFM gained 6.8% and 9.3% in R@10 over WRMF, respectively, which confirms the value of spatial context in POI recommendation. Thirdly, the autoencoder baselines (CDAE and Mult-VAE) did not exploit coordinates at all, yet they surpassed the geography-aware matrix factorization methods on the Gowalla and Yelp datasets. Our proposed model, SAE-NAD, combines the nonlinear modeling capacity of the autoencoder family with explicit geographical information, which enables it to outperform both groups.

To further understand the contributions of each component in our proposed model, we conducted an ablation study. We evaluated four variants: (i) AE, which removes both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder, leaving a plain autoencoder; (ii) SAE, which keeps only the self-attentive encoder; (iii) NAD, which keeps only the neighbor-aware decoder; and (iv) the full SAE-NAD model. Figure 3 shows the MAP@10 and R@10 values for these variants on the Gowalla dataset. The plain AE achieved MAP@10 = 0.0671, whereas adding the self-attentive encoder raised this value to 0.0749 (+11.6%). Adding the neighbor-aware decoder further raised the MAP@10 value to 0.0772 (+15.1%). The full SAE-NAD model achieved MAP@10 = 0.0845, which is 25.9% above the plain AE. The two components thus contribute complementary rather than redundant information, as the gain of the combined model is nearly additive. Similar patterns were observed on the Foursquare and Yelp datasets.

We also compared the multi-dimensional attention mechanism in our proposed model with a standard single-vector additive attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and with uniform weighting of checked-in POIs. Replacing multi-dimensional attention with single-vector attention reduced R@10 by 3.9% on the Gowalla dataset and 4.4% on the Foursquare dataset. Uniform weighting reduced R@10 by 7.8% and 8.6% on the two datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the multi-dimensional attention mechanism in our proposed model. The effectiveness of the decoder in our proposed model, SAE-NAD, relies on the interplay between two key components: the semantic similarity between points of interest (POIs) and their geographical proximity. To demonstrate this, we conducted ablation studies where we removed either the RBF kernel or the POI-embedding inner product from the decoder. The results showed that using the RBF kernel alone, without the inner product, led to a 5.7% decrease in MAP@10 on the Gowalla dataset, while using the inner product alone, without the RBF kernel, resulted in a 6.9% decrease. These findings underscore the importance of considering both factors in the decoder to achieve optimal performance.

We also investigated the sensitivity of SAE-NAD to several hyperparameters, including the latent dimension $d$, the number of attention dimensions $r$, and the RBF kernel bandwidth. Our analysis revealed that increasing the latent dimension $d$ from 20 to 100 led to improved performance, with R@10 rising from 0.1189 to 0.1317 on Gowalla. However, further increasing $d$ to 200 did not yield significant gains, with R@10 reaching 0.1314. Based on these results, we fixed $d$ at 100 for our main experiments. The number of attention dimensions $r$ also had a notable impact on performance, with R@10 improving steadily from $r = 1$ (0.1262) to $r = 5$ (0.1317). Nevertheless, increasing $r$ beyond 10 led to a slight decline in performance, likely due to overfitting caused by highly sparse check-in histories.

The RBF kernel bandwidth played a crucial role in balancing the geographical influence of POIs. Very small values made the kernel too localized, failing to propagate useful information to neighboring POIs, while very large values rendered the kernel nearly uniform, treating distant POIs similarly to close ones. The optimal bandwidth was found to be at intermediate values, with results varying by less than 3% within the neighborhood of the optimum, indicating reasonable robustness. Additionally, we observed that the dropout rate had a moderate effect on performance, with values between 0.3 and 0.5 yielding the best results across all datasets.

To further evaluate the performance of SAE-NAD, we examined its effectiveness across different user activity levels. We split test users into three groups based on the number of training check-ins: inactive (fewer than 10), moderate (10-30), and active (more than 30). On Gowalla, the inactive group accounted for 41.2% of users, and SAE-NAD achieved an R@10 of 0.0963, outperforming Mult-VAE (0.0794) and PACE (0.0781) by 21.3% and 23.3%, respectively. The advantage of SAE-NAD narrowed for active users, with an improvement of 8.9% over Mult-VAE (0.1804 vs. 0.1657). These results suggest that the geographical neighbors and attention mechanism in SAE-NAD can effectively compensate for limited interaction history, particularly for sparse users.

In terms of efficiency, we compared the training cost of SAE-NAD with other models on a single NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti GPU. SAE-NAD converged in approximately 40 epochs on Gowalla, with an average of 11.3 seconds per epoch, resulting in a total training time of around 7.5 minutes. This is comparable to CDAE (about 6.8 minutes) and significantly faster than PACE (about 31 minutes), which requires joint training of user and POI embeddings with context prediction. The RBF kernel is computed once from POI coordinates and can be reused throughout training, adding only 9% to the per-epoch time of the plain autoencoder. These results indicate that the accuracy gains of SAE-NAD do not come at the cost of prohibitive computational overhead.

The experiments presented above demonstrate that combining a self-attentive encoder with a neighbor-aware decoder yields consistent improvements over strong baselines on three location-based social network (LBSN) datasets. SAE-NAD improved Precision@k, Recall@k, and MAP@k at every cutoff examined, with relative gains most pronounced on the sparsest dataset, where Recall@10 increased by roughly 8-12% over the strongest competing method. In this section, we interpret these results, relate them to prior work, and discuss limitations and implications.

Three key observations emerge from our findings. First, autoencoder-based collaborative filtering benefits from non-linear modeling of user-POI interactions. Linear and bilinear factorization approaches, including weighted matrix factorization and its geographically augmented variants, were consistently outperformed by neural approaches. This pattern supports the view that check-in behavior is governed by interacting factors, such as category preference, spatial convenience, and social or temporal routines, which a single inner product of latent vectors cannot easily capture. The performance gap between our model and these baselines reinforces this interpretation.

Second, the ablation results indicate that the two components of SAE-NAD contribute complementary gains. Replacing the multi-dimensional attention with mean pooling over checked-in POI embeddings reduced performance substantially, suggesting that treating all visited POIs as equally informative discards useful signal. A user's history typically mixes habitual visits with more preference-revealing ones, and attention weights learned in multiple subspaces allow the encoder to emphasize different subsets of the history for different latent aspects. Case studies showed that different attention dimensions concentrated on semantically coherent groups of POIs, such as dining venues versus transit-adjacent locations. However, these observations should not be taken as proof that each dimension encodes a distinct interpretable factor, as prior analyses have cautioned that attention weights are not always faithful explanations of model behavior.

Third, removing the neighbor-aware decoder or replacing the RBF kernel with a uniform or purely distance-thresholded alternative degraded accuracy. The decoder raises the predicted reachability of POIs that are both geographically close to and embedding-similar to a user's visited POIs, reflecting the first law of geography as it operates in human mobility. A key difference from earlier approaches is that geography is not imposed as a hard prior or a separate additive score, but rather enters multiplicatively with learned POI similarity. This design likely explains why our model outperformed methods that model geographical influence through independent distributions, such as the multi-center Gaussian formulation or the kernel-based approach.

The loss of an upper limb is a profound and life-altering event that significantly impacts an individual's ability to engage in daily activities, maintain relationships, and participate in leisure pursuits. The hand and arm play a vital role in manipulation, tactile exploration, and non-verbal communication, and their absence can result in a disability that extends far beyond the physical deficit. According to population estimates, over a million people in the United States are living with limb loss, and this number is projected to more than double by mid-century due to the increasing prevalence of vascular disease and diabetes (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Notably, while lower-limb amputation is primarily dysvascular in origin, upper-limb loss is often the result of traumatic injury, affecting younger, working-age individuals who have been involved in industrial accidents, road traffic collisions, or armed conflict (Dillingham et al., 2002; Atkins et al., 1996). As these individuals face decades of life with limb loss, the quality of their care has significant functional, psychological, and socioeconomic implications.

Prosthetic fitting is the most well-known intervention for upper-limb amputation, and the range of available devices has expanded to include passive cosmetic restorations, body-powered hooks, myoelectric hands, and advanced multi-articulating and pattern-recognition-controlled systems. Techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation have increased the number of intuitive control signals available to individuals with high-level amputations (Kuiken et al., 2009). However, despite advances in technological sophistication, sustained use of prosthetic devices has not been reliably achieved. Surveys and reviews spanning 25 years of literature have reported substantial rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment, often attributed to factors such as discomfort, weight, poor functional return, and inadequate training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Davidson, 2002). Satisfaction with prosthetic use is influenced by a range of factors, including the timing of fitting, the quality of follow-up services, and the user's preparedness to operate the prosthesis in daily life (Pezzin et al., 2004; McFarland et al., 2010). Furthermore, comparative evidence on myoelectric and body-powered devices suggests that neither is uniformly superior, highlighting the importance of user training and context in determining successful prosthetic use (Carey et al., 2015).

This situation underscores the critical role of rehabilitation in the care pathway for individuals with upper-limb amputation. Prosthetic rehabilitation is a structured, multidisciplinary process that begins at or before amputation and continues after definitive fitting. It encompasses a range of activities, including pre-prosthetic care, such as wound healing, edema control, desensitization, and maintenance of range of motion and strength. Subsequent training focuses on muscle control and signal acquisition, donning and doffing, controlled operation of the terminal device, and bimanual functional activities. Additionally, rehabilitation addresses phantom sensation and pain, as well as the psychosocial adjustment necessary for reintegration into work and community roles (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). As prosthetic technology becomes increasingly complex, the needs of users become more pronounced, and clinicians have noted that the evidence base for training approaches has not kept pace with engineering developments (Resnik et al., 2012).

Several rehabilitation strategies have been proposed or tested, including general conditioning programs, graded motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, mirror therapy, myoelectric training with biofeedback, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual reality or augmented reality environments in which users practice control before or alongside physical device use. Mirror therapy and related visual-feedback methods have been primarily investigated for phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007), while recent work suggests that virtual and augmented reality combined with myoelectric pattern recognition can improve control and alleviate pain (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016; Powell & Thakor, 2013). These approaches draw on different theoretical bases, including motor learning, cortical reorganization, and task-specific practice, and are applied in various settings and at different times after amputation. However, the resulting literature is characterized by fragmentation, with most studies being small case series or single-center studies with heterogeneous outcome measures, and incomplete descriptions of training content, intensity, and sequencing.

This fragmentation limits both clinical practice and research, as clinicians lack a consolidated summary of the components of rehabilitation programs, their delivery, and associated outcomes. Health systems, too, face challenges in deciding how to allocate resources between therapy services and devices, due to a lack of synthesized evidence on the added value of rehabilitation. Previous reviews have primarily focused on prosthesis design, control strategies, or user acceptance and abandonment (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Carey et al., 2015), while others have examined phantom limb pain interventions or lower-limb amputation. To our knowledge, few have systematically examined the content of rehabilitation programs specifically for individuals with upper-extremity amputations or considered the implications of this body of work for the importance of rehabilitation in successful prosthetic use.

The present review aims to address this gap by identifying and cataloging the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation reported in the literature, appraising the methodological quality of available studies, and arguing that rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision.
