Firstly, we sought to investigate the extent to which air quality warning systems influence protective behaviors among the general public, with a particular focus on estimating both intended and actual adherence to the accompanying health advice. Secondly, we aimed to identify the demographic and psychosocial factors associated with adherence and non-adherence, including self-reported reasons for following or not following the advice, and to interpret these findings within the context of the COM-B framework. To maintain a sharp focus on the warning systems themselves, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies in which participants were either using or aware of such systems, and excluded those that examined protective behaviors prompted solely by subjective perceptions of poor air quality.

Our review makes three significant contributions to the existing literature. Firstly, it provides the first systematic summary of adherence rates to health advice linked to air quality alerts, drawing a critical distinction between advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activity and broader protective behaviors. Secondly, it clarifies the utility of demographic characteristics in identifying individuals who are less likely to adhere to health advice. Finally, it identifies modifiable psychosocial facilitators and barriers, mapping them onto a behavioral framework to provide a foundation for the design and evaluation of more effective air quality communication strategies.

In conducting this systematic review, we adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, as outlined by Moher et al. in 2009. Given the anticipated heterogeneity of the literature in terms of design, populations, warning systems, and outcome measures, we planned a narrative synthesis in advance, following guidance from the Economic and Social Research Council on narrative synthesis in systematic reviews. Our findings were interpreted through the lens of the COM-B model of behavior, which posits that behavior is a function of interacting components, including capability, opportunity, and motivation. This model, which forms part of the Behaviour Change Wheel, suggests that behavior can be understood as the product of these interacting components, and provides a useful framework for understanding the complex factors that influence adherence to health advice.

Our eligibility criteria were carefully defined to ensure that only relevant studies were included in the review. We considered studies eligible if they assessed either intended or actual adherence to health advice accompanying an air quality warning system, where such advice encouraged individuals to reduce their exposure to air pollution. This could include advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activity, avoid busy roads, stay indoors, or use preventative medication. We also included studies that examined predictors of adherence, including demographic and psychosocial factors, as well as self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. To be eligible, studies had to report original data, be published in English in a peer-reviewed journal, and involve participants who were members of the general public, including those with pre-existing conditions such as asthma. We excluded studies that examined only protective behaviors arising from subjective perceptions of poor air quality, as well as those that did not involve participants who were aware of or using a warning system.

Our search strategy was comprehensive, involving a systematic search of multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, from inception to August 2016. We combined three concept blocks using Boolean operators, focusing on air quality terms, warning terms, and behavioral terms. Search terms were adapted to the controlled vocabulary of each database, and reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched. We also conducted forward citation tracking in Google Scholar and screened the first 100 results of Google Scholar queries using the main search terms.

Study selection was a rigorous process, involving the export of records to reference management software, the removal of duplicates, and the screening of titles and abstracts against our eligibility criteria. One reviewer screened all titles and abstracts, while a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subsample, with agreement assessed using Cohen's kappa. Full texts of potentially relevant articles were obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third author. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were carefully recorded.

Data extraction was a systematic process, involving the development and piloting of a standardized extraction form on three studies. Extracted information included country and setting, study design, sampling method and sample size, participant characteristics, type of warning system, and the content of the accompanying health advice. We also extracted information on adherence rates, demographic and psychosocial predictors tested, and self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. One reviewer extracted data, while a second reviewer checked all entries for accuracy. Where studies reported adherence to multiple behaviors, we separated adherence to the advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activities from adherence to a wider range of protective behaviors. Where adherence was reported for subgroups only, we extracted rates by subgroup and calculated the overall rate as a weighted proportion where sufficient information was available. For each category, we calculated the range and median of reported adherence proportions across studies.

Throughout this review, we have sought to provide a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the factors that influence adherence to health advice linked to air quality alerts. By examining the complex interplay between demographic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors, we hope to provide a foundation for the development of more effective air quality communication strategies, ultimately contributing to improved public health outcomes. The findings of this review have significant implications for policymakers, public health practitioners, and researchers, highlighting the need for tailored approaches to air quality communication that take into account the diverse needs and characteristics of the population. By prioritizing the development of effective air quality communication strategies, we can work towards reducing the adverse health effects of air pollution and promoting healthier behaviors among the general public. The assessment of methodological quality was a crucial step in our research, and to ensure rigor, two reviewers evaluated the included studies independently. Given the diversity of study designs, we employed an adapted version of the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies, developed by the Effective Public Health Practice Project (Thomas et al., 2004), for quantitative studies, and the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist (CASP, 2013) for qualitative studies. Our evaluation focused on several key domains, including selection bias, study design, confounding control, and the validity and reliability of data collection tools, as well as the appropriateness of analysis. Each domain was rated as strong, moderate, or weak, and an overall rating was assigned. We paid particular attention to the methods used to measure adherence, noting whether validated or piloted instruments were used, and the potential for recall and social desirability bias inherent in self-reported behavior. It's worth noting that the quality ratings were not used as a basis for excluding studies, but rather to inform our interpretation of the synthesis.

The heterogeneity of the studies, in terms of warning systems, populations, outcome definitions, and time frames for recall, precluded the use of meta-analysis. Instead, we opted for a narrative synthesis, which was conducted in four stages. The first stage involved developing a preliminary description of the study findings through tabulation. In the second stage, we grouped the studies by outcome type, distinguishing between intended and actual adherence, as well as the reduction of outdoor activity versus wider protective behaviors. The third stage involved exploring relationships within and between studies, including the role of demographic variables, such as age, sex, education, income, ethnicity, and health status, in predicting adherence. Finally, in the fourth stage, we assessed the robustness of the synthesis, taking into account study quality, sample size, and consistency across settings.

In coding the psychosocial predictors and self-reported reasons, we employed an inductive approach, followed by deductive mapping onto the COM-B domains. We gave greater weight to barriers and facilitators identified in multiple studies, and considered a factor to be a consistent predictor if it was significantly associated with adherence in the same direction in the majority of studies that tested it. Where findings conflicted, we reported them as inconsistent. The coding was performed by one reviewer and reviewed by a second, with any disagreements resolved through discussion.

Our database searches and supplementary strategies, including reference list screening, citation tracking, and contact with experts, yielded a total of 6,412 records. After removing 1,327 duplicates, we screened 5,085 titles and abstracts, excluding 4,902 as irrelevant, primarily because they focused on air pollution exposure or health outcomes without a warning system. The remaining 183 full-text articles were assessed, and 162 were excluded, mainly due to the following reasons: participants were not using or aware of a warning system (n = 71); protective behavior was attributed only to subjective perception of air quality (n = 38); no adherence or predictor data were reported (n = 29); the study was a commentary, protocol, or conference abstract (n = 16); and the study was not available in English (n = 8). Ultimately, 21 studies were included in the final synthesis.

The majority of the included studies (17) investigated actual adherence, while three examined intended adherence, and one assessed both. Most studies (n = 16) employed a cross-sectional survey design, with the remaining studies using a cohort or panel study design (n = 2), qualitative interviews or focus groups (n = 2), or a mixed-methods approach (n = 1). The studies were conducted in various regions, including North America (n = 14), Europe (n = 4), Asia (n = 2), and Australia (n = 1). Sample sizes ranged from 28 (in qualitative studies) to 5,038 participants, with a median of 412. The populations studied were diverse, with 11 studies focusing on general adult samples, and 10 targeting at-risk groups, such as individuals with asthma or chronic respiratory or cardiovascular disease (n = 6), parents of children with asthma (n = 3), and older adults (n = 1).

The warning systems used in the studies typically involved air quality indices communicated through various channels, including media, websites, smartphone applications, telephone alerts, or school and workplace notices. Most studies employed a numerical or color-coded index, such as the US Air Quality Index or the Canadian Air Quality Health Index. Adherence was nearly always self-reported, with only three studies using objective or semi-objective measures, such as time-activity diaries, accelerometry, or hospital records. Our quality appraisal revealed that 9 studies were of moderate quality, while 7 were of low quality, with common weaknesses including non-representative sampling, low response rates, unvalidated questionnaires, and recall bias. Only 5 studies were rated as higher quality.

The actual adherence to advice on reducing or rescheduling outdoor activities during poor air quality episodes was reported in 15 studies, with a wide range of adherence rates, from 9.7% to 57% (median = 31%). Notably, adherence tended to be lower in general-population samples (median = 27%) compared to samples of individuals with respiratory conditions (median = 41%), although this difference was not formally tested due to heterogeneity in measurement and reference periods. In some studies, fewer than one in five respondents reported modifying outdoor activity, as seen in surveys of Canadian adults aware of the Air Quality Health Index (McDermott et al., 2006; Radisic & Newbold, 2016). Adherence exceeded 50% only in one study of individuals with asthma who actively subscribed to an alert service (Wen et al., 2009).

The adherence to a wider range of protective behaviors was reported in 13 studies, including avoiding busy roads, closing windows, using air conditioning or air filters, wearing masks, and taking preventative or reliever medication. Adherence rates ranged from 17.7% to 98.1% (median = 46%), with the highest figure coming from a study conducted in heavily polluted urban settings where mask use or staying indoors was commonly reported. Indoor-based behaviors, such as closing windows and staying inside, were generally reported more often than behaviors that required spending money or changing routine, such as using a mask (typically below 25%) or changing commuting mode (below 15%). Among individuals with asthma, 25-60% reported adjusting medication use in response to alerts. The three studies that reported intended adherence found that 55-70% of respondents said they would change their behavior if an alert were issued, which was generally higher than the actual adherence reported in comparable populations.

Finally, six studies reported the proportion of people who had received or knew about alerts, with awareness ranging from 14% to 72% (median = 44%). Among those aware, a substantial proportion did not know what the alert meant or how to respond, highlighting the need for clear and effective communication of warning systems to promote adherence to protective behaviors. Overall, our findings highlight the complexities of promoting adherence to warning systems and the need for tailored approaches that take into account the specific needs and contexts of different populations. The interpretation of index values is a crucial aspect of air quality warning systems, yet the relationship between these values and adherence to recommended health advice is complex. A thorough examination of the existing literature reveals that demographic predictors, such as age and gender, do not consistently predict adherence. For instance, older age was associated with greater adherence in three studies, while in one study, it was linked to lower adherence, and in six studies, no association was found. Similarly, women were more likely to adhere to health advice in three studies, with odds ratios ranging from 1.3 to 2.1, whereas in six studies, no significant association was observed. Education and income, assessed in eight and six studies, respectively, were found to have significant associations in only two and one study, respectively, and these associations were in opposing directions.

In contrast, the presence of a chronic respiratory or cardiovascular condition emerged as a reliable demographic and clinical correlate of adherence. In six out of eight studies, individuals with such conditions were more likely to adhere to health advice, with odds ratios ranging from 1.5 to 3.4. This finding highlights the importance of considering the health status of individuals when designing air quality warning systems. Psychosocial predictors, examined in 16 studies, played a significant role in determining adherence. Knowing where to check air quality indices was a strong facilitator, with individuals who knew where to find this information being two to four times more likely to adhere to health advice. This finding is consistent with the idea that access to information is a critical factor in determining health behaviors.

Believing that one's symptoms were caused or worsened by air pollution was also associated with adherence in five out of six studies. Additionally, higher perceived severity of air pollution, including concern about its health effects, was linked to adherence in six out of eight studies. Receiving advice from a healthcare professional, such as a doctor or nurse, was another significant facilitator, with individuals who received such advice being more likely to modify their behavior. Other facilitators, such as perceived susceptibility, prior experience of symptoms during poor air quality, and perceived effectiveness of recommended behaviors, were reported less frequently.

However, several barriers to adherence were also identified. Lack of understanding of the indices, including confusion about numerical scales, color categories, and thresholds for action, was a common issue. Two studies found that exposure to general health messages, such as those emphasizing that air quality in the area was generally "good" or that the risk was confined to vulnerable groups, reduced both concern about air pollution and perceived personal susceptibility, leading to lower adherence. Low perceived self-efficacy or external locus of control, where individuals believed that they could not meaningfully reduce their exposure to air pollution, was reported in five studies. Reliance on sensory cues, such as visible haze, smell, or how the air feels, rather than official indices, was another barrier, with individuals often continuing normal activities when the air looked or smelled clean despite elevated index values.

The COM-B model, which posits that behavior arises from the interaction of capability, opportunity, and motivation, provides a useful framework for interpreting these findings. Capability factors, such as knowledge of where to find the indices and understanding of what they mean, were prominent barriers. Motivation factors, including symptom attribution, perceived severity, and susceptibility, self-efficacy, and locus of control, were also significant. Opportunity factors, such as lack of time and social and occupational constraints on changing routines, were reported in fewer studies. This systematic review highlights the complexity of factors influencing adherence to air quality warning systems and the need for a comprehensive approach that addresses capability, opportunity, and motivation.

The findings of this review have important implications for the design and implementation of air quality warning systems. By understanding the demographic and psychosocial factors associated with adherence and non-adherence, policymakers and healthcare professionals can develop targeted interventions to improve public health outcomes. For instance, providing clear and accessible information about air quality indices, as well as promoting awareness of the health effects of air pollution, could help to increase adherence to health advice. Additionally, addressing the barriers to adherence, such as low perceived self-efficacy and external locus of control, could help to empower individuals to take action to reduce their exposure to air pollution.

In conclusion, this systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the factors influencing adherence to air quality warning systems. By examining the demographic and psychosocial predictors of adherence, as well as the barriers to adherence, this review highlights the need for a nuanced and multifaceted approach to improving public health outcomes. By addressing the capability, opportunity, and motivation factors that influence adherence, policymakers and healthcare professionals can develop effective interventions to reduce the health impacts of air pollution. Ultimately, this review demonstrates the importance of considering the complex interplay of factors that influence health behaviors and the need for a comprehensive approach to promoting public health.

The production of speech is a complex process that involves a coordinated sequence of movements of the articulators, including the lips, jaw, tongue, velum, and larynx. As these articulators move, they continuously reshape the vocal tract, the airway that extends from the glottis to the lips, thereby modulating airflow and creating different resonant cavities. The time-varying shape of the vocal tract plays a crucial role in determining the acoustic properties of the speech signal, as demonstrated by Fant (1970) and Stevens (1998). Consequently, understanding the mapping between vocal tract geometry and acoustics remains a central problem in speech science, with significant implications for phonetics, speech technology, clinical assessment, and the study of language variation (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2016).

To tackle this problem, researchers have relied on various instrumentation techniques to observe articulation, including electromagnetic articulography, ultrasound, X-ray microbeam, and video of the face. While these methods provide valuable insights, they each capture only a partial view of the articulatory process, focusing on flesh-point trajectories, the tongue surface, or the external lips (Whalen et al., 2005; Stone, 2005). In contrast, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers a non-invasive and radiation-free means of visualizing the entire vocal tract, including regions such as the pharynx and velum that are difficult to access using other modalities. Recent advances in fast acquisition and reconstruction have made real-time MRI (rtMRI) of speech a practical reality, enabling the capture of dynamic articulation in the midsagittal plane during natural, continuous speech (Narayanan et al., 2004; Bresch et al., 2008; Lingala et al., 2016).

The availability of large rtMRI corpora, such as the USC-TIMIT database and related multi-speaker collections, has facilitated the quantitative study of articulation across many speakers (Narayanan et al., 2014). However, most computational work on rtMRI speech data has relied on hand-designed or semi-automatic representations of the vocal tract, including air-tissue boundary segmentation, cross-distance functions along the vocal tract midline, and region-of-interest time series that capture constriction formation at the lips, tongue tip, tongue body, and velum (Kim et al., 2014; Bresch & Narayanan, 2009; Proctor et al., 2010). While these representations are interpretable and have supported insights into coarticulation, compensatory articulation, and the composition of articulatory gestures (Browman & Goldstein, 1992), they require segmentation or parameterization pipelines that may be sensitive to image quality and speaker anatomy, and may discard information that is not captured by the chosen parameters.

A complementary approach is to learn representations directly from the image sequences, allowing the data to determine which spatial and temporal features are informative about the speech sounds being produced. Deep learning provides a powerful toolkit for this strategy, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learning hierarchical visual features and achieving strong results in image recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015; He et al., 2016). For video data, the challenge is to also model temporal dynamics, with approaches including 3D convolutions (Ji et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015), two-stream networks combining appearance and motion (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), and architectures that couple per-frame CNN features with recurrent networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) are a prominent example of the latter, where a CNN extracts deep visual features from each frame, and a recurrent layer integrates them over time, making the model deep in both space and time (Donahue et al., 2015).

While LRCN models have been successfully applied to action recognition, video description, and other sequence-learning tasks, and have also been used for visual speech recognition from lip images (Assael et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017), their application to rtMRI of the full vocal tract has received relatively little systematic attention. This gap in the existing literature is significant, as studies of automatic recognition from articulatory data have mostly used point-tracking measurements or lip-region video, or have used articulatory features as auxiliary inputs to acoustic recognizers (King et al., 2007; Hueber et al., 2010). Work that learns directly from the full midsagittal rtMRI video to identify speech content is limited, and it is not well understood how standard video-classification architectures behave on this kind of data.

One of the key challenges in applying LRCN models to rtMRI data is that vocal tract videos differ significantly from the natural-scene videos for which these architectures were designed. The images are grayscale, the spatial layout is highly constrained and consistent across frames, and the discriminative information lies in subtle, spatially localized constrictions and their timing rather than in large-scale object motion or scene context. Moreover, the sequences of interest, such as vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances, are short and the relevant dynamics are brief and coarticulated, so assumptions about the value of long temporal context or of pretrained appearance features may not carry over. It is therefore unclear whether design choices that benefit generic video and sequence classification, including network depth, recurrent configuration, and sequence length, transfer to speech.

This paper takes a step towards addressing this question by investigating whether speech content can be identified directly from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in rtMRI, using video action recognition techniques. We focus on identifying VCV sequences, which isolate consonant articulation in a controlled vowel context and are a standard probe of coarticulation and articulatory dynamics. Our approach involves formulating speech identification from rtMRI as a video classification problem and applying LRCN models to 2D rtMRI of VCV utterances from 17 speakers. We conduct a comparative evaluation of this class of models under various parameter settings and for several classification tasks, providing an empirical characterization of what matters for this data.

The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we demonstrate the feasibility of speech identification from rtMRI using LRCN models, which combines deep CNN feature extraction with recurrent sequence modeling. Second, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the performance of LRCN models under various parameter settings, including the CNN and recurrent components, and for several classification tasks. Third, we report that model behavior in speech classification differs markedly from that in generic sequence or video classification tasks, which suggests that architectures and training practices developed for natural video should be adapted for articulatory imaging. Together, these findings inform the design of data-driven models linking vocal tract shape geometry to speech acoustics, and highlight the need for further research into the application of deep learning techniques to rtMRI data. The study of vocal tract dynamics and speech production has long been a topic of interest in the field of linguistics and speech science. Recent advances in real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) have provided a unique opportunity to examine the articulatory movements of the vocal tract during speech production. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the acoustic mapping from articulation using a database of 2D rtMRI images of the midsagittal vocal tract acquired from 17 native speakers of American English. The database consists of vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences, which provide a rich source of information on the dynamics of speech production.

The image acquisition protocol followed established procedures (Narayanan et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2014), where participants lay supine in a scanner and a fast spiral gradient-echo sequence was used to image a single midsagittal slice that covered the lips, tongue, velum, larynx, and pharyngeal wall. The reconstructed image sequences had a temporal resolution of approximately 20-25 frames per second and a spatial resolution of a few millimeters per pixel. The images were stored as grayscale video and were accompanied by simultaneous audio recordings, which were used to segment the utterances. The audio signals were denoised using a noise-cancelling optical microphone and a denoising algorithm (Bresch et al., 2006), but were not used as input to any classifier.

Each speaker produced a set of VCV tokens with a symmetric vowel context, where the same vowel precedes and follows the consonant. The inventory of consonants spanned stops, nasals, fricatives, and approximants, and was crossed with the corner vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/. Each token was repeated several times in a carrier-free, isolated manner, and individual tokens were cut from the continuous recording using the acoustic signal. The clips were manually checked for visible motion artifacts, incomplete articulations, or acquisition failures, and tokens with such issues were discarded. The remaining clips were labeled with their VCV identity, consonant, and vowel context.

Preprocessing of the images involved cropping the frames to a fixed region of interest around the vocal tract, resizing them to 224 × 224 pixels using bilinear interpolation, and replicating them across three channels to facilitate the use of ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks (Deng et al., 2009). The intensities were normalized per speaker by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, which reduced inter-speaker differences in coil sensitivity and overall brightness. To account for variations in speaking rate, each clip was converted to a fixed length of T frames, with longer clips being uniformly subsampled and shorter clips being padded by repeating the last frame. The value of T was treated as a design parameter.

The main model used in this study was a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN; Donahue et al., 2015), which consists of a convolutional network that processes each frame independently and yields a fixed-length feature vector, followed by a recurrent network that maps the sequence of feature vectors to class probabilities. The convolutional network used was VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015), and the recurrent network was a long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The final hidden state of the LSTM network was fed to a softmax layer, and dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) was applied before the recurrent and output layers.

To place the LRCN results in context, we trained three reference models on the same splits: a frame-wise CNN that ignores temporal order, a late-fusion CNN that concatenates features over time (Karpathy et al., 2014), and a 3D convolutional network that learns joint spatiotemporal filters (Tran et al., 2015). These reference models allowed us to examine whether explicit sequence modeling is necessary to capture the dynamics of speech production.

The experimental design involved defining three classification tasks: VCV identification, consonant classification, and vowel classification. In the VCV identification task, the model predicted the full VCV label, requiring the inference of both the consonant and vowel context. In the consonant classification task, clips from all vowel contexts were pooled and labeled only by the consonant, requiring invariance to the surrounding vowel. In the vowel classification task, clips were labeled by vowel context regardless of consonant. For each task, we varied several parameters, including clip length T, the number of LSTM units and layers, the CNN backbone, initialization, and recurrence direction.

To estimate generalization to unseen speakers, we used speaker-independent evaluation, where the 17 speakers were partitioned into folds for cross-validation. In each fold, a subset of the remaining speakers was held out as a validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, and no test speaker data influenced model selection. We also ran a speaker-dependent condition, where tokens from every speaker were split across training and test sets by repetition, to quantify the gap caused by inter-speaker variability in vocal tract anatomy. Networks were trained by minimizing categorical cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015), and the initial learning rate was set to 1e-4 for pretrained layers and 1e-3 for newly initialized layers.

Overall, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the acoustic mapping from articulation using rtMRI images of the vocal tract. The results of this study have implications for our understanding of speech production and the development of speech recognition systems. By examining the dynamics of speech production in a detailed and systematic manner, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between articulation, acoustics, and perception. The experimental setup involved training deep learning models on a dataset of real-time MRI (rtMRI) images of the vocal tract, with the goal of identifying consonant and vowel sounds. To mitigate overfitting, we employed several regularization techniques, including weight decay and early stopping with a patience of 10 epochs. We also used mini-batches of 16 clips and monitored per-class performance to ensure that the models were not biased towards any particular class. The models were implemented in a standard deep learning framework and trained on a single GPU, with each configuration run multiple times with different random seeds to account for any variability in the results.

In terms of statistical analysis, we used classification accuracy on the held-out speakers as our primary metric, as well as macro-averaged F1 scores to guard against class-specific effects. We reported results as mean ± standard deviation across cross-validation folds and seeds, and examined confusion matrices aggregated over folds to characterize systematic confusions, such as those among consonants sharing a place of articulation. To assess differences between model configurations, we used paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, depending on the normality of the data, and adjusted p-values for multiple comparisons using the Holm-Bonferroni procedure. When comparing two classifiers on the same test clips, we used McNemar's test. We considered a difference to be significant if the adjusted p-value was less than 0.05.

Our experiments involved a 5-fold cross-validation setup, in which the 17 speakers in the rtMRI corpus were partitioned such that no test speaker appeared in training. Each fold was repeated with three random initializations, and we reported mean ± standard deviation. We evaluated our models on three tasks: consonant identification from the VCV clip (C-task, 8 classes), vowel-context identification (V-task, 3 classes), and joint identification of the full VCV token (VCV-task, 24 classes). The chance levels for these tasks were 12.5%, 33.3%, and 4.2%, respectively.

As a baseline, we used a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN) with a VGG-16 encoder pretrained on ImageNet, a single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units, and 20 frames per clip sampled uniformly. This model achieved 71.4 ± 2.8% on the C-task, 88.9 ± 1.9% on the V-task, and 63.7 ± 3.1% on the VCV-task. Notably, the vowel context was recognized much more reliably than the intervening consonant, consistent with the larger and more sustained tongue and jaw displacements of vowels in midsagittal images. Most joint-task errors came from consonant confusions, with only 7.9% of VCV errors involving an incorrect vowel with a correct consonant.

We also investigated the effect of the visual feature extractor on our models' performance. In a series of table-level comparisons across encoders, we found a pattern that differed from generic action recognition. With the LSTM fixed, the pretrained VGG-16 reached 71.4% on the C-task, while a ResNet-50 achieved 70.2 ± 3.0%, and a small four-layer CNN trained from scratch reached 72.6 ± 2.6%. The differences among these three were within one standard deviation and not significant. The VCV-task showed the same ordering, with the VGG-16 achieving 63.7%, the ResNet-50 achieving 62.5%, and the small CNN achieving 64.9%. These results suggest that deeper hierarchical features did not provide a significant benefit, even though they typically yield large gains on benchmarks like UCF-101.

Fine-tuning the pretrained backbones raised C-task accuracy by only 1.1 points for the VGG-16, whereas freezing them lowered it to 66.8 ± 3.3%. This suggests that ImageNet features transfer only partially to grayscale, single-view articulatory images. We also explored the effect of the recurrent configuration on our models' performance. Increasing the LSTM hidden size from 64 to 128, 256, and 512 units produced C-task accuracies of 67.9%, 70.1%, 71.4%, and 71.0%, indicating that performance saturated at around 256 units. Stacking two LSTM layers gave a negligible change, while a third layer reduced accuracy to 69.5% with higher variance. Bidirectional LSTMs provided a modest gain, which is plausible given that VCV identity depends on both the closing and releasing gestures around the consonant.

Replacing the LSTM with a GRU gave 71.0%, which was statistically indistinguishable from the LSTM. Notably, a frame-level baseline that averaged CNN features over time with no recurrence reached 64.3 ± 3.4% on the C-task. The recurrent layer thus contributed around 7 points, and 9 points when bidirectional, confirming that temporal ordering carries information beyond static posture. However, this benefit is smaller than the typical gap between frame-averaging and recurrent models in generic video classification.

We also investigated the effect of temporal sampling on our models' performance. Varying the number of frames per clip from 8 to 30, with a median of 46 at the native frame rate, produced C-task accuracies that plateaued at around 20-30 frames. Using all frames lowered accuracy and increased training time by 2.1×. Clips subsampled non-uniformly, with higher density around the consonantal constriction, achieved 74.1 ± 2.6% with 20 frames. This suggests that where frames are placed matters more than how many are used, in contrast to generic action recognition, where longer clips usually improve accuracy.

Furthermore, we examined the effect of spatial input and speaker variability on our models' performance. Cropping the image to a region around the vocal tract improved C-task accuracy from 71.4% to 74.8 ± 2.4%, suggesting that background and shoulder pixels are distracting. Intensity normalization per speaker added another 1.6 points, resulting in an accuracy of 76.4%. Per-speaker accuracy on the C-task ranged from 58.2% to 85.7%, with the weakest speakers being those with the lowest signal-to-noise ratios or atypical head positioning. Adding data augmentation, including random shifts, rotations, and brightness jitter, raised the mean to 78.0 ± 2.2%. However, temporal augmentation by speed perturbation reduced accuracy to 75.9%, suggesting that articulatory timing itself is discriminative.

Finally, we analyzed the per-class behavior and confusions of our models. In the best configuration, which included a bidirectional LSTM, cropped and normalized input, augmentation, and targeted sampling, accuracies were 80.3 ± 2.1% on the C-task, 91.6 ± 1.5% on the V-task, and 70.8 ± 2.9% on the VCV-task. Per-consonant F1 scores were highest for the bilabial /p/ and the velar /k/, which have visually salient closures, and lowest for the alveolar pair /t/-/d/. Confusion matrices showed that 64% of errors involved consonants that share a place of articulation, highlighting the challenges of distinguishing between similar sounds in the vocal tract. Overall, our results demonstrate the potential of deep learning models for articulatory feature recognition from rtMRI images, and highlight the importance of carefully designing the visual feature extractor, recurrent configuration, and temporal sampling strategy to optimize performance. The analysis of consonant errors reveals an intriguing pattern, where voicing counterparts with the same place and manner of articulation, such as /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, or /s/ and /z/, are frequently confused. This is not entirely unexpected, given that voicing is primarily controlled at the glottis, a feature that is not well-represented in midsagittal images. When these voicing pairs are merged into a single class, the accuracy of the C-task increases substantially, from 80.3% to 90.2% ± 1.7%. In contrast, errors related to place of articulation account for only 21% of the remaining confusions. These findings highlight the challenges of modeling speech articulation using visual data.

A comparison with generic video benchmarks reveals a notable divergence in the performance of different architectural components. While pretrained depth, longer clips, and larger recurrent stacks typically yield improvements in generic sequence classification, they provide little to no benefit in this context. Instead, compact encoders, tight spatial cropping, and a short, well-targeted temporal window prove to be more effective. This suggests that the visual cues present in articulatory data are distinct from those found in generic video classification tasks.

The present study investigates the ability of action-recognition architectures, specifically Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN), to identify vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences from dynamic vocal tract shaping in 2D real-time MRI (rtMRI). The main finding is that these models can extract linguistically meaningful information from articulatory video, but their behavior differs significantly from what is typically reported for generic video classification. The differences lie in the architectural components that contribute to performance, the importance of temporal context, and the types of classes that are confused.

In generic video classification benchmarks, such as UCF-101, the performance of CNN-RNN hybrids is often driven by appearance cues, including scene context, objects, and body pose. The recurrent layer adds a relatively modest gain by aggregating frame-level evidence. In contrast, vocal tract rtMRI offers none of these cues, as every frame shows the same anatomy in the same view. The class information lies in small, continuous deformations of the tongue, lips, velum, and larynx, as well as the timing of constrictions relative to one another. As a result, a deep visual extractor must be sensitive to subtle contour displacements, rather than object-level semantics.

This difference in visual cues may explain why features transferred from natural-image pretraining, which are strong for generic action recognition, are less advantageous in this context. The transferability of features declines as the source and target domains diverge, and grayscale mid-sagittal tissue boundaries are far removed from ImageNet statistics. We interpret the performance gap between speech and generic video tasks as largely a domain-mismatch effect, combined with the fact that the discriminative signal is spatially localized and low in contrast.

The temporal dimension also behaves differently in speech compared to generic video classification. In generic video, a few sampled frames are often sufficient to identify an action, whereas in speech, the identity of a VCV token depends on the timing of constrictions and the surrounding vowels. This coarticulatory structure, described by Öhman (1966) and formalized as overlapping gestures in articulatory phonology (Browman & Goldstein, 1992), means that the same consonant can produce different image sequences in different vowel contexts, while different consonants can share similar vowel transitions.

A model that relies on frame-level appearance will thus confuse tokens whose articulatory differences are brief and local, such as place contrasts among consonants formed with similar tongue-body configurations. Recurrent modeling is useful in principle, but its benefit depends on the quality of the per-frame representation and the frame rate and clip length being adequate to capture short constriction events. Our comparisons across parameter settings, such as sequence length and recurrent configuration, are consistent with this picture, suggesting that sensitivity to temporal sampling is greater than is typical in generic action recognition.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the database contains 17 speakers, which is large by rtMRI standards but small by deep learning standards. Inter-speaker differences in vocal tract anatomy, head position, and speaking style add variability that a small cohort cannot fully capture. Performance under speaker-independent evaluation is the more relevant measure of generalization, and it should be interpreted cautiously, as individual speakers may still be partly memorized by high-capacity networks.

Second, the data are 2D mid-sagittal images acquired at limited frame rates, which omits lateral channel shaping, such as the grooving involved in sibilants and lateral approximants, and some of the spatial detail in the oral cavity and pharynx. Temporal blurring at the frame rates used may also obscure rapid events like stop releases and taps. Third, VCV tokens are controlled, read stimuli, which isolate consonantal gestures cleanly but are far from continuous, spontaneous speech, in which reduction, prosodic modulation, and long-range coarticulation make the mapping from shape to phonetic identity less direct.

Fourth, we evaluated classification of discrete, pre-segmented tokens, which sidesteps the problems of segmentation and alignment that any practical system would face. Finally, we did not systematically compare against architectures that learn spatiotemporal features jointly, such as 3D convolutions or inflated two-stream networks, nor against explicit articulatory representations such as segmented contours or region-of-interest time series. These alternatives could change the relative conclusions.

Despite these caveats, the findings have several implications. For speech science, the ability of a general-purpose video model to separate VCV classes supports the view that vocal tract shape dynamics contain rich, learnable information about linguistic content. Analyzing which classes are confused and which image regions drive decisions could provide data-driven evidence on which articulators and time points are most informative for particular contrasts, complementing the hypothesis-driven analyses typical of articulatory phonetics.

For speech technology, the results represent a modest step toward mapping vocal tract geometry to acoustics. They resemble work on visual speech recognition from lip video and on articulatory-to-acoustic mapping from ultrasound and other modalities, but they use a view of the full vocal tract that includes the internal articulators. Such mappings could support silent-speech interfaces, assessment of disordered speech production, and articulatory-informed acoustic modeling. Methodologically, the contrast with generic video classification suggests that architectures and pretraining strategies should be designed for articulatory data instead of being imported unchanged. Promising directions include developing models that can capture the spatial and temporal nuances of vocal tract shaping, as well as exploring the use of multimodal data, such as audio and video, to improve the accuracy and robustness of speech recognition systems.

Phylogeography, the study of the processes that shape the geographic distribution of genealogical lineages, has become a crucial tool for understanding the emergence, dispersal, and diversification of pathogens across space and time. In the context of rapidly evolving organisms, such as RNA viruses, where evolutionary and epidemiological timescales overlap, phylogeographic analysis enables researchers to reconstruct the complex dynamics of disease transmission. This is particularly important for infectious diseases like influenza A, rabies, HIV-1, Ebola, and SARS-CoV-2, where the ability to track the movement of pathogens is essential for effective surveillance, control, and prevention.

Bayesian phylogeographic frameworks, which treat location as a discrete trait evolving along a phylogeny, have been successfully applied to various viral systems. These approaches rely on the analysis of genetic sequences, often obtained from public databases like GenBank, to infer the origins and spread of pathogens. However, the accuracy of these analyses depends critically on the quality of the geographic information associated with each sampled sequence. Unfortunately, the metadata provided with GenBank records, such as country, isolation source, and geolocation name, are often incomplete, inaccurate, or lacking in sufficient detail.

The limitations of GenBank metadata are well-documented. Submitters may omit crucial information, provide only country-level data, or enter free-text values that vary widely in format and granularity. Moreover, country-level resolution is frequently inadequate for modeling the transmission of viruses within a country or between neighboring regions. For instance, understanding the spread of a virus between provinces, cities, or even individual farms requires location data at a much finer scale. Furthermore, the country listed in a GenBank record may reflect the location of the sequencing laboratory rather than the origin of the host, and for viruses sampled from migratory animals or travelers, the place of infection may differ from the place of sampling.

Several studies have highlighted the importance of location granularity and accuracy in phylogeographic analyses. The choice of location scale and the precision of assigned locations can substantially alter inferred migration networks and root-location estimates. When metadata are insufficient, researchers often turn to the publications linked to GenBank records, which may provide more detailed information about the sampling campaign. However, extracting this information manually is a time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult-to-reproduce process, particularly for studies involving hundreds or thousands of sequences drawn from many articles.

Automating the extraction of geographic locations from text offers a promising solution to this problem. The computational task of recognizing place names in text, known as toponym recognition, is a crucial step in geographic information retrieval. Toponym recognition is conventionally treated as a form of named entity recognition (NER) and addressed using sequence labeling models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) and neural architectures. However, general-purpose NER systems often perform poorly on biomedical text, where geographic names are intermingled with names of strains, genes, hosts, and institutions that share surface forms with places.

The scarcity of annotated data for toponym recognition in virology articles is a significant obstacle. Manual annotation of geographic mentions requires domain expertise and is costly, making it impractical for large-scale analyses. Distant supervision, which generates training labels automatically by aligning an existing knowledge base with unlabelled text, offers an alternative. However, the use of weak labels derived from existing database records, such as GenBank metadata and gazetteers like GeoNames, is inherently noisy and may not provide the same level of accuracy as fully supervised models.

Two key gaps remain in the development of methods for extracting fine-grained geographic locations from the literature for virus phylogeography. First, there is no established method tailored to the peculiarities of virus-related articles, such as strain nomenclature, sampling descriptions, and host-related terminology. Second, it is unclear whether weak supervision derived from existing database records can approximate the accuracy of fully supervised models, thereby removing the annotation bottleneck. To address these gaps, we ask two questions: (i) to what extent can a supervised sequence labeling model with features tailored to virology articles detect geographic location mentions, and (ii) can a distant supervision approach, using weak labels derived from existing database records, achieve comparable accuracy to fully supervised models? Answering these questions is essential for developing more precise and scalable phylogeographic analyses, which can inform infectious disease surveillance, control, and prevention.

In an effort to address this question, our research makes several key contributions. Firstly, we present a supervised CRF-based sequence labelling approach that incorporates a range of innovative features designed to capture the lexical, syntactic, and document-level context of place names in virus-related articles. These features include those that help to distinguish sampling locations from places embedded in strain names or other entities, thereby improving the accuracy of our model. 

Our approach is based on a comprehensive understanding of the complexities involved in identifying sampling locations in scientific articles. We recognize that sampling locations are often reported in specific sections of an article, such as the Methods section, and that they can be embedded in strain names or other entities. To address these challenges, we have developed a range of features that take into account the context in which a place name appears. For example, our document-structure features encode the section type of the sentence in which a place name appears, while our sampling-context features flag trigger words that are commonly associated with sampling locations.

In addition to our supervised approach, we also introduce a distant supervision approach that derives training labels from GenBank metadata and gazetteer entries. This approach is designed to reduce the cost and time associated with manual annotation, while still achieving high accuracy. To filter out ambiguous and spurious matches, we propose novel noise-reduction methods that can be applied before model training. These methods include the use of logarithmic binning to capture the number of times a candidate string occurs in an article, as well as the use of document-level consistency features to capture the consistency of a candidate string across an article.

To evaluate the performance of both our supervised and distant supervision approaches, we compare them against a manually annotated gold standard of articles linked to virus-related GenBank records. Our results show that our supervised approach achieves an F-score of 0.81, while our distant supervision approach achieves an F-score of 0.66 without using manual annotations for training. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches in identifying sampling locations in scientific articles.

One of the key strengths of our research is the comprehensive dataset that we have constructed. Our dataset consists of 600 articles, stratified by virus family to ensure that no family contributes more than 20% of the sample. This prevents highly sequenced groups, such as influenza viruses and retroviruses, from dominating the data. We have also divided our dataset into a manually annotated gold-standard set, a development set, and a pool of articles used for distant-supervision training data. The gold-standard set consists of 150 articles that have been manually annotated by two trained annotators, with disagreements resolved by consensus with a third annotator, a virologist.

Our annotation guidelines are based on a clear distinction between toponym recognition and the more general task of geoparsing. We annotate every mention of a geographic location that refers to the place of origin of an infected host or of a viral isolate, including countries, administrative regions, cities, villages, and named natural features such as lakes. However, we do not annotate locations that appear only as part of a laboratory or institution name, locations used as adjectives in strain nomenclature without a sampling interpretation, or locations mentioned only in the context of prior literature.

In terms of our supervised sequence labelling approach, we treat the detection of sampling locations as a sequence labelling problem and train a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) implemented in CRFsuite. We estimate parameters using L-BFGS optimization with elastic-net regularization, and tune the L1 and L2 coefficients on the development set. Our baseline feature set is standard for named entity recognition, and includes features such as the lowercase token, lemma, prefixes and suffixes, word shape, capitalization, and part-of-speech tag. We also add membership features derived from a gazetteer built from GeoNames, as well as four feature groups designed specifically for the virological domain.

Our feature groups include document-structure features, sampling-context features, strain-name features, and document-level consistency features. We perform feature ablation on the development set by removing each group in turn, and evaluate the impact on performance. Our results show that each feature group contributes significantly to the accuracy of our model, and that the combination of all feature groups achieves the highest F-score.
