The process of identifying sampling locations in article text began with a straightforward, case-insensitive match of a seed string, which was then labeled as a sampling location, while all other tokens were marked as outside. A conditional random field (CRF) with the same baseline feature set was subsequently trained on these labels. However, this heuristic labeling approach is inherently noisy, prompting the development of three distinct noise-reduction methods, which were evaluated both individually and in combination. 

The first method, ambiguity filtering, involved removing seed strings that coincided with common English words or personal names. This was achieved by examining the frequency of the lowercase form of a string in a background corpus of 50,000 PubMed Central articles, as well as its GeoNames entry, to determine if it shared a name with a more populous non-location entity. For instance, a string like "Georgia" might be removed if it was found to be commonly used as a personal name or as a reference to a non-geographic entity.

The second approach, context-based filtering, retained a match only if the sentence contained at least one sampling-context trigger word, such as "isolated from" or "collected in," or if the match occurred in a Methods section or table caption. This strategy effectively reduced false positives arising from literature review passages, where geographic locations are often mentioned in a non-sampling context. By incorporating this contextual information, the model was able to better distinguish between relevant and irrelevant mentions of geographic locations.

The third method, frequency-based reweighting, assigned each seed string a weight inversely related to the proportion of its document occurrences that were matched outside sampling contexts. This was estimated using an expectation-maximization procedure over the pool of articles. Instances with weights below a certain threshold, set at 0.2 based on the development set, were relabeled as outside. This approach allowed the model to adapt to the varying frequencies of different seed strings and to reduce the impact of noisy labels.

To provide a comprehensive evaluation, both approaches were compared to two baselines: a gazetteer-only system that labels the longest GeoNames match, and the pretrained Stanford named entity recognizer with its LOCATION label. Neither of these baselines utilizes domain-specific training data, making them useful points of comparison for the proposed methods. 

The evaluation of all systems was conducted on a 150-article gold standard, which was annotated by human experts to provide a high-quality reference point. For the supervised model, 10-fold cross-validation was employed at the article level, with folds fixed across all comparisons to prevent sentences from the same article being split between training and test sets. In contrast, the distant-supervision models were trained once on the automatically labeled pool and then tested on the full gold standard. The performance metrics used included precision, recall, and F1, calculated under both exact-match and lenient (overlap) matching conditions. Scores were micro-averaged over all entities to provide a comprehensive overview of system performance.

To estimate the confidence intervals for F1, a nonparametric bootstrap over articles was used, with 1,000 resamples. Differences between systems were tested using approximate randomization, with 10,000 article-level shuffles, and results were considered significant at a two-sided P-value of less than 0.05 after Holm correction for multiple comparisons. This rigorous evaluation framework allowed for a detailed assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

Furthermore, performance was stratified by virus family and section type to examine the robustness of the models across different contexts. Error analysis was also conducted manually on a random sample of 100 false positives and 100 false negatives from each system, with errors categorized by cause, such as ambiguity, nested or abbreviated locations, and unlisted locations. This analysis provided valuable insights into the types of errors made by each system and highlighted areas for future improvement.

The manually annotated gold standard comprised 305 full-text articles linked to virus-related GenBank records, containing 6,412 toponym mentions annotated as geographic locations of infected hosts or sampling sites. Inter-annotator agreement, measured on a doubly annotated subset of 60 articles, was high, with a Cohen's κ of 0.88 and a pairwise F-score of 0.91. This level of agreement is consistent with that reported for comparable biomedical named-entity annotation tasks, indicating the high quality of the annotations.

The characteristics of the annotated corpus revealed that 71.4% of the mentions were country-level, 19.8% were province- or state-level, and 8.8% were finer-grained (city, village, or farm). Notably, only 38.2% of the annotated locations were recoverable from the GenBank "country" field of the associated records, highlighting the insufficiency of existing metadata for a majority of mentions. This finding is in line with earlier assessments of GenBank geographic annotations, which have consistently shown that the available metadata is often incomplete or inaccurate.

The supervised sequence labeling approach, implemented as a linear-chain CRF, was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation at the article level. A baseline CRF using only lexical features achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.68, and F-score of 0.72. The addition of part-of-speech and chunk features improved the F-score to 0.74, while the inclusion of gazetteer-derived features increased recall markedly, from 0.68 to 0.76, with a smaller gain in precision, yielding an F-score of 0.77. The innovative features introduced in this study, including section-based and trigger-term-based features, as well as word-embedding cluster features, yielded the largest additional gains, with the full feature set producing a precision of 0.85, recall of 0.78, and an F-score of 0.81.

The improvement over the lexical baseline was statistically significant, with a paired bootstrap test yielding a p-value of less than 0.001. Performance varied by granularity, with the F-score for country-level mentions being 0.87, compared to 0.76 for province- or state-level mentions and 0.58 for fine-grained mentions. Recall for mentions in tables and figure captions was substantially lower, at 0.52, than for running text, at 0.81, reflecting the unconventional formatting of tabular content after text extraction.

In contrast, the distant supervision approach generated training labels automatically by aligning article text with the geographic metadata of linked GenBank records, without manual annotation. Applied to 41,870 articles, the raw alignment yielded 187,300 candidate positive mentions. Training a CRF directly on these labels, without noise reduction, resulted in a precision of 0.49, recall of 0.64, and F-score of 0.56 on the gold standard. Manual inspection of 500 randomly selected automatically labeled mentions indicated that 31.6% were erroneous, most commonly due to a location appearing in the record matching non-geographic or irrelevant uses.

The application of the three noise-reduction methods, first individually and then in combination, resulted in significant improvements in performance. Excluding mentions in the title page, affiliations, and reference sections (positional filtering) increased precision to 0.57, while ambiguity filtering and frequency-based reweighting further improved performance. The combination of these methods yielded the best results, with a precision of 0.63, recall of 0.71, and F-score of 0.67. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed noise-reduction methods in improving the accuracy of the distant supervision approach.

Overall, the results of this study demonstrate the potential of both supervised and distant supervision approaches for identifying sampling locations in biomedical text. While the supervised approach achieved higher performance, the distant supervision approach offers a promising alternative for large-scale annotation tasks, particularly when combined with effective noise-reduction methods. Future work will focus on further improving the accuracy and efficiency of these approaches, as well as exploring their application to other domains and tasks. The geographic metadata associated with GenBank records are often too coarse to support fine-grained spatial inference, a significant bottleneck in virus phylogeography. To address this limitation, we evaluated two strategies for automatically recognizing geographic location mentions in linked articles. Our first approach employed a supervised conditional random field (CRF) sequence labeler, which leveraged domain-motivated features to achieve an F-score of 0.81, with a precision of 0.85 and recall of 0.78, on a manually annotated gold standard. In contrast, a distant-supervision approach, trained without manual annotation and utilizing novel noise-reduction steps, yielded an F-score of 0.66, with a precision of 0.69 and recall of 0.63. While both results are meaningful for downstream use, they differ significantly in terms of cost and error profiles.

To improve the performance of the distant supervision model, we explored several methods for reducing label noise. One approach involved filtering ambiguous toponyms through a disambiguation step, which removed candidate matches whose surrounding context was inconsistent with a geographic sense. This step resulted in a precision of 0.58 and an F-score of 0.61. Another method utilized a bootstrapped relabeling procedure, in which an initial model was used to re-score training instances and discard those with a posterior probability below 0.3. This approach produced a precision of 0.60 and an F-score of 0.62. Combining all three methods resulted in the best-performing distant supervision model, with a precision of 0.69, recall of 0.63, and F-score of 0.66 (95% CI: 0.64–0.68). Notably, this corresponded to a reduction in estimated label noise from 31.6% to 13.2% in the manual inspection sample, and an absolute F-score improvement of 0.10 over the unfiltered distant supervision system (p < 0.001).

A comparison of the two approaches revealed that the supervised model outperformed the best distant supervision model by 0.15 F-score points (0.81 versus 0.66; p < 0.001), primarily due to higher precision (0.85 versus 0.69) and recall (0.78 versus 0.63). However, the distant supervision system required no manual annotation, making it an attractive option when annotated data are scarce. Learning curves showed that the supervised model's F-score reached 0.74 with 50 training articles and 0.79 with 150 articles, approaching its plateau at approximately 250 articles. In contrast, the distant supervision model trained on all 41,870 articles exceeded the performance of the supervised model trained on 25 articles (0.66 versus 0.63), suggesting that the approach is a viable alternative when annotated data are unavailable.

We also explored the potential benefits of combining the two approaches, by pretraining on distantly labeled data and then fine-tuning on gold-standard data. This resulted in a modest additional improvement in a post hoc experiment with small training sets (F-score of 0.77 with 50 annotated articles, versus 0.74 for supervised training alone), although the benefit disappeared with more than 200 annotated articles. Both systems outperformed a rule-based baseline that tagged all gazetteer matches as locations (precision 0.31, recall 0.83, F-score 0.45), and a baseline based on the Stanford named-entity recognizer (Finkel et al., 2005) using its default location class (precision 0.66, recall 0.61, F-score 0.63). The supervised model's advantage over the Stanford recognizer was significant (p < 0.001), whereas the difference between the Stanford recognizer and the distant supervision approach was not (p = 0.18).

An error analysis of 300 randomly sampled errors from the supervised system revealed that 41% were false negatives involving fine-grained or uncommon place names absent from the gazetteer, 23% were false positives in which a location unrelated to host sampling was labeled, 19% were boundary errors in multiword names, and 17% resulted from annotation ambiguity or abbreviations. In contrast, the distant supervision system's errors were primarily caused by noisy training labels (47%) and incomplete labeling of locations not listed in the GenBank metadata (29%). These findings highlight the importance of addressing label noise and improving the coverage of gazetteers in order to enhance the performance of distant supervision models.

The 15-point F-score advantage of the supervised model is consistent with the general pattern that models trained on high-quality, in-domain annotations outperform those trained on automatically derived labels (Mintz et al., 2009; Ratner et al., 2017). Much of the gain appears to come from features that capture how locations are reported in virology articles, which differs from newswire, the genre on which general-purpose named entity recognizers are usually trained (Finkel et al., 2005). In methods sections and sequence-submission descriptions, locations often appear in compact forms such as strain designations, sampling-site lists, and parenthetical provenance statements. Contextual and gazetteer-informed features capture these patterns better than surface orthography alone, a known weakness of off-the-shelf taggers in biomedical text (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008).

The distant-supervision result is more modest in absolute terms but more notable given that it required no manual labeling. Distant supervision is attractive because it uses existing resources, here GenBank geographic fields and gazetteers, to generate training labels at scale. However, its main liability is label noise, which can be mitigated through noise-reduction methods. The precision of 0.70 suggests that most retained labels were correct, although the lower recall of 0.63 indicates that the approach is conservative and tends to miss locations that are not already represented in the metadata or gazetteer.

Our error analysis points to three recurring failure sources. First, ambiguity between geographic and non-geographic uses of place names, such as eponymous viruses and strains, and institutional affiliations, produced most false positives in both systems. Second, nested and compound expressions caused boundary errors, which strict span matching penalizes heavily. Third, historical or colloquial place names and abbreviations were poorly covered by gazetteers, reducing distant-supervision recall in particular. Because our evaluation counted only exact matches, the reported scores are probably conservative estimates of practical utility, since a researcher may still find value in a system that returns near-misses or related locations.

Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of both supervised and distant supervision approaches for automatically recognizing geographic location mentions in linked articles. While the supervised model outperformed the distant supervision model, the latter's ability to operate without manual annotation makes it an attractive option when annotated data are scarce. By addressing label noise and improving the coverage of gazetteers, it is possible to enhance the performance of distant supervision models and make them more effective in supporting fine-grained spatial inference in virus phylogeography.

The dissemination of scientific knowledge has traditionally relied on a limited number of channels, including printed journals, scientific meetings, and, more recently, journal websites and indexing databases. However, over the past decade, social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have emerged as important tools for disseminating research, with many medical journals now maintaining active accounts and sizable followings. The underlying assumption driving this trend is straightforward: by posting a brief message and link to a new article, journals can increase exposure to readers who might not have encountered the work otherwise, thereby boosting page views, downloads, and ultimately, citations.

This assumption is intuitive, and editors, publishers, and professional societies have largely embraced it, with social media activity now a standard component of the publication process for many journals, including those in cardiovascular medicine. Studies have consistently shown that articles mentioned on Twitter or other social platforms tend to accumulate more views, downloads, and citations than those that are not mentioned. For instance, research by Eysenbach, Shuai et al., and Fox et al. has demonstrated a positive association between social media attention and various metrics of article impact. These findings have, in turn, fueled the development of alternative metrics, which aggregate online attention to research outputs and are increasingly displayed alongside traditional bibliometric indicators.

However, it is essential to note that these associations are susceptible to confounding, as articles that attract social media attention may differ systematically from those that do not. For example, they may address topics of broad public interest, originate from well-known investigators or institutions with large online followings, or be more novel or clinically important. Furthermore, readers who encounter an article through social media may already be inclined to read it, which can further complicate the interpretation of observational comparisons. To address these limitations, randomization offers a more robust approach, allowing researchers to separate the causal effect of social media promotion from the characteristics of the articles and authors selected for promotion.

A previous randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation allocated original research articles to social media exposure or no exposure and compared 30-day page views between the groups. Although the investigators found no significant difference in page views between the arms, this result was somewhat surprising, given the favorable associations observed in observational studies. A subsequent trial in a different setting reported similar findings, suggesting that the null result was not unique to a single journal. However, the Circulation trial left an important question unresolved: whether the lack of effect reflected an intervention that was too weak to produce a measurable change or a true absence of benefit from social media exposure at any level of intensity.

This distinction is crucial, both scientifically and practically. If a light-touch approach fails due to inadequate intensity, then journals might reasonably expect that a more concerted effort would succeed, justifying the resources devoted to expanding followings and repeating posts. In contrast, if a more intensive strategy also fails to change readership, the case for social media as a driver of article traffic becomes considerably weaker, and journals may need to reconsider their expectations or goals. The importance of considering a dose-response perspective is well recognized in the evaluation of behavioral and communication interventions, where a negative trial of a low-intensity program is generally not considered sufficient to rule out the value of a more substantial one.

Social media campaigns in health are inherently heterogeneous, varying in reach, frequency, and engagement, and the effect of exposure is likely to depend on factors such as audience size and engagement, content delivery frequency, and algorithmic or paid amplification. Several features of platform behavior make intensity a plausible determinant of effect. For instance, on Twitter, the lifespan of an individual post is short, and a message may be seen by only a fraction of followers in the narrow window during which it is visible. On Facebook, organic reach to followers is limited, and paid promotion can substantially extend the audience of a post. Repeating messages at different times of day can increase the likelihood of being seen, and retweets by the journal account can extend visibility further. A larger follower base provides a larger potential audience for each of these actions.

In light of these considerations, we conducted a second randomized controlled trial at Circulation to determine whether a more intensive social media strategy increases 30-day page views of original research articles. Building on the design of the earlier trial, we randomized accepted manuscripts to social media exposure or no exposure and implemented a range of strategies to increase intensity, including expanding the journal's follower base through advertising and organic growth, presenting each exposed article in three separate posts, boosting posts on Facebook, and retweeting posts on Twitter. We also prespecified an interim analysis with stopping rules for futility and examined whether the effect of the intervention differed by manuscript type, geographic location of the corresponding author, timing of publication, and the presence of an accompanying editorial.

This study makes three key contributions. First, it provides randomized evidence on the effect of a substantially intensified social media intervention, addressing the principal limitation of the earlier trial. Second, it evaluates potential effect modification across article and author characteristics that might identify subsets of articles for which promotion is more effective. Third, it offers practical guidance for journals deciding how to allocate effort and resources to social media, contributing to a broader understanding of the role of social media in disseminating scientific knowledge and informing evidence-based decisions about the use of these platforms. By exploring the impact of social media on article readership and engagement, this research aims to provide valuable insights for researchers, journals, and the broader scientific community. The relationship between online attention and actual readership of scientific work has been a topic of interest in recent years. To explore this further, we conducted a prospective, parallel-group, single-center randomized controlled trial at Circulation, a weekly peer-reviewed cardiovascular journal of the American Heart Association. This trial was designed as a follow-up to an earlier study that investigated the impact of social media exposure on page views, which found no significant increase in 30-day page views with a standard-intensity strategy (Fox et al., 2016). Our study aimed to build upon these findings by implementing a more intensive social media strategy and examining its effect on article readership.

The unit of randomization in our study was the individual original research manuscript. We began randomizing articles published in January 2015, and the trial was conducted in accordance with the CONSORT recommendations for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010). To ensure the integrity of the study, we obtained exemption from formal institutional review, as the study involved no human participants and only utilized publicly available, aggregate journal web metrics.

Eligible articles for our study were original research manuscripts accepted for publication in Circulation and scheduled for release in the weekly print and online issues. We excluded other content types, such as editorials, letters, and case reports, from randomization, although we did record the presence of an accompanying editorial for each randomized article. Manuscripts were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either social media exposure (intervention) or no social media exposure (control). A statistician not involved in the social media activity performed the allocation using a computer-generated random sequence, stratified by article type to promote balance across arms.

Given that the intervention was delivered by journal staff, it was not possible to blind them to the randomization assignments. However, page view data were extracted objectively from the journal's web analytics, eliminating the potential for observer bias. Authors were not informed of the randomization assignments to prevent any potential influence on their behavior.

Articles assigned to the intervention arm received social media exposure through the journal's official Facebook and Twitter accounts. To increase the intensity of the intervention relative to the earlier trial, we employed several strategies. First, we expanded the follower base of both accounts through paid advertising campaigns and organic growth, such as regular posting of engaging content, cross-promotion across American Heart Association channels, and interaction with followers. We recorded follower counts at the start and end of the study period to document growth. Second, each intervention article was promoted in triplicate, with three distinct posts published on each platform at different times and on different days after publication, using varied wording and images to reduce redundancy and capture different audiences across time zones.

Third, on Facebook, we used paid promotion to boost posts and extend their reach beyond existing followers. Fourth, on Twitter, we retweeted the journal's posts from the journal account at later times to extend visibility. Each post included a short descriptive message, a link to the article on the journal website, and, where applicable, a graphical element such as the visual abstract or a key figure. To minimize variation in content between articles, posts were designed using a standardized template by the journal's social media editors.

In contrast, control articles received no promotion from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts. However, control articles were still subject to all other standard journal dissemination mechanisms, including table of contents e-mail alerts, press releases for selected articles, and the journal's website and print edition. While authors, readers, and outside organizations were not prevented from independently sharing any article on social media, we assumed that such activity would be evenly distributed across arms due to randomization.

The primary outcome of our study was the number of page views of the article during the first 30 days after publication, defined as the sum of full-text HTML and abstract views recorded by the journal's website analytics. We counted page views from the day of online publication. Secondary descriptive measures included the number of followers of each account, the reach and engagement of social media posts, and page views at other time points when available. We also recorded baseline covariates for each manuscript, including article type, geographic location of the corresponding author, the presence of an accompanying editorial, and the date of publication, categorized by trimester to account for potential temporal trends in readership and follower growth.

Our target enrollment was based on the number of original research articles expected to be published in Circulation across the calendar year, anticipating roughly 300 manuscripts. Given the practical limit on the available sample, our study was designed to detect a moderate difference in 30-day page views between arms. We prespecified an interim analysis once 50% of the anticipated manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. At this interim analysis, groups were to be compared on the primary outcome, and the trial would be stopped for futility if there was no evidence of a treatment effect, defined by conditional power calculations under the observed trend (Lachin, 2005). The rationale for the futility rule was to avoid continuing an intensive, resource-demanding intervention if its benefit was unlikely to emerge. We did not plan to stop the trial for efficacy, as our focus was on determining whether increased intensity would produce a benefit that the previous trial failed to demonstrate.

All analyses in our study followed the intention-to-treat principle, with articles analyzed according to their randomized assignment. We summarized baseline characteristics by arm using counts and percentages for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. To assess balance between arms, we used chi-square or Fisher exact tests for article type, corresponding author location, and editorial status. Given that page view counts are right-skewed, we summarized the primary outcome using medians and interquartile ranges and compared arms using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. As a sensitivity analysis, we log-transformed page views and compared arms with linear regression, reporting the ratio of geometric means with 95% confidence intervals. We also fit models adjusted for the stratification factor and baseline covariates to assess the robustness of the unadjusted comparison.

To evaluate whether the effect of the intervention varied across subgroups, we tested treatment-by-covariate interaction terms in regression models for manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, and presence of an accompanying editorial. By examining these interactions, we aimed to identify potential modifiers of the intervention's effect and provide insight into the conditions under which social media exposure may be most effective in increasing article readership. Ultimately, our study aimed to contribute to the ongoing discussion about the role of social media in promoting scientific research and to inform the development of effective strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of scientific work. The conduct of this study was guided by a prespecified protocol, which outlined the publication and editorial status of each interaction. Each interaction was subjected to separate testing, with the interaction P value reported accordingly. Subgroup analyses were considered exploratory in nature and, as such, were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. All statistical tests were two-sided, with a P value of less than 0.05 deemed statistically significant. The analyses were performed using SAS software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), which provided a robust framework for evaluating the data.

The study population and randomization process commenced in January 2015 and continued until the prespecified stopping rule was met. This rule, as outlined by Fox et al. (2015), called for an interim comparison of 30-day page views once 50% of the planned manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. The data and safety review, conducted on September 26, 2015, concluded that the intervention was unlikely to demonstrate a benefit with continued enrollment, leading to the trial being stopped for futility. In total, 152 original research manuscripts were randomized, with 74 (48.7%) assigned to social media exposure and 78 (51.3%) to the control arm. Every randomized manuscript was included in the analysis according to its assigned arm, ensuring that the integrity of the randomization process was maintained.

Article-level page-view data were available for all 152 manuscripts at 30 days, resulting in no manuscripts being lost to follow-up or excluded due to missing outcomes. Furthermore, no manuscripts crossed over between arms, which helped to minimize potential biases. Control manuscripts received no posts from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts, although the journal's usual non-social-media dissemination channels remained unchanged for both arms. This design allowed for a clear comparison of the effect of social media exposure on page views.

The balance of baseline characteristics between the two arms was a critical aspect of the study. Fortunately, randomization produced groups that were well balanced on the prespecified characteristics. The distribution of article types, including clinical, population science, and basic or translational studies, did not differ significantly between the social media and control arms (P=0.85). Similarly, the geographic location of the corresponding author, categorized by region, was comparable between the two arms (P=0.33). The proportion of manuscripts accompanied by a published editorial also did not differ between arms (P=0.80). Editorials are an important covariate, as they can increase the visibility of an article independently of social media activity. Overall, the balance of baseline characteristics suggested that chance allocation had not favored one arm over the other.

The primary outcome of interest was the number of 30-day page views. The distribution of page views was right-skewed, with a small number of highly viewed articles in each arm. To account for this, we summarized the outcome using medians and compared groups using methods suited to non-normal data. The median number of 30-day page views was 499.5 for manuscripts randomized to social media and 450.5 for control manuscripts, representing an absolute difference of 49 page views or approximately 10.9% relative to the control median. However, this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.38), and there was no evidence of a treatment effect. The distributions for the two arms overlapped extensively across the range of page views, with the upper tail of highly viewed articles present in both arms. The direction of the point estimate favored social media, but its magnitude was small compared to the variability in page views between articles. The estimate was also compatible with no effect, leading to the conclusion that the data do not support the idea that the intervention increased traffic.

The futility determination was based on this comparison, which showed that the observed difference was too small and the variability too large for the trial to have a reasonable chance of demonstrating a statistically significant benefit if enrollment continued to the originally planned sample. This finding was consistent with the results of an earlier trial of social media at the same journal, which also found no increase in page views (Fox et al., 2015). The present result therefore agrees with this earlier null finding, despite the intervention being more intensive in the current study. The lack of benefit was unexpected, given the larger follower numbers and more frequent posting in the current study.

We also conducted subgroup and interaction analyses to examine whether the effect of social media varied across prespecified subgroups. We tested treatment-by-subgroup interactions for manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, and editorial status. None of these interactions were statistically significant. The treatment effect did not differ by manuscript type (P=0.86), indicating that no category of original research gained or lost differentially from social media promotion. Similarly, the effect did not differ by the geographic location of the corresponding author (P=0.35), suggesting that the intervention did not preferentially increase views of articles from authors in particular regions. The effect of social media also did not vary by trimester of publication (P=0.34), which is notable given that the intervention changed over the study period as the follower base on both platforms grew. Finally, the presence or absence of an editorial did not modify the effect of social media (P=0.79), indicating that social media exposure did not boost views more for articles with an editorial than for those without.

In summary, this randomized trial of 152 original research manuscripts found that a more intensive social media strategy was not associated with a significant increase in 30-day page views. The arms were balanced on article type, author geography, and editorial status, and the median number of page views was 499.5 with social media and 450.5 without (P=0.38). The trial was stopped for futility, and treatment effects did not differ across manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, or editorial status. These results reproduce the null finding of the earlier trial, despite a larger follower base and more frequent posting. The findings suggest that social media exposure may not be an effective means of increasing page views for research manuscripts, at least in the context of this journal. The role of social media in promoting scholarly articles has been a topic of considerable interest in recent years, with many journals investing significant time and resources into maintaining a presence on platforms such as Facebook and Twitter. In an effort to better understand the impact of social media on article readership, we conducted a randomized controlled trial at Circulation, a leading journal in the field of cardiology. Our study built on an earlier trial, which found that a less intensive social media strategy had no significant effect on page views. We hypothesized that the null result may have been due to an insufficiently potent intervention, and therefore designed a new trial that incorporated several key changes.

First, we expanded the journal's follower base through a combination of paid advertising and organic growth, with the goal of increasing the reach of our social media posts. We also repeated each post three times, rather than just once, in an effort to increase visibility and engagement. Additionally, we paid to boost posts on Facebook, which allowed us to target specific audiences and increase the post's visibility in users' news feeds. Finally, we retweeted articles on Twitter, which helped to further amplify our message. Despite these changes, our results showed that the more intensive social media strategy had no significant effect on 30-day page views of original research articles. The median page views for articles in the social media arm were slightly higher than those in the control arm (499.5 vs 450.5), but the difference was small and not statistically significant.

One possible explanation for the lack of effect is that the audience reached by the journal's social media accounts may overlap heavily with readers who already follow the journal through other channels, such as tables of contents, email alerts, and direct website visits. In other words, the social media promotion may not have added many new readers to the mix, as those who are already engaged with the journal would have found the articles regardless of social media exposure. Another possibility is that the content of the social media posts was not engaging enough to drive significant traffic to the articles. Brief posts with a title and link may be easily overlooked in a crowded feed, and social media users may react to the post (e.g., by liking or sharing) without actually clicking through to the article.

It's also possible that the promotion of articles through social media is simply not effective in driving traffic, at least in the short term. This could be due to a variety of factors, including the fact that social media users are often bombarded with information and may not have the time or attention to engage with scholarly articles. Alternatively, the effects of social media promotion may be delayed, and may not be fully captured by our 30-day page view metric. For example, social media may influence outcomes such as awareness, discussion, and downstream citations, which are not directly measured by page views.

Our study had several limitations that should be taken into account when interpreting the results. First, the trial was conducted at a single journal with a specialized, predominantly professional readership, and the results may not generalize to journals with different audiences or to other social media platforms. Additionally, randomization occurred at the level of the manuscript, but social media is not a perfectly containable exposure, and articles in the control arm could still have been shared by authors, readers, institutions, or other accounts. This could have biased our estimates toward the null, and may have masked any potential effects of the social media promotion.

Despite these limitations, our study had several strengths. The prospective randomized design minimized confounding by article quality, topic, or author prominence, and the primary outcome and interim stopping rules were specified in advance. The trial also built directly on a prior experiment, and tested a specific hypothesis about the intensity of social media promotion. The results of our study have practical implications for journals, which often devote significant resources to social media on the assumption that it will increase readership. Our findings suggest that, at least for short-term page views, this investment may not yield returns, even when intensified.

Journals may reasonably decide to maintain a social media presence for other purposes, such as community building, public engagement, or brand visibility, but should not expect it to substantially increase traffic to individual articles. Authors and institutions, who possess personal networks and credibility that a journal account lacks, may be more effective promoters, and this deserves further study. Future trials could also test more engaging content formats, targeted promotion to defined audiences, promotion timed to coincide with meetings or news events, and the engagement of influential individual users. Outcomes beyond page views, including citations, altmetrics, and measures of knowledge translation, would help establish whether social media has value that traffic metrics fail to capture.

In conclusion, our study found that a more intensive social media strategy, incorporating a larger follower base, repeated posts, and paid boosting, did not increase 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. Combined with the previous trial, these data provide consistent randomized evidence that journal-led social media promotion has little effect on early article readership. Journals should evaluate such activity against goals other than page views, and consider alternative strategies for promoting their content and engaging with their audiences. By doing so, they can make more informed decisions about how to allocate their resources, and can work to maximize the impact of their research on the scientific community and beyond.

Empirical software engineering, a field that relies heavily on observable artifacts like source code, version histories, and defect reports, often derives claims about software development and maintenance that extend far beyond the data from which they were drawn. For instance, a technique that proves effective in a set of open-source projects is frequently presented as a universal solution, and results observed during one period are implicitly assumed to hold true in subsequent periods. However, this assumption is rarely tested, despite the fact that software projects are in a constant state of flux due to the introduction of new features, changes in team composition, refactoring, and evolving development practices. A critical question arises: will a researcher's conclusions remain valid a year from now for the same software projects? There are compelling reasons to doubt this. Previous research by Menzies and Shepperd (2012) has highlighted the instability of many findings in software analytics, citing "conclusion instability" as a major obstacle to building a cumulative body of knowledge. Subsequent studies have reinforced this notion, demonstrating that conclusions often vary significantly across different data sets, learners, and experimental configurations (Menzies et al., 2013; Shepperd et al., 2014; Tantithamthavorn et al., 2016). Findings that appear robust in one context may weaken or even reverse in another. Notably, most of this research has focused on variation across space, i.e., across projects, data sets, or methods, with relatively little attention paid to variation across time. This is a significant oversight, given that software evolves over time and the practical application of prediction models is inherently temporal.

Defect prediction, an active research area for over two decades, provides a particularly informative setting in which to investigate this problem. The primary goal of defect prediction is to identify files, modules, or changes that are likely to contain defects, enabling limited quality-assurance resources to be allocated effectively (Zimmermann et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2012). A substantial body of work has proposed new learners, features, and transfer strategies, reporting improvements over prior approaches. Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), which involves training a model on one or more source projects to predict defects in a different target project, has received significant attention due to its potential to address the common scenario where a project lacks sufficient historical data to train its own model (Turhan et al., 2009; Zimmermann et al., 2009; Nam et al., 2013). Comparative studies have identified approaches that appear to outperform others (Herbold et al., 2018; Hosseini et al., 2019), and these rankings are frequently taken as guidance for both researchers and practitioners. However, the conventional evaluation protocols used in defect prediction can obscure temporal instability. Standard methods, including k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits, ignore the chronological order of the data, allowing models to be trained on instances from the future of the instances being predicted – a form of information leakage that no practitioner could replicate in deployment (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019). Furthermore, defect labels are often derived with delay, as a defect may be discovered long after the code that introduced it was written. Evaluations that disregard this lag can overstate performance. Even when time is respected, evaluations typically report a single aggregate figure computed over the entire history, masking how performance fluctuates between releases or periods. A method that appears superior on average may only be superior in certain intervals. This aggregation, therefore, conceals exactly the temporal behavior on which a practitioner's decision to adopt a model depends.

This gap is significant for several reasons. Firstly, a defect predictor is deployed on future releases, so the relevant evidence is its performance on data that postdate its training. Secondly, if the ranking of techniques changes from one release to the next, a study that selects the "best" approach from one evaluation window cannot support a claim that this approach will remain the best. Thirdly, the metrics used to quantify performance may themselves behave differently over time. Defect-prone ratios shift between releases, and metrics such as F-Score are sensitive to class imbalance, whereas the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is more robust to it (Yao and Shepperd, 2020; Chicco and Jurman, 2020). Reporting only one metric may thus provide an incomplete view of stability. 

In this article, we empirically investigate the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models. To do this, we adopt a time-aware evaluation approach where models are trained only on data available in the past and evaluated only on data from the future. Instead of presenting a single aggregate result, we examine performance as a function of the evaluation period and compare how conclusions drawn in one period compare with those drawn in subsequent periods. We measure performance using three complementary indicators: F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and MCC. Our study is guided by three research questions: 

RQ1: How does the performance of cross-project defect prediction models vary across time periods? We quantify the variability of F-Score, AUC, and MCC when the same models are evaluated on successive periods of the same projects. 

RQ2: Are conclusions about the relative performance of defect prediction approaches stable over time? We examine whether the ranking of approaches, and the statistical significance of differences between them, persist across evaluation periods or change from one period to the next. 

RQ3: How sensitive is conclusion stability to the choice of performance metric? We compare the three metrics to determine whether instability is an artifact of a particular measure or a more general phenomenon. 

This work makes several contributions. Firstly, to our knowledge, it presents one of the first systematic investigations of time-based conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction, shifting the focus from stability across data sets to stability across time for the same projects. Secondly, it provides a time-aware evaluation procedure where training uses only past data and testing uses only future data, avoiding the leakage inherent in conventional cross-validation and allowing performance to be tracked period by period. Thirdly, it shows empirically that the performance of defect predictors, in terms of F-Score, AUC, and MCC, can vary significantly over time, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of conclusion stability in software engineering research. 

By exploring the temporal stability of defect prediction models, this study aims to provide insights into the dynamic nature of software development and the challenges of building reliable prediction models that can withstand the test of time. The findings of this research have significant implications for both researchers and practitioners, as they underscore the importance of considering time in the evaluation and deployment of defect prediction models. Ultimately, this work seeks to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable software engineering practices, ones that can adapt to the evolving nature of software projects and provide lasting benefits to the software development community. 

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. We first provide a detailed overview of the related work in defect prediction and conclusion stability, highlighting the key challenges and limitations of existing research. We then describe our research methodology, including the data sets used, the experimental design, and the performance metrics employed. Next, we present the results of our empirical study, discussing the variability of defect prediction performance across time periods and the stability of conclusions about the relative performance of different approaches. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications of our findings, the limitations of our study, and directions for future research. 

In conclusion, this article highlights the critical importance of considering time in software engineering research, particularly in the context of defect prediction. By examining the temporal stability of defect prediction models, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of software development, ultimately leading to the development of more reliable and effective software engineering practices. The findings of this study have significant implications for both researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the need for a more nuanced and time-aware approach to software engineering research. 

Overall, our research contributes to the growing body of literature on conclusion stability in software engineering, providing new insights into the temporal dynamics of defect prediction and the challenges of building reliable prediction models. As software development continues to evolve, it is essential that our research methods and practices adapt to these changes, incorporating a deeper understanding of time and its impact on software engineering phenomena. One of the primary concerns is the instability of conclusions drawn from these models, which can vary significantly depending on the period evaluated. In other words, the performance of a defect prediction model, as measured by metrics such as F-Score, AUC, and MCC, can fluctuate substantially over time, leading to inconsistent conclusions. Our study examines the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models through three research questions. The first question (RQ1) investigates how the performance of these models, as measured by F-Score, AUC, and MCC, varies across successive evaluation periods. The second question (RQ2) explores whether comparative conclusions, such as "learner A outperforms learner B," remain consistent across periods. The third question (RQ3) examines whether the magnitude of change between consecutive releases is associated with the change in predictive performance.

To answer these questions, we studied 10 open-source Java projects from the Apache Software Foundation, which satisfy four key criteria: at least five tagged releases, a public issue tracker with bug reports linked to commits, at least 100 classes per release, and a release history of at least three years. This yielded 74 releases, containing 61,204 class-level instances, which were published between 2008 and 2020. We computed 20 static product metrics for each class in each release, including the Chidamber-Kemerer suite, size and complexity measures, and coupling and cohesion indicators. Defect labels were derived using the SZZ algorithm, which identifies bug-fixing commits and maps them to the bug-introducing changes of the files they modify.

We adopted a strictly chronological protocol for our evaluation, where every release of every project served once as a test set. The training set consisted only of instances from releases of other projects, satisfying two conditions: the release date plus the 180-day labeling window precedes the release date of the test release, and the defect labels used for training were recomputed using only bug-fix information available at that cut-off. This removes both look-ahead in the instances and look-ahead in the labels, a subtle form of leakage that can occur when labels are collected after the prediction date.

To define evaluation periods, we grouped test releases into non-overlapping calendar half-years, yielding 22 periods between 2009 and 2020. We restricted our analysis to the 17 periods that contained at least three test releases, to ensure that per-period summaries were not dominated by a single release. Performance within a period was summarized by the median across its test releases. As a reference condition, we also ran a time-agnostic CPDP evaluation, where the training set comprised all releases of other projects regardless of date. This allowed us to quantify how much ignoring temporal ordering changes conclusions.

We selected four learners that are widely used in the defect-prediction literature: logistic regression, naïve Bayes, random forest, and a gradient-boosted decision tree ensemble. We also included a CPDP-specific approach, the nearest-neighbor relevancy filter, applied before fitting logistic regression. All metrics were log-transformed, and features were z-standardized using training-set statistics only. Class imbalance was handled by class-weighting in the loss function, rather than resampling, to keep the test distribution untouched and avoid synthetic instances. Hyperparameters were kept at library defaults to isolate temporal effects from tuning variability.

We report three complementary measures of performance: F-Score, AUC, and MCC. The F-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall for the defective class, while AUC measures threshold-independent ranking performance. MCC is a balanced correlation between observed and predicted classes that remains informative under class imbalance. By using three measures with different sensitivities to base rate and threshold, we can check whether instability is an artifact of the evaluation metric or a genuine property of the models. Our results provide new insights into the challenges of defect prediction and highlight the importance of considering the temporal context in which models are evaluated. In the realm of defect prediction, the accuracy of a model's performance is often summarized by a single metric, which can be either an absolute statement, such as "learner A achieves an AUC above 0.70," or a comparative statement, like "A outperforms B." A conclusion is considered stable if it holds true beyond the initial evaluation period in which it was drawn. To assess this stability, we employed four key indicators.

Firstly, we examined the dispersion of performance metrics across different periods. For each learner and measure, we calculated the range, interquartile range, and coefficient of variation (CV) of the period-level medians. Additionally, we counted the proportion of periods in which a performance threshold - such as an AUC of 0.70, an MCC of 0.30, or an F-Score of 0.40, as suggested by Hall et al. (2012) - was violated. This violation rate provides insight into the consistency of a learner's performance over time.

Secondly, we evaluated the comparative consistency of learner pairs across different periods. For every pair of learners and each period, we determined the winner based on their paired, per-release performance values. The significance of the differences between these values was tested using the two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945), with the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons at a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Effect sizes were quantified using Cliff's δ, which categorizes the effect as negligible (|δ| < 0.147), small (< 0.33), medium (< 0.474), or large (otherwise), according to Romano et al. (2006). A pairwise conclusion was deemed stable if the same learner consistently won with a non-negligible effect in at least 80% of the periods. Furthermore, we computed the learner ranking in each period and measured the agreement across periods using Kendall's coefficient of concordance W (Kendall & Smith, 1939) and the Spearman rank correlation between the rankings of consecutive periods.

Thirdly, we investigated the sign reversal rate, which is the fraction of learner pairs whose winner changed sign between consecutive periods, given that at least one period showed a significant difference. This metric helps in understanding how often the relative performance of learners changes over time.

Lastly, we analyzed the time-aware versus time-agnostic gap (RQ1-RQ2), which involves the paired difference in each performance measure between the two evaluation protocols, tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and the number of pairwise conclusions that differ between the protocols. This comparison is crucial for understanding the impact of temporal considerations on the evaluation of defect prediction models.

To characterize the degree of change in a product between releases, we compared the metric distributions of each test release with those of its immediate predecessor within the same project. For each of the 20 metrics, we computed the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between binned distributions, averaging these across metrics to obtain a release dissimilarity score. We also recorded churn-based descriptors, including the proportion of added, deleted, and modified classes. Then, we calculated the Spearman correlation (ρ) between dissimilarity and the absolute change in AUC, F-Score, and MCC relative to the previous release of the same project, reporting Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples). Additionally, we contrasted performance change for the upper versus lower quartile of dissimilarity using Mann-Whitney U tests with Cliff's δ. To mitigate dependence on a single labeling choice, we repeated the analysis with 90- and 365-day labeling windows and with quarterly periods, which alters the period boundaries. Conclusions were deemed robust only if they persisted across all variants.

Our research questions (RQ1 and RQ2) aimed to investigate the stability of cross-project defect prediction performance over time and whether conclusions about the relative ranking of learners remain stable. To address RQ1, we evaluated each of the five learners (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and a CART decision tree) under a time-aware cross-project protocol. For every target project and each evaluation window, models were trained exclusively on defect data from other projects observed before the window began and tested on the target project's modules created or changed during the window. This procedure yielded 1,214 train-test pairs across 41 projects and 24 consecutive windows of six months each. The performance metrics varied significantly across windows. Averaged over all learners and projects, the median F-Score was 0.41 (IQR 0.27-0.55), the median AUC was 0.67 (IQR 0.58-0.76), and the median MCC was 0.19 (IQR 0.06-0.33). These values are notably lower than those typically reported under time-agnostic cross-validation, where we obtained a median F-Score of 0.53, an AUC of 0.74, and an MCC of 0.31 on the same data. The difference was statistically significant for all three measures (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001) with moderate-to-large effect sizes (Cliff's δ = 0.38, 0.41, and 0.44 for F-Score, AUC, and MCC, respectively), consistent with earlier warnings that ignoring temporal order inflates estimates (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019).

The within-project variability over time was also substantial. For a given project and learner, the median range (maximum minus minimum) of AUC across windows was 0.29, and that of MCC was 0.41. In 63% of projects, the best-performing window had an MCC at least three times that of the worst-performing window, and in 18% of projects, MCC changed sign, indicating that the model performed better than chance in some windows and worse in others. The coefficient of variation of F-Score across windows averaged 0.46 (SD = 0.19), far higher than the 0.12 observed across ten repetitions of random cross-validation, suggesting that the variation was not solely due to stochastic training effects.

We also quantified the change in performance between consecutive windows. The absolute change in AUC had a median of 0.07 but a heavy tail, with the 90th percentile at 0.21, and 7.4% of transitions exceeding 0.30. Large changes frequently coincided with major releases. For transitions spanning a major release, the median absolute change in MCC was 0.16, compared with 0.07 for transitions within a release series (Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.001, δ = 0.35). This suggests that a substantive revision of a product can abruptly alter predictive performance, aligning with observations of concept drift in software data (Menzies et al., 2012; Turhan, 2012).

Addressing RQ2, we examined how often conclusions about the relative ranking of learners persisted from one window to the next. Most defect prediction studies draw conclusions of the form "learner A outperforms learner B." For each window, we ranked the five learners by mean AUC across target projects and tested for differences using a Scott-Knott ESD procedure (Tantithamthavorn et al., 2017). The top-ranked learner changed in 58% of consecutive windows, indicating a significant level of instability in the relative performance of learners over time. This finding highlights the importance of considering temporal factors when evaluating and comparing the performance of defect prediction models.

All analyses were implemented in Python (scikit-learn) and R, with fixed random seeds, ensuring reproducibility. The scripts and derived datasets are provided in a replication package, facilitating further investigation and validation of our findings. The evaluation of defect prediction models is a complex task, and our research highlights the importance of considering the temporal aspect of this evaluation. We analyzed the performance of various machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, SVM, and CART, on a large dataset of software projects. The results show that the ranking of these algorithms varies significantly across different time windows, with Random Forest being ranked first most often, but not always being statistically significantly better than other algorithms. In fact, in 11 out of 24 windows, at least one simpler learner was statistically indistinguishable from Random Forest.

To further investigate the stability of these rankings, we calculated Kendall's τ between rankings of adjacent windows, which had a median of 0.40, indicating a moderate level of correlation. However, in 21% of cases, the correlation was zero or negative, suggesting that the order of learners in one period offered little information about the next. This lack of stability is concerning, as it implies that the conclusions drawn from a single evaluation period may not be reliable.

To mimic a typical single-snapshot study, we randomly drew 1,000 individual windows and drew a "conclusion" about which learner was best. We then checked whether this conclusion was reproduced in a different window sampled from the following year. The results were striking: only 46% of such conclusions replicated, and the probability of replication declined as the temporal gap grew. This suggests that the choice of evaluation period can have a significant impact on the conclusions drawn about the relative performance of different algorithms.

We also investigated the effect of the evaluation metric on the stability of the conclusions. Our results show that the choice of metric, whether F-Score, AUC, or MCC, does not remedy the instability. In fact, the replication rate was similar across all three metrics, with 43% for F-Score, 46% for AUC, and 41% for MCC. This suggests that the instability is a fundamental property of the data, rather than a result of the choice of evaluation metric.

To better understand the sources of instability, we computed the Kendall's coefficient of concordance (W) of learner rankings across all 24 windows. The results show that AUC was the most stable measure, albeit with limited absolute stability, with a W of 0.47. In contrast, F-Score and MCC had lower W values, of 0.34 and 0.29, respectively. Moreover, the three metrics disagreed about the best learner in 37% of windows, highlighting the importance of considering multiple metrics when evaluating defect prediction models.

We also investigated the factors that contribute to the instability of the conclusions. Our results show that distribution shift, test-window defect rate, and code churn are all significant predictors of instability. A mixed-effects regression model explained 36% of the variance in MCC, with distribution shift being the strongest predictor. A one standard deviation increase in the KS statistic was associated with a 0.09 decrease in MCC, highlighting the importance of considering the distribution of the data when evaluating defect prediction models.

The class imbalance of the test data also changed over time, with the median defect rate ranging from 3% to 46% across windows within the same project. This change in class imbalance can have a significant impact on the evaluation metrics, particularly F-Score and MCC, which are sensitive to base rates. In contrast, AUC was less correlated with defect rate, suggesting that it may be a more robust metric in the presence of class imbalance.

To assess the robustness of our findings, we performed several sensitivity analyses. We repeated the analysis with three-month and twelve-month windows, and found that the qualitative findings were unchanged. We also applied standard transfer approaches, such as Burak filtering and transformation-based methods, before training, and found that these techniques improved median AUC but did not reduce the variability. Finally, we restricted the analysis to the 14 projects with at least 20 windows of data and more than 100 defective modules per window, and found that the results were similar to those obtained with the full dataset.

Overall, our results show that the conclusions drawn from cross-project defect prediction experiments depend on when the evaluation is performed. The performance of defect prediction models fluctuates considerably between consecutive evaluation periods, and the median F-score, AUC, and MCC values vary significantly across projects. The spread in MCC is particularly notable, as it is a more conservative indicator of classifier quality on imbalanced data. In several periods, a model that appeared adequate under F-score had an MCC close to zero, meaning its predictions were barely better than chance. This instability is consistent with earlier warnings that conclusions in software analytics rarely transfer across contexts, and highlights the importance of considering the temporal aspect of evaluation when drawing conclusions about defect prediction models.

The implications of our findings are significant. A researcher who evaluates defect prediction models at one point in time may draw different conclusions than one who evaluates at a different time, even on the same projects. This instability is arguably more troubling than the instability across datasets, as it suggests that the results of a single evaluation period may not be reliable. Our findings highlight the need for more robust evaluation methods that take into account the temporal aspect of software development, and for more careful consideration of the factors that contribute to instability in defect prediction models. By acknowledging and addressing these challenges, we can develop more effective and reliable defect prediction models that can be used to improve software quality.

Complex systems, whether in nature, society, or technology, are inherently composed of numerous interacting units, whose collective behavior cannot be fully understood by examining these units in isolation. The language of network science has been instrumental in describing such systems, with nodes representing individual units and links representing the interactions among them (Newman 2003; Boccaletti et al. 2006). However, the traditional formulation of network science has often relied on the assumption that a system can be represented by a single graph, implying a single type of interaction. This assumption has become increasingly recognized as overly restrictive, as real-world systems often involve multiple types of interactions. For instance, individuals in a society interact through various means, including face-to-face contact, online social platforms, and professional ties, while a transportation system may comprise airline, rail, and road connections among the same set of cities. Similarly, a cell relies on genetic, protein, and metabolic interactions among overlapping sets of molecular components. In each of these cases, a common set of nodes participates in multiple distinct layers of connectivity, and its role may differ significantly from one layer to another.

The multilayer or multiplex framework was developed to capture this complex structure (Kivelä et al. 2014; Boccaletti et al. 2014; De Domenico et al. 2013). This framework has revealed a range of phenomena that have no counterpart in isolated networks, including abrupt, cascading failures in interdependent systems (Buldyrev et al. 2010), altered percolation and robustness properties (Gao et al. 2012), modified synchronization and controllability, and rich interplay between coupled spreading processes, such as the spread of an epidemic and the diffusion of awareness about it (Granell et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2019). However, almost all of these advances presuppose that the multiplex topology is known. In practice, the connection structure of real systems is often only partially observable or entirely hidden, whereas time series of the nodal states are relatively easy to record. This motivates the inverse problem of network reconstruction: inferring the interaction structure from measured dynamics.

For single-layer networks, a substantial literature now exists, with approaches including driving-response and perturbation schemes (Timme 2007), methods based on correlation and information-theoretic measures (Bullmore and Sporns 2009; Schreiber 2000), and compressive sensing, which exploits the sparsity of real networks to recover topology from short data records (Wang et al. 2011; Han et al. 2015; Shen et al. 2014). Compressive sensing has been applied to various systems, including evolutionary games, epidemic spreading, and oscillator networks, and variants have been developed for hidden nodes and for identifying network structure from binary-state dynamics (Su et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2016). Related statistical strategies, including maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, have been proposed for diffusion and cascade networks (Gomez-Rodriguez et al. 2012; Netrapalli and Sanghavi 2012), for kinetic Ising-type systems and inverse problems in statistical physics (Roudi and Hertz 2011; Nguyen et al. 2017), and for reconstructing networks from epidemic outbreaks (Shen et al. 2014; Hoffmann et al. 2019). These studies have shown that, with appropriate dynamical models and sparsity-aware algorithms, accurate reconstruction can be achieved from limited data.

However, extending these ideas to multiplex networks is far from straightforward, and the problem remains largely open. One of the primary difficulties is that the observed data are a superposition of effects from several layers, making it challenging to disentangle the contributions of each layer. A node's state change at a given time reflects the combined influence of its neighbors in all layers, and the layer-specific contributions are not directly separable from the time series. Applying a single-layer method to such data would either produce an aggregated network in which layer identity is lost or yield spurious links through mixing of the layers. Another difficulty is dimensionality: the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of layers, making the inference problem harder precisely when each layer is only weakly constrained by the data. Furthermore, the layers can host dynamical processes of different kinds, with different transmission mechanisms and rates, so that a reconstruction framework must be able to attribute observed transitions to the appropriate process. Finally, real observations are limited in length and contaminated by noise, and any practical framework must be robust to both.

Existing multilayer studies have largely concentrated on structural inference from static or aggregated data, community detection, or the estimation of interlayer correlations, rather than on reconstructing the layer-resolved topology directly from dynamics. The present work addresses this gap by posing the following question: given only binary time series of the states of a set of shared nodes, subject to the coupled action of distinct dynamical processes propagating on different layers, can the full layer-resolved connectivity be recovered, and under what structural and dynamical conditions is the recovery accurate and robust? We focus on duplex networks, the simplest multiplex systems, which host two different types of spreading dynamics, as a prototypical setting that retains the essential difficulties described above while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Such coupled spreading is directly relevant to the interplay of disease and information or of competing contagions.

To tackle this problem, we develop a mean-field-based maximum likelihood estimation framework. The central idea is to write the probability of each observed node-state transition in terms of the unknown adjacency structure of both layers, using a mean-field approximation to render the likelihood tractable, and then to estimate the layer-specific connections by maximizing it. This formulation allows the contributions of the two layers to be disentangled through their differing dynamical signatures rather than through any prior knowledge of the layer assignment of links. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate the multiplex reconstruction problem for coupled spreading dynamics and provide a principled, likelihood-based solution that separates layer-specific structure from superposed binary observations. Second, we validate the framework on synthetic duplex networks with diverse topologies and on real-world multiplex networks, demonstrating accurate recovery from data of moderate length. Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of how reconstruction accuracy depends on structural parameters such as network size, mean degree, and interlayer correlation; on dynamical parameters such as spreading rates; and on the amount of data and the level of observational noise, thereby clarifying the regimes in which reconstruction is reliable. Together, these results extend data-driven network inference from single-layer to multiplex systems and provide a foundation for uncovering the hidden structure of complex systems. The architecture of complex systems, characterized by multiple interaction types, is a rich and dynamic field of study. To better understand these systems, we employed multiplex network models, which consist of multiple layers of interactions between nodes. Specifically, we focused on duplex networks, comprising two layers, denoted as α ∈ {1, 2}, with binary symmetric adjacency matrices A^α describing the connections between nodes. Each node exists in both layers, adhering to the standard multilayer formalism established by Kivelä et al. (2014) and Boccaletti et al. (2014).

To construct our synthetic duplex networks, we drew upon three distinct network models: Erdős–Rényi random graphs (Erdős & Rényi, 1959), Barabási–Albert scale-free networks (Barabási & Albert, 1999), and Watts–Strogatz small-world networks (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). We typically considered networks with N = 100–500 nodes and a mean degree of ⟨k⟩ = 4–10 per layer. Furthermore, we controlled the interlayer degree correlation by rewiring edges in layer 2 until a target Spearman correlation between node degrees across layers was achieved.

In addition to these synthetic networks, we also examined three empirical multiplex networks: the Kapferer tailor-shop network (Kapferer, 1972; Cardillo et al., 2013), the Pierre Auger Observatory collaboration network (De Domenico et al., 2015), and the C. elegans connectome with its electrical and chemical synaptic layers (Chen et al., 2006). Where necessary, we binarized edge weights and retained the largest common connected component.

To study dynamical processes on these networks, we utilized a prototypical coupled-spreading model, in which an information process on layer 1 interacts with an epidemic on layer 2 (Granell et al., 2013). Each node carries two binary variables at time t: awareness xi(t) ∈ {0,1} (unaware/aware, layer 1) and infection yi(t) ∈ {0,1} (susceptible/infected, layer 2). The awareness process follows an unaware–aware–unaware pattern, where an unaware node becomes aware with probability Pi^x(t) = 1 − ∏j [1 − λ aij^1 xj(t)], and an aware node reverts with probability δ. The infection process, on the other hand, follows a susceptible–infected–susceptible pattern, where a susceptible node becomes infected with probability Pi^y(t) = 1 − ∏j [1 − βi(t) aij^2 yj(t)], and an infected node recovers with probability μ.
