The coupling between the two processes enters through βi(t) = β if xi(t) = 0 and βi(t) = γβ if xi(t) = 1, with 0 ≤ γ < 1, effectively reducing susceptibility when a node is aware.

Unless otherwise specified, we set λ = 0.3, δ = 0.4, β = 0.3, μ = 0.4, and γ = 0.5. We employed synchronous updating and initiated each time series from random initial conditions, with 10% of nodes aware and 10% infected. After discarding the first 50 steps as transients, we recorded the subsequent T steps. The observed data consisted of binary matrices X ∈ {0,1}^{N×T} and Y ∈ {0,1}^{N×T}, with no knowledge of the underlying adjacency matrices A^1, A^2, or the interlayer coupling. To vary the amount of data, we used the ratio T/N, ranging from 0.5 to 10.

To address the potential issue of trajectories falling into an absorbing state, we applied a node-wise random reseeding of 1% of nodes at any step where prevalence fell to zero. We confirmed that our results were insensitive to this choice. 

The maximum likelihood formulation for estimating the network structure and parameters involves factorizing the transition probabilities across nodes and time. Given the time series data, we aimed to reconstruct the neighbor vectors ai^1 and ai^2 for each node i. Focusing on layer 2, we considered the times at which node i is susceptible, and the outcome yi(t+1) is Bernoulli with success probability Pi^y(t). The log-likelihood function for node i in layer 2 can be written as Li(ai^2) = Σ{t∈Si} { yi(t+1) ln Pi^y(t) + [1 − yi(t+1)] ln[1 − Pi^y(t)] }, where Si is the set of times at which node i is susceptible.

However, maximizing this likelihood directly is challenging due to the nonconvexity of the product inside Pi^y and its dependence on βi(t), which in turn depends on the awareness layer. To overcome this, we applied a mean-field approximation in two steps. First, we expanded the product in the limit of weak per-contact transmission, yielding Pi^y(t) ≈ βi(t) Σj aij^2 yj(t). Second, we replaced the instantaneous, state-dependent rate βi(t) with its conditional expectation given observed awareness, β̄i(t) = β[1 − (1 − γ)xi(t)]. This resulted in a likelihood that is concave in the relaxed variables aij^2 ∈ [0,1]. A similar expansion was used to derive the layer-1 likelihood in terms of λ and xj(t).

To prevent the linearized probability from exceeding one, we clipped it at 1 − ε, with ε = 10⁻⁶, to keep the logarithm finite. We also employed the same mean-field step for the 1 − P term in the case of dense neighborhoods, as described by Shen et al. (2014) and Han et al. (2015).

For joint estimation of parameters and structure, we recognized that the rate parameters (λ, β, γ) are generally unknown. We estimated them using an alternating maximization approach. With the parameters fixed, each row ai^α was obtained by projected quasi-Newton optimization (L-BFGS-B) with box constraints [0,1], starting from the uniform value ⟨k⟩/N. With the structure fixed, the parameters were updated by one-dimensional line searches on the summed log-likelihood over all nodes. Since information on γ is carried by the interlayer dependence of y on x, the two layers were coupled through this shared parameter, and iterations were repeated until the relative change in total log-likelihood fell below 10⁻⁵, typically requiring fewer than 20 cycles. Rows were computed independently, allowing the procedure to parallelize across nodes. We enforced symmetry of the undirected layers by averaging the estimates âij and âji.

To convert the estimated parameters to networks, we employed two methods. First, we sorted the N(N−1)/2 estimated values in each layer and located the largest gap in the sorted sequence. Alternatively, we used a two-component Gaussian mixture fit, and the two procedures agreed to within 1% in the reported metrics. Neither method required prior knowledge of the number of links.

To evaluate the performance of our reconstruction method, we used several metrics. Reconstruction accuracy was quantified layer by layer using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR), both computed from the continuous estimates, as well as the F1 score of the thresholded network. AUPR is particularly informative for sparse networks, where AUROC can be inflated by the large number of absent links (Davis & Goadrich, 2006). We tested the robustness of our method by varying T/N, ⟨k⟩, and interlayer degree correlation, as well as λ, β, and γ over their physically meaningful ranges. Additionally, we added observational noise by independently flipping each recorded binary state with probability η ∈ [0, 0.1]. 

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reconstructing the underlying network structure and estimating the model parameters, even in the presence of noise and varying data amounts. The ability to accurately infer the interlayer coupling and node states has significant implications for understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems, and our approach provides a valuable tool for analyzing and modeling these systems. The reconstruction of duplex networks from temporal data is a complex task, particularly when the underlying parameters are unknown or the true and assumed parameters do not align. To address this challenge, we compared our method, which utilizes mean-field maximum likelihood estimation (MF-MLE), to two baseline approaches: a single-layer reconstruction that disregards coupling and a compressive-sensing reconstruction, as proposed by Shen et al. in 2014. Our evaluation was based on 20 independent network realizations, each with 10 independent time-series realizations, and the results are presented as means with standard errors. 

To assess the differences between methods, we employed paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across realizations, applying Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons and considering significance at p < 0.01. Notably, for empirical networks, which are fixed, we resampled only the dynamical realizations. The MF-MLE framework was tested on duplex networks comprising N nodes and two layers, represented by adjacency matrices A^(1) and A^(2). The first layer hosts an awareness-type contagion, while the second layer hosts an epidemic-type contagion, with the two processes coupled as described in the interacting-spreading models of Granell et al. and reviewed in further detail by other researchers. 

Each node's state is binary, taking on values of 0 or 1 at each time step, and the only input to the reconstruction is the N×T binary state matrix. The framework replaces unknown neighbor states with their layer-wise mean-field averages and then maximizes the resulting log-likelihood to estimate the incoming links in both layers simultaneously. Performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and the F1 score at the optimal threshold, averaged over 20 independent network and dynamics realizations. Unless otherwise specified, our simulations used N = 100, a mean degree of ⟨k⟩ = 6 in each layer, infection probabilities of β1 = 0.3 and β2 = 0.25, and recovery probabilities of μ1 = μ2 = 0.4.

We began by examining duplex networks where each layer is an Erdős–Rényi (ER) random graph or a Barabási–Albert (BA) scale-free network. For ER–ER duplexes with uncorrelated layers, the AUC increased sharply with the amount of data. At T = 500 (T/N = 5), the AUC was 0.87 ± 0.03 in layer 1 and 0.84 ± 0.03 in layer 2, exceeding 0.99 in both layers at T = 2000 (T/N = 20). The F1 score followed a similar trend, rising from 0.71 at T = 500 to 0.96 at T = 2000. In contrast, a baseline that treats the two layers as a single aggregated network achieved an AUC of only 0.78 for the aggregated structure and was unable to assign links to the correct layer. Notably, links present in only one layer were assigned correctly in 97.4% of cases by MF-MLE at T = 2000, compared to 52% for the aggregated baseline, which is close to chance.

BA–BA duplexes proved somewhat more challenging to reconstruct at small T, with an AUC of 0.81 ± 0.04 in layer 1 and 0.79 ± 0.04 in layer 2 at T = 500. However, the AUC reached 0.98 at T = 2000. Hubs were recovered almost perfectly, with the degree of each hub node estimated with a relative error below 3%. In contrast, low-degree nodes contributed most of the false negatives, consistent with the notion that heterogeneous networks provide less information about weakly connected nodes in the data. Mixed ER–BA duplexes fell between the two cases, indicating that reconstruction accuracy is not strongly tied to the topology of the neighboring layer.

We also investigated the effects of structural parameters on reconstruction accuracy. At fixed T = 1000, increasing the mean degree from ⟨k⟩ = 4 to 12 lowered the AUC monotonically. In ER layers, the AUC fell from 0.99 to 0.91, likely due to the fact that denser networks produce more heterogeneous mean-field fluctuations, making the neighbor-averaged approximation less accurate. Larger networks with 50 to 400 nodes at fixed T/N = 10 showed only weak size dependence, with the AUC varying between 0.95 and 0.97. This suggests that the data requirement scales roughly linearly with N.

Interlayer degree correlation had a more pronounced effect on reconstruction accuracy. We varied the edge overlap between layers from 0 (uncorrelated) to 1 (identical layers). At zero overlap, the AUC at T = 1000 was 0.96, decreasing to 0.94 at an overlap of 0.5 and 0.88 at an overlap of 1.0. When the layers are identical, the two contagion channels cannot be distinguished from the data alone, resulting in a nearly degenerate likelihood. However, partial overlap affected the accuracy only mildly, indicating that the method is robust for moderately correlated layers, which are typical of real systems.

In addition to structural parameters, we examined the impact of dynamical parameters on reconstruction accuracy. The AUC depended non-monotonically on the infection probability. For layer 2 at T = 1000, the AUC was 0.82 at β2 = 0.05, peaked at 0.98 for β2 between 0.2 and 0.4, and declined to 0.93 at β2 = 0.8. At small β, few transmission events occur, making the data uninformative. At large β, the system saturates in the fully active state, and its time series exhibit little variability. Raising the coupling strength between the layers from 0 to 0.8 reduced the layer-2 AUC only slightly, from 0.97 to 0.95, suggesting that the interaction between the processes is captured by the likelihood and does not act as an unmodeled confounder. The best accuracy occurred when the stationary fraction of active nodes was between 0.2 and 0.6.

Finally, we applied our method to two empirical multiplex systems: the C. elegans connectome, with electrical and chemical synapse layers, and the London transport network, with Underground, overground, and DLR layers. The duplex versions were driven with the same two-process dynamics. For C. elegans, T = 5000 produced an AUC of 0.95 and 0.93 in the electrical and chemical layers, respectively, with F1 scores of 0.84 and 0.80. For the London network, whose layers are sparse, the AUC reached 0.97 at T = 4000, and the F1 score was 0.88. While the accuracy in these networks was lower than in comparable synthetic ones, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the MF-MLE framework in reconstructing duplex networks from temporal data. The performance of our reconstruction framework is notable, particularly when considering the challenges posed by strong clustering and degree heterogeneity, which can weaken the mean-field assumption. Indeed, at the same sampling ratio, we find that the framework is able to recover approximately 91% of the top-ranked hub nodes in the C. elegans chemical layer, as well as a similar fraction in the London transport layers. This achievement is a testament to the framework's robustness, especially given the complexities of these networks.

One of the key aspects of our framework is its ability to handle noise, which is inevitably present in real-world data. To model observational noise, we introduced errors into the recorded binary states by flipping each state independently with a probability p. Our results show that the area under the curve (AUC) decreases gradually as the noise level increases. For instance, in the case of ER-ER duplexes at T = 2000, the AUC decreased from 0.99 at p = 0 to 0.81 at p = 0.10. However, we also found that doubling the data length to T = 4000 can help to recover some of the lost accuracy, with an AUC of 0.90 at p = 0.10. This suggests that longer records can, to a substantial degree, compensate for the effects of noise.

In addition to observational noise, we also examined the impact of random omission of observations, where a fraction q of the time series entries are missing. Our findings indicate that the framework is relatively robust to such omissions, with an AUC of 0.96 at q = 0.2 and 0.90 at q = 0.4, both at T = 2000. Furthermore, we tested the framework's sensitivity to mis-specified dynamical parameters, where the values of β and μ used in the likelihood deviated by ±20% from the true values. The results show that the AUC is reduced by less than 0.03, indicating that the framework does not require precise knowledge of the spreading rates.

In summary, our quantitative findings suggest that, in synthetic duplex networks, an AUC above 0.98 is attainable with approximately 20 observations per node, and layer attribution is accurate to roughly 97%. However, the accuracy degrades gracefully with density, interlayer overlap, and noise, with the worst case occurring when the layers are identical. In empirical multiplex networks, the AUC remained between 0.93 and 0.97. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in reconstructing multiplex networks from observed dynamics.

The problem of recovering multiplex structure from observed dynamics is a complex one, and it has received relatively little attention compared to its forward counterpart. Our mean-field-based maximum likelihood framework addresses this challenge by reconstructing both layers of a duplex network from binary time series of coupled spreading processes. The tests on synthetic and empirical multiplex topologies demonstrate that, given sufficient data, the framework can recover intralayer connectivity in both layers with high accuracy, even when the two dynamical processes are entangled through shared nodes and their mutual influence.

One of the central difficulties in multiplex reconstruction is that the state transition of a node depends on neighbors in several layers at once. This means that the observed outcome is a composite of contributions that cannot be attributed to a particular layer without a model of how layers interact. Earlier approaches to single-layer reconstruction, such as compressive sensing and Bayesian inference, treat the system as one coupled network. In contrast, our results suggest that treating layers separately within a likelihood function is feasible when the coupling between layers is expressed through a known or parameterized dynamical rule.

The mean-field approximation is a crucial component of our framework, as it makes the problem tractable by replacing exact joint state probabilities with node-wise marginals. This locality allows the approach to scale to larger systems, because the inference for each node is an independent problem of dimension proportional to the number of candidate neighbors across layers. The parameter analysis provides a coherent picture of what controls performance, with reconstruction accuracy improving with the length of the time series and degrading as the networks become denser.

Our findings also highlight the importance of the spreading rates, with accuracy depending on the dynamically active regime between extinction and saturation. Observational noise, modeled as random flips of recorded states, lowers accuracy gradually rather than abruptly, suggesting that the estimator is reasonably robust. This is encouraging for practical use, where state classification is rarely perfect.

However, several limitations of our framework should be acknowledged. First, the framework assumes that the functional form of the dynamics is known, including the structure of the cross-layer coupling. In practice, the mechanisms by which layers influence one another are often uncertain, and model misspecification could bias the inferred links. Combining our approach with model selection or nonparametric estimates of transition probabilities would be a natural extension.

Second, the mean-field approximation neglects dynamical correlations between neighboring nodes, which can become significant in networks with high clustering or strong community structure. In such cases, the approximation may underestimate or misattribute link strengths. Third, we considered duplex systems with a one-to-one correspondence between nodes in the two layers and with binary, unweighted links. Many real multiplexes have more than two layers, partially overlapping node sets, weighted or directed edges, and time-varying connectivity, and each of these features adds parameters and potential non-identifiability.

Fourth, the data requirements, though modest relative to what exhaustive inference would demand, remain nontrivial. Observing the states of all nodes at fine temporal resolution is possible in simulations and some digital settings but difficult in field epidemiology or social data. Hidden nodes and partially observed states are important cases that the present formulation does not address, although related work on single-layer networks suggests that such cases can be handled with additional machinery.

Finally, a threshold on estimated link strengths is needed to convert continuous estimates into a binary structure, and the choice of this threshold affects the reported accuracy. We used criteria that are standard in the field, but we cannot exclude some sensitivity of the results to this choice. Despite these limitations, our framework provides a valuable tool for reconstructing multiplex networks from observed dynamics, and its performance demonstrates the potential for meaningful insights into the structure and behavior of complex systems.

The widespread collection of personal data by online services, healthcare providers, retailers, and social platforms has led to the creation of detailed databases that describe individual behavior. These databases are often shared or released, with the justification that identifiers have been removed or replaced with pseudonyms. However, a growing body of research suggests that this form of anonymization provides weak protection against privacy breaches. One of the earliest and most influential studies in this area was conducted by Sweeney in 2002, who demonstrated that a small number of quasi-identifiers, such as ZIP code, birth date, and sex, can be used to single out most individuals in a population. This work motivated the development of formal notions of anonymity, including k-anonymity.

Subsequent studies have further highlighted the limitations of anonymization. For example, Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) showed that an anonymized release of movie ratings could be linked to public profiles on a separate platform using only a handful of approximate observations per user. They later applied the same principle to social-network graphs (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2009). These studies demonstrate that privacy leakage is often not a property of a single dataset, but rather arises from the statistical dependence between the released data and auxiliary information available to an adversary.

Differential privacy (Dwork, 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014) provides a framework for understanding and mitigating privacy risks, but it is not widely used in practical data-sharing settings. As a result, there is a need for a principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible, in order to assess the risk of sharing data. Two broad lines of work address this question. The first is algorithmic and empirical, focusing on the design of heuristics that exploit similarity between records or neighborhoods in graphs, and evaluating their performance on real data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008, 2009; Ji et al., 2016). The second is information-theoretic, seeking to understand the fundamental limits of correlation between two databases, and how much information is required to align them.

In graph settings, information-theoretic approaches have produced sharp thresholds for matching correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs (Pedarsani & Grossglauser, 2011; Cullina & Kiyavash, 2016; Korula & Lattanzi, 2014). For databases with feature vectors, Cullina, Mittal, and Kiyavash (2018) characterized the fundamental limits of alignment under a permutation model, and Dai et al. (2019) obtained analogous results for jointly Gaussian features. These results suggest that the mutual information between corresponding records is the key quantity that governs matching, and that matching becomes possible once the number of attributes per record is large enough relative to the logarithm of the number of records.

However, existing analyses often rely on specific distributional assumptions, such as Gaussian features, Bernoulli or Erdős–Rényi structure, or independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) entries. These assumptions are convenient, but often unrealistic. Real-world attributes, such as time-stamped ratings, location traces, or sequential medical measurements, are heterogeneous and temporally correlated, requiring models that permit richer dependence. This paper addresses this gap by studying the matching of two high-dimensional databases in which each row corresponds to a user and each column corresponds to an attribute. One database is released with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation, and the other serves as the adversary's auxiliary information. The relation between corresponding entries is described by an arbitrary joint distribution, and the dependence across the attributes of a given user is allowed to be non-i.i.d.

Our central question is: under what conditions on the joint distribution and on the relative sizes of the database dimensions can an adversary recover the unknown permutation with vanishing probability of error, and when is this provably impossible? Answering this question for general distributions, rather than for isolated families, would yield a unified criterion for the privacy risk of correlated releases. To address this question, we develop a typicality-based approach, which rests on concentration of measure (Ledoux, 2001; Boucheron et al., 2013). When the number of attributes grows, empirical statistics of a pair of rows concentrate sharply around their expectations. This is the mechanism behind the asymptotic equipartition property and the notion of typicality used in the proofs of channel coding theorems (Cover & Thomas, 2006).

We exploit this concentration phenomenon to develop a matching scheme that declares a pair of rows to be a match when they are jointly typical, and then selects the permutation consistent with these declarations. A union bound over the competing permutations, combined with laws of large numbers for the relevant empirical averages, yields explicit conditions under which the scheme succeeds. This typicality-based strategy was introduced for pairs of correlated graphs by Shirani et al. (2019), and we extend it here to databases with general entry distributions.

The contributions of this work are fourfold. First, we propose a general matching scheme and achievability result, showing that if the number of users grows at most exponentially in the number of attributes, with a growth rate strictly below a limiting information quantity of the source, then the scheme recovers the permutation with probability tending to one. For i.i.d. entries, this quantity is the mutual information between a pair of corresponding entries. Second, we prove a matching converse, identifying a class of joint distributions for which, when the database growth rate exceeds the same information quantity, the probability of correct matching vanishes for any matching scheme. Together with the achievability result, this yields a sharp phase transition between the regimes where de-anonymization is feasible and infeasible.

Third, we evaluate the conditions for i.i.d. databases, recovering known thresholds as special cases and thereby validating the general framework. We then treat Markovian database models, in which entries within a row are temporally correlated. The relevant threshold is an information rate expressed through the stationary distribution and transition kernel of the underlying chain. The analysis shows how memory in the data changes the number of attributes needed for reliable matching relative to an i.i.d. model with the same marginals. Finally, our proof technique extends beyond the cases treated, using only typicality and concentration of measure, and can be applied to other models and settings.

Overall, this work provides a unified framework for understanding the privacy risks of correlated data releases, and sheds light on the fundamental limits of correlation between two databases. The results have important implications for the design of data-sharing protocols and the assessment of privacy risks in a variety of applications, from healthcare and social media to finance and marketing. By providing a principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible, this work can help to inform the development of more effective privacy protections and data-sharing strategies. The theoretical framework presented in this paper is grounded in fundamental principles of probability theory, including the laws of large numbers. A key advantage of this approach is that it does not rely on closed-form likelihood computations or specific parametric families, making it broadly applicable whenever empirical averages concentrate. This flexibility opens up new avenues for exploring various dependence structures. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a rigorous formulation of the database model and the concept of matching reliability. Section 3 introduces the matching scheme and presents an achievability theorem, while Section 4 focuses on proving the converse. Section 5 delves into the specialization of these results to independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) models and Markov models, and Section 6 discusses the implications and outstanding problems.

To initiate this exploration, we consider a database model comprising two databases, D⁽¹⁾ and D⁽²⁾, each with m rows (representing users) and n columns (denoting attributes). Specifically, row i of D⁽¹⁾ is denoted by Xi = (X{i1}, …, X{in}) ∈ 𝒳ⁿ, where 𝒳 is a finite alphabet. The corresponding row in the second database, Yi = (Y{i1}, …, Y{in}) ∈ 𝒴ⁿ, is drawn from another finite alphabet 𝒴. The rows of the pair (Xi, Yi) are independent across users, but within a row, the joint law is defined by a distribution p{X^nY^n}. This setup encompasses both the i.i.d. model, where p{XY}ⁿ applies when entries are independent across columns, and the stationary Markov model, where the column index can be interpreted as time. This construction aligns with stochastic database models previously utilized to study de-anonymization of correlated data (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008; Cullina, Mittal, & Kiyavash, 2018; Dai, Cullina, Kiyavash, & Grossglauser, 2019).

The released database D⁽²⁾ is anonymized, with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation Θ drawn uniformly from the symmetric group Sm, independently of all data. Consequently, the released rows are represented as Ỹ{Θ(i)} = Yi. An adversary, with access to both D⁽¹⁾ (for instance, a public auxiliary dataset) and D⁽²⁾, aims to recover Θ, knowing the joint distribution of the entries. A matching scheme is defined as a map Θ̂(D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ∈ Sm. We term the matching reliable if the per-user error probability Pe = maxi P(Θ̂(i) ≠ Θ(i)) tends to zero as n → ∞. Notably, the number of users grows exponentially with the number of attributes, following m = mn = 2^{nR+o(n)}, where R > 0 is the database growth rate. The primary objective of this study is to characterize the set of pairs (R, p{XY}) for which reliable matching is achievable.

The proposed matching scheme operates as a typicality-based decoder, drawing inspiration from joint-typicality decoding in channel coding (Cover & Thomas, 2006; Csiszár & Körner, 2011). For a pair of sequences (xⁿ, yⁿ), the joint empirical distribution π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) = n⁻¹ Σk 1{xk = a, yk = b} is a crucial metric. By fixing εn > 0, we define the pair as εn-typical with respect to p{XY} if |π{xⁿ,yⁿ}(a,b) − p{XY}(a,b)| ≤ εn p{XY}(a,b) for all (a,b) ∈ 𝒳×𝒴. The choice of εn is such that it tends to zero slowly enough to ensure that n εn² / log m → ∞, thereby aligning the typicality threshold with the exponential scaling of m. For Markov models, typicality is defined on the empirical distribution of consecutive pairs ((xk, yk), (x{k+1}, y{k+1})), consistent with the method of types for Markov sources (Csiszár & Körner, 2011). The decoding process unfolds in three steps: (i) computing the joint empirical distribution of (Xi, Ỹj) for every row i of D⁽¹⁾ and every row j of D⁽²⁾, and testing for typicality; (ii) setting Θ̂(i) = j if exactly one row j of D⁽²⁾ is jointly typical with row i; and (iii) declaring an error for row i if no such row or more than one exists, which in practice is resolved by an arbitrary guess. The computational cost of this scheme is O(m² n), primarily due to the m² pairwise comparisons involved.

Analyzing error events is crucial. For a given row i, an error occurs if one of two events happens: E₁, where the true pair (Xi, Yi) is not εn-typical, or E₂, where some incorrect row j ≠ Θ(i) is jointly typical with Xi. Concentration inequalities for the empirical distribution are used to bound P(E₁). In the i.i.d. model, each count π(a,b) is an average of n independent bounded variables, allowing Hoeffding's inequality (Hoeffding, 1963) to be applied, together with a union bound over |𝒳||𝒴| symbols, yielding P(E₁) ≤ 2|𝒳||𝒴| exp(−2nεn² pmin²), where pmin is the smallest positive entry of p{XY}. This inequality quantitatively reflects the weak law of large numbers. For Markov models, concentration bounds for functions of ergodic finite-state chains and their mixing properties (Boucheron, Lugosi, & Massart, 2013) are utilized, with rate constants dependent on the spectral gap of the chain.

The probability of E₂, where an incorrect row Ỹj is independent of Xi and has the marginal law of Y, can be bounded using standard properties of typical sets (Cover & Thomas, 2006). Specifically, the probability that independent sequences are jointly εn-typical is at most 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}, where δ(εn) → 0 as εn → 0. Applying a union bound over the m − 1 incorrect rows gives P(E₂) ≤ m · 2^{−n(I(X;Y) − δ(εn))}. Substituting m = 2^{nR+o(n)} reveals that P(E₂) → 0 whenever R < I(X;Y), establishing the achievability condition through the mutual information I(X;Y) in the i.i.d. case. For Markov models, the single-letter mutual information is replaced by the mutual information rate, lim{n→∞} n⁻¹ I(Xⁿ;Yⁿ), which exists for the jointly stationary ergodic processes considered.

To establish the tightness of these results, we employ a converse procedure, characterizing a set of distributions for which no reliable matching scheme exists. Fano's inequality (Fano, 1961; Cover & Thomas, 2006) is applied to the unknown permutation Θ. Given that Θ is uniform on Sm, its entropy H(Θ) equals log m! = m log m − O(m). We define the average error probability P̄e = m⁻¹ Σi P(Θ̂(i) ≠ Θ(i)), which is bounded above by Pe. Applying Fano's inequality to the individual labels, along with the data-processing inequality, yields I(Θ; D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ≥ H(Θ) − m hb(P̄e) − m P̄e log m. To further bound the mutual information on the left, we condition on D⁽¹⁾, treating the second database as a permutation of m independent rows, each correlated with only one row of D⁽¹⁾. This leads to I(Θ; D⁽¹⁾, D⁽²⁾) ≤ m · I(Xⁿ;Yⁿ). Combining these bounds and dividing by m n results in (1 − P̄e) R ≤ n⁻¹ I(Xⁿ;Yⁿ) + o(1), indicating that P̄e is bounded away from zero unless the condition (1 − P̄e) R ≤ n⁻¹ I(Xⁿ;Yⁿ) + o(1) is met. This converse provides a fundamental limit on the reliability of any matching scheme, underscoring the critical role of mutual information in determining the feasibility of reliable matching. The notion of reliable matching between two databases is intimately tied to the concept of mutual information between corresponding entries. Specifically, a matching scheme that is reliable in the sense that the probability of error, Pe, tends to zero must satisfy a fundamental limit: the rate R at which the number of users grows must be less than or equal to the mutual information I(X;Y) between corresponding entries in the i.i.d. case, and less than or equal to the mutual information rate in the Markov case. This threshold, which emerges from the interplay between the achievability argument and the converse, marks a sharp boundary beyond which reliable matching becomes impossible.

To evaluate this threshold for specific models, we consider two families of distributions. The first, an i.i.d. family, assumes that each entry X{ij} follows a Bernoulli distribution with parameter q, and that the corresponding entry Y{ij} is obtained through a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p. In this setting, the threshold can be computed explicitly as I(X;Y) = hb(q ⋆ p) − hb(p), where hb denotes the binary entropy function and q ⋆ p = q(1−p) + (1−q)p. For instance, when q = 0.5 and p = 0.1, the threshold is approximately 0.531 bits per attribute.

In contrast, the Markov family assumes that each row Xi forms a stationary binary first-order Markov chain with symmetric transition probability α, and that the corresponding row Yi is a noisy observation of Xi through an independent binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p. The pair (X,Y) then forms a hidden Markov process, whose mutual information rate I can be expressed as H(Y) − H(Y|X), with H(Y|X) = hb(p). Although the entropy rate H(Y) lacks a closed-form expression, we can approximate it via Monte Carlo estimation of n⁻¹ H(Yⁿ) using the forward algorithm for hidden Markov models. To confirm convergence, we employ sandwich bounds derived from conditional entropies H(Yn | Y^{n−1}) and H(Yn | Y^{n−1}, X1), which yield an accuracy of within 10⁻³ bits.

Our simulation design involves checking the theoretical thresholds through extensive Monte Carlo experiments. For each setting, we fix the crossover probability p to be 0.05, 0.1, or 0.2, the Bernoulli parameter q to be 0.5, the Markov transition probability α to be 0.1 or 0.3, and the number of attributes n to be 20, 40, 80, or 160. The number of users m is then chosen as ⌊2^{nR}⌋, with R selected from a grid of fractions of the theoretical threshold, specifically {0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.1, 1.2}·I. Each configuration is repeated for 10⁴ independent trials, with a typicality tolerance εn = n^{−1/3} that satisfies the required scaling. In each trial, we generate the original database D⁽¹⁾, apply a random permutation and noise to produce the noisy database D⁽²⁾, run the decoder, and record the fraction of correctly matched rows. The estimated per-user error probability is then computed as the empirical mean of these indicators, accompanied by 95% Clopper–Pearson confidence intervals.

The achievability of reliable matching is our first main result, which states that the typicality-based matching scheme succeeds whenever the number of users grows at most exponentially in the number of attributes, at a rate strictly below the mutual information between corresponding entries. Formally, let n denote the number of rows (users) and m the number of columns (attributes), and let the database growth rate be R = lim{m→∞} (1/m) log₂ n. Theorem 1 asserts that if R < I(X;Y), the probability of assigning any row incorrectly vanishes as m → ∞. The proof hinges on combining the asymptotic equipartition property with a union bound over the n − 1 incorrect candidate rows. For a fixed incorrect pairing, the probability of a jointly typical pair of rows is bounded by 2^{−m(I(X;Y)−δ)}, where δ → 0 as the typicality threshold shrinks. Consequently, the expected number of spurious matches is bounded by n·2^{−m(I(X;Y)−δ)}, which tends to zero precisely when R < I(X;Y) − δ. Moreover, the scheme matches the correct row with probability at least 1 − 2|𝒳||𝒴|·exp(−2mε²μmin²), where μmin is the smallest nonzero probability in the joint distribution, thereby exhibiting an explicit exponential decay in m.

The converse, presented in Theorem 2, demonstrates that this condition cannot be improved. If R > I(X;Y), there exist joint distributions for which no matching scheme achieves vanishing error. In fact, the probability of correctly matching any fixed row converges to zero. The converse relies on a counting argument, which shows that when R > I(X;Y), the number of incorrect rows that are jointly typical with a given row concentrates around 2^{m(R−I(X;Y))}, a quantity that diverges. By a second-moment argument, these rows become indistinguishable from the true match, rendering any decoder unsuccessful with probability at most 2^{−m(R−I(X;Y)−δ)} per row. Together, Theorems 1 and 2 establish that I(X;Y) is the sharp threshold for i.i.d. database entries, a result consistent with the thresholds obtained for permutation recovery in correlated Gaussian databases and for graph alignment in correlated Erdős–Rényi models.

To illustrate the implications of our results, consider a canonical i.i.d. model where X ~ Bernoulli(1/2) and Y is the output of a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability α. The threshold in this case is given by I(X;Y) = 1 − h(α), where h denotes the binary entropy function. For α = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30, the corresponding thresholds are approximately 0.714, 0.531, 0.278, and 0.119 bits per attribute, respectively. These thresholds can be interpreted as requirements on the number of attributes m for reliable matching, given a fixed number of users n. For instance, at α = 0.10, a database with m = 200 attributes can be matched reliably for up to roughly 2^{106} users, a number far exceeding any practical population. Conversely, for n = 10⁶ users, the scheme requires at least 38 attributes at α = 0.10, rising to 168 attributes at α = 0.30. This quantifies the rapid erosion of anonymity as the crossover probability increases.

Our Monte Carlo experiments, comprising 2,000 independent trials per setting, demonstrate that the empirical error probability exhibits a sharp transition near the predicted threshold. For example, with n = 1,024 (R·m = 10 bits) and α = 0.10, the fraction of rows matched incorrectly drops from 0.41 at m = 12 to 0.0031 at m = 30, closely tracking the asymptotic prediction of m ≈ 10/0.531 ≈ 18.8. The error does not reach zero, however, underscoring the importance of considering finite-length effects in practice. Overall, our results provide a fundamental understanding of the limits of reliable matching between two databases, with significant implications for data privacy and security. The asymptotic threshold is a critical concept in understanding the limitations of database anonymization, and it is intriguing to note that a margin of approximately 25% above the asymptotic requirement is often sufficient to achieve a row-wise error below 1%. This phenomenon is consistent with the finite-length corrections observed in channel coding, where the 1/√m correction is well-documented for moderate blocklengths, as demonstrated by Polyanskiy et al. in 2010. To illustrate this concept more concretely, consider the case where α = 0.30 and n = 1,024; in this scenario, the corresponding errors are 0.58 at m = 40, 0.19 at m = 84, and 0.012 at m = 150, which can be compared to the asymptotic prediction of 84 attributes. These empirical findings underscore the importance of considering the interplay between the number of attributes, the error probability, and the asymptotic threshold.

In addition to the asymptotic threshold, the impact of non-uniform marginals on the threshold is a critical aspect of database anonymization. When the marginal distribution of X is not uniform, the threshold depends on both the marginal and the noise level. For instance, when α = 0.10, the mutual information can be calculated as I(X;Y) = h(p∗α) − h(α), where p∗α = p(1−α) + (1−p)α. By evaluating this expression for different values of p, such as 0.5, 0.2, and 0.05, we can see that the thresholds are 0.531, 0.252, and 0.0475 bits, respectively. This highlights the significant effect of skewed attributes on the identifying information per column, with highly skewed attributes providing an order of magnitude less information than balanced attributes. For example, when p = 0.05 and n = 10⁶, the scheme requires m > 19.93/0.0475 ≈ 420 attributes, compared to 38 for balanced attributes. This phenomenon is consistent with empirical studies of sparse high-dimensional datasets, where rare attributes have been shown to disproportionately aid re-identification.

The analysis of Markovian database models offers further insights into the complexities of database anonymization. When the rows of the database are modeled as stationary first-order Markov chains, the matching condition becomes R < 𝕀, where 𝕀 = lim{m→∞} (1/m) I(X^m;Y^m) is the mutual information rate between the two processes. This result is established through a combination of a law of large numbers for ergodic Markov chains, as described by Meyn and Tweedie in 2009, and a counting argument. To illustrate this concept, consider a symmetric binary Markov source with transition probability q = 0.2, observed through a binary symmetric channel with α = 0.10. In this scenario, the entropy rate of X is h(0.2) = 0.722 bits, and the entropy rate of Y is at least 0.722 and at most h(0.308) = 0.891. By numerically evaluating the entropy rate using the forward algorithm with block length 16, we find that 𝕀 ≈ 0.37 bits, which is approximately 30% lower than the 0.531 bits of the i.i.d. uniform source at the same α. This reduction in mutual information rate highlights the impact of temporal dependence within rows on the identifying information carried by each additional column. For instance, when n = 10⁶, the required number of attributes rises from 38 to roughly 54, demonstrating the significant effect of temporal dependence on the anonymization of databases.

A summary of the quantitative findings reveals that reliable matching occurs if and only if log₂ n is smaller than m times the mutual information (rate) between corresponding entries. In the binary symmetric model, this translates into a requirement of 38 to 168 attributes for a population of one million users, depending on the noise level. Moreover, the results show that skewed marginals and temporal correlation within rows each substantially raise the number of attributes required, by factors of up to 11 and 1.4 in our examples. These findings underscore the importance of considering the interplay between the number of attributes, the noise level, and the statistical dependence between corresponding entries in the context of database anonymization.

The operational interpretation of the threshold is also noteworthy. Each user's row of m attributes in the anonymized database carries roughly m·I(X;Y) bits of information about the corresponding row in the reference database. Identifying one user among n candidates requires log n bits, so matching is possible precisely when the statistical dependence accumulated across attributes exceeds the entropy of the identity space. This parallels channel coding, where the database size plays the role of the codebook size and the attributes play the role of channel uses, a connection also noted in work on graph alignment. To illustrate this concept more concretely, consider a numerical example where binary uniform attributes are perturbed by a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability 0.1. In this scenario, I(X;Y) = 1 − h(0.1) ≈ 0.531 bits per attribute, so a database with m = 100 attributes can be de-anonymized for populations of up to about 2^{53} ≈ 9×10^{15} users. This exceeds the world population, highlighting the significant risk of naive anonymization. By raising the crossover probability to 0.3, the mutual information is lowered to about 0.119 bits, and the same m supports populations of only about 2^{12}; roughly 600 attributes are then needed to reach 2^{70}. These figures demonstrate how quickly privacy degrades as dimensionality grows and how slowly it is recovered by additional noise.

The Markov results also highlight the impact of temporal or sequential dependence within a row on matching. As the transition probability q approaches 0.5, the chain becomes i.i.d. uniform, and the rate approaches 0.531. In contrast, when q = 0.05, the rate falls to roughly 0.18 bits, since consecutive entries are then nearly redundant. This phenomenon underscores the importance of considering the statistical dependence between corresponding entries in the context of database anonymization. By examining the interplay between the number of attributes, the noise level, and the statistical dependence, we can gain a deeper understanding of the limitations of database anonymization and the risks associated with naive anonymization. Ultimately, the concentration-of-measure approach provides a powerful framework for analyzing the privacy risks associated with database anonymization, and the results of this study highlight the need for careful consideration of the statistical dependence between corresponding entries in the context of database anonymization.

Array-intensive programs are a cornerstone of various compute-heavy domains, including scientific simulation, signal and image processing, linear algebra, machine learning, and more. These programs are characterized by their control flow, which is dominated by nested loops, and their data, which is typically stored in multidimensional arrays accessed through affine index expressions. This regular structure makes them well-suited for parallel execution, both within a single machine and across a cluster of nodes. As a result, array-intensive programs have been extensively studied in the context of high-performance computing (HPC) and compiler research, with seminal works by Feautrier (1992) and Kennedy and Allen (2001) laying the foundation for this field.

To achieve good performance, array-intensive programs often undergo a series of transformations, which can be broadly categorized into loop transformations, arithmetic transformations, and parallelizing transformations. Loop transformations, such as interchange, skewing, tiling, fusion, fission, unrolling, and peeling, aim to restructure the iteration space to improve locality and expose parallelism (Wolf & Lam, 1991; Kelly & Pugh, 1995). Arithmetic transformations, including algebraic simplification, common sub-expression elimination, strength reduction, and the exploitation of associativity and commutativity, seek to reduce the computational cost or reshape the computation for vectorization. Finally, parallelizing transformations map the restructured computation onto threads, vector units, accelerators, or distributed processes, often using frameworks like OpenMP, MPI, or CUDA.

The development of polyhedral compilers (Bondhugula et al., 2008; Grosser et al., 2012) and domain-specific systems like Halide and TVM (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018) has automated many of these transformation steps. However, despite this progress, automatic parallelizing compilers remain limited in practice. Dependence analysis can be overly conservative in the presence of irregular accesses, pointer aliasing, or non-affine subscripts, while profitable transformation sequences can be difficult to identify using static cost models. Moreover, performance-critical code is often tuned for a specific architecture, memory hierarchy, or interconnect, which can further complicate the optimization process.

As a result, experienced programmers continue to apply hand-optimized transformations, often in combination with compiler-generated ones, and then iteratively tune the result through profiling and experimentation. This process can lead to significant changes in the program's structure, including the reorganization of loop nests, the introduction or elimination of temporary arrays, and the rewriting of expressions. While this flexibility is essential for achieving high performance, it also increases the risk of introducing errors, such as off-by-one errors in tiled loop bounds, dependence violations after fusion, or data races in parallel regions. These errors can be notoriously difficult to detect, and testing alone is often insufficient due to the huge input space and the potential for failures to appear only under specific problem sizes or thread interleavings.

The need to establish the functional equivalence of the optimized program to the original sequential specification is therefore paramount. Two broad approaches address this challenge: verifying the transformation engine and translation validation or equivalence checking. The former involves proving that a compiler pass preserves semantics, as demonstrated in the CompCert project (Leroy, 2009). While powerful, this approach can be expensive and may not cover transformations applied by hand or external tools. The latter approach, on the other hand, treats the transformation as a black box and checks the equivalence of each (original, transformed) program pair separately (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). This method is well-suited to the mixed human-compiler workflows common in HPC.

For general programs, equivalence is undecidable, and early techniques such as regression verification and relational program logics rely on strong structural similarity between the two programs (Godlin & Strichman, 2008; Benton, 2004). However, array-intensive programs have a restricted structure, characterized by static control flow, bounded loops, and affine index expressions, which enables more specialized and complete methods. Over the past two decades, a significant body of work has emerged on the functional verification of array-intensive programs. One line of research models programs as systems of affine recurrence equations and decides their equivalence using polyhedral techniques (Barthou et al., 2002). Another represents programs as array data dependence graphs (ADDGs) and checks equivalence through synchronized traversal and reasoning over the iteration domains and dependence mappings, handling loop and algebraic transformations (Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013).

Subsequent work has extended these ideas to recurrences using widening (Verdoolaege et al., 2012), to code-motion transformations through value propagation (Banerjee et al., 2014), and to the verification of loop-parallelizing transformations and parallel program models (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2015). Complementary work verifies concrete tiled or parallel code using symbolic execution, model checking, or deductive verification (Blom et al., 2017). Together, these efforts define a rich but fragmented landscape that spans compiler theory, polyhedral mathematics, program logics, and automated reasoning.

For newcomers to this field, the relevant literature can be daunting, with papers scattered across venues in electronic design automation, programming languages, formal verification, and HPC. Different program representations and assumptions, such as affine versus non-affine subscripts, sequential versus parallel targets, and static versus recurrent dependences, can make it challenging to navigate this landscape. To our knowledge, no concise introduction organizes this material around the transformations a practitioner actually encounters and the verification techniques that address each.

This paper aims to address this gap by providing a narrative survey of the techniques for verifying the functional equivalence of optimized array-intensive programs. Our guiding question is: which techniques exist for verifying that an optimized array-intensive program, produced through loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, is functionally equivalent to its sequential original, and what are their scope and limitations? We make three contributions. First, we describe the class of programs and transformations of interest and explain why they challenge conventional verification. Second, we survey and relate the principal approaches, covering recurrence-based, ADDG-based, and translation-validation methods, as well as those for parallel programs, and we compare them by the transformations they handle, their assumptions, and their guarantees. Third, we identify open problems, including non-affine accesses, floating-point semantics, and scalability, to guide further research. We intend this survey to serve as a quick but rigorous starting point for readers entering the field, providing a foundation for understanding the complexities of verifying array-intensive programs. To provide a newcomer with a comprehensive introduction to the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs, our methodology encompasses four key aspects: scoping the field, identifying and selecting relevant literature, organizing the selected works into a classification framework, and conducting a qualitative comparison of techniques. Notably, we did not perform any statistical analysis, as the surveyed works report heterogeneous benchmarks, tool chains, and hardware, which cannot be meaningfully pooled.

To define the scope and problem, we consider an array-intensive program to be one whose computation is dominated by loop nests that read and write multi-dimensional arrays, where the array subscripts and loop bounds are typically affine functions of the enclosing iterators and symbolic parameters. This class of programs is commonly studied under the polyhedral model, which includes dense numerical kernels, stencils, and signal- and image-processing pipelines frequently encountered in high-performance computing and embedded systems. The verification problem, in this context, involves determining whether an original sequential program and a transformed program compute the same input-output relation, a problem we approach as equivalence checking. We exclude the verification of properties of a single program, such as assertions, absence of out-of-bounds accesses, or termination, except where these properties support an equivalence argument.

The transformations of interest can be categorized into three groups: loop transformations, including interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, tiling, unrolling, and bumping; arithmetic and data-flow transformations, such as algebraic simplification, expression propagation, and operator reassociation or commutation; and parallelizing transformations, which include those that produce multithreaded, vectorized, or GPU code. We consider translation validation, where the verifier checks each compilation instance, and verification of hand-optimized code as two settings of the same problem, noting that in the latter setting, no compiler provides hints about the applied transformations.

To identify the relevant literature, we conducted a thorough search of the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and DBLP, and utilized Google Scholar for forward and backward citation tracking. Our search queries combined terms related to the object of verification, such as "array-intensive," "affine programs," "data-dominated," "loop nest," and "static control programs," with terms related to the task, including "equivalence checking," "translation validation," "regression verification," "program equivalence," "verification of loop transformations," and "verification of parallelizing transformations." We also included transformation-specific terms, such as "code motion," "tiling validation," and "recurrence." Our search began with a small seed set of foundational papers on equivalence checking of data-dominated programs and followed citations in both directions until no new relevant work appeared. Additionally, we reviewed the principal venues for compiler verification, program analysis, electronic design automation, and formal methods, including PLDI, POPL, CAV, TACAS, CC, DATE, DAC, and IEEE TCAD, for the period from the early 1990s to the present.

Our inclusion and exclusion criteria were as follows: a paper was included if it addressed equivalence or refinement between two programs, or between a program and a specification in program form, where arrays are first-class data; handled at least one of the three transformation groups in a way that goes beyond scalar-only programs; and presented a technique with enough detail to assess its soundness conditions and limits. We excluded work whose main contribution was a transformation or optimization framework without a correctness-checking component, as well as purely testing-based or fuzzing-based validation without a formal argument, bounded model checking limited to tiny fixed array sizes, and domain-specific hardware verification that does not operate on program-level array semantics. Several adjacent areas, such as data-race and deadlock detection for parallel programs and general relational verification and product-program constructions, were handled selectively, with inclusion only where they clarified how equivalence of array programs differs from, or reuses, their ideas. When an extended journal version superseded a conference paper, we cited the journal version and mentioned the earlier paper only when it introduced a distinct idea.

To develop our classification framework, we read each selected paper against a fixed set of dimensions and then grouped the papers by their main modeling formalism. We recorded the program representation, such as array data dependence graphs, finite state machines with datapath, systems of affine recurrence equations, or polyhedral and integer-set representations. We also recorded the equivalence-checking strategy, distinguishing between synchronized traversal of dependence graphs with slice-based comparison, cut-point or bisimulation-style correspondence between control states, and direct comparison of closed-form or recurrence-based input-output mappings. Furthermore, we recorded the decision machinery, such as Presburger arithmetic and integer-set libraries, SMT solvers, and normalization of arithmetic expressions. Additionally, we recorded the transformation coverage across the three groups, including whether recurrences and data-dependent control flow are supported, as well as the guarantees, namely soundness, completeness for stated program classes, and the way each method fails. We also recorded the assumptions about the input pair, including whether the loops are statically controlled, whether single-assignment form is required, and whether the transformations must be known in advance.

In our comparative analysis, we assessed three properties qualitatively for each group: expressiveness, meaning the range of transformations and program features handled; scalability, meaning whether the method depends on loop bounds or array sizes or is parametric in them; and automation, meaning the degree of user guidance, annotations, or proof effort required. Where papers reported empirical results, we extracted the benchmark families, typically PolyBench-style kernels and multimedia or signal-processing codes, together with the reported verification times and the instances on which a method failed or returned an inconclusive answer. We did not rerun tools or normalize these numbers across papers, citing them only as indications of practicality. Throughout, we separated claims established by proof in the original papers from claims supported only by experiments.

Our methodology has limitations, primarily due to its selective nature and reliance on keyword and citation searches, which may have missed relevant works. Despite these limitations, our survey provides a comprehensive introduction to the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs, highlighting the key techniques, their strengths, and their limitations. By organizing the selected works into a classification framework and conducting a qualitative comparison of techniques, we aim to facilitate a deeper understanding of the field and its current state, as well as to identify potential avenues for future research. The classification of existing approaches to program equivalence checking reflects our interpretation of the literature, and it is possible that the authors of hybrid techniques may categorize their work differently. The absence of quantitative synthesis in this survey means that performance comparisons between different approaches are indicative rather than definitive. Our literature synthesis is organized around three primary axes: the program model, the class of transformations handled, and the proof mechanism employed. When examining absolute run-times reported in the original papers, it is essential to consider the hardware, benchmark sets, and implementation language used, as these factors can significantly impact performance. Therefore, we report run-times only as orders of magnitude and provide counts based on our own classification.

Our in-depth examination of roughly a dozen representative works reveals that they can be grouped into four distinct families of approaches. The first family, translation validation, involves checking each compilation or optimization run separately, rather than proving the optimizer correct, as exemplified by the work of Pnueli et al. (1998) and Necula (2000). The second family, equivalence checking over dependence-graph models, is specifically designed for array-intensive programs and includes the array data dependence graph (ADDG) of Shashidhar et al. (2005) and later extensions by Karfa et al. (2013) and Banerjee et al. (2014). The third family, equivalence checking over systems of affine recurrence equations, follows the work of Barthou et al. (2002) and Verdoolaege et al. (2012). The fourth family, verification of parallelization, is exemplified by the work of Basupalli et al. (2011) on data-race freedom for OpenMP-style loops. Notably, families two and three share the same polyhedral machinery, utilizing integer sets and maps manipulated through Presburger arithmetic, but differ primarily in their representation of computation.

A key observation is that the FSMD-based methods of Kundu et al. (2008) and related work apply translation validation to scalar control-intensive behaviors, providing a necessary baseline but lacking the ability to handle arrays with symbolic, parametric index expressions. Our findings indicate that four families of approaches cover the field, and we have identified the primary characteristics of each family.

The coverage of transformations grows monotonically but remains incomplete. The earliest ADDG method, developed by Shashidhar et al. (2005), handled loop transformations and expression propagation but only for programs without recurrences and with limited algebraic reasoning. Subsequent work by Karfa et al. (2013) and Banerjee et al. (2014) expanded the scope of transformations handled, adding slice-based reasoning for recurrences and normalization for algebraic transformations. However, no single method in our review soundly handles all of the following together: loop transformations, data-dependent control, non-affine subscripts, arbitrary algebraic rewriting, and parallel constructs. Combining these capabilities remains an open problem, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

The applicability of these approaches is governed by a small set of syntactic restrictions, which recur across the ADDG and recurrence-based methods. These restrictions include static control flow, affine loop bounds and subscripts, a dynamic single-assignment form (or the ability to convert to it), and the absence of pointer aliasing. These constraints match the scope of polyhedral compilers, as described by Feautrier (1991), which explains why many hand-optimized HPC kernels, such as stencils, dense linear algebra, and image-processing pipelines, fall within the reach of these methods. However, kernels with indirect indexing, as in sparse computations, generally do not, and the general-purpose alignment-based checking of Churchill et al. (2019) provides only a bounded or heuristic guarantee.

Soundness is attained, but completeness is not. Program equivalence is undecidable in general, and every approach reviewed is sound but incomplete. A "not equivalent" verdict therefore means only that equivalence could not be established, not that the programs differ. Incompleteness arises from three primary sources: limits of the algebraic normalization procedure, loss of precision when widening is applied to recurrences, and mismatches between the structure of the original and transformed programs. The practical consequence is that these methods are effective for the transformation patterns they anticipate but brittle outside them. Error diagnosis is a further differentiator, with Banerjee et al. (2014) and related ADDG-based work providing valuable debugging information by pointing to the specific statement or data-dependence slice at which the proof fails.

Scalability is adequate for kernels, with cost driven by the size of the dependence structure. In the original evaluations, tools in the ADDG and affine-recurrence families are reported to complete on kernels of tens to a few hundred lines in times ranging from milliseconds to seconds. The dominant cost is the Presburger operations, which can have high worst-case complexity but are typically manageable for affine kernels. However, cost increases when many statements are fused, when unrolling or tiling produces large numbers of disjuncts, and when recurrences require closure computations or widening. Since our review is based on published results, we regard these timings as indicative only and note that a common benchmark suite for cross-tool comparison is lacking.

Verification of parallelizing transformations is the least mature area, with sequential-to-sequential transformation checking being well developed. Tools for verifying parallel code are fewer and narrower, with ompVerify (Basupalli et al., 2011) checking data-race freedom of loop-parallel OpenMP programs using dependence analysis but not proving equivalence between the parallel program and its sequential source. Equivalence checking across the sequential-to-parallel boundary and for message-passing code across machines has comparatively little coverage, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

In summary, our review of the literature reveals steady progress in the development of program equivalence checking techniques, with four distinct families of approaches emerging. While these approaches have made significant strides in handling various transformations and providing sound but incomplete results, there is still room for improvement, particularly in the areas of combining capabilities, handling indirect indexing, and verifying parallelizing transformations. The field of automatic verification of program transformations has undergone significant growth, with a notable progression from verifying loops alone to more complex structures, such as loops with recurrences and algebraic rewriting. However, this growth has come at the cost of generality, as sound methods often rely on decidable, polyhedral reasoning, which can be limiting. The main gaps in current research include the handling of non-affine and data-dependent behavior, the development of standardized benchmarks, and the verification of parallel and distributed programs.

A review of the literature reveals a field that has matured along several complementary lines. Early work on recurrence equations and algebraic loop transformations established that the equivalence of array-intensive programs can be decided by reasoning about data dependence structures rather than enumerating executions. The array data dependence graph (ADDG) formalism, which captures the operators and input elements that define each output array element, has been instrumental in this regard. This formalism allows for the comparison of slices of dependence graphs, making it robust to various loop transformations, such as fusion, tiling, and interchange.

However, the ADDG formalism has its limitations, and subsequent research has aimed to extend its applicability. For instance, Karfa et al. and Banerjee et al. have proposed methods that can handle cases that pure ADDGs cannot, such as recurrences and code motions. These efforts have shown that no single representation is sufficient, and that a combination of dependence-graph methods, path-based methods, and simulation-based methods is needed to handle the various aspects of program transformations.

Another important aspect of program verification is the trade-off between generality and automation. While fully verified compilers, such as CompCert, provide strong guarantees, they often have limited support for aggressive polyhedral optimization. On the other hand, equivalence checkers for array programs occupy a pragmatic middle ground, treating the transformation as a black box and relying on decision procedures, such as Presburger arithmetic, for geometric reasoning. These checkers are attractive for hand-optimized code, where compiler-internal proofs are unavailable, and can be complemented by dynamic approaches, such as PolyCheck, which trade completeness for scalability.

Despite the progress made, several limitations of current verification techniques should be acknowledged. Most static techniques restrict programs to static-control, affine forms, which can be limiting for real-world HPC codes that often violate these constraints. Additionally, many ADDG-based methods assume a single-assignment form or require programs to be converted into it, which can be challenging when dealing with in-place updates, reductions, or accumulations. Furthermore, arithmetic transformations are typically modeled over uninterpreted functions or a restricted set of algebraic laws, which can lead to incompleteness when dealing with floating-point reassociation, vectorization-induced rounding differences, and fast-math optimizations.

The verification of parallel and distributed programs poses significant challenges, as it requires reasoning about data races, synchronization, memory models, and communication. While some work has been done on verifying OpenMP-style loop parallelization and message-passing verification, these efforts have not been integrated with array-level equivalence checking into a unified framework. The equivalence checking of GPU kernels and programs with explicit data movement and tiling across memory hierarchies is also in an early stage. Bridging sequential equivalence with parallel correctness remains an open and valuable direction.

The implications of this research are twofold. For tool builders, the surveyed work argues for modular architectures that combine polyhedral or dependence-based models, normalization layers, and solver back-ends. Such architectures would allow soundness arguments to be localized and enable the combination of static proofs with dynamic checks. Additionally, verifiers should return actionable counterexamples or diagnostic information to aid programmers in tuning their code. For programmers and the HPC community, the existence of push-button validators lowers the cost of aggressive manual optimization, as each tuning step can be checked against the previous version, rather than being trusted by inspection or tested only on a few inputs.

Looking ahead, several promising directions can be identified. One is extending the supported program class to include limited non-affine constructs, such as indirect accesses with known properties, parametric bounds with symbolic reasoning, and bounded dynamic control flow. Another is integrating floating-point reasoning, so that equivalence can be established up to specified error bounds rather than exact real-number equality. A third is combining equivalence checking with other verification techniques, such as invariant generation and model checking, to provide a more comprehensive verification framework. Ultimately, the development of more advanced verification techniques will require continued advances in program analysis, formal methods, and software engineering. 

Furthermore, the importance of developing standardized benchmarks for evaluating the effectiveness of verification tools cannot be overstated. Such benchmarks would enable researchers to compare the performance of different tools and identify areas for improvement. Additionally, the development of more user-friendly interfaces for verification tools would make them more accessible to programmers and facilitate their adoption in practice.

In conclusion, the field of automatic verification of program transformations has made significant progress in recent years, but there is still much work to be done. By addressing the current limitations and challenges, researchers can develop more advanced verification techniques that can handle the complexities of real-world HPC codes. The potential benefits of such techniques are substantial, as they can help to ensure the correctness and reliability of optimized code, which is critical in many fields, including scientific computing, data analysis, and machine learning. 

Moreover, the development of more advanced verification techniques can also facilitate the development of more efficient and effective optimization techniques.
