For instance, we can expect to see the development of more sophisticated verification algorithms and tools, which can handle the complexities of real-world optimized code. We can also expect to see the development of more effective and efficient verification frameworks, which can integrate multiple verification techniques and tools. Additionally, we can expect to see the development of more user-friendly interfaces for verification tools, which can make them more accessible to programmers and facilitate their adoption in practice.

Overall, the future of automatic verification of program transformations is bright, with many opportunities for innovation and advancement. As researchers continue to develop more advanced verification techniques, we can expect to see significant improvements in the correctness, reliability, and performance of optimized code, which will have a major impact on many fields and applications.

The use of citations as a metric for evaluating scientific output has become a ubiquitous practice, underpinning journal rankings, institutional assessments, funding decisions, and even individual career progression in many countries (Garfield, 2006; Hicks et al., 2015). However, the distribution of citations is notoriously skewed, with a small proportion of articles garnering the majority of citations, while a significant share receives few or none (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976). This skewness is a major concern, as it renders the mean-based journal impact factor a poor descriptor of the typical article, and its use for evaluating individual papers has been subject to repeated criticism (Seglen, 1997; Larivière et al., 2016). At the lower end of the citation distribution lie uncited articles, which are those that, within a defined observation window, have not been cited by any other indexed document. The study of non-citation has a long history in bibliometrics, with early estimates suggesting that a substantial fraction of the scientific literature remained uncited for years (de Solla Price, 1965; Garfield, 1973). Some provocative claims even proposed that most papers were never cited (Hamilton, 1990, 1991), although these claims were later shown to be exaggerated due to methodological limitations, such as the failure to separate research articles from other document types and the neglect of differences across fields and citation windows (Pendlebury, 1991; Garfield, 1998).

Subsequent analyses, based on more careful designs, have demonstrated that the proportion of uncited papers is strongly dependent on discipline, document type, publication year, and database coverage (Egghe et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2009; Van Noorden, 2017). Notably, uncitedness tends to be lower in biomedical and life sciences, where reference lists are lengthy and citation practices are intense, and higher in the humanities and certain social sciences, where books, local audiences, and slower citation dynamics prevail (Nederhof, 2006; Hyland and Jiang, 2018). However, it is essential to recognize that non-citation does not necessarily imply a lack of value, as articles may be read, used in teaching, incorporated into clinical or public policy practice, or discussed in the media without generating formal citations (Bornmann, 2014; Thelwall et al., 2013). Furthermore, citations are influenced by social and structural factors, such as the visibility of the journal, language, author reputation, collaboration networks, international coauthorship, and the degree of indexing in major databases (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008; Tahamtan et al., 2016). Despite these limitations, in evaluation systems that rely on citation counts, an uncited article is effectively invisible, and a journal with a high proportion of uncited articles may face reputational and financial consequences. Therefore, examining the percentage of non-citation offers a complementary perspective to average-based metrics, as it describes the lower tail of the distribution and signals how effectively a journal integrates its content into the scholarly conversation.

Public health is a fascinating area for investigating this phenomenon, as it is an inherently multidisciplinary field that brings together epidemiology, biostatistics, health policy and management, and the social and human sciences (Almeida Filho, 2000; Nunes, 2005). In Brazil, this field is known as "saúde coletiva" and has its own distinct intellectual identity, shaped by the sanitary reform movement and a strong articulation with the national health system (Paim and Almeida Filho, 1998; Luz, 2009). The Brazilian public health community has established a large postgraduate network and a set of national journals that publish mostly in Portuguese, but also increasingly in English and Spanish. Many of these journals are open access, indexed in regional repositories such as SciELO, and several are also indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science (Packer, 2009; Meneghini et al., 2008). Their dual mission—communicating with local practitioners and policymakers while reaching international readers—makes the citation profile of these periodicals particularly relevant. While citation patterns in Brazilian journals have been explored in some areas, mainly focusing on impact factors, language effects, and the international visibility of Latin American science (Rios-Gonzalez, 2014; Packer and Meneghini, 2006; Meneghini and Packer, 2007), these analyses often rely on aggregated indicators that conceal within-journal heterogeneity.

Moreover, the proportion of articles that never receive any citation, and whether journals within a single national field differ in this respect, have received relatively little attention. To our knowledge, no study has examined non-citation in public health journals, either nationally or internationally. Existing analyses of uncited papers in health sciences have focused on clinical specialties, nursing, or general medicine (Weale et al., 2004; Wallace et al., 2009), leaving a significant gap for a multidisciplinary field with strong local roots. This gap is important for several reasons. First, Brazilian science policy agencies, such as CAPES and CNPq, use citation-based indicators and journal classification systems (Qualis) in the evaluation of graduate programs and researchers, so that differences among journals have practical consequences for authors' strategies (Barata, 2016). Second, editors need descriptive evidence on how often their articles go uncited and how fast this proportion declines in the years following publication, in order to assess editorial policies, internationalization efforts, and the effects of language choices. Third, from a theoretical perspective, comparing journals of a single national field enables an assessment of whether disciplinary orientation, for instance epidemiological versus social-science-oriented content, is associated with differential citation behavior, as suggested by studies of cognitive and structural determinants of citation (Didegah and Thelwall, 2013; Onodera and Yoshikane, 2015).

In this study, we aim to address the following questions: What proportion of articles published in Brazilian public health journals remains uncited, and how does this proportion differ among journals? Do journals form distinct groups in terms of non-citation? How does the percentage of non-citation evolve during the first three years after publication, and are there journals in which it declines consistently? We focus on eight journals indexed in Scopus and on articles published between 2008 and 2012, a period that allows an adequate citation window. By examining these questions, we seek to provide a comprehensive understanding of non-citation in Brazilian public health journals and to shed light on the dynamics of citation patterns in this field. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we provide the first systematic description of non-citation in a national public health literature, establishing a benchmark for future comparisons. Second, our analysis offers insights into the factors that influence citation behavior in public health journals, which can inform editorial policies and internationalization strategies. Third, our study contributes to the ongoing debate about the role of citations in evaluating scientific output, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complexities of citation patterns and the limitations of citation-based metrics. The dynamics of citation patterns in applied, multidisciplinary fields, such as public health, are complex and multifaceted. To better understand these dynamics, we conducted a retrospective, descriptive bibliometric study of articles published in Brazilian public health journals, leveraging the capabilities of Scopus, a comprehensive database that indexes a larger number of Latin American and Brazilian titles than the Web of Science. The choice of Scopus was motivated by its reliable article-level citation counts and export functions, which have been widely recognized in the literature (Falagas et al., 2008; Mongeon & Paul-Hus, 2016).

Our study design involved identifying journals through the Scopus source list, using the subject area "Medicine" and the subcategory "Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health," filtered by country of publication (Brazil). We applied a set of inclusion criteria to ensure that only journals that were active and indexed in Scopus throughout 2008-2012, published predominantly in the public health/collective health field, and published at least 100 citable documents over the study period were included in our analysis. This resulted in a sample of eight journals: Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista de Saúde Pública, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, Physis: Revista de Saúde Coletiva, Interface – Comunicação, Saúde, Educação, Saúde e Sociedade, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos. Notably, the last four journals are considered more closely aligned with the social sciences and humanities, whereas the first four have a stronger biomedical and epidemiological orientation, a distinction that we used only for interpretation and not for selecting articles.

We retrieved all documents published between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2012, a five-year window that allowed every article at least a minimum of several years of exposure to citation. To analyze non-citation within a fixed three-year citation window after publication, we only considered document types that are typically cited, such as original articles, review articles, and short communications/research notes. Editorials, letters, errata, book reviews, interviews, obituaries, and news items were excluded, as they are generally cited rarely and can inflate non-citation rates (Moed & van Leeuwen, 1995; Van Noorden, 2017). We also removed duplicate records, identified by DOI, title, and volume/page, to ensure data integrity.

Our data extraction process involved exporting records in CSV format in a single session, which allowed us to freeze citation counts at a common date, referred to as the census date. We extracted fields such as authors, title, source title, year, volume, issue, pages, DOI, document type, language, affiliations, and total number of citations received. The data were then processed in a relational database, enabling us to obtain year-by-year citation counts for each article through the Scopus "citation overview" function. This function provides citations per calendar year, allowing us to reconstruct the citation history in the first three years after publication. We did not remove self-citations, as our aim was to describe the actual citation visibility of the articles in the database, and because the proportion of self-citations among low-cited articles is generally small in absolute terms (Aksnes, 2003).

To analyze the data, we defined non-citation as an article with zero citations recorded in Scopus at the census date. For each journal j, we calculated the overall percentage of non-citation as Pj = (Uj / Nj) × 100, where Uj is the number of uncited articles and Nj is the total number of citable articles published by journal j between 2008 and 2012. To describe temporal patterns, we also computed the percentage of articles of publication year t that remained uncited within a fixed window of three years after publication: P{j,t}^{(3)} = (U{j,t}^{(3)} / N{j,t}) × 100, with t = 2008, …, 2012. Using a fixed window rather than the total accumulated citations avoids the artefact that older articles have had more time to be cited (Glänzel & Schoepflin, 1995; Wang, 2013). Because the three-year window for the 2012 cohort extends beyond the census date for part of the sample, the census was set after the end of 2015, ensuring that all cohorts had a complete window.

In addition to the main outcome variable, we also computed secondary descriptive variables, including the number of articles per journal and year, language of publication, document type, and the mean and median number of citations per article. Given that citation distributions are highly skewed (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976), we preferred medians and interquartile ranges to means for summarizing central tendency. Our statistical analysis involved describing absolute and relative frequencies of articles and uncited articles by journal and by publication year, as well as computing 95% confidence intervals for proportions using the Wilson score method, which performs better than the Wald interval for small samples and extreme proportions (Newcombe, 1998).

To test for differences in the overall percentage of non-citation among journals, we used a chi-square test of homogeneity of proportions across the eight journals. Where the global test was significant, we carried out all pairwise comparisons (28 comparisons) using two-sample tests of proportions, with p-values adjusted by the Bonferroni–Holm procedure to control the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05 (Holm, 1979). Journals that did not differ significantly from one another after adjustment were grouped, allowing us to identify clusters of journals with similar non-citation patterns.

Our results provide insights into the dynamics of recognition of articles in Brazilian public health journals, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive model of citation determinants in applied, multidisciplinary fields. By applying statistical tests for differences in proportions, we were able to identify groups of journals with statistically distinguishable non-citation levels, moving beyond rankings based on raw percentages. Furthermore, our analysis of temporal trends in non-citation within the initial years after publication offers a nuanced understanding of the role of multidisciplinarity and editorial orientation in shaping citation patterns. These findings have important implications for editors, evaluators, and researchers, underscoring the importance of considering the complexities of citation dynamics in applied, multidisciplinary fields. Our analysis took a multi-faceted approach to identify statistically distinct groups of journals, adopting a conservative and pragmatic strategy that classified journals based on inferential evidence of difference rather than relying on arbitrary cutoffs. This methodological choice allowed us to sidestep the limitations of traditional cluster analysis. To examine the temporal trend of non-citation within a three-year window, we plotted the proportion of uncited articles, P{j,t}^{(3)}, for each journal and publication year. We then fitted a logistic regression model for each journal, using the uncited status (0/1) as the dependent variable and publication year (centered at 2008) as a continuous predictor. The exponentiated coefficient, exp(β1), yielded the annual odds ratio of non-citation, with values below one indicating a declining trend. To evaluate these trends, we employed Wald tests, supplementing our analysis with the Cochran–Armitage test for trend as a sensitivity check. Given the visual suggestion of non-monotonic patterns in some journals, we also conducted pairwise comparisons between the 2008 and 2012 cohorts using Fisher's exact test. For journals where neither a monotonic trend nor a difference between endpoints was detectable, we described the oscillating patterns qualitatively. Notably, with only five time points per journal, we refrained from attempting time-series modeling, recognizing the limitations of our dataset in this regard.

As an exploratory step, we compared the distribution of citations (excluding uncited articles) among journals using the Kruskal–Wallis test, followed by Dunn's post hoc test. This allowed us to investigate whether journals with lower non-citation rates also exhibited higher citation intensity. All statistical tests were two-sided, with a significance level set at 5%. Our analyses were performed in R (version 3.x), leveraging base functions and the packages dplyr, ggplot2, and binom. Since our study utilized only publicly available bibliographic metadata and did not involve human participants, ethical review was deemed unnecessary.

However, our method is not without its limitations. The coverage in Scopus, our data source, is limited, and citations from sources not indexed in the database, including many Brazilian journals, theses, and policy documents, are not captured. This means that an article classified as "uncited" is uncited within Scopus but not necessarily in all scholarly or practical contexts, a nuance highlighted by previous research (Hamilton, 1990; Nicolaisen & Frandsen, 2019). This limitation also implies that non-citation rates are likely overestimated for journals in the humanities, whose literature is less comprehensively covered in databases like Scopus. Therefore, our results should be interpreted as indicators of visibility within an international database rather than as measures of intrinsic quality or social impact.

The dataset we analyzed consisted of 6,213 documents published between 2008 and 2012 in eight journals, retrieved through a Scopus search. After excluding non-article items such as editorials, letters, errata, and other non-classified items, 5,478 citable articles remained for analysis. The journal Cadernos de Saúde Pública (CSP) contributed the largest number of articles (1,452, or 26.5%), followed closely by Revista de Saúde Pública (RSP; 1,138, or 20.8%) and Ciência & Saúde Coletiva (CSC; 1,046, or 19.1%). Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia (RBE) contributed 548 articles (10.0%), Interface 459 (8.4%), Physis 322 (5.9%), Saúde e Sociedade 311 (5.7%), and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos (HCSM) 202 (3.7%). Citation counts were extracted in 2015, resulting in an observation window that ranged from three years (for 2012 articles) to seven years (for 2008 articles) after publication.

Across all journals, we found that 1,064 articles (19.4%) had received no citations. The percentage of non-citation varied significantly among journals (χ² = 912.4, df = 7, p < 0.001), ranging from 5.7% in RSP to 58.1% in HCSM (Table 1). CSP had 6.2% uncited articles (90/1,452), while RSP had 5.7% (65/1,138). Intermediate values were observed for RBE (16.4%; 90/548) and CSC (17.2%; 180/1,046). Physis (32.3%; 104/322), Saúde e Sociedade (34.4%; 107/311), and Interface (36.8%; 169/459) formed a distinct tier, with HCSM being the extreme case, with 117 of 201 evaluated articles uncited (58.1%). Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction (28 comparisons; adjusted α = 0.0018) identified four statistically homogeneous groups. HCSM alone comprised the first group (58%), significantly different from every other journal (all p < 0.001). The second group consisted of Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade (32%–37%), with no significant differences among them (smallest adjusted p = 0.21 for Physis versus Interface). The third group comprised CSC and RBE (16%–17%; p = 0.74 between them), and the fourth group comprised CSP and RSP (about 6%; p = 0.68). Differences between adjacent groups were all significant (p < 0.001), with odds ratios relative to the reference group (CSP and RSP combined) being 2.9 (95% CI 2.3–3.7) for CSC and RBE, 8.4 (95% CI 6.7–10.6) for Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade, and 21.6 (95% CI 15.0–31.2) for HCSM.

When examining non-citation by publication year, we observed that the expected pattern of decreasing percentages with increasing time since publication was only partly present. This reflects both the age of the cohort and journal-specific dynamics. Across the whole set, non-citation was 26.8% for 2012 articles, 22.1% for 2011, 19.0% for 2010, 15.7% for 2009, and 14.0% for 2008. A trend test across years was significant (χ² for trend = 94.6, p < 0.001), but the slope varied among journals (journal × year interaction, likelihood-ratio test p < 0.001). Given the confounding effect of differing observation windows on journal-level comparisons across cohorts, we computed non-citation within the first three years after publication, applying an identical window to each cohort (Figure 1; Table 2). Under this criterion, non-citation was always higher than in the full-window analysis, and the ordering of journals was preserved.

Four journals displayed a clear decline in non-citation across the cohorts. In CSP, three-year non-citation fell from 21.4% for 2008 articles to 9.8% for 2012 articles (trend p < 0.001). Similarly, in CSC, it fell from 36.5% to 21.0% (p < 0.001), in RBE from 38.2% to 20.5% (p = 0.002), and in Physis from 61.0% to 38.6% (p = 0.01). For CSP and CSC, the decline was approximately monotonic, whereas RBE and Physis showed one-year reversals (RBE, 2010: 31.9% to 2011: 33.7%; Physis, 2010: 46.4% to 2011: 47.9%) that did not alter the overall trend. Three other journals oscillated without a sustained trend. RSP had 3-year non-citation of 12.1% in 2008, falling to 8.5% in 2009, rising to 13.4% in 2010, and ending at 11.9% in 2012; the 2008 and 2012 values were nearly identical (difference 0.2%). These patterns highlight the complexity of citation dynamics across different journals and years, underscoring the need for nuanced analysis that accounts for both temporal trends and journal-specific factors. The analysis of non-citation rates in Brazilian public health journals reveals a complex landscape, with significant variability across journals and over time. For instance, the proportion of non-cited articles in Revista de Saúde Pública ranged from 5.7% to 6.3% between 2008 and 2012, with no discernible trend (p = 0.94). In contrast, Saúde e Sociedade exhibited a more pronounced fluctuation, with non-citation rates ranging from 39.1% in 2009 to 54.0% in 2011, although the endpoints were similar (p = 0.93). Interface, on the other hand, displayed the largest swings, with values of 52.8% in 2008, 44.7% in 2009, 59.2% in 2010, 48.3% in 2011, and 53.1% in 2012, with the amplitude of oscillation being broader than in Revista de Saúde Pública. Notably, História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos maintained uniformly high three-year non-citation rates throughout the study period, ranging from 67.5% to 78.3%, with no discernible trend (trend p = 0.52).

The distribution of citations among articles also varied significantly across journals. For example, the median number of citations per article was 9 (interquartile range 4–18) for Revista de Saúde Pública, 8 (4–16) for Cadernos de Saúde Pública, and 4 (2–8) for Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia. In contrast, the median number of citations per article was significantly lower for journals such as Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade, with values of 2 (1–4), 2 (1–3), and 2 (1–3), respectively. Furthermore, the citation distributions were strongly right-skewed in every journal, with the top 10% of articles accounting for a substantial proportion of all citations, ranging from 31% in Revista de Saúde Pública to 52% in the smaller social-science-oriented journals.

The association between article and journal characteristics and non-citation rates was also explored. A multilevel logistic regression analysis revealed that the probability of non-citation decreased with increasing observation time (odds ratio per year 0.85; 95% CI 0.80–0.90). Articles in English or with English abstracts showed lower odds of non-citation (OR 0.62; 95% CI 0.51–0.75) than articles with Portuguese-only abstracts. Moreover, articles classified as original research had lower odds of non-citation than essays and other non-empirical contributions (OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.33–0.51). However, between-journal variance remained substantial after adjustment (intraclass correlation 0.31), indicating that these article-level variables explained only part of the differences among journals.

This study provides the first national description of non-citation in Brazilian public health journals, a field that had not been examined either in Brazil or internationally. The principal finding is heterogeneity, with non-citation rates ranging from 5.7% to 58.1% across journals. The journals fell into four statistically distinct groups, with Cadernos de Saúde Pública and Revista de Saúde Pública, the two oldest and best-established titles, having around 6% uncited papers. Ciência & Saúde Coletiva and Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia followed at 16–17%, while Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade lay between 32% and 37%, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos had roughly 58%.

These findings are best understood against the wider literature on uncitedness, which suggests that non-citation rates vary significantly across fields and journals. Earlier analyses by Hamilton (1990) and Pendlebury (1991) suggested that a large share of published papers were never cited, although those estimates were later criticized for treating journal-specific and field-specific differences as uniform and for ignoring the length of the citation window. More recent studies have shown that non-citation is strongly field-dependent, with the social sciences and humanities showing higher rates than the natural and biomedical sciences. The very high rate for História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos is therefore unsurprising, given its focus on the history of science and health humanities, which is poorly captured by Scopus.

The gradient found across journals suggests that disciplinary orientation matters, with journals closer to epidemiology and the biomedical and quantitative core of public health having lower non-citation rates. However, the observation that multidisciplinary journals attract more citations deserves tempering, as Ciência & Saúde Coletiva and Interface, both multidisciplinary journals, had markedly different non-citation rates. Other factors, such as publication volume, language policy, and the presence of English-language abstracts or full texts, likely contribute to the pattern. A comprehensive citation model for the field, perhaps a multilevel regression with article-level covariates nested within journals, remains to be formulated and tested.

The temporal analysis adds a further layer of complexity, with four journals (Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, and Physis) showing a clear decline in non-citation within three years of publication across the 2008–2012 cohorts. This may reflect real improvement in visibility, perhaps linked to Scopus indexing, wider use of electronic platforms, and increased pressure on researchers to publish in indexed outlets. However, it may also be partly artefactual, since the number of Scopus-indexed sources that cite Brazilian journals has grown over time. In contrast, three journals (Revista de Saúde Pública, Saúde e Sociedade, and Interface) oscillated but ended at similar levels in 2008 and 2012, suggesting that small journals or those with modest annual output may be more susceptible to fluctuations in citation rates.

In conclusion, this study highlights the complexity and variability of non-citation rates in Brazilian public health journals. The findings underscore the importance of considering disciplinary orientation, language policy, and other journal-level factors in understanding citation patterns. Further research is needed to develop a comprehensive citation model for the field, one that takes into account the nuances of journal and article characteristics, as well as the changing landscape of scientific publication and citation practices. By examining the dynamics of non-citation in Brazilian public health journals, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the factors that influence citation rates and the ways in which journals can improve their visibility and impact.

The role of universities in driving innovation and economic growth has become increasingly prominent, with the "entrepreneurial university" concept suggesting that institutions have undergone a significant transformation, prioritizing the capitalization of knowledge alongside traditional research and teaching missions (Etzkowitz, 2003; Etzkowitz et al., 2000). This shift has been accompanied by a growing trend towards "academic capitalism," where declining public funding and intensifying competition have led institutions and individual scholars to adopt more market-oriented behaviors in pursuit of resources (Slaughter & Leslie, 1997). While the commercialization of research has received considerable attention, with studies focusing on patenting, licensing, and spin-off formation (Shane, 2004; Perkmann et al., 2013), a more fundamental question remains understudied: to what extent do academics themselves exhibit an entrepreneurial disposition, and does this disposition contribute to increased research productivity?

Research productivity is a crucial aspect of an academic's career, as well as a key factor in determining the competitiveness of universities and national systems. Various individual and organizational factors, including gender, career stage, collaboration networks, institutional resources, and workload, have been linked to productivity (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005; Hesli & Lee, 2011). However, the dispositional and behavioral characteristics of researchers have received relatively little systematic attention. The concept of entrepreneurial orientation (EO) has been extensively studied in the management literature, where it is used to capture an actor's strategic posture through innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking (Miller, 1983; Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Meta-analytic evidence has shown a positive association between EO and performance in firms (Rauch et al., 2009), and this construct has been extended to the individual level, where it describes a person's propensity to pursue opportunities, act ahead of events, and tolerate uncertainty (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Yet, it remains unclear whether EO is also a significant predictor of scholarly output among academics.

There are compelling reasons to expect both a positive and a more nuanced relationship between EO and research productivity. On one hand, academic research involves identifying opportunities, mobilizing resources, and accepting uncertain returns, all of which are characteristic of entrepreneurial behavior. Academics who proactively seek out funding, collaborators, and publication outlets, and who are willing to take risks, may indeed accumulate more output over time. On the other hand, certain philosophical and sociological perspectives on science suggest that research is often conducted within established "paradigms," or circumscribed areas of study with shared assumptions, methods, and problem sets (Kuhn, 1962). Within these boundaries, "normal science" may involve incremental puzzle-solving, and journals and peer reviewers may reward conformity as much as novelty (Azoulay et al., 2011). If this is the case, the innovativeness dimension of EO may not be a reliable predictor of productivity, and some research may not be inherently innovative at all. The question of whether the various dimensions of EO matter equally, or whether only some translate into output, is therefore an empirical one that existing theory does not settle.

A related gap in the literature concerns the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process. The rise of digital platforms has created new opportunities for financing and conducting research, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D (Mollick, 2014; Belleflamme et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2013; Afuah & Tucci, 2012). These approaches may be particularly relevant in contexts where traditional funding is scarce. However, little is known about academics' willingness to adopt these methods or whether a technological propensity of this kind is associated with higher output. By treating this propensity as a distinct but complementary construct to EO, we can separate a general entrepreneurial posture from the specific readiness to use new tools for resourcing and conducting research.

These issues are particularly pertinent in developing-country contexts, where universities often face significant resource constraints. In South Africa, for example, universities operate with limited public funding relative to enrollment growth, heavy teaching loads, and a need to address historical inequities, all while facing strong performance incentives (Cloete et al., 2015). In this environment, academics who can mobilize alternative resources and act proactively may have a distinct advantage. Conversely, if unconventional financing and research methods are underutilized, this may signal untapped opportunities for a sector that cannot rely on increases in conventional funding. Research from such settings is also valuable because the entrepreneurship and higher education literatures have been dominated by evidence from advanced economies with very different funding and incentive structures.

Against this background, our study addresses two research questions. First, to what extent are academics entrepreneurial, and is a higher self-reported level of EO, and of each of its constituent dimensions, associated with higher research productivity? Second, is a greater propensity to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, associated with higher productivity, and how prevalent is the use of such methods? To answer these questions, we conducted a survey of academics at a large South African university, using a comprehensive purposive sampling process that yielded 292 usable responses. We estimated the relationships using ordinary least squares regression and assessed the robustness of the findings with bootstrapped standard errors and negative binomial regression, which is suitable for the count-based and over-dispersed nature of publication output (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).

Our study makes three key contributions. First, it extends entrepreneurship theory to a setting in which it has seldom been applied, demonstrating that EO, a construct developed to explain firm behavior, can be meaningfully measured among individual scholars and linked to a core academic outcome. In doing so, it responds to calls for closer synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory and for greater attention to the micro-foundations of the entrepreneurial university (Fini et al., 2018). Second, by disaggregating EO into its dimensions, the study contributes to the debate on whether innovativeness, in particular, is rewarded in paradigm-bound academic work. Our findings suggest that, although individuals with higher endowments of EO may be more productive, innovativeness is not significantly related to productivity, which complicates simple narratives about the role of entrepreneurship in academic research. Finally, our study highlights the importance of considering the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process, particularly in contexts where traditional funding is scarce. By exploring the relationship between technological propensity and research productivity, we can better understand the ways in which academics can leverage new tools and approaches to enhance their research output. The notion that scholarly success is inextricably linked to novelty is a pervasive one in academic circles. However, this perspective overlooks the complex interplay of factors that contribute to research productivity. Our study seeks to address this limitation by exploring the relationship between entrepreneurial orientation, technological propensity, and academic research productivity. Furthermore, by examining the use of crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, we provide insight into the technological propensity of academics, highlighting the potential for these methods to be underutilized. The implications of our findings are particularly relevant for university leaders and policymakers in resource-constrained systems, as they inform the design of research support, training, and incentive structures.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. First, we develop the theoretical background and hypotheses that underpin our investigation. Next, we describe the data, measures, and estimation strategy employed in our study. We then present the results and robustness tests, followed by a discussion of the implications, limitations, and directions for future research.

Our research design and sampling strategy were guided by the need to estimate associations between individual-level dispositions and self-reported performance outcomes in a defined population. To this end, we employed a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, which is well-suited for this purpose (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). The survey was administered to academic staff at a large, research-intensive public university in South Africa, a setting that combines formal research-output incentives with the resource constraints typical of developing-country higher education. This context is analytically useful, as it allows us to examine the intersection of research productivity and technological propensity in a resource-constrained environment.

A comprehensive purposive sampling procedure was applied to select participants. The sampling frame comprised all permanent and fixed-term academics, from lecturer to full professor, who were affiliated with a faculty or school and held a formal research mandate. Staff in purely administrative, support, or short-term teaching-only contracts were excluded, as were postdoctoral fellows, whose research mandates differ structurally. Purposive selection was preferred to probability sampling because the construct of interest, research productivity, is meaningful only for individuals with an opportunity to conduct research (Etikan et al., 2016). Within this boundary, an effort was made to include every eligible academic across all faculties to maximize disciplinary variation.

After deduplication and verification against the institutional staff directory, 1,214 eligible individuals were identified. Each was invited by personalized email to complete an online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. Two reminders were sent at ten-day intervals, resulting in a total of 317 questionnaires being returned. However, 25 of these were excluded due to substantial missing data or straight-lining, leaving 292 usable responses (an effective response rate of 24.1%). This response rate is comparable to those reported in other surveys of academic staff (Baruch & Holtom, 2008).

To assess non-response bias, early respondents (first quartile) were compared with late respondents (last quartile) on all focal variables, following Armstrong and Overton (1977). No significant differences were found (all p > 0.10), suggesting that non-response bias is unlikely to be a significant concern. Additionally, the sample was compared with institutional staff records for rank and faculty, and the distributions did not differ materially. A sensitivity analysis showed that a sample of 292 gave over 0.95 power to detect a medium effect (f² = 0.15) in a regression with up to 15 predictors at α = 0.05 (Cohen, 1988), exceeding the minimum of 50 + 8k observations suggested by Green (1991).

The measures employed in this study were designed to capture the key constructs of interest. The dependent variable, academic research productivity, was measured as the number of DHET-accredited research output units that respondents reported for the preceding three calendar years. These units include articles in accredited journals, books, book chapters, and peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and are fractionalized by authorship share. A three-year window was used to smooth annual volatility in publication outcomes (Abramo et al., 2011). Self-reports were verified, where respondents consented, against the institutional research-office repository for a random subsample of 40 respondents, and the correlation between the two sources was high (r = 0.93).

Entrepreneurial orientation (EO) was measured using the nine-item scale of Covin and Slevin (1989), adapted from the firm level to the individual-academic level in line with Bolton and Lane (2012). The scale operationalizes the three classical dimensions identified by Miller (1983): innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point Likert scale, with example items rewritten to reflect research behavior, such as "I favour novel research questions over well-established lines of enquiry" (innovativeness) and "I typically initiate research collaborations rather than respond to others" (proactiveness). Dimension scores were computed as item means, and an overall EO score was computed as the mean of all items (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996).

Technological propensity, specifically the propensity to apply novel technological methods, was measured using a five-item scale developed for this study, informed by technology-readiness research (Parasuraman, 2000) and the literature on open and crowdsourced innovation (Howe, 2006; Mollick, 2014). Items captured the extent to which respondents had used, or would consider using, crowdfunding to finance research, crowdsourced R&D or citizen-science data collection, online collaborative platforms, and open-data repositories. Responses were captured on a seven-point scale. Exploratory factor analysis (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation) of the items indicated a single factor (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin = 0.81; Bartlett's test χ² significant at p < 0.001), with an eigenvalue of 3.04 explaining 60.8% of the variance. Two items on crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D specifically were also analyzed separately due to their theoretical salience.

Control variables were selected for their established associations with research output (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005). These comprised age (years), gender (female = 1), academic rank (ordinal, 1 to 5), possession of a doctorate (yes = 1), years in academia, average weekly teaching hours, receipt of external research funding in the review period (yes = 1), and broad disciplinary cluster (natural sciences and engineering, health sciences, humanities and social sciences, and economic and management sciences), which was dummy-coded.

The reliability, validity, and common-method bias of our measures were assessed using various statistical techniques. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha (Cronbach, 1951) and composite reliability, with all scales exceeding the conventional threshold of 0.70 (Nunnally, 1978): overall EO α = 0.84, innovativeness α = 0.77, proactiveness α = 0.79, risk-taking α = 0.73, and technological propensity α = 0.86. Convergent validity was supported by average variance extracted values above 0.50 for all constructs, and discriminant validity was established using the Fornell and Larcker (1981) criterion. Common-method bias was evaluated following Podsakoff et al. (2003), with the dependent variable placed in a separate section of the questionnaire, respondent anonymity assured, and Harman's single-factor test showing that the first unrotated factor did not account for the majority of the variance. Our analysis revealed that the variance in research productivity accounted for by our predictors was 27.4%, which falls short of the 50% threshold. To further examine the relationships between our variables, we conducted a marker-variable test using an unrelated attitudinal item, but this did not yield any substantial changes in the correlations. 

We performed our statistical analysis using Stata 17, beginning with an examination of descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations. Notably, our data had fewer than 3% missing item-level responses for all variables, and Little's test supported the assumption that data were missing completely at random (p = 0.38). We addressed missing data using multiple imputation by chained equations. 

Our primary model was estimated using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, where research productivity was regressed on entrepreneurial orientation (EO), its three dimensions, technological propensity, and several control variables. Due to the right-skewed nature of publication counts, we transformed the dependent variable as ln(units + 1) for the OLS models, following the approach recommended by Wooldridge (2016). 

We estimated our models hierarchically, starting with a base model that included only control variables (Model 1), followed by the addition of overall EO (Model 2), its subsequent disaggregation into innovativeness, proactiveness, and risk-taking (Model 3), and finally the inclusion of technological propensity (Model 4). To evaluate the incremental explanatory power of each model, we examined changes in R² and conducted F-tests. To facilitate interpretation and mitigate non-essential collinearity, we mean-centred our predictors. 

We also checked for multicollinearity using variance inflation factors, all of which were below 2.6, well under the threshold of 10 suggested by Hair et al. (2019). While the Breusch–Pagan test indicated mild heteroskedasticity in some specifications, we addressed this by reporting heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors, as recommended by White (1980) and Long and Ervin (2000). Additionally, we inspected residual normality using Q–Q plots and the Shapiro–Wilk test and identified influential observations through Cook's distance; no case exceeded 4/n, and results remained unchanged when these cases were removed.

To further test the robustness of our results, we undertook two additional analyses. First, we employed nonparametric bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples to derive bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 95% confidence intervals for all OLS coefficients, thus relaxing distributional assumptions about the error term, as outlined by Efron and Tibshirani (1993). Second, given that research output is a non-negative count variable, we estimated negative binomial regression on the untransformed counts, preferring this approach to Poisson regression because the likelihood-ratio test of the dispersion parameter rejected equidispersion (α = 0.71, p < 0.001), in line with Cameron and Trivedi (2013). We reported incidence-rate ratios (IRRs) alongside coefficients. The consistency of sign, magnitude, and significance across the OLS, bootstrapped, and negative binomial estimates provided evidence of robustness.

All hypotheses were tested at α = 0.05 (two-tailed), and effect sizes were interpreted alongside p-values, following current recommendations (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016). Ethical clearance for this study was obtained from the university's research ethics committee prior to data collection. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was captured electronically. Responses were anonymized, and data were stored on encrypted institutional servers.

Our sample consisted of 292 usable responses, with 54.5% of respondents being women, and a mean age of 44.3 years (SD = 9.8). The average duration of holding an academic post was 11.6 years (SD = 8.4). Notably, 63.4% of the sample held a doctorate, and 38.7% were at senior lecturer rank or above. The mean annual research output, measured as accredited publication units per annum over the preceding three years, was 3.84 (SD = 3.52; median = 2.9; range = 0–21.5). This distribution was strongly right-skewed (skewness = 1.97) and overdispersed (variance = 12.39, against a mean of 3.84), which motivated our use of a count-based robustness test, as suggested by Cameron and Trivedi (2013).

All multi-item scales demonstrated acceptable internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha values exceeding the conventional threshold of 0.70 (Nunnally, 1978). Specifically, alpha was 0.81 for innovativeness, 0.78 for proactiveness, 0.74 for risk-taking, and 0.83 for technological propensity. On the seven-point scales, respondents reported moderately high levels of innovativeness (M = 5.21, SD = 0.94) and proactiveness (M = 5.07, SD = 1.02), but markedly lower levels of risk-taking (M = 3.96, SD = 1.17). This pattern is consistent with the risk-averse institutional context often attributed to academia (Lumpkin and Dess, 1996). Technological propensity was found to be relatively low (M = 3.18, SD = 1.41). Only 31.2% of respondents reported being aware of crowdfunding as a research-funding mechanism, and actual use was limited, with 12 respondents (4.1%) having used crowdfunding and 22 (7.5%) having used crowdsourced R&D, resulting in 34 (11.6%) having used at least one of these methods. 

Respondents who had used at least one such method reported higher mean research output (M = 5.62, SD = 4.31) compared to non-users (M = 3.60, SD = 3.35). This difference was statistically significant under a Welch correction for unequal variances (t(38.6) = 2.31, p =.026), with a medium effect size (Cohen's d = 0.55; Cohen, 1988).

Our examination of bivariate relationships revealed that research productivity was positively correlated with proactiveness (r =.33, p <.001), risk-taking (r =.26, p <.001), technological propensity (r =.22, p <.001), and, to a lesser extent, innovativeness (r =.12, p =.04). Among control variables, productivity correlated with academic rank (r =.29, p <.001), possession of a doctorate (r =.24, p <.001), and years in academia (r =.18, p =.002), but negatively with teaching load (r = −.17, p =.004). The EO dimensions were moderately intercorrelated, most notably innovativeness and proactiveness (r =.58, p <.001), though not to a degree suggesting problematic collinearity, as the highest variance inflation factor in the regression models was 2.31, well below the conventional cut-off of 10 (Hair et al., 2010) and the more conservative threshold of 5 (O'Brien, 2007).

Because all constructs were self-reported, we assessed common-method bias using Harman's single-factor test, which indicated that a single factor accounted for 24.6% of total variance, well below the 50% level at which concern is typically raised (Podsakoff et al., 2003). 

Table 3 presents the hierarchical OLS results. Model 1, containing only controls (age, gender, rank, doctorate, years in academia, disciplinary field, and teaching load), explained 16.0% of the variance in research productivity (R² =.160; F(8, 283) = 6.74, p <.001). Rank (β =.21, p <.001), doctoral qualification (β =.15, p =.01), and teaching load (β = −.13, p =.02) emerged as significant predictors. Model 2 added the three EO dimensions and technological propensity, and we found that the addition of these variables significantly enhanced the explanatory power of the model, as evidenced by the increase in R² and the significant F-test. The results of these analyses are presented in detail in the tables and figures accompanying this text, providing a comprehensive overview of our findings. Our regression analysis revealed a significant increment in explained variance, with the inclusion of the four entrepreneurial orientation dimensions raising the R² to 0.270 (adjusted R² = 0.239; F(12, 279) = 8.60, p < 0.001). This increment was itself significant (ΔR² = 0.110; F(4, 279) = 10.51, p < 0.001), indicating that these dimensions collectively contribute to the prediction of research productivity. However, it is essential to note that the Breusch–Pagan test indicated the presence of heteroscedasticity (χ² = 11.8, p = 0.001), which led us to utilize heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors throughout our analysis to ensure the accuracy of our estimates.

Among the entrepreneurial orientation dimensions, proactiveness emerged as the strongest predictor of productivity, with a coefficient of 0.92 (SE = 0.24, β = 0.24, p < 0.001). This suggests that for every one-point increase on the seven-point proactiveness scale, academics can expect approximately 0.92 additional publication units per annum, holding all other variables constant. Risk-taking and technological propensity also exhibited positive and significant relationships with productivity, with coefficients of 0.58 (SE = 0.20, β = 0.17, p = 0.004) and 0.47 (SE = 0.18, β = 0.14, p = 0.010), respectively. In contrast, innovativeness did not demonstrate a significant independent relationship with research productivity once the other predictors were included in the model (b = 0.21, SE = 0.21, β = 0.06, p = 0.32). The modest bivariate correlation between innovativeness and productivity appears to be an artifact of shared variance with proactiveness, rather than reflecting any direct contribution of innovativeness to productivity.

The effects of rank (β = 0.18, p = 0.001) and teaching load (β = −0.11, p = 0.04) remained significant, while the effect of having a doctorate weakened to marginal significance (β = 0.10, p = 0.07). Notably, age, gender, and disciplinary field did not exhibit significant relationships with research productivity in either model. To assess the robustness of these findings, we conducted two additional tests. First, we re-estimated Model 2 using nonparametric bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). The resulting bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence intervals excluded zero for proactiveness [0.46, 1.38], risk-taking [0.18, 0.99], and technological propensity [0.11, 0.84], but not for innovativeness [−0.21, 0.62]. Moreover, the bootstrapped standard errors differed from the HC3 estimates by less than 9% for every coefficient, indicating that our inferences were not sensitive to non-normal residuals.

Second, given that publication output is a nonnegative count with evident overdispersion, we estimated a negative binomial regression on the rounded output measure. The dispersion parameter was significantly greater than zero (α = 0.41; likelihood-ratio χ² = 148.3, p < 0.001), supporting the specification of a negative binomial model over a Poisson model. The results were substantively consistent with the OLS estimates, with each one-point increase in proactiveness associated with a 19% increase in expected output (IRR = 1.19, 95% CI [1.08, 1.31], p < 0.001). The corresponding increases were 11% for risk-taking (IRR = 1.11, [1.03, 1.20], p = 0.006) and 9% for technological propensity (IRR = 1.09, [1.02, 1.17], p = 0.014). Innovativeness, once again, did not exhibit a significant effect (IRR = 1.04, [0.94, 1.15], p = 0.43). The model fit was modest but acceptable (McFadden pseudo-R² = 0.08), and the direction and significance of all four focal coefficients matched those of the OLS and bootstrap estimates.

Across the three estimation approaches, our findings consistently indicated that higher self-reported proactiveness, risk-taking, and technological propensity are associated with higher research productivity, with proactiveness showing the largest and most stable effect. In contrast, innovativeness, often regarded as the defining characteristic of entrepreneurial orientation, did not independently predict productivity in any specification. The descriptive evidence also revealed that novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, were seldom utilized in this sample, despite the positive association between technological propensity and output. This study investigated whether academics who report higher entrepreneurial orientation and a greater propensity to adopt novel technological methods are more research productive. The evidence from 292 respondents at a large South African university offers qualified support for this hypothesis.

The aggregate entrepreneurial orientation measure was positively and significantly associated with research output in the ordinary least squares (OLS) model (β = 0.21, p < 0.01). This result was stable under bootstrapping with 5,000 replications, where the confidence interval excluded zero, and under negative binomial regression, where each one-unit increase in entrepreneurial orientation corresponded to an estimated 14% increase in the expected output count (incidence rate ratio = 1.14). The convergence of three estimators suggests that this finding is not an artifact of the skewed, over-dispersed distribution typical of publication counts (Cameron and Trivedi, 2013). Innovativeness, by contrast, was not significantly related to productivity, and the adoption of novel technological methods was low across the sample.

The positive entrepreneurial orientation–productivity relationship is consistent with the view that entrepreneurial dispositions are not confined to commercial settings but shape how individuals pursue opportunities in knowledge-producing organizations (Shane and Venkataraman, 2000; Etzkowitz, 2003). Meta-analytic evidence in firms shows that entrepreneurial orientation is positively related to performance (Rauch et al., 2009). Our results suggest an analogous mechanism at the level of the individual academic, where proactiveness and risk-taking, two core dimensions of entrepreneurial orientation (Covin and Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin and Dess, 1996), plausibly help scholars pursue collaborators, funding, and publication outlets before these are demanded of them, and persist through the high rejection rates and uncertain returns of peer review.

In this context, research productivity reflects not only ability and resources (Fox, 1983) but also an opportunity-seeking orientation. This orientation may be especially valuable in resource-constrained systems, where academics cannot rely on slack resources and must create opportunities themselves. The non-significant effect of innovativeness (β = 0.06, p = 0.38) is the most theoretically interesting result and warrants careful interpretation. One explanation draws on Kuhn's (1962) argument that most scholarly activity is "normal science" conducted within paradigms whose problems, methods, and standards of evidence are largely given. If so, productivity within a field may depend more on the efficient execution of well-defined research programs than on novelty of approach. Innovativeness may even carry costs in the short run, since unconventional topics or methods can face longer review cycles, narrower sets of receptive journals, and greater difficulty in securing funding.

Incentive structures may reinforce this, as seen in the South African subsidy arrangements that reward accredited publication units (Department of Higher Education and Training, 2015), potentially favoring incremental, high-throughput output over exploratory work. A second explanation is conceptual: innovativeness, as measured by self-reported openness to new ideas, may not map neatly onto the kind of novelty that is rewarded in academic research. This discrepancy may arise from the complex interplay between individual characteristics, organizational contexts, and the broader academic ecosystem, highlighting the need for further research into the nuances of entrepreneurial orientation and its relationship with research productivity.

Multi-view stereo (MVS) is a fundamental problem in computer vision, aiming to recover the dense three-dimensional geometry of a scene from a set of calibrated images. This technology has far-reaching implications for various applications, including autonomous driving, augmented reality, cultural heritage preservation, and large-scale urban modeling. Despite decades of research, producing accurate and complete depth maps remains a challenging task. Real-world scenes often contain occlusions, illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and large low-textured regions, where photometric cues are ambiguous. Moreover, MVS methods must be efficient enough to process high-resolution images and large image collections.

Traditional MVS methods can be broadly categorized into four groups based on scene representation: voxel-based, point cloud-based, mesh-based, and depth map-based approaches. Depth map-based methods, which process each reference image independently and fuse the resulting depth maps into a final point cloud, have proven to be the most flexible and scalable. Within this family, PatchMatch stereo has become a dominant approach. This method initializes random depth and normal hypotheses at each pixel and iteratively propagates good hypotheses between neighbors, allowing correct hypotheses to spread quickly across the image. Notable extensions of PatchMatch stereo include Gipuma, which introduced a diffusion-like propagation scheme, and COLMAP, which jointly estimates depth, normals, and pixel-wise view selection within a probabilistic framework.

In recent years, learning-based MVS has also gained significant attention. Methods such as MVSNet and its successors have achieved strong results on benchmarks by building plane-sweep cost volumes from deep features and regularizing them with 3D convolutions. However, these approaches have limitations, including high memory and runtime requirements, which grow rapidly with image resolution and depth range. Furthermore, their generalization to scenes unlike the training data is not guaranteed. In contrast, traditional PatchMatch methods remain attractive due to their training-free nature, ability to work at full resolution, and modest memory requirements.

However, PatchMatch-based MVS faces two significant challenges. The first challenge concerns hypothesis propagation and view selection. Existing checkerboard schemes often rely on a fixed, small neighborhood pattern, which can lead to spatially close and strongly correlated candidate hypotheses. These hypotheses may lie across depth discontinuities or in unreliable areas, resulting in sampled hypotheses that do not accurately reflect the local structure of the scene. Moreover, view selection is typically performed using a single global criterion per image or a per-pixel criterion computed from one hypothesis, which can be noisy and unreliable, particularly early in optimization.

The second challenge is the presence of low-textured regions, where photometric consistency measures, such as normalized cross-correlation, are almost uninformative. Enlarging the window size can help, but it also blurs details and increases the computational cost. Planar priors derived from sparse, reliable points and triangulation can be used to improve completeness in low-textured areas, but they depend on the quality of the sparse points and the validity of the piecewise-planar assumption. A natural alternative is a multi-scale strategy, which can help recover reliable estimates in low-textured areas while preserving fine details.

In this paper, we investigate how a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while maintaining the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. Our approach combines a stronger single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. We present a basic MVS method, ACMH, which uses Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection. The adaptive checkerboard sampling selects candidate hypotheses from a wider neighborhood, improving propagation efficiency and robustness near discontinuities. The multi-hypothesis joint view selection uses the whole set of candidate hypotheses to infer the view subset used for cost aggregation at each pixel, resulting in a more stable and informative selection.

We also propose ACMM, which embeds ACMH in a multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency. Depth maps are estimated first on coarse images, where low-textured areas can be matched reliably. Geometric consistency across views is then used to filter the estimates and guide optimization at finer scales, ensuring that reliable coarse estimates are retained and propagated to the finest scale. To correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales, we introduce a novel detail restorer, which identifies regions where the upsampled estimates are inconsistent with finer-scale evidence and restores thin structures and boundaries through hypotheses generated at the finer scale.

Our method is evaluated on standard benchmarks, including ETH3D and Tanks and Temples, and achieves state-of-the-art performance among traditional approaches, while being competitive with learning-based methods. The results demonstrate that our approach can recover depth in low-textured areas as well as in fine details, with good computational efficiency. Overall, our work provides a principled way to address the challenges of PatchMatch-based MVS, enabling the recovery of accurate and complete depth maps in a wide range of scenarios. 

The key to our approach is the combination of a strong single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. By using adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis joint view selection, we can improve the efficiency and robustness of hypothesis propagation and view selection. The multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency ensures that reliable coarse estimates are retained and propagated to the finest scale, while the detail restorer corrects erroneous estimates and restores thin structures and boundaries.

In conclusion, our work demonstrates that a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can be designed to obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while maintaining the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. The proposed approach has the potential to be widely adopted in various applications, including autonomous driving, augmented reality, and cultural heritage preservation. Future work can focus on further improving the efficiency and accuracy of the approach, as well as exploring its applications in other fields. 

Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in recovering depth in low-textured areas and fine details. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art traditional approaches and is competitive with learning-based methods. The approach is also computationally efficient, making it suitable for large-scale applications. 

In addition to the technical contributions, our work also provides a detailed analysis of the challenges of PatchMatch-based MVS and the limitations of existing approaches. The paper discusses the importance of hypothesis propagation and view selection, as well as the need for a multi-scale strategy to recover reliable estimates in low-textured areas. The analysis provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in the field of computer vision and MVS.

Overall, our work provides a significant contribution to the field of MVS, demonstrating the potential of a PatchMatch-based framework to obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details. The proposed approach has the potential to be widely adopted in various applications, and future work can focus on further improving its efficiency and accuracy.

The paper provides a detailed analysis of the challenges of PatchMatch-based MVS and the limitations of existing approaches. The analysis provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working in the field of computer vision and MVS. The proposed approach has the potential to be widely adopted in various applications, and future work can focus on further improving its efficiency and accuracy.

In the future, we plan to explore the use of other machine learning techniques, such as reinforcement learning and generative models, to improve the efficiency and accuracy of the approach. We also plan to investigate the use of other sensors, such as lidar and radar, to provide additional information for the MVS algorithm. Additionally, we plan to explore the applications of the proposed approach in other fields, In the context of depth estimation, a crucial aspect is the ability to accurately reconstruct a scene from a set of images. Our approach involves estimating a depth map for each image in a sequence, with each image serving as a reference point. This process leverages a structure-from-motion pipeline, as described by Schönberger and Frahm (2016), to determine the poses and intrinsics of the cameras. A key component of our method is the representation of each pixel as a plane hypothesis, denoted as θp = (np, dp), which consists of a unit normal and a depth value. This formulation is reminiscent of the slanted-plane model used in PatchMatch stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Barnes et al., 2009).

Our pipeline can be broken down into three primary components: a basic estimator, referred to as ACMH, a multi-scale geometric consistency scheme built upon it, termed ACMM, and a detail restorer that operates between scales. The ultimate goal is to filter and fuse the depth maps into a point cloud. To achieve this, we first define a matching cost for each hypothesis θp. This cost is calculated as the photometric cost, denoted as cj(p, θp), which represents the difference between a patch around pixel p in the reference image Iref and the corresponding warped patch in source image Ij. The photometric cost is computed using the normalized cross-correlation (NCC) with bilateral weights over spatial and intensity distance, as proposed by Schönberger et al. (2016). To reduce computational complexity, we employ an 11×11 patch sampled with a stride of two pixels, similar to the approach used by Xu and Tao (2019).

One of the innovative aspects of our method is the introduction of adaptive checkerboard sampling. Unlike the standard checkerboard scheme (Galliani et al., 2015), which propagates from a fixed set of neighbors and is limited to a local, fixed-shape region, our approach allows for more flexibility. We maintain the red-black update order to facilitate parallel GPU computation. For each pixel in the active color, we define eight sampling areas: four V-shaped areas near the pixel and four strip-shaped areas that extend farther along the axes and diagonals. Within each area, we select a small set of same-color candidate pixels and retain the one with the lowest matching cost. This process yields eight candidate hypotheses per pixel, which can originate from distances beyond the immediate neighborhood. The strip-shaped areas enable correct hypotheses to cross small occlusions or weakly textured gaps, while the V-shaped areas preserve local structure.

Another critical component of our approach is the multi-hypothesis joint view selection. Earlier methods often select views from a single hypothesis (Zheng et al., 2014) or a fixed neighborhood, which can lead to the inclusion of occluded or badly overlapping views that corrupt the aggregated cost. In contrast, we utilize all eight candidate hypotheses jointly. For each candidate i and source view j, we compute a cost cij, resulting in an 8×(N−1) cost matrix. We then apply an iteration-dependent threshold τ(t) = τ₀·exp(−t²/α) to determine whether a view is "good" for a candidate. The threshold starts loose and tightens as the iterations converge. A view is added to the pixel's aggregation subset if it is good for at least n₁ candidates, which exploits the structured-region evidence. Conversely, a view whose cost exceeds a hard upper bound for any candidate is rejected to guard against occluders. Each selected view receives a weight wj based on the number of candidates for which it is good, and these weights are carried over to later iterations as a prior.

The aggregated cost of candidate i is computed as ci = Σj wj cij / Σj wj. We evaluate the eight candidates under the new view subset and retain the one with the lowest cost for the pixel. To further refine the hypotheses, we form a small set of combinations of the current depth and normal, a randomly drawn depth and normal, and a perturbed version of the current ones. We then evaluate all combinations under the selected view subset and retain the one with the lowest cost. The hypotheses are randomly initialized at the coarsest scale, and each scale runs a fixed number of iterations (three in our experiments), alternating between red and black passes.

To address the issue of photometric costs being ambiguous in low-textured regions at fine scales, we employ a multi-scale geometric consistency guidance scheme, referred to as ACMM. We construct an image pyramid with K scales, downsampling factor two, and scaled camera intrinsics. The ACMH estimator is run from the coarsest scale, and the result at scale k is bilinearly upsampled to serve as initialization for scale k−1. To prevent the finer-scale photometric cost from overwriting good coarse estimates in textureless areas, we introduce a geometric consistency term. This term uses the upsampled depth maps of the source views to compute a reprojection error cgeo,j for each pixel p in the reference image. The guided cost used at scale k is a combination of the photometric cost cphoto,j and the geometric cost cgeo,j, balanced by a parameter η. The reliable coarse estimates from the coarser scale act as a constraint on the finer-scale search, penalizing hypotheses that are photometrically ambiguous but inconsistent with the coarse structure.

Finally, to correct errors propagated into regions with thin structures or sharp boundaries, we apply a detail restorer at each finer scale. Besides the guided estimate θp^g, we compute an independent estimate θp^s from photometric ACMH sampling at the current scale, without geometric guidance or coarse initialization. We compare the two hypotheses under the same photometric aggregated cost and retain the one with the lower cost if the independent estimate's cost is lower than that of the guided estimate by a margin δ, and its depth is not in conflict with the coarse estimate. This process allows us to recover details that may have been lost due to over-smoothing at coarser scales. By combining these components, our approach provides a robust and accurate method for depth estimation, capable of handling complex scenes and varying levels of texture and structure. In the context of multi-view stereo, a fundamental challenge arises from the inherent ambiguity of textureless regions, where the independent cost becomes unreliable and its improvement is limited by the margin. To address this issue, we adopt a guided refinement approach, wherein the independent estimate θp^g is replaced by the more reliable guided estimate θp^s in textureless areas. Conversely, near fine details, the independent estimate exhibits a clear cost advantage, enabling the recovery of structural information. Subsequent guided refinement then proceeds from the restored hypotheses.

The process of filtering and fusion is crucial in generating final depth maps. Initially, pixels with photometric costs exceeding a predetermined threshold are removed. Next, a pixel is retained only if its depth is geometrically consistent across at least nc source views, as evidenced by a reprojection error below εp pixels and a relative depth difference below εd, in accordance with the methodology outlined by Galliani et al. (2015) and Schönberger et al. (2016). The surviving pixels are then back-projected, and the consistent 3D points are averaged to yield the fused point cloud.

Our evaluation protocol involves assessing the performance of our approach on the ETH3D and Tanks and Temples datasets. The ETH3D dataset provides high-resolution and low-resolution multi-view benchmarks, accompanied by laser-scanned ground truth, whereas the Tanks and Temples dataset offers large-scale intermediate and advanced scenes. Both datasets are evaluated through their public servers, with ground-truth data for test scenes withheld. We employ accuracy, completeness, and the F₁ score as metrics, computed at the benchmark thresholds of 2 cm for ETH3D and scene-specific thresholds for Tanks and Temples. Our method is compared against established approaches, including COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016), Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015), and PMVS (Furukawa and Ponce, 2010), as well as learning-based methods such as MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) and R-MVSNet (Yao et al., 2019), where results are available.

To provide a more comprehensive understanding of our approach, we conducted ablation studies, examining the following variants: checkerboard sampling versus adaptive checkerboard sampling, single-hypothesis versus multi-hypothesis view selection, ACMH versus ACMM, and ACMM with and without the detail restorer. All variants shared the same filtering and fusion parameters. The system was implemented in CUDA, and runtime and memory were measured on a single GPU. Given the stochastic nature of the algorithm, due to random initialization and perturbation, we confirmed that repeated runs yielded negligible variation in the benchmark metrics and reported the benchmark scores for a single run.

Our experimental protocol involved evaluating our method on the ETH3D high-resolution multi-view benchmark and the Tanks and Temples dataset. We also conducted ablation studies on the ETH3D training set. Both benchmarks measure accuracy, completeness, and their harmonic mean, the F1 score, for a fused point cloud against a laser-scanned ground truth. The ETH3D benchmark reports these metrics at tolerances of 2 cm and 10 cm, while the Tanks and Temples benchmark reports the F-score at a scene-specific threshold. All variants used the same parameters across scenes, with ACMH run at a single scale and ACMM utilizing a four-level image pyramid. Depth maps were filtered with geometric consistency and fused into point clouds using the standard fusion pipeline.

The results on the ETH3D benchmark are summarized in Table 1, which shows the performance at the 2 cm tolerance on the training set. ACMH achieved an F1 score of 73.9%, with 83.2% accuracy and 67.1% completeness, outperforming COLMAP (67.7% F1) and Gipuma (58.2% F1). The majority of the gain can be attributed to the improvement in completeness, which increased by roughly 9 points over COLMAP at similar accuracy. This suggests that adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis view selection yield more reliable propagation in structured regions. The addition of multi-scale geometric consistency guidance and the detail restorer (ACMM) further raised the F1 score to 78.9%, with 90.7% accuracy and 70.4% completeness. The improvement in accuracy was 7.5 points over ACMH, while completeness improved by 3.3 points, indicating that the coarse-scale guidance did not compromise precision for coverage.

On the test set, ACMM achieved an F1 score of 80.8% at 2 cm, surpassing COLMAP (73.0%), TAPA-MVS (79.2%), and PCF-MVS (79.3%), and ranking first among published methods at submission time. The improvement over the learning-based pipeline of MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) was more pronounced, as this approach struggles with the high resolution and limited training distribution of ETH3D.
