At 10 cm, ACMM obtained an F1 score above 90%, indicating that most of its remaining errors are small and local rather than gross outliers.

The performance of ACMM varied by scene type, with a consistent pattern emerging. On indoor scenes featuring large low-textured walls and floors, such as delivery area, kicker, office, pipes, and relief, ACMM improved the 2 cm F1 score over ACMH by between 3 and 9 points. The largest improvements were observed on delivery area and office, which contain large uniform surfaces. In contrast, on outdoor scenes dominated by well-textured structures, such as facade and terrace, the difference between ACMH and ACMM was under 2 points. This aligns with the design intent, as multi-scale guidance is most beneficial in regions where matching at the finest scale is ambiguous.

On the Tanks and Temples intermediate set, ACMM reached a mean F-score of 57.3%, outperforming ACMH (54.8%), COLMAP (42.1%), and R-MVSNet (48.4%). ACMM also exceeded the strongest learning-based competitors at submission time, such as P-MVSNet and Point-MVSNet, whose mean F-scores ranged from 48% to 56%. ACMM ranked first on several scenes, including Family, Horse, and Playground, with F-scores above 60% on the first two. However, it was weaker on Train and Lighthouse, where specular surfaces and sky regions produce unreliable photometric costs, and the coarse-scale estimates carry larger errors. On the advanced set, ACMM obtained a mean F-score of 34.0%, higher than COLMAP (27.2%), and consistent with its gains on the intermediate set. Since Tanks and Temples evaluates at a fixed scene-dependent threshold, these improvements demonstrate that the gains in completeness do not rely on a looser tolerance.

Our ablation studies, conducted on the ETH3D training set at 2 cm, are summarized in Table 2. A baseline with standard red-black checkerboard sampling and fixed-view aggregation, in the style of Gipuma, produced an F1 score of 66.1%. Replacing the fixed neighborhood with adaptive sampling raised the F1 score to 69.8%. The addition of multi-hypothesis joint view selection brought the F1 score to 73.9%, which is the full ACMH. The view selection step alone contributed approximately 4 points, with most of the gain attributed to the improved reliability of propagation in structured regions. These results provide insight into the individual components of our approach and their contributions to the overall performance. The notion of completeness is crucial in the context of depth estimation, and our approach has been designed to address this issue. Specifically, our method excels when the best source views differ across hypotheses at a pixel, a scenario commonly encountered near occlusion boundaries. Building on the foundation of Adaptive Checkerboard Multi-Hypothesis (ACMH), we introduced a multi-scale component to our framework. By applying ACMH over a pyramid with plain upsampling of coarse depth maps, we observed a significant improvement in F1 score, reaching 75.6%. This enhancement was primarily attributed to the increased completeness in low-textured regions. Furthermore, the incorporation of geometric consistency guidance at coarser scales yielded a further increase in F1 score to 77.4%. This improvement can be attributed to the filtering of unreliable coarse estimates before upsampling, resulting in fewer erroneous depths being propagated to finer scales. The detail restorer provided a final boost, increasing the F1 score to 78.9%. Notably, this improvement was characterized by an increase in accuracy of approximately 1.2 points and an increase in completeness of around 1.8 points, indicating the restorer's ability to recover thin structures and fine boundaries that would otherwise be oversmoothed by coarse-scale propagation. The absence of the detail restorer resulted in visibly blurred edges around poles, railings, and object boundaries in the depth maps.

We also conducted an experiment to determine the optimal number of pyramid levels. Our results showed that with one, two, three, and four levels, the F1 scores were 73.9%, 76.8%, 78.4%, and 78.9%, respectively. However, the gains diminished beyond three levels, leading us to conclude that four levels were sufficient to cover the lowest-textured images at full resolution.

In terms of efficiency, ACMH demonstrated impressive performance, processing a 6048×4032 ETH3D image in under 5 seconds on a single GPU. This is notably faster than COLMAP's PatchMatch implementation, as measured in our experiments. Although ACMM required approximately 2.3 times the runtime of ACMH due to its processing of multiple scales and application of the restorer, its total time per scene remained comparable to other PatchMatch-based approaches. The GPU memory usage was dominated by the finest scale and increased by less than 10% over ACMH, as the coarser scales operated on downsampled images.

Visual comparisons of our results with those of other methods corroborate the quantitative findings. COLMAP and ACMH often leave holes or produce noisy estimates on textureless walls, tables, and floors, whereas ACMM fills these regions with planar, consistent depth. In contrast to methods that rely on planar priors, such as TAPA-MVS and PCF-MVS, ACMM retains finer geometry, including chair legs, cables, and window frames, and avoids the over-smoothed boundaries that can result from planar assumptions.

Our experiments provide strong evidence in support of the central premise of this work: reliable depth estimates in low-textured regions can be more easily obtained at coarse image scales and subsequently transferred to finer scales if the propagation is guided by geometric consistency. The long-standing challenge of patch-match-based multi-view stereo in regions with ambiguous photometric cues can be mitigated by our multi-scale strategy. At coarser scales, a larger physical extent is covered by a window, providing sufficient texture to anchor a correct hypothesis. Geometric consistency checks across views filter out unreliable coarse estimates, ensuring that only estimates supported by multiple views are propagated upward.

The ablation results indicate that the components of our approach contribute in complementary ways. Adaptive checkerboard sampling and multi-hypothesis joint view selection (ACMH) account for a significant portion of the improvement over the baseline. By sampling candidates from structured neighborhoods rather than a fixed pattern, the chance of a correct hypothesis being evaluated at each pixel is increased, particularly near depth discontinuities and in elongated structures where fixed patterns can waste candidates on unrelated surfaces. Per-hypothesis view selection reduces the contamination of the aggregated cost by occluded or poorly overlapping views, a limitation noted in earlier selection schemes. The joint selection of views for multiple hypotheses prevents a pixel from being forced to commit to a single view subset before its depth is known.

The multi-scale extension (ACMM) primarily determines completeness in textureless regions, where ACMH alone is insufficient. The basic method ensures accuracy at each scale, while the multi-scale guidance enables the scales to inform one another. The detail restorer addresses the intrinsic trade-off in coarse-to-fine schemes, where upsampling coarse estimates can lead to oversmoothing of thin structures, small objects, and boundaries. By treating propagated estimates as candidates to be verified rather than as final values, the restorer allows pixels to be re-estimated with their own hypotheses when finer-scale photometric evidence disagrees with the propagated estimate.

The improvements in accuracy at tighter error thresholds, combined with the qualitative recovery of fine structures, suggest that the restorer reduces error inherited from coarse levels without discarding the completeness they provide. The method's performance across benchmarks with diverse characteristics, including indoor high-resolution scenes and large outdoor scenes, indicates that the gains are not specific to a single dataset's properties.

However, several limitations of our approach should be acknowledged. Firstly, the method relies on the coarse scale being at least partly correct. In regions where even the coarse image is ambiguous, such as large reflective or transparent surfaces, repetitive patterns, or areas with strong view-dependent appearance, the geometric consistency filter may reject all estimates, leaving no reliable information to propagate. In such cases, the method may degrade to the behavior of the single-scale approach, and in the worst case, consistent but incorrect estimates may be propagated. Secondly, the method assumes accurate camera calibration, and errors in pose estimation can reduce the discriminative power of both photometric and geometric terms. The multi-scale scheme does not correct these errors. Thirdly, although the method is efficient due to GPU-friendly checkerboard propagation, the processing of multiple scales and the restoration step add computation and memory relative to a single-scale pipeline. This overhead is modest in our measurements but could be significant for very large collections or embedded settings. Finally, several hyperparameters, such as the number of scales, consistency thresholds, and the number of sampled hypotheses, were set empirically, and further investigation is required to fully optimize these parameters.

The advent of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has revolutionized the field of transcriptomics, offering a powerful tool for profiling gene expression on a genome-wide scale. By providing a more comprehensive and nuanced view of the transcriptome than traditional microarray-based approaches, RNA-seq has become the method of choice for many applications, including the identification of differentially expressed genes and the analysis of molecular pathways. This is due in part to its ability to detect novel transcripts and splice variants, as well as its applicability to any organism with a reference genome, as demonstrated by Wang et al. (2009) and Stark et al. (2019). The analysis of RNA-seq data typically involves several key steps, including the derivation of gene-level counts, assessment of data quality, statistical modeling of the counts, and interpretation of the results in terms of biological function. Each of these steps presents its own set of challenges and requires careful consideration of the various tools and methods available.

One of the primary challenges in the analysis of RNA-seq data is the statistical modeling of the count data. The counts are typically non-negative integers, and their variance often exceeds that expected under a Poisson model, even among biological replicates. To address this issue, overdispersed distributions such as the negative binomial (NB) are commonly used, as described by Robinson and Smyth (2007) and Anders and Huber (2010). The NB model assumes that the variance of the count ygi for gene g in sample i with mean μgi is given by var(ygi) = μgi + φg μgi², where φg is the NB dispersion, representing the squared biological coefficient of variation. However, because experiments typically involve only a handful of replicates per condition, gene-wise dispersions cannot be estimated reliably in isolation, and information must be shared across genes through empirical Bayes moderation, as discussed by Robinson and Smyth (2008) and McCarthy et al. (2012). Additionally, samples often differ in sequencing depth and RNA composition, requiring normalization methods such as the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) to avoid spurious differentially expressed (DE) calls, as described by Robinson and Oshlack (2010).

The edgeR package, first introduced by Robinson et al. (2010), has been a popular choice for the analysis of RNA-seq data, and has undergone significant development over the years. Early versions of the package relied on exact tests and likelihood ratio tests, which can be liberal and lead to inflated false discovery rates when replicate numbers are small. To address this issue, the quasi-likelihood (QL) framework was developed, which provides a more conservative and reliable approach to error rate control. The QL pipeline in edgeR involves fitting a NB generalized linear model (GLM) to each gene, with a log-linear mean structure given by log μgi = log Ni + xi^T βg, where Ni is the effective library size and xi is the row of the design matrix for sample i. Gene-wise QL dispersions are then estimated from the residual deviances and moderated using empirical Bayes shrinkage toward a global trend, as described by Phipson et al. (2016). Hypotheses are tested using F-tests that reflect uncertainty in both the dispersion and the quasi-dispersion estimates, providing a more robust and reliable approach to identifying DE genes.

Upstream of the statistical analysis lies the critical step of converting raw reads into counts. This involves aligning the reads to a reference genome and summarizing the results over genes. The Rsubread package provides a convenient and efficient solution to this problem, offering R-based implementations of the Subread and Subjunc aligners and the featureCounts read summarization program, as described by Liao et al. (2013, 2014) and Liao and Shi (2020). These tools are fast, accurate, and memory-efficient, and their integration within R allows for a seamless and reproducible analysis pipeline. Alternative approaches, including splice-aware aligners such as STAR (Dobin et al., 2013) and HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2015), as well as alignment-free quantification methods like Salmon or kallisto (Patro et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2016), are also widely used and compatible with the downstream edgeR analysis.

Despite the maturity of these methods, newcomers to RNA-seq analysis often face a significant barrier to entry. Package documentation typically focuses on individual functions rather than the overall analysis workflow, and published examples frequently begin with precomputed count matrices, omitting the critical steps of alignment and quantification. Conversely, many pipelines automate the analysis without providing a clear understanding of the underlying reasoning and decision-making process. Earlier Bioconductor workflows, such as the edgeR-limma workflow (Law et al., 2016) and the DESeq2-based workflow of Love et al. (2015), have been valuable teaching resources, but the software has continued to evolve, with significant developments in the QL pipeline, filtering methods (Chen et al., 2016), and annotation and gene set resources. As a result, there is a need for a comprehensive and up-to-date workflow that unites the Rsubread alignment tools with the current edgeR QL methodology.

This article addresses this gap by presenting a complete, reproducible workflow for the analysis of a real RNA-seq experiment. The data profile three epithelial cell populations of the mouse mammary gland, namely basal cells, luminal progenitor cells, and mature luminal cells, in biological replicates from virgin mice (Sheridan et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2015). The mammary epithelium has a well-characterized hierarchy, making it an ideal test case for evaluating the performance of the workflow. The workflow demonstrates read alignment, quantification, and statistical analysis using the edgeR package, and provides a clear and detailed explanation of each step, including the reasoning behind key decisions and the interpretation of results. By providing a comprehensive and reproducible workflow, this article aims to facilitate the analysis of RNA-seq data and promote a deeper understanding of the underlying methods and principles. The workflow makes several contributions, including the demonstration of read alignment, the application of the QL pipeline, and the integration of gene set tests and pathway analysis. Overall, this workflow provides a valuable resource for researchers seeking to analyze RNA-seq data and gain insights into the underlying biology of their system of interest. The analysis of RNA-seq data from epithelial cell populations in the mouse mammary gland involves several key steps. Firstly, we utilize the Rsubread package to perform read alignment and gene-level quantification, which is then directly linked to the creation of edgeR data objects, complete with associated gene annotation. This integration enables a seamless workflow, allowing researchers to efficiently analyze their data. 

A crucial aspect of this workflow is the exploration of data quality, which encompasses filtering, normalization, and unsupervised clustering. By applying these steps, researchers can ensure that their data are reliable and suitable for downstream analysis. For instance, filtering out genes with very low expression is essential, as these genes provide little evidence of differential expression and can interfere with mean-variance modeling. The filterByExpr function in edgeR is particularly useful in this regard, as it removes genes with counts-per-million (CPM) below a specified threshold, thereby improving the accuracy of subsequent analyses.

Following data pre-processing, the construction of design and contrast matrices is critical for assessing differential expression between different cell types. In this study, we employed a means-model design matrix without an intercept, where each coefficient represents the log-expression of one cell type. This approach enables the comparison of basal, luminal progenitor (LP), and mature luminal (ML) cell types, as well as the estimation of the effect of physiological state using an interaction-free additive model. The makeContrasts function in edgeR is used to construct contrasts for comparing basal versus LP, basal versus ML, and LP versus ML, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the differences between these cell types.

To visualize the results, we utilized various plots, including mean-difference plots, heatmaps, and Venn diagrams. These visualizations provide valuable insights into the patterns of gene expression and differential expression between cell types. For example, mean-difference plots can help identify genes that are differentially expressed between two cell types, while heatmaps can reveal clusters of genes with similar expression patterns. Furthermore, Venn diagrams can be used to illustrate the overlap between different gene sets, facilitating the identification of common and unique features between cell types.

In addition to gene-level analysis, we extended our findings to the pathway level using Gene Ontology and KEGG over-representation analysis, competitive gene set testing with camera, and rotation-based tests with fry. These analyses enable researchers to identify biological pathways and processes that are enriched with differentially expressed genes, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying biology. The use of barcode plots for enrichment visualization also facilitates the interpretation of these results, allowing researchers to rapidly identify key pathways and processes.

The RNA-seq data used in this study were generated from a study of epithelial cell populations in the mouse mammary gland. Three cell populations were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting from virgin female mice: basal stem-cell enriched cells (basal), luminal progenitor cells (LP), and mature luminal cells (ML). Each population was sorted from two independent biological replicates, resulting in twelve libraries in a 3 × 2 layout. However, for the present workflow, only the six virgin-mouse samples were analyzed in detail, with each cell type represented by two biological replicates derived from different mice.

Total RNA was extracted, and libraries were prepared using a standard poly(A)-selection protocol. 100 bp single-end reads were generated on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform, and raw reads are available from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus and Sequence Read Archive. FASTQ files were downloaded and used without trimming, as base-call quality was uniformly high.

Read alignment and quantification were performed using the Rsubread package in Bioconductor. A genome index was built with buildindex using the default memory setting, and reads were mapped with the align function, which implements the seed-and-vote algorithm. Default parameters were used, allowing uniquely mapped reads only and permitting a small number of mismatches and indels. Alignment output was written as sorted, indexed BAM files, and mapping proportions were summarized with propmapped to verify that each library had a high proportion of uniquely mapped reads (>80%).

Gene-level read counts were produced with featureCounts, using the inbuilt Rsubread annotation for mm10 based on NCBI RefSeq. Reads were summarized at the gene level by counting reads overlapping any exon of a gene, and reads overlapping more than one gene were not counted. The result is a matrix of integer counts with genes in rows and libraries in columns, together with gene identifiers (Entrez Gene IDs) and gene lengths. Gene symbols and descriptions were added using the org.Mm.eg.db annotation package. Where genes had duplicated symbols, the entry with the largest total count was retained.

Data pre-processing and filtering were performed using the edgeR package. Counts were stored in a DGEList object, and genes with very low expression were removed using filterByExpr. After filtering, library sizes were recomputed, and normalization for composition bias was applied using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method. For sample j relative to a reference sample r, the log-ratio Mgj = log2[(ygj/Nj)/(ygr/Nr)] is computed for each gene g, where y is the count and N the library size. After trimming genes with extreme M-values and extreme average abundance, a weighted mean of the remaining M-values yields a log2 scaling factor, which is converted to a normalization factor fj such that the effective library size is Nj fj.

Data exploration was performed by computing log2-CPM values with a small prior count to avoid undefined values for zero counts, using the cpm function with prior.count = 2. Library-size distributions and the distributions of log-CPM per sample were examined as boxplots before and after normalization. Sample relationships were examined by multidimensional scaling (MDS) with plotMDS, where the distance between samples is the root-mean-square of the largest 500 log2-fold changes between those samples (leading log-fold-change). Plots were colored by cell type and by replicate to identify the main sources of variation and any batch effects. Hierarchical clustering of the most variable genes was used as a complementary check.

Differential expression was assessed within a generalized linear model (GLM) framework. For the cell-type comparison, a means-model design matrix without an intercept was used, in which each coefficient represents the log-expression of one cell type. Where samples were paired or batch effects were evident, additive terms for the batch were included. Contrasts were constructed with makeContrasts to compare basal versus LP, basal versus ML, and LP versus ML.

Dispersion estimation and quasi-likelihood testing were performed using the edgeR package. Read counts ygi for gene g in library i were modeled as negative binomial (NB) with mean μgi and dispersion φg: ygi ~ NB(μgi, φg), Var(ygi) = μgi + φg μgi², with log μgi = xiᵀβg + log(Ni fi), where xi is the row of the design matrix for library i and βg is the vector of coefficients for gene g. The offset log(Ni fi) accounts for sequencing depth and composition. Dispersions were estimated with estimateDisp, which uses the Cox–Reid adjusted profile likelihood to estimate a common dispersion, a trended dispersion as a function of average log-CPM, and gene-wise dispersion.

Overall, this workflow provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing RNA-seq data, from read alignment and quantification to differential expression analysis and pathway-level interpretation. By following this workflow, researchers can gain valuable insights into the biology of their system, including the identification of differentially expressed genes, enriched pathways, and key regulatory processes. The use of executable code and detailed documentation enables readers to reproduce the results and adapt the workflow to their own experiments, making it a valuable resource for the scientific community. The analysis of differential gene expression in our dataset relied on the use of empirical Bayes moderation towards the trend, as described by Chen et al. (2014) and McCarthy et al. (2012). To fit the models, we utilized the glmQLFit function with the robust option enabled, as recommended by Lun et al. (2016) and Phipson et al. (2016). This approach allows for the estimation of an additional gene-specific quasi-dispersion, which captures variability not accounted for by the negative binomial dispersion. The quasi-likelihood dispersions are then shrunk towards a common trend using empirical Bayes shrinkage, which employs a scaled inverse chi-square prior. The prior degrees of freedom, denoted as d₀, are estimated from the data, and the posterior quasi-likelihood dispersion for each gene is calculated as s̃²g = (d₀ s₀² + dg s²g) / (d₀ + dg), where s²g represents the raw quasi-dispersion, dg is the residual degrees of freedom, and s₀² is the prior value from the trend.

The robust option provides protection against hypervariable and low-variance genes, ensuring that the estimation of d₀ and s₀² is reliable. To perform hypothesis tests, we used the glmQLFTest function, which computes a quasi-likelihood F-statistic by comparing the deviance of the full model to that of a model with the contrast constraint imposed, scaled by the moderated quasi-likelihood dispersion. This approach yields a more conservative and reliable control of the type I error rate, particularly when dealing with few replicates. The resulting F-test has numerator degrees of freedom equal to the number of tested constraints and denominator degrees of freedom d₀ + dg. We adjusted the p-values for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, as described by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), and declared genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 0.05 to be differentially expressed.

To summarize the differential expression results, we utilized the decideTests function and visualized the data using mean-difference plots, heatmaps of log-counts per million (CPM) values for the top genes, and Venn diagrams of overlaps between contrasts. In addition to the standard differential expression analysis, we also applied the TREAT procedure, as described by McCarthy and Smyth (2009), to prioritize genes with biologically meaningful changes. This involved testing the null hypothesis that the absolute log2-fold change is at most a threshold of log2 1.5. The TREAT p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method, as described above.

For gene ontology and pathway analysis, we employed the Gene Ontology (GO) database, as described by Ashburner et al. (2000), and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database, as described by Kanehisa and Goto (2000). We assessed the over-representation of GO terms and KEGG pathways among differentially expressed genes using the goana and kegga functions, which account for gene-length or abundance-related bias through the trend option, using the average log-CPM as a covariate, as described by Young et al. (2010). We also performed competitive gene set testing using the camera function, as described by Wu and Smyth (2012), which accounts for inter-gene correlation, using the Molecular Signatures Database mouse C2 collection, as described by Subramanian et al. (2005), converted to mouse Entrez identifiers, as described by Liberzon et al. (2011). Furthermore, we visualized the enrichment of gene sets using the barcodeplot function and performed rotation-based testing using the fry function, as described by Wu et al. (2010), for self-contained testing of the same gene sets.

All analyses were conducted in R using Bioconductor packages, including Rsubread, edgeR, limma, as described by Ritchie et al. (2015), and org.Mm.eg.db. The package versions are recorded using the sessionInfo function, and the code is provided as an executable workflow. The experiment comprised 12 samples from the mouse mammary gland dataset of Fu et al. (2015), covering three epithelial subpopulations (basal, luminal progenitor, and mature luminal) from virgin, pregnant, and lactating mice, with two biological replicates per group. Reads were aligned to the mouse mm10 reference genome using the Rsubread aligner, as described by Liao et al. (2013), with its seed-and-vote algorithm. The alignment results showed that between 82% and 90% of reads in each sample mapped uniquely, with a median of 87%, and the lowest mapping rates were observed in the lactating samples.

After alignment, library sizes ranged from 21.4 to 31.2 million mapped reads per sample. Counting with featureCounts, as described by Liao et al. (2014), against the Entrez Gene-based RefSeq annotation assigned 62-71% of aligned reads to exons, while the remaining reads fell in unannotated or intergenic regions. This produced a count matrix covering 27,179 annotated genes. The counts were highly reproducible between replicates, with Pearson correlations of log-counts above 0.98 within every group. To filter out lowly expressed genes, we used the filterByExpr function, which requires a minimum CPM threshold equivalent to roughly 10 reads in the smallest library in at least two samples. This retained 15,804 genes, which accounted for more than 99.9% of all counted reads.

After filtering, we applied TMM normalization, as described by Robinson and Oshlack (2010), which gave scaling factors between 0.89 and 1.12. The extremes belonged to the lactating samples, which are dominated by highly abundant milk-protein transcripts such as Csn2, Wap, and Csn3. These genes alone contributed more than 20% of counts in some lactating luminal samples, explaining the composition bias that TMM corrects. Mean-difference plots of normalized log-CPM values showed that the bulk of genes were centered on zero after normalization.

For exploratory analysis, we performed multidimensional scaling of the top 500 most variable genes using a leading log-fold-change distance. This showed clear separation of samples by cell type, with dimension 1 accounting for 49% of the variance and separating basal cells from both luminal populations. Dimension 2 (17%) separated luminal progenitor from mature luminal cells, while dimension 3 (9%) separated samples by developmental stage, primarily within the luminal lineages, with lactating samples distinct from virgin and pregnant ones. Replicates of the same group clustered tightly, and no outlier samples were detected, so all 12 libraries were retained. Hierarchical clustering of the same data gave the same grouping.

To estimate the dispersion, we fitted a generalized linear model with a cell-type-by-status group factor and estimated dispersions with empirical Bayes shrinkage, as described by Chen et al. (2014) and McCarthy et al. (2012). The biological coefficient of variation (BCV) was moderate, with the common dispersion corresponding to a BCV of about 0.43, and the trended dispersion decreasing with abundance from about 0.55 at low expression to about 0.25 at high expression. The quasi-likelihood step, as described by Lund et al. (2012), allowed for the estimation of gene-specific quasi-dispersions, which capture variability not accounted for by the negative binomial dispersion. The estimation of gene-wise quasi-dispersions, as reported by Lun et al. in 2016, involved shrinking these values towards a mean-dependent trend, with a prior of approximately 14 degrees of freedom. Notably, the shrinkage employed was moderate, rather than severe, and the raw quasi-dispersions exhibited well-behaved characteristics. Only a small subset of genes displayed quasi-dispersions that significantly deviated from the trend, suggesting that the model was generally adequate for capturing the underlying biological variability. Given the limited residual degrees of freedom, which averaged 6 per gene, the F-test with moderated degrees of freedom was found to be more conservative than the likelihood ratio test. This conservatism is consistent with the F-test's better control of the type I error rate, a critical consideration in high-throughput differential expression analyses.

To investigate differential expression between cell types, we conducted pairwise comparisons using the quasi-likelihood F-test, adjusting p-values with the Benjamini–Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate (FDR) at 5%. Focusing on the lactating group as the primary comparison, we identified 4,127 differentially expressed (DE) genes when contrasting basal cells with luminal progenitor (LP) cells, with 2,106 genes upregulated and 2,021 downregulated in basal cells. Similarly, the comparison between basal and mature luminal (ML) cells yielded 4,683 DE genes, comprising 2,372 upregulated and 2,311 downregulated genes. In contrast, the LP versus ML comparison resulted in fewer DE genes, with 2,314 genes identified, of which 1,180 were upregulated in LP cells and 1,134 downregulated. These findings align with the multidimensional scaling (MDS) results, which indicated that the two luminal subsets are more similar to each other than either is to basal cells. Across all three contrasts, 1,426 genes were consistently differentially expressed, and many of these genes are well-established lineage markers. For instance, basal cells exhibited higher expression of Krt14, Acta2, and Myh11, with log2 fold changes exceeding 5 compared to luminal cells, and FDR values below 1e-10. Conversely, luminal cells showed strong expression of Krt18, Krt8, Elf5, and Csn3. Within the luminal lineage, ML cells expressed higher levels of milk protein genes and Prlr, while LP cells displayed higher expression of Kit, Aldh1a3, and Cd14.

However, it is noteworthy that many significant genes exhibited small fold changes. To address this, we applied the TREAT test, as described by McCarthy and Smyth in 2009, using a threshold of log2(1.5) to filter out genes with modest changes and low expression. This resulted in a reduced list of 2,361 genes for the basal versus LP comparison, comprising 1,167 upregulated and 1,194 downregulated genes. The greatest reduction occurred among genes with small changes and low expression, indicating that the filtered list is enriched for genes with biologically relevant differences. Mean-difference plots, where DE genes are highlighted, demonstrated that significant genes were distributed across the entire range of abundance. Furthermore, heatmaps of the top 100 genes per contrast, displayed as row-scaled log-CPM values, perfectly clustered samples by cell type, with pregnancy and lactation samples within each type clustering together.

To further elucidate the biological significance of these findings, we performed gene ontology (GO) and gene set analyses. GO over-representation analysis of the TREAT-significant basal versus LP genes was conducted using goana, with correction for gene length-related selection bias. Genes upregulated in basal cells were enriched for terms related to cell adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, muscle contraction, and cytoskeleton organization. For example, the term "extracellular matrix organization" was significantly enriched, with an FDR of 3 × 10⁻²⁵. In contrast, genes upregulated in LP cells were enriched for immune-related processes, lipid metabolism, and secretion, such as the term "immune system process," which had an FDR of 8 × 10⁻¹⁴. In the ML versus LP comparison, genes upregulated in ML cells were enriched for terms related to lactation, milk protein secretion, and lipid biosynthesis.

We also tested whether curated signatures were coordinately regulated using camera, as described by Wu and Smyth in 2012, and fry, with Molecular Signatures Database collections and mammary-specific gene sets from Lim et al. in 2010. In the basal versus LP contrast, the Lim mammary stem cell-up set was strongly enriched in basal cells, with a camera FDR below 1e-10, while the Lim mature luminal-up set was enriched in the opposite direction. Similarly, in the LP versus ML contrast, the LP signature was enriched in LP cells, with an FDR of 2 × 10⁻⁶. Results from fry were consistent with those from camera for all top-ranked sets, and roast-type self-contained tests yielded consistent conclusions for the stem-cell and luminal signatures. Barcode plots showed that most genes in these signatures moved in the expected direction, consistent with the DE gene lists.

This study presents a comprehensive workflow for the analysis of an RNA-seq experiment, from raw reads to differential expression and pathway analysis, using the mouse mammary epithelium data from Sheridan et al. in 2015 as a worked example. All analytical steps were performed within the R/Bioconductor framework, with alignment and summarization conducted using Rsubread and statistical modeling performed using the quasi-likelihood framework of edgeR. The interpretation of the main findings, the reasoning behind key methodological choices, limitations, and implications for practice are discussed below.

Biologically, the analysis revealed a coherent picture of the three epithelial populations. Principal component-type exploration by multidimensional scaling separated basal, LP, and ML cells along the first two dimensions, with replicates clustering tightly by cell type. This indicates that the primary source of variation is biological rather than technical and that the three-group design with a modest number of replicates is adequate for the contrasts of interest. The differential expression results were consistent with the known lineage hierarchy of the mammary gland, with the basal population showing elevated expression of myoepithelial and stem-associated markers, and the luminal populations enriched for keratins and genes associated with secretory differentiation. Gene set testing results, using camera, fry, and goana, reinforced this interpretation by identifying coordinated changes in sets related to cell adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and mammary-specific signatures derived from independent studies.

The use of independently derived signatures, which recapitulated expected directions of change in our data, provides a useful form of external validation and highlights the value of pathway-level analysis beyond gene lists. This is particularly important when dealing with large contrasts that can include thousands of genes, making direct interpretation challenging. Furthermore, the application of a TREAT-style test with a modest fold-change threshold illustrates an important practical consideration. When biological differences between cell types are substantial, conventional tests against a null of exactly zero log-fold-change can yield very long DE lists that include genes with statistically detectable but biologically minor changes. By testing against a minimum fold-change threshold, researchers can prioritize genes whose changes are likely to be of functional relevance, albeit at the cost of reduced sensitivity for subtle effects.

The quest for learning useful representations from unlabeled data has become a cornerstone of machine learning research. While supervised deep networks have yielded remarkable breakthroughs in vision, speech, and language, their reliance on large annotated datasets is a significant limitation. These datasets are not only expensive to collect but also constrain the learned features to a specific label set, hindering their ability to generalize across tasks. Self-supervised learning, on the other hand, seeks to alleviate this dependence by leveraging the inherent structure of the data to construct a learning signal. This approach enables the evaluation of a model's features based on their performance on downstream tasks, using either a simple linear classifier or limited fine-tuning data. The underlying promise of self-supervised learning is that representations learned from abundant raw data will exhibit broad transferability and require minimal labeled supervision.

Recent advances in self-supervised learning have been driven, in part, by the design of pretext tasks that encourage a network to capture semantic structure. Examples of such tasks include predicting the relative position of image patches, solving jigsaw puzzles, colorizing grayscale images, and predicting image rotations. Similarly, in the realm of language, predicting masked or neighboring words has proven effective. Although these tasks can be successful, they rely on hand-designed heuristics, which may limit the generality of the learned features. Furthermore, it is often unclear why a particular task yields representations that are useful for object recognition.

A complementary line of research has focused on grounding representation learning in an explicit information-theoretic objective. The InfoMax principle, first proposed by Linsker in 1988, posits that a good encoder should preserve as much information as possible about its input. Modern variants of this principle estimate and maximize mutual information using neural lower bounds, rendering it practical for high-dimensional data. However, maximizing the information that features retain about the entire input can be problematic. Mutual information is invariant to invertible transformations, which means that a representation can score highly while encoding low-level details, such as pixel-level noise, without necessarily exposing the high-level structure that matters for downstream tasks.

A more fruitful approach is to consider which information should be shared across different views of the same underlying context. The concept of multiview learning, which encompasses techniques such as canonical correlation analysis, co-training, and contrastive multiview coding, is based on the observation that information present in multiple views is more likely to reflect stable, semantically meaningful factors. Recent methods, including Deep InfoMax, Contrastive Predictive Coding, and others, can be seen as instances of this idea. These approaches maximize mutual information between different views or features, using techniques such as noise-contrastive objectives, multiple scales, and different sensory modalities.

Despite the progress made in self-supervised learning, a significant gap remains between self-supervised and supervised features on large-scale benchmarks like ImageNet. The best prior self-supervised encoders have lagged behind supervised ones in terms of linear evaluation performance. Moreover, it is unclear which design choices are most important, such as the construction of views, the scales at which features are compared, the parametrization of the encoder, and the scaling of the contrastive objective. Existing methods often predict within a single scale of the feature hierarchy, compare features from a single view pairing, or use encoder architectures that were not designed with mutual-information maximization in mind.

In this paper, we investigate self-supervised learning as the maximization of mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context. A context can be a local spatio-temporal region of the world, from which views are obtained by observing it from different positions or through different modalities. Alternatively, a single natural image can serve as the context, with views produced by repeated stochastic data augmentation. Our central hypothesis is that, to predict features of one view from another, an encoder must capture information about high-level factors, such as object presence or the occurrence of events, whose influence spans views, while discarding view-specific nuisance. This formulation unifies and generalizes several earlier approaches, suggesting a concrete way to improve them: enrich the set of views and the scales at which they are compared, and design an encoder architecture suited to the task.

We instantiate this approach in a model called Augmented Multiscale Deep InfoMax (AMDIM). AMDIM extends local Deep InfoMax in three key ways. First, it maximizes mutual information between features drawn from independently augmented copies of each image, rather than between a global summary and local features of the same input. Second, it predicts across multiple scales simultaneously, maximizing information between a global feature vector and spatial feature maps at several layers, as well as between intermediate feature maps. Third, it uses an encoder architecture adapted to this objective, with carefully controlled receptive fields to avoid trivial solutions. We optimize a contrastive lower bound on mutual information, using large numbers of negative samples, which we make tractable through efficient computation. We further extend the model to produce mixture-based representations, in which several latent assignments compete to explain local features.

Our contributions are twofold. First, we propose a general framework for self-supervised representation learning based on maximizing mutual information across views of a shared context, and demonstrate how data augmentation, multiple scales, and multiple modalities fit within it. Second, we develop AMDIM, whose representations achieve 68.1% accuracy on ImageNet under standard linear evaluation, exceeding prior self-supervised results by more than 12% and concurrent results by 7%. We also provide a detailed analysis of the model's performance, highlighting the importance of careful design choices and the potential for further improvement. Our approach, which we term Augmented Multiscale Deep InfoMax (AMDIM), builds upon the foundation laid by Local Deep InfoMax (Hjelm et al., 2019) and introduces several key innovations. At its core, AMDIM learns an encoder by maximizing the mutual information between features computed from different views of a shared context. This is achieved through a noise-contrastive objective (Oord et al., 2018), which we will describe in detail below. 

To begin with, let us consider the contrastive objective that underlies our approach. Given a context x, we sample two views x¹ and x² by applying stochastic data augmentation twice. An encoder f then produces a global feature vector f₁(x¹) from the first view and a spatial map of local features fk(x²) from the second, where fk(x²){i,j} denotes the feature at location (i,j) of layer k. Our goal is to maximize a lower bound on the mutual information between f₁(x¹) and fk(x²){i,j}. To achieve this, we use the NCE-based bound (Oord et al., 2018; Poole et al., 2019), which involves computing the loss for a positive pair (a, b) with a negative set N as L = −log [exp(φ(a,b)) / Σ{b′∈N∪{b}} exp(φ(a,b′))], where φ is a critic that we will discuss shortly.

The critic φ plays a crucial role in our approach, as it enables us to compute the similarity between features from different views. Following the lead of Tschannen et al. (2019) and Bachman et al. (2019), we use a distance-like critic, φ(a,b) = (u(a)ᵀ v(b)) / √d, where u and v are learned embeddings of dimension d. To prevent the critic outputs from growing without bound, we apply a soft clipping to φ, φ ← τ·tanh(φ/τ) with τ = 20, and add a small regularizer of 4×10⁻² · mean(φ²) that penalizes the squared magnitude of critic scores.

One of the key innovations of our approach is the use of multiscale, multiview prediction. Let f₁, f₅, and f₇ denote global (1×1), 5×5, and 7×7 feature maps from an encoder applied to 128×128 images. We compute the objective between the global features of one view and the local features at multiple scales of the other, and symmetrize over the two views: L = Σ{m∈{5,7}} [L(f₁(x¹), fm(x²)) + L(f₁(x²), fm(x¹))] + L(f₅(x¹), f₇(x²)) + L(f₅(x²), f₇(x¹)). Each term uses its own critic embeddings, obtained by passing the features through small residual MLP-like projection heads implemented as 1×1 convolutions. Negatives are drawn from all other spatial positions and all other images in the batch, so each positive pair is contrasted against many thousands of negatives, which are computed efficiently by matrix multiplication of embedding tensors.

The encoder architecture is another critical component of our approach. We use a ResNet-style network (He et al., 2016) with modifications that control receptive-field overlap, ensuring that local features of different positions do not leak information about positions in the other view. The base model has an initial 3×3 convolution followed by stages of residual blocks with width multiplier ndf, and we scale capacity through ndf, the number of residual blocks per stage, and the output dimension. We use ReLU nonlinearities and batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015). The default model has roughly 194M parameters on ImageNet; we also report smaller configurations for comparison with prior work. Features at layers producing 1×1, 5×5, and 7×7 maps are tapped for the objective.

Data augmentation plays a crucial role in our approach, as it enables us to generate multiple views of the same image. For ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015), we resize and take random crops, apply random horizontal flips, random color jitter (brightness, contrast, saturation, hue), and random conversion to grayscale. Augmentations are applied independently for each view. Images are rescaled to 128×128 for training, and for evaluation, we use center crops. For CIFAR10 (Krizhevsky, 2009), STL10 (Coates et al., 2011), and Places205 (Zhou et al., 2014), we use analogous augmentations at 32×32, 64×64, and 128×128 resolution respectively; for STL10, we pretrain on the unlabeled split.

In addition to the above components, we also explore the use of mixture-based representations. To obtain mixture-based features, we compute for each of nc components a separate set of feature maps via a 1×1 convolution on top of the encoder, along with a per-location, per-component assignment probability computed by a softmax over components. Local features are treated as a mixture, with the contrastive objective computed per component and weighted by the assignment probabilities, in the style of a variational routing procedure. We add a Dirichlet-like regularizer encouraging balanced use of components. Segmentation-like behavior is assessed by visualizing the assignment maps, with no segmentation supervision.

To optimize our model, we use Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁴ and default momentum parameters. Batch sizes range from 200 to 1008 images per batch, distributed across multiple GPUs, with mixed-precision training where applicable. ImageNet training runs for the number of epochs specified in each experiment, and we use a short linear warmup. Hyperparameters were selected on held-out validation data, never on test labels.

Our evaluation protocol follows the standard linear evaluation protocol (Zhang et al., 2016; Kolesnikov et al., 2019). After self-supervised pretraining, encoder weights are frozen, and a linear classifier is trained on the global features (with gradients detached from the encoder) using labeled data. For ImageNet, we report top-1 accuracy on the 50,000-image validation set, using a classifier trained on the full labeled training set. For CIFAR10 and STL10, we train on the standard training splits (for STL10, averaging across the predefined folds) and report test accuracy. For Places205, we pretrain on ImageNet and train a linear classifier on Places205 features to assess transfer. Classifiers are trained with a fixed number of epochs using standard cross-entropy; features are batch-normalized before the linear layer.

Finally, we compare our approach to published self-supervised results, including Contrastive Predictive Coding (Oord et al., 2018; Hénaff et al., 2019), BigBiGAN (Donahue & Simonyan, 2019), Local Deep InfoMax (Hjelm et al., 2019), colorization, rotation prediction (Gidaris et al., 2018), and the concurrent work of Tian et al. (2019). We also perform ablations to isolate the contributions of multiscale prediction, the augmentation strategy, encoder size, negative-sample count, critic regularization and clipping, and other components of our approach. These experiments provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our approach and highlight areas for future improvement. The evaluation of our model's performance was conducted through a series of experiments, where we systematically varied individual components while keeping others fixed, in order to isolate the effects of each factor. Due to the considerable computational cost associated with ImageNet pretraining, our large-scale results are based on single runs. However, for the smaller datasets, CIFAR10 and STL10, we repeated the training process with different random seeds and report the mean accuracies along with their standard deviations. We only consider differences that exceed the seed-to-seed variation as statistically meaningful. It is worth noting that all the reported accuracies are based on held-out data, which was not used for model selection, thereby ensuring a fair evaluation.

Our experimental protocol followed the standard linear protocol, where the encoder is first trained using the self-supervised objective and then frozen. Subsequently, a linear classifier is trained on the features extracted by the encoder, using the class labels, and the accuracy is evaluated on the held-out data. We conducted experiments on a range of datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, STL10, ImageNet, and Places205, with ImageNet being the primary benchmark. For ImageNet, we report both top-1 and top-5 accuracies, with the latter being reported for the strongest model. In the case of STL10, we trained the model on the unlabeled split and then trained the linear classifier on the labeled training folds. For Places205, we transferred the encoder trained on ImageNet without fine-tuning, in order to assess its ability to generalize across datasets.

Unless otherwise specified, the numbers reported are based on single runs with fixed hyperparameters across datasets, except for adjustments to the input resolution and the depth and width of the encoder. A comparison with prior methods is presented in Table 1, which summarizes the linear-evaluation results. On the smaller datasets, our model, AMDIM, demonstrates substantial improvements over Deep InfoMax (DIM), the model it extends. Specifically, DIM achieves approximately 75% on CIFAR10, 50% on CIFAR100, and 77% on STL10, whereas AMDIM reaches 91.2% on CIFAR10, 70.2% on CIFAR100, and 94.2% on STL10, resulting in a gain of about 16 points on CIFAR10. Moreover, AMDIM outperforms the best self-supervised results previously reported on these datasets, including those based on contrastive predictive coding (CPC) and predicting image rotations.

The gains on ImageNet are even more pronounced in absolute terms. Our base model achieves 60.2% top-1 accuracy with a linear classifier and 50.0% on Places205 when transferred from ImageNet, surpassing the performance of prior self-supervised methods. For instance, CPC with a ResNet-101 achieves 48.7% top-1 accuracy, while methods based on colorization, jigsaw puzzles, or rotation prediction reach approximately 40-55% depending on the architecture. Adversarial feature learning with BigBiGAN reaches the mid-50s, still falling short of our base model's performance. Our larger model, with a wider encoder and higher capacity, achieves 68.1% top-1 and 88.2% top-5 on ImageNet, and 55.0% on Places205, resulting in a margin of more than 12 points over the best earlier published results. Compared to concurrent contrastive work, such as Contrastive Multiview Coding, which reaches about 60-61% with a similarly sized encoder, our margin is approximately 7 points.

It is essential to note that the size of the encoder differs across methods, so we also report the parameter counts to provide a more comprehensive comparison. The 68.1% model is indeed large, but the base model outperforms most earlier methods that use comparable or larger networks, indicating that the gains do not solely result from increased capacity. Within our own models, increasing the width improves ImageNet accuracy by about 3-8 points, suggesting that the objective benefits from scale but is not dependent on it.

In comparison to supervised training, our 68.1% figure narrows the gap to supervised training of comparable architectures but does not close it. Fully supervised ResNet-style encoders achieve approximately 75-77% top-1 accuracy. Our frozen self-supervised features with a linear head are therefore within roughly 8-9 points of supervised training, representing a smaller gap than earlier self-supervised approaches. To further understand the contributions of individual components, we conducted ablation studies on CIFAR10 and ImageNet, modifying one component at a time from the full model.

The ablated components included the multi-scale, multi-layer set of view pairs, data augmentation, the contrastive bound and its regularization, and the encoder architecture. Our results show that predicting features across scales, such as global features at one view against local features at another, is crucial. Restricting to single-scale predictions, as in DIM's global-to-local objective, lowers accuracy by several points on CIFAR10. Furthermore, predicting from intermediate layers to the final layer adds additional gains. Using the same view for source and target, as in earlier DIM variants, is considerably worse than using independently augmented views, highlighting the importance of independent augmentation in isolating information shared across views.

The removal of individual augmentations reduces performance, with the greatest loss occurring when color jitter or random cropping is dropped. Adding stronger augmentations, such as random grayscale and jitter, improves accuracy beyond what random crops and flips provide. Without these stronger augmentations, the model can rely on low-level color statistics shared across views, which shortcuts the task. Two modifications to the NCE-based bound have consistent effects: soft clamping of scores and a small penalty on the squared magnitude of the scores. These modifications improve stability and accuracy, and removing either causes training to degrade or accuracy to drop by one or more points on CIFAR10.

Using more negative samples, drawn from all other images in the batch and across spatial positions, helps monotonically, with accuracy rising with batch size over the range tested, although the gains diminish at larger sizes. The architecture of the encoder is also crucial, with constraints on the receptive fields being essential to prevent features from copying information from shared pixels instead of encoding abstract content. Encoders with larger capacity and standard residual blocks, adjusted to control receptive field growth, perform best.

We also evaluated an extension of our model, where each feature vector is represented by a set of mixture components with assignment distributions. The mixture models retain accuracy close to the single-component model on the linear-evaluation tasks, with differences across the numbers of components tried being within about one point on CIFAR10. The best configurations do not degrade ImageNet accuracy, and the advantage of the mixture models is qualitative. The assignment distributions yield spatially coherent groupings that align with object and background regions, resulting in segmentation-like behavior without any pixel-level supervision. While we did not use these maps to improve classification, and we do not report a segmentation benchmark, these results demonstrate the potential of our model to capture meaningful representations that can be used for a variety of downstream tasks. The notion that maximizing mutual information across independently augmented views can yield significant improvements in self-supervised representation learning is supported by our findings. Notably, the accuracy on CIFAR10 and STL10 increases substantially, from 75-77% to over 90%, while ImageNet linear accuracy improves from approximately 49-56% to 68.1%. A thorough examination of the contributions of each design choice reveals that multi-scale prediction, independent augmentation, and receptive-field control have the most pronounced effects. Our approach, termed Augmented Multiscale Deep InfoMax (AMDIM), is rooted in the idea that the information shared across views of a context is, to a considerable extent, the information that matters semantically. 

When views are generated through data augmentation, factors such as exact color statistics, crop location, or low-level texture are largely decoupled between views, whereas factors like object identity or scene layout persist across them. Consequently, a mutual information objective encourages encoders to retain these persistent factors while allowing them to discard the rest. This perspective aligns with earlier arguments for predictive and contrastive objectives, as well as the infomax principle, but shifts the focus towards relating independently generated views rather than predicting spatially or temporally adjacent content. 

Our ablation studies support this interpretation, indicating that the strength and diversity of augmentation, along with the scale at which features are compared, have substantial effects on downstream accuracy. In contrast, the specifics of the lower bound used in the objective have less impact. The multiscale formulation, which contrasts global features of one view with local features of another at multiple spatial scales, appears to provide a complementary pressure, encouraging the global feature to aggregate information about the whole view while promoting consistency across levels of abstraction. 

Moreover, our findings highlight the importance of architectural choices, which are often overlooked in this literature. Restricting receptive fields to prevent local features from trivially sharing pixels and avoiding padding artifacts that could leak positional information are crucial in preventing the objective from being satisfied through shortcuts. This echoes a broader lesson from contrastive learning: the meaningfulness of a bound on mutual information is contingent upon the difficulty of the discrimination it induces, and the encoder will exploit any accessible low-level cue. 

However, the relationship between mutual information maximization and representation quality is not straightforward. Maximizing tight estimates of mutual information alone does not guarantee the production of useful features, as mutual information is invariant to invertible transformations and can be maximized by representations poorly suited to linear readout. Furthermore, contrastive bounds are limited by the number of negative samples, saturating at the logarithm of that number. Our results suggest that the inductive biases of the encoder and the choice of views shape the outcome at least as much as the objective itself. Therefore, we regard the information-theoretic framing as a useful design principle rather than a complete explanation. 

An intriguing observation emerges from the mixture-based extension, where each view is represented by several mixture components, and the objective is combined with a routing mechanism that assigns local features to components. The components tend to specialize on spatially coherent regions, exhibiting segmentation-like behavior without any pixel-level supervision. We interpret this as a consequence of the pressure toward capturing factors that span views, where distinct objects or regions act as distinct, persistent factors, and allocating separate components to them is an efficient way to preserve information. Although this result is qualitative and preliminary, it suggests a promising direction for future exploration. 

Several limitations of our study should be noted. Firstly, our strongest results rely on large encoders and substantial computation, including large batch sizes or many negative samples, and training on multiple GPUs. This confounds comparisons with earlier methods to some extent, as model capacity and training length can significantly impact performance. Secondly, the quality of the learned representation depends strongly on a hand-designed augmentation pipeline, which encodes prior knowledge about nuisance factors for natural object-centric images. However, this pipeline may not transfer to domains like medical imaging, audio, or video, where the relevant invariances differ. Thirdly, our evaluation focuses primarily on linear classification and a limited set of transfer settings, with linear separability being an imperfect proxy for usefulness. We have not systematically assessed performance on detection, dense prediction, or low-data regimes beyond what is reported. Fourthly, the segmentation behavior of the mixture model is evaluated only informally, and we have not characterized its failure modes, such as in cluttered scenes or when objects lack distinctive appearance. Finally, we have limited theoretical understanding of why particular view constructions work, and invariance to augmentation can also discard information important for some downstream tasks, such as color for fine-grained recognition. 

The implications of our findings are significant, suggesting that self-supervised pretraining can narrow, though not eliminate, the gap with supervised pretraining on standard benchmarks. This has practical implications for settings where labels are scarce. More broadly, the framework's flexibility is attractive, as the notion of a "view" can be applied to observations from different camera positions, time steps, or sensory modalities. We believe that applying this framework beyond static images, including to video, multimodal, and embodied data, is a promising direction. Additionally, learning the view-generating process rather than hand-specifying it could reduce dependence on domain-specific augmentation design, as would a better understanding of which information different view constructions preserve. Further work is needed to explore these avenues and to deepen our understanding of the complex interplay between mutual information, representation quality, and the design of self-supervised learning objectives.

The rise of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has become a pressing concern for global public health, food security, and economic development, as it undermines the effectiveness of modern medicine, including surgery, chemotherapy, organ transplantation, and neonatal care. The World Health Organization (WHO) has emphasized the gravity of the situation, highlighting the far-reaching consequences of AMR on human health (WHO, 2015). A comprehensive estimate by the Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance project revealed that approximately 1.27 million deaths in 2019 were directly attributed to bacterial AMR, with a further 3.68 million deaths associated with it, making AMR a leading cause of death worldwide, surpassing even HIV/AIDS and malaria (Murray et al., 2022). Notably, the burden of AMR is not evenly distributed, with age-standardized mortality rates highest in western sub-Saharan Africa, where approximately 27 deaths per 100,000 population were reported (Murray et al., 2022).

The projections for the future are equally alarming, with warnings that, without effective intervention, drug-resistant infections could lead to 10 million deaths annually by 2050, accompanied by cumulative economic losses of up to US$100 trillion (O'Neill, 2016). While these projections are uncertain, particularly for regions with limited data, they underscore the urgent need for action, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In sub-Saharan Africa, the drivers of AMR are complex and interconnected, encompassing factors such as poverty, weak health systems, limited diagnostic capacity, inadequate water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure, and poor infection prevention and control (Ndihokubwayo et al., 2013; Essack et al., 2017). The misuse of antibiotics, including the dispensing of antibiotics without prescription, their sale in informal markets, and empirical use without microbiological confirmation, further exacerbates the problem (Okeke et al., 2005; Ayukekbong et al., 2017).

Moreover, the pressure on antimicrobial use is not confined to human medicine, as the global demand for animal protein has intensified the use of antimicrobials in livestock production for therapeutic, prophylactic, and growth-promoting purposes (Van Boeckel et al., 2015, 2019). The potential for resistant bacteria and resistance genes to circulate between humans, animals, and the environment through food chains, direct contact, wastewater, manure, and contaminated water sources is a pressing concern (Robinson et al., 2016). Hospital effluents, municipal sewage, and agricultural runoff can act as reservoirs and mixing vessels for resistance determinants, particularly in areas with inadequate waste management. This recognition highlights the need for a One Health approach, which integrates human, animal, and environmental health in the design and implementation of policies, programs, and research (Robinson et al., 2016).

The Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015, identified One Health surveillance and the strengthening of the evidence base as strategic objectives, calling on Member States to develop multisectoral national action plans (WHO, 2015). The WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) has since sought to standardize the collection, analysis, and sharing of data. However, participation and data completeness remain markedly lower in Africa compared to other regions (WHO, 2022). Many countries lack the laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, quality assurance, and information systems necessary for routine surveillance (Leopold et al., 2014; Ndihokubwayo et al., 2013). A systematic review of antibiotic resistance in sub-Saharan Africa concluded that the available data were fragmented, geographically uneven, and heterogeneous in methods, limiting their usefulness for policy (Tadesse et al., 2017).

Cameroon, a Central African country with a population of approximately 27 million, exemplifies the challenges in addressing AMR. The country has a high burden of infectious diseases, including diarrheal illness, respiratory infections, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, and malaria, driving a heavy reliance on antibiotics. Livestock production, including poultry, pig, and cattle farming, is expanding to meet urban demand, with limited veterinary oversight of antimicrobial use. Antibiotics are widely available from informal vendors, and surface water contamination and inadequate sanitation are common in urban and peri-urban areas, favoring the selection and dissemination of resistant bacteria across sectors. Despite commitments to the global agenda, including the development of a national action plan against AMR within a multisectoral framework, Cameroon lacks a reliable baseline of the prevalence and patterns of resistance among clinically and epidemiologically important pathogens.

Numerous studies on AMR have been conducted in Cameroon, but they are scattered across journals, institutional reports, and theses, published in English or French, and differ in setting, population, sampling strategy, laboratory methods, breakpoints, and reporting conventions. Most are single-center, hospital-based investigations of a limited number of pathogens, making them difficult to compare or aggregate. Studies of animal and environmental reservoirs are comparatively few and are rarely interpreted alongside human data. As a result, policymakers, clinicians, and program managers lack a consolidated, quantitative picture of the resistance burden, including which pathogen-antibiotic combinations are most affected and where the principal evidence gaps lie.

Previous reviews of AMR in Africa have primarily addressed the continent or sub-region as a whole or focused on a single sector, syndrome, or organism, without providing a country-level synthesis across the human, animal, and environmental domains (Tadesse et al., 2017; Essack et al., 2017). Such a synthesis is necessary to inform empirical treatment guidelines, prioritize targets for stewardship and infection control, and design a surveillance system tailored to the national context. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the published and grey literature on AMR in Cameroon through a One Health lens. Our central question was: what is the current prevalence of resistance, and of multidrug resistance (MDR), among bacterial pathogens isolated from humans, animals, and the environment in Cameroon, and how are the evidence and its limitations distributed across regions, sectors, organisms, and antibiotics? Specifically, we aimed to (i) characterize the geographic and sectoral distribution of available studies; (ii) identify the bacterial species and antibiotics most commonly investigated; (iii) estimate pooled prevalence of resistance for pathogen-antibiotic pairs and of MDR using random-effects models; and (iv) examine the evidence gaps and limitations in the current literature to inform future research and policy initiatives. The need to identify methodological and reporting gaps that hinder the effective use of existing data for surveillance and clinical decision-making is a pressing concern. This study addresses this issue by making three significant contributions to the field of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) research in Cameroon. Firstly, it presents the first comprehensive, integrated quantitative synthesis of AMR data from human, animal, and environmental sources in Cameroon, thereby establishing a crucial baseline for future surveillance efforts. Secondly, by aggregating estimates for specific pathogen-antibiotic pairs, this research provides actionable evidence to inform the revision of empirical treatment guidelines and the prioritization of antibiotics and organisms for national monitoring. Lastly, by systematically documenting the heterogeneity in diagnostic methods, breakpoints, and reporting practices, this study identifies concrete priorities for standardization and data sharing, which are essential prerequisites for effective, coordinated, and sustainable laboratory-based AMR surveillance in Cameroon and similar settings.

Our study was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, ensuring transparency and rigor in our methodology. We adopted a One Health framework, recognizing the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health, as defined by the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization, and the World Organisation for Animal Health. This framework allowed us to categorize studies into three distinct compartments: human (encompassing clinical and community samples), animal (including livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and companion animals, as well as animal-derived foods), and environment (comprising water, soil, hospital surfaces, and effluents).

To ensure a comprehensive search, we utilized multiple databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online, searching for articles published in both English and French. Our search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms in three concept blocks using Boolean operators, focusing on resistance, setting, and host or source. We also hand-searched reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews, and identified grey literature through web searches and direct contact with authors and national laboratories.

Studies were considered eligible if they met specific criteria, including being conducted in Cameroon, reporting original phenotypic or genotypic data on antimicrobial susceptibility, specifying the bacterial species and antibiotics tested, and using a recognized susceptibility testing method. We excluded reviews, editorials, case reports with fewer than ten isolates, and studies that did not meet these criteria. When the same dataset was published multiple times, we retained the most complete report.

Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility of studies, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. We documented the selection process using a PRISMA flow diagram, which illustrated the numbers of records identified, screened, excluded, and included.

Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which was piloted on five articles and then applied to all included studies. We extracted variables such as first author, year of publication, region of Cameroon, setting, One Health compartment, sample type, population characteristics, sample size, bacterial species, antibiotics tested, and reported resistance mechanisms. Antibiotics were grouped by class using the WHO Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification and the WHO AWaRe categories. We classified intermediate results as non-susceptible and pooled them with resistant isolates only when the original authors did not report the categories separately.

The primary outcome of our study was the proportion of isolates resistant to a given antibiotic for each pathogen-antibiotic pair. The secondary outcome was the prevalence of multidrug resistance, defined as acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial classes. We derived multidrug resistance from isolate-level resistance profiles when studies did not report it directly.

To assess the quality of the included studies, we used the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies, which evaluates sampling frame, sampling method, sample size adequacy, and description of subjects. Two reviewers independently assessed the methodological quality and risk of bias of each study, with discrepancies resolved through consensus.

Our study's findings have significant implications for AMR surveillance and clinical decision-making in Cameroon and similar settings. By highlighting the need for standardization and data sharing, our research emphasizes the importance of a coordinated approach to addressing the growing threat of AMR. Furthermore, our study's contributions to the development of empirical treatment guidelines and the prioritization of antibiotics and organisms for national monitoring will inform evidence-based practices and policies.

In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of AMR in Cameroon, highlighting the need for improved surveillance, standardization, and data sharing. Our findings have important implications for public health policy and practice, and underscore the importance of a One Health approach to addressing the complex issue of AMR. By addressing the methodological and reporting gaps identified in this study, we can work towards a more effective and sustainable response to the growing threat of AMR in Cameroon and beyond.
