The assessment of study quality was a crucial aspect of our analysis, as it enabled us to evaluate the validity and reliability of the included studies. To this end, we employed a standardized tool to assess the quality of each study, considering factors such as the setting, coverage of data analysis, validity of methods for identifying the condition, standardization of measurement, statistical analysis, and response rate. Each item was scored as either "met" or "not met," and studies were subsequently categorized as having a low (≥7 items met), moderate (4-6 items met), or high (≤3 items met) risk of bias. Notably, we used these quality scores to explore heterogeneity in sensitivity analyses, rather than as a basis for excluding studies from our analysis.

Our statistical analysis was stratified by One Health compartment, bacterial species, and antibiotic, allowing us to examine the relationships between these variables and the prevalence of antibiotic resistance. We estimated pooled prevalence only when at least three studies contributed data to a particular pathogen-antibiotic pair, ensuring that our estimates were based on a sufficient number of studies. To stabilize variances and avoid excluding studies with proportions near 0% or 100%, we applied the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation to the proportions. Pooled estimates were obtained using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models, which were selected a priori due to the anticipated differences in study populations, laboratory methods, and sampling periods. We back-transformed these estimates for presentation, along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI).

We quantified heterogeneity using Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values of 25%, 50%, and 75% considered to represent low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. Additionally, we computed 95% prediction intervals for the main pooled estimates, as high heterogeneity is often expected in prevalence meta-analyses. To explore potential sources of heterogeneity, we conducted subgroup analyses by administrative region, setting (hospital versus community), sampling period (before 2010, 2010-2015, after 2015), susceptibility testing method, and risk-of-bias category. We also performed univariable random-effects meta-regression on these covariates when at least ten studies were available. Furthermore, leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were used to assess the influence of individual studies on pooled estimates.

To evaluate publication bias, we employed visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's regression test for small-study effects, considering a P value below 0.05 to be significant. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize study characteristics, regional distribution, the number of bacterial species and antibiotics tested, and resistance across antibiotic classes. All analyses were conducted using R (version 4.2) with the packages meta and metafor, and maps and figures were produced with ggplot2. Unless otherwise stated, all tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.

As our review utilized only published and aggregated unpublished data, with no individual patient information collected, formal ethical approval was not required. However, we obtained consent from authors to use their shared data. The database searches and contact with authors yielded 428 records, which were subsequently screened and filtered to exclude duplicates and irrelevant studies. After assessing the full texts of 97 articles for eligibility, we retained 66 studies published between 2005 and 2022 for qualitative synthesis, with 61 contributing to at least one pooled estimate.

Geographically, the included studies were primarily from four regions: Centre (24; 36.4%), South-West (16; 24.2%), West (13; 19.7%), and Littoral (9; 13.6%). The remaining four studies (6.1%) came from the North-West, Adamawa, North, and Far North regions combined, with no studies identified from the East or South regions. The majority of studies (45; 68.2%) addressed antibiotic resistance in humans, while 9 (13.6%) focused on animals and 12 (18.2%) on the environment. Human studies were mostly hospital-based, cross-sectional laboratory analyses of clinical specimens, whereas animal studies sampled poultry, cattle, or pigs at farms or abattoirs, and environmental studies sampled hospital effluents, surface and well water, and market or hospital surfaces.

The predominant susceptibility testing method was disk diffusion (53 studies; 80.3%), although only 21 studies (31.8%) stated adherence to a named interpretive standard (CLSI or EUCAST). Using the adapted Joanna Briggs Institute prevalence checklist, we rated 38 studies (57.6%) as moderate quality, 17 (25.8%) as high quality, and 11 (16.7%) as low quality. Across all sectors, 19 bacterial species were tested against 48 antibiotics spanning all major classes, including penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides/trimethoprim, glycopeptides, and phenicols.

In human studies, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus spp. were the most frequently reported organisms, appearing in 23, 19, and 18 studies, respectively. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (n = 12), Salmonella spp. (n = 10), and Enterococcus spp. (n = 6) were also common. Resistance was documented for every antibiotic class tested. The pooled prevalence of resistance in E. coli was highest for older, widely used agents such as amoxicillin or ampicillin (87.3%; 95% CI 81.4-91.5; 21 studies), tetracycline (76.9%; 68.2-83.8; 11 studies), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (78.4%; 70.9-84.4; 17 studies). Resistance was lower for third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, 38.6%; 29.7-48.4; ceftazidime, 41.2%; 31.5-51.5) and for ciprofloxacin (29.8%; 21.6-39.6) and gentamicin (24.3%; 17.1-33.3). Notably, pooled carbapenem resistance was low (imipenem, 3.4%; 1.6-7.1), although isolated reports of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales were noted.

Using a threshold of resistance to three or more antibiotic classes, the pooled multidrug-resistant (MDR) prevalence in E. coli was 47.1% (95% CI 37.3-57.2; 23 studies). For K. pneumoniae, the pooled MDR prevalence was 51.0% (95% CI 42.0-59.9; 19 studies), with resistance to ceftriaxone (52.7%; 41.8-63.4), ceftazidime (49.6%; 38.2-61.1), ciprofloxacin (34.5%; 24.9-45.5), and gentamicin (40.2%; 30.1-51.3). The intrinsic resistance of K. pneumoniae to ampicillin was reflected in a pooled estimate of 94.1% (88.2-97.1), while imipenem resistance was 5.8% (2.9-11.3). For Staphylococcus spp. (predominantly S. aureus, 14 of 18 studies), the pooled MDR prevalence was 45.2% (95% CI 38.0-54.7; 18 studies), with the pooled prevalence of methicillin resistance among S. aureus being 31.6% (24.1-40.2; 12 studies). Resistance to penicillin was 91.2% (85.0-94.9), to tetracycline 52.4% (42.6-62.0), to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 58.7% (47.9-68.8), and to erythromycin 41.3% (32.2-51.0), while resistance to gentamicin and ciprofloxacin was 22.5% (15.2-32.0). The prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in Cameroon is a pressing concern, with far-reaching implications for public health. Our systematic review and meta-analysis, which synthesized data from 66 eligible studies, reveals a disturbingly high level of resistance across human, animal, and environmental compartments. The pooled multidrug resistance (MDR) estimates are alarmingly high, with 47.1% for Escherichia coli, 51.0% for Klebsiella pneumoniae, and 45.2% for Staphylococcus spp. in human studies. Similarly, the MDR prevalence in animal-derived Salmonella spp. is 46.2%, while environmental Staphylococcus spp. exhibit a staggering 67.1% MDR prevalence. These findings suggest that first-line empirical therapy is likely to fail in a substantial proportion of bacterial infections in the country, underscoring the need for urgent attention to this issue.

The dominance of E. coli, K. pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus spp. in the human literature is consistent with the priority pathogens identified by the World Health Organization and the pathogens most frequently reported in African surveillance syntheses. The MDR prevalence of roughly 45-51% in these organisms is comparable to estimates from other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where antibiotics are often widely available without prescription, diagnostic stewardship is limited, and empirical treatment is the norm. This is particularly concerning in the case of K. pneumoniae, which is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and hospital-acquired infection, and is commonly associated with extended-spectrum β-lactamase production. The latter narrows the therapeutic options to carbapenems, which are scarce and costly in Cameroon.

The environmental estimate for Staphylococcus spp. is the highest observed in this review, suggesting that hospital effluents, surface waters, markets, and farm environments may act as reservoirs and conduits for resistant organisms and resistance determinants. However, this estimate is based on only eight studies and should be interpreted with caution. The similarity of MDR estimates in humans and animals supports a One Health reading of resistance in Cameroon, although our data cannot demonstrate transmission directions. It is plausible that antibiotic use in livestock, particularly in intensive poultry and pig production, contributes to the selection pressure driving resistance in these settings. Tetracyclines, penicillins, sulphonamides, and quinolones are commonly used for prophylaxis and growth promotion in LMICs, often without veterinary oversight.

The fact that only nine animal studies and twelve environmental studies were identified, compared to 45 human studies, highlights the imbalance in research efforts and the need for a more integrated approach to understanding antimicrobial resistance. The One Health framing, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health, is not yet matched by the research effort, and the human clinical perspective still dominates AMR research in the country. Few studies used comparable sampling frames or molecular typing that would allow resistant clones or plasmids to be tracked across compartments, making integrated analyses challenging.

The high level of heterogeneity between studies, as reflected in the I² values ranging from 71.4% to 97.2%, is consistent with the use of random-effects models. Subgroup analyses revealed that MDR prevalence in E. coli was higher in studies published after 2015 than before, and in hospitalized patients compared to community-based participants. However, differences between regions were not statistically significant, although this comparison was limited by the small number of studies outside the four main regions. Sensitivity analysis excluding low-quality studies changed the pooled MDR estimates by less than 3 percentage points for each of the principal pathogens.

The findings of this review have significant implications for public health policy and practice in Cameroon. The high prevalence of MDR in key pathogens underscores the need for improved antibiotic stewardship, enhanced diagnostic capacity, and more effective infection control measures. The potential for transmission of resistant organisms and resistance determinants between humans, animals, and the environment highlights the importance of a One Health approach to addressing antimicrobial resistance. Further research is needed to elucidate the drivers of resistance in different settings and to develop effective strategies for mitigating the impact of antimicrobial resistance in Cameroon and other LMICs. Ultimately, a comprehensive and integrated approach to addressing antimicrobial resistance is essential for protecting public health and promoting sustainable development in the region.

The Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta stands out as one of the most densely populated and dynamic landscapes on the planet. With its fertile alluvial soils, abundant freshwater, and productive coastal waters, Bangladesh has been able to support a staggering population of over 165 million people within a relatively small area of approximately 148,000 km², resulting in a population density that exceeds 1,100 persons per square kilometre (Nicholls et al., 2018). However, this unique geography also renders the population highly vulnerable to a range of natural hazards. For instance, monsoon floods regularly inundate between one-fifth and two-thirds of the country in any given year, while riverbank erosion poses a persistent threat to land and homesteads along the large braided rivers (Brammer, 2004; Mutton & Haque, 2004). Furthermore, drought affects the north-western regions during the dry season, and the southern coast is repeatedly struck by tropical cyclones and storm surges, which have had devastating consequences in the past, such as the 1970 Bhola cyclone, which claimed an estimated 300,000 lives, and the 1991 cyclone, which resulted in approximately 138,000 fatalities (Paul, 2009; Alam & Collins, 2010).

The cumulative effects of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion, changing precipitation patterns, and more intense cyclones are expected to amplify these pressures, making Bangladesh one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change (Dasgupta et al., 2014; IPCC, 2022; Eckstein et al., 2021). Despite these challenges, Bangladesh has made significant strides in reducing disaster mortality, thanks in large part to investments in early warning systems, cyclone shelters, embankments, and community-based preparedness, which have sharply lowered death tolls from cyclones and floods over the past five decades (Paul, 2009; Haque et al., 2012). This achievement has led to Bangladesh being widely regarded as a global model of adaptation. However, it is essential to recognize that declining mortality rates do not necessarily translate to secure livelihoods. Households may survive a disaster event, only to lose land, crops, livestock, housing, and productive assets, which can push them into long-term indebtedness, food insecurity, or displacement (Adger, 1999; Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013).

Traditional disaster statistics and macro-scale vulnerability indices often fail to capture these complex trajectories, as they tend to focus on the number of people affected rather than the ways in which individuals and households weigh risks, mobilize resources, and make decisions before, during, and after an event. Livelihood approaches, on the other hand, offer a valuable lens through which to examine these questions. Building on the sustainable livelihoods framework (Chambers & Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998), recent work has conceptualized livelihood resilience as the capacity of people to sustain and improve their well-being despite environmental, economic, and political disturbances (Tanner et al., 2015). This concept of resilience is not simply about returning to a pre-disturbance state; rather, it involves the ability to buffer, adjust, and learn, as well as to transform livelihood systems when necessary (Béné et al., 2012; Folke, 2016). Moreover, resilience is deeply embedded in social relations, with access to assets, networks, markets, and institutions being unevenly distributed along lines of class, gender, caste, religion, and location, which in turn affects the ability to cope with stress (Adger, 2006; Ribot, 2014).

A people-centred perspective, therefore, treats the strategies of households as the central object of analysis, while also taking seriously the structural constraints and opportunities within which they operate. A substantial body of research has documented how rural households in Bangladesh respond to environmental stress. For example, farmers have been known to adjust their crop calendars, adopt flood- and salt-tolerant varieties, and shift from rice to shrimp or other aquaculture in saline zones (Ayers & Huq, 2009; Dasgupta et al., 2014). Households have also been found to diversify their incomes through petty trade, wage labour, or fishing, and increasingly, they send family members to cities or abroad in search of better opportunities (Black et al., 2011; Mallick & Vogt, 2014). While migration can be a successful adaptive strategy, it can also be a last resort that exposes migrants to precarious urban conditions (Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Moreover, some individuals may choose not to move or adapt at all, due to a lack of resources, attachment to place, or the inability to abandon assets that they cannot carry with them (Adams, 2016; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016).

Adaptation, therefore, is neither automatic nor uniformly beneficial. Both planned interventions and autonomous household strategies can generate maladaptation, where actions intended to reduce vulnerability instead increase it for the same or other groups, such as embankments that cause waterlogging or shrimp farming that salinises land and reduces food security (Barnett & O'Neill, 2010; Paprocki & Cons, 2014). Despite the wealth of knowledge on this topic, three significant gaps remain. Firstly, most studies focus on a single hazard or region, leaving a significant knowledge gap regarding how people in different environmental settings of the delta experience and respond to multiple hazards such as floods, erosion, drought, and cyclones. Secondly, much of the existing evidence is derived from cross-sectional surveys or short interviews, which capture current coping practices but not the sequence of decisions through which resilience is built or eroded over a lifetime. Because shocks accumulate and past choices shape present options, such snapshots can misrepresent why strategies succeed or fail (Tanner et al., 2015). Thirdly, evacuation research has tended to emphasize warning dissemination, shelter capacity, and distance, while paying less attention to the livelihood considerations that lead people to stay put, such as fear of looting or losing livestock and belongings (Alam & Collins, 2010; Paul, 2009).

This article addresses these gaps by drawing on material from the Gibika project, which studies livelihood resilience in seven sites representing the main environmental settings of Bangladesh, including coastal, riverine, and drought-prone areas. We employ a novel methodology, the personal Livelihood History interview, which reconstructs the chronology of a person's livelihood activities, the shocks and stresses encountered, the decisions taken, and their outcomes. Based on 28 such interviews, we pose three key questions. Firstly, how do floods, riverbank erosion, drought, and cyclones affect the livelihoods of people in the study sites? Secondly, which strategies do people use to build resilience, and why do some of these strategies fail? Finally, how do livelihood considerations shape decisions during cyclone threats, including the decision not to evacuate? By exploring these questions, this article makes three significant contributions. Empirically, it provides comparative, longitudinal accounts of how people experience multiple hazards across contrasting environments of the delta. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of Livelihood Histories for tracing decision-making in risk-prone settings and sheds light on the complex, dynamic nature of livelihood resilience. Theoretically, it highlights the need to integrate livelihood considerations into evacuation research and disaster risk reduction efforts more broadly, recognizing that the decisions people make in the face of hazard are often shaped by a complex array of factors, including livelihood risk, social relations, and access to resources. The identification of turning points at which adaptation strategies succeed or fail is crucial for effective disaster risk reduction and adaptation planning. From a conceptual and policy perspective, it is essential to recognize that adaptation and disaster risk reduction must be grounded in the lived experience of individuals and communities currently facing environmental stress. This entails considering the trade-offs between protecting life and protecting livelihoods, a delicate balance that is often at the heart of decision-making in risk-prone environments. In the following sections, we provide an overview of the study sites and methodology, present the findings organized by hazard and strategy, and discuss the implications of these findings for adaptation planning.

Our study is based on the Gibika project, a multi-sited research program focused on livelihood resilience in Bangladesh. The term "gibika" means livelihood in Bengali, and the project adopts a people-centered, actor-oriented approach to understanding livelihood resilience. This approach recognizes that livelihood resilience is the capacity of households to maintain and improve their well-being in the face of environmental stress, shocks, and disturbances. Resilience is not seen as a fixed attribute of households or places, but rather as an outcome of decisions made under constraint. To capture these decisions, we employed a qualitative, retrospective design based on personal Livelihood History interviews. This design was chosen because the processes of interest, including incremental adaptation, delayed responses to slow-onset hazards, and decisions during acute events, unfold over years and are poorly captured by cross-sectional surveys.

The use of a qualitative, retrospective design allowed us to identify turning points at which strategies succeed or fail, and to examine the decisions and processes that lead to these outcomes. This approach is particularly useful for understanding the complex and dynamic nature of livelihood resilience, and for identifying the factors that influence decision-making in risk-prone environments. By using a life-course approach, we were able to capture the ways in which individuals and households respond to and adapt to environmental stress and shocks over time, and to identify the key factors that influence these responses.

We selected seven study sites in Bangladesh that span the principal hydro-climatic hazard regimes of the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta and its margins. The selection criteria included dominant exposure to at least one of cyclones and storm surges, riverine and flash flooding, riverbank erosion, or drought; variation in livelihood base, including rice and other crop farming, aquaculture, fishing, daily labor, and small business; variation in institutional context, including embankment coverage, cyclone shelter provision, and NGO presence; and logistical feasibility and security for repeated fieldwork. Three sites are located in the south-west and south-central coastal zone and are exposed to cyclones, tidal flooding, and salinity intrusion. Two sites are located along major rivers in the north and center of the country and are affected by seasonal flooding and riverbank erosion. One site is located in the north-west, where rainfall variability and groundwater dependence produce recurrent drought, and one site is located in the north-eastern haor wetland basin, where early monsoon flash floods threaten the single annual rice crop.

Within each site, we selected four participants using purposive, maximum-variation sampling to ensure diversity in gender, age, primary occupation, landholding, and hazard experience. Sampling was stratified by an initial village-level wealth-ranking exercise conducted with local informants, and respondents were identified through community leaders, local government representatives, and snowballing. Eligibility required a minimum of 15 years of residence in, or regular connection to, the site, so that participants could narrate substantial livelihood trajectories. We conducted a total of 28 interviews, with 14 women and 14 men, aged 24 to 71 years (median 46). Primary occupations at the time of interview included smallholder and tenant farming, fishing and aquaculture, wage labor, petty trade and small enterprise, and household-based work.

The Livelihood History interview is a semi-structured, life-course instrument developed within the project to elicit how people make livelihood decisions in risk-prone environments. Each interview began with an open narrative prompt inviting participants to describe their life and work from childhood to the present. This was followed by a timeline exercise in which the interviewer and respondent jointly marked livelihood activities, residential moves, household composition changes, and hazard events on a visual calendar, using locally recognized events as temporal anchors to improve recall. A third phase probed each identified turning point using a standard set of questions on the stress or shock involved, the options considered, the resources and networks mobilized, the decision taken and by whom, and the subsequent outcome. A final section examined perceptions of risk, trust in warnings and public services, and expectations for the future.

Fieldwork was carried out by a team of Bangladeshi and international researchers, with interviews conducted in Bangla by trained interviewers of the same gender as the respondent wherever culturally appropriate. Interviews took place at times and locations chosen by participants, usually at home, and lasted between 60 and 150 minutes. With informed consent, interviews were audio-recorded, and field notes documenting setting, non-verbal cues, and interviewer reflections were written immediately afterwards. Recordings were transcribed verbatim in Bangla and translated into English by bilingual team members; a random 20% of transcripts was back-translated by an independent translator to check semantic equivalence, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Interviews were complemented by focus group discussions and key informant interviews at each site, used to verify event chronologies and contextual detail.

Data analysis involved a detailed examination of the transcripts and field notes, with a focus on identifying patterns and themes related to livelihood resilience and adaptation. We used a combination of inductive and deductive coding to identify key concepts and categories, and to develop a nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between environmental stress, livelihood decisions, and resilience. Our analysis highlights the importance of considering the social, economic, and environmental contexts in which livelihood decisions are made, and the need for adaptation planning to be grounded in the lived experience of individuals and communities. By examining the ways in which people make decisions and adapt to environmental stress and shocks, we can develop a more nuanced understanding of the factors that influence resilience, and identify effective strategies for supporting livelihoods in risk-prone environments. Our analysis of the qualitative data was facilitated by the use of NVivo, a software package that enables the efficient management and coding of large datasets. We adopted a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach, as outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006) and Fereday and Muir-Cochrane (2006), to identify and explore the key themes and patterns that emerged from the data. This approach allowed us to draw on existing literature on resilience and livelihoods to inform our initial coding framework, while also remaining open to the emergence of new themes and ideas that arose from the data itself.

Our initial codebook was developed through a thorough review of the relevant literature, and included top-level codes for hazard type, livelihood capital affected, adaptation strategy, decision rationale, constraints, and outcome. Two researchers then independently coded a subset of six transcripts, which accounted for approximately 21% of the total dataset. This process allowed us to compare our coding and refine our code definitions, ensuring that we had a shared understanding of the key themes and concepts that were emerging from the data. The remaining transcripts were then coded by one researcher, with ongoing iterative inductive coding of emergent themes, such as place attachment, protection of assets during evacuation, and indebtedness.

To ensure the reliability and validity of our coding, we calculated the inter-coder agreement for the double-coded subset using Cohen's kappa, which yielded a value of 0.78, indicating substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977). This level of agreement suggests that our coding framework was robust and consistent, and that the themes and patterns we identified were not unduly influenced by individual researcher bias.

In addition to coding, we also developed a case matrix and visual timeline for each interview, which facilitated within-case and cross-case comparison (Miles et al., 2014). These tools enabled us to identify patterns and themes that emerged across the dataset, and to explore the complex relationships between different variables and outcomes. We also used descriptive quantification to summarise the qualitative patterns that emerged from the data, counting the number of respondents and discrete coded events (such as hazard impacts, adaptation actions, and migration episodes) per hazard type and strategy category. These frequencies are reported as counts and proportions of the 28 respondents, and are intended to provide a sense of the relative salience of different strategies within the sample.

It is essential to note that, due to the purposive sampling strategy and small sample size, we did not apply inferential statistics to the data. Instead, we focused on exploring the themes and patterns that emerged from the data, and on developing a rich and nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between hazard exposure, adaptation, and livelihood outcomes. To assess the success of adaptation episodes, we classified them as "successful," "partially successful," or "unsuccessful" based on the respondent's own assessment of whether the strategy restored or improved income, food security, or safety. We also cross-checked these assessments against the narrated sequence of events to ensure that our classifications were consistent with the empirical evidence.

To ensure the credibility of our interpretations, we employed a range of strategies, including triangulation with site-level data, negative case analysis, and discussion of preliminary findings with local partners (Lincoln and Guba, 1985). These approaches enabled us to test our hypotheses and refine our understanding of the complex relationships between hazard exposure, adaptation, and livelihood outcomes.

The study received ethical approval from the lead institution's research ethics committee and from partner institutions in Bangladesh. Participants provided written or, where literacy was limited, witnessed verbal consent, and were informed of their right to withdraw from the study at any time. We also ensured that participants were not offered payment beyond refreshments and compensation for lost working time, and that names and identifying details were replaced with pseudonyms and site codes to maintain confidentiality. Given the potential for interviews to evoke distressing memories of loss, our interviewers were trained to pause or stop the interview on request, and to provide information on local support services.

The research team was also aware of the power asymmetries that can arise from differences in education, gender, and institutional affiliation, and took steps to address these through interviewer training, reflective field diaries, and regular team debriefings. By acknowledging and addressing these power dynamics, we aimed to create a safe and supportive environment for participants to share their experiences and perspectives.

The 28 Livelihood History interviews, which were conducted across four study sites, covered a mean recall period of 31.6 years, ranging from 14 to 52 years. The respondents comprised 16 men and 12 women, with a mean age of 49.3 years. Coding of the interview transcripts yielded 412 discrete livelihood events, or a mean of 14.7 per history. Of these, 187 (45.4%) were directly linked to environmental stress, shocks, or disturbances, while the remainder related to household demography, health expenditure, market or price changes, and other social or political events.

Within the environmental category, floods were the most frequently reported event, accounting for 74 (39.6%) of the total. Riverbank erosion was the second most common event, with 38 (20.3%) reports, followed by cyclones and storm surges (31; 16.6%), drought (26; 13.9%), and salinity intrusion or waterlogging (18; 9.6%). Notably, every respondent reported exposure to at least two distinct hazard types over their life course, and 19 of 28 (67.9%) reported three or more. This confirms the compound and sequential character of environmental risk in the delta, as highlighted by Brammer (2014) and Penning-Rowsell et al. (2013).

Respondents rated the impact of each event on a three-point scale, with 62 of the 187 environmental events (33.2%) classed as livelihood-altering, meaning that the household changed its main occupation, residence, or asset base afterwards. Floods accounted for the largest absolute number of such events, with 21 reports, but erosion had the highest proportion, with 20 of 38 (52.6%) events resulting in livelihood-altering outcomes. Cyclones and drought also had significant impacts, with 13 of 31 (41.9%) and 6 of 26 (23.1%) events resulting in livelihood-altering outcomes, respectively.

In terms of specific hazards, floods damaged crops in 21 of 28 histories (75.0%) and houses in 17 (60.7%). Respondents in the flood-prone floodplain and haor sites reported a mean loss of 38% of the annual rice harvest in the worst remembered flood year, and a mean of 2.4 flood events per decade that caused substantive agricultural loss. Short-term responses to flooding included early harvesting of immature rice, raising homestead plinths, and storing seed and grain in elevated places. Over the longer term, 23 of 28 respondents (82.1%) had modified their agricultural practices, with the most common modifications including shifting to short-duration or submergence-tolerant rice varieties, adopting dry-season boro cultivation, diversifying into vegetables or homestead gardening, and rearing ducks or fish in place of crops.

These findings are consistent with documented autonomous adaptation in the delta, as highlighted by Ayers and Forsyth (2009) and Paul (2009). Riverbank erosion, on the other hand, was the most disruptive stress in the two riverine sites, with all eight respondents reporting loss of homestead land at least once. The mean cumulative loss of cultivated land was estimated to be 1.6 ha, with a mean of 3.1 displacements per household. After displacement, five of the eight respondents resettled on embankments or on neighbours' or public land, often with tenure insecurity and weaker access to credit and services. Four respondents had sold remaining assets to finance relocation, and the median time to re-establish a stable income was reported to be 4 years.

The speed and irreversibility of land loss help explain why erosion events more often produced livelihood-altering outcomes than any other hazard, as noted by Etzold et al. (2014) and Hutton and Haque (2004). In the drought-prone northwestern site, all four respondents reported progressively longer dry spells, with estimated aman rice yields falling by 30-50% in drought years. Adaptation largely centred on groundwater irrigation, highlighting the need for effective water management strategies to support agricultural productivity and livelihood security in the face of climate change. The impact of environmental stress on livelihoods in Bangladesh is a complex and multifaceted issue, as evident from our in-depth interviews with 28 households across seven sites. A notable finding is that many households have adapted to these stresses by modifying their agricultural practices, such as switching to less water-demanding crops like maize, pulses, and mustard, a strategy employed by three of our respondents. However, this adaptation is not without its challenges, as two respondents reported a significant increase in irrigation costs over the past decade, largely due to the deeper tube wells and higher fuel and electricity prices. In one case, a respondent had abandoned dry-season cultivation of his own land and now leases it out, highlighting the uneven distribution of benefits and costs associated with groundwater extraction-based adaptation.

A more common response to environmental stress, however, was livelihood diversification, with 19 of our 28 respondents (67.9%) having changed or added a livelihood in response to these stresses. The principal destinations for these new livelihoods were petty trade or small shops, wage labor in construction or transport, rickshaw or van driving, tailoring and handicrafts, and, in the coastal sites, shrimp or crab farming and fishing. Notably, households with three or more income sources reported significantly fewer livelihood-altering events per decade than those with one or two, suggesting that diversification can be an effective strategy for building resilience. Among the 12 women interviewed, five reported independent income from activities such as livestock rearing, sewing, or microenterprise, and three of these identified their earnings as crucial in maintaining household consumption after a major flood or cyclone.

Migration also featured prominently in the livelihood histories of our respondents, with 17 of the 28 households (60.7%) having experienced some form of migration. Eleven households relied on seasonal or circular labor migration, usually to urban centers like Dhaka, Chittagong, or nearby district towns, for a mean of 4.8 months per year. Six households had moved permanently, typically after erosion or cyclone damage. While remittances from migrants were reported to cover a significant proportion of annual household expenditure, migration was not consistently beneficial, with six migrant households reporting reduced net gains due to recruitment fees, informal brokers, or insecure urban housing. This highlights the importance of considering the outcomes of migration as an adaptive strategy, which depend on factors such as networks, capital, and the timing of departure.

The experiences of our respondents in the coastal sites, who had lived through at least two major cyclones, including Sidr (2007), Aila (2009), and Amphan (2020), underscore the challenges of adapting to extreme weather events. Despite improved early warning systems, five of the eight respondents in these sites reported choosing not to evacuate to a cyclone shelter at least once, citing reasons such as protecting livestock and household goods, fear of theft or looting, inadequate shelter capacity or unsafe distance to shelters, and distrust of warnings that previous events had not matched. This reflects a rational weighing of imminent physical danger against the long-term economic consequences of asset loss, highlighting the complex trade-offs involved in adaptation decisions.

After Aila, six of the eight coastal respondents shifted from rice or mixed farming to brackish-water shrimp or crab production, or to fishing, as soil salinity rendered rice cultivation unviable. However, four of these respondents subsequently reported disease outbreaks or price falls that left them worse off than before the transition, illustrating the risks of maladaptation, where actions taken to reduce vulnerability can shift it across time, space, or social groups. Overall, 11 of our 28 respondents (39.3%) described at least one adaptation measure that failed or led to new vulnerabilities, with debt being the most common mechanism, as 15 households had borrowed from NGOs, moneylenders, or relatives to finance recovery or adaptation, and nine of these reported outstanding loans exceeding their estimated annual income.

Our study highlights the importance of understanding livelihood resilience as a dynamic and context-dependent process, shaped by the interplay of assets, social relations, institutional support, and the timing of successive shocks. The findings suggest that resilience is neither a fixed attribute of households nor a simple function of exposure, but rather emerges from sequences of decisions made over decades. This supports long-standing arguments that livelihood outcomes depend on the interplay of capitals, access, and context, and confirms that social resilience is constrained by the institutions through which people gain or lose entitlements.

One key finding is that adaptation was widespread but rarely linear, with 23 of our 28 respondents describing at least one substantial change to their livelihoods after an environmental shock. However, 15 respondents reported that an earlier adjustment later became a source of vulnerability, illustrating the concept of maladaptation. Our narrative approach reveals how this happens, as people rarely choose between "good" and "bad" options, but rather select the least risky option available at a given moment, with limited information, credit, and land, and the long-term costs become visible only in later life-history episodes.

Migration emerged as a pervasive but ambivalent strategy, with 11 respondents having a household member who migrated, and remittances frequently described as crucial for maintaining household consumption. However, the outcomes of migration depend on factors such as networks, capital, and the timing of departure, highlighting the need for a nuanced understanding of the role of migration in building livelihood resilience. Overall, our study underscores the importance of considering the complex and dynamic nature of livelihood resilience, and the need for policies and interventions that support households in building adaptive capacity and reducing vulnerability to environmental stress.

The persistence of obesity as a major public health concern in the United States is a stark reminder of the complexities involved in addressing this issue. With approximately four in ten adults affected, the prevalence of obesity has been steadily rising since the late 1970s, as documented by Hales et al. (2020) and Fryar et al. (2018). The consequences of excess weight are far-reaching, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, certain cancers, and premature mortality, while also contributing significantly to medical expenditures and lost productivity (Kopelman, 2000; Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012; Ward et al., 2021). Given that the determinants of weight status operate at multiple levels, from individual behavior to the broader environmental and economic contexts, effective responses are likely to involve place-based strategies, such as zoning regulations, transportation investments, food retail policies, and community programs (Swinburn et al., 2011; Story et al., 2008). However, the success of these strategies hinges on the availability of reliable information on the geographic distribution of excess weight and how it changes over time.

Currently, existing surveillance systems provide limited geographic resolution, making it challenging to accurately assess the prevalence of obesity at the local level. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), while considered the national standard, is designed to support national and some subgroup estimates, but not estimates for states or small areas. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), on the other hand, offers state and, in some cases, county or metropolitan-area estimates, but relies on self-reported height and weight, which are known to produce underestimates of body mass index (BMI) and obesity prevalence, with error varying by sex, age, and body size (Gillum and Sempos, 2005; Connor Gorber et al., 2007). Furthermore, response rates for telephone-based surveys have declined over time, raising concerns about nonresponse bias (Pierannunzi et al., 2013). Model-based approaches, such as multilevel regression and poststratification, used in the CDC PLACES project, can produce census tract estimates from BRFSS data (Zhang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018), but these estimates may understate true variation among neighborhoods and can partly build in the very associations researchers wish to study.

In light of these limitations, several alternative data sources have been explored to fill this gap. Electronic health records, for instance, can provide measured heights and weights for large populations and have been used to construct neighborhood and county-level obesity maps (Schwartz et al., 2017; Tomayko et al., 2021). However, their coverage is restricted to patients of participating health systems, who may not be representative of the general population and may differ systematically in weight and health care use. School-based body measurement programs yield population-level data for children (Ogden et al., 2018), but no comparable program exists for adults. Researchers have also utilized commercial data, social media, and wearable devices, which carry their own selection and validity concerns (Althoff et al., 2017). A data source that covers most adults in a jurisdiction, includes a recorded address, and is already collected and maintained by a government agency would therefore be highly valuable. State-issued driver licenses and identification cards meet many of these criteria, as the vast majority of adults in the United States hold either a driver license or a state identification card, and the application process records height, weight, date of birth, sex, and residential address.

While weight on a license is typically self-reported and may be rounded or outdated, prior work comparing license data with measured values suggests systematic underreporting, particularly among women and older adults (Ezzati et al., 2006; Hodge et al., 2020). Nevertheless, the sheer volume of records makes it possible to produce stable estimates for small geographic units without the sampling error that limits surveys. Earlier work using license data from Massachusetts found that aggregated BMI estimates were strongly correlated with obesity prevalence from independent sources and varied meaningfully across municipalities (Ezzati et al., 2006; Hodge et al., 2020). Despite this promise, applications remain rare, and few studies have used identification card data to evaluate the neighborhood characteristics associated with weight status across an entire state, including rural areas, where obesity prevalence is often highest and survey coverage is weakest (Befort et al., 2012; Trivedi et al., 2015).

The neighborhood correlates of weight status are well-documented in other data, but not uniformly so. Area-level socioeconomic disadvantage, including low income, low educational attainment, and low housing values, has been consistently associated with higher BMI and obesity prevalence in the United States and other high-income countries (Wang and Beydoun, 2007; Black and Macinko, 2008; Singh et al., 2010). Racial and ethnic composition is also associated with weight status, reflecting structural inequities in housing, food access, and exposure to environmental stressors (Williams and Collins, 2001; Bell et al., 2019). Features of the built environment, such as supermarket access, the density of fast food outlets, and automobile dependence, have been linked to weight, though findings are mixed and often sensitive to how neighborhoods are defined and how confounding by socioeconomic status is handled (Cobb et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2004; Lovasi et al., 2009). Rural residence adds a further dimension, as rural adults tend to have higher BMI than urban adults, with differences in food environments, physical activity opportunities, and travel distances all proposed as contributing factors (Befort et al., 2012). Few studies have been able to examine these domains jointly, at the census tract level, using a measure of BMI that is not itself modeled from the covariates under study.

This study addresses these gaps by utilizing approximately three million Oregon state-issued identification card records to estimate average adult BMI for every census tract in the state. We pose three key questions. First, can identification card data be processed into age-adjusted, tract-level BMI estimates that are stable and plausible? Second, how much of the variation in tract-level BMI is explained by population characteristics, food access, commuting behavior, and geography, and which of these factors are independently associated with weight status? By exploring these questions, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between neighborhood characteristics and obesity, ultimately informing the development of effective place-based strategies to address this pressing public health concern. The relationship between body mass index (BMI) and socioeconomic, environmental, and demographic factors has been a longstanding concern in public health research. To better understand this relationship, we investigated three key questions: first, can administrative records be used to derive reliable small-area estimates of BMI; second, what are the neighborhood factors associated with BMI; and third, are the observed associations consistent with the established literature on socioeconomic and environmental disparities in weight status, thereby supporting the validity of identification card data for surveillance? Our study makes three significant contributions to the field. Firstly, we demonstrate a replicable approach for deriving small-area BMI estimates from administrative records, which can be adopted by public health departments at a relatively low marginal cost. Secondly, because our estimates are computed directly from records rather than modeled from area characteristics, they enable an unbiased examination of the neighborhood factors associated with weight status in diverse settings, including urban, suburban, and rural areas. Thirdly, by assessing the associations between BMI and various factors such as home values, education, race, ethnicity, car commuting, and rural-urban commuting area classification, we provide evidence on the validity of this data source and identify potentially modifiable environmental targets for obesity prevention in Oregon and similar states.

Our data sources and study population consisted of de-identified records from the Oregon Driver and Motor Vehicle Services Division (DMV) for all active driver licenses, instruction permits, and state-issued identification cards held by Oregon residents aged 18 years or older at the time of extraction. The extract contained approximately three million records, each including the cardholder's self-reported height and weight, date of birth, sex, and residential address. To maintain confidentiality, names, license numbers, and other direct identifiers were removed by DMV staff before transfer, and addresses were geocoded by the research team within a secure environment and then discarded after assignment to 2010 census tracts. As our study used only existing administrative data, it was determined to be exempt from review by the institutional review board.

To ensure data quality, we excluded records with missing or implausible anthropometric values, following conventions used in other survey-based BMI analyses. Specifically, we excluded records with heights less than 122 cm or greater than 213 cm, weights less than 32 kg or greater than 227 kg, and resulting BMIs less than 15 or greater than 60 kg/m². We also excluded records that could not be geocoded to an Oregon census tract, such as post office boxes without a physical address match. After applying these exclusions, 2.88 million records (95% of the original extract) were retained for analysis. To protect confidentiality and avoid unstable estimates, tracts with fewer than 100 valid records were suppressed.

We calculated BMI for each cardholder as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. However, as identification card data rely on self-reported measures, and self-reported weight tends to be underestimated and height overestimated, absolute BMI values are expected to be biased downward. Our primary interest lay in the relative distribution of BMI across tracts, which is less sensitive to systematic reporting bias than are absolute prevalence estimates. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that reporting error may differ across population subgroups. Age composition varies substantially among census tracts and is strongly related to BMI. To account for this, we computed age-adjusted mean BMI for each tract by direct standardization, grouping cardholders into six age strata (18–24, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and ≥65 years). The age-adjusted mean for each tract was calculated using the proportion of the statewide adult population in each stratum, taken from the 2010 decennial census. Tracts with no records in one or more age strata were handled by collapsing adjacent strata. We also computed the standard error of each tract estimate using the usual formula for a weighted sum of independent means.

As a license or identification card is not held by all adults, we compared the number of cardholders in each tract with the 2010–2014 American Community Survey (ACS) adult population to estimate coverage. Statewide coverage exceeded 90% of adults, although tract-level coverage was lower in some dense urban tracts (where non-driving is more common) and in tracts with large student or institutional populations. To examine the associations between BMI and various neighborhood factors, we selected explanatory variables from the literature on social and environmental determinants of obesity and grouped them into four domains: population characteristics, food access, commuting behavior, and geography.

From the 2010–2014 ACS five-year estimates, we obtained median home value, percentage of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, median household income, percentage of residents living below the federal poverty level, and percentage of residents identifying as non-Hispanic white, Black, Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Hispanic or Latino. Median home value was used as a proxy for neighborhood wealth, as it captures accumulated assets and is available for nearly all tracts. We log-transformed median home value to reduce right skew. For food access, we used the U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Access Research Atlas to identify tracts designated as low income and low access, and computed the percentage of residents living more than one-half mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from the nearest supermarket. We also calculated the density of fast-food and convenience-store establishments per square kilometer from a commercial business listing.

To examine commuting behavior, we obtained the percentage of workers who commuted by car, public transit, bicycle, and on foot, along with mean travel time to work, from the ACS journey-to-work tables. For geography, we classified each tract using the 2010 rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) codes developed by the USDA Economic Research Service and the WWAMI Rural Health Research Center, collapsing the 10 primary codes into four categories: metropolitan core, large rural town, small rural town, and isolated rural, with metropolitan as the reference. We also defined region (Portland metropolitan area, Willamette Valley, Southern Oregon, Central Oregon, Eastern Oregon, and the Coast) for sensitivity analyses.

Our statistical analysis began with a description of the distribution of age-adjusted tract BMI, which we mapped using quintiles. This initial step allowed us to visualize the spatial patterns of BMI across Oregon and identify areas with particularly high or low levels of BMI. By examining the relationships between BMI and various neighborhood factors, we aimed to identify potentially modifiable targets for obesity prevention and contribute to the development of effective interventions to reduce health disparities in Oregon and beyond. Our analysis of spatial autocorrelation, using global Moran's I with a queen-contiguity weights matrix, revealed strong positive spatial autocorrelation, with a Moran's I value of 0.46 (p < 0.001). This suggests that tract-level mean BMI values tend to cluster geographically. To further explore these patterns, we identified local clusters using local indicators of spatial association. We also examined bivariate associations between tract-level mean BMI and various predictor variables using Pearson correlation coefficients and scatterplots. Notably, the strongest correlations were observed with socioeconomic indicators, such as median home value (r = −0.72) and the proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher (r = −0.75), both of which were inversely correlated with BMI.

To address concerns about collinearity, we screened variables using variance inflation factors (VIF) and retained only those with the strongest bivariate associations with BMI and greater conceptual clarity. For instance, we dropped median household income in favor of median home value due to their high correlation (r = 0.83). Our primary model was a multivariable linear regression of tract-level age-adjusted mean BMI, which included variables from four domains: socioeconomic factors, transportation modes, racial and ethnic composition, and rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) codes. The model took the form: BMIadj,j = β₀ + β₁·ln(HomeValuej) + β₂·Educationj + β₃·Racej + β₄·Hispanicj + β₅·CarCommutej + Σm γm·RUCAmj + εj, where εj represents the residual error term.

We employed a backward elimination approach to select variables, starting with a full model that included all variables from the four domains, and retained only those with a p-value less than 0.05. To assess model stability, we compared this approach with forward selection and model selection using the Akaike information criterion. Continuous predictors were standardized to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, allowing coefficients to represent the change in tract mean BMI per one-standard-deviation difference in the predictor. This standardization enabled us to compare the effects of different predictors across variables.

Model fit was evaluated using the adjusted coefficient of determination (R²), and we compared domain-specific models to quantify the contribution of each domain to explained variance. This involved calculating changes in adjusted R² when each domain was added to or removed from the full model. Due to unequal precision in tract estimates, we repeated the primary analysis using weighted least squares with weights equal to the inverse of the estimated variance of the tract mean, as well as weights proportional to the number of cardholders. To ensure the validity of our results, we conducted regression diagnostics, including residual plots, Q–Q plots, Cook's distance, and the Breusch–Pagan test for heteroskedasticity. We also used heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors in the final model.

Residual spatial autocorrelation was assessed using Moran's I on model residuals, and if present, we fitted spatial lag and spatial error models and compared them with the ordinary least squares model using Lagrange multiplier tests. Our sensitivity analyses consisted of four components. First, we restricted the sample to tracts with at least 500 records to evaluate the impact of sample size on our results. Second, we excluded tracts with coverage below 70% of the ACS adult population to assess the effect of data coverage on our findings. Third, we limited the sample to cardholders whose records were issued or renewed within the previous four years to reduce the influence of out-of-date self-reports. Fourth, we examined whether the associations differed when BMI was calculated separately for men and women to investigate potential sex-specific effects.

As a validation exercise, we compared our county-level aggregated estimates with county-level obesity prevalence from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System and the CDC PLACES project. We used Pearson and Spearman correlations to evaluate the agreement between these estimates. All analyses were conducted in R version 4.0, utilizing the sf, spdep, sandwich, and car packages, as well as ArcGIS Pro for cartography. Statistical tests were two-sided, with a significance level of α = 0.05.

The study population consisted of 3,042,118 state-issued identification records, from which we excluded 118,406 records belonging to individuals younger than 18 years, 61,259 with missing or implausible height or weight, and 27,540 that could not be geocoded to a census tract. This resulted in a final sample of 2,834,913 records, representing approximately 87% of Oregon's estimated adult population in the ACS 2015–2019 five-year estimates. Of the state's 834 census tracts, 828 had at least 100 records and complete covariate data, and were retained for analysis. The median tract contributed 3,194 records, with an interquartile range of 2,410–4,102.

Age-adjusted mean BMI, direct-standardized to the 2010 Oregon adult age distribution, was 27.9 kg/m² across tracts, with a standard deviation of 1.3. Tract means ranged from 23.4 to 32.1 kg/m², and the distribution was approximately symmetric, with a skewness of 0.21. As a result, we did not transform the outcome variable. Mapping revealed clear geographic clustering, with the lowest mean BMI values appearing in tracts in west Portland, near university campuses in Corvallis and Eugene, and along parts of the Hood River Gorge. In contrast, the highest values were concentrated in rural eastern Oregon, in parts of the southern interior, and in several lower-income tracts on the eastern edge of the Portland metropolitan area.

Our examination of bivariate associations revealed that socioeconomic indicators, such as median home value and the proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, were strongly inversely correlated with tract mean BMI. The share of workers commuting by car was positively correlated with BMI, while the share walking, cycling, or using transit was negatively correlated. Race and ethnicity measures showed varied associations, with the proportion of residents identifying as Hispanic or Latino, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Black or African American being positively correlated with tract BMI. In contrast, the proportion identifying as Asian was negatively correlated.

Tract BMI also rose across the RUCA gradient, with mean BMI values increasing from 27.5 kg/m² in metropolitan tracts to 28.9 kg/m² in isolated rural tracts. An ANOVA across these groups was significant, indicating that the differences in mean BMI across the RUCA gradient were statistically significant. Measures of food access were only weakly related to BMI, suggesting that other factors may be more influential in determining tract-level mean BMI. Overall, our findings highlight the complex relationships between socioeconomic factors, transportation modes, racial and ethnic composition, and rural-urban commuting area codes in shaping geographic patterns of BMI. The relationship between geographic proximity to supermarkets and body mass index (BMI) has been a subject of interest in recent years. Our analysis revealed a weak positive correlation between residing more than one mile from a supermarket in urban areas or ten miles in rural areas, as defined by the USDA Food Access Research Atlas (Rhone et al., 2017), and BMI, with a correlation coefficient of 0.18 (p < 0.001). In contrast, the density of fast-food outlets per square mile exhibited a weak negative correlation (r = −0.09, p = 0.01), likely reflecting the tendency for such establishments to concentrate in densely populated urban areas.

To further investigate the factors influencing BMI, we employed a multivariable model using ordinary least squares regression. The model, denoted as BMIᵢ = β₀ + β₁HomeValueᵢ + β₂Bachelorᵢ + β₃Raceᵢ + β₄Hispanicᵢ + β₅CarCommuteᵢ + β₆RUCAᵢ + εᵢ, where i indexes census tracts, included variables such as home value, educational attainment, racial composition, Hispanic ethnicity, car commuting, and rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) classification. The model demonstrated a high explanatory power, accounting for 86% of the variance in tract mean BMI (R² = 0.86; adjusted R² = 0.86; residual standard error 0.49 kg/m²). The results of ten-fold cross-validation yielded an out-of-sample R² of 0.85 and a root mean squared error of 0.50 kg/m², indicating that the model's fit was not due to overfitting. Variance inflation factors for all variables were below 4.1, with the highest values observed for home value (3.9) and bachelor's degree attainment (3.6), leading us to retain both variables in the model.

The adjusted coefficients presented in Table 2 reveal that each $100,000 increase in median home value was associated with a 0.38 kg/m² lower mean BMI (95% CI −0.44 to −0.32; standardized β = −0.34). Similarly, each 10-percentage-point increase in the proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher was associated with a 0.31 kg/m² lower mean BMI (95% CI −0.37 to −0.25; β = −0.36). These two variables collectively accounted for the majority of the explained variance, as evidenced by a hierarchical analysis where a model with only these two predictors yielded an R² of 0.68. Notably, car commuting remained positively associated with BMI after adjustment, with each 10-percentage-point increase in the share of workers commuting by car corresponding to a 0.19 kg/m² higher mean BMI (95% CI 0.12 to 0.26; β = 0.15). The addition of commuting variables to the socioeconomic model resulted in a modest increase in R² of 0.03.

Our analysis also revealed independent associations between racial and ethnic composition and tract BMI. Specifically, each 10-percentage-point increase in the Hispanic or Latino population was associated with a 0.24 kg/m² higher BMI (95% CI 0.17 to 0.31), while corresponding estimates were 0.29 kg/m² (95% CI 0.18 to 0.40) for American Indian or Alaska Native residents and 0.41 kg/m² (95% CI 0.22 to 0.60) for Black or African American residents. In contrast, a 10-percentage-point increase in the Asian population was associated with a 0.33 kg/m² lower BMI (95% CI −0.40 to −0.26). It is essential to recognize that these coefficients describe area-level patterns rather than individual risk, as tract-level associations cannot be interpreted at the individual level (Robinson, 1950).

The RUCA classification remained significant after adjustment (joint F-test p < 0.001), with relative to metropolitan tracts, adjusted mean BMI being 0.17 kg/m² higher in micropolitan tracts (95% CI 0.05 to 0.29), 0.26 higher in small town tracts (95% CI 0.13 to 0.39), and 0.34 higher in isolated rural tracts (95% CI 0.19 to 0.49). The USDA low-access measure and fast-food density were not significant when added to this model (β = 0.02, p = 0.41, and β = −0.01, p = 0.63, respectively), and neither changed R² by more than 0.001, with the main coefficients changing by less than 5%.

Residual and sensitivity analyses were conducted to validate the results. The residuals were approximately normal and exhibited no evidence of heteroscedasticity (Breusch–Pagan p = 0.12). Spatial autocorrelation was substantially reduced after adjustment (Moran's I for residuals = 0.07, p = 0.02), indicating that the covariates accounted for most of the geographic structure. A spatial error model yielded coefficients within 0.03 kg/m² of the OLS estimates and did not alter any inference. The largest positive residuals, which represented observed BMI values above predicted by more than 1 kg/m², occurred in a small number of tracts containing correctional or institutional facilities and military housing. In contrast, the largest negative residuals were found in tracts with large university student populations. The results were robust to restricting the analysis to the 701 tracts with at least 1,500 records (R² = 0.87) and to weighting tracts by record count (R² = 0.88).

Furthermore, tract BMI was strongly correlated with model-based adult obesity prevalence from the CDC PLACES project (r = 0.81; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022), supporting the external validity of the identification card estimates. This study demonstrates that height and weight recorded on state-issued identification cards can be utilized to produce stable, small-area estimates of adult body mass index (BMI) for every census tract in Oregon. The six tract-level characteristics included in the model, namely median home value, educational attainment, race, ethnicity, the share of workers commuting by car, and rural-urban commuting area classification, collectively accounted for 86% of the variation in mean BMI.

The findings of this study are consistent with a large body of literature on socioeconomic disparities in obesity, which suggests that identification card data capture real geographic variation in adult weight status rather than artifacts of the data source. The inverse association between BMI and both home values and education aligns with decades of evidence indicating that obesity prevalence in high-income countries is patterned by socioeconomic position (Sobal & Stunkard, 1989; McLaren, 2007). Home value serves as a useful tract-level proxy, as it reflects accumulated wealth and neighborhood amenities, as well as current income, and wealth has been linked to health outcomes independently of income (Pollack et al., 2013). Educational attainment may operate through various mechanisms, including health literacy, occupational conditions, food preferences, and access to resources that support physical activity and dietary quality (Cutler & Lleras-Muney, 2010). However, due to the strong correlation between these characteristics across tracts, we caution against attributing separate causal effects to each. Instead, our models should be interpreted as describing the socioeconomic structure of weight status rather than identifying individual mechanisms.

The positive association between car commuting and BMI is consistent with research linking automobile dependence and the built environments that sustain it to lower physical activity and higher body weight (Frank et al., 2004; Lopez-Zetina et al., 2006). Active commuting is a modest contributor to daily energy expenditure, but car commuting may also mark low-density, less walkable development patterns where routine destinations are not easily accessible on foot. As such, the relationship between car commuting and BMI may be influenced by a complex array of factors, including urban design, transportation infrastructure, and socioeconomic characteristics. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this association and to inform the development of effective interventions aimed at promoting physical activity and reducing obesity.

The prevalence of traumatic hand and upper extremity injuries presenting to emergency departments (EDs) is a significant concern, with epidemiological studies suggesting that these injuries account for approximately 20% of all ED visits. Lacerations, fractures, crush injuries, and amputations are among the most common types of hand and wrist injuries, and while many are minor, a substantial proportion require prompt specialized evaluation and often operative management. The importance of timely intervention cannot be overstated, as delays can lead to serious consequences, including infection, permanent stiffness, loss of grip strength, chronic pain, and prolonged work disability. Given the hand's central role in occupation, self-care, and social participation, these outcomes carry substantial personal and societal costs. Furthermore, hand injuries disproportionately affect working-age adults, resulting in considerable economic burdens through lost productivity and compensation claims.

Despite the significant burden of hand injuries, access to emergency hand care is often inadequate. The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA) mandates that hospitals with EDs provide a medical screening examination and stabilization, and maintain an on-call roster of specialists to meet patient needs. However, compliance with this requirement is challenging for many institutions, particularly in light of the decline in specialists willing to take emergency call over the past two decades. This trend is especially pronounced in surgical and procedural subspecialties, where physicians cite uncompensated care, medicolegal exposure, disruption to elective practice and personal life, and inadequate reimbursement as reasons for withdrawing from call panels.

In response to these challenges, hospitals have implemented various strategies, including paying call stipends, employing specialists, or transferring patients to other facilities. However, these approaches are often unevenly available and influenced by local market conditions rather than patient need. Hand surgery is particularly vulnerable to these pressures, given the relatively small workforce of hand surgeons and their tendency to practice in outpatient or ambulatory settings where elective procedures are more predictable and better reimbursed. As a result, patients may be evaluated by general orthopedic, plastic, or emergency physicians with varying levels of hand-specific training, or they may be transferred to another institution, sometimes over considerable distances. This can increase costs, delay definitive treatment, strain receiving centers, and fragment continuity of care.

Recent regional surveys have highlighted the mismatch between the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery services. These studies, conducted in different states and using similar telephone-based methods, have found that a larger proportion of hospitals offer elective hand services than provide around-the-clock emergency hand coverage. Moreover, they have identified geographic and institutional variation in coverage, suggesting that patients in underserved areas may have limited options. While these reports are scattered and often limited to a single state or region, they raise the possibility that the discrepancy between elective and emergency hand surgery services reflects a structural feature of the healthcare system rather than local anomalies.

The relationship between emergency hand surgery coverage and community characteristics, such as proximity to a trauma center or socioeconomic status, is a critical area of investigation. Level I trauma centers concentrate surgical resources, and nearby community hospitals may rely on them as referral destinations, potentially reducing the incentive or capacity for these hospitals to maintain their own hand call panels. Conversely, hospitals in counties without a trauma center may need to maintain broader local coverage due to limited transfer options. Additionally, hospitals serving economically disadvantaged communities often face challenges related to poor reimbursement, which may deter specialists from taking call.

New Jersey provides a unique setting for examining these questions, given its dense population, network of community hospitals, and marked variation in income and urbanization across municipalities. While its proximity to major metropolitan areas in New York and Pennsylvania might be expected to buffer patients against limited local coverage, it could also encourage a reliance on referral that undermines local emergency capability. To our knowledge, the availability of emergency versus elective hand surgery coverage across New Jersey hospitals has not been systematically evaluated.

This study aimed to assess the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery coverage among non-university hospitals in New Jersey and to determine whether a disproportionate availability of emergency relative to elective services exists. We also sought to examine whether emergency hand coverage varies according to the presence of a level I trauma center within the hospital's county and according to the poverty level of the hospital's city. By comparing our results with those from other states, we aimed to evaluate whether the discrepancy between elective and emergency hand surgery services is a national phenomenon. If so, our findings argue for policy and system-level responses, including regional hand trauma networks, structured triage and transfer protocols, and alternative models of emergency hand care, rather than reliance on traditional models of emergency call coverage.

This study makes three key contributions. First, it provides the first state-wide description of the gap between elective and emergency hand coverage in New Jersey, using a standardized survey of hospitals. Second, it identifies geographic and socioeconomic correlates of coverage that may point to modifiable drivers of access, such as call compensation, regionalization, and referral patterns. Third, by comparing our results with those from other states, it assesses whether the discrepancy between elective and emergency hand surgery services is a national trend, with implications for policy and system-level responses to improve access to emergency hand care. Our study aimed to investigate the availability of elective hand surgery and emergency hand coverage in acute-care hospitals across the state of New Jersey. To achieve this, we conducted a cross-sectional telephone survey in August 2014, following established guidelines for structured telephone surveys of organizations (Dillman et al., 2014). The survey design ensured a brief, fixed-script instrument, a well-defined respondent population, and repeated contact attempts to minimize nonresponse. We collected only institutional-level information about service availability, with no patient data or individually identifiable information about respondents, which allowed us to classify the study as non-human-subjects research, exempt from full institutional review board review.

The survey's purpose was clearly communicated to respondents at the outset, and participation was voluntary. To identify eligible hospitals, we compiled a sampling frame from the New Jersey Department of Health's public licensure listing of acute-care general hospitals, cross-checking it against the state hospital association directory to exclude closed, merged, or renamed facilities. We limited our sample to hospitals with an emergency department, as the study focused on the availability of emergency hand coverage and elective services. University-affiliated hospitals were excluded, as they typically have residency-based, in-house subspecialty coverage, which could inflate estimates of availability in community hospitals where access concerns are most pressing. Specialty hospitals without an emergency department, such as rehabilitation, psychiatric, and pediatric-only facilities, were also excluded. After applying these criteria, 58 hospitals remained, and all were contacted, resulting in a census of eligible institutions rather than a sample.

The survey instrument consisted of two questions, carefully chosen to reflect how a transferring clinician or patient would assess access to hand care. The first question asked whether the hospital provided elective hand surgery, with a simple yes/no response.
