As the demand for IoMT systems continues to grow, there will be a need for new and innovative solutions that can meet the technical, regulatory, and social challenges of this rapidly evolving field. This can be achieved through the development of new wireless communication standards, the creation of new technologies and applications, and the integration of IoMT systems with other technologies such as artificial intelligence and blockchain.

In addition to the development of new technologies and applications, it is also essential that we create new use cases and applications that take advantage of the unique capabilities of the IoMT. This can be achieved through the development of new business models, the creation of new industries and markets, and the integration of IoMT systems with other technologies and systems. By creating new use cases and applications, we can unlock the full potential of the IoMT and create a future where healthcare and wellness are personalized, proactive, and preventive.

The integration of IoMT systems with other technologies such as artificial intelligence and blockchain is also critical to the future of the IoMT. This can be achieved through the development of new applications and use cases that take advantage of the unique capabilities of these technologies, as well as through the creation of new business models and industries that are based on the integration of IoMT systems with other technologies. By integrating IoMT systems with other technologies, we can create a future where healthcare and wellness are personalized, proactive, and preventive, and where the unique capabilities of the IoMT are fully realized.

In the final analysis, the future of the IoMT is dependent on our ability to address the technical, regulatory, and social challenges that currently hinder the widespread adoption of IoMT systems. By working together to develop new technologies, applications, and use cases, we can create an IoMT that is safe, secure, and beneficial for all. This will require a concerted effort from researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, as well as a commitment to prioritizing the needs and interests of users. By doing so, we can unlock the full potential of the IoMT and create a future where healthcare and wellness are personalized, proactive, and preventive. The nominal data rate is often cited as a key performance metric, but it is essential to recognize that this estimate represents an idealized lower bound, excluding protocol overhead, retransmissions, and duty-cycle effects. Consequently, we focused on theoretical throughput, rather than application-layer throughput, to ensure consistency throughout our analysis. When empirical values from the literature were available, such as packet delivery ratio and latency, we opted to summarize them using medians and ranges instead of pooled means, given the diversity of test conditions employed in the studies (Higgins et al., 2019). This approach allowed us to account for the variability in experimental setups and provide a more nuanced understanding of the data.

To address our third research question, we developed a taxonomy of IoMT applications, adapting the framework proposed by Islam et al. (2015). Our classification system comprised five categories: chronic-disease management (encompassing conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease), remote patient monitoring, fitness and wellness, elderly and assisted living, and medication adherence. We identified vendors through a comprehensive search of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration device databases, CE-marking registries, trade-press listings, and product documentation. A vendor was included in our analysis if it marketed a currently available product that utilized one of the studied PAN technologies and was positioned for health or clinical use. Each product was carefully coded for its wireless technology, sensed physiological variable, regulatory status, and intended user (clinician or consumer). To ensure accuracy, coding was performed by one author and verified against manufacturer documentation by a second author.

Our quality appraisal and synthesis of the included studies involved evaluating each study on four criteria, scored on a scale of 0 to 2: clarity of experimental setup, reproducibility of reported parameters, relevance to clinical use, and consideration of security and privacy. Studies with total scores below 4 out of 8 were retained for context but not used for quantitative statements. Our synthesis was primarily descriptive, involving the tabulation of counts and proportions of studies by technology, year, and application domain. We also assessed temporal trends in the share of publications per technology using simple linear regression on annual proportions, with significance set at α = 0.05. Although the number of annual data points is relatively small, we interpret these trends as exploratory and worthy of further investigation. All calculations were performed using Python 3, with the pandas and SciPy libraries.

It is essential to acknowledge the limitations of our method. Restricting the review to English-language sources and selected databases may introduce publication and language bias. Moreover, manufacturer-supplied specifications represent best-case performance and may not reflect the complexities of clinical environments, where body shadowing and interference can significantly impact device performance. The vendor landscape is also subject to rapid change, so our catalogue represents a snapshot of the market as of the search date.

Our comparative characterization of PAN standards focused on three dominant standards in IoMT: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), IEEE 802.15.4/ZigBee, and IEEE 802.15.6 for Body Area Networks (BANs). Although all three operate in or near the 2.4 GHz band, they exhibit substantial differences in throughput, energy profile, topology, and suitability for in-body or on-body communication (Latré et al., 2011; Movassaghi et al., 2014). BLE, introduced in Bluetooth 4.0 and later, utilizes 40 channels of 2 MHz width, with three advertising channels, and provides a 1 Mbps physical-layer rate. The more recent Bluetooth !!!!!!!! 5 adds a 2 Mbps mode and a coded PHY, extending the nominal line-of-sight range to approximately 240 m (Bluetooth SIG, 2019). However, application-layer throughput is significantly lower than the raw rate, with measurements of BLE connections commonly reporting 5–100 kbps in practice, depending on connection interval and the number of packets per event (Gomez et al., 2012). The standard supports a star topology and, with the introduction of the Mesh profile, enables many-to-many networking. Peak radio currents are typically in the range of 10–15 mA, and sleep currents fall below 1 µA. According to Gomez et al. (2012), a sensor transmitting one reading per second could operate for more than a year on a 230 mAh coin cell.

In contrast, IEEE 802.15.4 defines a 250 kbps PHY at 2.4 GHz across 16 channels, 40 kbps at 915 MHz across 10 channels, and 20 kbps at 868 MHz on a single channel (IEEE, 2015). The maximum PHY frame is 127 bytes, leaving roughly 102 bytes of MAC payload after addressing and security overhead. ZigBee, which builds upon the IEEE 802.15.4 standard, adds network and application layers that support star, tree, and mesh topologies, with theoretical addressing of more than 65,000 nodes. Typical transmit current is in the range of 25–35 mA, resulting in energy per bit of the same order as BLE only when duty cycles are very low. Siekkinen et al. (2012) found BLE to be more energy efficient than ZigBee for small, infrequent transfers, reporting approximately 0.15 µJ/bit for BLE, and higher costs for ZigBee under comparable beacon-less operation. However, ZigBee's mesh capability provides an advantage in multi-room facilities, such as hospital wards, where single-hop BLE links require additional gateways.

IEEE 802.15.6, ratified in 2012, was specifically designed for BANs and specifies three PHY layers: Narrowband (NB), Ultra-Wideband (UWB), and Human Body Communications (HBC). NB data rates range from approximately 75.9 kbps to 971.4 kbps, while UWB supports rates from roughly 0.5 Mbps to over 12 Mbps. The standard targets transmit power at or below 0 dBm and a packet error rate below 10% for 256-octet payloads at stated receiver sensitivities (IEEE, 2012). Its star topology with up to two-hop extension, and its three security levels (unsecured, authentication only, and authentication plus encryption), are tailored to body-worn sensors. Kwak et al. (2010) projected that 802.15.6 could achieve markedly lower energy consumption per delivered bit than 802.15.4 for periodic medical traffic, although few commercial chipsets implement the standard, limiting empirical validation.

The BAN literature consistently reports a set of requirements that are critical to the development of effective IoMT solutions. Typical on-body communication ranges are 1–3 m, and implanted links, commonly operating in the 402–405 MHz Medical Implant Communication Service band, function over distances below 2 m through tissue (Movassaghi et al., 2014). Body shadowing produces path loss 20–40 dB greater than free-space propagation at 2.4 GHz for non-line-of-sight on-body links (Hall & Hao, 2006), which explains the frequent need for relay nodes and retransmission. Required data rates vary by modality, with ECG sampling at 250 Hz with 12-bit resolution per lead producing approximately 3 kbps per lead, and a 12-lead ECG producing roughly 36 kbps. EEG with 32 channels at 256 Hz yields approximately 100 kbps, and uncompressed audio or video streams for telemedicine exceed 1 Mbps. In contrast, temperature, glucose, and SpO2 sensors generate fewer than 1 kbps (Latré et al., 2011). Both BLE and 802.15.4 satisfy the throughput needs of these applications, although the choice of technology ultimately depends on a range of factors, including energy efficiency, topology, and security requirements. The realm of personal area networks (PANs) is a crucial component of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), as it enables the seamless communication between various medical devices and sensors. When it comes to vital-sign monitoring, for instance, UWB-class links are not necessarily required, whereas high-bandwidth imaging or neural applications demand more robust connections. Moreover, latency tolerances vary significantly across different applications, with delay budgets of under 125 ms for ECG-based alarms and under 250 ms for interactive applications, accompanied by reliability targets above 99% for critical alerts, as highlighted by Latré et al. in 2011.

A closer examination of the existing standards reveals that only 802.15.6 defines explicit prioritization, with eight user priority levels, whereas BLE and ZigBee rely on application-level management or guaranteed time slots in 802.15.4 beacon-enabled superframes, allowing up to seven dedicated slots. This distinction is noteworthy, as it underscores the unique requirements of various medical applications.

Our comprehensive survey of 46 IOMT applications and products from both academic and commercial sources provides valuable insights into the current landscape. These applications can be broadly categorized into five clinical functions: remote patient monitoring (37%), chronic disease management (24%), fitness and wellness tracking (17%), medication adherence and smart dispensing (11%), and in-hospital asset and patient tracking (11%). Notably, among the products that disclosed their PAN technology, BLE was the most prevalent, appearing in 31 of 46 entries (67%), followed by IEEE 802.15.4/ZigBee-based or proprietary 802.15.4 systems (15%), ANT/ANT+ or NFC (11%), and no entry used IEEE 802.15.6 natively. This finding confirms the gap between standardization and commercial adoption, as suggested by chipset availability.

The vendor landscape is characterized by moderate concentration, with consumer-grade wearables and continuous glucose monitors from companies like Apple, Fitbit, and Medtronic accounting for 41% of the entries, while enterprise and hospital-oriented platforms from Philips, GE Healthcare, and Cisco accounted for 26%. Specialized startups and academic prototypes made up the remaining 33%. Market projections cited in the literature suggest that the global IoMT sector was approximately USD 41 billion in 2017, with expected annual growth above 20% through the early 2020s, consistent with the density of BLE-enabled entries in our catalogue.

However, our analysis also reveals several challenges across the surveyed systems. Security and privacy provisions were unevenly documented, with only 46% of the entries explicitly reporting link-layer or application-layer encryption, usually AES-128. Furthermore, 33% described authentication or pairing mechanisms beyond default settings, highlighting the need for more robust security measures. Interoperability was another concern, as only 28% of the entries cited conformance to a health-specific profile, while the remainder relied on proprietary data formats, complicating integration with electronic health records.

The interpretation of our findings suggests that the IoMT landscape is characterized by a set of trade-offs among throughput, energy consumption, topology, interoperability, and security. No single PAN technology satisfies the full set of clinical requirements, and instead, the landscape is marked by a complex interplay between different technologies. BLE offers a nominal physical-layer rate of 1 Mbit/s, rising to 2 Mbit/s in Bluetooth 5, and is built into virtually every smartphone, explaining its dominance in consumer-grade wearables. ZigBee, on the other hand, operates at a nominal 250 kbit/s in the 2.4 GHz band, with its main strengths being mesh routing and very low duty cycles, making it suitable for ambient and in-home monitoring.

A second key finding is the gap between standardization and deployment. Although IEEE 802.15.6 is technically better matched to clinical BAN requirements, commercial IoMT products overwhelmingly use BLE, proprietary sub-GHz links, or ANT+. Silicon availability, smartphone integration, and developer ecosystems have proved more decisive than protocol fitness. Our survey of vendors and applications is consistent with this: remote patient monitoring, fall detection, medication adherence, and chronic disease management all rely mainly on commodity radios, with intelligence and storage pushed to gateways and cloud back-ends.

The coexistence of different technologies is another critical aspect, as BLE, ZigBee, ANT, and Wi-Fi all share the 2.4 GHz ISM band, and hospital environments add dense interference from infusion pumps, imaging equipment, and visitors' devices. Experimental studies have shown that IEEE 802.15.4 packet loss can rise sharply when it overlaps with high-duty-cycle Wi-Fi channels. Adaptive frequency hopping in BLE mitigates this, though it does not remove it. Alarm-critical signals, such as arrhythmia alerts, therefore cannot depend on an unmanaged shared band without application-level acknowledgment and redundancy.

The implications of our findings are significant for practitioners, suggesting a layered selection strategy rather than a single-technology choice. High-rate or smartphone-mediated applications such as ECG patches and continuous glucose monitors are best served by BLE. Facility-wide or home-wide sensing with many static nodes favors ZigBee-style mesh networking. Implanted or strictly on-body systems with stringent power and safety limits should adopt, or at least track, IEEE 802.15.6. Because device lifetimes in healthcare often exceed a decade, procurement should also weigh a standard's maintenance trajectory and vendor roadmap, not only current performance. Security and privacy emerge as critical considerations, underscoring the need for more robust measures to protect sensitive medical data. Ultimately, our study highlights the complex interplay between different PAN technologies and the need for a nuanced understanding of their strengths and limitations in the context of IoMT applications.

Understanding the relationships between events in a text is a crucial aspect of natural language processing, as it enables us to grasp the underlying narrative structure and extract meaningful information. Consider, for instance, a news report on an earthquake, which typically includes mentions of the quake itself, the collapse of buildings, rescue operations, and subsequent aid pledges. While some of these mentions refer to the same real-world occurrence, others describe distinct events linked by time, causation, or narrative structure. Recovering these relationships is essential for various downstream applications, such as summarization, question answering, knowledge base population, and storyline extraction. In this paper, we focus on two specific event relations: Event Coreference, which involves grouping event mentions that refer to the same event, and Event Sequencing, which orders the subevents of a larger event in the sequence in which they are narrated within a script-like structure.

Event coreference resolution has been a topic of interest in the natural language processing community over the past decade, with early work adapting entity coreference techniques to events. This involved using pairwise classifiers over various features, including lexical, syntactic, and argument-overlap features. More recent systems have incorporated distributed representations and neural architectures, and shared tasks such as the TAC-KBP Event Nugget track have provided a standardized evaluation framework. A common feature of nearly all this work is the decoding strategy employed, which typically involves linking each mention to at most one antecedent, resulting in a forest structure where each tree corresponds to a coreference cluster. This approach is well-suited for coreference, as it is an equivalence relation, and a single link to any earlier member of the cluster is sufficient to determine membership.

In contrast, event sequencing has received relatively less attention, and has been studied under different guises. Research on narrative schemas and scripts has focused on learning typical orderings of events from large corpora, while temporal relation research has classified pairwise relations such as BEFORE and AFTER between events on a document timeline. Our notion of sequencing differs from these approaches, as we are interested in how the subevents of a complex event follow one another in the discourse. For instance, an attack may be followed by an injury, an arrest, and a trial. These sequences are not equivalence classes, as a subevent may follow several preceding events, and a given event may participate in more than one sequence when a narrative branches or converges.

Moreover, the relation is non-transitive in the sense that a direct link between consecutive subevents carries information that would be lost if links were inferred from distant order. This difference exposes a gap in the current approach to event sequencing, as decoding with the same antecedent-tree structure used for coreference would restrict each event to having only a single predecessor, and the output would be unable to represent branching or merging within a script. Relaxing the structure entirely, as in independent pairwise classification, would yield outputs that may be inconsistent and ignore global properties of the relation.

Existing temporal ordering work often resolves such inconsistencies with global inference, such as integer linear programming, but these approaches are typically designed for a single relation type and do not provide a shared decoding framework that can also handle coreference. As a result, the two relations are generally modeled by separate pipelines with incompatible assumptions, despite their interaction: coreferent mentions should occupy the same position in a sequence, and sequence links between mentions should be consistent with their cluster membership. These observations lead us to our central research question: can a single decoding framework, more general than the antecedent tree, represent and learn both event coreference and event sequencing, while remaining competitive with specialized systems on each?

To address this question, we propose a graph-based decoding algorithm, where events are treated as nodes, and relations are predicted as edges in a directed acyclic graph. The permitted topology of the graph is determined by the task, and the decoder operates over edge scores without depending on how those scores are produced. This allows for flexible feature sets, including lexical, discourse, argument, and embedding-based features, and enables task-specific features to be added without changing the inference procedure. The model is trained with a structured, margin-based objective, ensuring that learning matches the decoding used at test time.

We evaluate our approach on both event coreference and event sequencing tasks. On the TAC-KBP 2015 event coreference task, our system achieves state-of-the-art performance under the standard metrics. For event sequencing, we create a new dataset and evaluation framework, as existing datasets and metrics are not well-suited for our notion of sequencing. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our graph-based decoding algorithm in capturing both event coreference and event sequencing, and highlight the potential for a unified framework to represent and learn these two related but distinct relations.

The implications of our work are significant, as it enables the development of more sophisticated natural language processing systems that can extract and represent complex event relationships. By providing a shared decoding framework for event coreference and event sequencing, we can improve the performance of downstream applications such as summarization, question answering, and storyline extraction. Furthermore, our graph-based decoding algorithm can be applied to other related tasks, such as temporal relation extraction and narrative schema learning, and can be extended to incorporate additional features and relations.

In conclusion, our research demonstrates the importance of developing a unified framework for event coreference and event sequencing, and highlights the potential of graph-based decoding algorithms in capturing complex event relationships. By addressing the limitations of existing approaches and providing a more general and flexible framework, we can advance the state-of-the-art in natural language processing and enable the development of more sophisticated and effective systems for extracting and representing event relationships. Our work presents a novel approach to event coreference and sequencing, outperforming a strong baseline that leverages temporal ordering and oracle information. The key contributions of our research are fourfold. Firstly, through a comprehensive analysis of annotated data and experiments, we demonstrate that the traditional tree-like decoding structure commonly employed in event coreference is ill-suited for event sequencing. This is because event sequencing often involves multiple valid predecessors, which cannot be adequately captured by a single-parent constraint. Secondly, we introduce a graph-based decoding algorithm that unifies the two tasks, allowing for flexible feature sets and accommodating the complexities of event relationships. Thirdly, our system achieves state-of-the-art results on the TAC-KBP 2015 dataset for both coreference and sequencing tasks, surpassing a strong oracle-informed temporal baseline. Finally, we discuss the challenges that remain in studying event relations, including the issues of annotation sparsity, ambiguity in event granularity, and error propagation from upstream event detection.

We evaluated our coreference system on the TAC-KBP 2015 Event Nugget corpus, which comprises newswire and discussion-forum documents annotated for event nuggets and within-document event coreference. Following the shared-task protocol, we trained our model on the 2015 training release and tested it on the official 2015 evaluation set. To fine-tune our model, we held out 10% of the training documents as a development set for feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. The final model was retrained on the full training set with the selected settings. For the main experiments, we used gold event mentions as input to the coreference system. Additionally, we report results on system-predicted mentions from a sequence-labeling nugget detector to demonstrate how mention errors propagate.

Event sequencing was studied on the same documents as coreference, allowing the two tasks to share mentions and coreference clusters. A sequencing link connects an event to the event that immediately follows it in the narrative script of the document. Annotators marked a link only when the later event could be inferred to happen after the earlier one. Notably, links are defined between coreference clusters rather than individual mentions, as coreferent mentions denote a single event. Furthermore, because a story can branch, an event may have multiple successors and predecessors. We split the data at the document level in the same way as for coreference and computed inter-annotator agreement using Cohen's κ on a doubly annotated subset.

The traditional approach to coreference relies on a latent antecedent tree, where each mention selects a single antecedent from the preceding mentions or a dummy root that starts a new cluster. However, this single-parent constraint is unsuitable for sequencing, as it discards valid links and makes the output dependent on arbitrary tie-breaking. To address this limitation, we decode over a general directed graph, where the set of nodes represents mentions for coreference and clusters for sequencing. For each candidate pair, the model scores the edge using a task-specific weight vector, and an edge is included when its score exceeds a threshold. The threshold is tuned on the development set.

For coreference, we maintain the tree constraint of at most one incoming edge per mention, using the highest-scoring antecedent when its score exceeds the threshold, and otherwise linking to the dummy root. This makes the tree decoder a special case of the graph decoder. In contrast, sequencing places no limit on in-degree or out-degree but requires the graph to be acyclic. We consider candidate edges in descending score order and skip an edge if it would close a cycle. Although this greedy procedure is not guaranteed to find the optimal directed acyclic graph (DAG), exact search is NP-hard in general, and preliminary experiments showed that greedy search produced the same graphs as beam search on over 97% of documents. To keep the sequencing graph compact, we apply transitive reduction to the output, removing an edge when a path exists with both component edges selected.

Both tasks are trained using a structured perceptron with averaged weights. For coreference, the gold annotation provides only clusters, not antecedent choices, so the correct structure is latent. We define the latent gold antecedent for each mention as the highest-scoring gold-coreferent predecessor under the current weights. The update at each mention is based on the difference between the predicted antecedent and the latent gold antecedent. We use a cost-augmented variant, where erroneous links to the dummy root and erroneous non-root links receive different margin penalties, which are tuned for the trade-off between precision and recall. For sequencing, the gold structure is observed at the cluster level, so no latent selection is needed. The update is based on the predicted score and the gold label for each pair of clusters.

Our feature set for coreference follows previous work, including lexical match and lemma features. We also explore the use of additional features, such as semantic role labeling and named entity recognition, to improve performance. The sequencing features are designed to capture the temporal relationships between events, including the use of temporal expressions and the narrative structure of the document. By combining these features with the graph-based decoding algorithm, we achieve state-of-the-art results on both coreference and sequencing tasks.

In conclusion, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of a graph-based approach to event coreference and sequencing, outperforming a strong baseline and achieving state-of-the-art results on the TAC-KBP 2015 dataset. However, there are still challenges to be addressed, including annotation sparsity, ambiguity in event granularity, and error propagation from upstream event detection. Future work should focus on developing more robust and accurate methods for event detection and representation, as well as exploring the application of our approach to other domains and languages. The resolution of event coreference and sequencing is a complex task that relies on a multitude of features to accurately identify and order event mentions in a document. Our approach leverages a range of features, including overlap of triggers, WordNet synonymy, cosine similarity of pre-trained word embeddings, event type and realis agreement, sentence and token distance, and argument overlap derived from a semantic role labeler and an entity coreference system. These features are computed on mention pairs and are used to inform the clustering of event mentions. In addition to these pairwise features, we also compute sequencing features on cluster pairs, which capture the relationships between clusters. These features include the event types of both clusters, the order of their first mentions, the minimum sentence distance, and discourse connectives and temporal expressions near each trigger.

To aggregate these pairwise mention features, we take the maximum and mean over all mention pairs in the two clusters. This allows us to capture the most salient features of each pair and to represent the relationships between clusters in a compact and meaningful way. We also add features that capture the relationships between clusters that share a participant, including the participant's role in each event. Furthermore, we include the signed difference of the clusters' positions in the document, which provides a sense of the overall structure of the document and the relationships between events.

One of the key advantages of our approach is that the decoder scores each edge independently, which means that any pairwise or cluster-level feature set can be used without changing the inference procedure. This allows us to test different feature groups separately and in combination, and to evaluate their contribution to the overall performance of the system. In our ablation studies, we found that the flexible feature set is a key component of our system, and that the addition of argument and entity-compatibility features, as well as discourse features, significantly improves performance.

To evaluate our system, we compared it to a range of baselines, including the top-ranked TAC-KBP 2015 systems, a tree-based latent antecedent model, and a mention-pair model with closest-first clustering. We also used a strong oracle-informed temporal baseline, which takes gold coreference clusters and orders them by the textual position of their first mention. This baseline provides a sense of the upper bound of performance, and allows us to evaluate the effectiveness of our system in comparison to a gold standard.

In terms of evaluation metrics, we used the official TAC-KBP scorer, which reports MUC, B³, entity-based CEAF, and BLANC, together with their unweighted average. We also reported precision, recall, and F1 over cluster-level links, as well as a variant that computes the same measures over the transitive closure of both gold and system graphs. This allows us to capture the nuances of event coreference and sequencing, and to evaluate the performance of our system in a comprehensive and meaningful way.

Our experimental setup involved evaluating event coreference on the TAC-KBP 2015 Event Nugget evaluation data, following the official protocol. We trained our classifier on the 2015 training documents, plus the 2014 annotation release, with 20% of the training documents held out for tuning. The test portion contains 202 documents with 3,670 gold coreference clusters. We report the official scorer's metrics, as well as the AVG score, which is the mean of the four F1 values.

The results of our evaluation show that our system reaches an AVG F1 of 53.9, with MUC 31.4, B³ 49.8, CEAF-e 50.6, and BLANC 43.3. This is 1.6 points above the strongest system we compare against, and 3.2 points above the best official 2015 submission. The gain over the best prior system is statistically significant, and is mainly due to improvements in MUC and BLANC, the two metrics most sensitive to link-level recall.

We also compared our graph decoder with other decoding strategies under identical features and the same pairwise classifier. A simple closest-first clustering of pairwise decisions gives an AVG of 48.2, while a best-first (antecedent-tree) decoding trained with a latent-antecedent perceptron reaches 51.8. Our graph decoder reaches 53.9, which is significantly better than the other decoding strategies. The graph decoder differs from the tree decoder in allowing a mention to retain links to multiple antecedents within a cluster, and the tree-to-graph gain of 2.1 AVG points is significant.

Most of the gain appears as higher recall, with pairwise link recall on gold within-cluster pairs rising from 41.7 to 48.9, while precision falls only from 56.3 to 54.8. Cluster-level analysis shows that the gain is concentrated in larger clusters, with B³ F1 rising from 44.2 to 49.5 for clusters of four or more mentions. For singletons and pairs, the two decoders are statistically indistinguishable.

The flexible feature set also plays a crucial role in our system, with the addition of argument and entity-compatibility features, such as shared agent or patient, yielding a significant improvement in performance. Starting from a baseline with only lexical and surface features, the system scores 47.6 AVG. Adding argument and entity-compatibility features yields 50.9, while adding discourse features gives 52.2. These results demonstrate the importance of incorporating a range of features into the system, and highlight the effectiveness of our approach in resolving event coreference and sequencing.

In conclusion, our system demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the task of event coreference and sequencing, and highlights the importance of incorporating a range of features and using a flexible decoding strategy. The results of our evaluation show that our system is able to effectively capture the nuances of event coreference and sequencing, and provides a sense of the overall structure of the document and the relationships between events. Future work will focus on further improving the performance of our system, and exploring the application of our approach to other tasks and domains. The incorporation of features derived from the sequencing relation has a notable impact on our model's performance, yielding a final score of 53.9 (+1.7) when added to the existing feature set. This improvement is not merely a byproduct of other features, as removing these sequencing-derived features results in a return to the 52.2 configuration. The availability of these features is a direct consequence of our decoder's explicit graph representation of events, rather than a tree-like structure of antecedent choices. This distinction is particularly relevant when examining the task of event sequencing, where the suitability of a tree-like structure is called into question.

An analysis of the gold annotation reveals that, among events with at least one gold predecessor in their sequence, a substantial proportion (37.4%) have two or more predecessors, while 28.9% have two or more successors. This complexity is not adequately captured by a decoder that selects a single antecedent per mention, as in traditional tree-based coreference decoding. Such an approach would have a maximum attainable link recall of 62.6%, even with a perfect scorer. In contrast, our graph decoder is not constrained by this structural ceiling, allowing it to better model the intricacies of event sequencing.

The results of our sequencing experiments are presented in Table 2, where we compare our model to a strong temporal-based, oracle-informed system. This baseline system utilizes gold event mentions and gold coreference clusters, ordering events by their gold temporal relation (when available) and by textual order otherwise, linking each event to its immediate temporal neighbor. Despite its access to oracle information, this system achieves only 34.6 link F1 (precision 41.8, recall 29.5), highlighting the limitations of relying solely on temporal order to determine script-like sequences. A tree-decoding variant of our model, which uses a single best predecessor per event, reaches 36.9 F1 (precision 46.2, recall 30.7), consistent with its recall ceiling. In contrast, our graph decoder, using only predicted mentions and predicted coreference clusters, achieves 42.3 F1 (precision 45.1, recall 39.8). This represents a significant improvement of 7.7 points over the oracle-informed baseline and 5.4 points over the tree variant (p < 0.01). Notably, recall improves most, with a 10.3-point increase over the baseline and a 9.1-point increase over the tree variant, while precision remains roughly equivalent to that of the tree variant.

We also examined the performance of our graph decoder when using gold mentions and gold coreference, in order to estimate the impact of upstream errors. The results show that link F1 rises to 48.7 and sequence-level F1 to 26.4, indicating that approximately 6 link-F1 points are lost due to mention detection and coreference errors. Furthermore, our analysis of chain-length accuracy reveals a monotonic drop in performance: link F1 is 51.0 for sequences of length two to three, 41.5 for lengths four to six, and 30.2 for longer sequences. This suggests that errors accumulate as the number of required links grows.

The interaction between the two tasks is also noteworthy. Using predicted coreference clusters in sequencing features, instead of none, improves sequencing F1 from 39.5 to 42.3 (+2.8). Replacing predicted clusters with gold clusters raises it to 44.1, indicating that coreference quality is a moderate bottleneck. Conversely, the sequencing-derived features add 1.7 AVG points to coreference, as noted above. While we did not attempt joint optimization, these pipeline results with one-way feature sharing in each direction demonstrate the potential benefits of integrating the two tasks.

Our error analysis involved manually inspecting 100 sampled errors from each task. In coreference, we found that 41% of false merges involved events of the same type with similar arguments but distinct real-world occurrences, and 27% of missed links involved mentions that required inference beyond lexical overlap. In sequencing, 36% of false positives were links to events that were plausible successors but belonged to a different script instance in the same document, and 29% of missed links involved events separated by more than three sentences. Additionally, annotator agreement on sequencing links is lower than for coreference (Cohen's κ of 0.61 vs. 0.74 on a double-annotated subset of 20 documents), suggesting that part of the remaining error reflects genuine ambiguity in the task rather than model failure.

The central finding of this study is that the decoding structure matters, and that the appropriate structure depends on the relational semantics of the task. Event coreference is an equivalence relation, where each mention either begins a new event or attaches to an earlier mention of the same event, making a latent antecedent tree or a set of disjoint trees a natural and efficient approximation. In contrast, event sequencing differs in two key ways: a script-like sequence is not partitioned into disjoint clusters, and a given event may be linked to more than one predecessor or successor. Forcing each mention to choose a single antecedent therefore discards valid links by construction, limiting recall regardless of the local scorer's quality. Our error analysis supports this interpretation, as the tree-restricted variant lost most of its recall on mentions with multiple gold predecessors, which are more frequent in sequencing than in coreference.

The graph-based decoder avoids this limitation by scoring candidate edges jointly and enforcing only the constraints required by the relation (transitivity and symmetry for coreference, acyclicity and sparsity for sequencing). This approach echoes earlier work on global inference for temporal and discourse relations, but extends it by demonstrating that one decoding framework can serve two relations with different structural properties.

In interpreting our empirical results, we note that our coreference system reached state-of-the-art performance on TAC-KBP 2015. We attribute this improvement mainly to the decoder's ability to use pairwise evidence from mentions that are not adjacent in an antecedent chain, rather than to the feature set, which is deliberately conventional. Ablations are consistent with this view, and removing graph-level consistency terms yields similar results. These findings highlight the importance of careful decoder design and the potential benefits of integrating multiple tasks in a single framework.

The management of hand burns is a complex and challenging aspect of burn care, owing to the unique anatomy and function of the hand. As one of the most common injuries encountered by burn centers, hand burns account for a disproportionate share of long-term disability, with even small burns in this region capable of causing substantial functional loss. The hand's thin dorsal skin, limited subcutaneous tissue, and superficial tendon and joint structures render it particularly vulnerable to deep injury, and the consequences of such injuries can be far-reaching, affecting not only employment and self-care but also psychosocial recovery.

Historically, the primary goal of burn care was survival, with advances in fluid resuscitation, infection control, nutritional support, and early excision steadily reducing mortality from major burns. As survival rates improved, attention turned to the quality of survival, and the management of the burned hand underwent a significant shift. Initially, the aim was to preserve life and prevent sepsis, with limb loss often accepted as an unavoidable consequence of deep injury. However, as our understanding of burn care evolved, the goal became salvage of the digits themselves, and more recently, functional digital salvage – preserving not only viable fingers but also fingers that are mobile, sensate, and useful.

This progression has placed greater emphasis on the quality and timeliness of care in the first hours and days after injury, as early decisions largely determine the eventual functional outcome. Among these early decisions, the recognition and treatment of burn-related ischemia of the upper extremity is particularly time-sensitive. Full-thickness and deep circumferential burns can produce an inelastic eschar that cannot accommodate the edema that follows injury and resuscitation, leading to compromised venous outflow and arterial inflow, and potentially resulting in nerve and muscle ischemia. In the hand, elevated pressures in the interosseous and thenar compartments and within the digits can cause ischemic necrosis of intrinsic muscle, with subsequent claw deformity and contracture, even when the overlying skin appears to have survived.

Escharotomy, the incision of constricting eschar to restore perfusion, has been a mainstay of burn management since the work of Pruitt and colleagues, and it is widely taught as a limb- and digit-saving procedure. Contemporary reviews describe its technique, indications, and adjuncts, including fasciotomy for deeper compartment involvement and carpal tunnel release when median nerve compression is suspected. Clinical signs such as diminished or absent Doppler signals, delayed capillary refill, pain with passive stretch, and progressive sensory change are commonly used to trigger intervention, although their sensitivity and specificity can be imperfect, particularly in sedated, intubated, or hypotensive patients.

Beyond escharotomy, the literature has outlined a set of principles for the acute care of the burned hand, including elevation to limit edema, early splinting in a protective position, and early range-of-motion exercise guided by occupational therapy. Prompt excision of nonviable tissue and early autografting or other coverage, as well as close surveillance for infection and vascular compromise, are also essential components of burn care. Reports from large burn centers suggest that adherence to such protocols yields good functional outcomes in most patients, and that the majority of hand burns, including many deep burns, can be salvaged. Early tangential excision and grafting, in particular, has been associated with shorter hospital stays, reduced contracture formation, and improved return of function compared with delayed or conservative approaches.

Despite the effectiveness of these protocols, some patients still lose digits or portions of the hand despite timely, appropriate care. Amputation in the burned hand may be primary, performed at initial debridement for clearly nonviable parts, or secondary and delayed, performed days to weeks later after tissue that appeared salvageable declares itself as necrotic or chronically infected. The latter scenario is more challenging for clinicians and patients, as it follows an intervention intended to preserve the digit. Delayed amputation after a technically successful escharotomy raises several questions, including whether it reflects progression of the original thermal injury, microvascular thrombosis not relieved by decompression, or underlying mechanisms of injury.

Electrical burns, for example, cause deep, often noncontiguous tissue destruction that cannot be judged from the cutaneous appearance, and they have long been associated with high amputation rates in the upper extremity. Alternatively, delayed amputation may reflect an incomplete or delayed escharotomy, inadequate postoperative perfusion monitoring, or other deficiencies in the early care process. These explanations have different clinical implications, and distinguishing between them is crucial for improving patient outcomes. If late amputation is mainly a consequence of injury depth and mechanism, it represents a limit of current therapy that patients and families should be counseled about. If it reflects remediable process failures, it identifies targets for quality improvement.

The literature on outcomes after hand escharotomy is sparse and largely descriptive, with most published series addressing the technique or indications rather than functional results. Few studies have followed patients who have undergone upper-extremity or hand escharotomy to determine the frequency of delayed amputation or the patient and injury characteristics associated with this outcome. Existing reports rarely separate amputations performed at presentation from those performed after a period of attempted salvage, making it difficult to estimate the rate of treatment failure after a decompressive procedure. Consequently, clinicians lack realistic benchmarks for counseling patients and auditing their own results, and it remains unclear whether demographic factors, burn size, or burn depth and mechanism identify patients at higher risk.

A more nuanced understanding of the outcomes after hand escharotomy is essential for improving patient care and informing clinical decision-making. By examining the factors that contribute to delayed amputation and the effectiveness of current treatment protocols, clinicians can refine their approach to burn care and develop more effective strategies for preserving hand function and reducing the risk of long-term disability. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay between injury, treatment, and outcome is necessary to optimize the management of hand burns and improve the quality of life for patients affected by these devastating injuries. The current study seeks to address a significant knowledge gap in the field of burn care by investigating the frequency of delayed digital amputation among patients who have undergone upper-extremity and hand escharotomy. To achieve this, we conducted a retrospective review of the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center Patient Registry, spanning a six-year period from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2005. Our primary objective was to determine the incidence of delayed digital amputation in burned hands where neurovascular compromise had been identified and escharotomy performed. Additionally, we aimed to examine whether patient demographics, such as age and sex, or total body surface area (TBSA) burned, were associated with subsequent amputation, and to characterize the depth and mechanism of the burns affecting the hands.

Our hypothesis was that amputation following escharotomy would be relatively rare and that it would be more closely related to the depth and mechanism of injury rather than patient demographics or burn size. This study makes three key contributions to the existing literature. Firstly, it provides an estimate of the rate of delayed amputation after hand escharotomy from a single regional burn center with a well-defined registry population, a quantity that has not been well documented in previous studies. Secondly, it distinguishes between failures of salvage and primary amputation, allowing for a more nuanced discussion of the limitations of decompressive therapy. Thirdly, it relates these outcomes to the principles of acute hand burn care, including splinting, timely and complete escharotomy, early excision and grafting, and occupational therapy, and considers the circumstances under which amputation may remain necessary despite adherence to these principles.

The study was designed as a retrospective, single-center cohort study at the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center, a referral facility for acute burn care serving a mixed urban and rural catchment area. Data were obtained from the center's prospectively maintained Patient Registry, which records demographic, injury-related, operative, and outcome data for all admissions. The study period spanned from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2005, and was designed and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for cohort studies. The institutional review board approved the protocol and waived the requirement for individual informed consent due to the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data for analysis.

The study population consisted of all patients admitted with an acute burn injury who underwent escharotomy of the upper extremity and hand during the study period. Patients were included if they had a thermal, electrical, chemical, or contact burn of one or both upper extremities, underwent escharotomy of the hand, including the digits, as documented in the operative record, and had sufficient documentation of the hospital course and follow-up to determine the final disposition of each digit. Patients who underwent escharotomy of the forearm or upper arm alone, without involvement of the hand, were excluded from the primary analysis. We also excluded patients who had traumatic amputations at presentation and those whose digits were judged nonviable and amputated at the first operative procedure. This approach ensured that the study addressed only digits considered salvageable at the time of escharotomy. Furthermore, patients who died before definitive assessment of digital viability were excluded, as the outcome of interest could not be established in these cases. The hand was the primary unit of analysis, and patients with bilateral involvement contributed two hands to the study.

Clinical management of the patients followed the center's standard burn care protocol throughout the study period. All patients were resuscitated according to Advanced Burn Life Support principles, with fluid volumes titrated to hourly urine output. Burn size, expressed as percentage total body surface area (TBSA), was estimated on admission using the Lund and Browder chart and revised after initial debridement when indicated. Burn depth was classified clinically as superficial, partial-thickness, or full-thickness, and electrical injuries were identified from the mechanism recorded at admission and analyzed as a separate category due to their distinct pattern of deep tissue injury. Affected extremities were elevated above heart level and splinted in the intrinsic-plus (safe) position, unless the injury required a different position. Neurovascular status of every burned extremity was assessed at admission and then hourly during the first 24 to 48 hours, a period that coincides with maximal edema formation during resuscitation.

The assessment included inspection of color and tissue turgor, capillary refill, subjective report of pain and paresthesia, pain with passive stretch of the digits, and pulsatile Doppler flow in the palmar and digital arches. Escharotomy was undertaken when circumferential or near-circumferential full-thickness or deep partial-thickness burns were accompanied by absent or diminishing Doppler signals, progressive loss of sensation, pallor or cyanosis, or a tense, noncompliant appearance of the digits or hand, in keeping with accepted indications. The escharotomy technique involved making incisions with a scalpel or electrocautery through the eschar and into the subcutaneous fat, carried to the depth at which the underlying tissue was able to expand. Digital escharotomies were placed on the midaxial line, on the ulnar side of the thumb and index finger and on the radial side of the middle, ring, and little fingers, to avoid scarring on the primary contact surfaces. Dorsal hand escharotomies were made in the second and fourth intermetacarpal spaces to release the interosseous compartments, and extension across the wrist, forearm, and upper arm was performed when circumferential involvement required it. Carpal tunnel release was added when median nerve compromise was suspected.

Complete release was defined as extension of the incisions across the entire length of constricting eschar, with documented restoration of Doppler signals or improvement in perfusion after the procedure. The date and time of escharotomy relative to injury, and the extent of release, were abstracted from the operative notes. Because intrinsic muscle ischemia can occur despite adequate skin release, the operative notes were also reviewed for any additional fasciotomy. After escharotomy, wounds were dressed with topical antimicrobial agents, and the patients received standard postoperative care, including pain management, wound care, and rehabilitation. The outcomes of interest, including delayed digital amputation, were determined through review of the medical records and follow-up data. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the management of acute hand burns and the factors associated with delayed digital amputation, highlighting the importance of timely and complete escharotomy, as well as the need for careful consideration of the circumstances under which amputation may be necessary despite optimal care. The management of severe hand burns often necessitates a multidisciplinary approach, incorporating surgical interventions, such as escharotomy and grafting, alongside occupational therapy to optimize outcomes. In our study, patients who underwent escharotomy for hand burns were typically treated with early tangential or fascial excision and autografting, once their physiological condition allowed. This was complemented by occupational therapy consultations, which focused on custom splinting and the initiation of active and passive range-of-motion exercises to prevent contractures and promote healing. For digits with progressive demarcation or necrosis, a watchful waiting approach was adopted until the line of demarcation became clear, at which point elective amputation was performed at the level of viable tissue to prevent further complications.

To better understand the factors influencing outcomes in these patients, we undertook a retrospective review of our institutional registry and medical records. A single reviewer extracted data using a standardized form, which was then verified by a second reviewer to ensure accuracy. The variables collected included demographic information (age, sex), details of the burn injury (mechanism, percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) burned, depth of hand burn), the presence of inhalation injury, laterality, time from injury to escharotomy, extent of escharotomy, timing of excision and grafting, and length of hospital stay. For each hand, we noted whether neurovascular compromise was documented before escharotomy, whether perfusion was restored post-escharotomy, and whether any digit required amputation.

The primary outcome of interest was the rate of delayed amputation of one or more digits in hands that had undergone escharotomy, where the digit was initially judged to be salvageable. Delayed amputation was defined as any digital amputation performed after the initial escharotomy, attributable to subsequent necrosis as documented in operative and pathology records. The amputation rate was calculated as the number of hands requiring delayed amputation divided by the total number of hands that underwent escharotomy. Secondary outcomes included the number and level of digits amputated, as well as the association between amputation and various factors such as burn depth, burn mechanism, TBSA, age, and sex.

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software. Continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations or medians with ranges, depending on their distribution. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Comparisons between patients who did and did not require delayed amputation were made using the Student t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and the Fisher exact test for categorical variables, given the anticipated small number of events. Additionally, point-biserial correlation coefficients were used to examine the associations between TBSA, age, and the likelihood of amputation. Because hands from the same patient are not statistically independent, comparisons were repeated at the patient level, considering a patient to have had an amputation if either hand was affected. Due to the limited number of outcome events, a multivariable regression model was not developed, and the analysis was thus descriptive and hypothesis-generating. All tests were two-tailed, with a P value less than 0.05 considered statistically significant.

The registry search identified 34 patients who underwent upper extremity or hand escharotomy between 2000 and 2005, all of whom met the inclusion criteria. These patients had a total of 57 burned hands, with 23 patients (68%) having bilateral hand involvement and 11 (32%) having unilateral involvement. The cohort consisted of 24 men (71%) and 10 women (29%), with a mean age of 41.2 years (SD 16.8, range 19–78). Four patients were older than 65 years. The mean TBSA burned was 28.4% (SD 17.9, median 24%, range 4%–75%), with 11 patients (32%) having a TBSA burned greater than 40%, and 9 patients (26%) suffering from an inhalation injury. Flame burns were the most common mechanism of injury, affecting 18 patients (53%), followed by electrical injury in 6 patients (18%), scald in 5 (15%), contact burn in 3 (9%), and chemical burn in 2 (6%). Notably, the 6 patients with electrical injury accounted for 8 of the 57 hands (14%), with the remaining 49 hands (86%) resulting from thermal or chemical injuries.

Burn depth was assessed from operative and clinical documentation for each hand, revealing that 21 hands (37%) had full-thickness injury involving at least part of the dorsal hand or digits, while 36 hands (63%) had deep partial-thickness injury. Circumferential or near-circumferential digital involvement was documented in 31 hands (54%), consistent with earlier series where escharotomy was typically reserved for deep, circumferential injuries with evidence of impaired perfusion.

All 57 hands underwent escharotomy due to clinical neurovascular compromise, as indicated by loss or diminution of Doppler signals in the digital arteries (47 hands, 82%), pallor or delayed capillary refill (38 hands, 67%), and tense swelling with progressive paresthesias in the 19 patients (56%) who were awake and able to cooperate with examination. Forearm or carpal tunnel decompression was performed in 41 hands (72%) in addition to hand and digital incisions, with dorsal interosseous compartment release in 29 hands (51%) and digital escharotomies in 52 hands (91%). The mean number of digits per hand that underwent escharotomy was 3.6 (range 1–5). The median time from injury to escharotomy was 4.0 hours (interquartile range 2.5–8.0, range 1–18 hours), with 49 hands (86%) decompressed within 8 hours of injury. Thirty-one patients (91%) were treated at or transferred directly to the burn center before escharotomy, while 3 patients (9%) underwent the procedure at a referring facility. Restoration of Doppler signals or capillary refill was documented immediately after release in 54 of 57 hands (95%), with the 3 hands without immediate reperfusion all belonging to patients with electrical injury, each of whom subsequently required amputation.

In terms of acute management, early splinting in the intrinsic-plus position was documented for 52 hands (91%), generally within 24 hours of admission. Occupational therapy consultation occurred a median of 1 day after admission (range 0–4). Tangential or fascial excision and autografting of the hand were performed at a median of 5 days after injury (range 2–14) in 49 hands (86%), with 41 hands (72%) excised within the first 7 days. The remaining 8 hands (14%) either healed without operative intervention, were managed nonoperatively, or underwent excision after the acute care period. Split-thickness skin grafts were used in the majority of cases for wound closure.

Overall, our study highlights the importance of prompt and aggressive management of severe hand burns, including early escharotomy and grafting, alongside meticulous wound care and occupational therapy. The findings also underscore the challenges posed by electrical injuries, which were associated with a higher risk of amputation despite timely intervention. Further research is needed to optimize outcomes for these complex injuries, potentially through the development of more sophisticated predictive models and tailored treatment protocols. The management of burned hands poses significant challenges, and the decision to perform escharotomy is often critical in determining outcomes. In our study, 57 hands in 34 patients underwent escharotomy, and while this procedure is generally regarded as a limb- and digit-salvage intervention, our findings suggest that it does not guarantee the survival of every digit. Notably, 6 hands (approximately 10%) ultimately required delayed digital amputation, despite timely recognition of neurovascular compromise and technically adequate escharotomy. This outcome highlights the importance of considering the depth and mechanism of the original injury, as these factors appear to influence the effectiveness of decompression.

The hands that required amputation belonged to 5 patients, with one patient undergoing bilateral amputations. A total of 11 digits were amputated, with a median of 2 digits per affected hand. The amputations were performed at varying levels, including the proximal interphalangeal joint, proximal phalanx, and ray resection of the small finger. In each case, the digit had initially appeared salvageable, with return of perfusion after escharotomy, but subsequently progressed to dry gangrene or deep infection with exposed, nonviable bone or joint. The median time to amputation was 19 days after injury, underscoring the need for close monitoring and prompt intervention in the management of burned hands.

In contrast, 51 hands (89.5%) maintained all digits through the end of follow-up, which had a median duration of 14 months. The hands that underwent amputation required a median of 2 additional operations beyond the amputation procedure, compared with 1 additional operation in hands that did not require amputation. To better understand the factors associated with amputation, we compared the characteristics of patients with and without amputation. Our analysis revealed that mean total body surface area (TBSA) burned was similar between the two groups, with 31.2% (SD 20.1) in patients who required amputation and 28.0% (SD 17.8) in those who did not (p = 0.71). Similarly, mean age was 44.6 years (SD 15.3) for the amputation group and 40.7 years (SD 17.1) for the remainder (p = 0.62).

We also examined the relationship between amputation and other factors, including inhalation injury, TBSA greater than 40%, and time to escharotomy. However, none of these variables were significantly associated with amputation. In contrast, burn depth and mechanism showed clear associations with amputation. All 6 amputated hands (100%) had full-thickness injury, compared with 15 of 51 preserved hands (29.4%). This translates to an amputation rate of 28.6% (6 of 21) among hands with full-thickness burns and 0% (0 of 36) among hands with deep partial-thickness burns (Fisher exact p = 0.002). Additionally, electrical mechanism was associated with amputation, with 3 of 8 electrically injured hands (37.5%) requiring amputation, compared with 3 of 49 hands (6.1%) with thermal or chemical injury (p = 0.03).

The association between electrical injury and amputation is biologically plausible, as current passing through tissues can cause deep, progressive tissue necrosis that exceeds what is evident on initial examination. This is consistent with the established observation that conduction injury produces severe tissue damage that can lead to delayed amputation. In our series, the 3 electrical cases were the 3 hands in which perfusion did not return after release, and all involved high-voltage exposure (greater than 1,000 V) with deep muscle injury evident at exploration. The remaining 3 amputated hands, from 2 patients, resulted from flame injury with full-thickness circumferential digital burns.

To assess functional outcomes in preserved hands, we reviewed occupational therapy documentation for 44 of the 51 hands with all digits preserved. Median total active motion of the digits at last evaluation was 78% of the expected normal value, with 36 of 44 hands (82%) achieving return to independent performance of basic activities of daily living. However, 9 hands (20%) required secondary reconstruction, including contracture release and web-space revision. Notably, hands treated with excision and grafting within 7 days had better median total active motion than those excised later, although this comparison was descriptive and not adjusted for burn depth.

Our findings refine the traditional view of escharotomy as a definitive limb- and digit-salvage procedure. While decompression is necessary and often prevents ischemic loss, it does not guarantee the survival of every digit. The depth and mechanism of the original injury appear to set a ceiling on what decompression can achieve. In our cohort, amputation after an initially successful escharotomy was associated with full-thickness and electrical burns, whereas TBSA, age, and sex showed no relationship to amputation. The lack of association with TBSA may seem counterintuitive, as large burns can generate greater systemic edema and resuscitation requirements, both of which raise the risk of extremity compartment syndrome. However, our study population was selected on the basis of having already required escharotomy, and within such a population, the main determinant of subsequent digital viability is probably local tissue injury, such as circumferential full-thickness involvement, thrombosis of the digital vessels, and direct thermal or electrical damage to deep structures, rather than the extent of injury elsewhere.

In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of considering the depth and mechanism of the original injury in the management of burned hands. While escharotomy is a critical intervention in preventing ischemic loss, it does not guarantee the survival of every digit. The association between electrical injury and amputation is biologically plausible, and our findings suggest that this mechanism of injury may be a key factor in determining outcomes. Further research is needed to better understand the factors that influence digital viability and to develop strategies for improving outcomes in patients with burned hands.

Social Prescribing (SP) has emerged as a vital service in primary care, where patients with non-clinical needs are referred to local services and activities provided by the third sector, encompassing community, voluntary, and social enterprise organizations. The fundamental aim of SP is to foster partnership working between the health and social sectors, thereby addressing the broader determinants of health, such as poverty, housing, and social isolation, which often fall outside the realm of traditional medical interventions. By adopting this approach, SP seeks to enhance the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities, particularly those with complex needs and multiple long-term conditions.

The concept of SP has gained significant traction in recent years, with a growing recognition of its potential to reduce health inequalities, improve patient outcomes, and alleviate pressure on healthcare services. In the UK, for instance, the National Health Service (NHS) has committed to implementing SP services as part of its broader strategy to promote integrated care and community-based services. Similarly, in countries such as the US and Australia, SP-like initiatives are being implemented to address the social determinants of health and promote more holistic approaches to healthcare. Despite this growing interest, however, the evidence base supporting the implementation and delivery of SP services remains weak. Previous studies have highlighted the complexity of SP services, which often involve multiple stakeholders, organizations, and sectors, and require careful navigation and coordination to ensure effective referrals and support.

The complexity of SP services is multifaceted, involving not only the coordination of multiple stakeholders but also the need to navigate diverse organizational and sectoral boundaries. Effective implementation and delivery of SP services, therefore, depend on a deep understanding of the facilitators and barriers that influence their success. However, there is a significant gap in knowledge regarding the specific factors that facilitate or hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, particularly in general practice settings. This gap is significant, as it hinders the development of effective SP services that can meet the complex needs of patients and communities. Moreover, the lack of evidence on the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery limits the ability of commissioners, managers, and providers to design and deliver high-quality services that can promote partnership working between the health and social sectors.

The research question guiding this systematic review – What are the facilitators and barriers of implementing and delivering Social Prescribing services in general practice settings involving a navigator? – is crucial in providing insights into the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services. Answering this question can inform the development of effective strategies to overcome the challenges associated with the implementation and delivery of SP services. This review contributes to the existing literature on SP services in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery, which can inform the development of effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors. Secondly, it identifies the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services, which can help commissioners, managers, and providers design and deliver high-quality services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities. Finally, it highlights the need for more high-quality research on SP services, particularly in general practice settings, to address the weak evidence base and promote more effective and sustainable services.

The findings of this review have important implications for policy and practice developments. For example, they can help commissioners and managers develop effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors and design high-quality SP services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities. Additionally, they can inform the development of training and support programs for navigators and other healthcare professionals involved in SP services, enhancing their skills and knowledge in promoting partnership working and addressing the social determinants of health. Overall, this review aims to contribute to the growing body of research on SP services and promote more effective and sustainable services that can improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities.

The systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A comprehensive search strategy was developed to identify studies that reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services. The search strategy involved a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to Social Prescribing, primary care, and the third sector, and was designed to capture studies that evaluated the implementation and delivery of SP services, including those that involved a navigator or link worker. Eleven databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus, were searched in June and July 2016.

In addition to the database searches, the grey literature was searched using the Google search engine and the websites of relevant organizations, such as the National Health Service (NHS) and the King's Fund. The reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also searched to identify additional studies. The study selection process involved two stages. In the first stage, the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies were screened against the inclusion criteria by one reviewer. Studies that clearly did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded at this stage. The full search strategy and inclusion criteria are detailed in the supplementary material, providing transparency and facilitating replication of the review.

Studies were included if they reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services, were written in English, and were published in a peer-reviewed journal or as a report. There were no date restrictions applied to the search, ensuring that all relevant studies, regardless of publication date, were considered for inclusion. The inclusion of studies published in peer-reviewed journals or as reports ensured that only high-quality, rigorously peer-reviewed research was included in the review. The systematic review methodology employed in this study provides a robust and transparent approach to identifying, evaluating, and synthesizing the existing evidence on the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery. By shedding light on the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services, this review aims to inform the development of effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors and improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities. The initial stage of our systematic review involved screening titles and abstracts against a set of predefined inclusion criteria, with those that failed to meet these criteria being excluded from further consideration. Following this, the full texts of the remaining studies were assessed by two reviewers (KW and JB) to determine their eligibility for inclusion. Any disagreements that arose between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus, ensuring that the study selection process was both rigorous and transparent. To facilitate this process, we utilized a PRISMA flow diagram, as recommended by Moher et al. (2009), to document the various stages of the review.

To evaluate the quality of the included studies, we employed the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) Version 2011, developed by Pluye et al. (2011). This tool is specifically designed to assess the methodological quality of studies that utilize mixed methods, quantitative, or qualitative designs. The MMAT evaluates studies based on four key criteria: the clarity of the research question, the appropriateness of the study design, the adequacy of the sampling strategy, and the quality of the data analysis. Each study was evaluated by two reviewers (KW and JB), with any disagreements being resolved through discussion and consensus.

The findings of the included studies were synthesized using a narrative approach, incorporating thematic analysis as described by Thomas and Harden (2008). This involved identifying, coding, and categorizing the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services reported in the included studies. The codes and themes were developed inductively from the data, with the analysis being iterative and recursive. The resulting narrative summary provided a comprehensive overview of the range of facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services.

To extract data from the included studies, we developed a data extraction form based on the research question and inclusion criteria. One reviewer (KW) conducted the data extraction, with a second reviewer (JB) checking the extracted data for accuracy and completeness. We also conducted a statistical analysis, using descriptive statistics such as frequencies and percentages to describe the study characteristics and the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. This analysis was performed using SPSS Version 22 (IBM Corp, 2013).

Our systematic review identified eight studies that met the inclusion criteria, all of which were published in English between 2015 and 2017. These studies were conducted in the United Kingdom (n = 7) and Australia (n = 1), with the majority (n = 6) employing a qualitative design.
