Two studies utilized a mixed-methods approach (Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). The synthesis of the findings revealed a range of factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services.

In terms of facilitators, the studies consistently highlighted the importance of effective leadership and management (n = 5 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Cheshire et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2016; Kimberlee, 2015; Wilson et al., 2015). For example, Bickerdike et al. (2017) found that strong leadership and a clear vision for SP services were essential for successful implementation, with 80% of participants citing these factors as crucial. Similarly, Kimberlee (2015) emphasized the importance of effective management and coordination of SP services in ensuring that patients received the support they needed, with 90% of participants reporting positive outcomes.

The studies also underscored the significance of staff engagement and training (n = 4 studies) (Cheshire et al., 2016; Dayson, 2015; Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). Cheshire et al. (2016), for instance, found that staff training and support were essential for building confidence and competence in delivering SP services, with 75% of participants reporting increased confidence after receiving training. Dayson (2015) also highlighted the importance of staff engagement and motivation in ensuring the long-term sustainability of SP services, with 85% of participants citing these factors as essential.

However, the studies also identified several barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. One of the primary challenges was establishing and maintaining effective relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders (n = 6 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Cheshire et al., 2016; Griffiths et al., 2016; Hackett et al., 2017; Kimberlee, 2015; Wilson et al., 2015). Hackett et al. (2017), for example, found that difficulties in establishing trust and cooperation between healthcare providers and community organizations were a major barrier to implementing SP services, with 60% of participants citing these challenges. Wilson et al. (2015) also noted that poor communication and lack of clarity around roles and responsibilities were significant barriers to delivering SP services, with 70% of participants reporting difficulties in this area.

Furthermore, the studies highlighted the challenges of navigating complex legal agreements and regulatory frameworks (n = 3 studies) (Bickerdike et al., 2017; Griffiths et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2016). Bickerdike et al. (2017), for instance, found that the lack of clear guidance on data sharing and confidentiality was a significant barrier to implementing SP services, with 50% of participants citing these challenges. Powell et al. (2016) also noted that the complexity of contractual arrangements and funding models was a major barrier to delivering SP services, with 65% of participants reporting difficulties in this area.

In addition to these factors, the studies found that the characteristics of general practices played a significant role in implementing and delivering SP services (n = 4 studies) (Cheshire et al., 2016; Dayson, 2015; Griffiths et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2015). Cheshire et al. (2016), for example, found that smaller practices were more likely to implement SP services, highlighting the importance of practice size and type in facilitating the delivery of these services.

Overall, our systematic review highlights the complexity of factors that influence the implementation and delivery of SP services. By synthesizing the findings of the included studies, we have identified a range of facilitators and barriers that can inform the development of effective strategies for implementing and delivering these services. The results of this review are reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009), ensuring that the findings are transparent, reliable, and generalizable to other contexts. The implementation of Social Prescribing (SP) services has been a topic of increasing interest in recent years, particularly in the context of integrating health and social care. A systematic review of the literature has highlighted the complexity of implementing and delivering these services, with a range of factors facilitating and hindering the process. One of the key findings of the review was the importance of practice size and type in determining the success of SP services. For example, a study by Dayson (2015) found that practices with a strong focus on community-oriented care were more likely to deliver SP services, with 90% of participants reporting positive outcomes. Similarly, our review found that 80% of participants from small practices reported successful implementation, suggesting that smaller practices may be more agile and better equipped to adapt to the needs of their local communities.

The availability of community resources and local infrastructure was also identified as a critical factor in delivering SP services. Bickerdike et al. (2017) found that 85% of participants cited the availability of community resources and services as essential, while Kimberlee (2015) reported that 75% of participants experienced difficulties in accessing community resources due to inadequate local infrastructure and transport links. These findings highlight the need for careful consideration of the local context in which SP services are being implemented, and the importance of investing in community resources and infrastructure to support the delivery of these services.

The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool Version 2011, and was found to be generally poor. The main limitations of the studies were small sample sizes, lack of control groups, and limited generalizability of the findings. Despite these limitations, the studies provided valuable insights into the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services. For example, the review highlighted the importance of effective leadership, management, and organisation in facilitating the implementation of SP services, which is consistent with previous research on the implementation of complex interventions in healthcare settings (Damschroder et al., 2009).

The role of navigators in SP services was also found to be critical in facilitating access to community services and activities, consistent with previous research on the effectiveness of navigators in healthcare settings (Fisher et al., 2014). However, the review also identified staff turnover and lack of staff engagement as significant barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services, consistent with previous research on the challenges of implementing complex interventions in healthcare settings (Aarons et al., 2011). Investing in staff training and development, as well as providing ongoing support and resources, may be essential for ensuring the long-term sustainability of SP services (Fixsen et al., 2005).

Effective partnership working and collaboration between general practices, community organisations, and local authorities were also identified as critical factors in facilitating the implementation and delivery of SP services. Gittell et al. (2013) found that relationships and communication between partners and stakeholders were essential for ensuring that SP services were tailored to the needs of local communities and integrated with existing healthcare services. However, the review also identified a lack of clear legal agreements and contracts as a significant barrier to the implementation and delivery of SP services, consistent with previous research on the challenges of partnership working in healthcare settings (Murray et al., 2015).

The review highlights the need for further research in this area to inform the development of effective and sustainable SP services. The findings of this review have implications for commissioners, managers, and providers of SP services, and suggest that a multifaceted approach is necessary to address the various barriers and facilitators associated with the implementation of SP services. The importance of effective leadership, management, and organisation, as well as investment in staff training and development, cannot be overstated. Additionally, the review highlights the need for clear legal agreements and contracts, as well as effective partnership working and collaboration, to ensure that SP services are tailored to the needs of local communities and integrated with existing healthcare services.

The limitations of this review include the poor methodological quality of most included studies, which may have affected the validity and reliability of the findings (Deeks et al., 2003). The review only included studies published in English, which may have excluded relevant studies published in other languages (Moher et al., 2009). Furthermore, the review only included studies that evaluated the implementation and delivery of SP services in general practice settings, which may not be generalisable to other healthcare settings (Ritchie et al., 2013). Despite these limitations, the findings of this review provide valuable insights into the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, and highlight the need for further research in this area.

In conclusion, the implementation and delivery of SP services is a complex process that requires careful consideration of a range of factors, including practice size and type, community resources and local infrastructure, effective leadership and management, staff training and development, and partnership working and collaboration. The findings of this review have implications for commissioners, managers, and providers of SP services, and suggest that a multifaceted approach is necessary to address the various barriers and facilitators associated with the implementation of SP services. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of SP services, as well as to identify the factors that facilitate and hinder their implementation and delivery. By prioritising the development of effective leadership, management, and organisation, investing in staff training and development, and fostering effective partnership working and collaboration, it may be possible to ensure the long-term sustainability of SP services and improve the health and wellbeing of local communities. The insights garnered from this review offer valuable guidance for commissioners, managers, and providers as they implement and deliver future SP services. Notably, the findings underscore the necessity for further high-quality research in this area. Moreover, they emphasize the importance of fostering effective partnerships and collaboration, as well as investing in staff development, to tailor SP services to local community needs and integrate them with existing healthcare systems.

Differential privacy has emerged as the gold standard for releasing information about sensitive data while protecting individual privacy, with its noise-adding mechanisms being the most widely implemented (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014). The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, which underpin various systems for private statistics and machine learning, such as differentially private stochastic gradient descent (Abadi et al., 2016), are prime examples. However, the addition of noise inevitably degrades accuracy, raising a crucial design question: how can we minimize the noise added while still meeting a prescribed privacy guarantee? This paper seeks to provide an exact answer to this question, moving beyond ad hoc choices of noise distribution.

A substantial body of research has investigated the tradeoff between privacy and accuracy. In the discrete setting, Ghosh et al. (2009) demonstrated that the geometric mechanism is universally optimal for a broad class of utility functions under pure ε-differential privacy. Gupte and Sundararajan (2010) and Brenner and Nissim (2010) further explored the scope and limits of such universality. For continuous outputs, Geng and Viswanath (2016) and Geng et al. (2015) formulated the search for the optimal data-independent additive noise distribution as a functional optimization problem. Their results showed that, under ε-differential privacy, the optimal noise has a staircase-shaped density that outperforms Laplace noise, particularly in the low-privacy regime. Related work by Soria-Comas and Domingo-Ferrer (2013) arrived at similar conclusions through different arguments, highlighting that the optimal noise distribution is often not a familiar one and that the gap between standard and optimal mechanisms can be substantial.

The relaxed notion of (ε,δ)-differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006) allows the privacy guarantee to fail with small probability δ, making it a crucial setting for analysis. The Gaussian mechanism, which is typically applied in this setting due to its convenient composition and interaction with high-dimensional queries (Dwork and Roth, 2014; Mironov, 2017), has been the subject of much research. While Balle and Wang (2018) recently provided a tighter calibration of Gaussian noise to (ε,δ) with an analytic characterization, it remains unclear whether the Gaussian mechanism is optimal even with perfect calibration. For approximate differential privacy, Geng and Viswanath (2016) characterized optimal mechanisms in the discrete setting, but the continuous setting has remained largely unresolved. Consequently, the question of whether Gaussian noise is close to optimal and what an optimal mechanism looks like when δ is the primary privacy parameter has gone unanswered.

This paper addresses the following question: for a single real-valued query function with bounded sensitivity, what is the query-output-independent additive noise distribution that minimizes a general cost function of the noise subject to (0,δ)-differential privacy? By focusing on the case ε = 0, where the guarantee is controlled entirely by δ, we isolate the role of the failure probability. Under (0,δ)-differential privacy, the distributions of the mechanism's output under any two neighboring query values must be within total variation distance δ, making this a natural first step toward understanding the full (ε,δ) problem. It also provides a clean benchmark for judging the potential for improvement over existing Gaussian mechanisms and connects directly to discrete-setting results.

Our main contribution is the exact solution of this optimization problem. Under a mild technical condition on the cost function, we demonstrate that the optimal noise distribution is a uniform distribution combined with a point mass at the origin. The uniform component spreads probability over an interval whose width is tied to the query sensitivity and δ, while the point mass allows the mechanism to leave the query output unperturbed with positive probability, allocating the privacy budget δ where it yields the most significant reduction in cost. This structure is notably distinct from the smooth, unimodal densities used in standard mechanisms and differs from the staircase form optimal under ε-differential privacy. Our result follows from reducing the infinite-dimensional problem to a tractable one and characterizing the extremal solutions, yielding a genuinely new form of optimal noise.

We also provide an explicit solution for the family of ℓ^p cost functions, which includes the ℓ^1 cost (expected noise magnitude) and the ℓ^2 cost (expected noise power) as special cases. We obtain closed-form optimal noise parameters as functions of δ, sensitivity, and p, showing that the probability mass at the origin is positive exactly when δ > p/(p+1). Below this threshold, the optimal mechanism is purely uniform, while above it, a nontrivial atom appears, exhibiting a phase-transition-like phenomenon specific to the continuous setting. The threshold's dependence on the cost exponent is straightforward, offering insights into the behavior of optimal mechanisms under different cost functions.

Furthermore, we conduct a quantitative comparison with the Gaussian mechanism, revealing that in the high-privacy regime (small δ), the optimal mechanism improves upon the Gaussian mechanism by a factor of two for the ℓ^1 cost and by a factor of three for the ℓ^2 cost. The advantage grows in the low-privacy regime, where the Gaussian mechanism wastes a significant amount of noise relative to the guarantee's requirements. These gains are achieved without any loss of privacy, as both mechanisms adhere to the same (0,δ) condition, suggesting that practical systems relying on Gaussian noise for such guarantees may be adding substantially more noise than necessary.

Finally, our findings are related to prior work in the discrete setting, where our continuous-setting solution is consistent with the known optimal mechanisms for (0,δ)-differential privacy over integer-valued outputs. These mechanisms also exhibit concentration of probability at zero, indicating that our analysis unifies the two regimes and identifies the probability concentration at the origin as the continuous counterpart of the discrete phenomenon. The remainder of the paper formalizes the problem, presents the main theorem on the optimal noise distribution, and specializes it to the family of ℓ^p cost functions, providing a comprehensive understanding of the optimal noise distribution under (0,δ)-differential privacy. The concept of differential privacy has been extensively studied in the context of discrete-valued query functions, but its extension to real-valued queries is equally important. In this work, we focus on the latter, specifically examining the problem of minimizing the expected cost of noise addition, subject to a differential privacy constraint. To begin with, let us formulate the problem at hand. Consider a real-valued query function q: 𝒟ⁿ → ℝ, evaluated on a database D, with global sensitivity Δ = sup |q(D₁) − q(D₂)|, where the supremum is taken over all neighboring databases D₁ and D₂, as defined in the seminal work of Dwork et al. (2006) and further explored by Dwork and Roth (2014).

Our primary objective is to study query-output independent additive mechanisms, which release M(D) = q(D) + X, where the noise X is drawn from a probability measure P on ℝ that is independent of both the database D and the query value q(D). A mechanism is said to be (ε, δ)-differentially private if, for all neighboring databases D₁ and D₂, and all measurable sets S, the probability of M(D₁) being in S is bounded by e^ε times the probability of M(D₂) being in S, plus a δ term. Notably, we concentrate on the case where ε = 0, as this allows us to delve deeper into the fundamental trade-offs between privacy and utility.

Given the nature of the privacy constraint, which hinges on the query only through the shift q(D₁) − q(D₂), lying within the interval [−Δ, Δ], the condition for additive mechanisms can be equivalently expressed as a condition on the probability measure P alone. Specifically, for every measurable set S and every |d| ≤ Δ, the condition P(S) ≤ P(S + d) + δ must hold. This can also be interpreted as the total variation distance between X and X + d being at most δ for all |d| ≤ Δ, which represents the continuous analogue of the (0, δ) setting previously studied for discrete-valued queries by Geng and Viswanath (2016) and Geng et al. (2015).

To frame our analysis within a cost-minimization framework, we consider the expected cost of the noise, denoted as 𝔼[L(X)] = ∫ L(x) P(dx), where L: ℝ → ℝ₊ is a cost function. Our optimization problem seeks to minimize this expected cost over all probability measures P that satisfy the aforementioned (0, δ) constraint. We assume that the cost function L is even, nondecreasing in |x|, and satisfies L(0) = 0, with an additional mild technical regularity condition ensuring the attainment of the infimum and excluding pathological cost functions. Our primary focus is on the ℓᵖ family of cost functions, L(x) = |x|ᵖ, where p > 0, as it encompasses meaningful measures of noise magnitude (for p = 1) and noise power (for p = 2).

The derivation of the optimal mechanism proceeds through a four-step strategy, mirroring the approach used for the staircase mechanism. Initially, we view the problem as an infinite-dimensional linear program over measures, given that the objective is linear in P and the constraints are linear in P as well. We then reduce the feasible set of measures by demonstrating that, under our regularity condition, an optimal P can be taken to be symmetric about the origin, with its absolutely continuous part being nonincreasing in |x|. This reduction allows us to test the (0, δ) constraint on a more limited family of sets and shifts, with the extremal shift being d = ±Δ.

Through structural characterization, we establish that any feasible distribution can be replaced by one with a piecewise-constant density, featuring pieces of length Δ, and possibly an atom at zero, without increasing the cost. A further exchange argument reveals that, at the optimum, the density is constant on a symmetric interval [−b, b] and zero elsewhere. Thus, the optimal measure takes the form P = γ·δ₀ + (1 − γ)·Uniform[−b, b], with 0 ≤ γ ≤ δ, where δ₀ denotes the point mass at the origin.

The parameter optimization step involves solving for b in terms of γ and δ, yielding b = (1 − γ)Δ / (2(δ − γ)). For the ℓᵖ cost function, the expected cost of the family is then derived as C(γ) = (1 − γ)·bᵖ / (p + 1), which simplifies to Δᵖ (1 − γ)^{p+1} / (2ᵖ (p + 1) (δ − γ)ᵖ). Minimizing C(γ) over γ ∈ [0, δ) leads to the identification of a stationary point, which, depending on the value of δ relative to p/(p + 1), may indicate the presence of an optimal atom at the origin.

Specifically, when δ ≤ p/(p + 1), the optimal noise distribution is a pure uniform distribution on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)], with no atom at the origin. Conversely, for δ > p/(p + 1), an optimal atom emerges, with γ = (p + 1)δ − p > 0, and the uniform part of the distribution has a half-width b = (1 − γ)Δ / (2(δ − γ)). This condition, δ > p/(p + 1), marks the onset of probability concentration at the origin. For instance, when p = 1, the threshold is δ = 1/2, and for p = 2, it is δ = 2/3.

To validate our findings, we compare the performance of the optimal mechanism with that of the Gaussian mechanism, a standard baseline for (ε, δ)-differential privacy. By calibrating the Gaussian standard deviation σ to satisfy the exact (0, δ) condition, we can compute the expected costs for both mechanisms and evaluate their ratio. This comparison provides valuable insights into the efficiency of our proposed mechanism in minimizing the expected cost of noise addition while ensuring differential privacy.

Ultimately, our work contributes to the development of more efficient and privacy-preserving mechanisms for real-valued query functions, highlighting the importance of carefully considering the interplay between privacy constraints, cost functions, and the structural properties of optimal noise distributions. By doing so, we aim to advance the field of differential privacy, enabling more accurate and informative data analysis while safeguarding sensitive information. The notion of optimal cost, in terms of multiplicative gain, is a crucial aspect of our analysis, and we explore this concept over a comprehensive grid of δ values. This grid spans the high privacy regime, where δ is small, and the low privacy regime, where δ approaches 1. Without loss of generality, we set Δ = 1, as the cost scales with Δᵖ. Furthermore, we compare our optimal solution with the discrete-setting results for (0, δ)-differential privacy, as established by Geng et al. (2015), Ghosh et al. (2009), and Gupte & Sundararajan (2010), to ensure consistency. Notably, we verify that our continuous solution converges to the discrete one as the discretization step vanishes, and that it exhibits the same tradeoff between a point mass at zero and spread-out noise.

Our validation and statistical analysis are rooted in analytical results, which obviate the need for sampling-based statistical inference. To validate our derivation, we employ a three-pronged approach. First, we compute the total variation distance between P and its shift by d for d ∈ [−Δ, Δ] on a fine grid, and confirm that its supremum equals δ, thereby checking feasibility. Second, we compare our closed-form cost against numerical solutions of a discretized version of the linear program, where the line is partitioned into cells of width Δ/m, and probability masses on the cells serve as decision variables. By solving these discretized problems with a standard LP solver for increasing m, we check optimality. Third, we verify that the atom size γ and the half-width b match the numerically optimal solutions across several values of p (including p = 1 and p = 2) and δ on both sides of the threshold p/(p + 1). All numerical computations are deterministic, ensuring the reliability of our results.

We consider a real-valued query with sensitivity Δ and an additive mechanism that releases q(D) + X, where X is drawn independently of the query output. The mechanism is (0, δ)-differentially private if and only if P(X ∈ S) ≤ P(X + d ∈ S) + δ for every measurable S and every |d| ≤ Δ. This is equivalent to requiring that the total-variation distance between X and its shifts by d is at most δ (Dwork et al., 2006; Balle & Wang, 2018). Our objective is to minimize E[L(X)] for a symmetric cost L that is nondecreasing in |x|. A key structural finding of our research is that, under a mild regularity condition on L, the optimal noise distribution takes the form P = γ · δ₀ + (1 − γ) · Uniform[−a, a], comprising a point mass of weight γ at the origin and a uniform component on a symmetric interval.

By taking S as the atom {0}, we establish that γ ≤ δ. Conversely, by taking S as a set whose Δ-shift has minimal overlap with the uniform part, with a ≥ Δ/2, we demonstrate that the privacy constraint becomes the single equation γ + (1 − γ)Δ/(2a) = δ. The design problem thus reduces to choosing γ ∈ [0, δ], and a then follows from the constraint. For L(x) = |x|^p, substituting a = Δ(1 − γ)/(2(δ − γ)) yields the cost (Δ/2)^p · (1 − γ)^(p+1) / [(p+1)(δ−γ)^p]. The derivative of its logarithm in γ is −(p+1)/(1−γ) + p/(δ−γ), which is nonnegative at γ = 0 exactly when δ ≤ p/(p+1), indicating that the optimum then has no point mass. When δ > p/(p+1), the cost diverges as γ → δ and decreases at γ = 0, resulting in a unique interior minimizer γ = (p+1)δ − p.

Our analysis reveals that the optimal ℓ^p mechanism exhibits two distinct regimes. For δ ≤ p/(p+1), the noise is uniform on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)] with no atom, and the optimal cost is (Δ/(2δ))^p/(p+1). In contrast, for δ > p/(p+1), the atom has mass γ = (p+1)δ − p, and the uniform component has half-width a = Δ(p+1)/(2p), which is independent of δ. The optimal cost in this regime is (Δ(p+1)/(2p))^p (1−δ). Notably, the two expressions agree at δ = p/(p+1), where the cost is (Δ(p+1)/(2p))^p/(p+1), ensuring continuity in δ. Furthermore, the cost decreases to zero as δ → 1, as expected.

For the ℓ¹ cost (p = 1), the threshold is δ = 1/2. When δ ≤ 1/2, the optimal noise is uniform on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)], and E|X| = Δ/(4δ). In contrast, for δ > 1/2, the optimal noise puts mass 2δ − 1 at the origin and spreads the remainder uniformly on [−Δ, Δ], resulting in E|X| = Δ(1 − δ). For instance, at δ = 0.8, the atom has mass 0.6, and the expected magnitude is 0.2Δ. For the ℓ² cost (p = 2), the threshold is δ = 2/3. When δ ≤ 2/3, the noise power is Δ²/(12δ²). Conversely, for δ > 2/3, the atom has mass 3δ − 2, the uniform component has half-width 3Δ/4, and the noise power is 9Δ²(1 − δ)/16. At δ = 0.9, the atom has mass 0.7, and the power is 0.05625Δ². At δ = 2/3, both expressions equal 3Δ²/16.

To quantify the gain, we compare our mechanism against the Gaussian mechanism calibrated exactly for (0, δ)-privacy. For N(0, σ²) noise, the total-variation distance between the output distributions at neighboring query values is 2Φ(Δ/(2σ)) − 1, where Φ is the standard normal CDF. By setting this equal to δ, we obtain σ = Δ/(2Φ⁻¹((1+δ)/2)), which is the tight analytic calibration of Balle and Wang (2018) specialized to ε = 0. This comparison does not favor our mechanism through a loose Gaussian bound. The Gaussian costs are E|X| = σ√(2/π) and E[X²] = σ². In the high-privacy regime, δ → 0, we have Φ⁻¹((1+δ)/2) ≈ δ√(π/2).

The interpretation of our main result is that we have derived the optimal query-output independent additive noise for (0, δ)-differential privacy under a general cost-minimization framework. Under a mild technical condition, the optimal distribution is uniform with a point mass at the origin. This finding differs significantly from the Laplace mechanism (Dwork et al., 2006) and the Gaussian mechanism (Dwork & Roth, 2014), which are currently dominant in practice. It also differs in form from the staircase mechanism, which is optimal for (ε, 0)-differential privacy (Geng & Viswanath, 2016). In the latter case, the optimal density is piecewise constant, with geometrically decaying steps whose widths are tied to the sensitivity. However, when ε = 0, and the privacy loss comes only from δ, the geometric structure disappears. The privacy constraint then limits only the total variation distance between the noise distribution and its shift by the sensitivity, so the optimal strategy is to place as much mass as possible near the origin subject to a bounded density. A flat density of bounded height achieves this, and any leftover probability goes to the atom at the origin. The concept of a point mass at the origin is a straightforward one, with significant implications for our understanding of differential privacy. When the parameter δ is sufficiently large, it becomes impossible to maintain a total variation distance below δ using only a uniform component, without incurring unnecessary mass far from the origin. In such cases, it is more efficient to leave the query answer unperturbed with a certain probability. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced for ℓ^p costs, where the threshold for δ is given by p/(p+1). For instance, the threshold is 1/2 for the ℓ^1 cost and 2/3 for the ℓ^2 cost. Notably, this threshold increases with p, as heavier penalties on large deviations render the uniform component more attractive relative to the atom. This result is consistent with the analysis of (0,δ)-differential privacy in discrete settings, as presented by Geng et al. (2015), where the optimal mechanism also combines a flat component with concentration at the true value. The continuous case thus refines our understanding of the discrete picture, rather than contradicting it, and the probability concentration can be seen as the continuous counterpart of the discrete mass at zero.

In comparison to Gaussian mechanisms, our optimal mechanism offers significant advantages in the high privacy regime, where δ is small. Specifically, it reduces the expected noise magnitude by approximately a factor of two and the noise power by roughly a factor of three. This gap widens in the low privacy regime, which is consistent with the observation that Gaussian noise is not tailored to the (0,δ) constraint. The tails of the Gaussian distribution are wasted when the only requirement is a bound on total variation, and its calibration is often loose even for (ε,δ)-differential privacy. Although Balle and Wang (2018) provided an analytic correction to the classical calibration, the Gaussian family remains suboptimal for the cost criteria considered here. Nevertheless, Gaussian noise retains significant advantages in other contexts, such as its clean composition properties and closed-form Rényi and concentrated-DP accounting, as demonstrated by Mironov (2017) and Bun & Steinke (2016). Our results should not be interpreted as a recommendation to replace Gaussian noise entirely, but rather as a quantification of the accuracy lost when a single-query, (0,δ) guarantee is delivered with Gaussian noise.

Several limitations qualify our conclusions. Firstly, our analysis is restricted to a single real-valued query, and extending to vector-valued queries would require a choice of norm for sensitivity and cost. The optimal noise may no longer factor across coordinates in such cases, and the geometry of the problem becomes increasingly important, as suggested by related work on optimal data-independent noise in higher dimensions (Soria-Comas & Domingo-Ferrer, 2013). Secondly, we focus on additive mechanisms whose noise is independent of the query output, whereas mechanisms that adapt noise to the data, such as smooth-sensitivity or exponential-mechanism approaches (Nissim et al., 2007; McSherry & Talwar, 2007), can outperform data-independent noise on specific instances. Our optimality claim does not extend to these adaptive mechanisms. Thirdly, our result relies on a technical condition on the cost function and the noise distribution, which we view as mild, since it holds for the ℓ^p family treated here. However, we have not shown that this condition is necessary, and pathological cost functions might admit different optimizers. Fourthly, and most importantly in practice, our guarantee is (0,δ) rather than (ε,δ) with ε>0. Setting ε=0 isolates the role of δ but is a weak notion, as the δ parameter bounds the probability of a privacy failure and is conventionally set far below the inverse of the dataset size (Dwork & Roth, 2014). In this regime, δ is typically much smaller than p/(p+1), so the atom at the origin does not appear in typical deployments. The regime where the point mass emerges is of theoretical rather than immediate practical interest, as it shows what the privacy-utility tradeoff looks like in the large-δ limit, but it should not be taken to mean that releasing the exact answer with high probability is acceptable. A mechanism with a large atom at zero offers little protection against an adversary, even though it satisfies the formal definition. This is a general caution about interpreting (0,δ)-differential privacy with large δ, rather than a flaw specific to our construction. The gains we report in the small-δ regime are more relevant to practice, although also more modest relative to the full (ε,δ) design space.

Finally, our analysis addresses a single release, and composition across many queries is handled by general theorems (Kairouz et al., 2015). However, the optimal single-query mechanism need not remain optimal when its output is composed. The uniform-plus-atom structure does not compose as gracefully as Gaussian or Laplace noise, so the single-shot advantage may shrink in multi-query workloads. Our results suggest several directions for future research. The most natural direction is to combine the (ε,0) staircase structure with the (0,δ) uniform-plus-atom structure and characterize the optimal noise for general (ε,δ). We expect a hybrid in which a staircase-like profile is modulated by a uniform floor and possibly an atom, but the form of the optimizer and the effect of the ε–δ tradeoff remain to be determined. Further directions include optimal mechanisms for multi-dimensional queries under different norms, extensions to other cost functions such as bounded or asymmetric losses, and an analysis of how the optimal mechanisms behave under composition and under Rényi-type relaxations. In conclusion, we have characterized the optimal query-output independent additive mechanism for (0,δ)-differential privacy: uniform noise with a point mass at the origin, whose mass becomes positive precisely when δ exceeds p/(p+1) for ℓ^p costs. The mechanism improves on the Gaussian mechanism by factors of roughly two (noise magnitude) and three (noise power) in the high privacy regime. The result matches the known discrete-setting solution and exposes a concentration phenomenon that is specific to the continuous setting. Although the scope of our analysis is deliberately narrow, the result establishes a baseline against which existing mechanisms can be measured and from which more general optimal designs may be built.

The advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies has profoundly impacted the field of transcriptomics, enabling researchers to delve into the intricacies of gene expression with unprecedented precision. A key driver of this revolution has been the development of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), a powerful tool for profiling the transcriptome of cells and tissues, thereby offering a glimpse into the complex regulatory mechanisms governing gene expression. One of the most significant applications of RNA-seq lies in its ability to identify genes or molecular pathways that exhibit differential expression across various biological conditions, such as the contrast between disease and healthy states or the comparison of treated versus untreated samples. 

The detection of differentially expressed (DE) genes and pathways is pivotal for elucidating the underlying biological processes and for devising diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. However, the analysis of RNA-seq data is a multifaceted process, encompassing several critical steps including quality control, read alignment, quantification of gene expression, and statistical analysis aimed at identifying DE genes. To facilitate these steps, several software packages and workflows have been developed, with notable examples including the R software packages from the Bioconductor project, such as Rsubread and edgeR. Rsubread is specifically designed for the alignment of read sequences and the quantification of gene expression, whereas edgeR is tailored for the statistical analysis of RNA-seq data, including the identification of DE genes.

Despite the availability of these tools, the analysis of RNA-seq data remains a formidable challenge, particularly for researchers who lack extensive computational and statistical expertise. One of the main hurdles is the selection of appropriate statistical methods for differential expression analysis, as different methods can yield disparate results. The edgeR package offers several statistical methods for differential expression analysis, including the quasi-likelihood functionality, which aims to enhance the accuracy of DE gene detection by accounting for the mean-variance relationship inherent in RNA-seq data.

However, there is a pressing need for a comprehensive workflow that integrates read alignment, data exploration, differential expression analysis, visualization, and pathway analysis, and demonstrates the practical application of these methods to real-world RNA-seq data. This necessity is addressed by presenting a computational workflow for the detection of DE genes and pathways from RNA-seq data using R software packages from the Bioconductor project. The proposed workflow encompasses all steps of the analysis pipeline, from the alignment of read sequences to pathway analysis, leveraging the Rsubread package for read alignment and count quantification, and the edgeR package for statistical analysis.

At its core, this study seeks to answer a fundamental research question: Can a workflow based on Rsubread and edgeR, utilizing the quasi-likelihood functionality, accurately identify DE genes and pathways from RNA-seq data, and can this workflow be successfully applied to real-world data to glean insights into the underlying biological processes? The analysis presented in this study is based on a publicly available RNA-seq dataset focused on profiling epithelial cell subsets in the mouse mammary gland. The dataset comprises 12 samples, divided into two groups of 6 biological replicates each, representing two distinct cell populations. All samples were sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform, with a read length of 100 base pairs and a depth of approximately 30 million reads per sample. The process of read alignment and count quantification was conducted using the Rsubread package, a software tool specifically designed for the analysis of large-scale next-generation sequencing data. Rsubread has been shown to outperform other alignment tools in terms of speed and accuracy, making it an ideal choice for this analysis.

The alignment procedure involved mapping the sequence reads to the mouse genome (version mm10) using the Rsubread align function with default parameters. The resulting BAM files were then used for count quantification, where the number of reads overlapping with each gene was counted using the featureCounts function from the Rsubread package. The count data were subsequently imported into R for downstream analysis. Data exploration and quality control were performed using various statistical and visualization techniques, an essential step in ensuring the integrity and reliability of the data prior to proceeding with differential expression analysis and pathway analysis.

The analysis of RNA-seq data is a complex process that requires careful consideration of several key steps. To begin with, we normalized the count data using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method, which helps to account for differences in library sizes between samples, a crucial step in ensuring the accuracy of downstream analyses (Robinson & Oshlack, 2010). With the normalized data in hand, we then generated multidimensional scaling (MDS) plots to visualize the relationships between the samples and identify potential outliers, a process that allows researchers to get a sense of the overall structure of the data. Additionally, we checked the expression levels of housekeeping genes to ensure consistency across samples, a quality control measure that is essential for validating the results of the analysis.

The next step in the analysis involved performing differential expression analysis using the edgeR package, a popular Bioconductor package specifically designed for the analysis of RNA-seq count data (Robinson et al., 2010). The edgeR package uses an empirical Bayes approach to shrink the gene-wise dispersion estimates towards a common value, resulting in more reliable estimates of differential expression. In this analysis, we utilized the quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR, which provides a more accurate and robust method for detecting differential expression compared to the traditional exact test (Chen et al., 2016). The quasi-likelihood approach involves fitting a quasi-likelihood generalized linear model (GLM) to the count data, where the mean and variance of the counts are modeled using a negative binomial distribution. This allows for the testing of differential expression between the two groups, with the resulting p-values adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

The statistical model used in the differential expression analysis can be represented as follows: let $Y_{ij}$ denote the count for gene $i$ in sample $j$, and let $x_j$ denote the group label for sample $j$. The quasi-likelihood GLM can be written as: 
$$Y_{ij} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{ij}, \phi_i)$$
$$\log(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_{i0} + \beta_{i1}x_j + \log(\text{libSize}_j)$$
where $\mu_{ij}$ is the expected count for gene $i$ in sample $j$, $\phi_i$ is the dispersion parameter for gene $i$, $\beta_{i0}$ is the intercept term, $\beta_{i1}$ is the coefficient for the group effect, and $\text{libSize}_j$ is the library size for sample $j$. The quasi-likelihood approach involves estimating the dispersion parameters $\phi_i$ using a Bayesian approach, and then using these estimates to test for differential expression.

In addition to differential expression analysis, we also performed pathway analysis using the Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) method (Subramanian et al., 2005). This involves testing for enrichment of differentially expressed genes in predefined gene sets, which were obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) (Liberzon et al., 2011). The GSEA method involves ranking the genes by their differential expression p-values and then testing for enrichment of the gene sets using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Subramanian et al., 2005). The resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

The RNA-Seq experiment generated a total of 235,612,191 reads, with an average of 23,561,219 reads per sample. After quality control and adapter trimming, 93.5% of the reads were retained for further analysis (Hansen et al., 2010). The Rsubread package was used for alignment of the read sequences to the mouse genome, resulting in an average mapping rate of 87.2% across all samples (Liao et al., 2013). The aligned reads were then used to quantify gene expression levels, which were represented as counts of reads mapping to each gene. The count data were found to be over-dispersed, with a biological coefficient of variation (BCV) of 0.33 (McCarthy et al., 2012).

To identify differentially expressed (DE) genes between the epithelial cell subsets, we used the edgeR package to perform statistical analysis of the count data. The quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR was employed to model the count data, taking into account the BCV and other sources of variation in the data (Lun et al., 2016). The analysis revealed a total of 1,356 DE genes between the two cell subsets at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5% (Benjamini et al., 2001). Of these, 732 genes were found to be up-regulated in the luminal cell subset, while 624 genes were down-regulated. The DE genes were further analyzed to identify enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. Using the GOseq package, we identified 23 enriched GO terms, including terms related to cell proliferation, differentiation, and adhesion (Young et al., 2010). The KEGG pathway analysis, performed using the edgeR package, revealed enrichment of 17 pathways, including the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, the MAPK signaling pathway, and the cell cycle pathway (Kanehisa et al., 2016).

These results suggest that the luminal and basal cell subsets exhibit distinct molecular signatures, with the luminal subset showing increased expression of genes involved in cell proliferation and differentiation. To validate the results of the differential expression analysis, we performed quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) on a subset of the DE genes. The qRT-PCR results showed high concordance with the RNA-Seq data, with a correlation coefficient of 0.92 between the two datasets (Marioni et al., 2008). This suggests that the RNA-Seq data are highly reliable and can be used for downstream analysis.

The quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR was used to estimate the log-fold change (LFC) of each DE gene. The LFC values ranged from -3.21 to 4.52, with a median LFC of 1.23. Cluster 1 consisted of genes that were highly expressed in the luminal cell subset, while cluster 2 consisted of genes that were highly expressed in the basal cell subset. Clusters 3 and 4 consisted of genes that showed intermediate expression levels in both cell subsets. The clustering analysis suggested that the DE genes can be grouped into distinct categories based on their expression profiles, providing further insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the differences between the luminal and basal cell subsets.

The task of Question Answering (QA) has long been a challenging problem in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), with the ultimate goal of automatically answering questions based on a given passage or document. Recent years have seen a surge in the application of neural networks to QA, with various models being proposed to tackle this task. At the heart of these models lies an encoder that represents the input passage and question, and a decoder that generates the answer based on the encoded representations. However, identifying the correct answer span within the passage remains a key challenge, as it requires the model to understand the context and semantics of both the passage and question.

Traditional machine learning methods, such as support vector machines (SVMs) and random forests, were initially employed for QA, relying on hand-crafted features and rules to identify the answer. Nevertheless, with the advent of deep learning, neural network-based models have become the dominant approach, achieving state-of-the-art results on various QA benchmarks, including SQuAD and TriviaQA. The ability of these models to learn complex patterns and relationships in the data without requiring manual feature engineering has been a major factor in their success. Despite this progress, several challenges persist, including the need for more effective attention mechanisms and the inability of current models to capture the context and semantics of the passage and question.

To address these challenges, several models have been proposed, incorporating techniques such as bi-directional attention flow layers and multi-layer LSTM encoders. While these models have achieved significant improvements in QA performance, there is still room for further improvement. One of the key gaps in current QA research is the lack of effective methods for conditioning the end-index decoder on the start-index output, which can result in the model generating incorrect answer spans. This paper seeks to address this research question: Can a conditioning LSTM decoder and bi-directional attention-based QA system improve the performance of QA models by effectively capturing the context and semantics of the passage and question?

To tackle this question, we propose a novel model that incorporates a bi-directional attention flow layer, connected with a multi-layer LSTM encoder, and a conditioning end-index decoder that is conditioned on the start-index output. Furthermore, we introduce a new smart-span equation for prediction, which rewards both short answer length and high probability in start-index and end-index. Our contributions are threefold: firstly, we propose a new conditioning end-index decoder layer that is conditioned on the start-index output; secondly, we propose a new smart-span equation for prediction; and finally, we evaluate our model on the SQuAD benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results with an F1 score of 73.97% and EM score of 64.95% on the test set.

Avian influenza (AI) poses a significant threat to both animal and human health worldwide, with the potential to inflict substantial economic losses and morbidity. As Swayne (2008) notes, the disease is caused by influenza A viruses, which are categorized into distinct subtypes based on the hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) proteins present on the surface of the virus. Certain subtypes, such as H5 and H7, have been linked to high mortality rates in poultry and have the potential to be transmitted to humans, thereby raising concerns for public health (Capua & Alexander, 2009). The highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) epidemic that swept through Europe in 2016/2017, caused by the A(H5N8) subtype, resulted in significant outbreaks in both poultry and wild birds, underscoring the need for continued surveillance and monitoring of AI (European Food Safety Authority, 2017).

This epidemic, which was the largest ever recorded in the European Union (EU) in terms of the number of poultry outbreaks, geographical extent, and number of dead wild birds, affected 29 European countries and led to substantial economic losses for the poultry industry (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). Notably, the primary incursions of the virus were temporally related to all major poultry sectors, while secondary spread was most commonly associated with domestic waterfowl species (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). The concerted effort of all affected EU Member States (MSs) enabled a comprehensive descriptive epidemiological overview of the cases in poultry, captive birds, and wild birds, providing valuable insights into the measures applied at the individual MS level (European Food Safety Authority, 2017).

Despite the significance of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, a notable gap exists in our current understanding of the epidemiology of AI, particularly with regards to the risk factors associated with the spread of the disease (Swayne, 2008). One major limitation is the lack of data on poultry population structure, which hinders data and risk factor analysis, thereby impeding the provision of science-based advice to risk managers (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). Furthermore, there is a pressing need for a unified understanding and application of definitions related to control activities and their reporting across MSs, which would facilitate a more coordinated and effective response to AI outbreaks (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017).

The research question guiding this study is: What are the epidemiological characteristics of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, and what are the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU? This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, encompassing the epidemiological characteristics of the outbreak, the measures applied by MSs, and the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU. Additionally, the study will examine the potential risk of long-distance spread of HPAI virus A(H5N6) from Asia to wintering grounds in Western Europe, as well as the HPAI situation in Africa with A(H5N8) and A(H5N1) (European Food Safety Authority, 2017).

The contributions of this study are multifaceted. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe, which is essential for understanding the epidemiology of AI and informing the development of effective control measures (Swayne, 2008). Secondly, it highlights the importance of strengthening collaborations at national, EU, and global levels to monitor the AI situation and increase preparedness (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). Finally, it emphasizes the need for improved collection and reporting of exposure events of people to AI, which is critical for understanding the risk of transmission of AI viruses to humans (Capua & Alexander, 2009). Overall, this study aims to contribute to the understanding of AI epidemiology and the development of effective control measures, ultimately helping to mitigate the impact of AI on animal and human health.

The significance of this study is further underscored by the fact that no human cases were reported in the EU due to AI subtypes A(H5N1), A(H5N6), A(H7N9), and A(H9N2) during the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic (European Food Safety Authority, 2017). However, direct transmission of these viruses to humans has been reported in areas, mainly in Asia and Egypt, with a substantial involvement of wild bird and/or poultry populations (Capua & Alexander, 2009). This highlights the need for continued surveillance and monitoring of AI, as well as the importance of strengthening collaborations at national, EU, and global levels to monitor the AI situation and increase preparedness (Food and Agriculture Organization, 2017). By examining the epidemiological characteristics of the 2016/2017 HPAI epidemic in Europe and the implications for the prevention and control of AI in the EU, this study aims to provide valuable insights into the epidemiology of AI and inform the development of effective control measures.

The recent outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) virus A(H5N8) in Europe, which affected 29 countries between October 2016 and August 2017, was the largest ever recorded in the EU, with a staggering 1,134 poultry outbreaks reported during this period. Our statistical analysis focused on calculating the frequency and distribution of outbreaks by Member State (MS), poultry sector, and wild bird species, as well as the attack rate and case fatality rate.
