Aphasia, a complex and heterogeneous condition characterized by language-cognitive impairments resulting from stroke, has been the subject of extensive research in the fields of neurology, linguistics, and cognitive psychology. The pioneering work of Benson (1979) and Goodglass (1993) laid the foundation for our understanding of this multifaceted disorder. However, despite the significant advances made in recent decades, the diagnostic criteria for aphasia remain somewhat fragmented, with most research focusing primarily on the lesion correlates of language deficits, while paying relatively little attention to the patterns of paraphasias exhibited by individuals with aphasia.

This disparity in research focus has resulted in a limited understanding of the intricate relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their underlying neural bases. To address this knowledge gap, it is essential to consider the complex interplay between language deficits, such as anomia, alexia, and agrammatism, and paraphasias, including semantic, phonological, and neologistic errors. The diagnostic criteria for aphasia typically encompass a combination of these language deficits and paraphasias, yet most studies have investigated the neural correlates of language deficits in isolation, without considering the patterns of paraphasias exhibited by individuals with aphasia.

Recent studies have begun to redress this imbalance by exploring the neural correlates of specific types of paraphasias, such as semantic and phonological errors. For example, Jefferies and Lambon Ralph (2006) and Schwartz et al. (2009) have made significant contributions to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying these types of errors. However, these studies have often relied on experimenter-derived methods to combine across error types, which may not accurately capture the complex patterns of paraphasias exhibited by individuals with aphasia. Furthermore, the use of a priori categories to classify paraphasias may not account for the inherent variability and individual differences in error patterns, as noted by Nickels (2002).

To overcome these limitations, a data-driven approach is necessary to integrate patient impairments and their pattern of errors into a unified model of chronic post-stroke aphasia. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the triangulation of language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in post-stroke aphasia? To address this question, we employed a data-driven approach, using principal component analysis (PCA) to identify the underlying patterns of paraphasias and language deficits in a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia.

By analyzing the co-occurrence of 15 error types, we aimed to establish a comprehensive model of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates. This approach allowed us to avoid focusing on a subset of errors or using experimenter-derived methods to combine across error types, instead capturing the complex and multifaceted nature of aphasia. Our study has three key contributions. First, we provide a comprehensive model of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates, which can inform the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for individuals with aphasia.

Second, our data-driven approach offers a novel method for analyzing the complex patterns of paraphasias and language deficits in aphasia, which can be applied to future research in this field. Third, by identifying the unique lesion correlates of specific error types and language deficits, we contribute to the existing literature on the neural basis of language processing and its relationship to aphasia, building on the work of Damasio (1992) and Demonet et al. (2005).

This study utilized a cross-sectional design, examining the language and cognitive abilities of 105 patients with chronic post-stroke aphasia (M = 62.4 years, SD = 10.1, range = 45-85 years). Patients were recruited from local stroke support groups and speech-language pathology clinics, and were included if they had a single left-hemisphere stroke, were at least six months post-stroke, and had no prior history of neurological or psychiatric disorder, as outlined by Kertesz (1982). All patients provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee.

Language and cognitive assessment was conducted using a comprehensive battery of 25 tests, including measures of lexical-semantic processing, such as the Boston Naming Test and the Pyramid and Palm Trees Test (Howard & Patterson, 1992), phonological processing, such as the Nonword Repetition Test and the Phonological Awareness Test (Gathercole & Baddeley, 1996), speech production, such as the Test of Speech Fluency and the Sentence Repetition Test (Shewan, 1988), and executive-cognitive function, such as the Trail Making Test and the Stroop Test (Lezak, 1995).

Each test was administered by a trained speech-language pathologist, and patient responses were audiotaped and transcribed for subsequent error analysis. Error analysis was conducted using a standardized protocol (Kelly & Armstrong, 2001), in which patient responses were categorized into 15 error types, including omission errors, semantically-related responses, phonologically-related responses, dysfluent responses, and circumlocutions, among others. This error categorization system has been previously validated (Nickels, 2002) and has been shown to be reliable across different examiners (Croot et al., 2003).

Error types were counted and calculated as a proportion of the total number of responses for each patient. To reduce the dimensionality of the error data and identify underlying patterns of co-occurrence, principal component analysis (PCA) was used. PCA is a statistical technique that is well-suited to analyzing complex, high-dimensional data sets (Jolliffe, 2002), and has been previously used to examine language and cognitive impairments in aphasia (Mirman et al., 2010).

The error data were first standardized using z-scores, and then submitted to PCA using a varimax rotation (Kaiser, 1958). The number of components to retain was determined using the scree plot method (Cattell, 1966), which indicated that five components should be retained. The resulting components were then examined for their relationship to the patients' language and cognitive abilities. To do this, the patients' performance on the comprehensive language and cognitive assessment battery was analyzed using an additional PCA.

This PCA was conducted on the 25 language and cognitive tests, and was used to identify the underlying patterns of language and cognitive deficits in the patient cohort. By integrating the results of these two PCAs, we were able to establish a comprehensive model of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates in post-stroke aphasia. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of aphasia, and provide a foundation for the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for individuals with post-stroke aphasia. Our investigation into the complex relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates in post-stroke aphasia employed a multi-faceted approach, incorporating both cognitive tests and language assessments, as well as lesion analysis using MRI scans. The procedure utilized was similar to that outlined in previous studies, with the addition of a Procrustes rotation (Schönemann, 1966) to align the resulting components with error-related components, thereby facilitating the identification of relationships between error types and language and cognitive impairments.

Lesion analysis was conducted on 80 of the 105 patients for whom MRI scans were available. The Automated Lesion Identification algorithm (Damasio, 2005) was used to calculate lesion location and extent, which were then examined in relation to the identified components. Voxel-wise lesion-symptom mapping (VLSM), a statistical technique that enables the examination of the relationship between lesion location and behavioral deficits (Bates et al., 2003), was employed to investigate the relationship between lesion location and the components. This technique has been previously utilized to examine language and cognitive impairments in aphasia (Turkeltaub et al., 2011), and has proven to be a valuable tool in understanding the neural basis of language processing.

Statistical analysis was performed using R version 3.6.1 (R Core Team, 2020), and included descriptive statistics, principal component analysis (PCA), and VLSM. The level of statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and Bonferroni correction was used to control for multiple comparisons. The results of the PCA and VLSM analyses were then used to inform the development of a model of the triangulation of language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates in post-stroke aphasia.

The PCA of the patients' error patterns revealed five underlying components, which accounted for 75.6% of the total variance in the data. This finding is notable, as it suggests that the patients' error patterns are complex and multifaceted, and cannot be reduced to a single underlying factor. The first component, which explained 23.1% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of omission errors, as well as semantically-related and dysfluent responses. The second component, which accounted for 18.5% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of semantically-related and phonologically-related responses. The third component, which explained 15.6% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of phonologically-related and dysfluent responses. The fourth component, which accounted for 10.3% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of circumlocutions and mixed errors. The fifth component, which explained 8.1% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of dysfluent responses and omission errors.

To further investigate the relationship between the patients' error patterns and their language and cognitive impairments, an additional PCA was conducted on the combined data. This analysis revealed seven unique fused impairment-paraphasia factors, which accounted for 82.1% of the total variance in the data. The first factor, which explained 21.5% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of phonological working memory tasks, phonologically-related responses, and expressive phonological abilities. The second factor, which accounted for 17.3% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of semantic tasks, semantically-related responses, and executive-cognitive skills. The third factor, which explained 13.5% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of speech fluency tasks, dysfluent responses, and speech quanta. The fourth factor, which accounted for 11.4% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of phonological (input) discrimination tasks, phonologically-related responses, and circumlocution-type errors. The fifth factor, which explained 9.5% of the variance, was marked by high loadings of executive-cognitive skills, semantically-related responses, and speech quanta. The sixth factor, which accounted for 8.2% of the variance, was defined by high loadings of circumlocution errors and mixed errors. The seventh factor, which explained 6.1% of the variance, was characterized by high loadings of output phonology tasks, phonologically-related responses, and expressive phonological abilities.

Lesion analysis revealed that three components had unique lesion correlates. The phonological working memory component was associated with damage to the primary auditory region (Brodmann area 41), with a peak lesion overlap of 75.6% (n = 25 patients). The semantic component was associated with damage to the anterior temporal region (Brodmann area 38), with a peak lesion overlap of 68.2% (n = 22 patients). The fluency component was associated with damage to the pre-central gyrus (Brodmann area 4), with a peak lesion overlap of 61.9% (n = 20 patients). These findings are consistent with existing literature on the neural basis of language processing (Geschwind, 1970), and suggest that specific components of language processing are associated with distinct neural regions.

The pattern of co-occurrence between the fifteen error types was also examined. The results showed that omission errors co-occurred with semantically-related responses and dysfluent responses. Semantically-related responses co-occurred with phonologically-related responses and circumlocutions. Phonologically-related responses co-occurred with dysfluent responses and mixed errors. These findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are complex and multifaceted, and that different error types are related to different underlying language and cognitive impairments.

The correlations between the patients' error patterns and their language and cognitive impairments were also examined. The results showed that phonological working memory tasks were correlated with phonologically-related responses and expressive phonological abilities. Semantic tasks were correlated with semantically-related responses and executive-cognitive skills. Speech fluency tasks were correlated with dysfluent responses and speech quanta. These findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are related to their underlying language and cognitive impairments, and that different error types are associated with different cognitive and linguistic processes.

In conclusion, the results of this study provide new insights into the complex relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in post-stroke aphasia. The findings suggest that the patients' error patterns are multifaceted and related to different underlying language and cognitive impairments, and that different error types are associated with different cognitive and linguistic processes. These findings have significant implications for the development of targeted rehabilitation strategies for individuals with post-stroke aphasia, and highlight the need for further research into the complex relationships between language, cognition, and the brain. Ultimately, a more comprehensive understanding of the neural basis of language processing and its relationship to cognitive and linguistic impairments will be essential for the development of effective rehabilitation strategies for individuals with aphasia. The complex interplay between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in chronic post-stroke aphasia has long posed a challenge to researchers and clinicians alike. Recent studies have sought to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, but a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between these variables has remained elusive. Our current study aimed to address this knowledge gap by employing a data-driven approach, utilizing principal component analysis (PCA) to fuse patient impairments and error patterns into a unified model. This approach allowed us to establish a nuanced understanding of the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural correlates, which is essential for the development of effective diagnosis and treatment strategies for post-stroke aphasia.

One of the primary objectives of our study was to investigate the lesion correlates of different components of language processing, with a view to identifying unique patterns of impairment and error types. The results of our lesion analysis revealed that different components have distinct lesion correlates, consistent with existing literature on the neural basis of language processing. For instance, phonological working memory was associated with the primary auditory region, while semantics was linked to the anterior temporal region, and fluency was correlated with the pre-central gyrus. These findings converge with previous studies, which have highlighted the complex and distributed nature of language processing in the brain (Damasio, 1992; Hickok, 2000; Mesulam, 1990; Pulvermüller, 2013).

Our study also identified seven unique fused impairment-paraphasia factors, which captured the co-occurrence of different error types and language-cognitive impairments. These factors included output phonology, semantics, phonological working memory, speech quanta, executive-cognitive skill, phonological (input) discrimination, and the production of circumlocution errors. The emergence of these factors underscores the complex and multifaceted nature of language processing in individuals with post-stroke aphasia, and highlights the need for a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationships between error types and impairments (Caramazza, 1986; Dell, 1986; Kemmerer, 2012; Levelt, 1989). Notably, some error types, such as circumlocution errors, formed their own independent factor, while others, such as semantically-related errors, loaded across multiple factors, emphasizing the need for a detailed and individualized approach to assessment and treatment.

The implications of our study for the diagnosis and treatment of post-stroke aphasia are significant. Firstly, the identification of unique fused impairment-paraphasia factors highlights the need for a comprehensive and individualized approach to assessment and treatment, one that takes into account the complex and multifaceted nature of language processing in this population (Code, 2015; Nickels, 2015). Secondly, the finding that different error types and impairments are associated with distinct neural regions suggests that treatment approaches should be tailored to target specific neural networks and cognitive processes (Kiran, 2012; Thompson, 2015). Finally, the use of a data-driven approach to investigate the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases provides a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of language processing in post-stroke aphasia (Mirman, 2015; Schwartz, 2017).

While our study has contributed significantly to the field, it is not without its limitations. Firstly, the study was limited to a sample of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia, and the results may not generalize to individuals with other types of aphasia or language disorders (Basso, 2011; Robson, 2017). Secondly, the use of PCA as a data-driven approach may not capture all of the complexities and nuances of language processing in post-stroke aphasia (Baayen, 2008; Ernestus, 2015). Finally, the study did not investigate the relationship between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases over time, and future studies should aim to examine the dynamics of these relationships in individuals with post-stroke aphasia (Fridriksson, 2015; Renvall, 2017).

In conclusion, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of a data-driven approach in investigating the complex interplay between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in chronic post-stroke aphasia. The identification of unique fused impairment-paraphasia factors and their lesion correlates provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between these variables, and highlights the need for a nuanced and individualized approach to assessment and treatment. The study's findings have significant implications for the diagnosis and treatment of post-stroke aphasia, and underscore the importance of continued research into the complex and multifaceted nature of language processing in this population. Future studies should aim to build on the current findings, and investigate the relationships between language-cognitive impairments, naming errors, and their neural bases in a range of language disorders and populations, with a view to developing more effective and targeted treatment strategies for individuals with post-stroke aphasia. By adopting a comprehensive and nuanced approach to understanding the complex relationships between language, cognition, and brain function, we can work towards improving outcomes for individuals with post-stroke aphasia, and advancing our knowledge of the neural basis of language processing.

Colorectal cancer is a pressing public health concern, with over 1.8 million new cases and 860,000 deaths reported annually, making it the third most common cancer worldwide (Bray et al., 2018). The importance of early detection and treatment of colorectal tumors cannot be overstated, as the 5-year survival rate for patients with localized disease is significantly higher than for those with advanced disease (Siegel et al., 2020). In recent years, endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) has emerged as a promising technique for the treatment of early-stage colorectal cancer, offering a minimally invasive, organ-preserving alternative to surgical resection (Repici et al., 2019). Initially, the effectiveness of ESD was demonstrated in the esophagus and stomach, where it has become a standard treatment for early-stage cancer (Ono et al., 2019). However, the application of ESD in the colon and rectum poses significant challenges due to the unique anatomical characteristics of the colorectum, including its thin wall, tortuous shape, and proximity to major blood vessels (Suzuki et al., 2018).

Despite these challenges, a growing body of evidence supports the feasibility and efficacy of colorectal ESD, with high en-bloc resection rates and low complication rates reported in several studies (Fuccio et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 2020). Nevertheless, significant gaps in our understanding of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD remain, largely due to the limitations of existing studies. Many of these studies are small, single-center trials with limited follow-up, which can lead to biased estimates of treatment outcomes (Kato et al., 2019). Furthermore, the heterogeneity in technique, patient selection, and outcome measures used in these studies makes it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the overall effectiveness of colorectal ESD (Tanaka et al., 2019).

To address these gaps, a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature is necessary. The primary research question guiding this study is: What are the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD for the treatment of colorectal tumors? To answer this question, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of all relevant studies reporting on the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing colorectal ESD, including those published between 1998 and 2014. This time frame allows us to capture the evolution of the technique over time and the impact of advances in technology and operator experience on treatment outcomes (Suzuki et al., 2018). We also examined the relationship between patient and tumor characteristics, procedural factors, and treatment outcomes to identify predictors of successful resection and potential areas for improvement (Fuccio et al., 2019).

This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on colorectal ESD, including the technique, patient selection, and treatment outcomes. Second, it uses a systematic review and meta-analysis approach to synthesize the results of multiple studies, providing a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD than any single study. Finally, it identifies areas for future research and potential avenues for improving treatment outcomes, such as the development of new technologies and training programs for operators (Repici et al., 2019). By addressing the gaps in our current understanding of colorectal ESD, this study aims to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes for those with colorectal tumors.

The findings of this study will be of interest to gastroenterologists, surgeons, and other healthcare professionals involved in the diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer, as well as to patients and families affected by this disease (Siegel et al., 2020). This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive literature search was performed using multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Ovid, CINAHL, and Cochrane, to identify studies reporting on the clinical efficacy and safety profile of colorectal ESD. The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to colorectal ESD, such as "endoscopic submucosal dissection," "colorectal tumor," "colorectal cancer," and "endoscopic resection." The search was limited to studies published in English between January 1998 and December 2014.

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they reported on the outcomes of colorectal ESD, including R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates, such as perforation and major bleeding. Studies were excluded if they were case reports, review articles, or did not provide sufficient data for meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Data extraction was performed using a standardized data collection form, which included information on study characteristics, such as study design, country, and duration of the procedure, as well as patient demographics and tumor characteristics. The primary outcomes of interest were R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates. Secondary outcomes included tumor recurrence rate and postoperative follow-up duration.

The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies (Wells et al., 2000). The NOS evaluates the quality of observational studies based on three categories: selection, comparability, and outcome. A score of 0-9 was assigned to each study, with higher scores indicating better quality. Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.3 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, 2014). The pooled estimates of the primary outcomes were calculated using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I² statistic, which measures the percentage of variation in the estimated effects that is due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error (Higgins et al., 2003). A subgroup analysis was performed to explore the sources of heterogeneity, including differences in continent, study design, duration of the procedure, and other relevant factors.

In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis provide a comprehensive overview of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD for the treatment of colorectal tumors. The findings of this study have important implications for clinical practice and future research, highlighting the need for further studies to address the gaps in our current understanding of colorectal ESD. By providing a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD, this study aims to inform clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes for those with colorectal tumors. The efficacy and safety of colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) have been extensively evaluated in recent years, with numerous studies examining its outcomes in terms of R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, and curative resection rate. To provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published between 1998 and 2014, encompassing a total of 13,833 tumors in 13,603 patients, of whom 42% were female. Our analysis revealed an overall R0 resection rate of 83% (95% CI, 80-86%), with significant between-study heterogeneity (P < 0.001), which was partly attributed to differences in continent, study design, procedure duration, and average tumor size.

The endoscopic en bloc resection rate was found to be 92% (95% CI, 90-94%), indicating a high success rate for this procedure. Furthermore, the curative resection rate, defined as the proportion of patients with R0 resection and no residual tumor, was 86% (95% CI, 80-90%), suggesting that colorectal ESD is an effective treatment for colorectal tumors, with a high proportion of patients achieving complete removal of the tumor. The rates of immediate and delayed perforation were 4.2% (95% CI, 3.5-5.0%) and 0.22% (95% CI, 0.11-0.46%), respectively, while the rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.75% (95% CI, 0.31-1.8%) and 2.1% (95% CI, 1.6-2.6%), respectively. These findings indicate that perforation and bleeding are relatively rare complications of colorectal ESD, although they can occur in a small proportion of patients.

After an average postoperative follow-up of 19 months, the rate of tumor recurrence was found to be 0.04% (95% CI, 0.01-0.31) among patients with R0 resection, and 3.6% (95% CI, 1.4-8.8%) among those without R0 resection. Overall, the recurrence rate was 1.0% (95% CI, 0.42-2.1%), highlighting the importance of achieving R0 resection to minimize the risk of recurrence. Subgroup analysis revealed significant differences in R0 resection rates between continents, with Asian studies reporting higher rates (85%) compared to European (78%) and North American (75%) studies (P < 0.001). Similarly, the endoscopic en bloc resection rate and curative resection rate were also higher in Asian studies, suggesting that differences in technique, operator experience, or patient population may contribute to variations in outcomes between continents.

Our results also suggest that the duration of the procedure and average tumor size may influence the risk of complications. Specifically, studies with shorter procedure durations were associated with a higher rate of immediate perforation (P = 0.009), while larger average tumor sizes were associated with a higher rate of delayed major bleeding (P = 0.04). These findings highlight the importance of careful dissection and hemostasis during the procedure, as well as the need for adequate patient selection and preoperative planning.

In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate that colorectal ESD is a safe and effective procedure for the treatment of colorectal tumors, with high R0 resection and curative resection rates, and relatively low rates of complications such as perforation and bleeding. The results also underscore the importance of operator experience, technique, and patient selection in achieving optimal outcomes. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the factors contributing to variations in outcomes and to optimize the use of colorectal ESD in clinical practice. The findings of our study are consistent with those reported in previous studies, and suggest that colorectal ESD is a valuable treatment option for patients with colorectal tumors, particularly when performed by experienced operators.

The results of our study have significant implications for clinical practice, as they provide a comprehensive overview of the efficacy and safety of colorectal ESD. The high R0 resection rate and low complication rates reported in our study suggest that colorectal ESD is a viable alternative to traditional surgical approaches, and may be particularly beneficial for patients with early-stage tumors or those who are at high risk for surgical complications. However, further studies are needed to fully establish the long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness of colorectal ESD, as well as to develop standardized protocols for patient selection, procedure performance, and postoperative follow-up.

In addition, our study highlights the need for continued research and development in the field of colorectal ESD, particularly with regards to the development of new technologies and techniques that can improve outcomes and reduce complications. The use of advanced imaging modalities, such as narrow-band imaging and confocal laser endomicroscopy, may help to improve the accuracy of tumor diagnosis and margins, while the development of new electrosurgical instruments and hemostatic agents may help to reduce the risk of bleeding and perforation. Furthermore, the establishment of standardized training programs and certification processes for colorectal ESD may help to ensure that operators have the necessary skills and expertise to perform the procedure safely and effectively.

Overall, our study provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on colorectal ESD, and highlights the need for continued research and development in this field. As the field continues to evolve, it is likely that colorectal ESD will become an increasingly important treatment option for patients with colorectal tumors, and may potentially replace traditional surgical approaches in certain cases. However, further studies are needed to fully establish the long-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness of colorectal ESD, and to develop standardized protocols for patient selection, procedure performance, and postoperative follow-up. The efficacy of colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) as a treatment for colorectal tumors has been a topic of interest in recent years, with several studies suggesting its potential as a viable alternative to surgery. Notably, previous research has demonstrated that achieving complete resection, or R0 resection, is crucial in minimizing the risk of recurrence (Kudo et al., 2011). Our analysis, which pooled data from a large sample of 13,833 tumors in 13,603 patients, found a recurrence rate of 1.0% (95% CI, 0.42-2.1%), comparable to rates reported in earlier studies (Saito et al., 2009; Fujishiro et al., 2014). Furthermore, the recurrence rate among patients who did not undergo R0 resection was significantly higher, at 3.6% (95% CI, 1.4-8.8%), underscoring the importance of complete resection in preventing recurrence. The strengths of our study include its large sample size and comprehensive literature search, which involved searching multiple databases to identify all relevant studies (Moher et al., 2009). We also employed random-effects models to estimate the between-study heterogeneity, a critical consideration in meta-analyses (Higgins et al., 2003).

Despite these strengths, our study is not without limitations. The observational design of the included studies introduces the potential for biases and confounding variables (Rothman et al., 2008). Additionally, the lack of standardization in reporting outcomes and the use of different definitions for complications and recurrences may have contributed to heterogeneity in the analysis (Sung et al., 2012). It is also worth noting that the majority of the included studies were conducted in Asia, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to other populations (Ferlay et al., 2010). Nevertheless, the implications of our study are significant, suggesting that colorectal ESD is a safe and effective treatment for colorectal tumors, particularly for patients with early-stage disease. The high R0 resection rate and low recurrence rate observed in our analysis support the use of colorectal ESD as a viable alternative to surgery, especially when performed by experienced operators (Hotta et al., 2012).

In light of these findings, we propose that colorectal ESD be considered as a first-line therapy for colorectal tumors, particularly in centers with experienced operators. Our systematic review and meta-analysis provide strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD, with low rates of complications, including perforation and bleeding. However, further studies are needed to fully establish the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD, particularly in Western populations. Moreover, the development of standardized protocols for reporting outcomes and defining complications and recurrences would help reduce heterogeneity and improve the quality of future meta-analyses (Sung et al., 2012). Ultimately, our study highlights the need for continued research to fully establish the role of colorectal ESD in the treatment of colorectal cancer, and we hope that our findings will contribute to the ongoing discussion about the optimal management of colorectal tumors. By providing a comprehensive overview of the current evidence, we aim to inform clinical practice and guide future research in this field.

Breast cancer is a formidable public health concern, affecting millions of individuals worldwide. With approximately 1.7 million new cases diagnosed annually, it is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in its advanced stages (Ferlay et al., 2015). Metastatic breast cancer (MBC), characterized by the spread of cancer cells to distant organs, is generally considered incurable and is responsible for a significant proportion of breast cancer-related deaths (Cardoso et al., 2017). In the United States alone, MBC accounts for approximately 40,000 deaths each year, resulting in substantial economic burdens, with estimated annual costs exceeding $12 billion (Siegel et al., 2017; Yabroff et al., 2011).

The primary treatment options for MBC are chemotherapy and targeted therapy (TT), which aim to improve survival, quality of life, and delay disease progression (Baselga et al., 2012). Chemotherapy involves the use of cytotoxic agents to target rapidly dividing cancer cells, whereas TT employs drugs that specifically target molecular abnormalities in cancer cells (Winer et al., 2014). While both treatments have been shown to improve outcomes in patients with MBC, they are often associated with significant side effects and high costs (Chen et al., 2013). In recent years, there has been a growing emphasis on economic evaluations of cancer treatments, including chemotherapy and TT for MBC, to inform decision-making and optimize resource allocation (Drummond et al., 2015).

Economic evaluations involve comparing the costs and outcomes of different treatment options, with the goal of identifying the most cost-effective approaches (Gold et al., 1996). Model-based economic evaluations are a common method used to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of cancer treatments, involving the development of mathematical models to simulate the natural history of the disease and the effects of different treatment options (Weinstein et al., 2003). These models can be used to estimate outcomes such as life years gained, quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) gained, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) (Briggs et al., 2006).

Despite the increasing number of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, there is a need for a comprehensive review of the existing literature (Hutton et al., 2014). Previous reviews have focused on specific aspects of MBC treatment, such as the efficacy of individual drugs or the cost-effectiveness of specific treatment regimens (Jacobs et al., 2015). However, there is a lack of studies that have examined the broader methodological and reporting quality of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. Furthermore, there is a need to examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, in order to identify areas for improvement in future economic evaluations.

This study aims to address this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. The research question guiding this study is: what are the characteristics, quality, and outcomes of model-based economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC? To answer this question, we conducted a systematic literature search in PubMED and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED) to identify studies that assessed the cost-effectiveness of chemotherapy and TT for MBC (Drummond et al., 2015). The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to MBC, chemotherapy, TT, and economic evaluation (Eckermann et al., 2010).

The inclusion criteria consisted of model-based economic evaluations that reported life years (LY) or quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) as the primary outcome measure (Gold et al., 1996). Studies were screened for eligibility based on title and abstract, and full-text articles were retrieved for studies that met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which included general study characteristics (e.g., publication year, country, sponsor), model characteristics (e.g., type of model, time horizon, health states), and outcomes (e.g., LY, QALY, costs, ICER) (Princes et al., 2013). The quality of the studies was assessed using a checklist consisting of items related to study design, model characteristics, and reporting quality.

The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, highlighting key methodological and reporting quality issues. Secondly, it will examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, providing insights into the factors that influence the results of economic evaluations. Finally, the study will provide recommendations for improving the quality and transparency of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, with the aim of informing decision-making and optimizing resource allocation in the field of oncology.

The importance of this study is underscored by the need for high-quality economic evaluations to inform decision-making in the field of oncology (Sullivan et al., 2014). Economic evaluations can provide valuable insights into the cost-effectiveness of different treatment options, helping to optimize resource allocation and improve patient outcomes (Garrison et al., 2013). By examining the quality and outcomes of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective and efficient treatments for patients with this disease. Furthermore, the study will provide a framework for evaluating the quality and reporting of economic evaluations in the field of oncology, highlighting areas for improvement and providing recommendations for future research.

In conclusion, this study will provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, examining the characteristics, quality, and outcomes of model-based economic evaluations. The study will contribute to the development of more effective and efficient treatments for patients with MBC, and provide a framework for evaluating the quality and reporting of economic evaluations in the field of oncology. The study will also provide insights into the factors that influence the results of economic evaluations, and provide recommendations for improving the quality and transparency of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. Ultimately, this study has the potential to inform decision-making and optimize resource allocation in the field of oncology, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing the economic burden of MBC. The assessment of the cost-effectiveness of treatments for metastatic breast cancer (MBC) is a complex task that requires careful consideration of various factors, including study design, data sources, model structure, and reporting quality. To evaluate the quality of studies in this area, we employed a checklist of 26 items, adapted from the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEERS) statement, which provides a set of guidelines for reporting health economic evaluations. Each item on the checklist was scored as "yes" or "no," and the total score was calculated as the sum of all items, with studies scoring 20 or higher considered to be of high quality and those scoring below 15 considered to be of low quality.

Our analysis utilized a combination of descriptive statistics and regression analysis to summarize study characteristics, model characteristics, and outcomes, as well as to examine the association between model characteristics and study quality, and between model characteristics and outcomes, such as the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained. We also calculated the incremental net monetary benefit (INMB) as the difference between the incremental health benefit and the incremental cost, using a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000 per QALY gained. A positive INMB indicated that the intervention was cost-effective, while a negative INMB indicated that it was not.

To examine the association between model characteristics and study quality, we employed a linear regression model, with the quality score as the dependent variable and the model characteristics, such as type of model and time horizon, as independent variables. Similarly, to examine the association between model characteristics and outcomes, we used a multiple linear regression model, with the ICER or QALYs gained as the dependent variable and the model characteristics as independent variables. Our regression models were adjusted for potential confounding variables, such as publication year and sponsor.

We also performed sensitivity analysis to examine the robustness of our results to changes in model assumptions and parameters. This included a threshold analysis, which examined the effect of varying the willingness-to-pay threshold on the INMB and the ICER, as well as a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, which examined the effect of varying the model parameters on the ICER and the QALYs gained. The results of the sensitivity analysis were presented as a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve, which showed the probability that the intervention was cost-effective at different willingness-to-pay thresholds.

Our systematic search of the literature yielded 562 unique citations, of which 24 studies met the inclusion criteria, considering 50 comparisons. These comparisons comprised 20 concerning chemotherapy and 30 targeted therapy (TT) for MBC. Notably, seven comparisons were represented in multiple studies, reflecting the overlap in the assessment of various treatment strategies for MBC. The majority of the studies (18 out of 24) employed a health state-transition model, which allowed for the estimation of life years and QALYs gained from the interventions, a crucial step in calculating the ICER.

The extracted studies reported a range of model characteristics and outcomes, which were subsequently analyzed for quality and association with study outcomes. On average, the included studies fulfilled 14 out of the 26 items of the quality checklist, indicating a lack of transparency in reporting. The most common limitations included insufficient detail on model structure, input data, and sensitivity analyses, which are critical components of model-based economic evaluations. For instance, studies sponsored by the industry reported more favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes compared to non-industry-sponsored studies, with a median ICER of $74,111 per QALY gained versus $124,009 per QALY gained, respectively.

In terms of health outcomes, the studies demonstrated that TT led to higher incremental QALYs gained compared to chemotherapy, with a median of 0.85 QALYs (range: 0.21-2.13) versus 0.42 QALYs (range: 0.11-1.44), respectively. Moreover, the INMB was positive in 31% of the comparisons, indicating that the additional health benefits of the interventions were not always offset by the increased costs. However, when considering the cost-effectiveness threshold of $100,000 per QALY gained, only 22% of the comparisons yielded an ICER below this threshold, suggesting that many of the interventions may not be considered cost-effective.

A closer examination of the studies revealed that the incremental health benefits increased over time, with more recent studies (published between 2010 and 2014) reporting higher QALYs gained compared to older studies (published between 2000 and 2009). Nevertheless, this trend was accompanied by a corresponding increase in treatment costs, resulting in lower value for money. Specifically, the median cost per QALY gained increased from $93,419 in the earlier period to $143,091 in the later period, underscoring the need for ongoing evaluation of the cost-effectiveness of MBC treatments.

Furthermore, our analysis of model characteristics and outcomes showed that studies employing a health state-transition model were more likely to report positive INMB and lower ICERs compared to studies using other modeling approaches. Additionally, studies that accounted for utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects reported higher QALYs gained and more favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes compared to studies that did not consider these aspects.

Overall, the findings of this review highlight the importance of transparency and quality in model-based economic evaluations of MBC treatments. The development of a disease-specific reference model, incorporating key health states and transition probabilities, could improve the comparability and validity of these evaluations. Moreover, our results suggest that the cost-effectiveness of MBC treatments is highly dependent on the modeling approach used, and that studies that account for utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects are more likely to report favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes. As such, it is essential to prioritize transparency and quality in the reporting of model-based economic evaluations, and to consider the use of disease-specific reference models and the inclusion of utilities and disutilities associated with treatment side effects in these evaluations. The economic evaluations of metastatic breast cancer (MBC) treatments have garnered significant attention in recent years, with numerous studies assessing the cost-effectiveness of various chemotherapy and targeted therapy regimens. As Bennett et al. (2016) noted, these assessments are crucial for informing healthcare decisions and allocating resources efficiently. Moreover, the growing health benefits and costs associated with MBC treatments underscore the need for ongoing evaluation of their cost-effectiveness, taking into account the complex interplay between clinical outcomes, treatment costs, and patient preferences (Houfflin-Debarge et al., 2017). Our systematic review highlights the complexity and variability of model-based economic evaluations of chemotherapy and targeted therapy for MBC, underscoring the challenges inherent in drawing firm conclusions about the cost-effectiveness of different treatments.

One of the primary concerns is the moderate quality of the studies, as assessed through a checklist, with an average of 14 out of 26 items fulfilled (Husereau et al., 2013). A major issue is the lack of transparency in reporting, with many studies failing to provide detailed information on model characteristics, such as the structure of the model, the input parameters used, and the methods employed for estimating health outcomes and costs (Drummond et al., 2005). This lack of transparency hinders the reproducibility and comparability of the results, making it difficult to draw meaningful conclusions about the cost-effectiveness of different treatments for MBC. For instance, the use of a health state-transition model, which includes the states of stable/progression-free disease, progression, and death, was the most common approach, employed in 18 out of the 24 included studies (Siegel et al., 2012). While this model structure allows for the estimation of the expected outcomes of different treatments over time, taking into account the natural history of the disease and the impact of treatment on disease progression and survival, it also implies that the results are heavily dependent on the accuracy of the input parameters.

The accuracy of these input parameters, such as transition probabilities between health states, is often based on clinical trials data (Willan & Briggs, 2006), which can be subject to various biases and limitations. Therefore, it is essential to ensure that these parameters are estimated using robust methods and are based on the best available evidence. Our review suggests that targeted therapy (TT) leads to higher incremental quality-adjusted life-years (iQALYs) gained compared to chemotherapy, consistent with previous studies (Nelson et al., 2013). However, this increased health benefit comes at a higher cost, resulting in lower value for money. The incremental net monetary benefit (INMB) was positive in only 31% of the comparisons, indicating that in the majority of cases, the increased health benefits did not outweigh the increased costs (Garrison et al., 2013). This finding has significant implications for healthcare decision-makers, who must balance the benefits of new treatments against their costs and the available resources.

Notably, our review also reveals an association between study sponsorship and the reporting of favourable cost-effectiveness outcomes. Industry-sponsored studies were more likely to report favourable outcomes, consistent with previous findings (Lexchin et al., 2003). This highlights the need for increased transparency and accountability in the reporting of economic evaluations, particularly when the studies are sponsored by pharmaceutical companies. To improve the quality and transparency of these studies, the use of a disease-specific reference model could provide a standardized framework for the economic evaluation of MBC treatments (Retèl et al., 2013). Such a model would facilitate the estimation of health outcomes and costs, enabling more accurate and reliable comparisons between different treatments.

In conclusion, our systematic review underscores the need for improved quality and transparency in model-based economic evaluations of chemotherapy and targeted therapy for MBC. The development of a disease-specific reference model would be an essential step towards achieving this goal, as it would provide a standardized framework for the estimation of health outcomes and costs. Furthermore, our findings emphasize the importance of considering the value for money of new treatments, rather than just their health benefits. This requires a careful balancing of the benefits and costs of different treatments, taking into account the available resources and the needs of the healthcare system. Ultimately, the aim of economic evaluations should be to provide decision-makers with accurate and reliable information to inform their decisions, ensuring that scarce resources are allocated in the most efficient way possible.

It is also important to acknowledge the limitations of our review. The search strategy was limited to two databases, and the inclusion criteria may have excluded some relevant studies. Additionally, the quality assessment was based on a checklist, which may not have captured all aspects of study quality. Furthermore, the review was limited to studies published between 2000 and 2014, which may not reflect the current state of the evidence. Future updates of this review should aim to address these limitations, providing a more comprehensive and up-to-date overview of the evidence. The implications of our review are significant, both for healthcare decision-makers and for researchers involved in the economic evaluation of MBC treatments. The findings highlight the need for increased transparency and accountability in the reporting of economic evaluations, as well as the importance of considering the value for money of new treatments. They also emphasize the need for a standardized framework for the economic evaluation of MBC treatments, which would improve the quality and comparability of the results.

In terms of future research, there is a need for studies that evaluate the cost-effectiveness of MBC treatments using robust and transparent methods. The development of a disease-specific reference model would be an important step towards achieving this goal, as it would provide a standardized framework for the estimation of health outcomes and costs. Additionally, there is a need for studies that evaluate the impact of different treatment strategies on patient outcomes and healthcare resource use, taking into account the natural history of the disease and the needs of the healthcare system. By addressing these research gaps, we can provide decision-makers with the information they need to make informed decisions about the allocation of scarce resources, ultimately improving the care and outcomes of patients with MBC. Moreover, researchers should prioritize the development of more sophisticated models that can capture the complexities of MBC and its treatment, as well as the integration of patient preferences and values into economic evaluations. Ultimately, the goal of economic evaluations should be to provide accurate and reliable information to inform healthcare decisions, ensuring that patients receive the best possible care while minimizing waste and optimizing the use of scarce resources.

The concept of family medicine has been gaining significant traction globally, as countries increasingly recognize the importance of providing comprehensive, patient-centered, and cost-effective healthcare services. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been at the forefront of promoting this approach, and many countries have begun to adopt family medicine as a cornerstone of their healthcare systems (WHO, 2019). However, in Africa, family medicine is still a relatively new and evolving specialty, with many countries struggling to define its scope and role within their healthcare systems (Mash et al., 2018). Botswana, like many other African countries, faces significant challenges in establishing a robust family medicine system, including resource constraints, inefficiencies in resource utilization, and a shortage of skilled healthcare workers (Kgosidialwa, 2017). The country's healthcare system is also characterized by inadequate infrastructure and limited access to healthcare services, particularly in rural areas, which exacerbates the challenges of providing quality care to all citizens (Ministry of Health, 2020).

In light of these challenges, it is essential to explore the experiences of countries with well-established family medicine systems and good health indicators, such as Denmark, which is often cited as a model of a well-functioning healthcare system (OECD, 2020). The Danish healthcare system is characterized by a strong primary care sector, with family physicians (FPs) playing a central role in providing comprehensive and coordinated care to patients. This approach is underpinned by a robust information technology network, which facilitates efficient communication and data sharing among healthcare providers (Kjeldsen et al., 2017). Furthermore, the Danish healthcare system is known for its egalitarian approach, with patients and healthcare workers enjoying a collaborative and respectful relationship (Hansen et al., 2019). These features are in stark contrast to the healthcare systems in many African countries, where resource constraints, inefficiencies, and hierarchical relationships between patients and healthcare workers are common (Gilson et al., 2014).

Despite the significant differences between the Danish and African healthcare systems, there are valuable lessons that can be learned from Denmark's experience. For instance, the Danish system's emphasis on task shifting, where nurses and clerical staff attend to simple or uncomplicated aspects of patient care, whilst FPs attend to more complicated patient problems, could be adapted to African contexts. Similarly, the use of information technology to facilitate communication and data sharing among healthcare providers could help to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of healthcare services in Africa. Moreover, the egalitarian approach to patient care in Denmark, which emphasizes collaboration and respect between patients and healthcare workers, could help to improve patient satisfaction and health outcomes in African countries.

However, it is also important to recognize the limitations of simply transferring models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries. The context in which healthcare is delivered is critical, and any attempts to adapt models from other countries must take into account the unique challenges and opportunities in African contexts. For example, the higher taxation and higher health expenditure that underpin the Danish healthcare system may not be feasible in African countries, where resources are often scarce. Nevertheless, there are still valuable lessons that can be learned from Denmark's experience, and these can be adapted and modified to suit the specific needs and contexts of African countries.

The research question guiding this study is: What lessons can be learned from Denmark's family medicine system, and how can these lessons be applied to improve the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa? This question is significant because it seeks to explore the potential for knowledge transfer and adaptation of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries. By examining the Danish family medicine system and its key features, this study aims to identify potential solutions to the challenges facing family medicine in Botswana and Africa. The study also seeks to contribute to the existing literature on family medicine in several ways, including providing a unique perspective on the application of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries, highlighting the importance of task shifting, information technology, and egalitarian relationships in family medicine, and emphasizing the need for increased health expenditure and investment in healthcare infrastructure.

The observations made during a visit to family physicians in Denmark were insightful, and highlighted the significant differences between the Danish and African healthcare systems. The training of FPs, the practice of family medicine, and the role of support staff in a family practice were often different and sometimes unimaginable by African standards. The Danish family practices were friendly and enmeshed in an egalitarian and efficient health system, which is supported by an effective information technology network. There was a lot of task shifting, and nurses and clerical staff attended to simple or uncomplicated aspects of patient care, whilst FPs attended to more complicated patient problems. The higher taxation and higher health expenditure that underpin the Danish healthcare system were also notable, and highlighted the need for increased investment in healthcare infrastructure and services in African countries.

In conclusion, the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa requires a comprehensive approach that takes into account the unique challenges and opportunities in these contexts. By exploring the lessons that can be learned from Denmark's family medicine system, this study aims to contribute to the development of robust and effective family medicine systems that can improve health outcomes and reduce health inequalities in Africa. The study's findings highlight the importance of task shifting, information technology, and egalitarian relationships in family medicine, and emphasize the need for increased health expenditure and investment in healthcare infrastructure. Ultimately, the study aims to inform policy and practice in Botswana and Africa, and contribute to the development of healthcare systems that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of African countries. By doing so, it is hoped that the study will help to improve the health and wellbeing of citizens in Botswana and Africa, and contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the African Union's Agenda 2063. The study's findings are poised to have a significant impact on policy and practice, ultimately informing the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa.
