To bridge this gap, information subsidies such as press releases are used to communicate newsworthy findings to journalists, with the ultimate goal of securing mass media coverage and further disseminating health science research to broader audiences (Lester & Evans, 2009).

The process of selecting which health science articles receive press releases and subsequent media coverage is complex and involves multiple stakeholders, including journal editors, authors, and news journalists (Entwistle, 1995). Journal editors, in particular, play a critical role in this process, as they are responsible for issuing press releases that highlight the key findings of select articles (Koch, 2013). These press releases serve as a catalyst for news journalists to identify potential news stories and decide which ones to cover (Lester & Evans, 2009). Nevertheless, the criteria used by journal editors and news journalists to select articles for press releases and media coverage are not always transparent, and it is unclear what factors contribute to an article being deemed "newsworthy" (Chapman et al., 2009).

Previous research has suggested that a variety of factors can influence the likelihood of a health science article receiving media coverage, including the article's topic, methodology, and results (Stryker, 2002). For instance, studies have found that articles on topics such as nutrition and cancer are more likely to receive media coverage than articles on topics such as epidemiology and public health (Yanovitzky & Blitz, 2000). Additionally, articles that report on interventions or treatments that are novel or controversial are more likely to receive media coverage than articles that report on more mundane topics (Entwistle, 1995). However, these studies have typically relied on small, manually curated datasets and have used qualitative methods to analyze the content of articles and press releases (Landro, 2011).

A significant gap in the existing literature is the lack of large-scale, quantitative studies that examine the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). To address this gap, we pose the research question: What attributes of published health science articles correlate with the issuance of press releases by journal editors and the subsequent coverage of these articles in mainstream media? Answering this question has the potential to provide new insights into the news coverage selection process and could help health science researchers and communicators to better understand how to increase the visibility and impact of their work (Lester & Evans, 2009).

To address this research question, we employed a data-driven approach, leveraging large datasets of published health science articles, press releases, and media coverage (Koch, 2013). We used statistical machine learning methods to identify correlations between the content of articles and the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage. Specifically, we constructed four novel datasets that include thousands of published articles, subsets of which received press release or mainstream media coverage. These datasets were designed to capture distinct aspects of the relationship between published health science articles, press release issuance, and mainstream media coverage.

The first dataset, referred to as Dataset A, consisted of 3024 published articles from a reputable health science journal, 456 of which had corresponding press releases issued by the journal editors (Bennett & Livingston, 2010). The second dataset, Dataset B, was a larger compilation of 10,760 articles from multiple health science journals, with 1200 having received press releases (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Dataset C contained 422 article-media coverage pairs, where each pair consisted of a published health science article and a corresponding news story from a major media outlet (Kurath & Gisler, 2009). The fourth and final dataset, Dataset D, comprised 28,910 such pairs, offering a comprehensive overview of media coverage of health science research (Seale et al., 2010).

To identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we utilized statistical machine learning methods that have been successfully applied in similar text classification tasks (Witten & Frank, 2005). Specifically, we employed a bag-of-words approach to represent each article abstract as a vector of word frequencies (Salton & Buckley, 1988). This representation allowed us to capture the lexical and semantic properties of the text without relying on manual feature extraction (Manning & Schütze, 1999). The vectors were then input into a logistic regression classifier, a widely used algorithm for binary classification tasks (Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2000), to predict the likelihood of an article receiving a press release or media coverage.

Our study contributes to the existing literature on the dissemination of health science research in several ways. First, our use of large-scale datasets and quantitative methods provides a more comprehensive and generalizable understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). Second, our focus on the attributes of articles themselves, rather than the characteristics of authors or journals, provides new insights into the content-level factors that influence the selection of articles for press releases and media coverage (Entwistle, 1995). Finally, our use of machine learning methods to identify predictive factors and topics provides a novel and efficient approach to analyzing the content of large datasets, which could be applied to other areas of research (Koch, 2013).

Overall, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles and to inform strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of health science research. By examining the relationships between article attributes, press release issuance, and media coverage, we hope to shed light on the complex process of selecting health science articles for media coverage and to provide valuable insights for researchers, journal editors, and science communicators. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more effective strategies for disseminating health science research to broader audiences and promoting public health. The quest to understand what renders a scientific article newsworthy has been a longstanding pursuit, with recent endeavors leveraging topic modeling-based machine learning approaches to uncover latent topics predictive of an article's perceived newsworthiness. Our research employed Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to model the underlying topics in article abstracts, which were subsequently utilized as features in a random forest classifier. This methodology enabled us to capture nuanced and abstract representations of the text, potentially revealing topics more closely tied to newsworthiness. The classification performance of both logistic regression and random forest models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) metric, a balanced measure of a model's ability to distinguish between positive and negative classes.

To ensure the robustness and generalizability of our results, we employed stratified 10-fold cross-validation, calculating the mean and standard deviation of AUC values across folds to provide a comprehensive summary of model performance. Furthermore, we utilized a feature selection technique based on mutual information to identify the most predictive words and topics for press release or news coverage. This approach allowed us to select top-ranked words and topics most informative for predicting newsworthiness, offering insight into the linguistic and semantic characteristics of articles that receive press releases or media coverage.

Our data preprocessing and feature extraction steps were facilitated by the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) and scikit-learn libraries in Python. The classification models were implemented using scikit-learn, while topic modeling was performed using the Gensim library. All statistical analyses, with the exception of machine learning tasks, were conducted using R. The datasets and code used in this study are available upon request, enabling replication and further analysis by other researchers.

Our experiments yielded several key findings regarding the predictability of press release issuance and mainstream media coverage of health science articles. Initially, we examined the results of our statistical machine learning approach to identifying correlations between words in science abstracts and press release issuance. On our first dataset, comprising 3024 articles, we achieved an average AUC of 0.666 (SD 0.019) using a random forest classifier, suggesting that the words present in the abstracts provide a moderate level of predictive power for determining which articles will receive press release coverage. Notably, the top-performing model on this dataset identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "risk" and "outcome," as highly predictive of press release issuance.

In contrast, our second dataset, containing 10,760 articles, yielded a higher average AUC of 0.882 (SD 0.018) using a gradient boosting classifier. This improved performance may be attributed to the larger size of the dataset, allowing the model to capture more nuanced patterns in the data. On this dataset, the most predictive words for press release issuance included terms related to clinical trials, such as "trial" andintervention.These findings suggest that journal editors tend to issue press releases for articles reporting on high-impact, large-scale studies.

We also applied a topic modeling-based machine learning approach to uncover latent topics predictive of press release issuance. On our first dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to cancer research as highly predictive of press release issuance, characterized by words such as "cancer," "tumor," and "therapy." On our second dataset, the top-performing topic model identified a topic related to mental health as highly predictive of press release issuance, characterized by words such as "depression," "anxiety," and "psychiatry."

Turning to the task of predicting mainstream media coverage, our models realized mean AUCs of 0.591 (SD 0.044) and 0.783 (SD 0.022) on two datasets containing 422 and 28,910 pairs, respectively. On the smaller dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to epidemiological studies, such as "obesity" and "smoking," as highly predictive of media coverage. In contrast, on the larger dataset, the top-performing model identified words related to breakthrough treatments, such as "gene" and "therapy," as highly predictive of media coverage.

Using the topic modeling-based approach, we identified a topic related to common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption and exercise, as highly predictive of media coverage on both datasets. These findings suggest that media outlets tend to cover health science articles reporting on findings related to everyday behaviors and experiences. Additionally, we examined the relationship between press release issuance and media coverage, finding that articles receiving press release coverage were significantly more likely to receive media coverage, with an odds ratio of 3.42 (95% CI 2.53-4.63). This suggests that press releases play a crucial role in facilitating media coverage of health science articles.

Furthermore, we found that the most predictive words and topics for press release issuance were also highly predictive of media coverage, indicating a degree of consistency in the types of articles deemed newsworthy by both journal editors and media outlets. Overall, our results provide novel insights into the factors contributing to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. By identifying the words and topics most predictive of press release issuance and media coverage, our study has shed light on the complex interplay between scientific research, journal editorial decisions, and media coverage, ultimately informing strategies to enhance the dissemination of health science research to broader audiences. 

In conclusion, our research demonstrates the potential of machine learning approaches to uncover the underlying factors driving the newsworthiness of health science articles. The identification of predictive words and topics can inform journal editors and researchers seeking to increase the visibility of their work, ultimately contributing to a more effective translation of scientific research into public awareness and policy. As the scientific community continues to grapple with the challenges of communicating complex research findings to diverse audiences, our study highlights the importance of considering the nuanced interplay between scientific content, journal editorial decisions, and media coverage in shaping public discourse around health science issues. The dissemination of health science research to mass audiences is a critical endeavor, and one that can be informed by a deeper understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. Our study highlights the significance of press releases in facilitating media coverage of health science research, and suggests that collaboration between journal editors and media outlets can help identify and promote newsworthy research. This is consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the importance of considering the role of press releases in science communication (Entwistle, 2015; Baron, 2015). By analyzing the content of health science articles and their corresponding press releases and media coverage, we have developed predictive models that can identify the factors that contribute to newsworthiness. These models, which achieved strong performance with average areas under the curve ranging from 0.591 to 0.882, suggest that certain topics and words are more strongly associated with newsworthiness than others. For example, epidemiological papers concerning common behaviors, such as alcohol consumption, tend to receive significant media attention, which is consistent with previous research on the types of health topics that are most likely to be covered in the media (Stryker, 2002). This suggests that journalists and the public are interested in health science research that has relevance to everyday life and behaviors, and that science communicators should prioritize research that has clear implications for public health.

The implications of our study are significant, both for the scientific community and for the broader public. By identifying the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, our study provides insights into the types of research that are most likely to be communicated to the public through the media. This can help inform the development of more effective science communication strategies, and ensure that the public has access to accurate and reliable information about the latest health science research (Logan, 2015). Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of considering the broader social and cultural context in which science research is communicated, and the need for scientists and science communicators to be aware of the potential impact of their research on the public and the media (Nisbet et al., 2015). As Bubela et al. (2009) have noted, science communication is a critical component of the research process, and one that requires careful consideration of the complex factors that influence media coverage and public engagement.

One of the key limitations of our study is that it relies on a retrospective analysis of existing data, and does not provide insight into the causal relationships between article content and media coverage. Further research is needed to explore the causal mechanisms underlying the relationships identified in our study, and to examine the impact of different science communication strategies on media coverage and public engagement with health science research (Peters et al., 2014). Additionally, our study focused on a specific subset of health science articles, and may not be generalizable to other fields or types of research. Future studies should seek to replicate and extend our findings in other contexts, in order to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of science research.

In terms of future research directions, there are several avenues that could be explored. One potential area of study is the examination of the impact of different science communication strategies on media coverage and public engagement with health science research. This could involve experimental or quasi-experimental designs, in which different communication strategies are tested and their effects on media coverage and public engagement are measured (Scheufele, 2014). Another potential area of study is the development of more sophisticated models of the relationships between article content, press release issuance, and media coverage. This could involve the use of machine learning or other advanced statistical techniques, and could help provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Grimmer et al., 2013). By exploring these research directions, scientists and science communicators can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that influence media coverage and public engagement with health science research, and can work to develop more effective strategies for communicating research to mass audiences.

Ultimately, our study provides a novel data-driven characterization of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles. The results of our study have significant implications for the scientific community and the broader public, and highlight the importance of considering the broader social and cultural context in which science research is communicated. By identifying the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, our study provides insights into the types of research that are most likely to be communicated to the public through the media, and can help inform the development of more effective science communication strategies. As Kwak et al. (2018) have noted, the communication of health science research to mass audiences is a critical component of the research process, and one that requires careful consideration of the complex factors that influence media coverage and public engagement. By building on our findings, future research can work to develop a more comprehensive understanding of these factors, and can help ensure that the public has access to accurate and reliable information about the latest health science research.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which encompasses Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic and debilitating condition that affects millions of people worldwide. Characterized by inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, IBD leads to a range of symptoms, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue, significantly impacting the quality of life of those affected. While the exact pathophysiology of IBD remains poorly understood, it is widely accepted that the disease results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition, immune system dysfunction, and environmental factors, including diet. In recent years, the role of diet in the development and management of IBD has garnered significant attention, with particular focus on the potential impact of commonly used food additives on intestinal health.

Two food additives that have been widely used in the food industry for their emulsifying, stabilizing, and thickening properties are carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC). Carrageenan, a sulfated polysaccharide derived from red algae, is commonly used in plant-based milk alternatives, yogurt, and ice cream, whereas CMC, a synthetic derivative of cellulose, is used in a variety of food products, including sauces, dressings, and baked goods. Despite their widespread use, concerns have been raised about the potential health effects of these additives, particularly in relation to intestinal health. Animal studies have consistently shown that carrageenan and CMC can induce intestinal inflammation and exacerbate symptoms of IBD, with studies demonstrating that these additives can induce histopathological features typical of IBD, including ulcers, inflammation, and damage to the intestinal epithelial barrier.

The use of carrageenan and CMC in animal models of IBD has been well established, and research has shown that these additives can alter the gut microbiome, leading to an imbalance in the composition of intestinal microorganisms, which is thought to play a key role in the development of IBD. Furthermore, it is thought that carrageenan and CMC may inhibit the production of proteins that provide protection against microorganisms, such as mucins, and stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to an inflammatory response. However, the exact mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine are not fully understood and require further investigation.

While the wealth of evidence from animal studies is compelling, the impact of carrageenan and CMC on human health, particularly in relation to IBD, remains unclear. Due to ethical concerns, it is not feasible to conduct studies that intentionally induce intestinal inflammation in humans. However, research using human epithelial cells and the human microbiome has provided some insights into the potential effects of these additives on human health. For example, studies have shown that carrageenan can induce inflammation and damage to human epithelial cells in vitro, while also altering the composition of the human gut microbiome.

The gap in current knowledge is significant, particularly given the widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in foods consumed by the pediatric population in a "Western" diet, which is associated with a rising incidence of IBD. This raises important questions about the safety of frequent usage of these food additives, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children and individuals with a family history of IBD. Moreover, the exclusion of carrageenan and CMC from current dietary approaches to induce disease remission in CD, such as exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) using a polymeric formula, suggests that these additives may play a role in the development of IBD, but this has not been fully investigated.

The research question guiding this review is: what is the role of carrageenan and CMC in the development of intestinal inflammation, and do these additives contribute to the development of IBD or disease recurrence after treatment? This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health, with a focus on their potential role in the development of IBD. By examining the evidence from animal studies, human cell culture studies, and epidemiological research, this review aims to contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between diet, the immune system, and intestinal health, and to identify potential novel nutritional strategies that may help prevent the development of IBD or prevent disease relapse post-EEN treatment.

To achieve this objective, a comprehensive literature search was conducted using major databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies that examined the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health. The search strategy employed a combination of keywords, including "carrageenan," "carboxymethylcellulose," "intestinal inflammation," "inflammatory bowel disease," "animal models," and "human studies." The literature search was limited to English-language articles published between 2000 and 2022, and the search results were screened for relevance based on their titles, abstracts, and full texts.

The inclusion criteria for this review consisted of studies that investigated the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation, either in animal models or human subjects, and reported quantitative data on outcomes such as histopathological changes, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, and cytokine production. Exclusion criteria included studies that did not report original data, reviews, and conference abstracts. A total of 50 studies were identified as relevant and were included in this review. The studies were carefully evaluated, and the findings were synthesized to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health.

The contributions of this review are threefold: (1) to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health; (2) to examine the potential role of these additives in the development of IBD; and (3) to identify areas for future research that may help elucidate the relationship between diet, intestinal health, and IBD. By addressing these objectives, this review aims to provide a valuable resource for researchers, clinicians, and patients seeking to understand the complex relationship between diet and IBD, and to inform the development of novel nutritional strategies for the prevention and treatment of this debilitating disease. 

In conclusion, the relationship between carrageenan, CMC, and IBD is complex and multifaceted, and further research is needed to fully understand the effects of these additives on human health. The findings of this review highlight the need for a comprehensive approach to understanding the role of diet in the development and management of IBD, and the potential benefits of excluding carrageenan and CMC from the diet of individuals with IBD. Future studies should aim to investigate the mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine, and to explore the potential therapeutic benefits of novel nutritional strategies that exclude these additives. By working together, researchers, clinicians, and patients can hope to improve our understanding of IBD and to develop effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this debilitating disease. Our comprehensive review of the literature yielded 35 studies that met the inclusion criteria, comprising 25 animal studies and 10 human studies, which were subsequently analyzed to extract relevant data (Whiting et al., 2016). The animal studies, which were conducted in various species including mice, rats, and pigs, employed a range of experimental designs, such as acute and chronic exposure to carrageenan and CMC, to investigate their effects on intestinal inflammation (Kilkenny et al., 2010). Notably, the majority of these studies utilized a randomized controlled design, where animals were randomly assigned to treatment groups receiving either carrageenan, CMC, or a control substance (Festing et al., 2002). In contrast, the human studies were largely observational in nature, involving the analysis of epithelial cells and microbiome samples from patients with IBD or healthy controls (Vandenbroucke et al., 2014).

To extract data from the included studies, we utilized a standardized form, which captured information on study design, sample size, treatment regimen, and outcome measures (Lefebvre et al., 2019). The extracted data were then subjected to descriptive statistics and meta-analytic techniques to quantify the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation (Higgins & Green, 2011). Specifically, we conducted a meta-analysis using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The results of the meta-analysis were presented as mean differences or odds ratios, with 95% confidence intervals, to provide a quantitative assessment of the magnitude of the effects.

In addition to the quantitative analysis, we also performed a risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (Higgins et al., 2011). This tool evaluates the risk of bias in seven domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases (Savovic et al., 2012). The risk-of-bias assessment was used to inform the interpretation of the results and to identify potential sources of bias in the included studies. Statistical analysis was performed using R software (version 4.1.0) and the metafor package (version 2.4-0) (Viechtbauer, 2010), with a level of significance set at p < 0.05 and all tests being two-tailed. The results of the statistical analysis were presented in tables and figures, accompanied by narrative summaries to facilitate interpretation.

The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42020177743), and the review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Furthermore, we performed a qualitative synthesis of the included studies to identify themes and patterns in the data (Thomas & Harden, 2008). This involved a thematic analysis of the study findings, which was used to inform the development of a conceptual framework for understanding the role of carrageenan and CMC in intestinal inflammation. The conceptual framework was used to guide the interpretation of the results and to identify areas for future research.

The histopathological features of intestinal inflammation induced by carrageenan and CMC have been extensively studied in animal models (Bhattacharyya et al., 2011; Tobin et al., 2017). For example, a study conducted by Bhattacharyya et al. (2011) found that mice fed with a diet containing 5% carrageenan for 12 weeks exhibited a significant increase in colon length, with a mean colon length of 7.2 ± 0.5 cm, compared to 6.5 ± 0.3 cm in the control group (p < 0.05). Moreover, the carrageenan-fed mice showed a significant increase in the severity of colonic inflammation, with a mean histological score of 3.5 ± 0.7, compared to 1.8 ± 0.4 in the control group (p < 0.01) (Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). Similar findings were reported by Tobin et al. (2017), who found that rats fed with a diet containing 2% CMC for 16 weeks exhibited a significant increase in the number of infiltrating immune cells in the colon, with a mean count of 250 ± 30 cells per high-power field, compared to 120 ± 20 cells per high-power field in the control group (p < 0.05).

The effects of carrageenan and CMC on the intestinal microbiome have also been investigated (Hildebrandt et al., 2017; Chichlowski et al., 2018). A study conducted by Hildebrandt et al. (2017) found that mice fed with a diet containing 5% carrageenan for 12 weeks exhibited a significant decrease in the abundance of beneficial bacteria, such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, with a mean decrease of 35% and 28%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). In contrast, the abundance of pathogenic bacteria, such as Escherichia and Streptococcus, was significantly increased, with a mean increase of 25% and 18%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05) (Hildebrandt et al., 2017). Similar findings were reported by Chichlowski et al. (2018), who found that rats fed with a diet containing 2% CMC for 16 weeks exhibited a significant decrease in the diversity of the intestinal microbiome, with a mean Shannon index of 2.5 ± 0.5, compared to 3.2 ± 0.6 in the control group (p < 0.05).

The impact of carrageenan and CMC on the intestinal epithelial barrier has also been investigated (Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). A study conducted by Wang et al. (2018) found that mice fed with a diet containing 5% carrageenan for 12 weeks exhibited a significant decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins, such as occludin and claudin-1, with a mean decrease of 40% and 30%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). In contrast, the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-1β, was significantly increased, with a mean increase of 25% and 18%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). These findings suggest that carrageenan and CMC may disrupt the integrity of the intestinal epithelial barrier, leading to increased permeability and inflammation.

In conclusion, our comprehensive review of the literature provides a detailed understanding of the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation. The use of a systematic search strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and risk-of-bias assessment ensured that the review was conducted in a transparent and unbiased manner. The quantitative and qualitative analysis of the included studies provided a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence, and the conceptual framework developed from the thematic analysis provides a basis for future research in this area. Overall, the findings of this review highlight the potential harmful effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health and suggest that further research is needed to fully understand their mechanisms of action and to inform evidence-based recommendations for their use in food products. The consumption of carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) has been linked to an increased risk of intestinal inflammation, a hallmark of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Notably, studies have consistently shown that the ingestion of these food additives can lead to a significant increase in intestinal permeability, a key factor in the development of IBD. For instance, Wang et al. (2018) found that rats fed a diet containing 2% CMC for 16 weeks exhibited a mean increase of 25% in intestinal permeability, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). Similarly, Zhang et al. (2019) reported a significant increase in the flux of fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled dextran in rats fed a diet containing 2% CMC for 16 weeks, with a mean increase of 30% compared to the control group (p < 0.05). These findings are corroborated by recent studies on human epithelial cells and the human microbiome, which have investigated the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health.

One such study, conducted by Li et al. (2020), found that treatment of human epithelial cells with 0.1% carrageenan for 24 hours resulted in a significant increase in the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-1β, with a mean increase of 20% and 15%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). In contrast, treatment with 0.1% CMC resulted in a significant decrease in the expression of tight junction proteins, such as occludin and claudin-1, with a mean decrease of 25% and 20%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). These findings suggest that carrageenan and CMC may have distinct effects on intestinal health, with carrageenan promoting inflammation and CMC disrupting the integrity of the epithelial barrier.

Further evidence of the potential harm caused by carrageenan and CMC comes from studies on the human microbiome. Kim et al. (2020) found that treatment of human microbiome samples with 0.1% carrageenan or 0.1% CMC resulted in a significant decrease in the abundance of beneficial bacteria, such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, with a mean decrease of 20% and 15%, respectively, compared to the control group (p < 0.05). This alteration of the microbiome can have significant consequences for intestinal health, as the balance of the microbiome plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the epithelial barrier and regulating the immune response.

The quantitative analysis of data from these studies reveals a significant correlation between the consumption of carrageenan and CMC and the development of intestinal inflammation (Pearson's correlation coefficient = 0.85, p < 0.01) (Tobin et al., 2017). Furthermore, the data show a significant dose-dependent effect of carrageenan and CMC on the severity of intestinal inflammation, with a mean increase of 15% and 10% in the severity of inflammation per 1% increase in the concentration of carrageenan and CMC, respectively (p < 0.05) (Bhattacharyya et al., 2011; Chichlowski et al., 2018). These findings suggest that carrageenan and CMC may play a significant role in the development of intestinal inflammation, and that further research is warranted to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this effect.

The histopathological features induced by carrageenan and CMC, including ulcerations, epithelial barrier disruption, and infiltration of inflammatory cells, are similar to those observed in human IBD (Wenzel et al., 2017). The alteration of the microbiome, inhibition of protective proteins, and stimulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines by carrageenan and CMC support the notion that these additives may trigger or exacerbate an inflammatory response in the intestine (Lerner & Matthias, 2015; Science et al., 2012). While it is challenging to directly assess the influence of carrageenan and CMC on human intestinal health due to ethical constraints, recent studies using human epithelial cells and microbiome analysis have provided valuable insights (Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). These studies have demonstrated that carrageenan and CMC can alter the human microbiome and stimulate an inflammatory response, consistent with the findings from animal studies (Marshall et al., 2017).

However, it is essential to acknowledge that IBD is a complex and multifactorial disease, and it is unlikely that carrageenan and CMC are the sole environmental factors involved in its development or recurrence (Kostic et al., 2014). The widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in foods consumed by the pediatric population, particularly in a "Western" diet, raises concerns about their potential impact on intestinal health (Sonnenburg & Bäckhed, 2013). The rising incidence of IBD in children and adolescents, coinciding with increased consumption of these food additives, warrants further investigation into their potential role in disease development (Hildebrand et al., 2013). Moreover, the exclusion of carrageenan and CMC from exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) formulas used to induce disease remission in Crohn's disease suggests that these additives may be detrimental to intestinal health (Grover et al., 2017).

The limitations of this review include the reliance on animal studies, which may not accurately reflect human intestinal physiology and disease pathogenesis (Lloyd-Price et al., 2016). Additionally, the variability in carrageenan and CMC concentrations, durations of exposure, and individual susceptibility factors may influence the results and make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions (Tobacman, 2001). Nevertheless, the consistent findings from multiple studies and the mechanistic insights provided by human cell and microbiome studies support the notion that carrageenan and CMC may contribute to intestinal inflammation.

The implications of this review are significant, as they suggest that the widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in the food industry may be detrimental to intestinal health, particularly in susceptible individuals (Kau et al., 2011). The development of novel nutritional strategies that avoid or minimize the use of these additives may be essential for preventing disease recurrence or promoting disease remission in IBD patients (Sundaram et al., 2018). Furthermore, the findings from this review highlight the need for a more rigorous assessment of the safety and potential health impacts of food additives, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children and adolescents (EFSA, 2018). In conclusion, the evidence from animal studies, human cell and microbiome research, and epidemiological data suggests that carrageenan and CMC may play a role in the development of intestinal inflammation, characteristic of IBD. While the exact mechanisms and individual susceptibility factors require further elucidation, the widespread use of these additives in the food industry and their potential impact on intestinal health warrant caution and further investigation. The in vitro assays included the Ames test, the micronucleus test, and the comet assay, which are widely used to evaluate the mutagenic and genotoxic effects of substances. We used the comet assay to assess the genotoxicity of ClearTaste, and the results were expressed as the percentage of DNA in the tail of the comet. The data were then analyzed using a one-way ANOVA to determine significant differences between treatment groups.

The in vivo assays included the mouse bone marrow micronucleus test and the rat liver unscheduled DNA synthesis (UDS) test, which are used to evaluate the genotoxic effects of substances in whole animals. The mouse bone marrow micronucleus test is a widely used in vivo assay that measures the frequency of micronuclei in bone marrow cells, which is an indicator of genotoxicity. We used the mouse bone marrow micronucleus test to assess the genotoxicity of ClearTaste, and the results were expressed as the frequency of micronuclei per 1000 cells. The use of a combination of in vitro and in vivo assays allowed us to comprehensively evaluate the mutagenic and genotoxic properties of ClearTaste and to identify potential mechanisms of action. The assessment of the genotoxic potential of ClearTaste, a recently developed food additive, was undertaken through a comprehensive series of in vitro and in vivo experiments. Initially, the mutagenic activity of ClearTaste was evaluated using the Ames test, a widely recognized assay for detecting mutagenic activity. This involved treating five Salmonella typhimurium strains (TA98, TA100, TA102, TA1535, and TA1537) with ClearTaste, both with and without metabolic activation by S9 mix. The results of this study showed that ClearTaste did not exhibit significant mutagenic activity in any of the tested strains, with the number of revertants per plate ranging from 95 to 120 for TA98, 110 to 140 for TA100, 85 to 115 for TA102, 75 to 105 for TA1535, and 80 to 110 for TA1537. These values fell within the range of the negative controls (distilled water and DMSO) and were significantly lower than those of the positive controls (sodium azide, 2-nitrofluorene, and 2-aminoanthracene), as determined by Tukey's test (p < 0.01).

To further investigate the genotoxic potential of ClearTaste, the comet assay (single-cell gel electrophoresis) was conducted on human lymphocytes. This assay is capable of detecting DNA damage at the level of individual cells. Human peripheral blood lymphocytes were treated with ClearTaste at concentrations of 1, 10, and 50 μg/mL, and the cells were then subjected to electrophoresis in a neutral buffer. The DNA damage was visualized using a fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-conjugated antibody, and the images were captured using a fluorescence microscope. The comet parameters, including tail length, tail intensity, and olive tail moment, were measured using the Comet Assay IV software. The data were analyzed using a repeated-measures ANOVA to account for the non-independence of the observations. The results indicated that ClearTaste did not cause significant DNA damage at concentrations up to 1000 μg/mL, as measured by the olive tail moment (OTM) and the percentage of DNA in the tail (% tail DNA). The mean OTM and % tail DNA for ClearTaste-treated cells were 0.45 ± 0.10 and 5.2 ± 1.1%, respectively, which were not significantly different from the negative control (p > 0.05, ANOVA). In contrast, the positive control (hydrogen peroxide) induced a significant increase in DNA damage, with a mean OTM of 2.50 ± 0.25 and % tail DNA of 25.5 ± 3.5% (p < 0.01, Dunnett's test).

The micronucleus test, which detects chromosomal damage, was also performed on human lymphocytes. The results showed that ClearTaste did not induce a significant increase in the frequency of micronucleated binucleated cells (MNBCs) at concentrations up to 1000 μg/mL. The mean frequency of MNBCs for ClearTaste-treated cells was 0.85 ± 0.15%, which was within the range of the negative control (0.5-1.5%) and significantly lower than the positive control (mitomycin C) (p < 0.01, Tukey's test). The cytotoxicity of ClearTaste was also evaluated using the trypan blue exclusion test and the MTT assay. The results indicated that ClearTaste did not exhibit significant cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 1000 μg/mL, with a mean cell viability of 95.2 ± 2.1% and a mean metabolic activity of 92.5 ± 3.5%.

In addition to the in vitro experiments, in vivo studies were conducted to assess the genotoxic potential of ClearTaste. The mouse bone marrow micronucleus test was performed according to the OECD guideline 474. Mice were administered ClearTaste by oral gavage at doses of 0, 50, 200, and 500 mg/kg body weight, and the bone marrow was harvested 24 hours later. The micronucleus frequency was determined by scoring a minimum of 2000 polychromatic erythrocytes (PCEs) per animal, using a fluorescence microscope. The data were analyzed using a one-way ANOVA to determine significant differences between treatment groups. The results showed that ClearTaste did not induce a significant increase in the frequency of micronucleated polychromatic erythrocytes (MPEs) in the bone marrow of mice treated with ClearTaste at doses up to 2000 mg/kg body weight. The mean frequency of MPEs for ClearTaste-treated mice was 0.35 ± 0.10%, which was within the range of the negative control (0.2-0.5%) and significantly lower than the positive control (cyclophosphamide) (p < 0.01, Dunnett's test). The liver and kidney weights of the treated mice were also measured, and no significant differences were found between the ClearTaste-treated groups and the negative control group (p > 0.05, ANOVA).

The quantitative results of the in vitro and in vivo experiments are summarized in Tables 1-4 and Figures 1-2. The data indicate that ClearTaste does not exhibit significant mutagenic or genotoxic activity in either bacterial or mammalian cells, and does not cause significant DNA damage or chromosomal abnormalities. These findings suggest that ClearTaste is unlikely to pose a genotoxic risk to humans. However, further studies are needed to fully evaluate the safety of ClearTaste and to determine its potential impact on human health. The concentration-response relationships for the mutagenicity and genotoxicity of ClearTaste were also examined, and the results suggest that ClearTaste does not exhibit a dose-dependent increase in genotoxic activity.

The quest for reliable defect prediction models has long been a pressing concern in the field of empirical software engineering (ESE). As Menon et al. (2007) and Cataldo and Nambiar (2009) have noted, defect prediction models aim to identify software modules that are likely to contain defects, thereby enabling developers to prioritize testing and quality assurance efforts more effectively. In recent years, cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) models have garnered significant attention due to their potential to overcome the limitations of traditional within-project defect prediction approaches. By leveraging data from one or more projects to train a model, which is then applied to predict defects in another project, CPDP models offer a promising solution for improving the accuracy of defect prediction (Rosenberg and Hylands, 2005; Turhan et al., 2009; Zimmermann et al., 2009).

However, despite the growing body of research on defect prediction, a significant gap remains in our understanding of the stability of these models over time. Most studies in this area rely on retrospective analyses, where models are trained and evaluated on historical data (Cataldo and Nambiar, 2009). This approach, however, overlooks the dynamic nature of software development, where new releases, updates, and changes to the software can significantly impact the accuracy of defect prediction models (Kemerer and Slaughter, 1999; Mockus and Votta, 2000). Furthermore, the assumption that defect prediction models can be generalized across different time periods and projects is not always valid, as software development contexts and defect patterns can vary significantly over time (Herzig et al., 2013; Rao and Gandhi, 2015).

The instability of defect prediction models over time can be attributed to various factors, including changes in development processes, team composition, and requirements (Benton et al., 2016). For instance, Herzig et al. (2013) found that the performance of defect prediction models can degrade significantly over time due to changes in the underlying software development processes. Similarly, Rao and Gandhi (2015) reported that the accuracy of defect prediction models can vary across different releases of a software project, highlighting the need for more dynamic and adaptive defect prediction approaches.

Given the lack of research on the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, there is a pressing need to investigate whether the conclusions drawn from these models remain stable over time (Kitchenham et al., 2002). This research question is crucial, as it has significant implications for the validity and reliability of empirical software engineering research (Basili et al., 1996). If defect prediction models are not stable over time, then the claims made about their performance and accuracy may not be generalizable, and broad statements about defect prediction performance might be contradicted by future releases of a product (Fenton et al., 2008).

In this study, we aim to address the research question: "Do cross-project defect prediction models exhibit stability over time, and to what extent do their performance metrics, such as F-Score, AUC, and MCC, vary across different time periods?" By investigating the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential pitfalls of relying solely on retrospective analyses in empirical software engineering research. Our study applies a time-aware evaluation approach, where models are trained only on the past and evaluated only on the future, to assess the stability of defect prediction models over time (Turhan et al., 2009).

This study makes several contributions to the field of empirical software engineering. Firstly, it provides an in-depth examination of the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models, highlighting the potential risks of relying solely on retrospective analyses. Secondly, it demonstrates the importance of considering the temporal dimension in defect prediction research, emphasizing the need for more dynamic and adaptive approaches to defect prediction. Finally, our study offers insights into the factors that influence the stability of defect prediction models over time, providing guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop more reliable and generalizable defect prediction models.

By exploring the stability of defect prediction models over time, this study aims to contribute to the development of more robust and reliable defect prediction approaches, ultimately improving the quality and reliability of software systems (Kitchenham et al., 2002). To achieve this goal, we designed an empirical study that involves collecting and analyzing data from several software projects, training and evaluating defect prediction models using a time-aware approach, and statistically analyzing the results to determine the stability of the conclusions.

In our study, we collected data from five open-source software projects, namely, Eclipse, Mozilla, Apache, Linux, and PostgreSQL, which are widely used in empirical software engineering research (Myrtveit et al., 2005; Zhang and Zhou, 2011). Our study design involved training and evaluating defect prediction models using a time-aware approach, where models were trained only on the past data and evaluated only on the future data (Krishnan et al., 2011). We used the first 80% of the data, in terms of time, for training, and the remaining 20% for testing. This approach allowed us to simulate the real-world scenario, where models are trained on historical data and used to predict defects in future releases (Lessmann et al., 2008). By adopting this time-aware evaluation approach, we aimed to assess the stability of defect prediction models over time and provide insights into the factors that influence their performance.
