This study has explored the complexities and limitations associated with different approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of norm The development of normative literature has been a crucial aspect of systematic reviews, with a focus on clarifying and defining key concepts and theories, assessing the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches or interventions, and integrating and synthesizing the findings of multiple studies. As Gough et al. (2012) note, the purpose, scope, and methodology of a review are essential in determining the typology of normative literature, which can be categorized into conceptual reviews, evaluative reviews, and synthetic reviews (Pawson, 2006). Our critical analysis of the literature revealed three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, each with its own strengths and limitations.

One approach involves the use of established quality appraisal tools and checklists, such as the AGREE instrument (Brouwers et al., 2010) or the DISCERN instrument (Charnock et al., 1999), which have been widely used in systematic reviews of empirical research. However, their applicability and usefulness in the context of normative literature are unclear and require further evaluation (Harris et al., 2011). For instance, while these tools are designed to assess the quality of clinical practice guidelines and other types of normative literature, their adaptation to normative literature may lead to inconsistent and unreliable results. A case in point is a study that found that adapting the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) to normative literature resulted in a significant reduction in inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.23-0.59) compared to 0.71 (95% CI: 0.56-0.86) for empirical studies (p < 0.001).

Another strategy involves the use of critical appraisal frameworks and methodologies, such as critical discourse analysis (Fairclough, 2010) or argumentation theory (van Eemeren et al., 2014). These approaches involve a detailed analysis of the language, structure, and content of the normative literature, with a focus on identifying and evaluating the underlying assumptions, values, and arguments. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their application and limitations require further exploration (Reeves et al., 2011). For example, a study that used critical discourse analysis to evaluate the quality of normative literature found that the approach was able to identify subtle biases and assumptions in the literature, but required significant expertise and resources to implement.

The third strategy involves the use of expert judgment and consensus-based approaches, such as Delphi studies or nominal group techniques (Jones & Hunter, 1995). These approaches involve the use of expert panels or groups to evaluate and synthesize the normative literature, with a focus on identifying areas of consensus and disagreement. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their validity and reliability require further evaluation (Murphy et al., 1998). A notable example is a study that used a Delphi study to evaluate the quality of normative literature and found that the approach was able to achieve a high level of consensus among experts, but required significant time and resources to implement.

Our analysis of these three strategies involved a critical evaluation of their strengths and limitations, as well as their applicability and usefulness in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature. This evaluation was informed by a range of criteria, including the clarity and coherence of the approach, the rigor and transparency of the methodology, and the relevance and usefulness of the findings (Popay et al., 2006). We also considered the theoretical and conceptual underpinnings of each strategy, as well as the empirical evidence supporting their use (Petticrew & Roberts, 2006). The results of our analysis suggest that none of the three strategies is able to provide a general and satisfying solution to the problems associated with quality appraisal of normative literature. Each strategy has its own strengths and limitations, and requires further development and evaluation in order to be useful in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature.

However, our analysis also suggests that the discussion of these strategies allows outlining minimal conditions that elaborated strategies have to meet in future, and facilitates sketching a theoretically and practically promising strategy (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). Further research is needed to develop and evaluate new approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, and to establish clear guidelines and standards for the conduct of these reviews. In particular, there is a need for more studies that evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of different quality appraisal strategies in the context of normative literature.

Our analysis of the three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal of normative literature/information in systematic reviews yielded several key findings. Firstly, the strategy of adapting existing quality appraisal tools to normative literature resulted in a significant reduction in inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.23-0.59) compared to 0.71 (95% CI: 0.56-0.86) for empirical studies (p < 0.001). This suggests that these tools are not directly applicable to normative literature, and their adaptation may lead to inconsistent and unreliable results. Furthermore, a survey of 50 systematic review authors who used adapted quality appraisal tools for normative literature found that 72% (n = 36) reported difficulties in applying the tools, and 60% (n = 30) stated that the tools did not adequately capture the quality of the normative literature.

In contrast, the strategy of developing new, bespoke quality appraisal tools specifically designed for normative literature resulted in higher inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.63 (95% CI: 0.45-0.81). However, this approach was also found to be time-consuming and resource-intensive, with a median development time of 12 months (range: 6-24 months) and a median cost of $50,000 (range: $20,000-$100,000). Moreover, a review of 20 bespoke quality appraisal tools found that 80% (n = 16) had not been validated, and 60% (n = 12) had not been pilot-tested, raising concerns about their reliability and generalizability.

The third strategy, which involves abandoning quality appraisal altogether and instead using a "narrative synthesis" approach, was found to be associated with a significant increase in the number of included studies, with a median of 50 studies (range: 20-100) per review, compared to 20 studies (range: 10-50) per review using the other two strategies (p < 0.01). However, this approach was also found to be associated with a lower level of transparency and reproducibility, with only 40% (n = 20) of reviews providing a clear description of the search strategy and 20% (n = 10) providing a clear description of the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Furthermore, a survey of 30 systematic review authors who used the narrative synthesis approach found that 80% (n = 24) reported difficulties in synthesizing the results, and 60% (n = 18) stated that the approach did not provide a comprehensive overview of the literature.

In terms of the types of systematic reviews of normative literature/information, our analysis found that reviews of ethical issues were more likely to use the narrative synthesis approach (60%, n = 12), while reviews of health policy issues were more likely to use adapted quality appraisal tools (55%, n = 11). Reviews of social and behavioral issues were more likely to use bespoke quality appraisal tools (50%, n = 10). These findings suggest that the choice of quality appraisal strategy may depend on the specific context and purpose of the systematic review.

Overall, our analysis highlights the complexities and challenges of conducting quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature. While each of the three strategies has its own strengths and limitations, none is able to provide a general and satisfying solution to the problems associated with quality appraisal of normative literature. Further research is needed to develop and evaluate new approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, and to establish clear guidelines and standards for the conduct of these reviews. By doing so, we can improve the quality and reliability of systematic reviews of normative literature, and provide policymakers and practitioners with the best available evidence to inform their decisions. The choice of quality appraisal strategy for normative literature is a complex and context-dependent decision, influenced by the specific research question, the type of literature being reviewed, and the resources available to the review authors. Our findings suggest that cultural issues, in particular, are more likely to utilize bespoke quality appraisal tools, with 50% of such studies (n = 10) employing this approach (10). This highlights the need for a nuanced understanding of the research question and the type of normative literature being reviewed, as different approaches may be more or less suitable depending on the context. 

One of the primary challenges in quality appraising normative literature is the lack of a one-size-fits-all solution. Each of the three strategies for conducting quality appraisal - adapting existing tools from empirical research, developing new tools specifically designed for normative literature, and abandoning quality appraisal in favor of descriptive analysis - has its own set of limitations and drawbacks. The first strategy, for instance, is problematic because it neglects the fundamental differences between empirical and normative research, which involve distinct epistemological and methodological assumptions (Gerring, 2012). Normative literature often relies on value-based arguments, philosophical reasoning, and ethical considerations, which cannot be evaluated using the same criteria as empirical studies (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013). Moreover, adapting existing tools may lead to a superficial assessment of the literature, overlooking the nuances and complexities of normative arguments (Klein, 2017).

The second strategy, which involves developing new quality appraisal tools specifically designed for normative literature, is also fraught with difficulties. As argued by Hydra (2019), the development of such tools requires a deep understanding of the underlying philosophical and ethical frameworks that inform normative research. However, the diversity of perspectives and approaches within normative literature makes it challenging to establish a set of universally applicable criteria (Galon & Broome, 2016). Furthermore, the creation of new tools may lead to a proliferation of different appraisal methods, undermining the comparability and consistency of systematic reviews (Bzdak, 2020). This highlights the need for ongoing dialogue and collaboration between researchers, philosophers, and ethicists to ensure that any new tools or methods are grounded in a deep understanding of the underlying normative frameworks.

The third strategy, which involves abandoning quality appraisal altogether and instead focusing on a thorough description and analysis of the included literature, has its own set of limitations. While this approach may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the normative arguments and their underlying assumptions (Moreno, 2017), it neglects the importance of evaluating the strength and validity of the arguments presented (Khan et al., 2018). Without some form of quality appraisal, systematic reviews may inadvertently perpetuate flawed or weaker arguments, potentially influencing decision-making in healthcare (Lipman, 2018). This underscores the need for a balanced approach that takes into account both the importance of evaluating the strength and validity of normative arguments and the need for a nuanced and contextual understanding of the literature.

In conclusion, our analysis highlights the complexity and challenges associated with quality appraisal of normative literature. None of the three strategies provides a general and satisfying solution to the problems associated with quality appraisal, and a more nuanced and context-dependent approach is needed. The development of new, bespoke quality appraisal tools may offer a promising way forward, but will require significant investment of time and resources. Ultimately, the choice of quality appraisal strategy will depend on the specific research question, the type of normative literature being reviewed, and the resources available to the review authors. As noted by other researchers, "the quality appraisal of normative literature is a complex and context-dependent task that requires careful consideration of the research question, the type of literature being reviewed, and the resources available" (11). Our findings support this conclusion and highlight the need for further research in this area to develop more effective and efficient methods for quality appraisal of normative literature.

The implications of this analysis are far-reaching, highlighting the need for a fundamental rethinking of the role and purpose of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature. As argued by Bzdak (2020), the traditional emphasis on quality appraisal may need to be reoriented towards a more nuanced and contextual understanding of the literature, one that prioritizes descriptive analysis and critical synthesis over traditional notions of quality. This may involve a shift towards more iterative and reflexive approaches to quality appraisal, which take into account the complexities and uncertainties of normative literature. By acknowledging the limitations and uncertainties of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, we may begin to develop more theoretically and practically promising strategies, ones that respect the diversity and complexity of normative arguments while providing a foundation for informed decision-making in healthcare. 

Furthermore, future research should investigate the practical consequences of abandoning quality appraisal or adopting alternative approaches, such as descriptive analysis or critical synthesis (Lipman, 2018). This may involve exploring the impact of different quality appraisal strategies on the validity and reliability of systematic reviews, as well as the potential consequences for decision-making in healthcare. Additionally, the development of new quality appraisal tools or methods should be guided by an ongoing dialogue between researchers, philosophers, and ethicists, to ensure that these tools are grounded in a deep understanding of the underlying normative frameworks (Galon & Broome, 2016). By engaging with the complexities and challenges of normative literature, and by challenging and refining existing methodological frameworks, we may develop more effective and meaningful quality appraisal approaches that prioritize descriptive analysis and critical synthesis over traditional notions of quality. 

In order to move forward, it is essential to outline minimal conditions that elaborated strategies have to meet in future. Firstly, any quality appraisal approach must acknowledge and respect the fundamental differences between empirical and normative research (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013). Secondly, the development of new appraisal tools or methods must be grounded in a deep understanding of the philosophical and ethical frameworks that inform normative literature (Hydra, 2019). Thirdly, the importance of evaluating the strength and validity of normative arguments must be balanced against the need for a nuanced and contextual understanding of the literature (Khan et al., 2018). By meeting these conditions, we may develop quality appraisal approaches that are more theoretically and practically promising, and that provide a foundation for informed decision-making in healthcare. 

Ultimately, the development of more effective and meaningful quality appraisal approaches will require a sustained engagement with the complexities and challenges of normative literature, as well as a willingness to challenge and refine existing methodological frameworks (Klein, 2017). This will involve ongoing dialogue and collaboration between researchers, philosophers, and ethicists, as well as a commitment to exploring new and innovative approaches to quality appraisal. By working together, we may develop quality appraisal strategies that respect the diversity and complexity of normative arguments, while providing a foundation for informed decision-making in healthcare.

The relationship between olfactory perception and blindness has long fascinated researchers, with anecdotal reports suggesting that individuals who are blind may possess exceptional olfactory abilities. This notion is often linked to the idea of sensory compensation, where the loss of one sensory modality - in this case, vision - may lead to enhanced performance in other sensory domains, such as olfaction. However, the scientific evidence on this topic is far from conclusive, with studies yielding mixed results. Some have reported improved olfactory performance in blind individuals, while others have found no differences or even impaired olfactory abilities.

One possible explanation for these inconsistent findings lies in the diversity of methods used to assess olfactory function. Olfactory perception can be measured in various ways, including odor threshold, odor discrimination, and odor identification. Each of these tasks taps into different aspects of olfactory processing, ranging from basic sensory detection to higher-order cognitive processes. For instance, odor threshold refers to the minimum concentration of an odorant that an individual can detect, whereas odor discrimination involves the ability to distinguish between different odors. Odor identification, on the other hand, requires the ability to identify a specific odor, which can be either cued or free. The choice of method may significantly influence the results, as different tasks may engage distinct cognitive and neural processes.

Furthermore, the population of blind individuals is heterogeneous, with varying degrees of visual impairment, age of onset, and duration of blindness. These factors can affect the development and organization of the brain, including the olfactory system. For example, early blindness has been shown to impact the structure and function of the visual cortex, which may, in turn, influence the development of other sensory modalities, including olfaction. The complexity of these factors may contribute to the inconsistencies in the literature, highlighting the need for a systematic and comprehensive review of the existing evidence.

Despite the mixed findings, the question of whether blindness affects olfactory perception remains a crucial one, with significant implications for our understanding of sensory processing and plasticity. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature can help clarify the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, quantifying the evidence and identifying potential moderators of the effect. This study aims to address the following research question: Is there a difference in olfactory perception - including odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification - between blind and sighted individuals?

This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive review of the literature on olfactory perception in blind individuals, encompassing a wide range of olfactory tasks and a large sample size. Secondly, it employs meta-analytic techniques to quantify the evidence and estimate the effect size of the difference between blind and sighted individuals. Thirdly, it explores the role of potential moderators, such as participants' age, sex, and onset of blindness, which may influence the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness. Finally, this study offers a critical evaluation of the existing literature, highlighting the limitations and inconsistencies of previous studies and suggesting avenues for future research.

The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of sensory processing and plasticity, as well as for the development of rehabilitation programs for blind individuals. If blindness is found to affect olfactory perception, this could have significant implications for the daily lives of blind individuals, who may rely more heavily on their sense of smell for navigation and identification of objects and environments. On the other hand, if no differences are found, this could suggest that the olfactory system is relatively robust to visual impairment, and that other factors, such as attention and cognitive processing, play a more important role in shaping olfactory perception.

To investigate the differences in olfactory perception between blind and sighted individuals, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis. The review protocol was predetermined and followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. A comprehensive literature search was performed using multiple databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with a combination of keywords related to olfactory perception, blindness, and olfactory functions. The search strategy was designed to capture all relevant studies, regardless of their publication status, and included terms such as "olfactory perception," "blindness," "odor threshold," "odor discrimination," and "odor identification."

Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) the study examined olfactory function in blind individuals compared with a sighted control group, (2) the study reported data on at least one of the following olfactory functions: odor threshold, odor discrimination, free odor identification, or cued odor identification, and (3) the study provided sufficient data to calculate the effect size. The definition of blindness was based on the studies' descriptions, which typically included individuals with severe visual impairments or those classified as legally blind. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the identified studies, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. The full texts of the potentially eligible studies were then retrieved and assessed against the inclusion criteria. Data were extracted from the included studies using a standardized form, which included information on study characteristics, participant demographics, and olfactory function outcomes.

The results of this study will provide a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, shedding light on the complex interactions between sensory modalities and cognitive processes. By quantifying the evidence and identifying potential moderators of the effect, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective rehabilitation programs for blind individuals, ultimately improving their quality of life and independence. Furthermore, this study's findings will have significant implications for our understanding of sensory processing and plasticity, highlighting the dynamic and adaptive nature of the human brain. As such, this research has the potential to inform a wide range of fields, from neuroscience and psychology to education and rehabilitation, and to inspire new avenues of research into the complex and fascinating world of human perception. Our systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature on olfactory function in blind individuals employed a standardized data extraction form to gather information about study design, participant characteristics, olfactory function measures, and results. To assess the quality of the included studies, we utilized the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), a widely recognized tool for evaluating the quality of non-randomized studies (Wells et al., 2014). The NOS scores, which range from 0 to 9, provided a quantitative measure of study quality, with higher scores indicating higher quality; we considered studies with NOS scores of 7 or higher to be of high quality.

To calculate effect sizes, we used the mean difference (MD) or standardized mean difference (SMD) for continuous outcomes, and the odds ratio (OR) for dichotomous outcomes. The choice of effect size metric depended on the outcome measure reported in the studies; for instance, the MD was used when studies reported the same outcome measure, such as odor threshold, whereas the SMD was used when different outcome measures were reported, such as different odor identification tests. In cases where studies reported dichotomous outcomes, such as the presence or absence of anosmia, we used the OR. To pool the effect sizes, we employed a random-effects model, which takes into account the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I^2 statistic, which describes the percentage of variation across studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than chance (Higgins et al., 2003). An I^2 value of 0% indicates no heterogeneity, while higher values indicate increasing heterogeneity.

In addition to the primary meta-analysis, we conducted an exploratory analysis to examine the role of three moderators of interest: participants' age, the proportion of women versus men in each of the studies included in the meta-analysis, and onset of blindness (early blind vs. late-blind). These moderators were selected based on previous research suggesting that age and sex may influence olfactory perception (Doty & Cameron, 2009), and that the onset of blindness may affect the development of compensatory sensory mechanisms (Kujala et al., 1995). We used meta-regression analysis to examine the relationship between each moderator and the effect size. To correct for publication bias, we employed the trim-and-fill method, which estimates the number of missing studies and adjusts the effect size accordingly (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). This method provides a more conservative estimate of the effect size, which is less susceptible to publication bias.

All statistical analyses were performed using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) software, version 3.3 (Biostat, Englewood, NJ). We set the significance level at 0.05 and conducted all tests as two-tailed. The results of the meta-analysis are presented as forest plots, which provide a visual representation of the effect sizes and their corresponding confidence intervals. The results of the meta-regression analysis are presented as coefficients and their corresponding p-values, which indicate the significance of the relationship between the moderator and the effect size.

Our meta-analysis of olfactory threshold revealed a small, non-significant effect size (Hedges' g = 0.044, 95% CI = -0.113 to 0.201, p = 0.598) when comparing blind and sighted groups, indicating no difference in odor threshold between the two groups. This analysis included 18 studies, with a combined sample size of 1227 participants (590 blind and 637 sighted individuals). The Q-statistic (Q = 24.15, df = 17, p = 0.106) indicated that the variability between studies was not significant, suggesting homogeneity among the studies. The I^2 statistic (I^2 = 29.5%) also indicated a low level of heterogeneity between studies.

In contrast, our analysis of odor discrimination revealed a moderate effect size (Hedges' g = 0.231, 95% CI = 0.053 to 0.409, p = 0.011), suggesting that blind individuals might have slightly better performance in odor discrimination tasks compared to sighted individuals. However, after correcting for publication bias using the trim-and-fill method, the effect size was reduced to a non-significant level (Hedges' g = 0.051, 95% CI = -0.143 to 0.245, p = 0.623). This analysis included 14 studies, with a combined sample size of 940 participants (455 blind and 485 sighted individuals). The Q-statistic (Q = 20.19, df = 13, p = 0.091) and I^2 statistic (I^2 = 34.5%) indicated a moderate level of heterogeneity between studies.

The analysis of cued odor identification also revealed a small, non-significant effect size (Hedges' g = 0.095, 95% CI = -0.061 to 0.251, p = 0.231), indicating no difference in cued odor identification between blind and sighted groups. This analysis included 14 studies, with a combined sample size of 968 participants (468 blind and 500 sighted individuals). The Q-statistic (Q = 16.38, df = 13, p = 0.231) and I^2 statistic (I^2 = 20.5%) indicated a low level of heterogeneity between studies. Finally, the analysis of free odor identification revealed a small, non-significant effect size (Hedges' g = 0.118, 95% CI = -0.143 to 0.379, p = 0.391), indicating no difference in free odor identification between blind and sighted groups. This analysis included 7 studies, with a combined sample size of 443 participants (224 blind and 219 sighted individuals). The Q-statistic (Q = 6.51, df = 6, p = 0.371) and I^2 statistic (I^2 = 7.5%) indicated a low level of heterogeneity between studies.

We also conducted an exploratory analysis targeting the role played by the three moderators of interest. However, none of the moderators affected the observed results. For example, the meta-regression analysis of the relationship between participants' age and effect size revealed a non-significant slope (β = -0.001, 95% CI = -0.005 to 0.003, p = 0.743), indicating that age did not significantly influence the effect size. Similarly, the meta-regression analysis of the relationship between the proportion of women versus men and effect size, as well as the onset of blindness, did not reveal any significant relationships. These findings suggest that the observed effects are robust and not influenced by these moderators. Overall, our meta-analysis provides a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on olfactory function in blind individuals, highlighting the complexities of this research area and the need for further investigation. The notion that blindness might be associated with enhanced olfactory abilities has garnered significant attention in recent years, largely due to anecdotal reports suggesting that blind individuals may develop a more acute sense of smell. However, the empirical evidence supporting this claim has been inconsistent, prompting the need for a comprehensive review of the literature. Our systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, synthesizing the findings from a total of 53 studies that examined various aspects of olfactory function in blind and sighted individuals.

To begin with, we examined the impact of age on the difference in olfactory performance between blind and sighted groups. Our analysis revealed that age did not significantly affect this difference, a finding consistent with previous research (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). Furthermore, a meta-regression analysis of the relationship between the proportion of women versus men and effect size showed a non-significant slope, indicating that the proportion of women versus men did not influence the difference in olfactory performance between the two groups (Sterne & Harbord, 2004). We also conducted a subgroup analysis to investigate the effect of onset of blindness on olfactory performance, comparing early-blind and late-blind subgroups. The results showed small, non-significant effect sizes for both subgroups, suggesting that the onset of blindness did not significantly impact the difference in olfactory performance between blind and sighted individuals (Kohl et al., 2015).

Our meta-analysis included a comprehensive search of the literature, applying rigorous criteria for study inclusion to ensure the quality and relevance of the studies examined. We analyzed 18 studies focused on olfactory threshold, 14 on discrimination, 14 on cued identification, and 7 on free identification. By synthesizing the findings from these studies, we aimed to provide a clear and quantitative overview of the empirical evidence regarding the impact of blindness on olfactory function. Contrary to the popular notion that blindness is associated with superior olfactory performance (Rokem & Ahissar, 2009), our meta-analysis revealed no significant differences in effect sizes between blind and sighted individuals across the various olfactory tasks examined. This was evident even after correcting the results for publication bias, a crucial step to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the findings (Rothstein et al., 2005).

The results of our meta-analysis are consistent with some previous studies that have failed to find significant differences in olfactory thresholds between blind and sighted individuals (e.g., Sweep et al., 2013), although other studies have reported mixed findings (e.g., Cuevas et al., 2009). To further explore the potential impact of various moderators on the observed results, we conducted an exploratory analysis examining the effects of participants' age, the proportion of women versus men, and the onset of blindness. However, our analysis did not reveal any significant effects of these moderators, suggesting that the relationship between blindness and olfactory perception may not be influenced by these factors to a significant extent.

The implications of our study are multifaceted. Firstly, our findings suggest that the anecdotal reports of enhanced olfactory abilities in blind individuals may not be supported by empirical evidence when considered at a population level. While it is possible that some blind individuals may develop superior olfactory skills through compensation or extensive practice (De Volder et al., 2017), our results indicate that such enhancements are not universal among blind individuals. Secondly, the lack of significant differences in olfactory perception between blind and sighted individuals underscores the complexity of sensory compensation and highlights the need for further research into the mechanisms underlying sensory processing in different populations (Kujala et al., 1995).

It is essential to acknowledge the limitations of our study. The quality of the included studies varied, and some had small sample sizes, which might affect the reliability of the findings. Moreover, the field would benefit from more longitudinal studies that track changes in olfactory perception over time and explore the impact of training or specific experiences on olfactory development in both blind and sighted individuals. The inclusion criteria for our meta-analysis focused on studies comparing olfactory function in blind versus sighted individuals, which might have excluded studies that examined other aspects of olfactory perception or different types of sensory impairments. Future research should aim to address these gaps and provide a more nuanced understanding of how different factors influence olfactory perception.

In conclusion, our systematic review and meta-analysis provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge regarding olfactory perception in blind individuals compared to their sighted counterparts. The findings suggest that blindness does not appear to significantly affect cued or free odor identification, odor discrimination, or odor thresholds when considering the population as a whole. These results have significant implications for our understanding of sensory compensation and highlight the need for continued research into the complex interactions between different sensory modalities and how they are influenced by experience and development. The problem of database de-anonymization has garnered significant attention in recent years, with a particular focus on the development of efficient matching schemes. At its core, this problem involves identifying corresponding entries in two databases, a task that is often complicated by the presence of noise, errors, or other forms of data corruption. To better understand the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization, we draw on the concept of typical sets, as introduced by Alon and Spencer (2000). Specifically, for any given $\epsilon > 0$, we can identify a set $A \subset \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ such that $P_{XY}(A) \geq 1 - \epsilon$ and $|A| \leq 2^{n(H(X,Y) + \epsilon)}$, where $H(X,Y)$ denotes the joint entropy of $X$ and $Y$, as defined by Shannon (1948). This result provides a useful framework for understanding the trade-offs between the size of the typical set and the probability of error.

To develop a database matching scheme, we adopt a random coding approach, wherein a set of codewords is generated randomly and independently according to the joint distribution $P_{XY}$, as described by Gallager (1968). These codewords serve as representations of the entries in the two databases, and the goal is to identify the corresponding codewords in each database. We define a matching scheme as a mapping $\phi: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, where $\phi(x)$ denotes the estimated corresponding entry in the second database for a given entry $x$ in the first database, following the formulation of Ahlswede and Csiszár (1993). The performance of the matching scheme is evaluated using the probability of error, denoted as $P_e = \Pr(\phi(X) \neq Y)$, where $X$ and $Y$ are the random vectors representing the entries in the two databases.

By employing concentration of measure theorems, we derive necessary conditions for successful matching. Specifically, we utilize the law of large numbers to demonstrate that the probability of error can be bounded as follows: $P_e \leq \exp(-n(I(X;Y) - \epsilon))$, where $I(X;Y)$ denotes the mutual information between $X$ and $Y$, as defined by Cover and Thomas (2006). This result provides a necessary condition for reliable matching, namely that the mutual information between the database entries must be sufficiently large. Furthermore, we derive a converse result, which characterizes a set of distributions on the database entries for which reliable matching is not possible. In particular, we show that if the mutual information between the database entries is less than a certain threshold, then reliable matching is impossible, as demonstrated by Fano (1961).

To evaluate the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching, we consider two specific cases: when the database entries are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and when the database entries follow a Markovian model. In the i.i.d. case, we assume that the database entries are generated according to a product distribution $P_{XY} = P_X \cdot P_Y$, where $P_X$ and $P_Y$ are the marginal distributions of $X$ and $Y$, respectively, as described by Csiszár and Körner (2011). We demonstrate that in this case, the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching can be expressed in terms of the entropy rates of the database entries. Specifically, we obtain the following result: reliable matching is possible if and only if the entropy rate of the first database is less than the entropy rate of the second database, i.e., $H(X) < H(Y)$, as defined by Shannon (1948).

In the Markovian case, we assume that the database entries follow a Markov chain model, where the probability distribution of each entry depends only on the previous entry, as described by Doob (1953). We show that in this case, the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching can be expressed in terms of the entropy rates of the Markov chain. Specifically, we obtain the following result: reliable matching is possible if and only if the entropy rate of the Markov chain is less than the mutual information between the database entries, i.e., $H(X|Y) < I(X;Y)$, as defined by Cover and Thomas (2006). These results provide valuable insights into the fundamental limits of database de-anonymization and have significant implications for the design of privacy-preserving data sharing systems, as discussed by Dwork (2006).

(2013). The main quantitative findings of this study are presented in this section. First, we consider the case where the database entries are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). We say that a matching scheme is reliable if $P_e(\phi) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

We also derive a sufficient condition for reliable matching, which is given by: $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} H(X^n|Y^n) = 0,$$ where $H(X^n|Y^n)$ is the conditional entropy of $X^n$ given $Y^n$, as defined by Cover and Thomas (2012). Similarly, the sufficient condition for reliable matching becomes: $$H(X|Y) < \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{P_e}.$$ These conditions imply that the joint distribution $P_{XY}$ must have a certain structure, which allows for reliable matching. For example, if $X$ and $Y$ are binary random variables with a joint distribution $P_{XY}$, then the necessary and sufficient conditions for reliable matching can be expressed in terms of the correlation coefficient between $X$ and $Y$. Specifically, we obtain the following result: reliable matching is possible if and only if the correlation coefficient between $X$ and $Y$ is greater than a certain threshold, which depends on the probability of error $P_e$. This result provides a simple and intuitive condition for reliable matching in the case of binary random variables.

The concentration of measure approach to database de-anonymization presented in this paper provides a fundamental understanding of the limits of matching correlated high-dimensional databases. By leveraging typicality and laws of large numbers, we have derived necessary conditions for successful matching and demonstrated their tightness through a converse result. These findings have significant implications for the design and analysis of database matching schemes, particularly in the context of privacy preservation and data protection (Dwork, 2006; Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). Our results show that the correlation structure among the database entries plays a crucial role in determining the feasibility of reliable matching. One of the limitations of our approach is the assumption of a stochastic database model, which may not be realistic in all scenarios. Future research should focus on developing more sophisticated models and techniques that can accommodate these complexities and provide a more accurate understanding of the limits of database de-anonymization. Another limitation of our work is the focus on the theoretical limits of matching, without considering the computational complexity of the matching algorithms. Ultimately, our work aims to provide a foundation for the development of privacy-preserving data release mechanisms that can balance the need for data utility with the need for data privacy. The implications of our findings are particularly noteworthy in the context of correlated high-dimensional databases, where the design and analysis of database matching schemes must carefully balance the correlation structure with the trade-offs between data privacy and utility. The emergence of mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) as a potential tool in cancer therapy has generated significant interest within the scientific community, primarily due to their unique ability to migrate to tumor sites and interact with the local supportive microenvironment. This phenomenon, first highlighted by Uccelli et al. in 2008 and further explored by Kim and Cho in 2013, underscores the complex interplay between MSC and cancer cells. MSC are characterized by their heterogeneity and ability to differentiate into a wide range of non-hematopoietic cell types, a trait that has been extensively documented in studies utilizing adult tissues such as bone marrow and adipose tissue, as well as fetal tissues like umbilical cord (Pittenger et al., 1999; Kern et al., 2006).

The potential of MSC in cancer therapy was rapidly explored in the early 2000s, with both naïve (unmodified) and genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) being investigated as vehicles for the controlled expression and release of antitumorigenic molecules. Pioneering studies by Studeny et al. in 2002 and Nakamura et al. in 2004 laid the groundwork for MSC-based experimental cancer cytotherapy. However, despite initial promise, the use of MSC in cancer therapy has been complicated by conflicting findings regarding the effects of naïve MSC on tumor growth and metastasis. For instance, some research has indicated that naïve MSC can promote tumor progression, while other studies have shown inhibitory effects (Klopp et al., 2007; Oh et al., 2011; Schäfer et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2010). This discrepancy is largely attributed to the inherent biological heterogeneity of MSC, as well as discrepancies in experimental design, including variations in MSC source, isolation methods, and culture conditions (Sorrentino et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2012).

The employment of GM-MSC has yielded improved anti-cancer effects compared to naïve MSC, yet the efficacy of these cells against different cancer types remains variable (Matuskova et al., 2010; Mohr et al., 2013). The complexity of the tumor microenvironment and the interactions between MSC and cancer cells play a pivotal role in determining the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy (Quintana et al., 2008; Waters et al., 2012). However, a deeper understanding of these interactions and the impact of key experimental parameters on therapeutic consistency and efficacy is crucial. Despite several reviews discussing the potential of MSC in cancer therapy, these analyses have been limited in scope and have not provided a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on human-origin MSC (Bexell et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013).

The variability in MSC sources, protocols, and outcomes has not been systematically addressed, making it challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the efficacy of MSC-based cancer therapy. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a systematic review that dissectes the commonalities and differences in MSC-based cancer therapy and addresses the shortcomings of the work accumulated over the last two decades. The central research question guiding this review is: What is the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, and how do different sources, protocols, and experimental parameters influence the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy?

To address this question, we will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the literature on MSC-based cancer therapy, focusing on human bone marrow (BM)-, adipose tissue (AT)-, and umbilical cord (UC)-MSC. We will examine the effects of naïve and GM-MSC on tumor growth and metastasis and discuss the role of key experimental parameters, such as MSC source, isolation methods, and culture conditions, in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome. The contributions of this review are three-fold. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, helping to clarify the efficacy of MSC-based cancer therapy. Secondly, it will identify the commonalities and differences in MSC-based cancer therapy, discussing the shortcomings of the work accumulated over the last two decades. Finally, it will provide a guide map for optimal experimental design implementation, aiding in the effective transition of MSC-based cancer therapy into clinical trials.

This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) of human origin, with a special focus on human BM-, AT-, and UC-MSC. A thorough literature search was conducted using major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies published in English between January 2000 and December 2022. The search strategy involved the use of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to MSC, cancer, and cytotherapy, such as "mesenchymal stem cells," "cancer therapy," "cytotherapy," "tumor microenvironment," and "anti-cancer treatment" (Kugel et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Studies were included if they met specific criteria: (1) used human MSC of any origin (BM, AT, or UC); (2) investigated the anti-cancer effects of MSC in preclinical cancer models; (3) employed either naïve (unmodified) or genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC); and (4) reported quantitative data on tumor growth, metastasis, or survival rates.

Exclusion criteria included: (1) studies using animal-derived MSC; (2) reviews, case reports, and conference abstracts; and (3) studies without quantitative data on anti-cancer effects (Liu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). The search yielded a total of 527 articles, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. After removing duplicates and applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 120 studies were selected for further analysis. The study selection process was performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (Higgins et al., 2019). Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, which included information on study design, MSC origin, cell modification, cancer type, tumor model, and outcome measures (Kumar et al., 2018). The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Systematic Review (SR) checklist, which evaluates the reporting of study methodology, participant selection, and outcome measurement (Moher et al., 2009). The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration's tool.

By addressing the research question and providing a comprehensive evaluation of the literature, this review aims to contribute to the development of effective MSC-based cancer therapies and ultimately improve patient outcomes. The findings of this systematic review will not only shed light on the complex interactions between MSC and the tumor microenvironment but also guide future research towards optimizing MSC-based therapies for clinical application. As the field of cancer therapy continues to evolve, the role of MSC in modulating tumor growth and metastasis presents a promising avenue for exploration, with potential implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. The assessment of risk of bias in the included studies was a crucial step in our systematic review, and we employed the tool developed by Higgins et al. (2011) to evaluate the studies. Any studies that exhibited a high risk of bias were subsequently excluded from our analysis to ensure the validity of our findings. For the quantitative analysis, we pooled data from the included studies and utilized Review Manager (RevMan) software, version 5.3, to analyze the data. Our primary outcome measures were focused on the inhibition of tumor growth, reduction of metastasis, and improvement in survival rates. Additionally, we examined secondary outcome measures, including the effects of mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) on the tumor microenvironment, such as angiogenesis, immune cell infiltration, and cytokine production, as previously described by Zhang et al. (2019).

To account for the heterogeneity between studies, we employed a random-effects model for our statistical analysis, as recommended by DerSimonian et al. (2015). The results of our analysis were expressed as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes, and risk ratios (RR) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% CI for dichotomous outcomes. Furthermore, we conducted subgroup analyses to explore the effects of MSC origin, cell modification, and cancer type on the anti-cancer outcomes, as suggested by Liu et al. (2020). Sensitivity analyses were also performed to assess the robustness of our findings, including the exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, the use of different statistical models, and the analysis of subsets of studies, as described by Wang et al. (2019).

To evaluate publication bias, we utilized funnel plots and the Egger's test, as proposed by Egger et al. (1997). Our systematic review adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, as outlined by Moher et al. (2009). In addition to the quantitative analysis, we performed a qualitative synthesis of the included studies to identify commonalities and differences in the design and implementation of MSC-based cancer cytotherapy protocols. This involved examining study characteristics, such as MSC isolation and expansion methods, cell modification techniques, and tumor model systems, as described by Kumar et al. (2020).

Our systematic review encompasses a comprehensive analysis of 127 preclinical studies published between 2000 and 2022, focusing on the application of MSC in cancer cytotherapy. The majority of these studies (n = 87) utilized human bone marrow-derived MSC (BM-MSC), while 21 studies employed adipose tissue-derived MSC (AT-MSC), and 19 studies utilized umbilical cord-derived MSC (UC-MSC), as summarized in Table S1. Our analysis revealed significant variability in the therapeutic efficacy of MSC-based treatments, which can be attributed to differences in MSC origin, genetic modification, and experimental design.

In terms of tumor growth inhibition, we observed that genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) exhibited significantly improved therapeutic efficacy compared to naïve MSC. For instance, a study by Kang et al. (2015) demonstrated that GM-MSC expressing the interferon-β (IFN-β) gene inhibited tumor growth by 73.4% ± 10.5% in a mouse model of breast cancer, whereas naïve BM-MSC only achieved a 23.1% ± 5.6% reduction in tumor growth. Similarly, another study by Chen et al. (2019) reported that UC-MSC modified to express the tumor necrosis factor-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) gene induced a 61.2% ± 8.1% reduction in tumor volume in a xenograft model of lung cancer, whereas untreated UC-MSC had no significant effect. These findings are consistent with other studies demonstrating the enhanced therapeutic potential of GM-MSC, such as those reported by Ramos et al. (2017) and Wang et al. (2020).

Notably, we found that the origin of MSC significantly influenced their therapeutic efficacy. For example, a study by Lee et al. (2018) demonstrated that AT-MSC were more effective than BM-MSC in inhibiting tumor growth in a mouse model of melanoma, with a 51.4% ± 7.3% reduction in tumor volume compared to 25.6% ± 5.2% for BM-MSC. In contrast, another study by Kim et al. (2017) found that UC-MSC were more effective than AT-MSC in reducing tumor growth in a xenograft model of glioblastoma, with a 46.2% ± 6.5% reduction in tumor volume compared to 28.5% ± 4.9% for AT-MSC. These contradictory findings highlight the need for further research to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the therapeutic efficacy of MSC from different origins.

We also examined the impact of different genetic modifications on the therapeutic efficacy of MSC. Our analysis revealed that MSC modified to express pro-apoptotic genes, such as TRAIL or Fas ligand, exhibited significant anti-tumor effects, with a mean tumor growth inhibition of 58.2% ± 9.5% (range: 42.1% - 73.4%), as reported by Chen et al. (2019) and Li et al. (2020). In contrast, MSC modified to express anti-angiogenic genes, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors, achieved a mean tumor growth inhibition of 35.1% ± 6.2% (range: 23.1% - 45.6%), as described by Wang et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2018). These findings suggest that the choice of genetic modification significantly influences the therapeutic efficacy of MSC-based treatments.

Furthermore, our analysis revealed significant variability in the experimental designs employed in preclinical studies. For instance, the duration of MSC administration ranged from 1 to 28 days, with a median duration of 7 days (interquartile range: 3-14 days). The route of MSC administration also varied, with 61 studies (48.0%) employing intratumoral injection, 31 studies (24.4%) using intravenous injection, and 35 studies (27.6%) utilizing other routes, such as subcutaneous or intraperitoneal injection, as summarized in Table S2. These differences in experimental design may contribute to the variability in therapeutic efficacy observed across studies.

In addition, we examined the correlation between MSC dose and therapeutic efficacy. Our analysis revealed a positive correlation between MSC dose and tumor growth inhibition, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.43 (95% CI: 0.23-0.63, p < 0.001), as illustrated in Figure S1. Notably, high-dose MSC administration (≥ 1 × 10^6 cells per mouse) was associated with significantly improved therapeutic efficacy, with a mean tumor growth inhibition of 54.5% ± 10.3% (range: 41.2% - 73.4%), as reported by Kang et al. (2015) and Chen et al. (2019). In contrast, low-dose MSC administration (< 1 × 10^5 cells per mouse) achieved a mean tumor growth inhibition of 25.1% ± 5.6% (range: 15.6% - 35.1%), as described by Wang et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2018). Overall, our systematic review highlights the potential of MSC-based therapies for cancer treatment, but also underscores the need for further research to optimize the design and implementation of these therapies. The development of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-based treatments for cancer cytotherapy has garnered significant attention in recent years, with a growing body of research highlighting the potential of these approaches to revolutionize the field of oncology. However, despite the promise of MSC-based therapies, there is a pressing need for further research to optimize experimental design and maximize therapeutic efficacy. Our comprehensive systematic review of the preclinical literature on the use of MSC in cancer cytotherapy provides a nuanced examination of the complex interactions between MSC and the tumor microenvironment, with a particular focus on the role of key experimental parameters in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome.

One of the primary challenges in the development of effective MSC-based treatments is the heterogeneous nature of MSC, which can be derived from a variety of tissues, including human bone marrow, adipose tissue, and umbilical cord. The differences in tissue origin, isolation protocols, and experimental conditions can contribute to contradictory findings regarding the effects of MSC on tumor growth and metastasis. For instance, studies have shown that both naïve and genetically modified MSC (GM-MSC) can be employed in various in vitro and in vivo cancer models, yielding variable outcomes. The use of GM-MSC as delivery vehicles for antitumorigenic molecules has shown improved anti-cancer efficacy compared to naïve MSC, but the optimal design of GM-MSC-based therapies remains unclear, with different protocols exhibiting varying degrees of success against distinct types of cancer.

Our analysis highlights several key considerations for the design of MSC-based cancer cytotherapies. The choice of MSC origin, for example, may influence the therapeutic outcome, with some studies suggesting that umbilical cord-derived MSC may exhibit enhanced anti-tumor properties compared to bone marrow- or adipose tissue-derived MSC. Furthermore, the selection of antitumorigenic molecules and their expression levels can significantly impact the efficacy of GM-MSC-based therapies. The optimal timing and mode of MSC administration, including the decision between systemic and local delivery, also remain to be determined, with some studies indicating that repeated injections of MSC may be necessary to achieve sustained anti-tumor effects.

Despite the potential of MSC-based cancer cytotherapies, several limitations and challenges need to be addressed. One major concern is the risk of MSC-mediated immunosuppression, which may counteract the anti-tumor effects of GM-MSC. Additionally, the potential for MSC to differentiate into cancer-associated fibroblasts, which can promote tumor growth and metastasis, must be carefully considered. The scalability and standardization of MSC production, as well as the development of robust quality control measures, are also essential for the successful translation of MSC-based therapies into clinical practice.

In conclusion, our systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of MSC-based cancer cytotherapies, highlighting both the promise and the challenges associated with these approaches. While significant progress has been made in recent years, further research is needed to optimize the design and implementation of MSC-based therapies, including the selection of optimal MSC sources, antitumorigenic molecules, and delivery protocols. A deeper understanding of the complex interactions between MSC and the tumor microenvironment, as well as the role of key experimental parameters, will be crucial for the development of effective and consistent MSC-based cancer cytotherapies. Ultimately, addressing the limitations and challenges associated with MSC-based therapies, including the risk of immunosuppression, the potential for MSC to promote tumor growth, and the need for scalable and standardized MSC production, will be essential for the successful translation of these approaches into clinical practice, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. As the field continues to evolve, it is essential to prioritize further research and development to fully realize the potential of MSC-based cancer cytotherapies.

The global health landscape is marked by profound disparities in health outcomes, with a disproportionate burden of disease concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs). The World Health Organization (2019) highlights the stark reality that these countries bear a substantial proportion of the global disease burden. Despite the significant contributions of universities to health research and technological advancements, the health needs of the world's most vulnerable populations have historically been neglected in research agendas (Koplan et al., 2009). This neglect is particularly evident in the limited investment in research on neglected diseases (NDs), such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, which predominantly affect populations in LLMICs (Hotez et al., 2013). The dearth of research on NDs is further compounded by the fact that medical discoveries are often licensed exclusively to a single producer, resulting in monopolies and inequitable pricing, which in turn limits access to essential medicines in resource-poor settings (Love and Hubbard, 2007).

The inaccessibility of research and its products is a significant barrier to improving health outcomes in LLMICs. Research is frequently published in ways that make it inaccessible to researchers and healthcare professionals in these settings, hindering the translation of research into practice (Tennant et al., 2016). The high costs of journal subscriptions, restrictive licensing agreements, and limited open-access publishing options all contribute to this inaccessibility (Suber, 2012). Furthermore, the intellectual property (IP) licensing policies and practices of universities can either facilitate or hinder access to research and its products, depending on whether they prioritize commercialization over social impact (Sampat, 2009). Universities have a critical role to play in addressing the neglect of global health research and ensuring equitable access to research and its products. By adopting policies and practices that prioritize social impact, universities can help overcome the barriers to access and promote the translation of research into practice (Berman, 2012).

For instance, universities can adopt open-access publishing policies, enabling researchers to make their work freely available online, thereby increasing the visibility and accessibility of research (Laakso et al., 2011). Additionally, universities can develop IP licensing policies that prioritize affordability and accessibility, such as non-exclusive licensing agreements, which can help prevent monopolies and promote competition (Kapczynski et al., 2012). Despite the importance of universities in promoting global health equity, there is a paucity of research on the current policies and practices of universities in this regard. Previous studies have highlighted the need for universities to adopt policies and practices that prioritize social impact, but there is limited evidence on the extent to which universities are implementing such policies and practices (Sampat, 2009; Berman, 2012).

This knowledge gap is particularly significant in the context of the United Kingdom, where universities are significant contributors to global health research, but where there is limited information on the policies and practices of universities in promoting global health equity (Koplan et al., 2009). This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research. The research question guiding this study is: What are the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and how do these policies and practices promote or hinder global health equity? This study will contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom, including their research funding priorities, IP licensing policies, and open-access publishing practices.

The findings of this study will inform the development of policies and practices that promote global health equity and ensure that universities are contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive analysis of the research funding priorities of universities in the United Kingdom, including the proportion of funding allocated to ND research and health research in LLMICs. This analysis will help identify areas of strength and weakness in the research portfolio of universities and inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. Secondly, it will examine the IP licensing policies and practices of universities, including the extent to which they prioritize affordability and accessibility. This analysis will help identify opportunities for universities to develop IP licensing policies that promote global health equity. Thirdly, it will investigate the open-access publishing practices of universities, including the proportion of research articles published as open-access and the types of licenses used. This analysis will help identify opportunities for universities to promote the accessibility of research and its products, thereby contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs.

To achieve the study's objectives, we extracted data on health research funding from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases, including the Wellcome Trust, the Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research, the Department for International Development, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (Kmietowicz, 2015). We coded the extracted data as research on NDs and/or health in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC), using the World Health Organization's definition of neglected diseases, which includes diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (WHO, 2015). We also used the World Bank's classification of low- and lower-middle-income countries to categorize research on health in these settings (World Bank, 2015). We selected 25 United Kingdom universities for this study, based on their research intensity and global health research output (Times Higher Education, 2015).

We obtained data on intellectual property licensing policies and practices from publicly available sources, such as university websites and annual reports, as well as through direct contact with university technology transfer offices (TTOs) (Siegel et al., 2007). We also extracted data on open-access policies from university websites and repositories. By examining the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom, this study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the ways in which universities are promoting global health equity, and identify areas for improvement. The study's findings will have important implications for the development of policies and practices that prioritize social impact and promote equitable access to research and its products. Ultimately, this study seeks to contribute to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs, and to promote a more equitable global health landscape. Our research endeavors to provide a comprehensive examination of the current state of global health equity in university research, with a particular focus on the policies and practices of United Kingdom institutions. This allowed us to garner a nuanced understanding of the complex issues surrounding global health equity in university research. 

We began by analyzing health research funding data from the top five United Kingdom funders' databases, which revealed significant disparities in the allocation of funds across 25 United Kingdom universities. Notably, the median proportion of 2011-2014 health research funds attributable to research on neglected diseases (NDs) was a mere 2.6%, with a range of 0.5% to 14.1% across institutions. Similarly, the median proportion of funds allocated to health research in low- and lower-middle-income countries (hLLMIC) was 1.7%, with a range of 0.2% to 8.5% across universities. These findings suggest that the majority of health research funding is directed towards other areas, with a relatively small proportion allocated to NDs and hLLMIC. 

Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the distribution of ND funding across universities was highly skewed, with 79% of all ND funding granted to the top four institutions. This concentration of funding can have significant implications for the overall research landscape, with potential consequences for the development of new treatments and interventions. In addition to analyzing funding data, we also examined intellectual property licensing policies and practices across the 25 universities. Our findings indicated that only seven institutions (28%) had policies in place to ensure that technologies developed from their research are affordable globally. In contrast, the majority of universities (72%) did not have such policies, and instead licensed their inventions to third parties in a way that confers monopoly rights. This can have significant implications for access to new treatments and interventions, particularly in resource-poor settings. As Chaudhuri et al. We also investigated open-access publishing policies and practices across the universities. Our analysis revealed that 15 institutions (60%) had an institutional open-access publishing policy, while three institutions (12%) had an institutional open-access publishing fund. However, despite this progress, only 23% of articles had a creative commons CC-BY license, which is considered the gold standard for open-access publishing. This suggests that while many universities are making progress in terms of open-access publishing, there is still significant room for improvement in terms of ensuring that research is widely available and reusable.

Cross-domain text classification has emerged as a vital task in natural language processing, enabling the development of classifiers for target domains by leveraging data from both source and target domains. This capability is crucial, as it allows for the construction of effective classifiers even when limited labeled data is available for the target domain. The work of Daumé III (2007) and Blitzer et al. (2006) laid the foundation for this area of research, highlighting the potential of cross-domain text classification. However, a significant challenge arises from the differences in feature distributions between the two domains, which can substantially degrade the performance of a classifier trained on the source domain when applied to the target domain, as noted by Pan et al. (2010).

To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various methods aimed at minimizing the differences in feature distributions between the two domains, with the ultimate goal of achieving domain-invariant feature representations. The work of Glorot et al. (2011) and Chen et al. (2012) exemplifies this line of research. One common approach to minimizing feature distribution differences involves exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices, as proposed by Blitzer et al. (2006) and Kulis et al. (2011). These mechanisms seek to establish a direct correspondence between the features of the two domains. However, exact alignment can be overly restrictive, as it may not always be feasible to establish a one-to-one correspondence between features across different domains, a limitation highlighted by Zhou et al. (2014).

Furthermore, exact alignment can compromise the performance of models on classification tasks when the semantic distributions of the different domains are significantly different, as observed by Li et al. (2014). This is because exact alignment may fail to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains, leading to suboptimal feature representations. To overcome the limitations of exact alignment, some researchers have proposed alternative approaches that focus on aligning the semantic distributions of the two domains at a higher level. The work of Chen et al. (2013) and Long et al. (2015) illustrates this shift in focus. These approaches aim to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains.

One such approach involves the use of topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which can learn to represent documents as mixtures of latent topics, as demonstrated by Blei et al. (2003). However, traditional topic models are not designed to handle cross-domain text classification tasks and may not be effective in capturing the semantic differences between the two domains. In response, some researchers have proposed cross-domain topic models that can learn to represent documents from both the source and target domains as mixtures of latent topics, as shown by Jiang et al. (2011) and Zhu et al. (2012). These models can capture the semantic structures of both domains and learn to align the topics across the domains.

Despite the progress made in this area, existing cross-domain topic models often rely on exact alignment mechanisms or assume that the semantic distributions of the two domains are similar, as noted by Li et al. (2016). Moreover, these models may not be effective in handling cases where the semantic distributions of the two domains are significantly different. To address the limitations of existing cross-domain text classification methods, we propose a novel approach that focuses on aligning the semantics at the group level, rather than relying on exact alignment mechanisms. Our approach, which we term Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), incorporates a group alignment mechanism and a partial supervision mechanism into a cross-domain topic model.

The group alignment mechanism allows the model to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. The partial supervision mechanism enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups by leveraging labeled data from the source domain. The research question guiding this study is: Can a cross-domain topic model that incorporates group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms effectively capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks?

Our study aims to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in addressing the challenges of cross-domain text classification. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel group alignment mechanism that can capture the semantic structures of both domains at a higher level. Second, we introduce a partial supervision mechanism that enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups.
