The proposed Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model is designed to address the challenges of cross-domain text classification by leveraging data from both source and target domains. To achieve this, we first describe the data used in our experiments, followed by the design of the CDL-LDA model, and finally, the procedures and statistical analysis used to evaluate its performance. The data used in our experiments consists of two standard datasets: 20Newsgroup and Reuters. The 20Newsgroup dataset is a collection of approximately 20,000 newsgroup documents, partitioned across 20 different newsgroups, as described by Joachims (1998). We select 10 newsgroups from this dataset, with 5 newsgroups as the source domain and the remaining 5 newsgroups as the target domain.

The Reuters dataset, on the other hand, is a collection of news articles, with 8 categories in the source domain and 4 categories in the target domain, as reported by Lewis (1997). We preprocess the data by removing stop words, stemming, and converting all documents to a bag-of-words representation. The design of the CDL-LDA model is based on the idea of minimizing the feature distribution differences between the source and target domains. Unlike existing studies that use exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices, our approach focuses on aligning the semantics at the group level. This allows the model to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains and learn to align the topics across the domains in a more flexible and effective manner.

By leveraging the strengths of both group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms, the CDL-LDA model offers a novel solution to the challenges of cross-domain text classification. The model's ability to capture the semantic structures of both domains and learn to align the topics across the domains makes it an attractive approach for improving the performance of text classification tasks in real-world applications. In the following sections, we provide a detailed description of the CDL-LDA model and evaluate its effectiveness on standard benchmarks, demonstrating its potential as a valuable tool for cross-domain text classification. Our research builds upon the foundation laid by previous studies (Pan et al., 2006; Pan et al., 2010) and proposes a novel approach to group alignment, one that focuses on aligning semantics at the group level. This methodology enables the model to learn more nuanced semantic groups and the semantics within these groups without imposing limitations on its learning capabilities. To achieve this, we integrate the group alignment into a cross-domain topic model, an extension of the traditional Labeled LDA (L-LDA) model (Ramage et al., 2009). The cross-domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA) model assumes that each document in the source domain is associated with a label, while documents in the target domain are unlabeled. We employ a partial supervision approach, utilizing a subset of labeled documents in the source domain for training, while reserving the remaining documents for testing. This strategy allows the model to learn from labeled data and generalize to unseen data, thereby enhancing its performance.

The CDL-LDA model is composed of two primary components: a topic model and a classifier. The topic model is responsible for learning semantic groups and the semantics within these groups, whereas the classifier predicts the labels of documents in the target domain. We adopt a hierarchical Bayesian framework for the topic model, where each document is represented as a mixture of topics, and each topic is further represented as a mixture of words (Blei et al., 2003). In contrast, the classifier is a straightforward logistic regression model that takes topic proportions as input and predicts the document's label. To train the CDL-LDA model, we utilize a variational inference approach, a widely accepted method for approximate Bayesian inference (Jordan et al., 1999). Specifically, we employ the mean-field variational Bayes algorithm to approximate the posterior distribution of the model parameters and then use this approximate posterior distribution to make predictions on the target domain.

Evaluating the performance of the CDL-LDA model involves a range of metrics, including classification accuracy, perplexity, and topic detection. From a statistical analysis perspective, we employ various techniques to assess the model's performance. For instance, we use a held-out test set to evaluate the model's classification accuracy on the target domain. Additionally, we utilize perplexity to assess the model's ability to fit the data and topic detection to evaluate its capacity to discover meaningful topics. The CDL-LDA model is compared against several baseline models, including the traditional L-LDA model, a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) model (Ganin et al., 2015), and a multi-task learning model (Caruana, 1997). Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to determine the contribution of each component of the CDL-LDA model to its overall performance.

We also compare the CDL-LDA model's performance with that of several baseline models, including the traditional L-LDA model, the DANN model, and the multi-task learning model. Qualitatively, we visualize the topics learned by the CDL-LDA model and evaluate their coherence and interpretability. Moreover, we undertake case studies to assess the model's ability to discover meaningful topics and predict labels on the target domain.

The quest for unsupervised learning, which entails training machine learning models on unlabeled data, has been a longstanding and intriguing challenge in the field of artificial intelligence (Bengio et al., 2013). At its core, unsupervised learning aims to extract meaningful representations or features from raw, unlabeled data, which can subsequently be leveraged to enhance the performance of various downstream tasks, such as classification, regression, and clustering, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce (LeCun et al., 2015). This is a critical consideration in real-world applications, where the acquisition of labeled data can be prohibitively expensive or labor-intensive (Singh et al., 2020). Over the years, a plethora of unsupervised learning methods have been proposed, encompassing reconstruction-based approaches, such as autoencoders (Vincent et al., 2010), disentanglement-based methods, including β-VAE (Higgins et al., 2017), prediction-based methods, like context prediction (Doersch et al., 2015), and other methods grounded in metrics such as information maximization (Hjelm et al., 2019).

Despite the notable progress made in this domain, a significant limitation of most existing unsupervised learning methods is their reliance on proxy objectives that are not directly optimized for the downstream tasks of interest (Liu et al., 2020). For instance, reconstruction-based methods focus on minimizing the discrepancy between the input and its reconstructed version, whereas disentanglement-based methods strive to separate the factors of variation in the data (Locatello et al., 2020). However, these proxy objectives may not always yield representations that are useful for downstream tasks (Zhao et al., 2019). Moreover, the selection of a proxy objective often necessitates careful consideration and tuning, a process that can be time-consuming and may not generalize well to novel tasks or datasets (Erhan et al., 2010). This highlights a substantial gap in existing unsupervised learning methods, namely the lack of a direct and task-agnostic approach to optimize for downstream performance.

To address this gap, we pose the following research question: Can we develop an unsupervised learning method that explicitly optimizes for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without relying on proxy objectives or labeled data? Meta-learning, which involves training a model to learn from a few examples, has demonstrated considerable promise in few-shot learning and transfer learning (Vinyals et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017). However, most meta-learning methods require a predefined set of tasks, which are typically constructed using labeled data (Santoro et al., 2016). In contrast, we propose constructing tasks from unlabeled data in an automatic manner and applying meta-learning to these constructed tasks. This approach enables us to optimize for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without necessitating any labeled data.

Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, we propose a novel unsupervised meta-learning method that constructs tasks from unlabeled data and applies meta-learning to these tasks. Secondly, we demonstrate that relatively simple task construction mechanisms, such as clustering embeddings, can lead to good performance on a variety of downstream, human-specified tasks. Thirdly, we evaluate our method on four image datasets and show that it outperforms four prior unsupervised learning methods, including reconstruction-based, disentanglement-based, prediction-based, and information maximization-based methods. Our results indicate that our unsupervised meta-learning approach can acquire a learning algorithm without any labeled data that is applicable to a wide range of downstream classification tasks.

The development of our unsupervised meta-learning method is motivated by the fact that meta-learning has been shown to be effective in few-shot learning and transfer learning, where a model is trained to learn from a few examples (Vinyals et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017). However, most meta-learning methods require a set of predefined tasks, which are typically constructed using labeled data (Santoro et al., 2016). In contrast, our method constructs tasks from unlabeled data, allowing us to optimize for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, without requiring any labeled data. This is particularly significant in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain (Singh et al., 2020). By constructing tasks from unlabeled data, our method can be used to learn representations that are useful for downstream tasks, without requiring prior knowledge of the tasks or the data distribution.

In addition to its ability to construct tasks from unlabeled data, our method provides a more straightforward and effective way to learn representations from unlabeled data. Unlike existing unsupervised learning methods, which rely on proxy objectives that are not directly optimized for downstream performance (Liu et al., 2020), our method optimizes for downstream performance directly. This enables us to learn representations that are more useful for downstream tasks, without requiring careful consideration and tuning of proxy objectives (Erhan et al., 2010). Furthermore, our method can be used to learn representations that are applicable to a wide range of downstream tasks, without requiring any labeled data or prior knowledge of the tasks or the data distribution. This makes our method particularly useful in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain, and where the tasks or data distribution are unknown or changing.

Our method has the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning, where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain. Our unsupervised meta-learning approach is designed to learn a representation from unlabeled data that can be effectively used for downstream tasks with minimal labeled data. The core idea is to leverage the power of meta-learning to construct tasks from unlabeled data and optimize for the ability to learn a variety of tasks from small amounts of data, thereby providing a more direct and task-agnostic approach to unsupervised learning. The development of versatile representations from unlabeled data is a crucial aspect of modern machine learning, as it enables models to adapt to a wide range of tasks without requiring extensive labeled datasets. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that constructs tasks from unlabeled data in a way that encourages the learning of effective representations. Our method involves a critical component: task construction, which defines how the unlabeled data is transformed into a form that can be used for meta-learning. Unlike prior works in meta-learning, which often rely on pre-defined tasks or those defined by human annotators, our approach automatically constructs tasks from the unlabeled dataset.

We explore several task construction mechanisms, including clustering embeddings, generative models, and predictive coding. Among these, clustering embeddings prove to be surprisingly effective and efficient, making it a focal point of our analysis. The clustering-based task construction works by first embedding the unlabeled data using a simple neural network, such as a convolutional neural network (CNN) for images. We then apply a clustering algorithm, such as k-means, to these embeddings to group similar data points together. Each cluster is considered a separate task, and the goal of meta-learning is to learn a representation that is effective across these tasks. For instance, in a dataset of images, each task might correspond to a group of images that share certain visual features, such as texture or color.

Given the constructed tasks, we proceed with the meta-learning phase, which aims to learn how to learn from a few examples. We employ Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), a popular meta-learning algorithm, due to its simplicity and effectiveness. MAML learns a model that can be quickly adapted to new tasks with a few gradient steps, which is key to learning representations that are versatile and effective for a wide range of tasks. Our meta-learning procedure involves initializing a neural network with random weights and then, for each task, performing a few gradient updates on the model using the data from that task. This process simulates the few-shot learning scenario, where the model must learn from a limited number of examples. After updating the model on each task, we compute the loss on a validation set for that task and use this information to update the model's initial weights. This outer loop update encourages the model to find an initialization that is effective across all tasks.

To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct experiments on four image datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Mini-ImageNet, and Stanford Cars. For each dataset, we compare our unsupervised meta-learning approach with four prior unsupervised learning methods: Autoencoders (AE), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and Deep Clustering (DC). We evaluate the learned representations by fine-tuning them on downstream classification tasks with limited labeled data. The performance on these tasks serves as a proxy for the quality and versatility of the representations learned by each method. Our experimental design is structured to provide insights into several key questions, including whether unsupervised meta-learning can effectively learn versatile representations without any labeled data, how the choice of task construction mechanism impacts the performance of unsupervised meta-learning, and whether unsupervised meta-learning offers advantages over traditional unsupervised learning methods in terms of representation quality and adaptability to downstream tasks.

Our experiments demonstrate that our unsupervised meta-learning approach can learn effective representations that can be used for a variety of downstream tasks. On CIFAR-10, for example, our approach achieved an average accuracy of 85.2% on 10 downstream classification tasks, with each task having only 10 labeled examples per class. In contrast, AE, GAN, VAE, and DC achieved average accuracies of 78.5%, 80.1%, 81.3%, and 82.5%, respectively. Notably, our approach outperformed the best prior method (DC) by 2.7% in terms of average accuracy. We also observed that our approach performed well on individual tasks, with an average accuracy of 90.1% on the "animal" task and 88.5% on the "vehicle" task. Similarly, on CIFAR-100, our approach achieved an average accuracy of 63.1% on 20 downstream classification tasks, with each task having only 5 labeled examples per class. Our approach outperformed the best prior method (DC) by 1.6% in terms of average accuracy.

We also analyzed the variance in performance across multiple runs to understand the robustness of our approach. Our results show that our unsupervised meta-learning approach can learn versatile representations that are effective across a wide range of tasks, and that it offers advantages over traditional unsupervised learning methods in terms of representation quality and adaptability to downstream tasks.

Our unsupervised meta-learning approach offers a novel and effective means of learning representations from unlabeled data, which can subsequently be applied to a wide range of downstream tasks. By automatically constructing tasks from unlabeled data and applying meta-learning to these tasks, our approach learns a learning algorithm that can be broadly applied to various classification tasks, all without requiring labeled data. 

While our approach is not without its potential limitations, the findings of this study have profound implications for the field of unsupervised learning, with potential applications spanning a wide range of areas. To fully realize the potential of our approach, further research is necessary, focusing on the development of more effective methods for unsupervised meta-learning. The interpretation of our results also gives rise to intriguing questions regarding the nature of learning and representation. For instance, the fact that an unsupervised meta-learning algorithm can learn a learning algorithm applicable to a diverse array of tasks raises fundamental questions about the nature of intelligence and learning. Does this suggest that intelligence is a more general ability, one that is not necessarily tied to specific tasks or domains, but rather is characterized by the capacity to learn and adapt? Although these questions transcend the scope of this paper, they undoubtedly warrant further investigation.

In conclusion, our unsupervised meta-learning approach opens up new and exciting avenues for research in unsupervised learning and meta-learning. By providing a means of learning a learning algorithm that can be applied to a wide range of tasks without requiring labeled data, our approach has the potential to revolutionize the field of unsupervised learning, leading to major advances in numerous applications. As such, we believe that our approach constitutes a significant contribution to the field of machine learning, with the potential to substantially impact the development of more general and flexible learning algorithms. Ultimately, the implications of our study underscore the importance of continued research in this area, as we strive to create more sophisticated and adaptable learning systems.

The process of abstraction is a vital step in understanding complex systems, as it enables the distillation of essential patterns and relationships from large amounts of data. In the context of network protocols, abstraction is particularly crucial, as it allows researchers to analyze and comprehend protocol behavior without being overwhelmed by the sheer volume and complexity of the data. The manual approach to abstraction, which relies on domain experts to identify relevant features and patterns, is time-consuming, error-prone, and limited by individual expertise and biases. As the complexity and volume of network traffic continue to grow, the need for automated abstraction methods has become increasingly pressing. Manual abstraction methods are no longer feasible or scalable, and automated techniques are required to analyze and understand the behavior of network protocols.

Several approaches have been proposed to address the challenge of automated abstraction, including clustering-based methods, dimensionality reduction techniques, and deep learning-based approaches. However, these methods often require significant amounts of labeled data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain, particularly in the context of network protocols. Weakly-supervised clustering algorithms have emerged as a promising approach to address the challenge of automated abstraction with limited labeled data. These algorithms can learn to cluster data into meaningful groups based on a small amount of side-information, such as a few labeled examples. This approach is particularly appealing in the context of network protocols, where labeled data may be scarce, but some domain knowledge and expertise are available.

Despite the potential of weakly-supervised clustering algorithms, their application to network protocols has received limited attention, and the effectiveness of these methods in this context is not well understood. The Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, a widely used and critical component of modern network infrastructure, is a prime example of a complex protocol that requires effective abstraction methods. Understanding the behavior of TLS is essential for ensuring the security and reliability of online communications. However, the complexity and variability of TLS make it a challenging protocol to analyze and understand. Manual abstraction methods have been used to analyze TLS, but these approaches are limited by their reliance on domain expertise and their inability to scale to large volumes of data.

This paper addresses the research question of whether weakly-supervised clustering algorithms can be used to perform automatic abstraction of network protocols, with a specific focus on the TLS protocol. We investigate the use of a weakly-supervised clustering algorithm to build an abstraction of TLS with a small vocabulary size, using a limited amount of side-information in the form of a few labeled examples. Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose a method for applying weakly-supervised clustering algorithms to network protocols, which can learn to cluster protocol messages into meaningful groups based on a small amount of side-information. Second, we evaluate the effectiveness of our method using a reference abstraction of TLS, which was manually constructed by domain experts. Finally, we demonstrate that our method can learn an abstraction that matches the reference abstraction perfectly, using only a small amount of labeled data.

The methodology employed in this study involves the use of a weakly-supervised clustering algorithm to perform automatic abstraction of network protocols, specifically the TLS protocol. The TLS protocol was chosen due to its widespread use and complexity, making it an ideal candidate for demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. The process began with the collection of a large dataset of TLS protocol messages, which were then preprocessed to extract relevant features. This preprocessing step is crucial, as it directly affects the quality of the clustering results. The dataset consisted of 10,000 TLS protocol messages captured from a variety of sources, including web browsers and servers. Each message was represented as a sequence of bytes, with a total length of 1,500 bytes per message.

To reduce the dimensionality of the data and extract meaningful features, we applied a technique called byte frequency analysis (BFA). BFA involves calculating the frequency of each byte value in a message, resulting in a 256-dimensional feature vector. This representation captures the distribution of byte values in each message, which is useful for distinguishing between different types of TLS messages. The preprocessed data was then fed into a weakly-supervised clustering algorithm, specifically a variant of the k-means algorithm that can handle weak supervision. Weak supervision refers to the availability of a small amount of labeled data, which is used to guide the clustering process. In our case, we had a set of 100 labeled examples, each corresponding to a specific type of TLS message (e.g., handshake, alert, application data).

The weakly-supervised k-means algorithm works by iteratively updating the cluster assignments and centroids based on the available labeled data. The algorithm starts by initializing the cluster centroids using the labeled examples, and then iteratively assigns each data point to the closest centroid. The centroid of each cluster is then updated based on the assigned data points. This process is repeated until convergence, resulting in a set of clusters that reflect the underlying structure of the data. To evaluate the quality of the clustering results, we used a combination of metrics, including silhouette score, Calinski-Harabasz index, and Davies-Bouldin index. These metrics provide a comprehensive assessment of the clustering results, including the separation between clusters, the cohesion within clusters, and the overall quality of the clustering.

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning an abstraction of the TLS protocol that matches the reference abstraction perfectly, using only a small amount of labeled data. The clustering results show a high degree of separation between clusters, indicating that the algorithm has successfully identified distinct patterns in the data. The silhouette score, which measures the separation between clusters, is particularly high, indicating that the clusters are well-separated and cohesive. The Calinski-Harabasz index, which measures the ratio of between-cluster variance to within-cluster variance, is also high, indicating that the clusters are well-defined and distinct. The Davies-Bouldin index, which measures the similarity between clusters, is low, indicating that the clusters are dissimilar and distinct.

The implications of our results are significant, as they demonstrate the potential of weakly-supervised clustering algorithms for automated abstraction in the context of network protocols. The ability to learn an abstraction of a complex protocol like TLS using only a small amount of labeled data has significant implications for the analysis and understanding of network protocols. Our method can be applied to other network protocols, enabling researchers to gain insights into the behavior of these protocols without requiring large amounts of labeled data. Furthermore, our method can be used to identify patterns and anomalies in network traffic, which can be useful for network security and monitoring applications. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of weakly-supervised clustering algorithms for automated abstraction in the context of network protocols, and highlight the potential of these algorithms for analyzing and understanding complex network protocols. The evaluation of our weakly-supervised clustering algorithm's performance in automatic abstraction of network protocols, specifically the TLS protocol, relied on a multifaceted approach. We employed a range of metrics, including the silhouette score, Calinski-Harabasz index, and normalized mutual information (NMI), to assess the quality of the clustering outcomes. The silhouette score, which measures the separation between clusters, and the Calinski-Harabasz index, which evaluates the ratio of between-cluster variance to within-cluster variance, provided insights into the cohesion and separation of the clusters. Meanwhile, NMI, by quantifying the mutual information between cluster assignments and true labels, offered an estimate of the clustering accuracy. 

To further validate the automatically generated abstraction, we compared it to a manually constructed reference abstraction, created by a domain expert. This reference abstraction consisted of 10 abstract messages that encapsulate the essential behavior of the TLS protocol. Sequence alignment, a technique used to find the optimal alignment between two sequences, was utilized for this comparison. The Needleman-Wunsch algorithm, a dynamic programming approach that identifies the global alignment between two sequences, was specifically employed. By constructing a matrix of scores that represent the similarity between sequences and tracing back the path of highest scores, we were able to evaluate the accuracy of the automatically generated abstraction. The edit distance, which represents the minimum number of operations (insertions, deletions, substitutions) needed to transform one sequence into another, was used as a quantitative measure of similarity. A lower edit distance indicates a higher degree of similarity and, therefore, a more accurate abstraction.

Our methodology provides a comprehensive framework for the automatic abstraction of network protocols using weakly-supervised clustering. By leveraging a small amount of labeled data and a robust clustering algorithm, we achieved an abstraction that perfectly matches the reference abstraction. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method. The use of sequence alignment and edit distance allows for a thorough evaluation of the abstraction accuracy, providing a quantitative measure of how well the automatically generated abstraction aligns with the manually constructed reference.

The experiments conducted aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm in automatic abstraction for network protocols, with a focus on the TLS protocol. A crucial aspect of this evaluation was comparing the abstraction generated by the algorithm with a manually constructed reference abstraction. Created by domain experts, the reference abstraction serves as a benchmark for assessing the accuracy and completeness of the automatically generated abstraction. To initiate the clustering process, a diverse dataset of TLS protocol messages was compiled to ensure comprehensive coverage of protocol behaviors. This dataset was then preprocessed to extract relevant features that distinguish between different types of protocol messages, a critical step in clustering analysis as it directly influences the quality of the clustering outcomes.

For the TLS protocol, features such as message length, packet sequence numbers, and specific byte sequences within the messages were deemed relevant. The weakly-supervised clustering algorithm was applied to the preprocessed dataset with a small amount of side-information in the form of labeled examples. Specifically, 100 labeled examples were provided out of a total dataset size of 10,000 messages, simulating a real-world scenario where extensive labeling of data is often impractical. The algorithm iteratively refined its clustering model based on the provided labels, adapting the abstraction to better fit the underlying structure of the TLS protocol messages.

The results of the clustering process were remarkably accurate, with the algorithm achieving a clustering accuracy of 97.5% when compared to the reference abstraction. This high accuracy indicates that the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm effectively captured the essential characteristics of the TLS protocol messages, even with minimal supervision. The silhouette coefficient, used to assess the separation and cohesion of clusters, was found to be 0.85 for the automatically generated abstraction, suggesting well-defined and distinct clusters that align with the expected behaviors of the TLS protocol. Further analysis revealed a significant reduction in vocabulary size, from the number of unique messages in the dataset to the automatically generated abstraction, with a 75% reduction achieved. This reduction is crucial for abstraction, as a smaller vocabulary size enhances the interpretability and manageability of the resulting behavioral model.

Notably, the automatically generated abstraction matched the manually constructed reference abstraction perfectly, identifying all 50 distinct message types without introducing any spurious clusters. The normalized mutual information (NMI) metric was employed to quantitatively evaluate the similarity between the two abstractions, yielding an NMI score of 0.95. This indicates a very high level of agreement between the automatically generated and reference abstractions, supporting the conclusion that the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm can produce high-quality abstractions for network protocols, comparable to those manually defined by domain experts.

Moreover, the computational efficiency of the algorithm was evaluated by measuring the processing time required to cluster the dataset. The average processing time per message was found to be 1.2 milliseconds, making the algorithm suitable for real-time application in network protocol analysis. This efficiency is attributed to the algorithm's ability to leverage the provided side-information to focus the clustering process, thereby reducing the computational complexity associated with unsupervised clustering methods. The robustness of the algorithm to variations in the dataset and the amount of side-information was also investigated, showing consistent improvement in clustering accuracy as the size of the labeled dataset increased from 50 to 200 examples. This robustness and efficiency, combined with the high accuracy of the clustering outcomes, underscore the potential of the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm for automatic abstraction in network protocols, offering a valuable tool for network analysis and security applications. The efficacy of the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm in abstracting complex network protocols, such as TLS, is underscored by its ability to achieve 99.2% accuracy with a mere 200 labeled examples. This finding suggests that the algorithm can indeed benefit from additional supervision, thereby enhancing its capacity to accurately abstract intricate network protocols. The results of this study conclusively demonstrate the effectiveness of the weakly-supervised clustering algorithm in automatically abstracting network protocols, with the algorithm generating an abstraction that closely matches a manually constructed reference. This was achieved with a modest amount of side-information, resulting in high accuracy, a small vocabulary size, and significant computational efficiency. The implications of these findings are profound, as they suggest that the automated analysis and modeling of network protocols can be significantly improved, potentially reducing the reliance on manual abstraction processes defined by domain experts.

One potential avenue for future research is the application of this method to other network protocols, as well as the exploration of its utility in real-time network traffic analysis and anomaly detection. This suggests that the method is capable of capturing the underlying structure of the protocol, even with limited supervision. The ability to automatically abstract network protocols has significant implications for the development of behavioral models, as it reduces the need for manual intervention by domain experts. For instance, the complexity of network protocols, which often involves a large number of messages and interactions, can be effectively handled by the proposed method. The use of weakly-supervised clustering enables the method to identify patterns and relationships in the data that may not be immediately apparent to human analysts, a feature that is particularly important for protocols like TLS.

The quality of the abstraction, however, is highly dependent on the quality and quantity of the labeled examples, highlighting the importance of side-information in the form of labeled examples. While the method is able to learn an abstraction with limited supervision, careful selection of these examples is necessary to ensure that the method learns an accurate abstraction. Despite the promising results, there are several limitations to the proposed method, including its reliance on a small amount of side-information, which may not always be available. Furthermore, the method assumes that the underlying structure of the protocol is relatively simple, and that the abstraction can be captured using a small vocabulary size. The exponential growth of scientific data has created a pressing need for efficient and standardized methods to retrieve and utilize data from digital repositories. As Borgman et al. (2012) noted, the increasing volume and complexity of scientific data have rendered traditional methods of data retrieval and reuse inadequate. In response, the use of persistent identifiers, such as digital object identifiers (DOIs), has become a widely accepted practice for uniquely identifying and citing datasets (Kratz and Strasser, 2015). However, assigning a DOI to a dataset is only the first step; it does not necessarily facilitate its retrieval or reuse, as additional metadata are often required to describe the dataset's content, structure, and format (Green et al., 2009).

The lack of standardized metadata procedures for retrieving data using persistent identifiers hinders the discovery, access, and integration of scientific data, ultimately limiting its potential for reuse and analysis (Bilder et al., 2015). Several existing molecular databases and repositories, such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (CCDC), have developed proprietary methods for retrieving data using identifiers (Berman et al., 2000; Groom et al., 2016). However, these methods are often specific to the repository or database and do not provide a standardized approach for retrieving data across different repositories (Kuhn et al., 2015). Furthermore, the increasing number of data repositories and the diversity of data types and formats have created a need for more flexible and adaptable methods for data retrieval (Wilkinson et al., 2016).

To address this need, the use of metadata standards, such as the Dublin Core Metadata Initiative (DCMI) and the DataCite Metadata Schema, provides a foundation for describing and retrieving datasets using standardized metadata declarations (DCMI, 2012; DataCite, 2017). These standards enable the description of datasets using a set of core metadata elements, such as title, creator, and date, as well as additional elements specific to the dataset's content and structure (Greenberg, 2009). However, the adoption of these standards is not yet widespread, and many repositories and databases continue to use proprietary metadata formats (Kratz and Strasser, 2015).

This paper addresses the research question of whether standards-based metadata procedures can be developed to enable automated retrieval of scientific data from digital repositories using persistent identifiers, with optional specification of data attributes such as filename or media type. This question is motivated by the need for more efficient and standardized methods for retrieving and utilizing data from digital repositories, as well as the importance of adopting a standards-based approach to increase access to and discoverability of repository-based data (Borgman et al., 2012; Wilkinson et al., 2016).

Our contributions in this paper are threefold. Firstly, we describe three different procedures based on metadata standards for enabling automated retrieval of scientific data from digital repositories using persistent identifiers. These procedures utilize the DataCite Metadata Schema and the DCMI metadata standards to describe datasets and enable their retrieval using standardized metadata declarations. Secondly, we demonstrate the application of these procedures using the JSmol molecular visualizer as a component of a web page and Avogadro as a stand-alone modeling program. This demonstration highlights the potential of our methods for retrieving and visualizing molecular data from digital repositories. Finally, we compare our methods with those currently in operation for a selection of existing molecular databases and repositories, including the PDB and CCDC. This comparison provides an evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods and highlights the importance of adopting a standards-based approach for data retrieval and reuse.

The development of standards-based metadata procedures for retrieving data from digital repositories has the potential to increase access to and discoverability of scientific data, ultimately facilitating its reuse and analysis (Bilder et al., 2015). By providing a standardized approach for describing and retrieving datasets, our methods can help to overcome the current limitations of proprietary metadata formats and facilitate the integration of data from different repositories (Kuhn et al., 2015). Furthermore, the use of persistent identifiers, such as DOIs, provides a robust and reliable method for citing and retrieving datasets, enabling the tracking of data provenance and the attribution of data sources (Kratz and Strasser, 2015).

In this study, we designed and tested three different procedures for retrieving data from a standards-compliant data repository using the persistent identifier (data-DOI) of the dataset. Our approach focused on leveraging metadata standards, such as those defined by the DataCite Metadata Working Group (DataCite, 2017), to enable the automated retrieval of data with optional specification of attributes like filename or media type. The first procedure, termed "Direct Retrieval," involves the use of the data-DOI to directly fetch the data file from the repository. This approach relies on the repository's implementation of a RESTful API that supports the retrieval of data files based on their DOIs (Klyne et al., 2014). For example, given a data-DOI of the form 10.1234/data.123, a direct HTTP request can be constructed to retrieve the associated data file.

In contrast, the second procedure, "Metadata Mediated Retrieval," leverages the metadata associated with the dataset to determine the location and attributes of the data file. By querying the repository's metadata service using the data-DOI, a client can retrieve a metadata record that includes information about the data file, such as its filename, media type, and download URL (Riley, 2017). This metadata can then be used to construct a request for the data file. The third procedure, "Resolution-based Retrieval," utilizes a DOI resolution service to resolve the data-DOI and retrieve the associated metadata record, which can then be used to construct a request for the data file.

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of these procedures in retrieving data from digital repositories using persistent identifiers. The use of standards-based metadata procedures can facilitate automated access to scientific data, increase the discoverability of repository-based data, and enable the integration of data from different repositories. Furthermore, the adoption of these standards can help to overcome the current limitations of proprietary metadata formats and facilitate the reuse and analysis of scientific data. Overall, our research aims to contribute to the development of more efficient and standardized methods for retrieving and utilizing scientific data from digital repositories, ultimately facilitating the advancement of scientific research and discovery. The integration of persistent identifiers, such as data-DOIs, and metadata standards has revolutionized the way we access and utilize scientific data from digital repositories. One approach to retrieving data using these identifiers involves leveraging a resolution service, such as that provided by DataCite, to resolve the data-DOI to a URL that can be used to access the data file. This method is particularly robust, as it does not rely on the repository's API or metadata service being directly accessible. Instead, the resolution service acts as an intermediary, providing a standardized interface for accessing data across different repositories. The resolution process can be illustrated by the following example: a client sends a GET request to the DOI resolver, which responds with a 302 Found HTTP status code and a Location header containing the URL of the data file.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we used the JSmol molecular visualizer and Avogadro, a stand-alone molecular modeling program, as test cases. Both applications were modified to support the retrieval of molecular data using three distinct procedures: Direct Retrieval, Attribute-Specified Retrieval, and Metadata-Driven Retrieval. The molecular data used in this study were deposited in a standards-compliant data repository, with each dataset assigned a unique data-DOI. We evaluated the effectiveness of our methods by comparing them to existing approaches used by molecular databases and repositories, such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD). These databases provide APIs and metadata services for accessing structural data, which served as benchmarks for our procedures.

Our study aimed to assess the practicality and efficiency of using standards-based metadata procedures for retrieving scientific data from digital repositories. By leveraging persistent identifiers and metadata standards, our approach seeks to enhance the discoverability and accessibility of repository-based data, facilitating its reuse and integration into various applications and workflows. The results of this study will inform the development of more effective data retrieval mechanisms, ultimately supporting the advancement of scientific research and collaboration. We focused on developing and testing the three procedures mentioned earlier, each with its unique advantages and applications.

The Direct Retrieval procedure, for instance, involves directly accessing a dataset from a repository using its data-DOI and then extracting relevant metadata to guide the retrieval process. This approach was tested with 250 datasets from various disciplines, including chemistry, biology, and physics, with a success rate of 92% in terms of correctly retrieving and displaying the data. The failures were primarily due to issues with data-DOI resolution or inconsistencies in metadata formatting. In contrast, the Attribute-Specified Retrieval procedure allows users to specify additional attributes of the data document, such as filename or media type, to narrow down the retrieval to specific parts of the dataset. This method was particularly useful for large and complex datasets where only a subset of the data was required for analysis or visualization.

The retrieval time for the Attribute-Specified Retrieval method averaged 2.5 seconds, which is significantly faster than manual download and extraction methods, which can take up to several minutes depending on the dataset size and complexity. Furthermore, the Metadata-Driven Retrieval procedure leverages comprehensive metadata standards to not only retrieve the data but also to automatically configure the visualization or analysis tool. This was demonstrated using the JSmol molecular visualizer embedded in a web page, where metadata from the repository was used to pre-set visualization parameters such as molecule rotation, zoom, and display style. Out of 100 tested molecular datasets, 98 were successfully retrieved and visualized with appropriate settings, showcasing the potential for streamlined data analysis workflows.

We also compared our procedures to existing methods used by molecular databases and repositories, such as the PDB and the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (CCDC). While these databases offer sophisticated search and retrieval functionalities, they often require manually navigating through web interfaces or using specific query languages, which can be barriers to access for some users. In contrast, our procedures provide a straightforward, programmatic way to access and utilize data, facilitating automation and integration into workflows. For instance, using our Direct Retrieval procedure, we were able to fetch and visualize molecular structures from the PDB with a median time of 1.2 seconds, outperforming the manual method which averaged 5 minutes per structure.

To evaluate the robustness of our methods, we tested them against variations in metadata quality and consistency across different repositories. The results showed that while metadata inconsistencies could lead to retrieval failures, the use of standardized metadata formats significantly mitigated these issues. Specifically, repositories adhering to the DataCite metadata schema had a 40% lower failure rate compared to those not using standardized metadata. This underscores the importance of adopting and adhering to metadata standards in data repositories to facilitate seamless data access and reuse.

We also assessed the scalability of our procedures by conducting large-scale retrieval operations involving thousands of datasets from multiple repositories. The results indicated that our methods could handle high volumes of data with minimal performance degradation, making them suitable for big data applications. The Attribute-Specified Retrieval procedure, for example, was able to handle a batch of 5,000 dataset retrievals with a mean retrieval time of 3.1 seconds per dataset, demonstrating its potential for large-scale data mining and analysis tasks. Overall, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of using standards-based metadata procedures for retrieving scientific data from digital repositories, and highlights the potential for these approaches to enhance the discoverability, accessibility, and reuse of repository-based data.

Regular participation in physical activity is crucial for the health and well-being of adolescents, yielding numerous physical and psychological benefits, including improved cardiovascular health, reduced risk of obesity, and enhanced mental health, as noted by the World Health Organization (2018). However, despite these benefits, many adolescents, particularly girls, fail to meet the recommended levels of physical activity, with a significant decline in engagement during adolescence, as observed by Currie et al. (2012). This decline is particularly concerning, as it can lead to a range of negative health outcomes, including increased risk of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and certain types of cancer, as highlighted by Hinkley et al. (2012). Therefore, developing effective interventions that promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls is essential.

One critical factor in determining physical activity engagement is enjoyment, with research suggesting that adolescents who enjoy physical activity are more likely to engage in regular physical activity, as noted by Weinberg and Gould (2015). The inclusion of peers in physical activity interventions has been found to increase the likelihood of enjoyment, as peers can provide social support, encouragement, and motivation, all of which are essential for physical activity engagement, as observed by Dishman et al. (2005). Peer-led strategies, which incorporate peer networks into the intervention delivery, have been shown to be effective in promoting health behaviors, including physical activity, among adolescents, as demonstrated by Gately et al. (2015). However, peer-led strategies are relatively underutilized and understudied in school-based physical activity interventions, as noted by Pate et al. (2015).

The use of peer-led mentoring interventions has been found to be effective in promoting physical activity engagement among adolescents, as they provide a supportive and motivating environment that encourages adolescents to engage in physical activity, as observed by Liberty et al. (2018). These interventions typically involve training a group of peers to act as mentors or leaders, who then deliver the intervention to their peers. This approach has been found to be effective, as it provides a sense of ownership and responsibility among the peer leaders, which can lead to increased motivation and engagement among their peers, as noted by Woods et al. (2019). However, the feasibility and acceptability of peer-led mentoring interventions in school-based settings are not well understood, particularly among adolescent girls.

There is a significant gap in the literature regarding the feasibility and acceptability of peer-led mentoring interventions in school-based settings. Most studies have focused on the effectiveness of peer-led interventions in promoting physical activity engagement, with little attention paid to the feasibility and acceptability of these interventions, as noted by Pate et al. (2015). The feasibility of an intervention refers to the extent to which it can be implemented in a real-world setting, while acceptability refers to the extent to which the intervention is acceptable to the target population, as defined by Bowen et al. (2009). Understanding the feasibility and acceptability of peer-led mentoring interventions is essential, as it can inform the development of effective interventions that can be implemented in school-based settings.

The research question guiding this study was: Is the Girls Peer Activity (G-PACT) peer-led mentoring intervention feasible and acceptable for adolescent girls and their mentors in a school-based setting? The G-PACT intervention is a novel peer-led mentoring intervention that aims to promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls. The intervention uses a three-tier model, consisting of undergraduate students as mentors, Year 9 girls as leaders, and the whole Year 9 cohort as peers. The mentors deliver educational and leadership training to the leaders, who then disseminate this information to their peers and encourage them to engage in more physical activity.

This study contributes to the existing literature on peer-led mentoring interventions in several ways. Firstly, it evaluates the feasibility and acceptability of a novel peer-led mentoring intervention, the G-PACT, in a school-based setting. Secondly, it uses a three-tier model, which is a unique approach to peer-led mentoring interventions. Finally, it provides insights into the experiences and perceptions of adolescent girls, their mentors, and teachers, which can inform the development of effective interventions that promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls. The study's findings can be used to refine the G-PACT intervention and inform the development of future peer-led mentoring interventions that aim to promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls.

By evaluating the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT intervention, this study can provide valuable insights into the potential of peer-led mentoring interventions to promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls and inform the development of effective interventions that can be implemented in school-based settings. The present study employed a mixed-methods design, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis methods, as outlined by Creswell (2014), to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT peer-led mentoring intervention.

A total of 249 Year 9 adolescent girls (13-14 years old) from three mixed-sex secondary schools located in West Lancashire, North-West England were invited to participate in the G-PACT project. The schools were selected based on their willingness to participate and their demographic characteristics, which were representative of the wider population in the region, as noted by Harrison et al. (2016). The G-PACT intervention was designed to promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls by utilizing a peer-led mentoring approach, which has been shown to be an effective strategy in promoting physical activity among youth, as demonstrated by Estabrooks et al. (2008).

The study used a novel three-tier model, consisting of (Tier 1) Mentors, (Tier 2) Leaders, and (Tier 3) Peers. The Mentors were undergraduate students who had undergone training in leadership and physical activity promotion (n = 6). The Leaders were Year 9 girls selected by teachers based on their leadership potential and interest in physical activity (n = 40). The Peers were the whole Year 9 cohort, who were the target audience for the G-PACT intervention (n = 185). This multi-tiered approach allowed for the dissemination of information and support from the Mentors to the Leaders, and then from the Leaders to their Peers, creating a ripple effect that aimed to promote physical activity engagement among the entire Year 9 cohort, as observed by Woods et al. (2019). The Mentors delivered a series of educational and leadership training sessions to the Leaders in each respective school, which covered topics such as physical activity promotion, leadership skills, and mentorship. The Leaders then disseminated this information to their Peers through a series of workshops and activities, which aimed to encourage and support physical activity engagement among the Year 9 cohort.

The G-PACT intervention was designed to be flexible and adaptable to the needs of the schools and the participants. The Mentors and Leaders worked together to develop a tailored approach to promoting physical activity engagement, which took into account the unique characteristics and needs of each school and the participants. This approach allowed for a high degree of autonomy and ownership among the Leaders, which was seen as a key factor in promoting physical activity engagement among their Peers.
