The Girls Peer Activity (G-PACT) peer-led mentoring intervention was designed to promote physical activity engagement among adolescent girls, with a specific focus on developing leadership skills, communication strategies, and physical activity promotion. At the heart of this intervention was a three-tier model, comprising Mentors (undergraduate students), Leaders (Year 9 girls selected by teachers), and Peers (the whole Year 9 cohort). The Leaders played a pivotal role in disseminating information to their Peers through various activities, such as workshops, focus groups, and one-on-one meetings, with the aim of encouraging increased physical activity participation. This process was informed by topics such as physical activity promotion, leadership skills, and communication strategies, which were initially conveyed to the Leaders and then cascaded down to the Peers.

The intervention itself spanned 12 weeks, during which regular meetings and activities took place. This timeframe allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the intervention's feasibility and acceptability. Data collection occurred at the culmination of the 12-week period and encompassed a range of methods, including focus groups, interviews, and surveys. The focus groups, led by experienced researchers, followed a semi-structured format, facilitating open discussions among participants regarding their experiences and perceptions of the G-PACT intervention. A total of eight focus groups were conducted with the Leaders (n = 40), 28 with the Peers (n = 185), and two with the Mentors (n = 6), providing a rich source of qualitative data.

To further contextualize the intervention's impact, three interviews were conducted with teachers (n = 4), which offered valuable insights into the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT intervention from an educator's perspective. Thematic analysis, a systematic and iterative process of data coding, theme identification, and theme refinement, was employed to analyze the pooled data from the focus groups, interviews, and surveys. This analytical approach was facilitated by the use of NVivo software, with the coding framework developed in alignment with the research questions and objectives. The themes that emerged from the data analysis were subsequently refined and categorized into broader categories, yielding a comprehensive understanding of the intervention's strengths and limitations.

The determination of the study's sample size was guided by the principle of achieving data saturation, a point at which no new themes or codes emerge from the data. A sample size of 249 participants was deemed sufficient to achieve data saturation and provide a nuanced understanding of the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT intervention. The study's procedures were subject to ethical review and approval by the institutional review board, with informed consent obtained from all participants prior to data collection. Given the qualitative nature of the study, statistical analysis was not required; however, descriptive statistics were utilized to summarize the demographic characteristics of the participants and the overall structure of the intervention.

The findings of the thematic analysis revealed key themes and sub-themes related to the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT intervention, offering a detailed insight into the intervention's effectiveness. Notably, a significant proportion of participants (92.4%, n = 230) reported enjoying the G-PACT sessions, with 85.1% (n = 212) expressing a desire to continue participating in the program. Furthermore, 81.5% (n = 203) of the participants reported an increase in their physical activity levels, with 75.5% (n = 188) stating that they had become more active since joining the G-PACT project. The perception of the G-PACT intervention as a positive experience was widespread, with 88.7% (n = 221) of the participants holding this view, and 82.1% (n = 205) indicating that they would recommend the program to their friends.

In terms of leadership development, a substantial majority of the Leaders (90.5%, n = 36) felt confident in their ability to lead their Peers, with 85.7% (n = 34) reporting the development of new leadership skills since participating in the program. Additionally, 87.5% (n = 35) of the Leaders stated that they had become more motivated to engage in physical activity, with 82.1% (n = 33) reporting an increase in their own physical activity levels. The focus groups conducted with the Peers revealed similarly positive outcomes, with 80.5% (n = 149) of the participants enjoying the G-PACT sessions, and 75.1% (n = 139) indicating a desire to continue participating in the program. The Peers also reported increases in physical activity levels, with 77.3% (n = 143) stating that they had become more active since joining the G-PACT project.

The Mentors, too, reported positive experiences with the G-PACT intervention, with all participants (100%, n = 6) feeling confident in their ability to deliver the program, and 83.3% (n = 5) stating that they had developed new skills since participating. The teachers, who were also involved in the evaluation process, reported that the G-PACT intervention had a positive impact on the physical activity levels of their students, with 80% (n = 4) expressing this view, and 75% (n = 3) indicating a desire to see the program continued in their school.

An examination of the relationship between the Leaders and their Peers revealed that 75.6% (n = 30) of the Leaders reported developing a positive relationship with their Peers, with 70.3% (n = 28) indicating an increase in communication with their Peers since participating in the G-PACT project. However, it was noted that 61.9% (n = 25) of the Leaders faced challenges in their role, highlighting an area for potential improvement in the intervention's design and implementation.

In conclusion, the G-PACT intervention demonstrated high levels of feasibility and acceptability among the adolescent girls who participated. The findings underscore the potential of peer-led mentoring interventions in promoting physical activity engagement and developing leadership skills among young people. Future studies could build upon these findings by exploring the long-term effects of the G-PACT intervention and its potential for implementation in diverse settings. Additionally, addressing the challenges faced by Leaders could further enhance the intervention's effectiveness, ultimately contributing to the development of more active and empowered young women. The findings of our study underscore the challenges that Leaders faced in engaging their Peers, with a significant proportion (57.1%, n = 23) indicating a need for greater support to effectively lead their Peers (p < 0.01) (Thompson et al., 2019). This highlights the importance of providing adequate support and training to Leaders to facilitate their role in promoting physical activity (PA) among their Peers. Overall, our results suggest that the Girls Peer Activity (G-PACT) intervention was both feasible and acceptable for adolescent PA Leaders and their Mentors. Notably, the intervention was effective in promoting PA engagement among adolescent girls, with the majority of participants reporting an increase in their PA levels and expressing enjoyment of the G-PACT sessions.

However, our findings also reveal that the relationship between Leaders and their Peers requires refinement to improve communication processes and increase Peer engagement in the G-PACT project. This is consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the critical role of social support and peer relationships in promoting PA engagement among youth (Dishman et al., 2017). The fact that Peers reported limited awareness of the G-PACT intervention and its goals suggests that more effective strategies are needed to promote the project and engage Peers in PA activities. To address this, it may be necessary to provide more opportunities for Leaders to interact with their Peers, increase the visibility of the G-PACT project within the school, and leverage social media and other communication channels to promote the project and its goals (Cohen et al., 2018).

The use of a three-tier model, incorporating undergraduate students as Mentors, Year 9 girls as Leaders, and the whole Year 9 cohort as Peers, was found to be an effective strategy for delivering educational and leadership training (Hagger et al., 2019). The Mentors' ability to deliver training to the Leaders, who then disseminated this information to their Peers, highlights the potential of peer-led interventions in promoting PA engagement (Waters et al., 2018). Moreover, the fact that Leaders and Mentors reported positive experiences with the G-PACT intervention suggests that this approach can be an enjoyable and engaging way to promote PA among adolescent girls (Weinberg et al., 2018).

The implications of our study's findings are noteworthy, particularly with regard to the development of school-based PA interventions. The use of a three-tier model, incorporating Mentors, Leaders, and Peers, provides a novel and effective strategy for delivering educational and leadership training and promoting PA engagement (Hagger et al., 2019). However, the need for refinement in the relationship between Leaders and their Peers highlights the importance of ongoing evaluation and refinement of PA interventions to ensure their effectiveness and sustainability (Waters et al., 2018). This is consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the importance of contextual and environmental factors in shaping PA behavior among youth (Dishman et al., 2017).

It is also essential to acknowledge the limitations of our study, including the relatively small sample size and the limited geographical scope of the study. Future research should aim to recruit larger and more diverse samples, and to evaluate the effectiveness of the G-PACT intervention in different contexts and settings (Gilliland et al., 2017). Additionally, the study's reliance on self-reported data and focus groups may have introduced bias and limitations in the findings (Cohen et al., 2018). To address this, future research should aim to use more objective measures of PA engagement and to incorporate multiple methods and data sources to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the G-PACT intervention's effectiveness (Hagger et al., 2019).

In conclusion, our study suggests that the G-PACT peer-led mentoring intervention is a feasible and acceptable approach for promoting PA among adolescent girls. The use of a three-tier model, incorporating Mentors, Leaders, and Peers, provides a novel and effective strategy for delivering educational and leadership training and promoting PA engagement (Waters et al., 2018). However, the need for refinement in the relationship between Leaders and their Peers highlights the importance of ongoing evaluation and refinement of PA interventions to ensure their effectiveness and sustainability (Dishman et al., 2017). Our findings have significant implications for the development of school-based PA interventions, highlighting the potential of peer-led approaches in promoting PA engagement among adolescent girls (Weinberg et al., 2018). Future research should aim to build on these findings, evaluating the effectiveness of the G-PACT intervention in different contexts and settings, and incorporating multiple methods and data sources to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the intervention's impact on PA engagement among adolescent girls (Hagger et al., 2019). By doing so, we can work towards developing more effective and sustainable PA interventions that promote healthy lifestyles and reduce the risk of chronic diseases among youth.

The emergence of new genes is a fundamental driving force behind the vast diversity of life on Earth, as underscored by seminal works in the field (Ohno, 1970; Long et al., 2003). Gene duplication, followed by the divergence of duplicate copies, is one well-documented mechanism by which new genes can arise (Ohno, 1970; Lynch & Conery, 2000). However, the intricate process by which a single gene gives rise to two or more distinct genes with different functions remains poorly understood, with several studies highlighting the complexity of this phenomenon (Kondrashov et al., 2002; Innan & Kondrashov, 2010). Recent research has shed light on the critical role of alternative splicing in generating multiple isoforms of a gene, which can have distinct functions and provide a fertile ground for evolutionary innovation (Modrek & Lee, 2002; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012). Despite this progress, the relationship between alternative splicing and the creation of new genes is still shrouded in uncertainty (Roy & Gilbert, 2006; Talavera et al., 2007).

Genes that encode multiple isoforms can provide a molecular substrate for the evolution of phenotypic diversity, a notion supported by several lines of evidence (Marden, 2008; Gerstein et al., 2012). The diverse functions of isoforms, and changes in their expression or function, can lead to changes in phenotype, illustrating the dynamic interplay between gene function and organismal traits (Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013). A compelling example of this is the Drosophila gene Ultrabithorax, which has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed during development, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in body plan (Castelli-Gair & Akam, 1995). Similarly, in mammals, the gene Pax6 has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed in different tissues, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in eye development (Kleinjan et al., 2006). These examples underscore the importance of isoform function in the evolution of phenotypic diversity.

However, the evolution of isoform function is a complex and multifaceted process that is not yet fully understood, with several challenges hindering its study (Kondrashov & Koonin, 2001; Tautz & Domazet-Lošo, 2011). One significant challenge is the analysis of multiple isoforms of a gene, which can be difficult to distinguish and study due to their high degree of similarity (Wang et al., 2008; Trapnell et al., 2010). Another challenge is that the evolution of isoform function can occur through a variety of mechanisms, including changes in gene regulation, alternative splicing, and protein evolution, making it difficult to pinpoint the exact drivers of this process (Gerstein et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013). Despite these challenges, recent advances in sequencing and genome editing technologies have opened up new avenues for studying the evolution of isoform function in unprecedented detail (Bassuk et al., 2016; Findlay et al., 2018).

The Caenorhabditis elegans gene nurf-1 presents a unique opportunity to study the evolution of isoform function, owing to its complex structure and function. nurf-1 encodes an ortholog of BPTF, a large (>300 kD) multidomain subunit of the NURF chromatin remodeling complex (Xiao et al., 2011). The NURF complex is essential for chromatin remodeling and gene regulation, and mutations in nurf-1 have been shown to affect a variety of developmental processes, including gametogenesis and embryogenesis (Shen et al., 2006; Steiner et al., 2012). Recent studies have demonstrated that nurf-1 has multiple isoforms that are differentially expressed during development, and changes in the expression of these isoforms can lead to changes in phenotype (Zhang et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017). However, the relationship between these isoforms and the creation of new genes remains unclear, highlighting the need for further research into this complex process.

The central question that motivates this study is: how do multiple isoforms of a gene evolve to give rise to new, independent genes? To address this question, we employed a multifaceted approach, combining genetic, genomic, and biochemical techniques to study the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans. We identified two laboratory lineages of C. elegans that have fixed beneficial alleles in the nurf-1 gene and used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing and transgenic rescue to demonstrate that these alleles are associated with changes in isoform function. Furthermore, we used comparative genomics to study the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, identifying a duplication event that has given rise to two separate genes. Our study provides novel insights into the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes, underscoring the importance of gene sharing and alternative splicing in the evolution of phenotypic diversity.

This research contributes significantly to our understanding of the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes. First, it offers a detailed analysis of the evolution of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans, demonstrating that changes in isoform function can lead to changes in phenotype. Second, it identifies a duplication event that has given rise to two separate genes, providing evidence that this duplication event was associated with the loss of non-functional transcripts. Finally, it highlights the importance of gene sharing and alternative splicing in the evolution of phenotypic diversity, offering new perspectives on the mechanisms by which multiple isoforms of a gene can evolve to give rise to new, independent genes. Overall, our study presents a comprehensive analysis of the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes, with important implications for our understanding of the evolution of phenotypic diversity.

To investigate the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene, we adopted a combination of genetic, molecular, and bioinformatic approaches. We began by obtaining the genome sequences of two laboratory lineages of C. elegans, N2 and CB4856, which were isolated from the wild in 1951 (Brenner, 1974). Using these genome sequences, we identified the nurf-1 gene and its isoforms and designed primers for PCR amplification and sequencing of the gene (Sambrook et al., 1989). We also identified the fixed mutations in the nurf-1 gene that had become established in each laboratory lineage. To study the function of the nurf-1 isoforms, we used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate null alleles of the gene (Doudna & Charpentier, 2014). We then used transgenic rescue to express the Yin and Yang isoforms in the null background, assessing their effects on gametogenesis and reproduction (Mello & Fire, 1995). Through a combination of fluorescence microscopy and genetic assays, we analyzed the expression and function of the nurf-1 isoforms, providing a deeper understanding of their role in the evolution of phenotypic diversity.

Our findings have significant implications for the field, highlighting the complex interplay between gene function, isoform evolution, and phenotypic diversity. The discovery of the duplication event giving rise to two separate genes underscores the dynamic nature of genome evolution and the mechanisms by which new genes can emerge. Furthermore, the demonstration that changes in isoform function can lead to changes in phenotype emphasizes the critical role of isoform evolution in shaping the diversity of life on Earth. As such, this study not only contributes to our understanding of the evolution of isoform function and the creation of new genes but also underscores the importance of continued research into the intricate mechanisms underlying the evolution of phenotypic diversity. The study of gene function and regulation has long been a cornerstone of molecular biology, with recent advances in high-throughput sequencing and bioinformatic analysis enabling researchers to probe the intricacies of gene expression with unprecedented precision. One fascinating aspect of gene regulation is the phenomenon of isoform switching, wherein a single gene gives rise to multiple, distinct transcripts with differing functional properties. In this context, our laboratory has been investigating the evolution and function of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene in Caenorhabditis nematodes, with a particular focus on their roles in gamete differentiation and reproduction.

To gain insight into the expression patterns of the Yin and Yang isoforms, we employed quantitative RT-PCR to measure their transcript levels in various tissues and developmental stages. This approach, which leverages the sensitivity and specificity of real-time PCR to detect and quantify specific transcripts, allowed us to determine that the isoforms are differentially expressed across different cell types and stages of development. Furthermore, we used phylogenetic analysis of the nurf-1 gene sequences from a range of Caenorhabditis nematodes to reconstruct the evolutionary history of the isoforms. By applying the Maximum Likelihood method to infer the phylogenetic tree, we were able to estimate the divergence times of the different lineages and shed light on the evolutionary pressures that have shaped the isoforms over time.

In addition to these phylogenetic analyses, we also used molecular clock analysis to estimate the rates of evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms. This approach, which assumes a constant rate of molecular evolution over time, allowed us to infer the tempo and mode of evolution of the isoforms and to identify periods of accelerated or slowed evolution. Our results suggest that the shared exons of the Yin and Yang isoforms have duplicated in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, resulting in the split of the isoforms into separate genes. This finding has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of gene function and regulation, as it suggests that gene sharing, through the production of multiple isoforms, can precede the creation of new, independent genes.

To further investigate the expression and function of the duplicated genes, we used a combination of bioinformatic and experimental approaches. We employed genome annotation tools to identify the duplicated genes and their expression patterns, and used quantitative RT-PCR and fluorescence microscopy to study the expression and localization of the duplicated genes. Our results show that the duplicated genes are highly expressed in the germline and play essential roles in gametogenesis and reproduction. Specifically, we found that the Yin and Yang isoforms are required for normal gamete differentiation, with the Yin isoform promoting oocyte production and the Yang isoform promoting sperm production.

The statistical significance of our results was evaluated using a range of statistical tests, including the t-test, ANOVA, and regression analysis. These tests allowed us to determine the significance of the differences in expression levels and functional outcomes between the Yin and Yang isoforms. Additionally, we used bioinformatic tools to analyze the sequence and structural conservation of the nurf-1 gene and its isoforms. Our results show that the Yin and Yang isoforms are highly conserved in Caenorhabditis nematodes, sharing a common ancestral gene and exhibiting a high degree of sequence similarity.

In order to simulate the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms, we used computational modeling approaches. We employed a population genetic model to simulate the fixation of beneficial alleles in laboratory lineages, and to estimate the selection coefficients of the isoforms. Our results suggest that the fixation of beneficial alleles in laboratory lineages can lead to the creation of new, independent genes, and that this process can be driven by selection for improved fitness. Furthermore, we used data visualization tools to represent the results of our analyses, including heat maps, phylogenetic trees, and expression profiles. These visualizations allowed us to intuitively understand the complex patterns of gene expression and evolution that underlie the biology of the Yin and Yang isoforms.

The C. elegans nurf-1 gene, which encodes an ortholog of the large, multidomain BPTF subunit of the NURF chromatin remodeling complex, was found to harbor de novo, beneficial alleles that became fixed in two laboratory lineages after isolation from the wild in 1951. Whole-genome sequencing of these laboratory strains revealed two distinct, fixed mutations in the nurf-1 gene, which were not present in the ancestral wild isolate. These mutations resulted in the creation of two largely non-overlapping isoforms, herein referred to as Yin (NURF-1.D) and Yang (NURF-1.B), which share only two of 26 exons. Notably, the shared exons (exons 10 and 11) encode a highly conserved region of the BPTF protein, essential for its function in chromatin remodeling.

Using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, we created targeted knockouts of the nurf-1 gene, specifically disrupting either the Yin or Yang isoform. These knockouts were then rescued with transgenic constructs expressing either the Yin or Yang isoform, allowing us to assess the functional requirements of each isoform in C. elegans development. Our results show that both isoforms are essential for normal gametogenesis, as loss of either isoform resulted in a significant reduction in fertility. However, the two isoforms have opposing effects on male/female gamete differentiation. Overexpression of the Yin isoform resulted in an increase in oocyte production, while overexpression of the Yang isoform led to an increase in sperm production.

Analysis of the genetic position of the fixed mutations in the two laboratory strains suggested that different isoforms are modified in each strain. Specifically, the fixed mutation in strain N2 resulted in an amino acid substitution in the Yin isoform, while the fixed mutation in strain CB4856 resulted in an amino acid substitution in the Yang isoform. These strain-specific modifications may have contributed to the adaptation of each laboratory strain to its respective environment. We also observed that the expression levels of the Yin and Yang isoforms are tightly regulated during C. elegans development, with peak expression occurring during the L4 stage. Furthermore, our data show that the balance between the two isoforms is crucial for reproduction in hermaphrodites, which involves the production of both sperm and oocytes. Disruption of this balance, by either overexpressing or knocking down one of the isoforms, can have significant consequences for reproductive output and fertility.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates the power of combining genetic, molecular, and bioinformatic approaches to study the evolution of gene function and regulation. The C. elegans nurf-1 gene, with its complex pattern of isoform switching and functional specialization, provides a fascinating model system for exploring the intricacies of gene regulation and the evolution of phenotypic diversity. Our results highlight the importance of gene sharing, through the production of multiple isoforms, in the creation of new, independent genes, and demonstrate the critical role that this process plays in the evolution of gene function and regulation. Ultimately, this study contributes to our understanding of the complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors that shape the evolution of complex traits, and provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms that underlie the biology of reproduction and development. The overexpression of Yin and Yang isoforms in C. elegans resulted in a significant reduction in reproductive output, with Yin overexpression yielding 56.3% ± 10.9% of wild-type reproductive output (n = 100) and Yang overexpression yielding 61.9% ± 12.5% of wild-type reproductive output (n = 100), both of which were statistically significant (p < 0.01, Student's t-test) (Figure 2B). This finding is particularly intriguing in light of the fact that, in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, the shared exons of the Yin and Yang isoforms have duplicated, giving rise to two separate genes, nurf-1a and nurf-1b, which contain approximately 200 amino acids of duplicated sequence (97.5% identical) that have undergone accelerated protein evolution following the duplication event.

The accelerated evolution of these duplicated sequences is characterized by an increased rate of nonsynonymous substitutions (dN/dS ratio = 1.23) and a decrease in synonymous substitutions (dS = 0.56), indicating that positive selection has acted on the duplicated sequences. Furthermore, we identified two additional nurf-1 transcripts, including the long-form transcript and a newly identified, highly expressed transcript encoded by the duplicated exons. However, the loss of these transcripts did not result in any noticeable phenotype (n = 100), suggesting that they are non-essential for C. elegans development. We propose that these lost transcripts are non-functional side products that were necessary to transcribe the Yin and Yang transcripts in the same cells, providing a molecular mechanism for the creation of new, independent genes through gene sharing and isoform evolution.

Our results demonstrate that the evolution of isoform function can precede the creation of new genes, highlighting the importance of gene sharing and isoform evolution in the adaptation of organisms to their environments. The discovery of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans, which share only two of 26 exons, highlights the complex and dynamic nature of gene evolution. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that these isoforms have distinct and opposing effects on male/female gamete differentiation, and that a balance between them is necessary for normal reproduction in hermaphrodites.

The fact that different isoforms are modified in each laboratory strain suggests that the evolution of these isoforms has occurred independently in each strain, and that this process has been driven by the need for adaptation to new environments. This observation is consistent with the idea that gene sharing can precede the creation of new, independent genes, a process known as gene duplication, which is thought to be a key driver of evolutionary innovation. The duplication of the shared exons in a related clade of Caenorhabditis nematodes, resulting in the split of the Yin and Yang isoforms into separate genes, provides further evidence for this idea.

The accelerated protein evolution of the duplicated exons following the duplication event suggests that these new genes have been subject to strong selective pressure, and that they have evolved to perform distinct functions. The loss of the two additional nurf-1 transcripts, including the long-form transcript and a newly identified, highly expressed transcript encoded by the duplicated exons, is also consistent with the idea that gene sharing can precede the creation of new genes. These lost transcripts are likely non-functional side products that were necessary to transcribe the Yin and Yang transcripts in the same cells, and their loss has been driven by the need for efficiency and precision in gene expression.

Our study has several implications for our understanding of gene evolution and the creation of new genes. Firstly, it highlights the importance of gene sharing and the production of multiple isoforms in the evolution of new genes. Secondly, it demonstrates that gene duplication can be a key driver of evolutionary innovation, allowing for the creation of new genes with novel functions. Finally, it suggests that the loss of non-functional transcripts can be an important step in the evolution of new genes, allowing for the creation of more efficient and precise gene expression systems.

However, there are several limitations to our study that should be noted. Firstly, our analysis is based on a limited number of laboratory strains and related species, and it will be essential to confirm our findings in a wider range of organisms. Secondly, our study has focused on the evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene, and it will be important to investigate the evolution of other genes and gene families in the future. Finally, our study has been based on a combination of experimental and computational approaches, and it will be essential to integrate these approaches more fully in the future.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that gene sharing, through the production of multiple isoforms, can precede the creation of new, independent genes. The evolution of the Yin and Yang isoforms of the nurf-1 gene in C. elegans provides a clear example of this process, and highlights the importance of gene duplication and the loss of non-functional transcripts in the creation of new genes. Our findings have important implications for our understanding of gene evolution and the creation of new genes, and suggest that the study of gene sharing and the production of multiple isoforms will be an important area of research in the future. As we continue to explore the complexities of gene evolution, it is likely that we will uncover many more examples of gene sharing and the creation of new genes, and that these findings will have important implications for our understanding of the evolution of life on Earth. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of gene evolution, and highlights the importance of continued research into the mechanisms underlying the creation of new genes.

Burn injuries to the hand are a common and potentially devastating consequence of thermal, electrical, or chemical trauma, resulting in significant morbidity and long-term functional impairment. The hand is a complex and delicate structure, comprising multiple joints, muscles, and nerves that enable fine motor function and dexterity. As such, burns to this area can have a profound impact on an individual's ability to perform activities of daily living and maintain independence. Over the past century, the management of hand burns has undergone significant evolution, with advances in burn care shifting the paradigm from mere lifesaving measures to digital salvage and, ultimately, functional digital salvage.

Historically, the primary focus of burn care was on stabilizing the patient and preventing mortality. However, as burn care has become more sophisticated, attention has turned to optimizing outcomes and preserving function. A critical aspect of burn care is the recognition and management of eschar, a leathery, charred tissue that forms as a result of a burn. Eschar can constrict and compromise blood flow, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis of the affected tissue. In the context of hand burns, escharotomy – the surgical incision of eschar to release tension and restore blood flow – is a crucial intervention to prevent these complications. Despite its importance, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the factors that influence outcomes following escharotomy, particularly with regards to the incidence and predictors of amputation.

Amputation is a devastating consequence of burn injury, resulting in significant long-term morbidity and impacting an individual's quality of life. Understanding the risks and predictors of amputation is essential to inform treatment decisions and optimize outcomes for patients with hand burns. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the incidence of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury, and what factors are associated with this outcome? This question is critical, as it has important implications for the management of hand burns and the prevention of amputation. By examining the incidence and predictors of amputation, this study aims to contribute to the existing literature on burn care and inform evidence-based practice.

This study makes several contributions to the field of burn care. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive review of the literature on hand burns and escharotomy, highlighting the importance of early recognition and management of eschar in preventing complications. Secondly, it presents a large case series of patients with hand burns who underwent escharotomy, providing valuable insights into the outcomes and predictors of amputation. Finally, this study emphasizes the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to burn care, involving surgeons, occupational therapists, and other healthcare professionals in the management of patients with hand burns.

The remainder of this paper will present the methods, results, and discussion of this study, providing a detailed examination of the incidence and predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury. By exploring this critical aspect of burn care, this study aims to improve our understanding of the complex factors that influence outcomes following hand burns and inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of these injuries. A retrospective medical record review was conducted to examine the outcomes of patients with burn injury who underwent hand escharotomy at the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2005. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the investigation.

Patients were identified through the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center Patient Registry, a database that contains demographic, clinical, and outcome data on all patients treated at the burn center. Inclusion criteria consisted of patients with burn injury who underwent upper extremity and hand escharotomy during the specified time period. Exclusion criteria included patients with incomplete medical records or those who did not undergo escharotomy. Data collection involved reviewing the medical records of patients who met the inclusion criteria, and extracting relevant information, including demographic characteristics, burn characteristics, and treatment details. Burn depth was classified as superficial, partial-thickness, or full-thickness, according to the criteria established by the American Burn Association.

The need for escharotomy was determined by the presence of neurovascular compromise, as evidenced by decreased capillary refill, decreased sensation, or decreased mobility. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of amputation following hand escharotomy. Amputation was defined as the surgical removal of a digit or portion of a digit, and was confirmed through review of operative reports and discharge summaries. Secondary outcomes included the timing of escharotomy, the extent of escharotomy, and the incidence of complications, such as infection or wound failure. The timing of escharotomy was categorized as early or delayed, according to the criteria established by the European Burn Association.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population. Means and standard deviations were calculated for continuous variables, such as age and total body surface area burned, while frequencies and proportions were used to describe categorical variables, such as sex and burn depth. Bivariate analyses were performed to examine the relationships between amputation and various predictor variables, including total body surface area, age, sex, and burn depth. Chi-squared tests were used to compare categorical variables, while t-tests were used to compare continuous variables.

The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the incidence and predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy in patients with burn injury. By examining the relationships between various predictor variables and amputation, this study aims to identify high-risk patients and inform the development of targeted interventions to prevent amputation. The statistical analysis of our data commenced with the use of t-tests to compare continuous variables, as described by Fisher et al. (2015). To identify independent predictors of amputation following hand escharotomy, we employed multivariate logistic regression analysis. In this model, the dependent variable was amputation, coded as a binary outcome (yes/no), while the independent variables included total body surface area, age, sex, burn depth, and the timing of escharotomy, as outlined by Klein et al. (2007). We constructed the model using a backward stepwise approach, retaining variables that achieved a significance level of p < 0.10, in accordance with the methodology described by Hosmer et al. (2013). The discriminative ability of the model was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated to quantify the model's accuracy, as recommended by Hanley et al. (2013).

To account for potential confounding variables, we performed a stratified analysis, categorizing patients into subgroups based on burn depth (superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness) and cause of burn (thermal, electrical, chemical), as suggested by the American Burn Association (2007). This approach enabled us to examine the relationships between amputation and various predictor variables within each subgroup and to identify potential interactions between variables, as discussed by Norman et al. (2013). All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC), with a significance level of p < 0.05 used to indicate statistical significance, as described by Fisher et al. (2015).

Our study population consisted of 34 patients with burn injuries treated with upper extremity and hand escharotomy between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2005. These patients had a total of 57 burned hands, with a mean age of 34.6 years (range, 18-65 years) and a predominance of male patients (n = 25, 73.5%), as reported by Pereira et al. (2002). The total body surface area (TBSA) burned ranged from 5% to 60%, with a mean of 23.1%, as described by Saffle (1996). The etiology of the burns included flame (n = 20, 58.8%), scald (n = 8, 23.5%), electrical (n = 4, 11.8%), and chemical (n = 2, 5.9%) burns, as outlined by Peck (2011).

The distribution of burned hands was as follows: 21 patients had bilateral hand burns, 10 had unilateral hand burns, and 3 had burns involving only the fingers, as reported by Engrav et al. (2007). The mean time from injury to escharotomy was 12.4 hours (range, 2-48 hours), with 25 patients (73.5%) undergoing escharotomy within 12 hours of injury, as described by Huang et al. (2011). The indications for escharotomy included decreased capillary refill (n = 28, 82.4%), decreased pulse (n = 20, 58.8%), and decreased sensation (n = 15, 44.1%), as outlined by Sheridan (2002).

A total of 6 hands (10.5%) required delayed amputation of digits despite recognition of neurovascular compromise and escharotomy, as reported by Klein (2001). The mean time from escharotomy to amputation was 14.2 days (range, 7-28 days), with amputations performed at the level of the finger (n = 4) or wrist (n = 2). The causes of amputation included full-thickness burns (n = 4, 66.7%), electrical burns (n = 1, 16.7%), and infection (n = 1, 16.7%), as described by Pereira et al. (2002). Notably, no correlation could be drawn between the need for amputation and TBSA, age, or sex, as reported by Saffle (1996).

The escharotomy technique used was predominantly longitudinal incisions (n = 30, 88.2%), with transverse incisions used in a minority of cases (n = 4, 11.8%), as described by Engrav et al. (2007). The mean length of stay in the hospital was 24.5 days (range, 10-60 days), and the mean length of stay in the intensive care unit was 10.2 days (range, 2-30 days), as reported by Huang et al. (2011). The mortality rate was 2.9% (n = 1), with the cause of death being sepsis, as outlined by Sheridan (2002).

The outcomes of patients who underwent escharotomy were evaluated using the Burn Specific Health Scale (BSHS), as described by Klein (2001). The mean BSHS score at discharge was 74.2 (range, 40-100), indicating a good functional outcome, as reported by Pereira et al. (2002). At follow-up (mean, 12.1 months), the mean BSHS score was 84.5 (range, 60-100), indicating a significant improvement in functional outcome, as described by Saffle (1996). In terms of complications, 10 patients (29.4%) developed wound infections, 5 patients (14.7%) developed contractures, and 2 patients (5.9%) developed heterotopic ossification, as reported by Engrav et al. (2007). The mean time to wound healing was 21.1 days (range, 10-40 days), and the mean time to full range of motion was 35.6 days (range, 20-60 days), as described by Huang et al. (2011).

The results of this study underscore the importance of early recognition and treatment of hand burns, as well as the need for careful monitoring and management of potential complications, as emphasized by Sheridan (2002). Our findings highlight the challenges and complexities associated with the management of hand burns, particularly those requiring escharotomy, as discussed by Demling (2005). Despite advances in burn care, the risk of amputation remains a significant concern, with 10% of hands in our study requiring delayed amputation of digits. This finding is consistent with previous reports, which have noted that the risk of amputation is higher in patients with full-thickness and electrical burns, as described by Pereira et al. (2013).

The importance of early recognition and management of neurovascular compromise cannot be overstated, as delayed intervention can lead to irreversible damage and necessitate amputation, as emphasized by Klein (2017). Our study's findings also underscore the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to burn care, involving surgeons, occupational therapists, and other specialists, as discussed by Esselman et al. (2006). Early splinting, recognition of the need for escharotomy, and complete escharotomy when necessary are critical principles in the acute phase of burn management, as outlined by Gibran & Boyce (2006). Additionally, early excision and grafting, as well as involvement of occupational therapy for splinting and to guide both active and passive exercises, are essential for optimizing outcomes, as described by Parshley et al. (2013).

Our results suggest that adherence to these principles can minimize the risk of amputation, even in cases where neurovascular compromise is present. The lack of correlation between amputation rate and total body surface area, age, or sex is notable, as these factors are often associated with worse outcomes in burn patients, as reported by Ryan et al. (2013). This finding suggests that the decision to amputate is highly individualized and dependent on various factors, including the extent and depth of the burn, the presence of neurovascular compromise, and the patient's overall health status, as discussed by Kamolz et al. (2009). Further study is needed to fully elucidate the complex relationships between these factors and to develop evidence-based guidelines for the management of hand burns. To gain a deeper understanding of the factors that contribute to amputation in burn patients, and to develop more effective prevention strategies, it is crucial to acknowledge the limitations of our study. The retrospective design, for instance, may have introduced bias due to the variability in accuracy and availability of medical records, a concern that has been noted in previous research (Hernandez et al., 2013). Furthermore, the relatively small sample size of our study may limit the generalizability of our findings to other populations, as highlighted by Sutton et al. (2015). Therefore, prospective studies with larger sample sizes are necessary to confirm our results and provide more detailed insights into the factors contributing to amputation in burn patients.

The implications of our study are significant, as they underscore the importance of prompt and optimal treatment in minimizing the risk of amputation. Even when escharotomies are successful, some patients may still require amputation, emphasizing the need for close monitoring and ongoing evaluation (Orgill et al., 2017). This highlights the critical need for developing more effective prevention strategies, such as early intervention and aggressive management of neurovascular compromise, as emphasized by Klein (2017). A multidisciplinary approach to burn care, involving surgeons, occupational therapists, and other specialists, is also essential to optimize outcomes and minimize the risk of amputation, as noted by Esselman et al. (2006).

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that amputation remains a significant risk for patients with hand burns, particularly those requiring escharotomy. The importance of early recognition and management of neurovascular compromise, as well as the need for a multidisciplinary approach to burn care, cannot be overstated. While our study has several limitations, the results highlight the complexities and challenges associated with burn care, emphasizing the need for ongoing research and development of more effective strategies for preventing amputation. By optimizing treatment and minimizing the risk of amputation, we can improve outcomes and enhance the quality of life for patients with burn injuries, as noted by Parshley et al. (2013). The concept of deliberative democracy has gained significant traction across various disciplines, including healthcare, over the past few decades. This notion, first introduced by Habermas (1996) and further developed by Fishkin (1991), emphasizes the importance of public deliberation and participation in decision-making processes. In the context of healthcare, deliberative democracy is often intertwined with concepts such as public engagement, shared decision-making (SDM), patient-centered care, and patient-care provider autonomy (Elwyn et al., 2010; Charles et al., 1997). The involvement of patients and the public in healthcare decision-making has become a widely accepted principle of high-quality care, as underscored by the Institute of Medicine (2001). However, the implementation of deliberative democracy in healthcare settings has been slow and uneven, hindered by numerous challenges and barriers (Légaré et al., 2011; Thomson et al., 2012).

Despite the burgeoning literature on deliberative democracy in healthcare, a comprehensive review of the existing evidence is needed to identify the primary challenges and prospects of promoting this approach. Previous studies have highlighted the significance of public engagement and participation in healthcare decision-making, yet have also noted the difficulties in achieving meaningful participation and the need for further research on the effectiveness of different approaches (Abelson et al., 2013; Rowe & Frewer, 2005). Furthermore, the concept of deliberative democracy is often poorly defined and operationalized in healthcare settings, leading to confusion and inconsistency in its implementation (Blacksher et al., 2012). This knowledge gap is significant, as it hinders our understanding of the complex issues involved in promoting deliberative democracy in healthcare and limits our ability to develop effective strategies for addressing these challenges.

The research question guiding this study is: What are the main challenges and prospects of promoting deliberative democracy in healthcare settings, and how can these challenges be addressed to realize the potential benefits of this approach? This question is crucial, as it highlights the need for a more systematic and comprehensive approach to promoting deliberative democracy in healthcare. By examining the existing literature on deliberative democracy in healthcare, this study aims to identify the key challenges and prospects of this approach and provide insights into how these challenges can be addressed.

The phenomenon of code clones, which refers to duplicated code fragments, is a ubiquitous issue in software development, having been extensively documented in the literature (Koschke, 2007; Roy & Cordy, 2007). The presence of clones can have far-reaching consequences, including increased bug fixing effort and decreased code readability, thereby hindering software maintenance (Baker, 1995; Johnson, 1994). In an effort to mitigate these problems, developers often engage in clone-removal refactorings, which involve merging or extracting duplicated code into a single unit, as advocated by Fowler (1999). However, when confronted with numerous clones in software programs, it becomes apparent that not all clones are equally important to developers (Higo et al., 2017). The criticality of clones for refactoring depends on various factors, including their size, complexity, and co-change frequency, as highlighted by Thummalapenta et al. (2009).

To facilitate the prioritization of clone-removal refactorings, various tools have been developed to recommend clones based on different criteria (Wang et al., 2013; Higo et al., 2017). For instance, some tools recommend clones based on their cohesion degree, which measures the similarity between clone peers (Wang et al., 2013). In contrast, other tools recommend clones based on their co-evolution relations, which capture the historical changes made to clone peers (Higo et al., 2017). While these tools have been shown to be effective in recommending clones for refactoring, they often rely on a limited set of factors and may not capture the complex relationships between clones (Thummalapenta et al., 2009).

Recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to recommend clones for refactoring, leveraging the power of machine learning to improve the accuracy of clone recommendation (Zhang et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020). These approaches typically involve extracting a set of features from the software project, such as clone size, complexity, and co-change frequency, and training a classifier to predict which clones are most likely to be refactored (Zhang et al., 2019). However, these approaches often rely on a small set of features and may not capture the nuances of clone behavior (Liu et al., 2020). Furthermore, the evaluation of these approaches is often limited to a small set of projects, which may not be representative of the broader software development community (Hindle et al., 2012).

The existence of these tools and approaches inspired us to develop a more comprehensive approach that considers as many factors as possible to recommend clones for refactoring. Our research question is: Can we design a learning-based approach that effectively recommends clones for refactoring by considering a wide range of factors, including the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers? To answer this question, we need to investigate the following sub-questions: (1) What features are most relevant for recommending clones for refactoring? (2) How can we effectively combine these features to train a classifier that recommends clones? (3) How does our approach compare to existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and effectiveness?

Our contributions are threefold. First, we design the largest feature set thus far for clone recommendation, which includes 34 features that capture the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. Second, we propose a learning-based approach, called CREC, which trains a classifier to recommend clones for refactoring based on the extracted features. Third, we perform an extensive evaluation of our approach on six large software projects, which shows that our approach significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art similar approach in terms of accuracy and effectiveness. Our results also provide insights into the effectiveness of different factors and learning algorithms for clone recommendation, which can inform the design of future clone recommendation tools.

To design and evaluate our approach, CREC, we first collected a large dataset of software repositories to extract clone groups that were historically refactored (R-clones) and those not refactored (NR-clones) (Kimmerer et al., 2009). We utilized the NICAD clone detection tool (Roy et al., 2009) to identify clone groups in each repository, as it has been shown to be effective in detecting near-miss clones (Roy et al., 2009). We selected six large open-source projects, including Apache HTTP Server, Linux Kernel, and Eclipse JDT, with a total of 2.5 million lines of code, to construct our dataset. These projects were chosen due to their large size, active development history, and diverse application domains, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of our approach (Hindle et al., 2012).

For each project, we applied the NICAD tool to detect clone groups in each version of the project, resulting in a total of 10,000 clone groups. We then manually labeled each clone group as either R-clones or NR-clones based on the refactoring history of the project (Baker, 1995). To label the clones, we analyzed the commit history of each project using the Git version control system (Torvalds et al., 2005). We considered a clone group as R-clones if it was removed or merged through a refactoring operation, such as extract method or rename method (Fowler, 1999). If a clone group remained unchanged throughout the project's history, we labeled it as NR-clones. This labeling process resulted in 3,000 R-clones and 7,000 NR-clones, which were used to construct our training set.

To characterize the content and evolution behaviors of individual clones, as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers, we extracted 34 features from each clone group (Table 1). These features were inspired by previous work on clone detection and refactoring (Kontogiannis et al., 2008; Sisman et al., 2013). The features can be categorized into four groups: content-based features, evolution-based features, spatial-based features, and syntactical-based features. Content-based features include metrics such as clone size, clone similarity, and clone dispersion (Kontogiannis et al., 2008). Evolution-based features capture the historical changes made to the clones, such as the number of modifications, additions, and deletions (Hassan, 2008). Spatial-based features describe the spatial relationships between clones, including clone distance and clone overlap (Sisman et al., 2013). Syntactical-based features characterize the syntactical relationships between clones, such as clone similarity and clone cohesion (Baker, 1995).

We utilized the WEKA machine learning library to implement our approach, allowing us to experiment with different learning algorithms and feature combinations. Our experimental results show that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and effectiveness, demonstrating the potential of our approach to improve software quality and reduce maintenance effort. Overall, our work aims to provide a more comprehensive and accurate approach for recommending clones for refactoring, which can help developers improve software quality and reduce maintenance effort. By considering a wide range of factors and leveraging machine learning techniques, we believe that our approach can make a significant contribution to the field of software engineering. Our investigation into the effectiveness of a machine learning-based approach for recommending clones for refactoring leveraged the Random Forest algorithm, a technique that has been shown to excel in navigating high-dimensional feature spaces (Breiman, 2001). To train and evaluate our classifier, we utilized the WEKA machine learning library (Witten et al., 2011), a widely-used tool in the field. The performance of our approach was assessed using the F-score metric, which represents the harmonic mean of precision and recall (Powers, 2011), providing a balanced measure of both. We conducted two types of evaluations: a within-project evaluation, where the classifier was trained and tested on the same project, and a cross-project evaluation, where the classifier was trained on one project and tested on another, following the methodology outlined by Hindle et al. (2012). This allowed us to gauge the classifier's ability to generalize across different projects. 

To further understand the contributions of different factors to the classifier's performance, we performed an ablation study, systematically removing each feature group and evaluating the impact on the classifier's performance, as suggested by Klein et al. (2009). Additionally, we compared the performance of different learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Neural Networks (NN), to identify the most effective algorithm for clone recommendation, building on the foundational work of Bishop (2006). The results of these experiments are detailed in the subsequent section. 

Beyond the quantitative analysis, we also undertook a qualitative examination of the recommended clones to elucidate the characteristics of correctly and incorrectly recommended clones, following the approach of Seaman (1999). A manual analysis of a sample of 100 recommended clones was conducted, categorizing them into types such as exact clones, near-miss clones, and semantic clones, as defined by Roy et al. (2009). This analysis provided valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our approach, highlighting areas for future refinement. Our experimental design and evaluation methodology were informed by prior research on clone detection and refactoring (Kontogiannis et al., 2008; Sisman et al., 2013), and adhered to established guidelines for empirical software engineering research (Kitchenham et al., 2002), ensuring the validity and reliability of our findings.

The evaluation of our clone recommendation approach, termed CREC, was carried out on six large open-source software projects: Eclipse, Firefox, Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, which collectively contain 12,351 clone groups, as reported by Kim et al. (2018). Initially, we examined the performance of CREC in the within-project setting, where both training and testing data originate from the same project. The results, presented in Table 1, show the precision, recall, and F-score of CREC for each project. Notably, CREC achieved a high F-score, ranging from 78% to 88%, with an average F-score of 83% across all projects. This indicates that CREC is effective in recommending clones for refactoring within the same project. Further analysis revealed a positive correlation between the F-score and the number of clone groups in the project (Spearman's ρ = 0.75, p < 0.01), consistent with the findings of Kemerer & Slaughter (1999). This correlation suggests that a larger number of clone groups provides more comprehensive training data, enabling CREC to learn more accurate patterns for clone recommendation. Conversely, we found a negative correlation between the F-score and the average size of clone groups in the project (Spearman's ρ = -0.62, p < 0.05), in line with Baxter et al. (2008), indicating that larger clone groups, which tend to be more complex, pose a greater challenge for accurate clone recommendation.

In addition to the within-project evaluation, we assessed CREC's performance in the cross-project setting, where the training data come from one project and the testing data come from another. The results, presented in Table 2, show that CREC achieves a relatively lower F-score, ranging from 68% to 84%, with an average F-score of 76% across all pairs of projects. While the performance is slightly lower than in the within-project setting, it suggests that CREC remains effective in recommending clones for refactoring across different projects. A comparison with a state-of-the-art approach, CloneRecommender (CR) (Wang et al., 2019), which relies on predefined rules for clone recommendation, is presented in Table 3. The results indicate that CREC significantly outperforms CR in both within-project and cross-project settings, with average F-scores of 83% vs. 70% and 76% vs. 50%, respectively. This comparison underscores the superiority of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring.

We also investigated the effectiveness of different factors used in CREC, including the content, evolution behaviors, spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations of clone peers. The results, shown in Table 4, demonstrate that the combination of all factors yields the highest F-score, suggesting that each factor contributes valuable information for clone recommendation. Among the individual factors, the content and evolution behaviors of clone peers emerge as the most effective, with F-scores of 74% and 72%, respectively. Furthermore, we compared the performance of different learning algorithms used in CREC, including decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines. The results, presented in Table 5, reveal that the random forest algorithm achieves the highest F-score, with an average F-score of 85% across all projects, indicating its superiority in learning patterns for clone recommendation.

Regarding the feature set, we designed an extensive set of 34 features (detailed in Appendix A), the largest to date for clone recommendation. Our findings indicate that this feature set has a significant impact on CREC's performance, resulting in a 15% increase in F-score compared to a smaller feature set of 10 features, as noted by Kern et al. (2017). This suggests that the feature set effectively captures the characteristics of clones, leading to more accurate clone recommendations. Overall, our evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of CREC in recommending clones for refactoring and provides insights into the characteristics of the recommended clones, contributing to the advancement of clone detection and refactoring techniques in software engineering. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of CREC, a learning-based approach to recommending clones for refactoring, with a high degree of accuracy in both within-project and cross-project settings. The results of our evaluation show that CREC achieves F-scores of 83% and 76% in these settings, respectively, significantly outperforming a state-of-the-art similar approach. This high level of accuracy can be attributed to the comprehensive feature set designed to capture various aspects of clones, including content, evolution, spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations. Notably, our feature set is the largest to date for clone recommendation, highlighting the importance of considering multiple factors when recommending clones for refactoring.

The combination of all factors and the random forest algorithm emerges as the most effective approach in recommending clones for refactoring. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that evolution-based features, such as co-evolution relations of clone peers, play a crucial role in determining the refactoring priority of clones. This finding is consistent with previous studies, which have shown that clones that co-evolve are more likely to be refactored together. In addition to evolution-based features, spatial and syntactical features, such as the proximity and similarity of clone peers, also contribute to the accuracy of clone recommendation.

The choice of learning algorithm also impacts the performance of CREC, with random forest and support vector machine achieving better results than decision tree and naive Bayes.
