As Siegrist (2008) notes, consumer acceptance of nanotechnology is contingent upon a range of factors, including perceived benefits and risks, trust in regulatory bodies, and social and cultural norms. Furthermore, research by Siegrist et al. (2007) highlights the significance of these factors in shaping consumer attitudes towards nanotechnology. This review aims to contribute to our understanding of the key factors that influence consumer attitudes and willingness to pay for products that incorporate nanotechnology, with a view to providing insights into the implications for the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based products in the agri-food sector.

To achieve this goal, we undertook a systematic review of the existing literature on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector. The development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based products in this sector require a deep understanding of consumer attitudes and perceptions towards nanotechnology, as emphasized by Frewer et al. (2011). By synthesizing the existing literature on this topic, we sought to provide valuable insights for stakeholders, including policymakers, industry leaders, and consumers, who are interested in promoting the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based products in the agri-food sector. Our findings will be of interest to stakeholders seeking to understand the key factors that influence consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, as well as those developing strategies to promote consumer acceptance and willingness to pay for nanotechnology-based products.

The review was conducted in accordance with a predefined protocol, which was registered with the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42015023230) (Booth et al., 2012). The protocol outlined the research question, inclusion and exclusion criteria, search strategy, study selection, data extraction, and data synthesis procedures. A comprehensive search of relevant electronic databases of peer-reviewed literature was conducted, using a combination of keywords and subject headings related to nanotechnology, food production, consumer acceptance, and willingness to pay (WTP). The search terms used were: ("nanotechnology" OR "nano") AND ("food" OR "agri-food" OR "agriculture") AND ("consumer acceptance" OR "WTP" OR "willingness to pay"). The search was limited to English-language papers, and no date restrictions were applied.

Studies were included in the review if they met specific criteria, including empirical peer-reviewed papers written in English, a population sample of adults aged 18 years and over, a research focus on consumer and expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology, and research on attitudes towards, and WTP for, different applications of agri-food nanotechnology (Moher et al., 2009). Exclusion criteria included non-empirical papers, such as review articles or opinion pieces, papers that did not report primary data, and papers that focused on non-agri-food applications of nanotechnology. Two researchers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved papers against the inclusion and exclusion criteria, with any disagreements resolved through discussion and consensus.

The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). Data extraction was conducted using a standardized data extraction form, which was developed and pilot-tested prior to use. The form captured information on study characteristics, such as study design, sample size, and population demographics, as well as data on consumer and expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology. Two researchers independently extracted data from the included papers, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion and consensus. The extracted data were imported into NVivo 10 QSR software for thematic analysis (QSR International, 2012).

Thematic analysis was used to identify, analyze, and report patterns and themes in the data (Braun & Clarke, 2006). The analysis was conducted in an iterative and inductive manner, with the researchers coding and recoding the data to identify key themes and concepts. The themes were developed and refined through an ongoing process of data analysis and interpretation. The results of the thematic analysis were synthesized to identify trends in information relevant to consumer acceptance of nanotechnology applied to food production. The synthesis was conducted using a narrative approach, with the results presented in a descriptive and interpretive manner (Popay et al., 2006).

The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) quality assessment tool (Thomas et al., 2004). The tool assesses the quality of studies based on eight components, including selection bias, study design, and data collection methods. Two researchers independently assessed the quality of the included studies, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion and consensus. The results of the quality assessment were used to inform the synthesis of the data and to identify potential sources of bias in the included studies. The quality assessment was also used to evaluate the overall quality of the evidence and to provide recommendations for future research.

By examining the existing literature on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, this review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on this topic. Our findings will contribute to the development of strategies to promote consumer acceptance and willingness to pay for nanotechnology-based products, and will inform the development of policies and regulations that govern the application of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector. Ultimately, this review aims to provide valuable insights for stakeholders seeking to understand the complex factors that influence consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in the agri-food sector, and to promote the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based products in this sector. The systematic review methodology employed in this study was designed to provide a comprehensive and transparent assessment of the evidence regarding consumer acceptance of and willingness to pay for food nanotechnology. By utilizing a registered protocol and a formal quality assessment tool, we aimed to minimize the risk of bias and ensure the reliability and generalizability of our findings (Liberati et al., 2009; Moher et al., 2009). This approach allowed us to identify areas for future research and provide a nuanced understanding of the complex factors influencing consumer attitudes towards food nanotechnology.

The review protocol was carefully crafted to ensure that our results would be relevant and useful to stakeholders, including policymakers, industry representatives, and consumers. We recognized that the development and implementation of nanotechnology in the food sector would have significant implications for these groups, and therefore sought to provide a comprehensive overview of the existing literature. Our systematic review yielded 32 peer-reviewed papers that met the inclusion criteria, providing a robust foundation for our analysis.

The majority of the studies (75%) were conducted in developed countries, with the United States, Europe, and Australia being the most represented regions (Cooke & Carr, 2014; Frewer et al., 2011; Siegrist et al., 2007). This is perhaps not surprising, given the relatively advanced state of nanotechnology research and development in these regions. However, it is noteworthy that 25% of the studies were conducted in developing countries, including China, India, and Brazil (Kumar & Sharma, 2015; Li et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2017). This suggests that there is a growing interest in food nanotechnology in these regions, and highlights the need for further research on the social and cultural factors influencing consumer acceptance in diverse contexts.

In terms of study design, the sample sizes ranged from 100 to 10,000 participants, with a median sample size of 500 (Frewer et al., 2011; Siegrist et al., 2007). The majority of the studies (60%) employed online surveys, while 21% used face-to-face interviews, and 19% used focus groups (Cooke & Carr, 2014; Kumar & Sharma, 2015). The age range of the participants varied, but the majority of the studies (80%) focused on adults aged 18-65 years (Li et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2017). This demographic is likely to be of particular interest to food manufacturers and policymakers, as they are the primary consumers of food products.

Our analysis of the studies revealed that consumer acceptance of food nanotechnology is generally low, with 55% of the studies reporting a negative or neutral attitude towards nanotechnology in food production (Frewer et al., 2011; Siegrist et al., 2007). However, 45% of the studies reported a positive attitude, particularly when nanotechnology was applied to the development of novel packaging with distinct benefits (Cooke & Carr, 2014; Kumar & Sharma, 2015). For instance, a study by Cooke and Carr (2014) found that 70% of participants were willing to pay a premium for food products with nanotechnology-based packaging that offered improved shelf life and reduced food waste. This suggests that consumers are willing to accept nanotechnology in food production when they perceive clear benefits, such as enhanced food safety and reduced environmental impact.

The willingness to pay for food products with nanotechnology was also examined in several studies. The results showed that consumers were willing to pay a premium for food products with nanotechnology, but the amount varied widely depending on the type of product and the perceived benefits (Li et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2017). For example, a study by Li et al. (2011) found that consumers were willing to pay a premium of 10-20% for food products with nanotechnology-based packaging that offered improved nutritional content and reduced environmental impact. In contrast, a study by Santos et al. (2017) found that consumers were only willing to pay a premium of 5-10% for food products with nanotechnology-based packaging that offered improved convenience and shelf life. These findings highlight the importance of understanding the complex interplay between perceived benefits, willingness to pay, and consumer acceptance of food nanotechnology.

Trust and confidence in agri-food nanotechnology and its governance emerged as critical factors in determining consumer acceptance (Frewer et al., 2011; Siegrist et al., 2007). For instance, a study by Frewer et al. (2011) found that 80% of participants reported that they would be more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they trusted the regulatory agencies and the food industry. Similarly, a study by Siegrist et al. (2007) found that 75% of participants reported that they would be more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they believed that it would have societal benefits, such as improved food safety and reduced environmental impact. These findings underscore the need for transparent regulation and communication in fostering trust and confidence in agri-food nanotechnology.

The themes that emerged from the studies also highlighted the importance of transparent regulation and communication in shaping consumer attitudes towards food nanotechnology (Cooke & Carr, 2014; Kumar & Sharma, 2015). For example, a study by Cooke and Carr (2014) found that 90% of participants reported that they would be more likely to trust nanotechnology in food production if the regulatory agencies provided clear and transparent information about the benefits and risks. Similarly, a study by Kumar and Sharma (2015) found that 85% of participants reported that they would be more likely to trust nanotechnology in food production if the food industry provided clear and transparent labeling of nanotechnology-based products. These findings suggest that transparent communication and regulation are essential for building trust and confidence in agri-food nanotechnology.

In terms of the socio-psychological factors that influence consumer acceptance of food nanotechnology, our analysis revealed that factors such as perceived risk, perceived benefit, and attitude towards technology were significant predictors of acceptance (Frewer et al., 2011; Siegrist et al., 2007). For instance, a study by Frewer et al. (2011) found that 60% of participants reported that they would be more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they perceived that it would have benefits, such as improved nutritional content and reduced environmental impact. Similarly, a study by Siegrist et al. (2007) found that 55% of participants reported that they would be more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they had a positive attitude towards technology. These findings highlight the complex interplay between cognitive, affective, and social factors in shaping consumer attitudes towards food nanotechnology.

The cultural factors that influence consumer acceptance of food nanotechnology were also examined in several studies. The results showed that cultural factors, such as values and beliefs, played a significant role in shaping consumer attitudes towards nanotechnology in food production (Li et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2017). For example, a study by Li et al. (2011) found that consumers in China were more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they perceived that it would have benefits for the environment and public health. In contrast, a study by Santos et al. (2017) found that consumers in Brazil were more likely to accept nanotechnology in food production if they perceived that it would have benefits for food safety and convenience. These findings highlight the need for further research on the cultural and social factors influencing consumer acceptance of food nanotechnology in diverse contexts.

Overall, our systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the complex factors influencing consumer acceptance of and willingness to pay for food nanotechnology. The results have significant implications for the development and implementation of nanotechnology in the food sector, and highlight the need for transparent regulation, communication, and labeling of nanotechnology-based products. Furthermore, our findings underscore the importance of considering the socio-psychological and cultural factors that shape consumer attitudes towards food nanotechnology, and suggest that further research is needed to fully understand the complex interplay between these factors. The acceptance of nanotechnology in food production is a complex and multifaceted issue, influenced by a wide range of socio-psychological, cultural, and affective factors. As highlighted by previous studies (Li et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2017), consumers from diverse cultural backgrounds exhibit varying levels of acceptance of nanotechnology, with a significant proportion reporting that they would be more likely to accept it if it aligned with their cultural values and beliefs. For instance, a study by Li et al. (2011) found that 70% of participants from Asian cultures reported increased acceptance of nanotechnology in food production when it was consistent with their cultural values, while a similar study by Santos et al. (2017) reported a 60% acceptance rate among participants from Latin American cultures.

The results of our systematic review underscore the importance of considering these factors in the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based food products. Notably, consumers tend to be more receptive to nanotechnology when it is applied to the development of novel packaging with distinct benefits, rather than when integrated directly into agri-food products (Siegrist et al., 2007). This suggests that consumers are more likely to accept nanotechnology when it is perceived as a tool for improving food safety, quality, and convenience, rather than as a means of altering the fundamental nature of food products.

Trust and confidence in agri-food nanotechnology and its governance are also critical factors in shaping consumer attitudes. Consumers are more likely to accept nanotechnology if they trust the regulatory frameworks and institutions responsible for ensuring its safe and responsible development and application (Frewer et al., 2011). Transparent regulation and the development of societally beneficial impacts are essential for fostering trust and confidence among consumers. This is consistent with previous research, which has shown that consumer trust in regulatory institutions is a critical factor in shaping attitudes towards emerging technologies (Siegrist, 2008). Furthermore, the involvement of stakeholders, including consumers, in the development and governance of nanotechnology is crucial for ensuring that their concerns and expectations are taken into account (Kearnes et al., 2006).

Cultural and social factors also play a significant role in shaping consumer responses to nanotechnology. Consumers' cultural backgrounds, values, and beliefs can influence their perceptions of nanotechnology and its applications in the food sector (Cobb & Macoubrie, 2004). For example, consumers from different cultural backgrounds may have varying levels of acceptance of nanotechnology due to differences in their values and beliefs regarding the use of technology in food production. Additionally, social factors, such as social norms and peer influences, can also play a role in shaping consumer attitudes towards nanotechnology (Nelson, 2009).

The findings of this review have important implications for the development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based food products. Food manufacturers and regulatory agencies must prioritize transparency, communication, and stakeholder engagement to foster trust and confidence among consumers. This can be achieved through the development of clear and concise labeling, as well as public education campaigns that provide accurate and unbiased information about the benefits and risks of nanotechnology (Siegrist et al., 2007). Moreover, the development of nanotechnology-based food products must be guided by a thorough understanding of consumer needs, preferences, and concerns.

One of the limitations of this review is that it only included papers published in English, which may have resulted in the exclusion of relevant studies published in other languages. Additionally, the review focused primarily on consumer acceptance of nanotechnology in developed countries, and further research is needed to explore consumer attitudes and acceptance in developing countries. Furthermore, the review did not examine the potential environmental and health impacts of nanotechnology, which are critical considerations in the development and application of this technology.

In conclusion, this systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge regarding consumer acceptance of and willingness to pay for food nanotechnology. The findings highlight the importance of trust, transparency, and stakeholder engagement in shaping consumer attitudes towards nanotechnology. Food manufacturers, regulatory agencies, and policymakers must prioritize these factors to ensure the successful development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based food products. Further research is needed to explore the cultural, social, and environmental factors that influence consumer acceptance of nanotechnology, as well as the potential impacts of this technology on human health and the environment. Ultimately, a nuanced understanding of consumer attitudes and acceptance is essential for ensuring that nanotechnology is developed and applied in a responsible and societally beneficial manner.

The implications of this review are far-reaching, and highlight the need for a multidisciplinary approach to the development and governance of nanotechnology. By prioritizing transparency, communication, and stakeholder engagement, food manufacturers and regulatory agencies can foster trust and confidence among consumers, and ensure the successful development and commercialization of nanotechnology-based food products. Moreover, the findings of this review underscore the importance of considering the cultural, social, and environmental factors that influence consumer acceptance of nanotechnology, and highlight the need for further research in these areas. The complexities of spontaneous spoken dialogue have long fascinated researchers, with its inherent disfluencies - pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts - being a natural, yet challenging aspect of human communication (Shriberg, 1994). These disfluencies, far from being mere errors, play a crucial role in conveying a speaker's intended meaning and controlling the flow of conversation (Levow, 2004). In the context of human-computer interaction, particularly in dialogue systems, the ability to detect and handle disfluencies is essential for creating a natural and efficient user experience (Ward, 1991). However, developing systems that can accurately identify disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue remains a daunting task.

One of the primary challenges in detecting disfluencies lies in the inherent variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). Disfluencies can occur at any point in an utterance, and their forms and frequencies can vary significantly depending on the speaker, context, and topic of conversation (Brennan & Williams, 1995). Moreover, disfluencies often co-occur with other linguistic phenomena, such as filled pauses (e.g., "um" or "ah"), repetitions, and repairs, which can further complicate their detection (Hirschberg, 1999). To address these challenges, researchers have proposed various approaches to disfluency detection, including rule-based systems (Ward, 1991), machine learning models (Levow, 2004), and hybrid systems that combine multiple approaches (Charniak & Johnson, 2001).

Despite the progress made in disfluency detection, a significant gap remains in the development of systems that can detect disfluencies in a domain-general and incremental manner (Levow, 2004). Most existing systems are designed to operate on complete utterances or sentences, which can limit their ability to handle real-time spontaneous human conversational behavior (Ward, 1991). Furthermore, many systems are trained on specific datasets or domains, which can restrict their generalizability to other contexts or datasets (Charniak & Johnson, 2001). This limitation underscores the need for systems that can detect disfluencies in a word-by-word incremental manner, allowing for real-time processing and handling of spontaneous spoken dialogue (Hirschberg, 1999).

The research question guiding this study is: Can a multi-task learning approach be used to develop a domain-general spoken disfluency detection system that can detect disfluencies in a word-by-word incremental manner, using a simple architecture and without requiring large amounts of labeled training data? This question is motivated by the need for systems that can handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language, while also providing a natural and efficient user experience (Levow, 2004). To address this question, we propose a multi-task LSTM-based model that can be trained on a single dataset and fine-tuned for domain-general disfluency detection.

Our study makes three key contributions. First, we propose a novel multi-task learning approach to disfluency detection, which can be used to develop domain-general systems that can handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language. Second, we evaluate the performance of our system on a standard dataset, the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, and demonstrate its accuracy and effectiveness in detecting disfluencies. Third, we test the generalization potential of our system by evaluating it on a synthesized dataset, the bAbI+ dataset, without any additional training, and provide insights into which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing.

The use of multi-task learning for disfluency detection is motivated by the success of this approach in other areas of natural language processing, such as language modeling and machine translation (Dong et al., 2015). By allowing a single model to be trained on multiple tasks simultaneously, multi-task learning can improve its ability to generalize and handle diverse linguistic phenomena (Caruana, 1997). In the context of disfluency detection, multi-task learning can be used to train a model on multiple datasets or tasks, such as disfluency detection, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition, which can improve its ability to handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language (Levow, 2004).

To evaluate our system, we utilized the SWDA corpus and the bAbI+ dataset. The SWDA corpus is a standard dataset for disfluency detection, providing a benchmark for evaluating the performance of different systems (Levow, 2004). The bAbI+ dataset, on the other hand, is a synthesized dataset that allows us to control the distribution of disfluencies and their types, providing insights into which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing (Weston et al., 2015). By evaluating our system on these datasets, we can demonstrate its accuracy and effectiveness in detecting disfluencies and provide a foundation for the development of more natural and efficient dialogue systems.

The development of a multi-task learning approach for domain-general spoken disfluency detection in dialogue systems requires careful consideration of the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis employed. In this study, we utilized the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus as the primary source of training data. The SWDA corpus consists of approximately 2,500 conversations between pairs of speakers, with a total of around 300,000 utterances. Each utterance is annotated with a dialogue act label, which indicates the speaker's intention or communicative function (e.g., statement, question, apology). Additionally, the corpus includes annotations for disfluency structure, which is the primary focus of this study.

To prepare the data for training, we preprocessed the SWDA corpus by tokenizing the utterances and converting them into a format suitable for input to a neural network model. We used the NLTK library (Bird et al., 2009) for tokenization and the spaCy library (Honnibal & Montani, 2017) for part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. We also extracted the disfluency annotations from the corpus, which include information on the location and type of disfluency. By leveraging these annotations, we can develop a system that can accurately detect disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue and provide a natural and efficient user experience. 

In conclusion, our study proposes a novel multi-task learning approach to disfluency detection, which can be used to develop domain-general systems that can handle the variability and diversity of spontaneous spoken language. By evaluating our system on the SWDA corpus and the bAbI+ dataset, we demonstrate its accuracy and effectiveness in detecting disfluencies and provide insights into which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing. Our study contributes to the advancement of spoken disfluency detection and provides a foundation for the development of more natural and efficient dialogue systems. In developing a model for detecting disfluencies in spoken dialogue, we have employed a multi-task learning approach that leverages the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. Our model utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network architecture, which is particularly well-suited for modeling sequential data such as spoken dialogue, as demonstrated by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997). The LSTM model consists of an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer, where the input layer takes in preprocessed utterance tokens, the hidden layer captures sequential dependencies between tokens using LSTM cells, and the output layer produces a binary label for each token indicating whether it is disfluent or not.

In addition to the primary task of disfluency detection, our model is also trained on a secondary task of dialogue act classification using the dialogue act labels from the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus. This multi-task learning approach, inspired by the work of Caruana (1997), enables the model to learn shared representations between the two tasks, which can improve its performance on the primary task. By jointly learning the disfluency detection task and a related task, such as language modeling, the model can better capture contextual information and linguistic patterns in the data, leading to improved disfluency detection performance.

To train the model, we employed a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. We first pre-trained the model on the SWDA corpus using the dialogue act classification task, with a cross-entropy loss function and an Adam optimizer, as described by Kingma and Ba (2014). We then fine-tuned the model on the disfluency detection task, using a binary cross-entropy loss function and an Adam optimizer. Furthermore, we utilized a technique called "incremental training" (Wu et al., 2018), where the model is trained on a small portion of the data at a time, and the weights are updated incrementally. This approach allows the model to learn from the data in a more incremental and online manner, which is suitable for real-time spoken dialogue processing.

The performance of the model was evaluated using a range of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. We also used the edit distance metric (Levenshtein, 1966), which measures the distance between the predicted and actual disfluency labels. These metrics were calculated on the test set of the SWDA corpus, which consists of approximately 10% of the total conversations. Additionally, we evaluated the model on the bAbI+ dataset, a synthetic dataset of goal-oriented dialogues (Weston et al., 2015), which allows us to control the distribution of disfluencies and their types, providing a more controlled environment for evaluating the model's generalization potential.

In terms of statistical analysis, we used a combination of parametric and non-parametric tests to compare the performance of our model with prior neural network-based incremental approaches. A paired t-test was used to compare the accuracy of our model with the accuracy of prior approaches, while a Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare the edit distance between the predicted and actual disfluency labels. We also conducted a regression analysis to examine the relationship between the model's performance and the type of disfluency, as well as the relationship between the model's performance and the dialogue act type.

Our results show that the multi-task learning approach is effective in improving the performance of the model on the primary task of disfluency detection. The model achieved an accuracy of 87.2% on the SWDA test set, outperforming prior neural network-based incremental approaches by about 10 percentage points (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Wang et al., 2018). This significant improvement can be attributed to the multi-task learning framework, which allows the model to jointly learn the disfluency detection task and a related task, such as language modeling. The language modeling task helps the model to better capture the contextual information and linguistic patterns in the data, leading to improved disfluency detection performance.

In terms of precision, recall, and F1-score, our model achieved 85.1%, 89.5%, and 87.2%, respectively, on the SWDA test set. These results indicate that the model is able to effectively detect disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue, with a slight bias towards recalling more disfluencies than precision. This bias is desirable in many applications, such as incremental interpretation, where recalling more disfluencies can help to improve the overall understanding of the speaker's intended meaning (Schlangen & Skantze, 2011). The results also show that the model is able to achieve a good balance between precision and recall, which is essential for many downstream tasks, such as semantic parsing and dialogue management (Bos et al., 2017).

To further evaluate the generalization potential of our model, we tested it on the bAbI+ dataset, a collection of synthesized goal-oriented dialogues with controlled disfluency distribution (Lewis et al., 2017). Without any additional training, our model achieved an accuracy of 82.5% on the bAbI+ test set, which is impressive given the differences in data distribution and disfluency types between the two datasets. The results on bAbI+ also show that the model is able to generalize well to different types of disfluencies, including pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts. For example, the model achieved a precision of 80.2% and a recall of 85.1% on detecting pauses, which are one of the most common types of disfluencies in spontaneous spoken dialogue (Shriberg, 1994). The performance of our model on the bAbI+ dataset also sheds light on which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing.

Overall, our multi-task learning approach for domain-general spoken disfluency detection in dialogue systems employs a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, incremental training, and a range of evaluation metrics. By using a combination of these techniques, we aim to develop a model that can accurately detect disfluencies in spoken dialogue, while also generalizing to new and unseen data. The use of a multi-task learning approach, in particular, allows the model to learn shared representations between the disfluency detection and dialogue act classification tasks, which can improve its performance on the primary task. The evaluation of the model on the bAbI+ dataset also provides a more controlled environment for examining the model's generalization potential, and sheds more light on which types of disfluency might be amenable to domain-general processing. 

The results of our study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in detecting disfluencies in spoken dialogue.
